Sports.title: Age-old rivalry bookends RLWC but will it end 18 years of supremacy?
Sports.content:
In the men's and women's Rugby League World Cup finals Australia will take on New Zealand; the last time both New Zealand teams won the tournament was back in 2008, nearly two decades ago; the finals take place on Sunday November 16

Australia vs New Zealand: Age-old rivalry bookends Rugby League World Cup but will it end 18 years of supremacy?

New Zealand are looking to lift the Rugby League World Cup for the first time since 2008

An age-old rivalry will bookend the Rugby League World Cup 2026 in the latest symbol that rugby league worldwide has grown but, ultimately, the contenders are still just contenders and the favourites remain just that.

In a sensational opener to the tournament, Australia clinched a dramatic 24-22 victory over New Zealand in front of the biggest Test crowd in 50 years, surpassing the previous benchmark set in 1974.

Now, the two men's teams will meet once again to decide who will be world champions. And in the women's tournament, the same showdown will decide who is on top.

Australia and New Zealand have contested the last four women's World Cup finals. In the men's, Australia have cemented their spot as ever with New Zealand returning to the final for the first time since 2013.

New Zealand's men's side have won the World Cup just once back in 2008. The women's side have won it on three occasions but not in 18 years, their last glory coming back in 2008 - the last year New Zealand were on top of the world.

Since then, it has been total and utter Australian domination. New Zealand Women head into their fifth final in a row against the Jillaroos. They do not want it to be a fifth loss in a row.

Image: The showdown between Tonga and Samoa was electric

Coming into this Rugby League World Cup, the talk was all about the new contenders, the ones that had been growing and growing and looked like, this time, they could take down the big boys. The talk was all about Tonga and Samoa showing the landscape of rugby league internationally had changed.

Throughout the group stage, they looked primed and their showdown in the final pool round, in which Tonga came away 20-18 victors, seemed to be the marker that they were here for the big win.

In the end, that match between the two nations ultimately became their final of sorts.

Following that, Tonga succumbed to New Zealand and Samoa fell short of Australia in the men's semi-finals. Exciting Samoa Women could not keep up in a 32-0 loss to New Zealand Women.

They edged closer in some respects but could not complete the job.

Image: Tonga and Samoa both made it out of the combined Pool B and C

The task is set for New Zealand's men - do what they did 18 years ago and release Australia's near two-decade long grip on the title.

Kalyn Ponga became the emblem of how the change to State of Origin eligibility would open up the international landscape as he could still play for Queensland but also represent his heritage. He did that valiantly by returning from a broken arm in that opening clash within just 22 days to star in the semi-finals.

What it would mean to him to complete the journey.

Image: New Zealand's Kalyn Ponga could complete the ultimate fairytale with victory

The World Cup storyline, for many, was going to be how a nation could defy the odds to win and send shockwaves globally.

While on the face of it New Zealand winning seems normal, it is anything but. They can still change the landscape, mark their moment, move the competition on.

A victory for them means Australia will be denied the chance to say they have been world champions for 20 years - surely that is as good a motivation as any?

One bookend is a win for Australia. Could the other bookend be glory for New Zealand?

Sports.title: Darts star Sheldon on brilliant Beau and the Littler effect hitting Ireland
Sports.content:
Katie Sheldon - nicknamed 'The Dublin Diamond' - is a pioneer of women's darts in Ireland at the tender age of 22.

As one of the hottest prospects to come out of the Emerald Isle, Sheldon has already competed on the Women's Series and at the Women's World Matchplay held at the iconic Winter Gardens in Blackpool.

Currently working as a wire assembler, Sheldon has already become the World Masters girls' champion and a two-time WDF World Cup team winner.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch Sheldon in action against Fallon Sherrock at the 2022 Women's World Matchplay

"I keep saying that one goal of mine is to pick up a PDC title, so a Women's Series. And along with that, it's trying to qualify for the Women's World Matchplay," she told Sky Sports, having taken part in the Netflix 'Beat Luke Littler' challenge in which she was given the chance to win £501,000.

It wasn't to be for Sheldon over one leg against 'The Nuke', but she has bigger dreams of emulating brilliant Beau Greaves, who finished a dominant season on the PDC Women's Series by winning 17 out of 24 events.

The Doncaster thrower will be at the Grand Slam of Darts where she has been drawn with Luke Littler and Niels Zonneveld. She also secured her qualification for the world championship at Alexandra Palace alongside 'Beat Luke Littler' winner Fallon Sherrock, Gemma Hayter, 'The Lancashire Rose' Lisa Ashton, and Belgian-born Swedish darts player, Vicky Pruim.

'Beau 'n' Arrow' made history in April by becoming the first woman to win a PDC ranking title at Players Championship 11 in Milton Keynes, defeating three former world champions, Rob Cross, Gary Anderson and Michael Smith.

She has risen to 75th in the PDC Order of Merit with the youngster closing in on the world's top 64, an achievement that would have ramifications for her future in the Women's Series with female players who break into the top 64 globally and hold a Tour Card restricted from playing in the Women's Series.

"She's really a great talent, and she's pushed us all," said Sheldon. "I think her being there has actually brought the standard up.

"Her being there has been a massive help to all of the women to progress their game, but I think it would be a sad loss to the Women's Series when she's gone."

Despite his success, Littler has threatened to boycott certain tournaments after being booed and whistled by vociferous crowds - not least in the Netherlands and Germany.

Sheldon accepts "it's a hard one to take" for players as well as Littler, himself.

She said: "When he first came on the scene, everyone was bigging him up and it was great, but then you're turning up to tournaments and people are booing him.

"People probably don't know what they're witnessing at the minute. The standard of darts is just crazy.

"I think if you are a fan, you should be going there to enjoy it. Don't get me wrong, everyone loves singing the songs, but I think there should be just that level of respect for the players when they're playing because at the end of the day, this is their livelihood as well.

"They want to be trying to perform the best for the fans, and they probably can't do that with all the boos.

"It's one of those things he has to deal with, which is kind of sad to see."

Sports.title: Cummins to address Khawaja 'Sandpapergate' claims on Friday
Sports.content:
Australia captain Pat Cummins has called a press conference for Friday to have his say on 'Sandpapergate' after former team-mate Usman Khawaja's explosive claims that the entire dressing room knew about the ball-tampering scheme that took place on the tour of South Africa in 2018.

Khawaja made the revelations in his new book 'Sabr', bringing the scandal back onto the agenda after eight years.

Cummins has been rested for the white-ball series' against England, which also begins on Friday with the first ODI in Perth, but has publicly invited a media grilling in Sydney for that same morning.

To view this content you can use the button below to allow Twitter cookies for this session only. Enable Cookies Allow Cookies Once

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Khawaja made his extraordinary claims ahead of the release of his autobiography 'Sabr'

"I'm training at Cricket Central (in Sydney) tomorrow morning before the Blues play in the Shield match," Cummins posted on X on Thursday. "Happy to speak with any and all media about the events of this week at 9.30 am.

"I've taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy's allegations so I can respond properly."

In the immediate aftermath of the Cape Town Test in 2018, in which Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball, only he, then captain Steve Smith and David Warner - who said on Monday that Khawaja's version of events was "100 per cent accurate" - were banned.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player David Warner took to his Instagram to back Khawaja's claims the entire team knew about 2018 ball-tampering plan (credit: @davidwarner31)

Khawaja's revelations have invited renewed speculation over the role of the bowling group who benefitted from the ball manipulation - with Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon having previously distanced themselves from the episode.

In 2021, the quartet issued a carefully worded statement responding to "rumour mongering and innuendo" in which they denied knowing that a foreign substance had been taken onto the field to alter the ball in order to try and make it swing.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player In 2018 footage emerged of Australia opener Cameron Bancroft using a foreign object to alter the condition of the ball against South Africa, later revealed to be sandpaper

Cricket Australia chairman David Boon has backed Cummins, saying his job as skipper is not under threat.

"We absolutely support Pat," Boon said in comments published by The Australian on Thursday. "He's been an exemplary captain, he's led the team ​with integrity and, you know, very successfully over the period of time that he's been captain, so there's no question of our confidence in him continuing on in that fact."

Starc: My recollection hasn't changed

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, after Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg insisted there would be no re-opening of the 'Sandpapergate' investigation, Starc said of Khawaja's claims: "I haven't really paid much attention to it to be fair.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mitchell Starc responds to Usman Khawaja's claims that Australia's entire dressing room knew about the ball-tampering scheme in Cape Town in 2018

"There are differing opinions of eight years ago. We were heavily grilled through the process, at the time and since.

"I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers but from where I stand my opinion hasn't changed, my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.

"As far as our statement said, we weren't aware of things being taken on the field. That's where I'll leave it.

"I will be sticking to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time eight years ago, so clearly there are differing versions from different people.

"We weren't aware of anything taken on the field to be tampered with. We saw it on the big screen in Cape Town.

"As far as the book is concerned, I haven't read it. I probably won't read it, so that's for Usman to elaborate on."

Image: Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon, Starc and Pat Cummins (left to right) issued a joint statement in 2021 denying knowledge of the scandal

On Khawaja saying the ball was also tampered with in the Test before the Cape Town fixture, at Port Elizabeth, now Gqeberha, Starc added: "That's the first I was aware of any of that."

Starc, Cummins, Hazlewood and Lyon are not part of the upcoming white-ball series at home to England.

Marsh not drawn on Khawaja claims | Root: It's all speculation

Captain of Australia for the three-match ODI series and five T20s against England, Mitchell Marsh - who was in the Test team that toured South Africa in 2018 - declined to comment at a press conference in Perth on Thursday.

Image: Australia white-ball captain Mitchell Marsh addressed the media on Thursday ahead of the team's first ODI against England in Perth

"I respect (Khawaja) for telling his story and for writing his book, and I don't sit here coming from a place of judgment on any of that," Marsh said ahead of Friday's series-opening ODI.

"It was a really tough time for Australian cricket. There's still a lot of people hurting. Now is not the time for me to share my story.

"My honest answer is because I've personally moved on. I respect that others probably haven't, but I have. And I hope that's respected."

He added: "Everyone's got their story. Some will be willing to share it, and others might not, purely on the basis of the fact that they've moved on. I think it's really important that at some stage we do."

In his book, Khawaja also said Australia experimented with lifting the seam on the ball during the 2017-18 Ashes at home to England, which they won 4-0 under the captaincy of Smith.

The ECB said 'no comment' when approached by Sky Sports News.

England's Joe Root said on Wednesday: "We obviously have no idea (about it).

"It's all speculation. I wasn't in that dressing room. I don't know what went on. I don't want to speculate, as I said. My focus is with this (ODI) team right now and what we've got coming up."

Cricket Australia: No compelling reason to re-open 'Sandpapergate' case

A statement from the Australian Cricketers' Association called the 2018 scandal a "low point for Australian cricket" for which Smith, Warner and Bancroft paid an "enormous" and "disproportionate" price.

The statement added: "There are no winners in this issue, and nothing can undo what happened. There are humans in the centre of this and we will be calling for the ongoing vitriol directed at those involved to come to an end."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, Nasser Hussain and Michael Atherton react to Usman Khawaja suggesting the whole Australian side knew about the Sandpaper scandal on their 2018 tour of South Africa.

Greenberg, who was not part of Cricket Australia at the time of the scandal, told Australian radio station SEN on the decision not to launch a fresh inquiry: "We don't see any compelling reason to open the investigation or revisit this again.

"I don't think there's anything that can be gained from that.

"We have said we're comfortable with the outcome of the investigation based on the information we've received. That includes what we've seen from Usman. Our position hasn't changed on that.

"There's absolutely no benefit in going back, that's the clear position of the CA board. I think it's fine, we've got to look ahead, and the matter was dealt with under a previous leadership back in 2018.

"Trying to second-guess decisions from a previous time or making an assessment through the prism of hindsight is not something we want to do."

Image: Speaking in 2021, Cameron Bancroft (right) said it was 'probably self-explanatory' that the bowlers were aware of the ball-tampering scheme

'Usman's version of events inconsistent with what others say'

The Cricket Australia CEO added: "When you cut to the core of the challenge that we face here, Usman's version of events is inconsistent with what others have had to say.

"I can assure you there are lots of other players who have a very, very different version of events and they have made that very public from the very start of 2018.

"They have been very consistent in their position right through until today. From my conversations with many over the weekend, I don't think that will change either.

"I think we end up at the same intersection point, which is that eight years ago people have a version of events which differ from each other.

"No one would like to get this chapter of Australian cricket closed more than me, but it is unlikely."

Uzzy’s book has created a lot of ruckus. I assume that will all play out in the next month or so and what will be will be. Everyone, at some stage, will have to discuss certain parts about this. Everyone’s got their story so I’m not sure if we are going to hear all of that.

Clarke: I want the truth to come out

Former Australia captain Michael Clarke hopes the truth comes to light, saying that chance was missed in the wake of the scandal in 2018 and then again three years later when Bancroft replied it was "probably self-explanatory" after being asked whether the bowling attack knew of the sandpaper use.

Clarke told 2DayFM: "[Australia fans] can't trust what's real. They don't know the truth until this gets reopened and the truth comes out. I would just like to see whatever the truth is for it all to come out, allow people to move on.

"For me, right now, there are more questions than answers. I want to know, firstly, did everyone know? Because certain players have come out and said they didn't. That's important information so we can get the truth.

"I can't believe we haven't heard from Cummins yet. Steve Smith lost his job. If this doesn't happen, Tim Paine never captains Australia. And neither does Cummins.

"Cummins would not have captained a game at this stage if 'Sandpapergate' didn't happen because Smith would still be captain."

Sports.title: Has Lawson saved his 2027 F1 seat with Brazil brilliance?
Sports.content:
After a superb weekend at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, Liam Lawson may have grabbed back control of his Racing Bulls seat.

Despite Lawson being on arguably the best run of form of his career and clearly outperforming his rookie team-mate Arvid Lindblad, there had been growing speculation over the first two legs of F1's Americas triple-header that Racing Bulls were going to replace the 24-year-old for the 2027 season.

The explanation for what on the surface would be a mystifying decision is that part of Racing Bulls' function as Red Bull's junior squad is to prepare young drivers from the organisation's academy for an opportunity with the senior team.

There's a highly-rated one in 19-year-old Bulgarian Nikola Tsolov awaiting an opportunity in F1 as he sees out the closing stages of an F2 championship battle.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch Liam Lawson perform a live gig in Texas ahead of US Grand Prix!

Perhaps more important than his F2 campaign was the fact that Tsolov impressed as he made his F1 practice debut in Mexico City, appearing to convince key figures that he is very much ready for motorsport's elite category.

Given the ultimate goal of the academy is to produce the next Max Verstappen, or at least another world champion, the fact Lawson has already had a go at Red Bull and failed to impress counts against him.

Lawson might be outpacing Lindblad at Racing Bulls, but there clearly remains hope that the 19-year-old Brit could develop into a driver that could cut it at Red Bull, where the second seat is currently occupied by Isack Hadjar, who has had a solid first campaign with the team.

Lawson delivers under pressure

For those reasons, Lawson arrived in Sao Paulo under extreme pressure, which he had admittedly increased by getting into an untimely spat with Verstappen during practice in Mexico.

Verstappen attempted a pass to gain superior track position, but instead of swallowing his pride and allowing the Dutchman to complete the unnecessary manoeuvre, Lawson fought back and the pair then collided, before each being given a one-place grid penalty for the incident.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and Red Bull's Max Verstappen made contact during FP2 at the Mexico City GP

More stinging than the penalty for Lawson was Verstappen, the most powerful individual in the Red Bull F1 system, reacting furiously as he told the media his former team-mate's actions weren't smart given he was 'fighting for his seat'.

A Lawson apology cleared the air before the race in Brazil, and since that moment the New Zealander hasn't put a foot wrong.

He drove a superb race in Mexico after starting at the back of the grid to finish seventh, ensuring he scores points in a fourth successive grand prix.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix

That form carried over to Brazil where wet conditions provided a huge challenge for the drivers, as he qualified fifth before being promoted to third on the grid as a result of penalties for some of the usual front-running drivers.

He seized an opportunity at the start, taking advantage of an error by pole-sitter Lando Norris to go second on the first lap. After that, he maximised the pace in his car to finish seventh, impressively battling Charles Leclerc on the final lap in a duel that saw the Ferrari driver overtake him but later be penalised for causing a collision between the pair.

Perhaps more than ever, the consensus in the paddock after Sunday's race was, 'how on earth could Racing Bulls be considering dropping a driver delivering so well?'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Charles Leclerc and Liam Lawson touch in the closing stages of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix

Speaking after the race, Lawson told Sky Sports F1: "I appreciate all the support. I've seen it over the last few weeks. It's honestly really nice to see. Obviously, I would love it if it was more from a team.

"But at the moment I'm just trying to enjoy driving the car because, with everything else going on, I don't really know what else I'm meant to do. I don't really know what else I'm meant to say to you guys (the media)."

Who is making the decision?

Whether or not the pressure put on the Red Bull and Racing Bulls hierarchy by Lawson's latest performance has told remains to be seen, but reports surfaced on Monday morning claiming he is now expected to keep his seat.

A further complicating element behind the saga is that the already unorthodox power structure at Racing Bulls (and Red Bull) has changed dramatically in the last 18 months.

Christian Horner was sacked as Red Bull team principal and Laurent Mekies was promoted from Racing Bulls to take his place in July 2025, before long-time Red Bull motorsport advisory Dr Helmut Marko, who had played a key role in driver line-up decision, was let go at the end of the season.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Liam Lawson said after the Mexico City GP earlier this month he has 'no assurance' of his future in F1 beyond 2026

Mekies insists that he is able to give "an opinion" but that the final decision lies with Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane.

"I've said it several times, the Racing Bulls driver decision is down to Racing Bulls," Mekies said on Sunday in Brazil.

"As much as we run a common junior programme, we are in the unique position where when the good guys are coming out from Racing Bulls, we obviously have the possibility to get them to be promoted to Red Bull Racing, as we have done with Max and as we have done with Isack, but how we get to that point is down to them in terms of the F1 stint.

"When it comes to Liam, I can only congratulate him for another very strong weekend. He has been on a fantastic run."

Permane, who recently signed a contract extension himself, appeared to suggest that Red Bull could benefit from a more patient approach with its junior drivers than was shown under Horner and Marko's leadership.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane says the team wants to 'apply science' to their decision on the 2027 driver line-up

Lawson was promoted from Racing Bulls to Red Bull at the start of the 2025 season but then dropped after just two races with the senior team.

Permane said: "Red Bull's had a very successful young driver programme, and I think, if I want to be... and I don't want to be critical of it, but I think if you guys are critical of it, maybe sometimes the drivers haven't been able to have enough time to settle, or maybe some snap decisions have been made.

"We're trying to apply a little bit of science, and that takes some time. So, we are looking at everything and studying, analysing, and time is on our side."

An announcement before Vegas?

Sky Sports F1 understands that Racing Bulls are intent on making a decision and announcing it before the next round, the Las Vegas Grand Prix, which takes place from November 19-21.

It remains unclear whether Permane himself has final say or whether Red Bull's shareholders will ultimately weigh in. There's the Thai Yoovidhya family, and then the bosses of Red Bull's sporting projects, led by Oliver Mintzlaff.

"We're not in a rush to do anything, and I'm very confident the right decision will be made," Permane added.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Liam Lawson teams up with Sky Sports F1's Simon Lazenby and Naomi Schiff to prank Racing Bulls team-mate Arvid Lindblad with a fake interview

"I realise it's frustrating for our drivers. I realise it's frustrating for everyone else, but we want to get it right, and we will get it right. I'm sure when we announce it in the coming weeks, everyone will be happy."

Mekies added on the topic: "It's a Racing Bulls decision. They have all the data, they are very experienced.

"Alan is a great guy. He understands racing better than most. It's probably fair that these guys are taking their time, because from a Red Bull perspective, there is no reason to rush."

'Lawson sacking would be one of most unjust in F1'

Sky Sports F1's Karun Chandhok says that Lawson losing his seat would be "one of the most unjust" decisions made by an F1 team.

"If Liam Lawson gets sacked, it would be one of the most unjust in Formula 1," Chandhok said.

"He's done a fantastic job this season. He's come back carrying the mental baggage of being sacked from the Red Bull top team, went back to the Red Bull earlier this year for three races and did a good job there. And he's delivered really, really well.

"I get the junior team is a university to prepare drivers for the top team. Today, they are a strong midfield team, have their own identity, own sponsors, own reasons to be competitive and not just be there to train drivers up."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player After Liam Lawson pranked Arvid Lindblad with a fake interview, Lindblad gets his revenge on his Racing Bulls team-mate with some challenges in the F1 Paddock

Sky Sports F1's Martin Brundle explained that there is often more context to driver decisions that may necessarily meet the eye for media and fans.

"I remember starting to beat Michael Schumacher at Benetton and I got biffed at the end of the year," Brundle said.

"It happens in this business for any number of reasons, sometimes commercial reasons, political future, and the teams are thinking a long way ahead and all the pieces of the jigsaw fit together in a way that don't always look obvious to us talking about it right now.

"But I think Liam's done a tremendous job for them."

Sports.title: Meeting of two lost souls: can Pochettino make it work at Manchester United? | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
Welcome, Mauricio, to the meat grinder. Or rather, welcome back. We’ve been expecting you. There is nothing surprising in the news Manchester United may be on the verge of appointing Mauricio Pochettino. United are always on the verge of appointing Pochettino. This is a club that has spent 13 years hiring and firing the same structurally doomed manager – same shellshocked eyes, same irresolvable macro-problems – and the last eight years almost but not quite doing this to Pochettino.

Well, maybe we’re finally here. Maybe he just needed to be broken enough to make it fit. And who knows, perhaps there is even a kind of accidental synergy here.

By now Pochettino has been thoroughly processed through the soul-extraction machinery of elite club football. He arrives at Old Trafford pre-minced, pre‑haunted, a 54-year-old already bruised by his experiences at Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and Levy‑era Spurs. This is a head coach so steeped in the blood of dysfunctional super-clubs that turning back is pretty much the same thing as heading on into its ultimate form in the west end of Manchester.

The problems at Old Trafford are of course unrelated to the appointment of the latest managerial avatar. The constant hiring and firing is a symptom not a cause. This is essentially a distraction, a false flag drawing attention from the avarice and incompetence of the executive tiers.

Still, though, it is necessary on these occasions to set out the reasons why the latest appointment probably won’t work. First up is the obvious sense of diminishing returns.

How do you solve a club that has won two major trophies in 10 years of steady downward progress? Easy. You hire a coach who has also won two major trophies in 13 years of steady downward progress. How do we get back to the dimly remembered recent past? We hire the dimly remembered recent past.

Does this feel like a magic bullet? At this stage hiring Pochettino is like booking the bloke who did Gangnam Style to play the Super Bowl. Yeah, huge fan. Remind me. Weren’t you quite big in 2013?

View image in fullscreen Pochettino at Spurs: ‘The world’s most handsome oil rigger.’ Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters

So much for all that then. It is more interesting to linger on the fact that, as ever with this great belching toxic volcano of a football club, there is always hope, and some kind of logic that says maybe this is the one. We see it every time. Ageing aura-master? Yep, do it. Hot young systems zealot? Get him in. Random ex-player, who will be transformed almost instantly into a damp, doomed figure crumpled on the touchline like a divorced dad at the school railings? We have a vacancy.

This time there are two things in Pochettino’s favour. First, the memory of his best days at Tottenham: the charisma, the barking laugh, the way of striding around looking like the world’s most handsome oil rigger. Plus of course the visceral, hard-running style of that early Spurs team, football as life, pain, exhaustion, delirium. There will be moments. Just give us some of these. In the end everyone here just wants to feel something.

Second, and more seductive, is the sense of some kind of shared redemption arc, a union of lost souls. Broken club, meet broken manager. You two are going to get along. This happens in movies, the Leaving Las Vegas dynamic: rock bottom, healing, redemption. Is this convincing? Do we have, of all things, not hope – obviously not that – but doomed hope?

Pochettino does have an incompleteness to his career. This is a manager who never manifested the full promise of those early years, headhunted by Southampton, then poached again by Spurs, where he offered a compelling injection of energy. That Pochettino was a hugely moreish figure. You wanted to hear him speak, clap his dimpled cheeks, to breathe in his Eau de Gaucho scent as he whispered gruff words in your ear about struggle and suffering, and maybe invited you to a barbecue later.

View image in fullscreen Mauricio Pochettino spent a year and a half working with galácticos at PSG. Photograph: Franck Fife/AFP/Getty Images

A decade on, Pochettino still has the air of someone looking for a home and a final form. It is an interesting exercise just trying to decide what really broke him. Maybe it was PSG, January 2021 to July 2022, still the source of his only major trophies.

In Paris Pochettino seemed to arrive pre-burnt out, required to make sense from a standing start of a bunch of supernova galácticos. This was High Decadence-era PSG, source of the original despot‑general Kylian Mbappé meme, and a time when Neymar seemed to be more or less continually dancing on crutches in an elite underground disco dressed in a solid gold bowler hat and shoes made from moon rock.

Those who know Pochettino reported a disillusionment with superstar egotism, the swagger of unproven young players, training that became a losing battle for intensity. And yes, there is a pre‑United klaxon here. How’s that going to work out? Does it seem like an obvious cultural fit?

Then again, maybe it was Chelsea that broke him, an ill-fitting season before a mutually agreed departure, shot through with frustration at an unbalanced squad and an incoherent hierarchy. Again, does this sound like a man ideally geared to make sense of a squad assembled under six managers and the interventions of pub-chat Big Sir Jim?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

You could even make a case it was Spurs that broke Pochettino, even if for five seasons this was his peak time in club management. The good times died at Tottenham because Pochettino couldn’t convince Daniel Levy of the need to build from a point of strength. That team was destined to eat itself. Pochettino was high on the Marcelo Bielsa school of football as a game of running, victory as a function of physical and emotional exhaustion.

In the end the thing that made Poch-era Spurs work was also the thing that killed it, a high-energy team that became a zombified entity, a squad of degraded parts, Pochettino himself already a little sad and war-weary.

So, welcome to Manchester then. Do any of those elements sound familiar? Maybe there is something interesting here. Maybe it’s a fit. United might be a ghost ship, trapped in a never-ending doldrums. Pochettino may also be the wrong side of his own prime. Hansi Flick won his first trophy at Bayern Munich in 2019, the same age as Pochettino. But long‑serving 54-year-old managers don’t tend to surge into their best years at this level.

View image in fullscreen Kobbie Mainoo has the press-resistant, quick-passing qualities to thrive under Mauricio Pochettino. Photograph: Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Getty Images

Then again, football is often emotion as much as detail, and Manchester United is definitely this right now, an entity that just needs to feel good, to give off heat, to keep rolling along. Pochettino’s arrival would at least be a story, a meeting of last chances and final saloons. Do we have an arc here?

If so, it needs to start with an extended action sequence. United are third from bottom of the Premier League. The squad is a random bin fire of divergent parts. On the plus side there is something astringent and purging about Pochettino’s best style, the high-intensity 4-2-3-1. There are even some players there that might fit.

Kobbie Mainoo has the necessary press-resistant, quick‑passing qualities. Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos are much better hard‑running midfielders than they’ve looked so far. Which isn’t saying much. They haven’t looked like this at all. Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo will be asked to hustle, which they can do. Benjamin Sesko hasn’t really got going. But Pochettino likes a big man.

The defence needs speed and a willingness to play a high line, meaning more than ever that Harry Maguire looks like a horse‑drawn train in a world of Ford Model Ts. Has Bruno Fernandes ever really been asked to play with more discipline and less risk? This will now happen.

And yes, we have been here before so many times. There is no magic bullet, no mega‑vaccine, no masterplan coming together in appointing Pochettino. Nobody is draining the swamp, flame‑throwing the boardroom, or raging at the managed mediocrity installed at every level.

Pochettino himself is like a walking vision of better times and diminished powers. But there are always other chapters, and in this case a sense of something that might just offer its own sense of shared theatre, private and public; a chance, however remote, to unbreak yourself.

Sports.title: Harry Kane’s England caps record: an illustrious career in numbers and charts
Sports.content:
Harry Kane will become the most capped player for England’s men when he features against Croatia at Wembley. Yet in the context of the grand history of international football, his record total will be relatively low.

Kane will draw level with players including Dani Alves, Eden Hazard and Paolo Maldini on 126 caps. Illustrious players, none of whom lead their country’s appearance standings. Neither do Kevin De Bruyne or Luís Figo, on 127, or Manuel Neuer with 128. It will be some time next year before England’s captain enters European football’s top 50 players for international caps, never mind the global standings.

And this is only in men’s football. Fara Williams made 172 appearances for England women’s team, with fellow Lionessess Jill Scott (161), Lucy Bronze (148), Karen Carney (144), Alex Scott (140), Casey Stoney (130) and Rachel Yankey (129) ahead of Kane too.

This is not to undermine Kane’s achievement. If anything, it enhances it. His standing within a wider context shows how hard it has been for anyone to play so many games for England’s men. Competition is fierce, with team success limited in the 49 years between winning the World Cup and Kane’s debut in March 2015. A good way to earn lots of caps is to go deep into tournaments, something England did not do regularly enough until the past decade.

England’s top caps collector stands alone among his countrymen in more ways than simply the headline figure. Kane’s tally of 36 appearances at major tournaments is the most by an Englishman. He leads the standings for the European Championship with 18 and is only one shy of Jordan Pickford’s record 19 at the World Cup. Kane recently signed a contract extension with Bayern Munich until 2029 so the idea of him adding to his tally at the 2030 World Cup at the age of 36 feels plausible.

He has also played 26 more competitive games for England’s men than anyone else. The comparison is unfair across the ages, or even against relatively recent times. Anyone who has represented the team since September 2018 will have had more opportunities to play competitive international football thanks to the introduction of the Nations League. Friendlies filled many windows in the past.

Players from yesteryear played fewer qualifiers too. Billy Wright amassed 105 caps between 1946 and 1959, missing three England matches in that period. Yet he played only 10 World Cup qualifiers, as many as England had for the 2022 tournament alone. The first European Championship did not take place until 1960. Nonetheless, Kane remains in front for competitive caps whether we include the Nations League or not.

Wright makes for another interesting comparison. By playing in 105 of England’s 108 matches in the span from his debut to his final game, the Wolves legend appeared in 97% of the possible matches across his international career. No player can hope to match that rate in the modern era, with a far greater focus on rest, recovery and rotation than occurred in Wright’s day.

Among players with at least 50 caps in more recent times, Des Walker played 92% of England’s matches between his first and last. David Platt featured alongside him in 41 of those games and played 82% of the possible total across his international spell. That puts Platt marginally ahead of Kane (81%), though the latter’s time with the national team has lasted almost as long as Walker and Platt’s combined. Nobody in the Premier League era has featured as regularly as Kane across at least a decade as an England player.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The 29 matches he has missed include 12 for which he was an unused substitute. Of the remaining 17, 12 were friendlies and one was in the second tier of the Nations League. When called for a match of significant consequence, Kane has almost always answered.

Playing so often may have been a detriment at times, particularly when looking off the pace at major tournaments. Was it worth Kane making 12 starts against the might of Andorra, Kosovo, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta and San Marino (with eight of the games away from home) if it cost him something when rather more was at stake?

That is a great unknown. What is known is that nobody has been more dedicated or integral to England in the modern era than Kane. His record tells us so.

Sports.title: Less drama, more listening, but is Kozo Tashima the candidate to topple Infantino?
Sports.content:
Not many remember Japan’s bid for the 2022 World Cup, when the country finished the race with only two of the final 22 votes. Kozo Tashima was involved then, and now the honorary president of the Japan Football Association is going it alone in the hope of ousting Gianni Infantino.

The 68-year-old Tashima is an unlikely insurgent and an unlikely challenger to Infantino. He is, however, a familiar and respected figure in Asian and global football politics, and ready to take the Fifa presidency out of the headlines into a quieter era.

In 2010, during the JFA’s failed World Cup bid, Tashima proved himself to be an affable campaigner, impressing with his efficiency and, in the words of an official from one European association, displaying a rare ability for a football leader to listen more than talk. He may not have the ability for an easy quip, or as much charm and charisma as Infantino or his predecessor, Sepp Blatter, but that could count in his favour.

Since entering the Fifa Council in 2015, Tashima has rarely made an international headline and it is this, he hopes, that will make a difference. Tashima is ready to put principles to the fore before March’s election. “It’s not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built,” Tashima said as he announced his candidacy for the Fifa presidency on 5 November. “What Fifa needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world.”

Tashima became the JFA’s technical director in 2002, moving up to the role of federation president as Japan became Asia’s leading football nation. Off the pitch, however, the power has moved westwards, from Tokyo to Riyadh, Doha and Manama. There has been disquiet about how the Asian Football Confederation has, from Japan’s perspective, become too close to Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

The feeling about Fifa is worse. JFA officials were dismayed at Infantino’s closeness to Donald Trump. Given how crucial a partner the United States has been to Japan in terms of security and as an export market for more than eight decades, the president’s actions in regards to tariffs and cosying up to China and North Korea went down badly in Tokyo, as did Trump’s favourability, going below 30% in May.

View image in fullscreen The close relationship between Gianni Infantino and Donald Trump has not gone down well in Japan. Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

The summer was the last straw, with the Folarin Balogun affair during the World Cup and then the leaking of Infantino’s plan to sell off the tournament’s commercial rights to private investors. Yet in October the JFA president, Tsuneyasu Miyamoto, the former defender who succeeded Tashima in 2024, followed the AFC leadership and backed Infantino. Miyamoto’s decision resulted in the resignation of the JFA vice-president, Takeshi Okada.

“I have always believed that sports should be noble and have cherished their social value,” said Okada, a former Japan defender and national team head coach. “However, the recent actions surrounding the Fifa World Cup have created a significant gap between my beliefs and the actions taken, and as a sportsman I could not accept them, which led me to this decision.”

Okada led Japan at the 2010 World Cup in South Africa but only after surviving calls from fans and the media for him to be sacked due to poor results in preparation for the tournament. Tashima’s support as JFA president was key to this and his loyalty was rewarded with seeing the Samurai Blue reach the knockout stages on foreign soil for a first time. Now it was Okada’s turn to back Tashima and he did just that as the latter announced his candidacy for the Fifa presidency, one that came as a surprise to most in Asia.

There is an expectation that Uefa’s candidate will be announced soon, but if no one is put up by Europe’s governing body then Tashima becomes the main challenger to Infantino’s supremacy, ahead of the former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega, who has also announced his candidacy. He would automatically get some support from Europe and Concacaf members but may not have the international connections to pick up enough votes elsewhere.

View image in fullscreen Takeshi Okada at the 2010 World Cup, where he led Japan to the knockout phase for the first time abroad. Photograph: Luca Bruno/AP

Tashima, who earned seven caps for Japan in the late 1970s and early 1980s, is not going to unite Asia, but there will also be backing for him from the east and south-east, where the JFA has worked hard over the years building relationships with national associations such as those of Singapore and Thailand. Tashima has put his chances of winning at between 20% and 30% but, as he said, this isn’t really about winning but about standing up for what is right.

If Tashima does win, there will be a Fifa president who looks to build consensus behind the scenes and make as few headlines as possible. There will also be no cosying up to world leaders, or certainly not any more than is absolutely necessary. Football fans may well appreciate a quieter, less visible, less controversial man at the top of the sport’s world governing body. Kozo Tashima could be that man.

Sports.title: Complaint filed to IRS in relation to Fifa head Gianni Infantino’s housekeeper
Sports.content:
A complaint has been filed to the United States Internal Revenue Service calling for an investigation into claims an individual on the Fifa payroll was working privately as a housekeeper for Gianni Infantino.

If the IRS investigates and finds the claims to be proven then Fifa could lose its tax-exempt status in the US. Fifa has 501(c)(4) status in the country, a category for organisations “created to promote community welfare for charitable, educational or recreational purposes”.

The complaint, which has been seen by the Guardian and is supported by a number of documents, claims an individual “performed domestic work exclusively for Fifa president Gianni Infantino and his wife, Leena Infantino, at their Miami residence, while receiving compensation or benefits through a Fifa-affiliated entity”, and argues that “senior leadership, acting in their official capacity and on behalf of Fifa, have abused the entity’s tax-exemption status”.

Quick Guide How do I 

The complaint goes on to argue: “If organisational funds or resources were used to pay for services benefiting a leader’s household, the arrangement raises serious questions about private benefit, financial reporting, compensation, and governance. The materials also raise questions about the accuracy of representations in employment, payroll, tax, and immigration records. We ask the agencies to investigate the underlying records and determine what occurred.” The IRS has been approached for comment.

The news comes as Fifa’s activities, and specifically Infantino’s involvement in the failed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme and his relationship with the Trump White House, are to come under intensified scrutiny from Democratic politicians in the US after the “blue wave” at the midterm elections. A spokesperson for the ranking member of the House judiciary committee, representative Jamie Raskin, said the committee had not requested documents related to the housekeeper but was “looking closely at those developments”.

A Fifa spokesperson said: “Matters related to the Fifa president’s personal and home life are private; however, for the avoidance of any doubt, the costs of any domestic staff are met by the Fifa president personally.”

The complaint, if taken up, would probably take months to complete and commonly the results of IRS investigations are not published. Any action taken as a result, however, would be in the public domain. The complaint was submitted by the Washington DC lawyer Abed Ayoub, who works in immigration law and has served as the national executive director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC). Last year the ADC was part of the campaign Game Over Israel, which called for Israeli football teams to be banned from international competition.

Fifa said: “We urge the media to act responsibly. As Fifa stated in August, it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president. Fifa welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a licence to amplify false allegations. Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading Fifa will continue to challenge it directly and vigorously.”

Infantino has been described by his predecessor, Sepp Blatter, as a “dictator” who “no longer knows any borders”. Blatter, Fifa’s president for 17 years before resigning amid a corruption scandal at the organisation, made the remarks in an interview with the German magazine Der Spiegel. He criticised the FFE scheme, the Fifa peace prize and, most significantly in his opinion, the overturning of Folarin Balogun’s suspension for a red card during the World Cup.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Sport in Focus Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“Fifa is suffering,” Blatter said. “It is currently led by a person who has allowed himself to be blinded.” He described the peace prize as “embarrassing”, saying: “Why would he do something like that? Infantino awards a peace prize to someone who wages war against Iran shortly afterwards?”

In assessing the FFE scheme, which was abandoned after an international outcry, Blatter said: “Infantino no longer knows any borders. He doesn’t understand any of this.” He described the Balogun controversy as “the worst”, saying: “Statutes can be interpreted. But rules of the game must apply to everyone, you can’t interpret them.”

FIfa has been approached for comment.

Sports.title: Danny Kelly, football broadcaster and renowned editor, dies aged 69
Sports.content:
The journalist and broadcaster Danny Kelly, who helped define coverage of music and football in the UK for a generation, has died at the age of 69.

Kelly edited the NME and Q magazine, and launched the Football 365 website before going on to be a presenter and pundit on the BBC and TalkSport. He had been receiving treatment for oesophageal cancer.

Tributes were led by Kelly’s longstanding broadcast partner Danny Baker. “My great friend, supreme broadcaster and funniest man I ever knew, Danny Kelly, died yesterday afternoon,” Baker wrote on social media, the pair having worked together on any number of radio, TV shows and podcasts. “I cannot believe I will never hear his voice again.”

Tottenham Hotspur paid emotional tribute to Kelly, a lifelong Spurs fan. A statement said: “The entire Tottenham family mourns the loss of one of our own, broadcasting legend Danny Kelly. Our thoughts and love are with his family and friends at this incredibly sad time.”

TalkSport, for which Kelly worked as a presenter for nearly two decades, said it was “heartbroken” by the news. “A cherished part of TalkSport for so many years, Danny brought extraordinary wit, warmth and knowledge to our airwaves,” the station said. “His passion for football, music and life was infectious, and his kindness touched everyone around him.”

Another broadcaster, the former Sky Sports host Richard Keys, said Kelly “was all of the things – and more – being said about him – ‘warm, witty and knowledgable’”.

View image in fullscreen Danny Kelly at the launch of the Football365 website in 1998. Photograph: Patrick Barth/Shutterstock

Kelly was born in north London in 1956 and first made his name writing about music. He began contributing to the NME in his 20s and went on to edit the agenda-setting weekly newspaper at the end of the 1980s. From there he took charge of the top-selling music monthly Q magazine, where he was named British magazine editor of the year.

Manic Street Preachers paid tribute to “a brilliant broadcaster-writer-ideas factory. Danny was editor of the NME when we first started getting press, a wonderful man, his musical knowledge was vast and deep, his radio voice has been part of our lives for so long … We will all miss him.”

In the second half of the 1990s, Kelly threw himself into the nascent world of digital media and launched Football365, which became one of the leading online voices on the sport. In the noughties, he spotted another development – podcasts – and launched the Game, a weekly football podcast, for the Times.

Over the past 15 years Kelly became best known as a radio presenter and podcast host, including presenting the Tottenham-focused show View from The Lane. Paying tribute to “our host, our leader” on its X account, the View from the Lane said: “We all loved him as much as he loved Spurs.”

Sports.title: US withdraw from U-17 World Cup in Qatar due to safety concerns
Sports.content:
The US men’s national team have pulled out of the Fifa U-17 World Cup, which is due to kick off in Qatar in just over a week. In a letter sent to players explaining the decision, the US Soccer Federation cited safety concerns for players and staff, referring them to the US state department’s travel advisory for Qatar, which encourages citizens to reconsider travel to the country “due to risk of armed conflict” and asks government employees to obtain special authorization to do so.

“Unfortunately, in light of current circumstances … we are no longer able to participate in the tournament,” US Soccer’s letter to players reads. “The wellbeing of our players and staff will always be our top priority.

“Please accept our deepest appreciation for your commitment to US Soccer and our shared disappointment about these circumstances.”

A US Soccer spokesperson said the federation would not go into details about how it reached its decision. The Guardian understands Fifa was informed of the federation’s decision on Wednesday.

Fifa’s regulations for the U-17 World Cups stipulate that qualified nations must participate in the tournament or be fined, with withdrawal within 30 days of the tournament’s start resulting in a fine of CHF20,000 (about $24,000). Fifa has been approached for comment.

The ongoing situation in the Middle East – involving interconnected conflicts among multiple states – has already led to postponements or cancellations of international sporting events. The 2027 Asian Cup, the continental soccer championship, was due to be held in Saudi Arabia in January 2027 but has been postponed nearly a year due to the conflict between the Saudis and the Houthi rebels, and the Iran war. More recently, Qatar pulled out of hosting rugby’s 2028 Nations Championship finals due to uncertainty around the conflicts. The final races of the Formula One season are still going ahead in the Middle East, on 29 November in Qatar and then 6 December in Abu Dhabi.

Multiple missile strikes by the Houthis on Riyadh’s international airport killed 13 people and wounded hundreds in October. Later that month, US diplomats were told to leave Saudi Arabia amid ongoing Houthi attacks.

Qatar has been acting as a mediator in talks between the US and Iran aimed at ending the countries’ conflict, which started with attacks by the US and Israel on Iran earlier this year. A tanker off the coast of Qatar was attacked in October amid thetensions.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The U-17 World Cup is still due to begin on 19 November in Doha. The US were placed in Group J along with Montenegro, Algeria and Chile. The US roster that was due to compete in the tournament does not contain any household names, but features a number of promising young players in MLS and abroad.

Sports.title: Top four teams in Fifa rankings set to be kept apart until semi-finals at 2027 Women’s World Cup
Sports.content:
The top four ranked teams will be separated until the semi-finals at the 2027 Women’s World Cup, ­provided they each win their group, after a change to the tournament’s draw procedure was confirmed by Fifa.

Spain, USA, Germany and England are ranked one to four in the world respectively, although USA and England still need to qualify for the tournament. The seedings will be based on the 7 December updated rankings, meaning the standings could change before the draw, which will take place on 11 December in Rio de Janeiro.

The top four sides were also ­separated until the semi-finals of the 2026 men’s World Cup, which consisted of 48 teams, but it was not announced until Wednesday that the same rule would apply to the 32-team ­women’s tournament. In the men’s World Cup the top four – Spain, Argentina, France, and England – all reached the semi-finals.

The record four-time champions USA face El Salvador on 27 November as they aim to confirm their place at the tournament next summer. A victory, coupled with no changes to the world rankings, would ensure USA would be placed in the opposite half of the draw to the defending cham­pions, Spain. That would mean if they win their groups the two teams could not meet until the final, which will be played at the ­Maracanã Stadium on 25 July. Neither Spain nor USA finished top of their group at the previous World Cup.

England, the 2023 runners-up, must beat Ukraine over two legs on 1 and 5 December to ensure their qualification. The European ­champions hold a 31-point advantage over fifth-placed Japan in the world rankings before the upcoming round of internationals.

France, the hosts Brazil and ­Sweden – who finished third at three of the past four World Cups, and face Scotland in their qualifying playoff in December – would complete the set of eight Pot 1 seeds for the eight groups, if the top eight remains as it is. ­Canada, ranked ninth in the world, could pounce on a Pot 1 spot if anyone slips up.

Fifa has also confirmed that the draw will take place at 1.30pm local time (11.30am EST/4.30pm GMT) on 11 December, at Rio de Janeiro’s Museum of Modern Art. Brazil, as hosts, will be placed in Group A and will contest the opening match at the Maracanã on 24 June.

After the eight Pot 1 sides, the next eight highest-ranked teams involved will be in Pot 2, with the next eight below them in Pot 3. Pot 4 will include three places for the winners of the inter-confederation playoff ­tournament that will conclude in March, along with the lowest-ranked sides involved. No group will be permitted to include more than one team from the same continent, except for European teams, of whom there can be a maximum of two per group.

Fifa also confirmed later on Wednesday that the uncontested bids to host the 2031 and 2035 Women’s World Cups have both passed their extensive bid evaluations.

The US, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica are bidding to jointly host the 2031 event and they received an overall score of 4.4 out of 5. The UK is the sole bidder for 2035 and the bid – which includes a proposal for Wembley to host the final – received a score of 4.3 out of 5.

No venue has yet been specified to stage the 2031 final. Both bids’ infrastructure, stadiums and accommodation were praised by Fifa. Fifa’s congress is expected to formally appoint them as hosts on 23 November.

Sports.title: League One clubs aim for further curbs on spending as budgets continue to spiral
Sports.content:
League One clubs want to introduce new spending restrictions to reduce losses by limiting investment from owners.

Clubs in the division voted to tighten the rules last summer by reducing spending limits from 60% to 50% of turnover, and removed a staggered approach to owner investment, so that only 50% of equity injections can be spent on squad costs, with the rest assigned to infrastructure projects. Less than six months later many want to go further.

The Guardian has learned that two proposed models are being ­con­sidered: a fixed cap on owner investment or introducing a version of the Premier League’s squad cost rules, with a £1 levy on clubs for every £1 spent above 50% of their revenue. Sporting sanctions would be applied if spending reached 60%, with the money raised from the levy redistri­buted to other clubs in the division.

The move to introduce more spending curbs comes despite a legal challenge to the existing rules from the Professional ­Footballers’ Association, which launched proceedings in August on the grounds that the clubs had failed to abide by the terms of their membership of the ­professional negotiating and consultative committee.

An attempt by League One and League Two to introduce salary caps of £2.5m and £1.5m respectively was withdrawn in 2021 after the PFA took them to an independent arbitration panel.

Discussions over stricter controls have been taking place for some time, but have been given fresh impetus by the publication last month of the State of the Game report. The first piece of work by the ­Independent Football Regulator showed that 94% of clubs in the EFL and National League are loss-making, and that 32 of the 96 would not survive for a month without owner funding.

The changes last summer reduced the percentage of clubs’ income that can be spent on wages, with mana­gers’ salaries included for the first time, but there is a renewed move to reduce losses, which averaged £7.5m per club in League One last season, up from £5.3m the previous season.

One owner said that further regulation was ­necessary because the clubs had shown ­repeatedly that they could not restrain themselves, pointing out that League One wage bills have increased by 15% this season, and that a top-six budget in the division five years ago would now rank in the bottom three.

Reading and Peterborough have long campaigned for tighter spending controls, but face opposition from clubs such as MK Dons and Wycombe, and it is unclear whether any proposal would gain the two-thirds majority required to be introduced.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

A source at another League One club warned that an unintended consequence would be to create a cliff edge in terms of financial resources with the Championship, which loosened its regulations last season by permitting owners an inject up to £33m over three years, an equity allowance that does not count towards the 85% wage spending/revenue limit.

League Two clubs are also involved in the discussions, although it is unclear whether they will choose to align with League One.

The EFL confirmed discussions were ongoing, although formal proposals have yet to be put to the clubs.

Sports.title: $440m franchise put up for sale after 33 years as relocation concerns grow
Sports.content:
Joey Saputo has put Major League Soccer team CF Montreal up for sale, and warns that the new buyer may decide to relocate the team.

Major League Soccer team CF Montreal has been put up for sale.

In a rare press conference on Monday, Canadian owner Joey Saputo was overwhelmed with emotion and fought back tears multiple times when confirming his decision to sell the team.

5 MLS side CF Montreal has been put up for sale just days after the 2026 regular season came to an end Credit: Getty



“This decision is neither driven by urgency, nor dictated by circumstance,” Saputo stated. “It’s the result of a careful and deliberate reflection on where we stand today, and more importantly, on the opportunities that lie ahead for the club.”

Saputo founded the club formerly known as the Montreal Impact in 1992, and joined the MLS in 2012 paying up the $40 million expansion fee to do so.

“After 33 years, I simply believe it is the time to pass the torch,” he added. “We believe this is the right time to welcome a new ownership group with the resources, vision and commitment to build on the strong foundation we’ve built."

During his ownership tenure, though, success has been few-and-far-between, having reached the MLS post-season on just four occasions, last doing so in 2022, in which they exited at the Conference Semifinals stage.



The club have a league-low valuation of $440 million, and this has showed through their struggle to compete with the big-market teams who have the capital to attract more high-profile talent.

Montreal, whose roster includes former Premier League and Newcastle United midfielder Matty Longstaff, finished with a league-low 6-8-20 record in the 2026 regular season.



For context, there are five clubs in the league who are valued at $1 billion or more.

This is spearheaded by Inter Miami - co-founded by MLS icon David Beckham and who have Argentina World Cup winners Lionel Messi, Rodrigo De Paul and other former European stars on their roster - who, per Forbes, are valued at $1.35 billion.



LAFC and LA Galaxy follow closely behind with valuations of $1.32 billion and $1.08 billion, respectively, with New York City FC ($1.02 billion) and Atlanta United FC ($1 billion) rounding out the top five.

In fact, 20 of the league's 30 teams are valued at $610 million or more, further showing the disparity between Montreal FC and their competitors.

5 Owner Joey Saputo held an emotional press conference on Monday where he revealed his intention to sell the team after 33 years Credit: Alamy

5 Montreal has struggled to compete with the MLS's powerhouses in recent seasons Credit: Getty



During his lengthy press conference, Saputo further explained that if he couldn't find a local buyer, then the Canadian team risks the wrath of relocation - something he doesn't want to happen, but one that would ultimately be out of his hands.

“I will not discount the club to the point of just giving it away just for the sake of giving it away,” Saputo said. “I want to be perfectly clear. I love this club. I will love this club to stay here.

"But if an owner comes in that doesn’t have the capacity to keep the club at the level that it needs to be at, and to spend the money that needs to be spent in order to bring in the players that this city wants to see, then at that point I’m not doing anyone a favor by selling it to someone just to keep it here.

“As much as I would love for this club to be here, if someone has the capacity to do it, and I feel that they have the capacity to do it, then I would love for this club to be here, and continue to build on what we did.



"But if there isn’t, and there’s an offer that comes in to relocate the club, and it’s in line with Major League Soccer and what they want to, then yeah, that’s where it’s going to be.”

Despite these comments, Saputo maintained his stance that he will exhaust all efforts into finding a buyer who "shares commitment to Montreal and who will ensure that the club remains in the city for many years to come.”

5 There is a realistic possibility that the new owner could relocate the team away from Montreal Credit: Getty

5 Montreal own their stadium, Stade Saputo, which could be advantageous in sale negotiations Credit: Getty



With that in mind, the 62-year-old - who in 2014 led a consortium that bought a controlling interest in Serie A side Bologna and became their president, doesn't appear to be in a huge rush to sell up.

Instead he appears to be prioritising the club's best interests and conducting the sales process in coordination with MLS as well as the club’s retained investment bankers.

As for how much he stands to make on a sale, that is to be determined with no fixed price currently publicized.

One factor that may yet become advantageous in the selling process, when looking at it through the lens of potential relocation, though, is that they fully own their 19,000 capacity Stade Saputo.



Both Sporting Kansas City and the Columbus Crew also own their own venues, and have made recent sales, with the Illig family selling 71 percent ownership of KC to Peter Malouk for $700 million back in January.

Furthermore, the Haslam family, who also own the NFL team Cleveland Browns, sold a 37 percent stake of the Crew at a valuation of $900 million.

Whilst both teams are ranked higher by Forbes with a $700 million and $805 million valuations, respectively, this nonetheless shows that Saputo stands to make a significant profit from the $40 million expansion fee he paid in 2012.

Craig Bellamy's men travel to Norway on Saturday before finishing their campaign with a home fixture against Portugal, whose record goalscorer Cristiano Ronaldo has retired from international football.
