World.title: Flamingos star Oluebube Umejiaku reveals emotional motivation behind World Cup Success
World.content:
Nigeria U-17 women’s national team star Oluebube Umejiaku has revealed that her determination to succeed in football is driven by a deeply personal ambition: to lift her mother out of hardship and give her a better life.

The 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup Golden Ball winner opened up about her difficult upbringing, the struggles her family endured and the emotional burden of watching her mother face insults and humiliation because of their circumstances.

Speaking in an interview with BBC News Pidgin, Umejiaku admitted that growing up in a family with limited financial resources was a major challenge, but insisted she would not let those difficulties derail her football dream.

For the Flamingos forward, giving up is simply not an option, especially when she considers the sacrifices her mother has made and the life she hopes to provide.

“It’s not easy coming out from a family that has nothing. It was a very big challenge for me to make it in life. No matter how, in this football career, I won’t give up. I cannot give up,” she said.

Umejiaku explained that her mother’s experiences remain her strongest motivation, particularly the way she is treated by people around them.

“I can’t give up because of my mother; she has suffered a lot. I need to take her out of where she is. People insult her, talk to her anyhow. Even when I’m there, they talk to her anyhow,” the youngster revealed.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Her ambition, therefore, goes beyond becoming a successful footballer or earning individual recognition. She wants to establish herself in the game so that her mother’s circumstances will change and the disrespect she has endured will become a thing of the past.

Praying for recognition to change her Mother’s story

The teenager disclosed that she regularly asks God to make her name known, believing that success in football will help her protect her mother from the treatment she has experienced.

She also recalled how her mother has urged her to remain calm whenever people insult her, warning her against reacting in a way that could create problems for her.

“I always talk to God to make people know my name, so they won’t insult my mother anyhow. She tells me not to reply them, to allow them insult her, so they won’t put me in any problem.

“I give God all the glory, and I thank God for life. I pray God gives me the strength, the mind, the ability to go forward in life,” she added.

It offers an emotional insight into the motivation behind one of the tournament’s most outstanding individual performances. While the Golden Ball has brought Umejiaku international recognition, the young forward’s ultimate ambition remains rooted in the desire to change her family’s story.

Mother’s encouragement fuelled Golden Ball campaign

Umejiaku also credited her mother with playing a significant role in her remarkable performance in Morocco, saying she received regular encouragement throughout Nigeria’s historic campaign.

Having started playing football at the age of seven, the Flamingos star admitted that she never imagined she would one day become the best player at a FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup.

Her mother’s constant calls and words of encouragement, however, helped strengthen her belief, particularly when she was urged to keep scoring goals for the team.

“When I started playing football at seven years old, I didn’t see myself winning the World Cup Golden Ball. When we won the tournament, my mother didn’t let me rest.

“Even during the tournament, she always called me to motivate me to score. Whenever she says, ‘I’ll score,’ I’ll score. So I’m very happy,” she said.

That encouragement appeared to follow Umejiaku throughout a competition in which she consistently delivered whenever Nigeria needed her.

Umejiaku’s decisive contributions to Nigeria’s historic triumph

From being a bench player to a starter, the forward was involved in a goal or assist in every match she featured in as the Flamingos became the first African nation to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup.

Although she was not included in the starting line-up for Nigeria’s opening 2-1 defeat to Poland, Umejiaku came off the bench to score the country’s first goal of the tournament.

She subsequently provided an assist in the 2-0 victory over Puerto Rico before finding the net again in Nigeria’s 3-1 win against defending champions Korea DPR.

Her influence continued into the knockout stages. She scored against Mexico in the round of 16 before winning the late penalty converted by captain Azeezat Oduntan to secure a 1-0 quarter-final victory over Venezuela.

Against Brazil in the semi-final, Umejiaku provided the assist for Nigeria’s third goal in a memorable 3-1 triumph that sent the Flamingos into their first-ever final.

She then delivered another decisive moment on the biggest stage, scoring Nigeria’s second goal in the 2-1 victory over Japan to seal the country’s historic world title.

Her consistency, influence, and ability to deliver key contributions throughout the tournament earned her the Golden Ball, recognising her as the competition’s outstanding player.

For Umejiaku, however, the individual honour and the World Cup triumph carry significance beyond football. They represent another step towards fulfilling the promise she has made to herself and her mother.

The Golden Ball may have announced her arrival on the global stage, but the young Nigerian is already looking beyond the applause and recognition. Her biggest victory, by her own account, will be giving her mother the better life she has always dreamt of.

World.title: Court sentences rapist to life imprisonment
World.content:
A Family Court in Calabar, Cross River State, has sentenced a 38-year-old man to life imprisonment for raping a 10-year-old girl.

Justice Blessing Egwu of Family Court 2 delivered the judgement on Tuesday, relying on Section 33 of the Cross River State Child Rights Law, 2023.

The convict, Nsikak Okon, was a customer of the survivor’s mother, according to James Ibor, a lawyer and co-founder of the Basic Rights Counsel Initiative (BRCI), who disclosed the conviction in a Facebook post on Wednesday.

Mr Ibor told PREMIUM TIMES the offence occurred on 12 July 2025 at Technical College Road, Ikot Effanga, Mile 8, Calabar.

He explained that the survivor’s mother discovered the child was bleeding and, after making inquiries, contacted BRCI for assistance.

The rights organisation subsequently supported the survivor and her family through the process of seeking justice.

In his Facebook post, Mr Ibor commended the Cross River State Government, the Nigeria Police Force and the state Attorney-General, Ededem Ani, for their roles in the case.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He also acknowledged the contributions of the Director of Public Prosecutions, Okoi Ukam, and Joseph Apajung, whom he praised for their diligence in ensuring that the perpetrator was held accountable.

Mr Ibor further commended members of his organisation for standing by the survivor and her family throughout the legal process.

He said supporting child survivors of sexual violence requires more than securing convictions, stressing the importance of protecting their privacy and ensuring they receive the necessary support to recover.

More rape convictions in Cross River

The latest judgement comes amid a series of life imprisonments against sexual offenders in recent months in Cross River.

In June, a Cross River State High Court sentenced a 41-year-old man, Endurance Sandy, to life imprisonment for raping an 11-year-old girl. The judgement was delivered by Justice Blessing Egwu.

Earlier in May, the same judge sentenced a 27-year-old man, Edidiong Nyojole, to life imprisonment for raping a 13-year-old girl in the Uwanse area of Calabar. The court also ordered him to pay N1 million in compensation to the survivor.

In April, another Cross River court sentenced a 46-year-old man, Imeh Sunday, to life imprisonment for raping his daughter. The court also ordered him to pay N1 million in compensation to the survivor.

Call for survivor-centred justice

While welcoming the latest judgement, Mr Ibor said the fight against sexual violence must extend beyond punishing offenders to protecting survivors and providing them with appropriate care.

He acknowledged the contributions of Safe Child Africa, ActionAid Nigeria and UNICEF Nigeria to efforts supporting survivors of sexual violence.

He said the safety, dignity and wellbeing of children must remain central to the response to sexual abuse.

The BRCI co-founder called for sustained collective efforts to prevent sexual violence and ensure that survivors and their families receive the support needed to heal and rebuild their lives.

World.title: Why Nigeria cannot fault CAF over “Player of the Year’ omissions – Kojo Williams
World.content:
Former Nigeria Football Association (NFA) chairman Kojo Williams has blamed the country’s disappointing performances on the international stage for Nigerian footballers’ absence from the 2026 CAF Men’s and Women’s Player of the Year nomination lists.

Mr Williams believes Nigeria has little justification to question the Confederation of African Football (CAF) over the omission, arguing that the country’s results over the past year have not been impressive enough to warrant representation among the continent’s leading individual performers.

The Super Eagles failed to secure qualification for the 2026 FIFA World Cup and finished third at the last Africa Cup of Nations, while the Super Falcons also endured a difficult period, missing out on qualification for the FIFA Women’s World Cup and failing to finish among the top three at the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations.

CAF recently unveiled its 10-man shortlist for the Men’s Player of the Year award, with several players who made significant contributions for their clubs and countries during the assessment period earning recognition.

The nominees include Yoane Wissa, Ismaël Saibari, Achraf Hakimi, Ismaïla Sarr, Sadio Mané and Amad Diallo, among other leading African stars.

Nigeria’s absence from the list has attracted attention, particularly with Super Eagles striker Victor Osimhen missing out despite his impressive contributions for club and country.

However, Mr Williams insists the omission should not come as a surprise, citing the national team’s inability to deliver major results during the period under consideration.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Speaking on ThePlayzone Podcast, the former football administrator said Nigeria’s performances over the past year had offered little basis for expecting players to feature among the nominees.

“It won’t be fair to me to say that I am surprised, but it all has to do with our performances, what we’ve done in the last year,” Mr Williams said.

“So if we’re not doing the right thing, of course, they won’t pick us. Did we qualify for the World Cup? We didn’t win the AFCON. You cannot fault that,” he stated.

Williams questions factors behind Osimhen’s omission

While acknowledging Nigeria’s shortcomings, Mr Williams also suggested that factors beyond individual performances can sometimes influence the African Player of the Year selection.

Osimhen’s absence from the shortlist has been particularly striking, given his contribution to Galatasaray’s success in the Turkish Super Lig and his performances for the Super Eagles at the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations, where he scored four goals.

The striker also played an important role as Galatasaray retained their domestic league title, further strengthening his credentials as one of Africa’s leading forwards.

Despite recognising Osimhen’s quality and achievements, Mr Williams suggested that competition from other African players, alongside the leagues in which nominees feature, could have influenced the selection.

“You know, sometimes they play politics. Yes, Victor did well in Europe, but you had the other guys from other teams like PSG, and maybe the league he’s playing in,” he said.

Mr Williams, however, was quick to acknowledge Osimhen’s standing in African football, recalling that the striker had previously won the continent’s top individual honour during his time at Napoli.

“Yes, he won African Footballer of the Year when he was playing for Napoli. He’s a great player,” he added.

Nigeria’s rich history at CAF Awards

The absence of Nigerian representatives from the latest nominations is a notable departure from the country’s proud history at the continental awards.

Nigeria has produced several winners of the men’s African Player of the Year honour, including Rashidi Yekini, Emmanuel Amuneke, Nwankwo Kanu, Victor Ikpeba, Victor Osimhen and Ademola Lookman.

The country’s women have also enjoyed considerable success, with Asisat Oshoala, Perpetua Nkwocha, Cynthia Uwak and Mercy Akide among the Nigerians who have claimed the women’s individual award.

For a country with such a rich tradition of producing continental stars, the latest omission represents a disappointing moment.

However, Mr Williams’ argument places the focus beyond individual brilliance, suggesting that the fortunes of the national teams and their performances in major competitions remain important considerations in how Nigerian football is perceived across the continent.

With the next CAF Awards ceremony approaching, Nigeria will hope that improved performances from its men’s and women’s national teams, alongside the achievements of its players at club level, will restore the country’s presence among Africa’s most celebrated football talents.

The prestigious event, which was previously scheduled for Monday, 7 December, has been brought forward by five days to 2 December.

The ceremony will begin at 7 p.m. Nigerian time, with Africa’s finest players, coaches, clubs and national teams expected to converge on Nigeria’s commercial capital for one of the biggest nights on the continent’s sporting calendar.

World.title: ANALYSIS: Beyond The Parties: How Nigeria can maximise Detty December
World.content:
Every December, Nigerian cities experience a surge in concerts, nightlife, travel and consumer spending. Hotels fill up, restaurants extend their hours, transport demand rises, and visitors from the diaspora return for what has become widely known as Detty December.

The season, however, should be treated as more than a collection of parties. It is a concentrated economic opportunity involving government agencies, event organisers, hospitality businesses, retailers, transport operators, sponsors and small enterprises.

The important question is no longer how many concerts were held or how lively Lagos became. It is how many visitors arrived, how long they stayed, what they spent, which businesses benefited, how many jobs were created and what lessons can improve the next season.

An economic marketplace

Detty December brings several markets together: aviation, road transport, accommodation, food, fashion, beauty, entertainment, security, logistics and digital payments.

The Lagos State Government estimated that tourism, hospitality and entertainment generated $71.6 million in December 2024, including approximately $44 million from hotels and $13 million from short-let apartments.

A separate assessment by MO Africa estimated that Lagos received about 1.2 million visitors during the period it studied in 2024. It put hotel revenue at approximately ₦54 billion, short-let earnings at ₦21 billion and combined tourism and entertainment revenue at about ₦111.5 billion.

MO Africa’s Economics of Euphoria: Lagos’ Detty December 2025 Report estimated consumer spending of ₦396.54 billion over 55 days, from mid-November 2025 to 10 January 2026. The report covered hospitality, entertainment, nightlife, dining, fashion and retail.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

These figures were derived from different periods and methodologies and should not be combined or compared directly. More importantly, consumer spending is not the same as government revenue or event-organiser earnings. Still, the estimates demonstrate that the festive economy extends far beyond ticket sales.

Lessons from the World Cup

The FIFA World Cup offers a useful lesson in planning around predictable demand. Host countries, tourism agencies, hotels, airlines, sponsors and retailers prepare years ahead, developing infrastructure, staffing, visitor services and commercial partnerships.

An International Monetary Fund analysis estimated that visitor spending and broadcasting revenue associated with the 2022 World Cup in Qatar ranged from $2.3 billion to $4.1 billion.

Detty December does not have to replicate the World Cup. The lesson is that a recurring event must be managed as an economic project. Nigeria knows that festive demand will rise every year; stakeholders should therefore prepare to capture, measure and retain more of its value.

Beyond promotion

Government’s responsibility should extend beyond sponsoring concerts or promoting Lagos as a destination. Visitors need safe transport, effective traffic management, sanitation, security, emergency services, stable power and reliable information.

Authorities can also publish verified event calendars, establish visitor-information platforms and create transparent opportunities for food vendors, craftspeople, drivers, performers and other small businesses.

Event organisers must equally build sustainable businesses rather than isolated shows. Revenue can come from tickets, sponsorships, hospitality packages, concessions, merchandise, brand activations and streaming rights.

Marketing should go beyond posting flyers or announcing performers. Organisers must understand their audiences, communicate practical information and demonstrate value to sponsors. Brands are more likely to invest repeatedly when they can identify the audience reached and measure the results.

Measure what matters

Detty December’s success should not be determined by crowd estimates or social-media impressions alone.

Visitor spending can be estimated using the number of visitors, their average daily expenditure and length of stay. Event revenue should be tracked through tickets, sponsorships and other income streams. Employment impact can be measured through contracts and paid shifts, while government revenue should reflect taxes, permits and lawful fees actually collected.

Every 30 December, stakeholders should hold a strategic review while the season remains active. They should assess visitor numbers, spending patterns, employment, business performance, sponsorship outcomes and problems affecting residents and tourists.

Because festivities often continue into January, the review should serve as a planning checkpoint rather than the date for declaring final figures. A comprehensive economic report can be published after the season, with its data and methodology clearly explained.

Building beyond December

Detty December can become the peak of a broader calendar of cultural, sporting, culinary and entertainment events rather than a once-a-year rush.

Planning and ticket sales can begin months earlier, with January used for evaluation. The rest of the year should support product development, infrastructure improvement and audience building.

The economic benefits must also be balanced against congestion, rising prices, noise, waste and pressure on housing. A sustainable festive economy must benefit visitors without making the city unliveable for residents.

The real success of Detty December is not simply what happens while the music is playing. It is the jobs, businesses, public revenue and lasting investments that remain after the applause.

Solomon Sanusi is a media marketing and growth strategist, entrepreneur and founder of Social Media Centre Marketing (SMC).

World.title: COP31: Nigeria ranks third among countries with highest registered participants at UN climate conference
World.content:
Nigeria ranks third among countries with the most registered participants at the ongoing 31st session of the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Turkey, with 1,506 delegates, according to provisional figures released for the summit.

Of this number, 573 participants were registered under the “Party” badge category, while 933 received “Party Overflow” badges.

The distinction between the two categories at UNFCCC conferences largely relates to participants’ formal status within national delegations and their roles in the negotiation process.

Participants with Party badges are generally designated government delegates. They comprise official negotiators, diplomats and other personnel directly appointed by a state party or observer state to represent their countries.

They are typically members of their countries’ official delegations and may participate actively in negotiations, take the floor and make interventions on behalf of their governments, subject to the rules governing the different negotiation sessions.

Party badges are usually pink, with the participant’s country indicated.

In contrast, Party Overflow badges are issued to additional participants registered through national governments but who are not necessarily part of the core negotiating delegation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

They may include advisers, researchers, business representatives, youth representatives and other experts associated with a country’s broader delegation.

Although registered through their respective governments, Party Overflow badge holders do not automatically enjoy the same negotiating privileges as official delegates.

Their access to negotiation spaces and sessions depends on accreditation rules and available capacity. They may, however, attend open sessions, visit national pavilions and participate in other conference activities.

The UNFCCC registration system tracks the two categories separately.

Not the first time

Nigeria’s emergence as the third-largest national delegation at the ongoing climate conference in Turkey has renewed questions about government spending on international conferences, particularly as millions of Nigerians continue to grapple with economic hardships.

A similar situation occurred at COP28 in Dubai in 2023, when Nigeria was among the countries with the highest number of registered participants, recording 1,411 delegates.

The country also ranked joint third behind the host country, the United Arab Emirates, and Brazil.

At the time, the Nigerian government said only 422 registered participants were government-funded.

The government has consistently maintained that not all participants registered under Nigeria’s delegation are state-sponsored, noting that the list also includes civil society representatives, businesspeople, researchers, and other stakeholders attending in different capacities.

However, the Nigerian government’s focal points at these conferences have yet to provide a comprehensive breakdown of how many participants’ trips are funded with public resources.

This lack of disclosure raises concerns about transparency and accountability in managing Nigeria’s participation in international climate negotiations.

It also limits public understanding of who represents the country in various negotiation groups and technical sessions, as well as who is responsible for advancing Nigeria’s positions on critical climate issues.

Some observers have also expressed concerns that Nigeria’s participation in these conferences sometimes goes beyond diplomatic engagement, with some registered participants allegedly treating the meetings as opportunities for international travel rather than meaningful negotiations.

They argue that inadequate technical knowledge, negotiating experience and understanding of diplomatic processes among some participants could undermine Nigeria’s ability to secure favourable outcomes from the annual climate negotiations.

COP31 records highest provisional attendance

With 92,934 participants registered, COP31 is provisionally the largest UN climate conference in history, surpassing COP28 in Dubai, which recorded more than 80,000 participants.

The provisional figure is based on participants registered to attend the summit in person. The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) releases the final attendance figures after the conference, based on participants who collect physical accreditation badges at the venue.

An analysis by Carbon Brief compares the provisional attendance figures for COP31 with final participant totals from previous climate conferences, dating back to COP1 in Berlin in 1995.

The UNFCCC participant lists are categorised according to the different groups and organisations represented at the summit. The largest category at COP31 comprises delegates representing parties, including nation-states and the European Union, that have ratified the convention and participate fully in climate negotiations.

This category accounts for 18,812 registered participants, making it the second-largest party delegation total recorded at a COP, after COP28.

Unsurprisingly, host country Turkey has the largest delegation at COP31, with 2,950 registered participants.

Brazil follows with 1,994 delegates, while Nigeria ranks third with 1,506 participants. China and Indonesia rank fourth and fifth, with 1,021 and 978 delegates, respectively.

Other countries in the top 10 are Australia (835), Uganda (627), Italy (607), Japan (588) and Kazakhstan (557).

The United Kingdom ranks considerably lower, with 255 registered participants.

At the other end of the list, North Korea has the smallest delegation, with just two participants, followed by Eritrea and Nicaragua with three each. San Marino and Trinidad and Tobago have four registered participants apiece.

However, the figures require some qualification. Some countries, including Brazil, allocate portions of their party badges to non-governmental organisations (NGOs), a practice that can bloat the size of their official delegations.

The provisional figures also indicate that male participants account for 59 per cent of party delegations, compared with 41 per cent for women.

According to Carbon Brief’s analysis, COP31 has a slightly less balanced gender representation than the previous two climate conferences.

Nevertheless, the figures broadly reflect a longer-term trend towards more balanced representation of men and women in national delegations attending UN climate negotiations.

World.title: Shehu Sani warns as Tinubu hails son’s turbaning in Kebbi
World.content:
Former Kaduna Central senator Shehu Sani has advised traditional institutions against conferring chieftaincy titles on serving government officials and their immediate family members.

The former senator, who is also the candidate of the All Progressives Congress (APC) for the district, gave the advice following the turbaning of a son of President Bola Tinubu, Seyi, as the Dan Zakin Gwandu, on Wednesday, by the Emir of Gwandu, Muhammadu Bashar, in Kebbi State.

Mr Sani said any traditional recognition or appreciation for public servants should take place after their tenure in office.

In a social media post, the outspoken former senator argued that awarding titles to people in power risks compromising the neutrality of traditional stools and diluting the merit behind such honours.

“People in Government and their family members should not be given traditional titles until they leave office; then they can be appreciated for their service with a title. That’s my opinion”, Mr Sani stated.

The title, which means “Son of the Lion of Gwandu”, was conferred on Seyi at the Abdullahi Fodiyo Palace in Birnin Kebbi.

The emir cited the recipient’s philanthropic activities, benevolence and contributions to community development for the honour.

According to a local news outlet, Kebbi Daily Updates, the emir said: “The title acknowledges his commitment to humanitarian causes, support for the less privileged and efforts to make a positive impact on the lives of people”.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

President Tinubu congratulates son

Meanwhile, President Tinubu has congratulated Seyi on the turbaning.

According to a statement by presidential spokesman, Bayo Onanuga, “President Tinubu thanked the Emir and the Gwandu Emirate Council for the honour, which the traditional ruler described as the first of its kind in the Emirate’s history”.

“The President noted that the honour carries a responsibility that extends beyond personal recognition and reflects the enduring bonds of friendship, mutual respect and unity among Nigeria’s diverse peoples.

“He acknowledged Seyi’s efforts in youth engagement, community development and empowerment, particularly through his involvement with the City Boy Movement and other initiatives supporting young Nigerians.

“As a father, I am pleased to see my son recognised by a traditional institution with such a distinguished history.

“But I also remind him that every honour comes with responsibility. The title of Dan Zaki Gwandu carries the values of courage, leadership and service. I urge him to live up to those values, remain humble and continue to dedicate himself to the well-being of others.

“Our traditional institutions remain important custodians of our history, culture and national unity. I thank the Emir of Gwandu and the good people of Kebbi State for extending this honour to my son,” the President says.

“President Tinubu encouraged Seyi to regard the title as a call to deepen his commitment to youth development, peaceful coexistence and service to Nigeria.

“He wished him wisdom, humility and strength as he assumes the responsibilities associated with the traditional title”, the statement read.

World.title: Court orders extradition of Nigerian to US over alleged wire fraud, others
World.content:
Federal High Court

The Federal High Court in Abuja has ordered the extradition of a Nigerian, Temitope Omotade, to the U.S. District Court of Minnesota to face his trial over allegations bordering on wire fraud, among others.

Justice Peter Lifu, in a judgment, held that the application made by the Attorney-General of the Federation (AGF) was meritorious.

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the AGF had made the application for the extradition of Omotade to the U.S.

He is a suspect in a superseding five-count indictment bordering on five counts in case number 22-CR-24 SRN/HB filed on Feb. 8, 2022, at the US District Court.

The offences in counts one, two and three bordered on mail and wire fraud in violation of Title 18 US Code, Sections 1341 and 1343, and 1349, which carries a maximum penalty of 30 years in prison in each of the counts.

Counts four and five bordered on aggravated identity theft and aiding and abetting, in violation of Title 18 US Codes, Sections 1028A (a)(1) and 2, which carries a maximum penalty of two years in prison for each count, consecutive to any other term of imprisonment imposed on the defendant.

In the AGF’s application, he contended that the request was grounded on an extradition packet and diplomatic notes from the US, including a sealed indictment from the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota and a warrant for Omotade’s arrest.

He argued that all statutory requirements under the Extradition Act have been met because the offences are non-political, non-trivial, and made in good faith.

He submitted that the Central Authority Unit had established that proper certifications and documentation, including affidavits from US officials, relevant statute copies, and passport details, accompanied the formal request.

Besides, the AGF said there were no pending local criminal proceedings in Nigeria against Omotade for the specified offences, and adequate assurances regarding nonprejudicial trial conditions in the US had been secured.

He asserted that the request and accompanying materials satisfied all conditions for the surrender of Omotade, who was the sole respondent in the suit marked FHC/ABJ/CS/494/2024.

The AGF maintained that the legal procedures complied with the Oaths Act and the Extradition Act, adding that the interest of justice dictated that the request be granted, “as the respondent is duly accused of the indictments brought against him abroad.”

But Omotade, in his counter-affidavit filed by his lawyer, prayed the court to dismiss the suit.

Omotade denied all allegations of mail fraud, wire fraud, conspiracy, and aggravated identity theft, maintaining that his connection to Roxanne Gilbert involved no criminal conduct or digital proceeds.

He contended that the extradition application lacked substantive proof and statutory backing for several reasons.

According to him, the supporting documents lack any blockchain analysis, financial trails, chat histories, or video calls, reducing the case to mere identification particulars like a passport data page and airway bill rather than active culpability, while pointing to potential identity theft by third parties.

He said he was under active specialist medical management for hepatic steatosis (fatty liver) and elevated liver functions, among other arguments.

He argued that his surrender would be unjust, oppressive and disproportionate given his fragile health and the physical rigours of international transfer and detention by the EFCC, among other arguments.

Delivering the judgment, Justice Lifu held that upon careful consideration of the affidavits, the documentary evidence, the submissions of learned counsel and the relevant provisions of the Extradition Act, he was satisfied that the AGF had established the necessary basis for Omotade’s extradition of the United States of America.

The judge observed that though Omotade cited health reasons in his arguments, he said the materials as presented in the record did not sufficiently establish that if Omotade surrendered himself, it would expose him to a grave and unavoidable medical consequence, or that the necessary medical attention could not be obtained in the requesting country.

He agreed with the AGF that medical care is available in the US and that Omotade had not discharged the burden of establishing that the extradition would be practically unjust or oppressive.

“In the absence of sufficient evidence establishing the asserted degree of risk, I am unable to hold that the respondent’s medical condition, standing alone, constitutes a legal bar to surrender in this case.

“I have equally considered the other restrictions contained in Section 3 of the Act,” the judge said.

Justice Lifu, therefore, held that no sufficient material had been established before the court to show that the request was made for the purpose of prosecuting or punishing Omotade on account of his race, religion, nationality, or political opinions, “or that any of the other applicable statutory restrictions necessarily preclude his surrender.”

According to him, the purpose of extradition proceedings is not to determine the respondent’s guilt in advance as noted earlier, nor to deprive him of the protections available under the law.

“It is to ensure that a request for surrender is examined judicially and that the person sought is surrendered only where the applicable statutory requirements have been satisfied.

“The respondent will retain the opportunity to contest the allegations against him in accordance with the law and procedure applicable to the criminal proceedings in the requesting country.

“The objections raised by the respondent do not, on the evidence and arguments presented, constitute sufficient grounds for refusing the application.

“Accordingly, an order is hereby made extraditing the respondent, Temitope Seyi Omotade, who is a subject in a superseding five-count indictment referred in this case to the United States District Court for the District of Minnesota, United States of America,” he ruled.

The judge also dismissed Omotade’s application for bail filed on Sept. 16. (NAN)

World.title: Trump to flex muscles on Asia tour after midterms losses
World.content:
President Donald Trump

After his party suffered a midterms hammering, President Donald Trump faces a new challenge: proving he is still the boss of US foreign policy on the global stage.

With Trump politically hamstrung as he enters the remaining two-year ‘lame duck’ period of his White House tenure, world leaders may be quietly wondering how to leverage the new balance of power in Washington.

The 80-year-old Republican heads to the ASEAN summit in the Philippines and APEC summit in China from a radically transformed and hostile political landscape at home after the Democrats seized both the House of Representatives and Senate.

Constitutionally banned from seeking a third term in the 2028 presidential race, the unpredictable billionaire could be all the more inclined to focus his energy on the international stage.

“After bad midterms, this is how presidents reset,” Edgard Kagan, an expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) told a news briefing.

– Iran, trade, China –

That is especially true for Trump on his Asian tour, where he is unlikely to be pressed publicly on domestic politics.

China has described the midterms as an “internal affair” and said it is “willing to continue working” with the United States after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress.

But the power shift in Washington will still be on leaders’ radars, said Joshua Kurlantzick, an expert in Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations.

“In private, many (Asian) leaders are relieved,” Kurlantzick wrote in an article this month.

“The Iran war has been particularly challenging for the United States’ Asian partners and allies, and they hope that after the midterm results US President Donald Trump’s decision-making on the issue will become more predictable.”

Trump has said several times since the midterms that renewed fighting between the United States and Iran is unlikely.

A Democratic-controlled Congress could also take a tougher stance towards China, Kurlantzick added, backtracking on the Trump administration’s “soft approach” to Beijing that has sparked unease among US allies in Asia.

Leaders in the world’s largest continent are also hoping to see Democrats push back on Trump’s barrage of tariffs on trading partners, which have stung Asian economies heavily reliant on exports.

Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries has urged Congress to reassert its authority over US trade policy.

The Democrats will not get an easy ride in undoing Trump’s policies, though.

The president enjoys broad authority over trade and holds veto power over congressional legislation — which he has vowed to use.

– High-profile meeting –

Trump relishes dramatic gestures and foreign policy provides an ideal arena for high-profile meetings, such as with Chinese and Russian leaders Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Trump told reporters this week he expects to meet Xi and Putin at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China scheduled for November 18-19.

The president said “denuclearization” and ending the war in Iran would be on the agenda.

But the bigger goal for Trump may well be a single photo of himself standing with the two other leaders he views as his great power equals, said Kurt Campbell, chair of The Asia Group and a senior diplomat during the Biden administration.

“I think in many respects this could be ‘the meeting is the message’,” Campbell said.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky, who watched in horror as the White House appeared to pivot towards Moscow this year, has warned against a “Yalta 2.0,” referring to Western leaders dividing Europe with the Soviet Union in 1945.

Victor Cha, president of geopolitics and foreign policy and Korea chair at CSIS, said the Republicans’ midterm defeat meant a high-profile meeting was all the more likely.

“One that he (Trump) has personally staked a lot of time over two terms has been on North Korea,” Cha said.

“There’s nobody else in the US government that makes policy on North Korea except the president, so I think that he’ll be focused on that sort of legacy issue.”

World.title: Who could potentially replace Jensen Huang if Nvidia ousts him?
World.content:
File: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang. Photo by Patrick T. Fallon / AFP.

Chip giant Nvidia’s board was reportedly meeting Wednesday to discuss the future of co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang after he dated an accused Chinese spy, according to US media.

The 63-year-old tech titan, who has led the key AI giant since it was founded in 1993, has been beleaguered with reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a data center executive who has been accused by US intelligence of working for China’s Ministry of State Security.

With Huang unexpectedly on the backfoot, and no known plan of succession at Nvidia, the field is wide open for a variety of replacements to lead one of the key AI players should the board decide to oust Huang.

Here are some of the names being suggested most frequently as Huang’s potential successor.

Internal hire

With over 40,000 employees, Nvidia could opt to go with an in-house pick to take the helm, including one of Huang’s dozens of direct reports.

Tech publications frequently cited Nvidia’s Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as an easy choice, if for no other reason than she is already among top leadership at the chip behemoth.

Another longtime Nvidia honcho is Ian Buck, who oversees the company’s data center clients. He was a key mind behind the software that keeps Nvidia-designed chips in demand.

Business magazine Inc. also lists Nvidia’s vice president of applied deep learning research, Bryan Catanzaro, as a possible pick.

A family affair

Huang could also try and position a member of his own family as his replacement, with more than one option for a bloodline succession.

His daughter Madison Huang is currently the senior director of product marketing at Nvidia and is among the names most suggested by analysts.

As a marketing leader, she had a multi-year stint at luxury conglomerate LVMH.

Jensen Huang’s son Spencer Huang could also be a potential successor. He currently works at Nvidia as the director of product management in the company’s robotics division.

Huang’s cousin, Lisa Su, could also be a viable candidate for selection – not only is she his first cousin, once removed, but she also has valuable expertise as the longtime CEO of semiconductor giant AMD.

Tech CEO swap

Su is not the only tech chief being bandied around as a possible replacement for Huang.

Rene Haas, CEO of UK chip design firm Arm, is another candidate being suggested by the tech press.

Speculation runs wide in Silicon Valley, where former Apple CEO Tim Cook – who stepped down from leading the tech giant in August after 15 years at the helm – is another person insiders say could potentially be tapped.

World.title: Student Loan: Parents, NANS offer tips on how to stop double dipping by beneficiaries
World.content:
By Adesina Wahab

Parents under the aegis of National Parent Teacher Association of Nigeria, NAPTAN, and the National Association of Nigerian Students, NANS, have offered tips on how to stop the practice of students benefitting from the Student Loan Scheme and still going ahead to collect tuition fees from their parents and guardians.

The practice, labelled double dipping by the Nigerian Education Loan Fund, NELFUND, which gives out the loans, is gradually becoming rampant and erasing the main reason the loan scheme was initiated – take the burden of tuition payment off the necks of parents and guardians.

Speaking with Thursday Learning, the Chairman of the Board of Trustees of NAPTAN, Chief Deolu Ogunbanjo, opined that such a practice negates the reason for the setting up of the scheme.

“The Student Loan Scheme was set up to give access to higher education to students who would otherwise drop out because of inability to pay fees. It is also to take the burden of fee payment off the necks of parents and guardians. Such happenings may not be totally eradicated. We know how rascally some young ones can be.

“I think the way out is to let the parents and guardians be aware when payments are made by NELFUND to beneficiaries. Let there be a means of notifying the parents that their children have benefitted from the scheme,” he said

Similarly, the National Public Relations Officer of NANS, Comrade Obidah David, also supported notification being sent to parents of beneficiaries.

“If it is a text message, they can send to parents and guardians of beneficiaries. Information on contacts of parents is always provided by students when registering. That is necessary in case of any emergency. Also, names of beneficiaries can be published whether in the traditional media or social media. There is nothing bad in that. It is for transparency, “ he stated.

Recall that recently, the Managing Director of NELFUND, Akintunde Sawyerr, said during a press briefing that the fund had identified cases of students allegedly accessing loan support while continuing to place the burden of tuition payments on their parents.

Describing the practice as unacceptable, Sawyerr said the fund was determined to end the situation and strengthen transparency in the administration of the scheme.

“This comment is based on our recognition that there are so many students out there who are double-dipping. They are taking from NELFUND and still stressing their parents. We are going to put an end to that,” he said.

Under the proposed arrangement, parents would be able to confirm whether their children’s school fees had been paid through NELFUND without necessarily having access to the actual amount involved.

Sawyerr said the initiative was intended to address concerns among parents who continued to shoulder the financial responsibilities of their children’s education despite the availability of government-backed loans.

The development comes as the Federal Government intensifies efforts to expand access to tertiary education through the student loan programme, designed to ease financial barriers and prevent eligible students from being denied higher education because of their inability to pay institutional fees upfront.

Under the arrangement, NELFUND provides loans for institutional charges, while upkeep allowances are processed separately to assist beneficiaries with their living expenses.

Sawyerr explained that the exercise would go beyond the fund’s routine public awareness campaigns, which primarily inform students about the availability of the loan scheme.

According to him, the new engagements would focus on educating students, parents and tertiary institutions on how the payment system works and the changes introduced to improve its administration.

“We can easily do a press release and say, ‘Hey, this is what we’re doing.’ But if we don’t educate the institutions, if we don’t educate the students, everybody will still be running behind,” he said.

“This is not sensitisation. This is re-education of the stakeholders and the students as to the changes that we have made in their favour,” he added.

The managing director said the workshops would help eliminate confusion surrounding institutional payments, upkeep allowances and the documentation required by beneficiaries.

Meanwhile, NELFUND’s Executive Director, Mustapha Iyal, provided further insight into the fund’s payment architecture, explaining that the system was designed to minimise intermediaries in the transfer of institutional fees. Iyal said the fund relied on students’ application identification numbers and wallet numbers for institutional payment processing rather than their conventional bank account numbers.

“To be clear, we don’t use account numbers. We use their application ID and wallet number,” he said.

World.title: Dollar to Naira exchange rate today, November 12, 2026
World.content:
The Nigerian naira opened trading on Thursday, November 12, 2026, under sustained demand pressure across both the official Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM) and the parallel market, maintaining the wider spread observed earlier in the week.

At the official window, data from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) shows the naira entering Thursday’s session around the ₦1,350.36 to ₦1,353.50 per dollar band. Early Thursday morning international currency feeds recorded spot quotes hovering near ₦1,345.72 per dollar, while official NFEM benchmarks reflect the closing figures from the prior trading session pending the day’s official fixing. Earlier in the week, trading at the official window saw intraday fluctuations between ₦1,349.25 and ₦1,354 per dollar, with interbank turnover reaching $248.07 million across 144 deals.

In the parallel market, commonly referred to as the black market, the naira continues to trade at a significant discount to the official rate. Currency dealers across Lagos and Abuja quoted the dollar between ₦1,411 and ₦1,420 for buying, while selling rates ranged from ₦1,419 to ₦1,430 per dollar depending on transaction volume and location.

This leaves an exchange rate gap of roughly ₦68 to ₦80 per dollar between the official NFEM benchmark and street-level rates.

Market analysts attribute the recent softening of the local currency to heightened seasonal foreign exchange demand from importers and travelers heading into the end-of-year period, alongside foreign portfolio investment outflows and a firmer US dollar globally. Despite the recent dip—which saw the parallel market touch a 10-month low of ₦1,430 per dollar this week—Nigeria’s gross external reserves remain sturdy at approximately $54.9 billion, well above the CBN’s full-year target of $51.04 billion, offering a substantial buffer to support market liquidity through the remainder of the fourth quarter.

Traders and businesses continue to monitor daily NFEM liquidity injections and CBN updates for direction as Thursday’s trading progresses.

World.title: My research effective for prostate, menopause therapy — Odimegwu, Gates Foundation Scholar
World.content:
Dr Joy Odimegwu

By Morenike Taire

Joy Odimegwu, a University of Lagos academic in the Department of Pharmacognosy, Faculty of Pharmacy, is a senior researcher with over 20 years of international experience with a passion for translating herbal medicine drug discovery from labs to markets to solve some of the world’s most pressing health care challenges, including drug resistant gynecological cancers and pain.

As a fellow of Mujeres Por Africa and Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, she sits at the intersection between biodiversity and cutting edge technology.

With a PhD in herbal medicine, Odimegwu is a herbal medicine expert who got a grant from Gates Foundation to train African researchers on women’s health. According to her, women’s health has always been regulated because it’s complicated and what is complicating it is the hormones which can be up in the morning, down by afternoon.

“It’s nature. It’s how we’re built, so it shouldn’t cause confusion. I didn’t know that other people were interested in the topic”, she told Vanguard. My area of research is biological patterns and I came across something very interesting. For many years they have been using broccoli to prevent certain gynecological cancers so as a researcher, I wanted to know what was in it. So, broccoli attacks inflammation and some people believe cancer is from inflammation”.

Odimegwu wanted to be sure broccoli that is grown in Nigeria is the same as that broccoli. “My first degree was in Botany so I know about plants. I did some research. I got some in Jos, carried some down to Lagos and carried out the research to find out if broccoli’s Sulforaphane could modulate hormones in animals. The result I got was what I presented in Brazil. I used rabbits, dehydrated the broccoli powder in such a way as to optimise the Sulforaphane. If you feed the rabbit for 30 days, checking the estrogen throughout, we found that type of estrogen stable (there are other types) while the control was all over the place.”

Clinical Studies

Now, her team is preparing for the clinical human studies and all her high school friends have signed up to support her. “Essentially, there’s a solution in our food. Already, Hormone Replacement Therapy is being marketed. They are calling it the gold standard. It’s time for somebody to talk about the contraindications. It’s not for everybody. In Nigeria, the first contraindication is poverty. So many people cannot afford it. The other contraindications are bleeding and many other things that if a woman has she should not take that Hormone Replacement Therapy. I have provided a solution, a natural one from food. We work with consistency because it takes a lot of time to get an effect. I produce it because I got a small grant from TETFUND to be able to produce and have been selling to family and friends because it’s not registered with NAFDAC yet”.

The feedback has been phenomenal, according to her. “I cannot even begin to talk about some of the things I have heard. I know why it’s like that – it’s concentrated. In vegetable, broccoli is 90 per cent water. If I am processing 10 grams, it’s not up to a gram powder so dehydration removes all the water and it concentrates the Sulforaphane. It’s safe in animal studies according to their organs after treatment because it’s food. If you are eating fresh broccoli, it would be hard to get enough amount of Sulforaphane. This person tells me she always feels full and after taking this powder in a week she notices that she’s lighter. If you eat vegetables often enough you will lose weight.

How it works

The Sulforaphane interacts with the estrogen receptors at the cellular level. For Odimegwu, the beautiful thing is that this has the effect of preventing certain cancers.

“So I am building a company to produce our vegetables in powder, concentrated. Because we’re so used to them, we can think, what is in it? There is a lot in it. From that nutritional aspect, I have been talking to a lot of people. I am very passionate about this, I use any opportunity that I am given to tell people that. As we are growing older, we also deal with insulin resistance, prolactin, androgens and testosterone start acting up. In the African context, what happens is, somebody has hormonal symptoms, goes to the hospital and if the doctor is not so experienced because you go through tests and nothing is showing, so it must be village people. But there’s a biological reason for what you are seeing.

“That not being able to see the problem compounds the problem and that is why I am very keen on talking about this to more people, educating people. Our mothers and grandmothers suffered this. Maybe they are chewing one thing, managing themselves. It’s part of ageing, there’s no problem. There’s actually a problem. Women should not suffer this”.

She shares the story of Bill Gates’ wife, one of the richest women in the world who was having menopausal symptoms missed by two doctors. It was the third one that caught it.

“She had suffered so much and this is the richest woman. Imagine someone so educated, well to do had to go through that, what of those that don’t have as much? In my fellowship, we believe that no woman, not even the least woman selling whatever in the village, should be left unsupported. Every woman should be supported”, she said.

World.title: How ISWAP’s southern expansion plot was foiled, commander killed in Ondo forest
World.content:
•Ohida, ISWAP commander (left) and Oba Falae

By Dayo Johnson, Akure

The elimination of Abdussamad Ohida, also known as Anwar, a senior commander of the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), alongside several of his fighters has brought major relief not only to the people of Ondo State but to the entire southern Nigeria.

Ohida, who took over the coordination of ISWAP’s central and southern regional activities following the 2023 arrest of his superior, Abu Ikrimah (Abu Uwais) inside an Ondo forest, was killed during an intelligence-led operation deep inside the Owo Forest, Ondo State, early this month.

Despite this breakthrough however, former Secretary to the Government of the Federation and now traditional ruler of Ilu-Abo in Akure North, Oba Olu Falae, has lamented that kidnapping and banditry still hold sway in rural communities

The operation was executed by a combined team of Nigerian Army troops, operatives of the Department of State Services (DSS), and officers of the Western Nigeria Security Network, codenamed Amotekun, with strategic intelligence backing from the United Kingdom.

A major blow against southern expansion, security analysts have described the operation as another major counter-terrorism breakthrough by Nigerian security agencies, at a time authorities are intensifying efforts to prevent terrorist groups from extending their operational footprint from the North-East into the South. According to security sources, the forces carried out a thorough clearance operation in the forest, aimed at dislodging entrenched terrorist cells and preventing planned attacks on communities in southern Nigeria.

Before the breakthrough, credible intelligence had indicated that Ohida was plotting to launch coordinated attacks on civilians during the festive period. The plot was designed to create a widespread atmosphere of insecurity that could undermine public confidence and disrupt preparations for the 2027 general elections.

His elimination has therefore foiled the group’s plans to launch major terrorist attacks in parts of southern Nigeria during the coming festivities.

The killing of Ohida came barely months after Nigerian and United States forces, in a joint counter-terrorism operation, killed another senior Islamic State commander, Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, in Borno State. For years, Ohida’s group had carried out several coordinated attacks against military formations, security installations and other soft targets as part of a deliberate strategy to establish or expand operational networks outside its traditional strongholds in northeastern Nigeria.

The latest operation is being viewed by security authorities as a decisive attempt to disrupt ISWAP’s desperate push to establish a new operational corridor in the South.

Trail of deadly attacks linked to Ohida

Ohida was accused of involvement in several high-profile attacks on security formations across the country. One of the alleged attacks was the December 31, 2025 attack on the Ipele Divisional Police Station in Owo, Ondo State, during which eight AK-47 rifles were reportedly carted away before the Police facility was bombed.

The killed terrorist was also linked to the April 23, 2022 attack on the Ogaminana Police Station in Adavi Local Government Area of Kogi State, where five policemen were killed in cold blood.

Other attacks attributed to him included the February 7, 2022 assault on the Okene Area Command and the December 24, 2020 attack on a naval checkpoint in Okene, where two naval officers were reportedly killed.

Security sources said Ohida had been on the wanted list for years and had perfected the use of Ondo’s thick forest reserves as a safe haven and launching pad for operations into Kogi, Edo and other parts of the South-West.

Aiyedatiwa’s 14-Day ultimatum

Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa had issued a 14-day ultimatum for bandits, kidnappers and other criminal elements to vacate the state’s forest reserves. The governor warned that failure to comply would trigger a coordinated security operation involving state security agencies, tactical teams and local hunters.

The raid carried out at the ISWAP camp that resulted in the killing of its leader, Abdussamad Ohida and his fighters came 19 days after the governor’s ultimatum elapsed.

In a statement issued by his Senior Special Assistant on Forestry, Bidemi Joshua Obayangban, Governor Aiyedatiwa commended the security agencies involved in the operation. He said the operation demonstrated his administration’s determination to reclaim the state’s forests from terrorists, kidnappers and other criminal elements. “The successful operation demonstrates that Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa’s 14-day ultimatum is yielding results. We commend the joint security forces for their courage and commitment in eliminating the ISWAP commander and members of his group. The government will continue to support security agencies until criminal elements are completely flushed out of Ondo State’s forests”, he said.

Kidnapping, banditry still hold sway in rural communities – Oba Falae

Despite the recent breakthroughs, insecurity in the state remains a serious challenge as gunmen and

suspected kidnappers have continued to target farm settlements and small communities, such as Imafon, Igushin, Ilado, Ilu-Abo, and Aba Oyinbo in Akure North, Owo and Ose council areas resulting in the abductions and deaths of farmers and residents.

Consequently, youths across communities in the state have staged protests over the incessant abduction for ransom, killings and rape of women on their way to farms by suspected herders. Insecurity across the state has taken a heavy toll on farmers, who can no longer tend their farms freely for fear of attack.

Disturbed by the development, the former Secretary to the Government of the Federation and now traditional ruler of Ilu-Abo in Akure North, Oba Olu Falae, lamented that kidnappers appear to be deliberately targeting wealthy residents who relocated to the community over the past decade because of its reputation for peace and stable electricity supply.

Falae also lamented the economic impact of the insecurity, noting that many residents are now afraid to visit their farms. Cocoa plantations and poultry operations, which are key sources of livelihood in the area, have been abandoned owing to fear of abduction.

He said: “People are afraid to go to the farm. Our hard-working residents cannot continue to live in fear; otherwise, we risk becoming beggars and food insecure.

“I am certain that the law will not abandon us and security agencies will not fold their arms. With determination, training and strategic action, we will rescue our people and safeguard our heritage,” Falae stated. The development has forced some families, who have been repeatedly targeted by gunmen, to flee their communities and put their homes up for sale.

Aiyedatiwa reveals foiled plot to bomb Govt House

In a related development, Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa has revealed that security operatives recently foiled an alleged plot to bomb the Ondo State Government House in Akure.

Governor Aiyedatiwa, who disclosed this during an appearance on a television personality programme, described the operation as one of several silent victories recorded in the state’s fight against insecurity.

He explained that the planned attack was uncovered about three to four months ago after intelligence reports alerted security agencies to suspicious activities by a group of youths allegedly plotting to target the seat of government.

According to the governor, the suspects initially lodged in a hotel within the state capital before relocating to a rented apartment, where security operatives later discovered materials and equipment believed to be connected to the planned operation.

“Following intelligence reports, the Police and Amotekun moved in, raided the location, arrested the suspects, and they remain in custody,” the governor said.

Aiyedatiwa noted that investigators are yet to establish the exact motive behind the alleged plot but stressed that the incident underscores the complex security challenges confronting the state and the need for constant vigilance. The governor said many successful security operations often go unnoticed by the public because attacks are prevented before they happen.

“So much work is being done. Security is one responsibility that leaders carry that is not so visible to everybody. It is only when there is a lapse that it will look as if the government has not been doing enough. We have been doing so much,” he said.

South-West governors closing ranks on security

Speaking on security efforts across the South-West, Aiyedatiwa said governors in the region are working together to strengthen safety, intelligence-gathering and joint operations.

“We are talking to ourselves; we are working,” he said, adding that recent meetings among the governors focused on enhancing collaboration through regional security outfits such as Amotekun and improving information sharing across state boundaries.

The governor also welcomed the conviction of four persons linked to the June 5, 2022 Owo church massacre, describing the judgment as a major victory for justice and the rule of law.

“For us in Ondo State, we are happy that this judgment is a victory for the rule of law and for all the victims attacked, not just in Owo, Ondo State, but all who have been attacked at one time or the other by these terrorists,” he said. The attack on St. Francis Xavier Catholic Church in Owo had claimed more than 40 lives and left many others injured after gunmen opened fire on worshippers during a Sunday service.

Amotekun commander renews call for state police

Speaking on the security situation, the Commander of Amotekun in Ondo State, Chief Adetunji Adeleye, renewed his call for the establishment of state policing, describing it as the most viable solution to Nigeria’s growing security challenges.

Adeleye, who doubles as Chairman of Amotekun Commanders in the South-West region, said the council had consistently maintained that decentralised policing remains the most effective strategy for tackling insecurity across the country.

According to him, local security structures possess better knowledge of their environments and are better positioned to identify and apprehend criminals operating within their communities.

“The position of the Council of Amotekun Commanders has always been that state policing remains the only viable solution to the present insecurity in the country. It is easier to identify criminals when security operations are rooted within the local communities,” he said.

Adeleye described the proposed state police structure as a major step towards decentralising Nigeria’s security architecture and strengthening grassroots intelligence-gathering.

“As far as the South-West is concerned, we are ready to adjust and conform with whatever framework is put in place to ensure the successful take-off of state policing,” he added.

The Ondo Amotekun boss noted that the corps had demonstrated the effectiveness of community-based policing through its operations across the state, disclosing that more than 500 suspected criminals had been arrested and prosecuted this year alone”, he said.

According to him, many of those prosecuted have been convicted and are currently serving various jail terms, a development, he said, validates the effectiveness of the Amotekun model.

However, residents remain apprehensive over desperate plans by Islamic groups still hiding in the thick forests to establish a new operational corridor in southern Nigeria, raising fresh concerns about the need for sustained surveillance and forest combing operations.

World.title: 4 dead, many hospitalised in Benue after consuming herbal mixture
World.content:
AI-generated image for illustration

By Peter Duru

Makurdi —No fewer than four persons have reportedly died, while 14 others are battling for their lives in hospital after allegedly consuming a suspected poisonous herbal mixture purchased in Oju township, headquarters of Oju Local Government Area of Benue State.

It was gathered that the incident occurred after three men, identified as Magani, Mohamed and Kala, allegedly sold herbal preparations suspected to contain poisonous substances to residents of the Igede community during the Ihiejwo market day in Oju township, last weekend.

According to the eyewitness, “The development gained attention when some of those, who drank the mixture and their loved ones raised the alarm on November 2, 2026, after several residents, who had purchased and consumed the herbal preparations started developing similar symptoms.

“While the first victim reportedly died Tuesday morning, the second died in the early hours of Wednesday, and the third and fourth victims died later on November 4, 2026.

“As we speak, over 14 other victims are currently battling for their lives, with many of them said to be in critical condition.”

He disclosed that the three suspects allegedly involved in the sale of the herbal mixture were apprehended by the leadership of the Igede Youth Council, in collaboration with the Oju Local Government Area Township Youth leadership, and subsequently handed over to the police in Oju.

“We have been told that the Oju Divisional Police Headquarters has transferred the case to the Benue State Police Command, where the suspects are currently undergoing investigation,” he said.

Speaking while handing over the suspects to the police, President of the Igede Youth Council, John-Frank Ozzidi, called on the Benue State government to ensure a thorough investigation of the incident and guarantee that justice was served.

Ozzidi said the Igede youths had deliberately refrained from taking the law into their hands, resisting the temptation to subject the suspects to jungle justice.

He explained that their decision to allow the law to take its course demonstrated their confidence in the state government to ensure justice is done in the matter.

The youth leader also urged political officeholders from the area to follow up on the case to ensure that the deceased victims got justice and that the circumstances surrounding the suspected poisoning were fully established.

Contacted, the Chairman of Oju council, Mr. Jackson Ominyi, confirmed the incident but said he was yet to obtain the exact number of fatalities.

Efforts to reach the Police Public Relations Officer, Peter Aondongu, for comments were unsuccessful, as he did not respond to enquiries at press time.
