At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

He further claimed that the county had written to the developer in 2023, 2024, and 2025 seeking engagement over the outstanding commitments.

Mutua Mutia, another former resident, said the prolonged dispute had left families frustrated, especially after they were promised they would return within a year.

"I have lived in Buxton since I was a young boy. My firstborn child is now more than 30 years old, and the history of Buxton is one that pains us. We were evicted with the promise that we would return after one year, but today it is seven years and we are still struggling," Mutia said.

The former residents are also demanding the reconstruction of an Early Childhood Development (ECD) centre demolished to pave the way for the project, as well as the construction of a promised community social centre.

Hussein said the county had yet to receive either facility or its share of the housing project.

"The county has not received its 10 per cent share to date. There was an agreement that the demolished ECD centre would be reconstructed and handed over to the county, alongside a community social centre, but we have not received either," he said.

The first phase of Buxton Point delivered 584 housing units in 2023, while the second phase is expected to provide between 1,400 and 1,500 additional apartments. Completion had been scheduled for August 2027.

However, GulfCap Real Estate Chief Executive Officer Chris Ochieng defended the developer's position, saying 492 housing units would be handed over to buyers by December.

While urging the county to stop politicising the project, Ochieng warned that the ongoing controversy risks disrupting the project’s completion and affecting hundreds of workers who depend on it for their livelihoods.

He said the county government's 10 per cent share would be transferred upon completion of the project.

He also maintained that the developer had supported displaced residents by providing Sh240,000 for relocation and offering them preferential rates to purchase apartments.

Ochieng said the continued involvement of county officials in the dispute was unfortunate, particularly at a time when 492 homeowners are expecting to take possession of their houses in December.

He noted that the controversy was not only creating uncertainty among prospective homeowners but also threatening the livelihoods of hundreds of people employed directly and indirectly through the project.

“It is very unfortunate that Mombasa County officials are bringing politics into a national project. We have 492 homeowners who expect to take possession of their units by December. Beyond the homeowners, hundreds of people depend on this project for employment and their daily livelihoods,” said Ochieng.

He called on the county leadership to allow the project to proceed without unnecessary political interference, arguing that Mombasa has previously witnessed housing projects that stalled despite significant public interest.

World.title: Sakaja defends Sh43.7b drop in Nairobi County's pending bills before Senate
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja tells Senate that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors. [File, Standard]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has told the Senate that pending bills in the city have been reduced from Sh118.79 billion to Sh75.07 billion through verification and payment.

Sakaja revealed that internal verification established that the Sh43.73 billion reduction was not achieved solely through payments but also involved legal assessments, court-ordered adjustments and the verification of disputed claims.

The governor, who appeared before the Senate County Public Accounts Committee at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi on Monday, said addressing the inherited debt required establishment of a verification committee to scrutinise the entire outstanding amount and establish the validity of the claims.

“The reduction of Nairobi County pending bills by Sh 43.73 billion was not achieved entirely through cash payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court-ordered reductions and disputed claims,” said Sakaja.

He told the Senate Committee chaired by Homa Bay Senator Moses Kajwang that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors and that he had constituted a committee to undertake an internal verification of the entire amount before payments were done.

Sakaja explained that the verification established that the reduction was not solely through payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court decisions and disputed claims.

“I would like to inform Senators that my administration has provided a detailed schedule accounting for the Sh43.73 billion pending bills reduction through adjustments and reconciliations,” he said.

The governor said that of this amount Sh1.63 billion related to legal assessments, while Sh19.14 billion represented government-guaranteed loans whose servicing had been suspended due to a lack of supporting documentation and loan schedules.

Sakaja told Senators that Sh19.2 billion related to LAPFUND interest and penalties which the County said had been reduced following a court consent that brought the claim down to approximately Sh8.2 billion.

He said that they had provided a signed indemnity form, in accordance with County Treasury rules governing misplaced payment documents, alongside a financial memo confirming that the works had been undertaken and payment made.

“The audit further raised concerns over Sh16.04 million in receivables from non-exchange transactions, which lacked sufficient supporting documentation,” said Sakaja.

The governor told senators that beyond the verification of pending bills his administration had also strengthened the county’s legal department to reduce expenditure on external legal services and protect public resources.

Sakaja noted that through the reforms, Nairobi saved approximately Sh8.48 billion in legal costs over two financial years by expanding its in-house legal capacity, handling more litigation internally and negotiating reductions in legal fees claimed by private advocates.

According to the County Assembly’s Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, of the 174 court cases concluded during the period under review, 84 were handled by the County’s in-house legal team, with 47 determined in Nairobi’s favour, representing a 56 per cent success rate.

Kajwang, commended the County for reducing its pending bills but asked the Governor to provide additional documentation supporting the payments and processes undertaken to account for the Sh43.73 billion reductions.

“The Senate County Public Accounts Committee requires further clarification on the verification exercise and the adjustments made to the outstanding debt,” said Kajwang.

World.title: Gachagua dismisses opposition divisions as 'polygamous family' rivalry
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County on November 8, 2026. [Peterson Githaiga, Standard]

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has dismissed claims of divisions within the Opposition, describing the disagreements among its leaders as normal sibling rivalry in a polygamous family, while insisting that the coalition remains united behind plans to field a single presidential candidate in the 2027 General Election.

Gachagua said the Opposition leaders were committed to working together to challenge President William Ruto, despite their differing opinions on the timing of selecting a joint presidential flagbearer and occasional disagreements among their political camps.

Speaking during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County, the former Deputy President likened the political differences to children from the same father competing for attention but eventually uniting whenever an external threat emerges.

“The Opposition is united to a man, and we have agreed that we will have a single presidential candidate. Everybody is committed, and we talk on a daily basis. The only challenge is normal petty problems,” he said.

He added that the disagreements should not be interpreted as a breakdown of the coalition, maintaining that such differences were healthy and expected in a broad political alliance.

“Ile shida kidogo ni ya boma, watoto wengi wa baba mmoja. Watoto huko ndani, oh, baba anakupenda kuliko mimi. Mbona ulinunua kiatu kabla mimi? Si hiyo ni kawaida kwa polygamous family?” he posed.

Gachagua said the bigger threat to Opposition unity was not necessarily disagreements among its principals but the conduct of their supporters, social media influencers and political bloggers, whom he accused of fuelling unnecessary tensions through insults and online confrontations.

He cautioned Opposition leaders against allowing overzealous supporters to dictate their political relationships, warning that unchecked political attacks could eventually weaken the coalition and undermine its common objective.

“If there is anything to separate us, it is our supporters and social media bloggers. Wanawakisha moto hakuna, watu wangu na wa Matiang'i wanatukanana na sisi tunakula breakfast pamoja,” he said.

He further claimed that some political influencers associated with his DCP party had been recruited and allegedly paid by individuals opposed to him to attack his leadership and the party.

Gachagua urged coalition principals to exercise restraint and avoid reacting to every provocation from supporters, insisting that political leaders must remain focused on the bigger picture.

“I want to ask leaders in the Opposition, be careful. Don't listen to overzealous supporters and influencers; they will lead you astray. Remain focused,” he warned.

On the question of selecting a joint presidential candidate, Gachagua revealed that differences remained over the appropriate timing, with Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka proposing that the flagbearer be identified before December, while Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna favoured February and Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua suggested May.

Gachagua, however, argued that selecting a candidate too early could expose the individual to political pressure and possible frustration from the government.

He proposed April next year as a more suitable time, maintaining that the coalition was united on the principle of having one candidate even if its leaders differed on the timing.

The DCP leader also dismissed arguments that academic qualifications, experience or political credentials should determine who becomes the coalition's presidential candidate, insisting that electoral numbers and the support of ordinary Kenyans would ultimately decide.

“As others say they have experience and an agenda in the Opposition, the deciding factor is the numbers. I'm with the people. You say you have capacity, but the person to decide is the voter,” he said.

He added: “Akili nyingi ni nzuri, but bila kura unaweza kaa nayo nyumbani.”

World.title: Mudavadi urges Western Kenya to unite, says region cannot remain on sidelines
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Prime CS Musalia Mudavadi. [File, Standard]

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi has urged Western Kenya to unite ahead of the 2027 General Election, saying the region must strengthen its political representation to have a greater say in national decision-making.

Speaking during a UDA delegates' meeting in Shitoto village, Mumias East, Kakamega County, he said Western Kenya could not afford to remain on the sidelines while decisions affecting the country were being made.

"2027 is the moment we must change the narrative. We must make sure that we are at the table where decisions are made. We cannot afford to remain spectators when the future of our country and our region is being determined," he said.

Mudavadi said parliamentary influence depended on numbers, arguing that electing more MPs would give the region a stronger voice in key parliamentary committees, including the Budget Committee.

"Parliament exercises authority in its own right. We want more MPs so that we can have a say in the Budget Committee and other important committees. These positions are secured through numbers, and numbers matter when decisions affecting the country are being made," he said.

Turning to the opposition, Mudavadi described its leaders as divided and challenged them to present clear manifestos outlining what they would offer Kenyans.

He said the divisions within the opposition would work in President William Ruto's favour as he seeks re-election in 2027, expressing confidence that he would win in the first round.

"We want Ruto to win without a petition. We want to thrash them in the first round," he said.

World.title: Family identifies two security officers involved in Abshir Abdi abduction
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

LSK president Charles Kanjama leads members in a protest over the disappearance of lawyer Abshir Abdi. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

The family of Nairobi lawyer Abshir Ahmedsadak Abdi has identified two security officers alleged to have taken part in their kin's abduction, even as his colleagues threatened mass protests to push for his release.

The Law Society of Kenya (LSK) said the two names have been forwarded to the police to aid in investigations and demanded that the office of the Inspector General of Police, Douglas Kanja, speed up the probe into the abduction.

"One is named Siad and the other is Hussein, and we want them released for investigation, arrest, prosecution, conviction, sentencing and imprisonment," said LSK.

The revelation came during a demonstration led by (LSK outside the office of the Deputy Inspector General of Police and other towns yesterday .

Abshir was forcibly taken on November 1 along Muchai Road, his vehicle was pursued and intercepted by armed individuals in two vehicles before he was seized.

While state security agencies have denied holding him in custody, court filings and colleagues suggest his abduction may be connected to his professional work representing clients in high-profile cases involving senior police officers.

Furthermore, the LSK presented additional names of security personnel linked to the incident, demanding immediate legal action against Chief Inspector Vitalis Kibet, Inspector Kennedy Kimani Karanja, Siad Mohammed, Abdurahman of the Anti-Terrorism Police Unit (ATPU), and KDF officer Ali Hussein.

The leadership voiced their frustration over the state's inaction and the alarming pattern of extrajudicial actions targeting officers of the court. Representatives insisted that lawyers must be allowed to execute their duties without fear of intimidation, torture, or abduction.

"We demand that the officers involved be handed over, arrested, prosecuted, and convicted. We will stand in the courts, in the streets, and in the boardrooms until abductions come to an end," they said in a statement.

The LSK has issued a stern ultimatum to the police command, including the president, DIG Gilbert Masengeli, Inspector General Douglas Kanja, and senior commanders. If Abshir is not released safely and the identified suspects are not formally charged in court by Monday, the LSK warned it will initiate private prosecutions itself.

Furthermore, the society threatened to bring activities to a complete shutdown and demand the immediate resignation of Kanja, Masingeli and Minister for Security Kipchumba Murkomen, carrying their demonstrations to Parliament and State House if necessary.

As court proceedings continue under a habeas corpus application at the Milimani High Court, the legal fraternity remains resolute: the protest at Jogoo House is merely the beginning of an unyielding campaign for justice and the rule of law.

In Nakuru, lawyers protested within the Law Courts, calling for his production.

“It is shocking that one of our colleagues was picked and today we do not know where he is. Unless we voice our concern, there will be complete lawlessness in the country,” said LSK member Ekaterina Handa. “Our lives matter and silencing lawyers is silencing justice. we will not relent until we get justice.”

Rift Valley LSK Chair Wangari Mwangi said it was shocking that the alleged abduction was captured on CCTV.

She rubbished the narrative that the missing lawyer was involved in a crime syndicate, maintaining that he should have been arrested and charged in court. [Additional reporting by Daniel Chege]

World.title: Goon financiers should be cursed and sent to hell, Chief Justice Koome says
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Chief Justice Martha Koome said goonism falls under serious organised crimes that goes against the Rome Statute and humanity. [Phares Mutembei, Standard]

Chief Justice Martha Koome now says those mobilising and financing goons should be cursed and thrown to hell.

Koome on Thursday said goonism falls under organised serious crimes that go against the Rome Statute and humanity.

She spoke at Kieganguru, Maara constituency, where she presided over the opening of the Maara law courts.

While calling on police to focus more on arresting the mobilisers and financiers, Koome said a time has come for the country to plead with God to protect the country and rescue the youth who are being misused and misled into organised gangs and goonism.

“Nobody gives birth to a child to be called a goon. Those organisers will go to hell, we curse them,” Koome said, adding, “If they will not go to hell they will meet God's justice. These are our children, and we reclaim them in the name of our Lord Jesus.”

According to her, the last time she checked, people are charged at the International Criminal Court with Organised crime.

She maintained that the best solution to the current goonism that wreaked havoc, especially in political meetings, is to arrest the organisers.

Koome said the courts cannot hold arrested goons without bail, yet the constitution grants them the right to bail or bond.

“When we arrest small people with petty crimes of causing disorder, the law allows us to release them on bail and bond, but when you bring the organisers, we will charge them under the Serious Crimes Act,” she said.

Koome said currently, the judiciary has gazetted a serious crimes division at the High Court to support Magistrates handling the cases.

“Let us look at the root cause of goonism across the country and rehabilitate those involved by getting them gainful employment,” she said.

Her sentiments, however, differ from those of Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen, who on Wednesday told the National Assembly that the judiciary was the weakest link in the fight against the menace.

Tharaka Nithi Governor Muthomi Njuki, in his remarks, supported Koome’s view of arresting the planners.

Njuki, who doubles up as the Council of Governors Chairperson, said politicians have had their time and organising goons against their opponents should not be condoned.

Using the analogy of a dog, Njuki said ‘every barking dog has an owner ’, and it is time serious action was taken against such characters at whatever level they are.

The county boss said CoG will work closely with county security teams to arrest the fast-rising menace and report all cases.

Security agencies have been under scrutiny regarding goons, with calls for their arrest and prosecution.

Earlier on, Koome and DCI boss Mohammed Amin differed on how to handle the goons during a National Council for Administrative Justice meeting as with the DCI boss also accusing the Judiciary of laxity and granting minor bail to arrested goons.

But Koome maintained the issue must be addressed lest it becomes a thorn in the flesh ahead of the 2027 elections.

World.title: IEBC warns UDA SG Hassan Omar over remarks on deceased voters
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

UDA Secretary General Hassan Omar meets Village Elders and Mabalozi wa Nyumba Kumi from Jomvu Sub-County’ on September 10, 2026. [Nehemiah Okwemba, Standard]

The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has issued a stern warning to Senator Hassan Omar after finding him in breach of the Electoral Code of Conduct over remarks he made at a political rally in Mombasa, cautioning that any repeat offence could attract tougher sanctions.

In a determination released on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, the Electoral Code of Conduct Enforcement Committee (ECCEC) found Omar guilty of breaching paragraphs 6(k)(i) and 6(l) of the Electoral Code of Conduct.

The committee consequently issued the senator with a formal and strict warning and severe caution, directing him to comply with the electoral regulations for the remainder of the applicable election period.

Omar was further instructed to refrain from language or conduct that could reasonably be understood as encouraging or normalising electoral malpractice or undermining public confidence in the integrity of the ballot.

The decision follows investigations into remarks the senator allegedly made during a public rally in Mombasa on September 11, 2026, which raised concerns over the possibility of encouraging electoral malpractice.

According to the commission, Omar was summoned to appear before the committee on October 21, 2026, to respond to the allegations. He honoured the summons and appeared in person, accompanied by his lawyer, where he was given an opportunity to explain his remarks and present his defence.

In reaching its determination, the committee considered the context in which the statements were made, Omar's explanation that his words were intended figuratively to encourage voter registration and participation, his subsequent clarification and the absence of evidence linking the remarks to an actual electoral incident.

However, the committee maintained that the language used could not be excused by the explanation offered.

It observed that the impugned words, considered in their original Kiswahili form and ordinary meaning, invoked the use of biometric identification details belonging to a deceased person to facilitate voting in that individual's name.

The committee consequently found the remarks inconsistent with the obligation under paragraph 6(l) of the Electoral Code to reassure voters about the integrity of the ballot.

The warning places Omar on clear notice that any recurrence of similar conduct could attract more severe sanctions under the Electoral Code of Conduct and applicable laws.

“The determination places Hon. Hassan Omar on clear and unequivocal notice that the warning issued by the Committee is intended to mark a firm boundary against any recurrence of similar conduct,” IEBC stated.

The commission further emphasised that political leaders and other electoral stakeholders have a constitutional right to campaign, criticise, debate, persuade and participate in political discourse.

However, it cautioned that political expression must be exercised responsibly, warning that statements perceived as advocating, encouraging or normalising electoral malpractice could undermine public confidence in the electoral process.

“As Kenya prepares for the 2027 General Election, the Commission calls upon all political leaders, candidates, political parties, supporters and other electoral stakeholders to exercise responsibility, restraint and vigilance in their public utterances and conduct,” the commission said.

The determination comes as political activities gradually intensify ahead of the 2027 General Election, with the electoral body seeking to strengthen compliance with regulations governing political campaigns and public conduct.

IEBC maintained that enforcement of the Electoral Code should not be interpreted as an attempt to suppress legitimate political competition or freedom of expression.

Instead, it said the measures were intended to safeguard democratic participation and ensure that every Kenyan could exercise their right to vote without intimidation, manipulation or interference.

The commission reiterated its commitment to protecting the sanctity of the ballot, assuring Kenyans that every vote must be protected and counted in accordance with the law.

It warned that it would continue enforcing electoral regulations firmly, fairly and without fear or favour, as preparations for the 2027 elections gather momentum.

World.title: Israel faces political chaos as Netanyahu’s grip on power weakens. What will it take to end the disarray?
World.content:
The wheels of Israel’s political machine are turning. But that doesn’t mean they’re going anywhere soon.

In the latest elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lost the parliamentary majority that kept him in power over the past four years. But his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, still faces a difficult task in unseating Israel’s longest-serving leader after being tasked with forming the next government.

On paper, Eisenkot has a clear majority, with 67 of 120 seats in Israel’s legislature, the Knesset. But those seats come from six ideologically diverse parties, from right-wing to Arab parties. That’s the challenge that Eisenkot, a neophyte politician, must address as he aims for the premiership: how to make these parties cooperate to both support him and help him govern.

For decades, Netanyahu commanded the loyalty of the political parties within his bloc. Even if they challenged him, he was adept at managing the disagreements and holding his coalition together.

Eisenkot has no such experience, and though he has veteran politicians within his bloc, he must now find a way to lead them toward a common goal: forming a government to replace Netanyahu.

Parliament members attend the Knesset opening ceremony. Ronen Zvulun/Reuters

How is a government normally formed?

In most elections in Israel – and in just about any parliamentary democracy – one party emerges with the clear backing of a majority of the parliament. In Israel’s Knesset, that amounts to at least 61 out of 120 seats. The leader of that party becomes the prime minister.

After the 2022 election, Netanyahu emerged with 64 seats. He then gained four more seats when an additional party joined his coalition. That gave him a commanding 68-seat majority, and the government lasted its entire term for the first time since 1988.

Netanyahu now has only 46 lawmakers supporting him, leaving him far short of the majority needed to govern. Eisenkot has 67 seats backing him, but it gets complicated because not all of those parties have agreed to work together.

Could Israel get a government that doesn’t have a parliamentary majority?

The election produced a complicated deadlock, leaving neither side with a clear path to forming a government.

Netanyahu’s 53-seat pre-election bloc shrank to 46 seats in the 120-seat Knesset after United Torah Judaism, an ultra-Orthodox party long loyal to the prime minister, declined to support him. The opposition won 67 seats, but 19 of those belong to the two Arab parties – the Joint List and Raam. That makes them pivotal to any attempt to replace Netanyahu.

However, many Jewish Israelis, including some of those opposed to Netanyahu, do not consider the Arab parties to be legitimate partners. Still, the Arab parties could support what’s called a minority government from the outside, providing it with a parliamentary safety net.

A demonstration by right-wing protesters outside the Israeli parliament in Jerusalem on Tuesday. Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images

A minority government holds fewer than the 61 parliamentary seats needed to support a stable coalition but remains in power after securing the backing of Knesset members who don’t sit in the cabinet. Israeli law requires only a simple majority to install a government, so a government can take office if its opponents are divided and abstain from voting. Removing one is harder: It requires a constructive majority of more than half the lawmakers who support an alternative government.

Gadi Eisenkot’s plan is to form what he calls a “national emergency government”: a minority government made of the four Jewish opposition parties, which together hold 48 seats: his own Yashar, Together – led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid; Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, and the left-wing Democrats, led by Yair Golan. The Arab parties wouldn’t be part of the coalition but would guarantee majority parliamentary support to keep it in power, in exchange for various concessions.

Israel has had minority governments in the past, but never immediately after an election. Yitzhak Rabin’s second government became a minority government after the ultra-Orthodox Shas party left his coalition in 1993. The government survived two more years with support from outside Arab parties.

Another possible variable is seeking the support of United Torah Judaism (UTJ), an ultra-Orthodox party. Though it is a traditional ally of Netanyahu, the party refused to recommend him during the post-election presidential consultations, opening a possibility that it could abstain from voting or even support an Eisenkot-led minority government, widening his safety net beyond the Arab parties. But it would likely demand concessions from Eisenkot.

Avigdor Liberman, leader of the Yisrael Beiteinu party, speaks to the media at at the Knesset on Tuesday. Kobi Wolf/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Who is blocking Eisenkot’s plan and could the ultra-Orthodox parties become kingmakers?

Eisenkot’s main obstacle now is Avigdor Liberman. The former minister of defense, foreign affairs and finance refuses to join any government dependent on the Arab parties, arguing that a minority government will be short-lived and will only strengthen Netanyahu.

Instead, he is proposing a different route: a 61-seat coalition that includes the ultra-Orthodox parties and excludes the Arab parties. He believes that once it is formed, some lawmakers from Netanyahu’s Likud party could defect.

Liberman has dropped his longstanding veto on the ultra-Orthodox parties, but his plan collides with one of the opposition’s core commitments: ending the blanket draft exemption for ultra-Orthodox men from mandatory military service. The ultra-Orthodox parties want to entrench that exemption, while Eisenkot, Liberman and others campaigned for universal service. Any deal would require a major ideological concession, and still appears distant, as Shas remains loyal to Netanyahu, even as UTJ signals an opening.

Liberman’s strategy risks undermining Eisenkot’s minority-government route, but the two are coordinating their next moves. Even before forming a government, the opposition plans to use its parliamentary majority to take control of the Knesset by replacing Netanyahu’s appointed speaker and other parliamentary officeholders, then begin advancing legislation.

Could Eisenkot and Netanyahu share power in a unity government?

Netanyahu has been applying heavy pressure against any Jewish-Arab political cooperation. In recent days, he has released two videos calling for a “national unity government.” But he only wants it on his terms: he insists on remaining prime minister and including his entire right-wing and ultra-Orthodox bloc.

Unity governments are traditionally formed by Israel’s two largest parties following a political deadlock. After the 1984 elections, Labor’s Shimon Peres and Likud’s Yitzhak Shamir famously governed together and shared the premiership under a rotation agreement. After the 1988 elections, they joined forces again.

Netanyahu has also led two such arrangements recently. In 2020, during the Covid crisis and after three inconclusive elections, Benny Gantz joined him for an emergency government. Gantz was supposed to take over and become prime minister after 18 months. But Netanyahu looked for a way out before stepping aside, forcing new elections by refusing to pass a state budget.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his wife Sara Netanyahu at the Knesset on Tuesday. Ronen Zvulun/Reuters

After the October 7, 2023 attack, Gantz and Eisenkot joined a war cabinet. The two resigned after eight months, citing frustration with Netanyahu’s handling of the Gaza war and lack of strategy.

Eisenkot has rejected Netanyahu’s national unity rhetoric as a “pathetic spin.” If Netanyahu genuinely wants to cooperate, he said, he should break with his extremist partners and join a government led by Eisenkot.

While Netanyahu appears unwilling to separate from his entire bloc, some analysts believe he may eventually be willing to part ways with National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, but not with Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and the ultra-orthodox parties. So far, he has given no indication he would make such a concession, and the opposition sees his unity appeals mainly as a tactic to undermine a government that could replace him.

Can Netanyahu still hold on?

For now, he remains in office as caretaker prime minister until a new government is sworn in.

Eisenkot has 28 days from last Sunday to negotiate with his bloc over cabinet posts, budgets and policies. He can ask for a 14-day extension. If he fails, the mandate passes to another candidate for 28 days.

If Netanyahu gets the mandate, he will likely try to lure a party or individual lawmakers from the opposition to join his bloc. Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman, and Golan have all declared they will not join him. With his bloc eight seats short, Netanyahu would need eight individual defectors, setting a high bar.

But time is on his side. If he fails, the mandate returns to the Knesset for another 14 days to try and suggest another candidate. If that fails as well, the political deadlock will lead Israel to another round of elections. During that period, Netanyahu would remain as caretaker prime minister.

World.title: AI data center opponents are cheering midterm results, but they say the fight isn’t over
World.content:
New York —

Texas resident Maggie Elizabeth Hill stayed up late on election night to watch the midterm results trickle in. But she was up early again the next morning, already thinking about how she could work with the state’s newly elected Democratic leaders to slow the development of AI data centers.

“I was so excited with the results,” said Hill, who earlier this year formed the data center watchdog group Don’t Drain Texas to help rural communities push back on data center projects. “I started brainstorming like, what can the lieutenant governor do? What are our routes to success here?”

The rapid buildout of AI data centers became a central issue in the months leading up to the midterms. Grassroots campaigns cropped up in communities nationwide, raising concerns about the local implications of massive new AI data center projects. Much of the resistance also served as an outlet for general distrust of AI and frustration with the power and wealth of tech billionaires.

Like Hill, data center opponents across the country see last week’s election results — where a staggering wave of populist, Democratic candidates won even in typically red stronghold areas — as a referendum on the issue and a significant win for their movement. They say concerns about AI data centers hiking electricity costs, harming the environment and impacting the livability of nearby communities drove members of their communities to the polls.

Nationwide, about a quarter of American voters said AI and data centers were “crucial” to their vote in the midterms, CNN’s Voter Poll found. When asked about building data centers in their communities, voters were opposed by a roughly 3-to-1 margin.

But data center opponents say the fight isn’t over.

Now, they will work to hold these newly elected officials accountable for their promises to rein in or put new guardrails around data center construction — or push them to take even harder lines. Many are seeking moratoriums on data center construction, but some simply want more transparency and greater benefits for nearby residents baked into the development process.

“I am an independent, and I definitely voted with… data centers at the top of my list, and I know so many people who are from rural communities who traditionally vote Republican who said that this was flipping them,” Hill told CNN.

A key election issue

Multiple candidates succeeded in tough races after making data centers central to their campaigns, including Democratic Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Annie Andrews of South Carolina. Democrats pulled off a massive upset in Hill’s state of Texas, winning the state’s high-profile Senate race and unseating Republican incumbents for governor and lieutenant governor.

“When the politicians stop speaking for the people or being responsive to the people, you’re going to see a recalibration, and I believe that happened certainly” in the midterms, said Nick Owens, an attorney who founded Conserve Ohio, a group that opposes large data center construction.

An aerial view of a data center on October 18, 2026, in Springfield, Ohio. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images A resident holds their notes while speaking against a proposed natural gas power plant that would be used to power a data center under construction during a public meeting in Ashville, Ohio, on August 19, 2026. Jessica Phelps/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Owens, a lifelong Republican and delegate for President Donald Trump at the 2024 Republican National Convention, added that Democrats “1,000%” did a better job speaking to voters about data centers ahead of the election. Meanwhile, GOP candidates had to contend with a link to Trump, who has dismissed concerns around data centers as a “hoax” and said communities who oppose them must want to be “backwards and poor.”

In Ohio, Democratic Gov.-elect Amy Acton ran on a “conditional moratorium” on data center development, which would require developers to cover energy generation costs and commit to transparency measures, among other guardrails, to have their projects approved.

But Owens said his group would push her to go further — using New York Gov. Kathy Hochul’s one-year moratorium on new AI data center construction in her state as a model. He’s also hopeful that Brown could contribute to progress on federal legislation around data centers, given his previous experience in the Senate.

‘Our fight doesn’t change’

Across the country, many activists oppose data centers because they want to preserve their community’s land and natural resources. That’s what motivates Nancy Thellman, whose family farm in an agricultural part of Douglas County, Kansas, is around a 15-minute drive away from a proposed hyperscale data center project.

“We have people who are trying so hard to keep their farms, to keep their skills, to keep the next generation on the farm, so that food can be grown,” Thellman said. She’s concerned about “data centers coming in and taking vast swaths of prime farmland out of production for a purpose that is not entirely understood or known for the future.”

Thellman and her grassroots group, the Douglas County Data Center Watchdogs, are optimistic that the election results in Kansas will give them a greater shot at pushing state legislators to revise or rescind controversial state Senate Bill 98, which passed last year, giving tax exemptions to data center developers.

Kansas last week elected its first Democratic senator in more than 90 years, as well as a Democratic attorney general. Democrat Cindy Holscher is in the lead for governor as the final votes are counted.

A view of a field with a sign against the construction of a data center in Leavenworth County, Kansas, on November 3, 2026. Nathan Howard/Reuters

Holscher, formerly a state senator, was among those who approved Senate Bill 98. But Thellman said she discussed the issue with Holscher during a cold campaign call from the gubernatorial candidate and was convinced the politician had changed her view. Holscher’s campaign site calls for a pause on data center development until more guardrails can be put in place and states that “big corporations don’t deserve taxpayer handouts.”

“She saw the error in that vote, and she made it very clear that should she be governor, she would place a statewide moratorium on data center development until reasonable guardrails could be put up,” Thellman said. “She was a politician who is brave enough and wise enough to change her mind and promise to legislate in a different way… We’ll hold her to it.”

Danielle Ray, lead organizer with the Louisville, Kentucky-based advocacy group No Data Center 502, told CNN that “our fight doesn’t change” following the election, although Democrats flipped nine seats in the statehouse. The group is fighting to stop a more than 1 million-square-foot data center project in the city.

“I believe that this has been part of the reason that some of the seats have been flipped in Kentucky,” Ray said. “But I think our concern is that it might cause folks to relax or think that the fight is over just because you know Democrats won (the) majority across the country.”

World.title: The trap in Trump’s Hegseth defense
World.content:
Deep into President Donald Trump’s news conference Monday, it became obvious why he’s so adamant in backing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth amid an impeachment storm.

Ultimately, Trump is defending himself.

To jettison the former Fox News anchor now would be to admit that the Iran war — of which Hegseth is the administration’s most vehement proponent — was a mistake. A sacking would also undermine Trump’s attempt to recast what is at best an inconclusive military adventure and at worst a strategic disaster.

Trump delivered his most forceful endorsement yet of Hegseth on Monday just after the president’s arch-foe, Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, introduced eight articles of impeachment against the defense secretary in the House. His vote of confidence came in another surreal public appearance that he described as a “little fun” as he again offered Ultimate Fighting Championship czar Dana White the job of press secretary, then said he was “sort of kidding.”

“But really, what has Hegseth done?” Trump asked reporters. “He won the war. He was in charge. He won the war in Venezuela, as I said, (in) 48 minutes. It was flawless. Nobody killed. And he certainly — I think he’s won the war in Iran, but he’s certainly winning the war.”

The special forces raid that extracted President Nicolás Maduro was daring and dangerous, but it was hardly a war. And the idea that the US has won in Iran — at least in a strategic sense — is questionable.

But Hegseth on Tuesday portrayed everything that his department had done as a massive success. He lavished praise on Trump and new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller at a press conference at the Pentagon. The defense secretary argued that Trump’s opponents had twice tried to eject the president from office (via first-term impeachments) and are now coming for him.

“Now they’re trying a third time, this time against a member of his Cabinet. They will fail again, and if standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week,” Hegseth said.

Hegseth is the Cabinet official most like Trump

President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth react during a cabinet meeting in the Cabinet Room at the White House on May 27. Evan Vucci/Reuters

Even before the defense secretary’s move Tuesday to make himself inseparable from Trump, there are political reasons why a president who is retreating into an ever-smaller inner circle may be loath to let him go.

The Pentagon chief is the Cabinet member who has most consciously succeeded in replicating Trump’s political id. He dared to kick the press out of the Pentagon; wages culture wars and anti-woke crusades; and seems determined to wear impeachment as a badge of honor. If Trump rejected the man who rebranded the Pentagon the “Department of War,” he’d be trashing his own brand.

Yet as he raged at the perceived unfairness of Hegseth’s position in the White House Briefing Room, Trump also highlighted a political trap closing around him. He’s fighting the last political battle: Millions of midterms voters just rebuked his war and his confrontational politics. By digging in, he may make his plight worse.

Both Trump and Hegseth seem to be living in their own chosen reality amid a war in which a smaller, less powerful, repressive regime has survived the US superpower onslaught. The war has cost tens of billions of dollars and counting; alienated US allies in the Gulf; and triggered an energy and cost of living crisis.

The president said on Sunday’s edition of CBS’ “60 Minutes” that he “wouldn’t change a thing” about the conflict. Hegseth told reporters Monday that he’d be happy to “litigate … the success” of administration military operations “all day long.”

Trump’s claims that he’s eradicated Iran’s nuclear program for good may take years to fully evaluate. But continuing to argue to voters that a war they hate is a triumph seems like an endlessly losing political proposition.

Massie lashes out at Hegseth

Rep. Thomas Massie takes a question from a reporter during a news conference to discuss articles of impeachment he introduced against Hegseth outside the US Capitol on November 9. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Impeachment is the gravest constitutional fate that can befall a public official. At least it was, in the normal political world that seemed to disingtegrate once Trump took office. Hegseth is accused, among other things, of illegally waging war in Iran in violation of constitutional war powers restrictions; of ignoring laws designed to mitigate civilian casualties; and of abusing his powers by overseeing “extrajudicial killings” against alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific.

Each of the articles of impeachment — which also cover strikes in Yemen and the attempt to punish Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly for telling service members they can refuse illegal orders — raises a genuinely serious constitutional debate.

“The reality is we’re not indicting him for being bad at his job. In fact, he was very effective at killing schoolchildren in Iran,” Massie said. “He was very effective at extrajudicial killings. There’s no argument in these impeachment articles that he’s ineffective. The argument here is that he’s broken laws and he’s violated the Constitution.”

But in a sense, Trump is correct: This is a deeply political process.

A longtime Trump antagonist, Massie drew the president’s ire for his successful efforts to pass a law opening the Epstein files to public view. The president was instrumental in cutting short Massie’s political career by backing a MAGA primary rival. “He’s a sick, sick guy. There’s something wrong with him, actually,” Trump said Monday, blasting Massie as a “stone-cold loser.”

Massie returns the compliment. And he lampooned Hegseth in predicting how he’d respond in a rare news conference the defense secretary has called for Tuesday. “I hope he addresses the eight articles and doesn’t get up and misquote the Bible in Quentin Tarantino fashion and do some pull-ups and, you know, call everybody fat and gay, like for being for this impeachment,” Massie told reporters.

The timing of Massie’s impeachment drive is also significant. After the Republican midterm wipeout, it will allow aggrieved lame-duck GOP lawmakers to cast a revenge vote against Trump and the war that propelled the loss of their jobs. A sizable group of Republican defectors could undermine Hegseth’s authority and raise the costs to Trump of standing by him.

Democrats are just loving the spectacle.

“I’m a hard yes, as I’ve made clear, on the impeachment resolution,” House Minority Leader and likely next House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries said Monday. He mocked the Iran war plan as “Operation Epic Failure,” adding that “Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America’s national security. And he’s the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed gas prices on everyday Americans, made the country less safe.”

House Democrats would gleefully vote to impeach any Trump official. But they’ll have to walk a fine line in the new Congress as they try to avoid overreaching in their planned Trump investigations while honoring voters’ demands to ease the affordability crisis.

But the current impeachment, brought by a Republican, essentially gives Democrats a free vote and insulates them against any political downside of pursuing the issue themselves.

Hegseth’s gamble — and why he may not ultimately survive

Hegseth arrives to hold a briefing at the Pentagon in Washington, DC, in March. Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters

Hegseth’s news conference, however, was a risk. Together with his hyper-aggressive videos he’s released in his own defense — apparently to catch Trump’s eye — he may deepen disquiet about his performance among GOP House members and inadvertently make the case for his impeachment.

He seems safe from being ejected from office in the short term, since a two-thirds majority to convict seems unlikely in any Senate impeachment trial.

But a defense secretary who has angered both parties over the war won’t be out of the woods. On Monday, Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer, who serves on the Armed Services Committee, told reporters he didn’t back impeachment but added: “Whether he should keep his job or not is up to either him and his family or the president,” he said.

And Hegseth could prove to be a liability when Trump needs to get defense spending requests through a Democratic Congress.

Massie told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins on Monday that he believed there was “a high probability” that Hegseth wouldn’t make it to the end of the year in office.

“They stand by them, until the day they don’t,” Massie said, predicting that the new Congress would call in officials who’d served under Hegseth “who’ve seen some things and know some things that aren’t even public yet.”

Then there’s the war that won’t end.

Trump showed Monday he’s still got no plan for a permanent peace, veering between predictions of an imminent deal; claims that it was not a real war anyway; and a warning he was “locked and loaded and ready to go” for a new assault.

If he can’t extricate himself, the war will besmirch his final two years in office. But turning a political page would be tricky with Hegseth still at the Pentagon.

The defense secretary’s most perilous moment may therefore come not after impeachment but at the moment when Trump can best protect himself not by defending Hegseth, but by pitching him overboard.

The story and headline have been updated with additional information.

World.title: Trump envoys to meet Putin in Moscow after latest Ukraine talks end with no breakthrough
World.content:
President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner said Wednesday he and Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff would travel to Moscow after talks in Abu Dhabi to end the Ukraine war ended with no clear breakthrough.

“Steve and I are going to travel to Moscow tomorrow to meet with (Russian) President Putin to go over what was discussed today and to try to make more progress on some of the issues that we discussed because we see some openings and some opportunities there,” Kushner said at a news conference in the UAE capital.

The announcement comes after two days of talks between Russian, Ukrainian and American negotiators, as the Trump administration ramps up efforts to end the nearly five-year conflict.

In recent weeks, Trump has announced significant concessions to Moscow, causing consternation in European capitals.

Kushner said that he and Witkoff would try to finalize humanitarian relief and prisoner releases, as well as push to bring European countries into the talks – a multilateral format that Moscow has so far resisted.

The president’s son in law – who acts as one of the country’s top diplomats despite holding no official role within the Trump administration – said he and Witkoff would also travel to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and discuss peace proposals from the Abu Dhabi talks.

Delegations from Russia, Ukraine and the United States attend peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday aimed at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine. Ukrainian Foreign Intelligence press office

“We’re going to be with President Zelensky to debrief with him and further explore some of the ideas that we that we came up with here today,” Kushner continued.

Speaking about Wednesday’s talks, which concluded after less than two hours, top Russian negotiator Vladimir Medinsky gave little indication that Moscow’s demands had changed.

“In some areas, we reached a mutual understanding. In others, we did not. This conversation will, without a doubt, continue,” Medinsky said.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s foreign intelligence chief and top negotiator Rustem Umerov thanked the US envoys for their efforts while touting progress over certain issues, including security matters.

But it’s clear that sticking points remain between the two sides. Another Ukrainian negotiator, Davyd Arakhamia, said that Russia clearly came to the talks with “very strict directives.”

“I’m in this process since 2022 and I can fairly say that this was one of the toughest ones,” Arakhamia added.

World.title: Egyptian Tax authority collects LE 14 billion through tax risk-assessment system: Official
World.content:
The Head of the Egyptian Tax Authority (ETA), Rasha Abdel-Aal, announced that the tax risk-assessment system has generated approximately LE 14 billion, noting that the ETA received around 750,000 voluntary disclosures, which contributed to a total tax yield of LE97 billion.

Speaking at a seminar organized by the Journalists Syndicate, Abdel-Aal added that the Tax Authority is undergoing a shift in its operational philosophy and approach to tax-related challenges.

This transition moves the focus beyond mere revenue maximization toward achieving a balance between increasing public treasury resources, safeguarding the interests of the business community, and streamlining its interactions with the tax system, she said.

The tax risk-assessment system stands as a cornerstone of the development and digital transformation plan currently being implemented by the ETA to modernize tax administration and enhance collection efficiency.

An effective system

The system leverages big data analytics and artificial intelligence systems to electronically screen taxpayer files, classifying them based on their level of tax compliance—all without human intervention.

This represents a significant paradigm shift, effectively ending the era of random, comprehensive audits for every single file.

The system operates through network connectivity and data integration, linking the Tax Authority’s own databases—most notably the e-invoicing and e-receipt systems—with those of other government entities, including the Customs Authority, the Commercial Register, banks, and investment authorities.

Through this integration, the system compares the actual transaction volumes of companies and individuals against the data provided in their tax returns, automatically flagging any unexplained gaps or discrepancies that may indicate potential tax evasion or undisclosed business activities.

Based on the findings of this analysis, field inspection and tax audit teams are directed exclusively toward high-risk files.

This has proven highly effective in identifying thousands of instances of non-compliance and ensuring the accurate and prompt collection of state treasury revenues.

Conversely, this mechanism offers a significant advantage to compliant taxpayers by sparing them from burdensome, routine audit procedures and fostering a stable, fair business environment.

These measures coincide with a package of tax facilitations introduced by the Finance Ministry and Tax Authority, aimed at building trust with the business community.

This policy seeks to encourage taxpayers—including those operating in the informal sector—to proactively file their tax returns and voluntarily regularize their tax status in order to benefit from the offered facilitations.

Furthermore, it aims to integrate the informal economy into the state’s formal system, thereby ensuring tax equity and bolstering the resources of the national economy.

World.title: Health Minister discusses training of Palestinian medical staff in Egyptian hospitals
World.content:
Health and Population Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar discussed with his Palestinian counterpart Majed Abu Ramadan ways to strengthen cooperation across all healthcare sectors and agreed on a plan to transfer Egypt’s expertise and experience to the Palestinian health sector, while continuing to provide humanitarian support to the Palestinian people.

During the meeting, Abdel Ghaffar underscored the deep-rooted fraternal ties between Egypt and Palestine, reaffirming Egypt’s commitment to providing all forms of support to help the Palestinian people through their current crisis.

For his part, the Palestinian health minister praised Egypt’s efforts and its humanitarian stance toward Palestine.

Health Ministry Spokesperson Hossam Abdel Ghaffar said the meeting saw an agreement on establishing a mechanism to receive Palestinian doctors from various specialties for training at Egyptian hospitals. The two sides also discussed the possibility of supplying the Palestinian side with ambulances equipped with the latest medical equipment.

The meeting also addressed telemedicine, describing it as an increasingly urgent technology for the Gaza Strip to speed up patient diagnoses and determine appropriate treatment, in addition to supporting cancer care and pharmaceutical supplies.

World.title: FM highlights food security as pillar of international peace, stability at G7 meeting
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty said food security is a fundamental pillar of international peace and stability, warning that conflicts, geopolitical tensions, climate change and disruptions to global supply chains are driving up food prices and placing mounting pressure on developing countries.

He outlined Egypt’s national efforts to strengthen food security by boosting agricultural production, diversifying import sources and upgrading storage and distribution systems.

Abdelatty made the remarks on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, while delivering a keynote address at a session on food security under the theme “Stability in the Middle East,” held as part of the G7 ministerial meeting in Paris.

The session brought together the foreign ministers of France, the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Germany, Italy and Japan, as well as the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy and the foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Brazil and South Korea.

Abdelatty said the region was beset by multiple conflicts and stressed that political solutions, dialogue and diplomacy were the only way forward, ruling out military solutions to these disputes.

He pointed to the catastrophic situation in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, Israel’s restrictions on the entry of aid into Gaza and settler violence in the West Bank.

He stressed the need to ensure the regular flow of food commodities and agricultural production inputs, while safeguarding freedom of navigation through vital maritime routes. He also rejected the use of food as a means of political pressure or as a weapon in conflicts, underscoring the need to protect civilians and agricultural facilities and ensure the delivery of humanitarian assistance.

Abdelatty said Egypt’s hosting of the 18th Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD COP18) in 2028 would offer an opportunity to strengthen international cooperation in addressing drought and promoting the water-food nexus and land restoration, particularly in Africa.

He also stressed the importance of providing developing countries with the financing needed to adapt to climate change without imposing additional debt burdens on them.

The foreign minister warned that food security challenges were worsening in developing food-importing countries, particularly in Africa and the Arab region, as a result of conflicts, displacement and water scarcity.

Citing the situations in Gaza and Sudan, he said these crises were having severe repercussions for food supplies and livelihoods. He called for safe, adequate, regular and unhindered access for humanitarian aid, alongside efforts to restore domestic production capacity and rehabilitate infrastructure.

Abdelatty affirmed Egypt’s readiness to contribute to strengthening regional food security, drawing on its strategic location, infrastructure, ports, transport and logistics networks, grain storage facilities and food-processing capabilities. These assets, he said, could support global trade flows and the distribution of food commodities.

World.title: Suez Canal Marina receives first cruise ship in Ismailia
World.content:
Suez Canal Authority Chairman Osama Rabie announced, Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that the Suez Canal Yacht Marina in Ismailia has received passengers aboard the cruise ship ASTORIA GRANDE during its voyage to several Egyptian ports, as part of the authority’s efforts to promote maritime tourism.

In a statement, the authority said the visit marks the cruise ship’s first stop and berthing in Ismailia. The vessel transited the Suez Canal in the early hours of the day as part of the northbound convoy.

The ship is 193 meters long, 27.6 meters wide, has a draft of six meters and can accommodate up to 1,300 passengers. The visit is significant as the marina is being used for the first time as a tourist berth in Ismailia, providing a facility for receiving visitors and completing the necessary procedures in coordination with all relevant authorities.

Rabie said the Suez Canal Authority is seeking to strengthen the canal’s position as a key hub for maritime tourism and logistics services by developing its yacht marinas, equipping waiting areas and providing the infrastructure needed to berth cruise ships, while coordinating with the relevant authorities to facilitate procedures.

He added that the Suez Canal Yacht Marina represents a promising addition to the authority’s efforts to promote maritime and yacht tourism in the region. It offers an integrated package of services designed to boost tourism through organized domestic tour programs in Ismailia and outbound excursions to various governorates across Egypt.

The ship is scheduled to remain in Ismailia for 24 hours. During the stop, 335 tourists will visit local attractions, including the Suez Canal Museum, Ismailia Gardens, Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq Mosque and the Evangelical Church, among other landmarks.

Another 327 tourists will take part in an organized tour of Cairo, visiting major attractions including the Grand Egyptian Museum, the Giza Pyramids, Khan el-Khalili bazaar and Al-Muizz Street, as well as taking a Nile cruise.

Rabie said the ship’s itinerary includes several Egyptian ports. Its next stop will be Sharm El Sheikh, followed by Aqaba in Jordan and then Hurghada, before it transits the Suez Canal again on its return journey.

World.title: Liberia’s Judges Sound the Alarm on Their Own Courts
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia — In late August, two pregnant women walked out of Monrovia Central Prison, the overcrowded jail on the Atlantic shore that Liberians call South Beach. Kebbeh Pewee and Annie Kollie had been held there while awaiting the outcome of their cases.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Their release drew attention only because of who was in the same prison. Former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, jailed in Liberia’s largest-ever cocaine investigation, had met the women inside. Her office said she had helped pay for their freedom. The Ministry of Justice said a judge had already ordered them released.



Whichever account is right, the episode showed something that rarely makes headlines. For most Liberians caught up in the justice system, the problem is not a high-profile trial. It is waiting — for a hearing, a lawyer, a judge, a ruling — often without the money to make the wait shorter.

Now some of the people best placed to know are saying so in public: Liberia’s own judges.

Opening the November 2026 court term in counties across the country, several circuit judges used their formal addresses to warn that corruption, favouritism, political interference and delay are eating away at public trust in the courts.

‘No Judge Is Above the Constitution’

In Liberia, each quarterly court term opens with a formal speech, known as a “charge”, in which the presiding judge reflects on the state of justice. Most are ceremonial. This month’s were not.

In Zwedru, the capital of Grand Gedeh County near the border with Côte d’Ivoire, Circuit Judge J. Kennedy Peabody said that filling state jobs with relatives and fellow tribesmen, and punishing staff who disagree, is corruption even when no money changes hands. Then he turned to his own branch.

“No Minister is above the Constitution. No Superintendent is above the Constitution. No Judge is above the

Constitution,” he said. “We cannot condemn retaliation in government institutions while tolerating retaliation within the justice system.”

In Monrovia, Judge Roosevelt Z. Willie of Criminal Court ‘A’ asked whether Liberia had learned anything from the failures of its justice system before the 14-year civil war. He revisited a 2006 International Crisis Group report that listed corruption, unqualified judicial staff, poor pay and a system in which money and political influence decided how citizens were treated. “Any country that does not learn from its past is doomed to fail,” he warned.

In Grand Kru County, on the south-east coast, Judge Peter W. Gbeneweleh cautioned against what he called the commercialization of justice. When people believe the courts are for sale, he said, they turn to mob violence, revenge and other forms of self-help.

They were not the first. In August, Judge Onesimus Banwon of Criminal Court ‘A’ — the same judge who ordered the two pregnant women freed — described South Beach as dangerously overcrowded, “not primarily by convicted criminals, but by pre-trial detainees.”

At the Bottom of the Pile

Liberia’s Constitution says an arrested person must be brought before a court within 48 hours and is presumed innocent. The numbers tell a different story.

As of September 2026, 2,848 of the 4,125 people held in Liberia’s prisons — about 69 per cent — had never been tried, according to Betty M. Lamin-Blamo, the nominee for Minister of Justice, who gave the figures at her Senate confirmation hearing last month. Some had not even been indicted. At South Beach alone, 1,312 of roughly 1,888 inmates were awaiting trial.

“These figures fall hardest on the poor, who cannot afford a lawyer or a bond,” she told senators.

The U.S. State Department’s most recent human rights report on Liberia, released in August 2025, found that about 60 per cent of pretrial detainees were held for more than two terms of court — roughly 180 days — without a hearing. It reported that some judges used the possibility of bail to solicit bribes, and that some magistrates asked complainants for money to transport the accused to and from detention.

For the poor, relief often comes from charity rather than the state. In October, a legal aid clinic run by the United Methodist Church secured the release of 63 pretrial detainees from South Beach through the judiciary’s Magistrate Sitting Program, which sends magistrates to hear cases of people held without trial.

The same pattern runs through everyday disputes over debts, wages and, above all, land. Less than a quarter of Liberia’s land is formally registered, according to the Liberia Land Authority, and conflicting deeds are common. A family fighting to keep a plot of land can spend years in court.

The public has noticed.

Afrobarometer, the independent pan-African survey network, found in its most recent Liberia survey, released in May 2025, that 52 per cent of Liberians see widespread corruption among judges and magistrates. The Bertelsmann Transformation Index, a German assessment of governance worldwide, says in its 2026 report that Liberians widely see their courts as serving the rich, and that influence peddling regularly decides cases.

Questions for the Top of the System

The circuit judges spoke from the lower courts. Their warnings point upward, to the five-member Supreme Court and the leadership of the judiciary.

Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay took office in August 2025, promising to tackle inefficiency, corruption and malpractice in the courts. More than a year later, judges in his own system are saying publicly that those problems persist.

The clearest test of the Court’s authority remains unresolved. On April 16, 2026, a Supreme Court justice ordered the House of Representatives to halt proceedings against Yekeh Kolubah, an outspoken lawmaker. The next day, the House expelled him anyway.

The Court’s own marshal had delivered the order to the offices of the Speaker and the Chief Clerk, where a receptionist and a computer operator received it. In May, the justice in chambers ruled that the House had not been properly served. The full bench heard Kolubah’s appeal on October 22 and reserved its ruling. Seven months after the expulsion, the Court has yet to say clearly whether its own order was defied.

For ordinary Liberians, the lesson is uncomfortable. If the country’s highest court cannot make its own orders stick with the Legislature, what chance does a market trader have of enforcing a judgment against a well-connected landlord?

High-profile criminal cases have raised their own concerns. In July, a court set aside a jury’s acquittal of former Finance Minister Samuel D. Tweah after finding jury misconduct. The arson trial of former House Speaker J. Fonati Koffa ended in a mistrial after the jury was disbanded. Both episodes raised questions about how juries are chosen, protected and supervised.

The U.S. State Department’s 2026 Investment Climate Statement describes a Supreme Court buckling under the volume of appeals, and notes widespread reports that court officials solicit bribes to act on cases.

The make-up of the bench adds another layer. If justices retire at 70 as the Constitution requires, every seat on the Supreme Court will have been filled by President Joseph Boakai by the time Liberians vote in October 2029, or shortly after. Two seats, including the Chief Justice’s, are due to open in the election year itself. A bench appointed entirely by the sitting president could be asked to rule on disputes over that election.

The Price in Lost Investment

The judges’ warnings landed in the same month as a blunt verdict from Washington. The State Department’s 2026 Investment Climate Statement on Liberia, published in early November, calls corruption the main brake on the country’s democratic consolidation and economic growth.

The report says Liberia’s Commercial Court, which hears disputes of US$15,000 and above, is severely backlogged, with cases taking two to five years. Judgments are hard to enforce, especially against government bodies. It notes regular media reports of executive interference in judicial matters.

The cost is not limited to foreign boardrooms. Because collateral is so hard to recover through the courts, the report says, banks demand security worth 150 to 200 per cent of a loan and charge interest of 18 to 25 per cent. That makes credit scarce and expensive for the Liberian shopkeeper or farmer who wants to grow a business.

Foreign companies have found a way around the problem: they avoid Liberian courts altogether. Investment contracts with the government often require arbitration outside the country. A Liberian citizen has no such option.

Liberia’s economy grew 5.1 per cent in 2025. But the investors who bring that growth can take their disputes abroad. Most Liberians are left with the courts their own judges are now warning about.

A Question for 2029

President Boakai came to power in January 2024 promising to fight corruption and restore the rule of law. When Liberians vote in October 2029, the courts are likely to be part of how that promise is judged.

The government points to steps under way. The Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission is pushing for a specialized criminal court for corruption cases, and a proposed amendment would remove the statute of limitations on corruption prosecutions. The Justice Minister-designate has promised to review pretrial detention files nationwide. “The State will either prosecute or release,” she told senators, urging them to pass a bill extending the terms of circuit courts to clear the backlog.

The State Department calls these efforts “nascent”. The judges who spoke this month suggest the deeper problem is not a shortage of laws or programmes, but whether those who run the system — ministers, lawmakers and judges alike — will be held to the rules they enforce on others.

That question matters most at South Beach, where more than 1,300 people presumed innocent are still waiting for their day in court.

Judge Peabody ended his address in Zwedru with a warning meant for every official, including those on the bench. “The public office you occupy is not your inheritance,” he said. “The employees you supervise are not your personal servants. The public funds you administer are not your family wealth.”
