World.title: Boakai Seals City Hall Shake-up as FPA Reported; NPP Chairman Battling Jewel Taylor Lands Gov’t Job
World.content:
Monrovia — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has nominated James Kpadeh Mulbah, General Manager of the Roberts International Airport (RIA), as Mayor of the Monrovia City Corporation (MCC), confirming a FrontPageAfrica report published Monday that Mulbah was set to take over City Hall.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The outgoing mayor, John-Charuk Siafa, has not been shown the door. In the same round of appointments announced Wednesday, November 11, by the Executive Mansion, Siafa was named Officer-in-Charge of the National Insurance Corporation of Liberia (NICOL).



At NICOL, Siafa takes over from Abdullah S. Swaray, who had been holding over as Acting Managing Director. The President extended special appreciation to Swaray for his service, according to the statement signed by Presidential Press Secretary Atty. Kula B.N. Fofana.

What FPA Reported

On Monday, FrontPageAfrica reported that Mulbah was poised to replace Siafa after nearly three years of public criticism of the mayor’s handling of the capital — over piling garbage, unpaid workers and contractors, and allegations of financial irregularities at the MCC.

The report also highlighted Siafa’s long-running defense: that the national government had never given the city corporation the money it needs to do its job.

Mulbah’s nomination requires confirmation by the Liberian Senate, as Siafa’s did in 2024. The Executive Mansion said the nominations and appointments are subject to Senate confirmation where applicable.

From the Airport to City Hall

Mulbah was appointed General Manager of RIA by President Boakai on February 28, 2024. Before government, he was best known as founder and CEO of Green Cities Incorporated, a waste segregation and recycling enterprise.

His name is not new in the race for City Hall. In late 2023, before Boakai’s inauguration, the Liberia Solid Waste Management Association (LISWA) urged the then President-elect to make Mulbah mayor, pointing to his background in sanitation and waste management.

Mulbah joined the ruling Unity Party (UP) in December 2025. He told journalists at the time that the UP was the first political party he had ever joined and that the President’s stance against corruption was a major reason for his decision.

A Rocky Tenure

Siafa, nominated by President Boakai on January 27, 2024, and commissioned in March that year as Monrovia’s 28th mayor, succeeded Jefferson Tamba Koijee with promises to clean the city, restore transparency and depoliticize the MCC. He has been widely reported to be a close relative of the President.

Some of the sharpest attacks on his tenure came from within the ruling party. In September 2025, Queen Johnson, Deputy Director for Records at the National Port Authority and a staunch UP member, publicly called for Siafa’s dismissal, labeling him corrupt and incompetent. In March 2026, another UP loyalist publicly branded the mayor a criminal amid allegations tied to an audit of the MCC.

MCC contractors also protested in front of City Hall on UN Drive over unpaid wages, and civil society groups criticized the dismissal of civil servants as political retaliation.

The mayor had defenders. The Civil Society of Liberia (CSNL) dismissed the corruption claims as propaganda driven by suspended staff and credited Siafa with improving waste management. The MCC has also disputed FrontPageAfrica’s reporting on the deteriorating City Hall, insisting the mayor inherited the facility in ruins.

The Funding Gap Mulbah Inherits

At his first budget hearing in April 2024, Siafa told lawmakers the MCC needed US$11,023,583 to function, including about US$8.2 million from the national government. The 2024 draft budget allotted the MCC US$3,777,965.

The 2026 national budget allocated US$4.5 million to the MCC — still well short of that estimate. In March 2026, Assistant Minister for Development Planning Wellington Barchu pledged to champion dedicated funding for solid waste management in the 2027 budget.

Mulbah is likely to inherit the same dilemma: a capital that residents say is drowning in waste, and a city government that says it has never been given the means to clean it.

A Reward for the NPP Chairman?

The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau post appears to have gone to George Sylvester Mulbah, National Chairman of the National Patriotic Party (NPP), who has led the push to replace former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor at the head of the party. The Executive Mansion statement lists the appointee only as “Mr. George Mulbah,” Commissioner.

The appointment comes weeks before the NPP’s December convention. Earlier this month, Mulbah announced there would be no Standard Bearer election there; delegates would instead elect a “political leader.” A senior partisan told FrontPageAfrica that no such post exists in the party’s constitution or by-laws.

Mulbah also declared that every party official had lost tenure — a statement critics read as including Howard-Taylor, who has held the Standard Bearer post.

Howard-Taylor, Vice President from 2018 to 2024, faces drug charges in Liberia’s widening cocaine-trafficking investigation, which she denies. Her case is on the docket of Criminal Court “C” as the courts’ November Term opens this week.

A group calling itself the Concerned Partisans of the NPP (CP-NPP) has demanded that the convention be postponed, warning that holding it now could feed perceptions that Howard-Taylor’s prosecution is politically motivated. The group has also alleged a push to hand the party to Vice President Jeremiah Koung.

Questions about Mulbah’s ties to the government predate Wednesday’s announcement. In September, CDC Secretary General Jefferson Koijee, Siafa’s predecessor at City Hall, publicly demanded that Mulbah say whether he holds a senior position in Vice President Koung’s office while leading the NPP.

Other Appointments

The President’s announcement also covered the following positions:

* Ministry of Foreign Affairs: Hon. Stephen J. H. Zargo and Hon. Jeremiah Solunteh, Ambassadors-Designate

* Ministry of Local Government: Mr. Wesley D. M. Nyenatoh, Sr., Superintendent, River Gee County; Mr. Elijah G. Freeman, Superintendent, Grand Cape Mount County. Outgoing Grand Cape Mount Superintendent Foley Kiatamba is to be reassigned.

* Ministry of Commerce and Industry: Mr. Ceebee C. D. Barshell, Deputy Minister for Public Services

* Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau: Mr. George Mulbah, Commissioner

* Agricultural and Industrial Training Bureau: Hon. Mike T. Swengbe, Deputy Director General for Technical Services

* Independent National Commission on Human Rights: Following vetting by the Chief Justice, Cllr. Philomena T. Williams, Mr. Shiwoh Kamara, Mr. Domah Cooper and Cllr. Mohammed E. Fahnbulleh (re-nominated) as Commissioners, filling four vacancies.

President Boakai urged the new officials to discharge their duties with integrity, professionalism and dedication, keeping the interests of the Liberian people at the center of their work.

World.title: Health Workers’ Union Sounds Alarm Over ‘Poor Welfare’, Demands US$500 Minimum Salary for Nurses and Midwives
World.content:
The Health Workers’ Union accuses the Boakai administration of neglecting healthcare professionals, questions the proposed US$135.8 million health sector allocation and warns of unspecified action if government fails to address its demands by January 2027.

MONROVIA — The Health Workers’ Union of Liberia has demanded a minimum monthly take-home salary of US$500 for degree-holding nurses and midwives, the immediate employment of more than 3,800 volunteer health workers and the passage of the long-delayed National Public Health Law.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The Union also warned that it could take unspecified action if the government fails to address its demands, escalating pressure on the administration of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai over the welfare and working conditions of healthcare professionals.



Speaking at a news conference in Monrovia on Tuesday, November 10, the organization accused the Government of Liberia of neglecting and marginalizing nurses, midwives, physician assistants and other healthcare professionals who continue to sustain the country’s health delivery system under difficult conditions.

Reading the Union’s statement, Meshach Karmo Jr. said thousands of qualified health professionals have remained in voluntary service for years without formal employment or regular compensation, while others receive salaries that do not reflect their academic qualifications, professional responsibilities and workloads.

“Let us state this clearly: Liberia cannot build a strong, resilient, and functional healthcare system while continuously neglecting, underpaying, and exploiting the very people responsible for delivering healthcare to its citizens,” the Union declared.

Karmo, who also serves as National Vice President for Administration of the Liberian Nurses Association, said healthcare workers routinely sacrifice their time, sleep, family life and personal safety to keep hospitals and clinics operational, attend to emergencies, deliver babies and save lives.

He lamented that despite these contributions, their welfare, dignity and professional advancement continue to receive inadequate attention from the government.

3,800 Volunteer Health Workers Await Employment

One of the Union’s major concerns is the prolonged unemployment of qualified healthcare professionals who have served in hospitals and clinics without formal employment.

The organization disclosed that some nurses, midwives, physician assistants and other trained health workers have spent five, six, seven and even eight years providing services without regular salaries or formal government employment.

It estimated that more than 3,800 volunteer health professionals and other personnel are currently awaiting employment.

The Union described the situation as exploitation disguised as professional experience, arguing that the government should not continue benefiting from the services of trained professionals while denying them formal employment and the opportunity to earn a living.

“Eight years of voluntary service is not a short waiting period. It is eight years of lost income, delayed professional advancement, family responsibilities left unattended, and dreams continuously postponed,” the organization said.

It called on the government to develop and implement a transparent, adequately funded and time-bound employment strategy to absorb qualified volunteer health workers into the public health system.

The Union also questioned the continued reliance on volunteers at a time when several health facilities across the country reportedly face shortages of trained personnel.

Demands US$500 Minimum Salary for Degree-Holding Nurses

Beyond employment, the Union expressed frustration over what it described as inadequate salaries for professional healthcare workers.

It said a nurse holding a Bachelor of Science degree could take home less than US$300 monthly despite years of training and significant responsibilities.

The organization argued that such compensation is insufficient to meet basic living expenses, support families and maintain the professional standards expected of healthcare workers, particularly amid rising living costs.

Consequently, it is demanding that the monthly take-home salaries of Bachelor of Science-qualified health professionals, particularly nurses and midwives, be increased to at least US$500.

“We are not demanding luxury. We are demanding fairness. We are not asking for privileges. We are demanding compensation that reflects our education, professional responsibilities, sacrifices, and contribution to national development,” Karmo emphasized.

He maintained that the proposed minimum salary was reasonable and long overdue, considering the responsibilities healthcare professionals carry in protecting the lives of Liberians.

Questions US$135.8 Million Health Sector Allocation

The Union also questioned whether the proposed 2027 National Draft Budget provides sufficient resources to address the employment and compensation challenges confronting the health sector.

According to figures cited by the organization, the proposed budget allocates US$135,827,541 to the entire health sector, with US$95,601,068 earmarked for the Ministry of Health.

Of the Ministry’s proposed allocation, US$47,923,812 is designated for employee compensation and salaries, compared with US$44,782,715 in the previous budget.

The proposed increase amounts to US$3,141,097.

Although acknowledging the increase, the Union described it as inadequate given the number of qualified health professionals awaiting employment and the need to improve salaries and working conditions.

It questioned how the additional allocation would accommodate more than 3,800 volunteer health professionals and other personnel awaiting absorption into the public workforce.

The organization is therefore calling on the Executive and Legislature to increase the employee compensation allocation in the 2027 budget and establish clearly defined budget lines and implementation plans to address employment and salary concerns.

It argued that increased allocations would have little impact if they did not translate into actual employment, improved compensation and better working conditions for healthcare professionals.

Accuses Senate of Delaying Public Health Law

The Union also criticized the Liberian Senate for what it described as an unacceptable delay in passing the proposed National Public Health Law, which it said has remained pending before the chamber for more than four years.

The organization argued that the legislation is essential to strengthening Liberia’s legal and institutional framework for public health protection, disease prevention, health security and the overall governance of the health sector.

It urged senators to demonstrate the necessary political will and legislative responsibility to conclude the process without further delay.

“The health of a nation must never become a casualty of legislative procrastination,” the Union declared.

Union Outlines Five Major Demands

In its statement, the organization presented five major demands to the government:

1. Immediate employment of volunteers: Develop and implement a transparent, adequately funded and time-bound plan to absorb qualified volunteer nurses, midwives, physician assistants and other health professionals into the public workforce.

2. Improved salaries: Increase monthly take-home salaries for Bachelor of Science-qualified health professionals, particularly nurses and midwives, to a minimum of US$500.

3. Increased budgetary allocation: Raise the employee compensation and salary allocation in the 2027 National Budget, with clear provisions for employment and improved remuneration.

4. Passage of the National Public Health Law: Prioritize and pass the legislation, which the Union says has remained before the Senate for more than four years.

5. Meaningful engagement: Establish genuine dialogue with the Health Workers’ Union and relevant professional associations to address the longstanding concerns of healthcare professionals.

Members Losing Patience, Union Rejects Claims of Compromised Struggle

The organization acknowledged growing frustration among its members, revealing that some healthcare workers are increasingly questioning the leadership, direction and effectiveness of its advocacy.

Some members, according to the Union, have also raised concerns about whether their struggle for improved welfare and professional recognition has been compromised.

However, the leadership insisted that it has neither abandoned nor compromised the campaign.

“We understand the frustration of our members because the leadership shares the same working conditions and financial difficulties confronting the broader health workforce,” the statement said.

The Union warned that it could no longer continue issuing statements, attending meetings and receiving government promises while the living conditions of its members deteriorate and thousands of qualified professionals remain unemployed.

“Our patience must not be mistaken for weakness. Our professionalism must not be mistaken for silence. And our commitment to serving humanity must never be exploited as an excuse to deny us our rights,” it declared.

The organization maintained that a functional healthcare system requires more than hospitals, ambulances, medical equipment and government policies. It must also prioritize the welfare of the people responsible for delivering essential medical services.

Threatens Unspecified Action by January

The Union’s concerns were reinforced by Theophilus T. Fayiah, President of the Liberia National Physician Assistant Association, who warned that healthcare professionals could resort to unspecified action if the government fails to make tangible progress by early January 2027.

Fayiah cautioned that the action could have serious consequences for the population and the country’s healthcare delivery system.

The Union called on President Boakai, the Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, and the Legislature to address its demands with urgency.

It stressed that its concerns extend beyond financial compensation to include professional dignity, fairness, job security and the government’s responsibility to those sustaining the national healthcare system.

The organization concluded that Liberia cannot achieve the quality of healthcare its citizens deserve while continuing to overlook the welfare of the professionals responsible for providing those services.

It insisted that the time for promises has passed and that concrete government action is now required.

World.title: Liberia Mobilizes African Diplomatic Support Ahead of December UN Security Council Presidency
World.content:
Ambassadors from 17 countries pledge regional backing as Liberia prepares to lead the 15-member Security Council, with calls to amplify Africa’s voice on global peace, security and institutional reform.

ACCRA, Ghana — Liberia is mobilizing diplomatic support from African and other international partners ahead of its assumption of the rotating Presidency of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) in December 2026, with ambassadors from 17 countries pledging to support the country’s leadership.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The commitment was made during an inaugural Diplomatic Breakfast Meeting hosted by the Embassy of Liberia in Accra, Ghana, on November 9, at the Labadi Beach Hotel.



The meeting brought together members of the Diplomatic and Consular Corps to discuss Liberia’s upcoming leadership of the 15-member Security Council and its implications for international peace, security and multilateral cooperation.

Participating ambassadors representing Sierra Leone, Nigeria, Rwanda, Kenya, Mozambique, Algeria, Sudan, South Sudan, Senegal, South Africa, Barbados, Zambia, Libya, the Sahrawi Republic, Namibia and Angola pledged their support for Liberia’s upcoming Presidency.

They urged President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to use the opportunity to advance not only Liberia’s national interests but also the broader aspirations of Africa, particularly in global discussions on conflict resolution, peacebuilding, sustainable development and reform of international institutions.

Liberia Seeks Stronger African Voice

Speaking at the gathering, Liberia’s Ambassador to Ghana, Musu Jatu Ruhle, thanked the diplomatic representatives for accepting the Embassy’s invitation and reaffirmed the government’s commitment to preparing for the December responsibility.

She said the Boakai administration, under the guidance of Foreign Affairs Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti, was making preparations to ensure Liberia effectively discharges its responsibilities during its Council Presidency.

Ruhle also acknowledged the contributions of African countries and international partners whose support helped Liberia secure its position on the Security Council.

She described the opportunity as both an honour and a responsibility, noting that Liberia’s own history of conflict and recovery offers important lessons for its engagement in international peacebuilding.

Liberia’s experience, she said, demonstrates that peace goes beyond the absence of war and requires dialogue, justice, reconciliation and opportunities for people to live with dignity.

According to Ruhle, these principles will inform Liberia’s approach during its leadership of the Council.

Women, Youth and Climate Security Among Priorities

The Ambassador outlined several priorities identified by Foreign Affairs Minister Nyanti for Liberia’s engagement at the Security Council.

They include increasing the participation of women and young people in conflict prevention and peacebuilding; addressing the connections between climate change, natural resources and conflict; strengthening security cooperation in West Africa and the Sahel; and supporting reform of the Security Council and stronger United Nations peacekeeping operations.

Ruhle emphasized that Africa has significant contributions to make to international peace and security but continues to face challenges that often transcend national borders.

She called for stronger cooperation among African governments, regional organizations and international partners, arguing that no country can independently address the continent’s complex security challenges.

She further stressed that Liberia’s presence on the Security Council must translate into meaningful African participation in global decision-making.

“Representation alone is not enough,” she said, emphasizing the need for African concerns to receive serious consideration and for the continent’s participation to produce practical outcomes.

Calls for African Cooperation

Ruhle acknowledged that African countries may not always agree on every international issue but said dialogue and mutual understanding could help them identify common ground on matters of shared interest.

She called for sustained engagement among African governments to strengthen their collective influence within the multilateral system.

As Liberia prepares to assume the Council’s Presidency, she said the country looks forward to working closely with African partners and other United Nations members.

She added that Liberia would approach the responsibility with a willingness to listen, a commitment to dialogue and an interest in building consensus.

The diplomatic gathering highlighted the importance of regional solidarity and coordinated engagement as Liberia prepares for its December leadership of the Security Council.

The upcoming Presidency provides Liberia an opportunity to contribute to international discussions on peace and security while advancing its stated priorities on African representation, climate-related security challenges, youth and women’s participation, and reform of the United Nations system.

World.title: News Analysis: Senator McGill’s Bid to Lead the CDC Tests the Party’s Credibility
World.content:
MONROVIA – When a political veteran sets his sights on a party’s top office, the usual questions concern votes, delegates and alliances. In the case of Senator Nathaniel F. McGill and the opposition Congress for Democratic Change (CDC), another question looms larger: how will the world react if the party’s next chairman is a man the United States government has sanctioned?

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

McGill, now the senator for Margibi County, was recently reported pledging support for the completion of a party headquarters. His chairmanship ambition therefore remains a prospective contest, but it has already prompted debate about the CDC’s direction as it prepares for the 2029 elections.



McGill is far from a newcomer. He climbed through the party’s senior ranks and served as National Chairman during the period that ended in the CDC’s historic 2017 victory. He then became one of the most powerful officials in the Weah administration, serving as Minister of State for Presidential Affairs. In 2023, he won the Margibi senatorial seat with 52,934 votes, about 39.89 per cent of the valid votes cast.

Supporters see a seasoned organiser who understands both the party and the machinery of government. Critics see a leader whose record carries costs the party may struggle to absorb. Both views deserve a fair hearing, but one issue stands apart because its consequences reach beyond Liberia’s borders.

The Treasury Designation

On 15 August 2022, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the US Treasury Department designated McGill under Executive Order 13818, which carries the Global Magnitsky framework targeting serious human rights abuse and corruption. According to the Treasury’s announcement, the action followed allegations involving unjustified government stipends and the distribution of undocumented cash to other officials for governmental and non-governmental activities. The Treasury also alleged that he used his official position to prevent the discovery of misappropriation.

Precision matters here. A sanctions designation is an administrative action by a government. It is not a criminal conviction by a court in Liberia or the United States, and the allegations have not been tested before a judge. McGill remains free to contest them and to seek reconsideration through the appropriate channels.

Even so, the designation is no footnote. It is a formal act by one of the world’s most influential governments, and it carries concrete legal effects. Treating it as routine political noise would be a serious misjudgement for any party hoping to return to power.

What the Sanctions Do and Do Not Mean

McGill’s name now appears on the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List. As a result, property and financial interests under US jurisdiction must generally be blocked, and US persons are broadly prohibited from transactions involving him unless authorised.

The legal picture requires nuance. Electing a sanctioned chairman would not automatically sanction the CDC as an institution. OFAC’s 50 per cent rule applies to entities owned, directly or indirectly, 50 per cent or more by blocked persons, and it does not extend to a party merely because a designated individual holds office within it. Nor would his election automatically bar every activity undertaken by non-US persons inside Liberia.

The practical risks lie elsewhere, particularly among the party’s overseas supporters. The CDC maintains networks among Liberians in the United States, including CDC-USA, and these supporters contribute to fundraising, organising and political engagement. Any transaction involving McGill that touches American citizens, banks or property could raise compliance questions. Banks, donors and event organisers often avoid risk rather than study the fine print, so a party led by a sanctioned chairman should expect added scrutiny and greater hesitation from partners abroad.

Why the Sanctions Could Be a Bad Omen

The deeper problem is reputational. Politics runs on perception, and perception travels across borders. Liberia’s relationship with the United States remains strategically important, touching development assistance, security cooperation, governance reform and investor confidence. Washington’s stance on corruption shapes how many partners view Liberian institutions and the people who lead them.

A party seeking power in 2029 must look like a credible government-in-waiting. It must persuade diplomats, donors and investors that it has learned from its time in office. If its chairman, the public face of the organization, appears on an American sanctions list over alleged corruption, the CDC begins that effort with a visible handicap. Several consequences could follow.

Loyalty to a leader does not erase international concern, and the party cannot simply campaign around the problem. Until the designation is lifted or amended, the CDC must treat it as a daily reality.

The Weah-Era Shadow

The sanctions do not stand alone. They sit within a broader record from McGill’s years in government. As Minister of State for Presidential Affairs, he stood at the center of presidential decision-making and party-government coordination. When an administration loses public favor, its chief political managers share the scrutiny. Critics, including some CDC partisans, complained that power had gathered among a small circle, that party stakeholders were sidelined and that internal criticism was poorly received.

Two episodes shaped public perception in particular. In January 2021, Representative Acarous Moses Gray criticized senior officials, including McGill, over alleged nepotism. The appointment of McGill’s sister, Rebecca McGill, as Deputy Minister of Finance for Administration became part of that debate. A family connection does not prove an unlawful appointment or an unqualified appointee. Still, the appearance of family advantage damaged a movement that had promised change.

Then came the elaborate tomb built for McGill’s late mother in 2021, which FrontPage Africa described in a July report. McGill reportedly said a friend built it. Available reporting does not show that state funds were used, and the difference between poor optics and proven misuse matters. Even so, the spectacle stirred public anger during a period of widespread hardship.

None of this is a permanent bar to leadership. Combined with the Treasury allegations, however, it forms a pattern that opponents are likely to exploit.

Reading the Margibi Numbers

Supporters often cite the Margibi victory as proof of McGill’s strength. The achievement is real, but the figures tell a more layered story. In the first round of the 2023 presidential election, George Weah received 56,272 votes in Margibi, or 41.76 per cent. Joseph Boakai won the county with 63,431 votes, or 47.08 per cent. McGill’s 52,934 votes fell about 3,338 short of Weah’s total. In other words, McGill won his Senate seat while the CDC’s presidential candidate lost the county.

That outcome points to personal appeal, local relationships and candidate-specific loyalty, which are common features of Liberian elections. It does not show that McGill betrayed his party, and no credible evidence has been offered to support such a claim. Indeed, he publicly reaffirmed his support for Weah after the first-round results.

The lesson is that winning a county is different from building a national machine. The CDC lost the 2023 runoff by only 20,567 votes, with Boakai and Jeremiah Koung of the Unity Party taking 50.64 per cent against 49.36 per cent for Weah and Jewel Howard-Taylor. The party remains a major force, and what it needs now is organization, discipline and renewed public trust. A chairman must be able to mobilize the entire country without carrying liabilities that push allies away.

Questioning the “Winning Chairman” Label

McGill’s allies often describe him as the winning chairman of 2017. That year, Weah took the runoff with about 61.5 per cent of the vote, ending twelve years of Unity Party rule and producing the first peaceful handover between living elected presidents in more than seven decades.

His role in that period is part of the record, but the victory had many authors. Weah’s personal popularity mattered, as did the party’s grassroots structures and the alliance with the National Patriotic Party and the Liberty Party. Crediting one man for the entire result is inaccurate. A good chairman is judged on unity, institution-building and lasting public confidence, and a single winning cycle does not prove those qualities.

One historical claim also needs correction. Published results for the December 2014 Margibi special senatorial election list Ansu Dao Sonii as the CDC candidate, and McGill does not appear among the candidates. Claims that he contested and lost that race cannot be supported by the record.

Leadership Style and Party Democracy

Beyond the sanctions, the party must ask whether McGill can reunite a divided house. Some critics accuse him of intolerance toward dissent and of favouring a close circle of allies. These remain allegations, not established findings, but delegates are entitled to ask hard questions:

Some accounts of his rise claim that positions were created to accommodate him, and others say he held two offices at once. These stories require proof from constitutional documents and convention records, and until that proof appears, they should not be treated as settled fact. The principle behind them still stands: a party must show that its procedures are stronger than any single personality.

The Boakai administration will be judged on corruption, economic management, jobs and public services. If it stumbles, the opposition will gain an opening. Public frustration, however, will not hand votes to the CDC automatically, because voters will compare both political establishments.

That is why the choice of chairman carries such weight. The CDC needs a face of renewal who can challenge the government with credibility. A leader whose record already raises questions about governance, and who sits under a foreign corruption designation, may struggle to carry that message at home or abroad.

The case for McGill rests on experience, relationships, institutional memory and his link to the 2017 triumph. The case against rests on the sanctions, the baggage of the Weah years, doubts about his leadership style and the risk of reopening old wounds.

Both sides raise fair points. Supporters can argue that he is capable and battle-tested, while critics can argue that the party cannot afford a leader who complicates its dealings with Washington and the wider international community while it rebuilds trust.

The sanctions are the sharpest edge of that debate. They are an allegation, not a conviction, and McGill may contest them. As long as they stand, however, they send a signal to donors, diplomats, diaspora supporters and voters. For a party that wants to project accountability, that signal could prove a bad omen.

The delegates will make the final call. If McGill shows real change, answers the reputational questions directly and commits to inclusive leadership, he can make a serious case. If his bid looks mainly like an effort to regain personal influence, the CDC may spend the road to 2029 explaining its past instead of offering a future.

World.title: Liberia: Togbah: ‘Bong Was Shortchanged Under Weah as Party Gatekeepers Blocked Its Leaders’
World.content:
MONROVIA – Jonah Togbah, a former member of the Congress for Democratic Change (CDC), says influential party figures in Bong County kept prominent local politicians out of government during the Weah administration. He says Wednesday’s appointments under President Joseph Nyuma Boakai show how quickly political fortunes can turn.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Togbah, who hails from Bong, said capable people who helped bring the CDC-led coalition to power in 2017 were denied a place in government. In his view, some party actors cared more about guarding their own influence than about widening opportunity.



His remarks follow the appointments Wednesday of two Bong sons to the Boakai government: Attorney George S. Mulbah, chairman of the opposition National Patriotic Party (NPP), and Ambassador Jeremiah C. Sulunteh.

Few ministers for a major county

Togbah began with Bong’s share of top executive jobs. Bong is the third most populous county in Liberia, and it produced Jewel Howard-Taylor, who was vice president for all six years of George Manneh Weah’s presidency. Even so, he said, only one Bong citizen, Dr. Mogana Flomo, served as a minister under Weah. Dr. Flomo was dismissed almost three years into the administration, and the county had no minister for the rest of the term.

Togbah called that outcome disappointing, given Bong’s role in the coalition’s victory and the presence of one of its own in the second-highest office in the country. “How does a county of this weight go for years without a minister?” he asked, in substance.

He acknowledged that the vice presidency and ministerial appointments are separate constitutional and political matters. He said the question remains why Bong’s influence did not produce wider representation in the executive branch.

Mulbah’s late appointment

Togbah then turned to Mulbah, whose NPP was one of two parties that joined Mr. Weah’s CDC to form the Coalition for Democratic Change. That coalition carried Weah to the presidency in 2017, and Mulbah and other NPP members played roles in building it.

Mulbah was named to head the Liberia Aviation Authority only about eight months before the Weah government left office in January 2024. Togbah said that timing raises questions about how seriously Bong stakeholders were accommodated.

He said the late consideration pointed to a deeper problem in the county’s party leadership. According to him, some powerful figures were uneasy with the rising profile of others who might challenge their standing or pursue separate political ambitions.

Sulunteh’s decision to join the CDC

Togbah also cited Sulunteh, who served as Liberia’s ambassador to the United States under former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf. When he endorsed and joined the CDC, the move was widely seen as significant, given his government experience and standing in Bong. His support for Weah in the 2017 campaign made him one of the Bong figures who helped broaden the coalition’s appeal.

But Togbah said Sulunteh did not receive the recognition he expected after crossing over. He alleged that certain influential actors in the county viewed Sulunteh’s growing relevance with suspicion. He said they treated his earlier service to the nation as if it counted for little because of his new CDC ties.

Party affiliation, Togbah argued, should not have decided who deserved recognition. He said Sulunteh’s experience and his contribution to the coalition should have counted when national service opportunities were distributed.

Yallah and the road to 2029

Togbah also named former Senator Henry W. Yallah, who lost the 2020 senatorial race in Bong. He said Yallah was among those expected to be considered for a government post after his defeat.

According to Togbah, some political actors were uncomfortable with the idea of Yallah remaining relevant through an appointment. He said that unease grew as calculations about the county’s future leadership and the 2029 elections began to take shape. He said that rivalry for influence created an atmosphere in which experienced people were pushed aside.

Criticism not aimed at Weah

Togbah took care to separate the former president from his criticism. He described Weah as a humble man who cared about ordinary Liberians, whatever their background or place of origin.

His complaint, he said, is with those entrusted with managing political relationships and coordinating CDC affairs in Bong. He said securing inclusion was the responsibility of influential party figures as well as the president.

Political leadership, he said, should not be reduced to protecting personal interests, consolidating influence or preventing other capable people from emerging. He argued that a successful administration should make room for people of varied backgrounds and ambitions to contribute to national development.

Loyalty held through 2023

Togbah said the alleged exclusion did not break the loyalty of those affected. Mulbah, Sulunteh and other stakeholders kept supporting Weah’s reelection bid in 2023, despite their disagreements and disappointments. He described that continued support as proof of political commitment, shown even when some felt their contributions had gone unrecognized.

The 2023 election, however, ended differently. Boakai, who served as vice president under Sirleaf, defeated Weah and became president. The change opened a new chapter for people whose ties to the previous government had been marked by disagreement and unmet expectations.

Thanks to Moye and Boakai

Togbah said the appointments of Mulbah and Sulunteh mark a major turn in their careers. He said they show that political setbacks do not necessarily determine the outcome of a person’s public service ambitions.

He gave particular credit to Senator Prince K. Moye, whom he said made recommendations that helped open doors for the two men. He thanked the senator for an intervention that, in his words, placed competence, inclusion and recognition of qualified people above past political differences.

He said Senator Moye’s role deserves recognition because appointing prominent Bong citizens should be viewed beyond partisan lines. In his view, it is a chance to strengthen the county’s participation in national governance.

Togbah also congratulated the two appointees, saying their new roles show the value of perseverance in public life. He thanked President Boakai for judging them worthy of national service, saying their backgrounds and contributions should be recognized regardless of past affiliations.

He said the appointments send a message that political differences should not permanently bar qualified Liberians from serving.

World.title: Liberia: Nimba University Suspends Student Leaders After Protest Against Senator Twayen
World.content:
Sanniquellie City, Nimba County — The administration of Nimba University, formerly Nimba County Community College, has concluded its investigation into the October 9 protest that disrupted a planned donation visit by Nimba County Senator Nya D. Twayen Jr.

By Franklin Doloquee

The university has suspended the chairmen of two campus-based political organizations over their alleged roles in the incident.



Emmanuel B. Nenwon, Chairman of the Students’ Liberation Party (SLP), has been suspended for two semesters, while Princeton G. Quiah, Chairman of the SUP-PROSA Alliance, has been suspended for one semester.

According to a document released by the university administration, Nenwon was penalized for allegedly refusing to honor a directive from Vice President for Administration Melvin Yealue to disperse an assembly.

The administration described his action as “disrespect to constituted authority.” Quiah was suspended for allegedly spreading false information against the Vice President for Administration, promoting instability and tarnishing the image of the university.

Several other students were also reportedly disciplined in connection with the protest. The administration said its actions were taken in line with the Nimba University Student Handbook.

What Happened on October 9

Tensions erupted at the university on Friday, October 9 when Senator Twayen and his entourage visited the campus to donate solar-powered lights and a Starlink Internet Facility intended to support students’ research and learning.

The visit, however, became controversial after students surrounded the senator’s convoy and prevented it from leaving the campus.

The disagreement reportedly centered on which student political organization should receive the donated items and formally present them to the university administration.

An eyewitness told journalists that members of the outgoing leadership of the Students’ Liberation Party complained that the senator had not informed them about the visit.

The incoming leadership of the Student Unification Party (SUP) also insisted that it should receive the items, arguing that the donation was connected to commitments made during the student council election.

The standoff reportedly lasted more than four hours, with university staff attempting to negotiate with the students and restore calm. Senator Twayen later confirmed that some student leaders had besieged him and his entourage, but said the situation was eventually brought under control.

Donation Put on Hold

Following the disruption, Senator Twayen said his office would suspend the planned donation until another time. He did not disclose when the solar-powered lights and Starlink internet package would be delivered.

The senator’s visit had been intended to provide practical support to students, particularly in areas of research, digital connectivity and campus lighting. Instead, the disagreement over the donation overshadowed the presentation and left the intended benefits uncertain.

The university administration condemned the students’ conduct, describing it as unacceptable and inconsistent with the discipline expected at an institution of higher learning. It also apologized to Senator Twayen for the treatment he received during the visit.

Administration’s Decision

The university’s decision to suspend the two student leaders has drawn mixed reactions across Nimba County.

Supporters of the administration’s action argued that the suspension will serve as a warning to students who attempt to disrupt official activities, intimidate public officials, or prevent development initiatives from reaching the institution.

They said the university must protect its academic environment and ensure that visitors, donors and government officials can carry out legitimate activities without obstruction.

Critics, however, believe the punishment may deepen tensions between the administration and student political groups.

Some have questioned whether the university adequately addressed the underlying disagreement over student representation and the handling of donations before imposing disciplinary measures.

Public Reaction in Nimba

The incident has sparked heated discussion on several community radio stations in Nimba County. Some callers condemned the students’ behavior, saying it was wrong to prevent a senator from carrying out a donation intended to benefit the same students.

Others described the students’ conduct in harsh terms, with some comparing it to the violence associated with Liberia’s civil conflict. Such comparisons reflect the strong emotions the incident has generated, though they remain opinions expressed by radio callers rather than established facts.

Some callers also urged President Joseph Boakai to intervene in the matter and review what they described as concerns over representation within the university’s administration.

These claims reflect broader public frustration, but they have not been independently verified. Other residents supported the university’s decision, arguing that disciplinary action was necessary to prevent similar incidents in the future and to reinforce respect for institutional authority.

Former County Inspector’s Comment

The incident also drew reaction from B. Mack Gbilwon, a former county inspector during the administration of former President George Weah and a student of Nimba University. In a Facebook post, Gbilwon appeared to defend the students’ position, arguing that Senator Twayen’s visit and donation were not timely.

He further described the donation as small. His comments were condemned by many Nimbaians, who accused him of supporting behavior that disrupted a development-oriented visit to the university.

Critics argued that, as a student of the institution, he should have encouraged dialogue and peaceful engagement rather than appearing to justify the blockade.

The incident has raised wider questions about the relationship between student political organizations, university authorities, and public officials in Nimba County. While students have a right to express concerns and participate in campus governance, the university administration has emphasized that grievances must be channeled through peaceful and recognized procedures.

In its earlier statement, the institution warned that it would not tolerate misconduct that undermines its academic mission, integrity or reputation.

For many residents, the issue is no longer only about the blocked donation. It has become a test of whether Nimba University can maintain discipline, protect educational opportunities and manage political competition among student groups without allowing disputes to disrupt development efforts intended for the benefit of students.

World.title: Liberia: LDEA Boss, Deputies Test Negative for Drugs Ahead of Senate Confirmation
World.content:
MONROVIA – Newly appointed Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA) Director General Daniel Dee Ziankahn, Jr. and his two deputies have tested negative for drugs as they prepare to appear before the Liberian Senate for confirmation.

By Edwin G. Genoway, Jr.

Ziankahn and his deputies, Precious Rue, Deputy Director General for Operations, and Prince Mulbah, Deputy Director General for Administration, underwent drug testing on Wednesday at the Wellness Health Center in Congo Town, outside Monrovia.



A team of journalists witnessed the testing process, and all three officials received negative results. Speaking after the test, Ziankahn said officers responsible for fighting illegal drugs must first demonstrate good character and discipline by setting an example for the public.

He said the decision to undergo testing before their confirmation was intended to show that the new leadership is prepared to follow the laws it is expected to enforce.

“As security officers, especially those fighting drugs, we need to lead the way and set the standards. As you can see here today, we came to do our drug test before going for confirmation,” Ziankahn said.

The LDEA’s fight against illegal drugs is built around four major areas: intelligence-led operations, drug prevention and demand reduction, institutional accountability and professionalism, and coordination with national and international partners under the National Anti-Drug Action Plan.

The agency’s intelligence-led operations are intended to stop the supply of illegal drugs by strengthening border security, monitoring major entry points and targeting trafficking networks that use Liberia as a transit route.

Its prevention and demand-reduction strategy focuses on educating the public, particularly young people, through school anti-drug clubs, community awareness campaigns, treatment and rehabilitation programs.

The agency also seeks to improve discipline and professionalism among its officers through drug testing, proper training and a zero-tolerance approach to corruption and misconduct.

Another key part of the strategy is cooperation among security institutions, health authorities, communities and other partners to ensure a coordinated national response.

Ziankahn has pledged to work with these strategies and strengthen their implementation to make the LDEA more effective, disciplined and professional.

He also urged officers of the agency to remain committed, focused and honest in carrying out their responsibilities, stressing that the fight against drugs must begin with accountability within the institution itself.

His appointment comes at a time when the LDEA has faced public criticism and questions about its leadership and effectiveness in fighting drug trafficking.

The leadership change followed the indefinite suspension of former Officer-in-Charge Fitzgerald Biago amid major cocaine seizures and investigations involving the agency’s previous administration.

The developments raised concerns about accountability, internal discipline and the agency’s ability to effectively fight the illegal drug trade. President Joseph Nyuma Boakai subsequently appointed Ziankahn and his two deputies in an acting capacity to take charge of the agency while the Senate confirmation process moves forward.

Meanwhile, some Liberians are expressing hope that Ziankahn’s appointment will bring meaningful changes to the LDEA and restore public confidence in an institution that plays a major role in protecting the country from illegal drugs.

Some believe his military and security background could help strengthen discipline within the agency, improve its operations and ensure that officers involved in drug enforcement carry out their duties professionally.

Others expect the new leadership to go beyond arresting street-level drug users and focus more attention on major dealers, suppliers and trafficking networks responsible for bringing illegal substances into the country.

There are also expectations that the new administration will investigate allegations of corruption within the agency, ensure that officers found guilty of misconduct are held accountable and prevent powerful individuals from interfering with drug investigations.

Young people and communities affected by drug abuse are also expected to benefit from stronger public education, prevention programs and rehabilitation services of the Zainkahn’s administration.

However, some Liberians believe the real test of the new leadership will not be its promises but its ability to produce visible results, including reducing the availability of illegal drugs, dismantling trafficking networks and rebuilding public trust.

For many observers, Ziankahn’s appointment presents an opportunity to change the public perception of the LDEA and strengthen the country’s fight against drug abuse and trafficking.

Zainkahn’s Senate confirmation still ahead, expectations are high that the new leadership will work with the agency’s anti-drug strategies and turn them into practical results.

World.title: It’s a full squad as Chipolopolo step up Burundi preps
World.content:
Chipolopolo have stepped up preparations for Friday’s Group I Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against Burundi, with Coach George Lwandamina now having a full squad in camp in Ndola.

All the players called in to replace the injured trio of Patson Daka, Lameck Banda and Gamphani Lungu have reported for duty.

Iraq-based Prince Mumba of Al Gharraf SC, Edward Chilufya of Hapoel Jerusalem and Derrick Bulaya of Green Eagles have all joined camp, boosting Lwandamina’s options ahead of the crucial double-header.

Zambia will, however, still be without Kingstone Mutandwa, Ackim Mumba and Jackson Phiri, who were ruled out of the back-to-back assignments due to injury.

Lwandamina has been leading the 30-member team in training, with the final 26 expected to make the cut for the home fixture.

Zambia hosts Burundi on Friday at the Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola at 15h00 CAT.

Algeria tops Group I with four points, one better than Zambia and Togo, while Burundi are rooted to the bottom on one point.

Only the top two teams will qualify to the PAMOJA 2027 AFCON to be hosted by Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.

Meanwhile, forward Kings Kangwa is back in camp after missing the first two qualifiers through suspension.

CAF have confirmed he will be eligible for the return leg against Burundi on 17 November in Bujumbura.

World.title: Zesco Targets 11,630MW By 2030, A Year Ahead Of The 10,000MW Deadline
World.content:
Zesco Limited has set itself a target of 11,630 megawatts (MW) of installed generation capacity by 2030. That would overshoot the Government’s 10,000MW goal under the Grow Zambia Agenda by 1,630MW and arrive a year before the 2031 deadline.

Managing director Eng. Justin Loongo outlined the plan when Minister of Electricity Mr Peter Kapala visited the utility’s headquarters in Lusaka. He said Zesco had aligned its planning with the national target but was now pursuing a higher figure through investment in solar, hydro, wind, thermal and other technologies.

The expansion would more than treble the 3,307MW of installed capacity the country had in 2021. Zesco director of transmission operations and trade Mr Lioko Sitali said the 2030 mix would include 4,126MW from solar, 3,970MW from hydropower, 3,234MW from thermal sources and 200MW from wind, among others.

Solar, on those numbers, would overtake hydropower as the largest single source of power. That would be a deep break for a country whose electricity has for decades depended on the water levels at Kariba and Kafue.

That shift is already under way. Mr Kapala welcomed the fall in hydropower’s share of the national energy mix from 85 per cent to 34 per cent, saying it showed real progress in diversifying generation after droughts exposed the risk of relying on a single source.

Mr Loongo said the utility was assessing renewable technologies and exploring partnerships and financing models to speed up the development and commissioning of new projects. He stressed that new plants would mean little without the lines to carry their power.

“As generation expands, we must also strengthen our transmission and distribution networks that deliver electricity to customers,” he said.

The managing director also pointed to private sector participation and regional power trading as central to meeting rising demand and strengthening national energy security.

One example is the 20-year power purchase agreement between Zesco and the Mineworkers Union of Zambia (MUZ) for a 120MW solar plant in Mufulira. The plant is being developed on MUZ-owned Mukuba Farm through Bashi Maini Investments Limited, trading as Mukuba Energy, with a first phase valued at US$120 million.

For Mr Kapala, the visit was also a chance to mark a financial recovery. He said the utility had been on the brink of collapse but had returned to profit following Government policy interventions, an achievement he said the country should be proud of.

“At a time when I was Minister of Energy, Zesco owed even US$2 billion,” Mr Kapala said. “In the next few years, we will be making millions of dollars in revenue for the Government. I pat the whole team on the back.”

He thanked President Hakainde Hichilema for leading efforts to revive the utility, comparing it with the Government’s revival of mines that had been dormant for more than 20 years.

Zesco’s customer base has grown from 1.2 million in 2022 to 1.5 million last year, and the utility is aiming for three million connections by 2030. Installed capacity is projected to reach 5,220MW by December.

The ambition faces sharp questions. Days before the announcement, Democratic Progressive Party president Mr Antonio Mwanza challenged the Government’s ability to reach even 10,000MW by 2031.

Using the Ministry of Energy’s October 2026 figure of 4,722MW, Mr Mwanza said Zambia would need to add a further 5,278MW, roughly 1,000MW every year. He said only about 840MW had been added since 2021, citing Energy Regulation Board (ERB) figures of 3,318.43MW in 2021 and 3,885.86MW in 2024.

He also drew a distinction that weighs on any capacity pledge: installed capacity is not the same as reliable supply. He pointed to a February 2026 ministerial statement that put available domestic generation at just 1,635MW, and warned that water levels, plant performance, maintenance and fuel supply all decide what actually reaches homes and businesses.

“Installed capacity cannot be equated with dependable electricity supply,” Mr Mwanza said.

Citing Zesco’s 2025 Integrated Report, the opposition leader noted 53 system disturbances during the year, 26 of them inside the utility’s own network. He also noted distribution losses of 575.89 gigawatt-hours, or 9.48 per cent of electricity purchased, at an estimated cost of K1.071 billion.

“The issue is not whether Zambia should aspire to 10,000MW. The issue is whether government can demonstrate a credible pathway to achieve it by 2031, and ensure that the resulting electricity is reliable, accessible and affordable,” he said.

The two positions now meet on a common point. Zesco’s own managing director has said that generation without transmission and distribution will not deliver power to customers, which is the gap Mr Mwanza says the country must close.

The first test comes before the end of the year. Zesco projects installed capacity of 5,220MW by December, a figure that will show whether the utility’s 2030 trajectory is on course.

World.title: M’membe Asks DPP To Seek Kafwaya Inquest As Three Months Pass Without Answers
World.content:
Three Months After Kafwaya Was Shot, M’membe Asks DPP To Seek An Inquest

Socialist Party president Dr Fred M’membe has formally asked the Director of Public Prosecutions to go to the High Court for an inquest into the killing of former Minister of Transport Mr Mutotwe Kafwaya. He says that three months after Mr Kafwaya was shot during a State security operation, no court has examined the force that ended his life.

In a letter delivered by hand to the National Prosecution Authority and stamped as received by its registry on Wednesday, Dr M’membe asked the DPP to apply under section 33 of the Inquests Act for an order that an inquest be held into the death of the former Lunte Member of Parliament.

Mr Kafwaya died on 14 August during a joint security operation at a house in Kabulonga, Lusaka, a day after the general election. It was not until 19 August that the Inspector General of Police confirmed he had been fatally wounded in that operation. Saturday marks three months since his death.

In that time, the letter says, no inquest has been opened. A postmortem examination was carried out, but its findings have never been made public, and the family has said it was not allowed to have a pathologist of its own present. As far as the public knows, no officer involved has been named, suspended or charged.

Dr M’membe, writing as party president, as a member of the legal profession and as a citizen, set that silence against the speed with which the State moved on everyone else in the house. By 16 August, the Government had announced that eleven people present at the property had been arrested and would face charges.

“Three months later, the force that ended Hon. Kafwaya’s life has not been examined by any court. The law must apply to all,” he said.

His letter rests on the plain wording of the Inquests Act. Under section 4, a coroner who is credibly informed that there is reasonable cause to suspect a violent or unnatural death must hold an inquest as soon as is practicable. Section 12 obliges any police officer who becomes aware of such a death to notify a coroner.

The law allows only one reason for delay, and Dr M’membe says it does not apply. Section 6 postpones an inquest only where someone has been, or is about to be, charged with the murder or manslaughter of the deceased. No one has been so charged, he notes, so nothing in the Act stands in the way.

Where a coroner has not acted, section 33(1)(a) allows the High Court, on an application made by or under the authority of the DPP, to order an inquest into any death if it considers this necessary or desirable. That is the step he wants the DPP’s office to take.

At the centre of his argument is the right to life. Article 12 of the Constitution protects it and permits the use of force only to the extent that is reasonably justifiable in the circumstances. Zambia is also bound by the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which require the State to investigate any death caused by its agents promptly, independently and transparently.

“Whether that standard was met in Kabulonga is a question that only an open judicial inquiry can properly answer,” Dr M’membe wrote.

He made three requests. First, that the DPP make or authorise an application to the High Court for the inquest. Second, that the office establish from the Inspector General of Police whether a coroner was ever notified of the death under section 12, and on what date. Third, that the postmortem and ballistic reports be released to the family and their lawyers without further delay.

The opposition leader framed the appeal around the constitutional independence of the office he was writing to. Article 180(7) provides that the DPP is not subject to the direction or control of any person or authority and must act in the public interest.

“I ask nothing of it on behalf of my party. I ask only that the law be followed. The family of Hon. Kafwaya, and the people of Zambia, look to your office to act without fear or favour,” he wrote.

The request goes to an office already deeply involved in the aftermath of that night. DPP Mr Gilbert Phiri is personally leading the prosecution of opposition leaders Mr Brian Mundubile, Mr Makebi Zulu and 16 others, arrested after the 14 August operations and facing charges relating to treason, sedition and terrorism.

Mr Kafwaya’s death has already been raised in those proceedings. In the constitutional bail case, defence lawyer Mr Sakwiba Sikota told the Lusaka High Court that Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu sought refuge at a United Nations facility because they feared for their lives after shootings at their homes and the former minister’s death.

The authorities maintain that the Kabulonga operation was lawful in its purpose, alleging that those arrested there were involved in an insurrection plot and that military-grade weapons were recovered during the raid. They have not publicly set out how Mr Kafwaya came to be shot.

The demand for answers did not begin with the Socialist Party. Former Cabinet minister Mr Given Lubinda has called for an independent inquest. In September, the European Parliament adopted a resolution urging Zambian authorities to establish independent and impartial investigations into the killing, a call the Government dismissed as premature.

In a separate statement, Dr M’membe asked the Human Rights Commission, which the Government says is overseeing the police investigation, to publish what it has found. He called on the Church, the legal profession and all political parties to unite behind one demand, that the law be followed, and urged President Hakainde Hichilema, as Head of State and Government, to let the law take its course.

He recalled a statement he made on 20 August, days after the death was confirmed, and repeated it.

“On 20 August I wrote that no crime can be committed in the name of elections or law enforcement. I say it again,” he said.

The letter was copied to the chairperson of the Human Rights Commission, the Minister of Home Affairs and Internal Security, the Inspector General of Police and the Kafwaya family. Dr M’membe said he would make the letter public and share the DPP’s response once it is received.

For Mr Kafwaya’s widow, Mrs Dinis Ng’andu Kafwaya, and their children, the questions remain the same as they were in August: how he died, who fired, and whether that force was lawful.

“Hon. Kafwaya’s family deserves the truth. So does Zambia,” Dr M’membe said.

The decision now rests with the DPP’s office, which must choose whether to take the application to the High Court before the death passes its third month without a single day in court.

The full text of the letter is reproduced below.

SOCIALIST PARTY

OFFICE OF THE PRESIDENT

Wednesday 11 November 2026

BY HAND

The Director of Public Prosecutions

National Prosecution Authority

Lusaka

Dear Director,

RE: REQUEST FOR AN APPLICATION UNDER SECTION 33 OF THE INQUESTS ACT, CHAPTER 36 OF THE LAWS OF ZAMBIA, FOR AN INQUEST INTO THE DEATH OF THE LATE HON. MUTOTWE KAFWAYA

I write as President of the Socialist Party, as a member of the legal profession and as a citizen of this Republic, to ask your office to act so that an inquest is held into the death of the late Hon. Mutotwe Kafwaya, former Minister of Transport and Member of Parliament for Lunte.

Background

Hon. Kafwaya died on 14 August 2026 during a joint security operation at a house in Kabulonga, Lusaka. On 19 August the Inspector General of Police confirmed that he had been fatally wounded during that operation. Three months have now passed. To the best of public knowledge no inquest has been opened. A postmortem examination was carried out, but its findings have not been made public, and the family has said that it was not able to have a pathologist of its own present. On 16 August the Government announced that eleven people present at the house had been arrested and would face charges. No comparable step has been taken to examine, before any court, the use of force that caused Hon. Kafwaya’s death.

The law

Section 4 of the Inquests Act provides that where a coroner is credibly informed that there is reasonable cause to suspect that a person has died a violent or unnatural death, the coroner shall hold an inquest as soon as is practicable. Section 12 requires a police officer who becomes aware of such a death to notify a coroner having jurisdiction. Section 6 postpones an inquest only where a person has been, or is about to be, charged with the murder or manslaughter of the deceased. To our knowledge no person has been so charged. Nothing in the Act therefore stands in the way of an inquest. Section 33(1)(a) provides that where the High Court, upon application made by or under the authority of the Director of Public Prosecutions, is satisfied that it is necessary or desirable to do so, it may order an inquest to be held touching the death of any person. Article 12(1) of the Constitution of Zambia protects the right to life. Article 12(3) permits the use of force only to the extent that is reasonably justifiable in the circumstances of the case. Whether that standard was met in Kabulonga is a question that only an open judicial inquiry can properly answer. Zambia is a State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, Article 4 of which protects the right to life, and to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Article 6 of which does the same. Both oblige the State to investigate any death caused by its agents promptly, independently and transparently.

What I ask of your office

a. That you make, or authorise, an application to the High Court under section 33(1)(a) of the Inquests Act for an order that an inquest be held into the death of Hon. Mutotwe Kafwaya.

b. That, in the meantime, your office establish from the Inspector General of Police whether a coroner was notified of the death under section 12, and on what date.

c. That your office use its good offices to ensure that the postmortem and ballistic reports are released to the family and their lawyers without further delay.

The independence of your office

Article 180(7) of the Constitution provides that the Director of Public Prosecutions shall not be subject to the direction or control of any person or authority, and shall have regard to the public interest. I ask nothing of it on behalf of my party. I ask only that the law be followed. The family of Hon. Kafwaya, and the people of Zambia, look to your office to act without fear or favour.

Response

I look forward to your response. As this is a matter of national importance, I will make this letter public, and I will share your response when it is received.

Yours faithfully,

Fred M’membe

President, Socialist Party

World.title: Proposed K22.7 billion allocation to agric sector receives kudos
World.content:
A Kasama based agricultural organisation has commended government for proposing a K22.7 billion allocation to agriculture, fisheries and livestock development in the 2027 National Budget.

Impanga Emayo Business Hub Director, Brian Changwe, says the development reflects government’s commitment to enhancing the agriculture sector as a key economic pillar as envisioned in the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Reverend Changwe said the set targets such as annual production of ten million metric tonnes of maize, three million tonnes of soya beans, one million tonnes of wheat and sugar will not only translate into food security but job creation as well.

“I am seeing three things here, there is food security, improved nutrition status and employment opportunities, the produce will need to be transported, we will have drivers, farm workers, loaders, and the like,” he explained.

Reverend Changwe has also welcomed the proposal to transition the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP) to a loan facility.

He has since advised small-scale farmers to embrace the development adding that the Ministry of Agriculture should carry out awareness on the new development.

“Usually, when people hear the term loan, they get worried but I believe this is something that our people should be sensitised on,” Reverend Changwe said.

He also praised government for promoting mechanisation and irrigation in the agriculture sector.

“This Grow Zambia Agenda is achievable with the interventions we are seeing from the government and for us as Impanga Emayo Business Hub, we believe in this too,” he stated.

Meanwhile, Reverend Changwe said the plan to realign the awarding of bursaries to the critical skills such as agriculture, tourism, mining and manufacturing to support the Grow Zambia Agenda is commendable.

World.title: Government warns against delays in implementation of projects
World.content:
Minister of Infrastructure and Urban Development, Collins Nzovu has warned that government will not allow delays in the implementation of infrastructure projects, especially where resources have been made available.

Mr Nzovu says delayed projects deny citizens the economic and social benefits of public investments.

He said this when he addressed Ministry staff, including officials from the Road Development Agency (RDA) and the National Council for Construction (NCC) at Mulungushi International Conference Centre in Lusaka.

The Minister called on staff to strengthen teamwork, coordination and accountability in implementing infrastructure projects.

He said collaboration among departments and institutions is critical to achieving the Government’s Grow Zambia Agenda.

“No single department or institution can successfully deliver infrastructure projects in isolation,” he said.

Mr Nzovu noted that the Ministry was central to the country’s development ambitions, which require reliable roads, railways, airports and other infrastructure to connect production areas to markets.

He also challenged engineers and planners to improve project designs and conduct thorough site assessments to avoid unnecessary variations, increased costs and delays.

Mr Nzovu pledged to support staff development through training, improved working conditions and career progression based on performance.

He urged employees to embrace a shared vision and take pride in their responsibilities, saying the success of the Grow Zambia Agenda depended on the Ministry’s ability to deliver quality infrastructure.

Meanwhile, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Infrastructure and Urban Development, Albert Malama has called for stronger collaboration between the Ministry and its statutory bodies to improve coordination and service delivery.

Prof Malama says effective engagement among staff and institutions is essential in advancing the Ministry’s mandate.

He noted that the meeting was the first of its kind to bring Ministry staff and statutory bodies together under one roof, with provincial officers participating virtually.

“This meeting is important as it is the first of its kind,” he said.

World.title: Serenje DEBS lauds free malpractice Grade 12 exams
World.content:
Serenje District Education Board Secretary (DEBS, Kellys Kapanga has disclosed that Grade 12 examinations are progressing well in the area, with no reported cases of examination malpractice.

Speaking in an interview with ZANIS, Mr Kapanga said the examinations are being conducted in accordance with the Examination of Zambia (ECZ) guidelines.

“We are not facing any major challenges. We have had the fuel for monitoring, while the other challenges are minor and we have been able to resolve them as they arose,” he explained.

Mr Kapanga said teachers assigned to invigilate the examinations have been adequately oriented on their roles and responsibilities to ensure the smooth conduct of the exercise.

He further disclosed that teachers from schools near the Central Business District (CBD) have been swapped to ensure candidates were invigilated by teachers from other schools.

Mr Kapanga said his office has conducted two monitoring exercises covering all the 14 examination centres in the district to ensure that the established guidelines are being followed.

The DEBs commended the government for the support rendered to his office, saying this has contributed to the efficient and effective administration of the examinations.

Mr Kapanga also applauded the community for working with his office to ensure that the examinations are conducted efficiently and without malpractice.

A total of 1,057 learners comprising 441 girls and 616 boys are sitting for their Grade 12 examination at 14 centres across Serenje District.

World.title: Govt. calls for increased promotion of Mwela Rock Monument
World.content:
Minister of Culture and Arts, Christopher Chibuye has called for improved revenue collection strategies and increased publicity for Mwela Rock Art National Monument in Northern Province to enhance its tourism potential.

Mr Chibuye says management of the site needs to review and strengthen its revenue projections to ensure that set targets are achieved.

Speaking in an interview with the media in Kasama just after visiting the site, Mr Chibuye emphasised the need for increased publicity and promotion of the country’s heritage sites to attract more visitors.

He said effective publicity would help raise awareness of the historical and cultural significance of the sites while boosting their visibility among local and international tourists.

Mr Chibuye observed that limited publicity remains one of the major challenges affecting the promotion of Zambia’s heritage sites.

He said the country needs to embrace strategic marketing and advertising through television, radio and other platforms, including engaging local artists to showcase its rich cultural heritage to the world.

Mr Chibuye further called for increased private sector investment in heritage sites, saying this would help improve facilities and enhance their attractiveness to both local and international tourists.

He said such investments would also contribute to tourism growth and create economic opportunities as the country works towards achieving its development aspirations under the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Meanwhile, National Heritage Conservation Commission Executive Director, Kagosi Mwamulowe said the Commission intends to increase the number of heritage sites covered under its preservation and promotion programmes.

Mr Mwamulowe said Mwela Rock Art National Monument is among the sites the Commission intends to pursue for inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

He said the move would enhance the site’s international recognition and strengthen efforts to preserve its historical and cultural significance.

Mr Mwamulowe added that the Commission remains committed to safeguarding Zambia’s heritage and ensuring that important historical sites are preserved for future generations.
