World.title: A mother at the counter, a widow at the door: Zambia must not grow used to this
World.content:
A mother at the counter, a widow at the door: Zambia must not grow used to this

Somewhere in Lusaka this week, a mother is waiting for a piece of paper.

She is Grace Nampokolwe Banda. Since 14 October, when her son Emmanuel, the man the country knows as Jay Jay, was taken in Mozambique, she has not seen his face. In her sworn affidavit she describes going from police station to police station, asking the same question at counter after counter, and leaving each time without an answer.

On Wednesday she finally had a court order in her hand. The State was told to bring her son before a judge. Morning came, and he did not appear. The judge gave the State until the afternoon, and still he did not appear. The State said he was too ill to be moved from a military hospital.

So now she waits for a doctor’s report. Not for her son, not for his voice, not for his hand, but for a document describing a body she is not allowed to see.

Let that sit for a moment. A mother in a constitutional democracy has had to hire lawyers and go to the High Court simply to establish that her child is alive, and on what terms the State is keeping him. The best the country could offer her on Wednesday was the promise of paperwork on Friday.

Whatever Jay Jay Banda is accused of, and he faces serious charges from 2024 that he must answer, his mother has done nothing wrong. Her only demand is the oldest one in law: show me my son.

Across town lives another woman whose wait has already ended in the worst way.

On 14 August, the day after Zambians voted, a security operation went into a house in Kabulonga. When it was over, former Minister of Transport Mutotwe Kafwaya was dead. For days his family did not know. His wife went to court seeking habeas corpus, asking the State to produce a husband who, it would later be confirmed, was already gone. That confirmation came on 19 August, five days after he was shot.

Read that again. A wife petitioned a court to bring her husband back, and the State’s answer was a death.

Three months later, Dinis Ng’andu Kafwaya and her children still do not know how he died. A postmortem was carried out, but its findings have never been published. The family says it was not allowed to have its own pathologist in the room. No officer has been named. No inquest has opened, though the law says one must be held into every violent death “as soon as is practicable”.

In those same three months, the machinery of the State has moved with remarkable speed against almost everyone else. Within two days of Mr Kafwaya’s death, eleven people from that house had been arrested and told they would face charges. Opposition leader Brian Mundubile, his running mate Makebi Zulu and 16 others have been held since August on charges that include treason.

A former ambassador, Martha Mwitumwa, has been charged with treason. Her daughter Esther was granted release by the High Court and then re-arrested by police inside the court building itself. The doors of justice opened for her, and then they closed again before she reached the street.

This is what should catch in every Zambian throat. It is not that the State is enforcing the law; that is its duty, and it must do it. It is that the law seems to run at two speeds. For the accused it is swift, certain and relentless. For the dead and the disappeared it is slow, silent and still “under investigation”.

Watch what happened in two courtrooms on the same Wednesday. In the High Court, the State raised yet another objection to the bail application of the 18 detainees, this time to strike out paragraphs about video footage of the raid on Mr Zulu’s home. A day earlier, the judges had thrown out its last objection. The application was filed on 14 October. It has still not been heard on its merits.

In the magistrate’s court, defence lawyers asked for time to take instructions. The DPP called it “deliberate machinations”. The lawyers withdrew, and two men who have been in custody for three months stood in the dock alone, arguing for their own right to be prepared.

When the accused ask for time, it is called a game. When the State takes three months and opens no inquest, it is called process.

The State has its case, and fairness demands that it be heard. It says the Kabulonga operation uncovered an insurrection plot and military-grade weapons. It says the accused are a flight risk and too influential to be released safely. It says being in the opposition puts no one beyond the reach of the law, and that the courts are open to anyone who wishes to test its conduct.

If all of that is true, the State has nothing to fear from the light. Let the postmortem be published. Let the ballistic report go to the family. Let a coroner sit in open court and hear how a former minister came to be shot dead in a house in Kabulonga. Let Jay Jay Banda be seen, on a stretcher if necessary, so that his mother knows he is breathing.

A government confident of its account does not hide the evidence that would prove it right.

The world has noticed, even if we have tried not to. The European Parliament voted 562 to one for an independent investigation into Mr Kafwaya’s death. Britain says it is watching the detention of UNIP leader Bishop Trevor Mwamba, whose family announced him missing and spent 48 hours not knowing whether he was alive. United Nations human rights officials have spoken. The Government calls this premature, and China’s ambassador says democracy should be judged by a country’s own people.

He is right about that last point. This is not a matter for Brussels or London. It is a matter for us. And the question every Zambian must answer honestly is this: are we comfortable with what we are becoming?

This is the country that buried a one-party state without a civil war. It handed over power peacefully at the ballot box more than once. Its citizens learned to say, with pride, that Zambia is a peaceful nation. A nation is not peaceful because it is quiet. It is peaceful because when a mother asks where her son is, she gets an answer. It is peaceful because when a husband is killed, his widow is not left to read about his death in a police statement.

Peace without answers is not peace. It is silence. And silence, as Fred M’membe warned this week, is not the same thing as contentment.

On Friday, the courts will sit again. A doctor’s report will be read. A ruling on a flash disk will be delivered. Somewhere in the National Prosecution Authority, a letter asking for an inquest is waiting for a reply.

And on Saturday, three months will have passed since Mutotwe Kafwaya left home and never came back.

His children will mark that day without a grave they understand. Jay Jay Banda’s mother will mark it without having seen her son. Eighteen families will mark it with a loved one behind bars, still waiting for a bail hearing that keeps receding like the horizon.

We can look away. Many already have. But a country is measured not by how it treats the powerful on their best days, but by how it treats the powerless on their worst. A mother at a police counter. A widow at the door. A family waiting for a body to be explained.

They are asking for nothing more than the truth. If we cannot give them that, we should at least have the decency not to call this normal.

By Lusaka Times Political Desk

World.title: Munetsi reflects on gruelling demands of English Championship
World.content:
ZIMBABWE international midfielder Marshall Munetsi has reflected on the gruelling nature of the English Championship, where teams are required to play matches every two or three days, leaving little time for training and recovery.

The Warriors captain says the congested fixture schedule makes squad depth crucial, with clubs needing at least two quality players in every position to remain competitive throughout the demanding campaign.

Munetsi, who is enjoying being back at Wolverhampton Wanderers after spending the second half of last season on loan at French side Paris FC, believes the club’s strength in depth has been key to their performances this season.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Insurers urged to build trust and embrace technology
World.content:
THE Southern Africa Insurance Indaba 2026 kicked off in Victoria Falls this Thursday morning with Insurance Institute of Zimbabwe (IIZ) president Clementine Chinyuku urging insurers across the continent to embrace innovation, strengthen consumer trust and expand access to affordable insurance amid evolving economic and technological risks.

Chinyuku said the industry needed to adapt to emerging challenges while ensuring that technological advancements are translated into meaningful benefits for policyholders.

Addressing delegates at the second edition of the Southern Africa Insurance Indaba, held under the theme “Futureproofing Africa’s Insurance: Building Resilient, Inclusive and Technology-Driven Markets”, Chinyuku said the sector needed to move beyond incremental reforms.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Local Government permanent secretary Muguti relieved of his duties
World.content:
Local Government and Public Works permanent secretary Tafadzwa Muguti has been relieved of his duties just two months after his appointment to the post.

The announcement was confirmed by Chief Secretary to the President and Cabinet Martin Rushwaya in a statement.

“In terms of Section 205, subsection (1) of the Constitution of Zimbabwe, His Excellency the President Emmerson Mnangagwa has appointed Dr Addmore Pazvakavambwa as permanent secretary in the Ministry of Local Government and Public Works,” said Rushwaya.

World.title: Garwe: Operation Chenesa to continue until residents “self-regulate”
World.content:
LOCAL Government and Public Works minister Daniel Garwe says Operation Chenesa will continue until Zimbabweans are used to living in a clean, orderly environment.

Addressing journalists in Harare this Wednesday, Garwe added that municipal police officers would soon have power arrest, offenders tried at council-run courts of law.

Garwe said earlier clean-ups lasted only a week or two because government assumed councils would take over.

World.title: Journalism is not a favour to those in power
World.content:
THERE is a troubling misconception among some people in positions of power that journalists should know when to stop asking questions, soften their reporting or, more importantly, look the other way.

Sometimes, the expectation comes through telephone calls, intermediaries and colleagues appealing for an end to stories considered damaging to someone’s reputation.

But journalism is not about protecting reputations.

THE National Athletics Association of Zimbabwe (NAAZ) says Ropafadzo Mzondo’s historic gold medal triumph at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games was no accident, but the result of deliberate planning, preparation and investment in young talent.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 12, 2026
World.content:
Kenya Discharges Last Ebola Patient, Begins 42-Day Countdown

Kenya has discharged its last Ebola patient, bringing the total number of recoveries to seven and marking a major step towards containing the outbreak. The country has now begun a 42-day countdown before it can officially be declared Ebola-free. No new confirmed cases have been reported since 20 October. Health authorities said that all 135 identified contacts have completed their 21-day monitoring period, with no evidence of wider community transmission. However, surveillance will continue at border crossings, airports and health facilities throughout the countdown. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) described it as an important achievement in the regional response to the outbreak. Kenya has also urged countries that introduced travel and visa restrictions over the outbreak to reconsider them.

Eswatini Gives Foreign-Owned Illegal Businesses 12 Months to Close



Eswatini has begun closing businesses owned by foreign nationals, particularly Asian traders, following the approval of a law aimed at increasing economic participation by emaSwati. The move comes after complaints from local traders that foreign-owned businesses are taking over traditional markets, increasing competition and threatening local livelihoods. Parliament has agreed that foreign business owners should be given at least 12 months to leave. But there are still disputes over how fast the law should be enforced. The government said the legislation is aimed at creating more economic opportunities for citizens amid widespread poverty and unemployment. The crackdown comes amid growing economic frustrations and calls for political reform in the kingdom.

Tundu Lissu Verdict - What It Means For Tanzania Democracy

On November 6, Tanzania's main opposition leader Tundu Lissu was sentenced to four years in prison for incitement following heavy unrest during the October 2025 elections. He was acquitted of treason charges that carried the death penalty. Lissu, who leads the opposition CHADEMA party, has rejected the verdict. He argued that incitement was not among the original charges brought against him. His party has indicated that it intends to appeal the conviction. The case follows Tanzania's disputed October 2025 elections, which were marred by deadly protests, an internet shutdown and a security crackdown. Political observers said that the verdict raises further concerns about political freedoms, opposition participation and the state of democracy in the country.

DR Congo Journalists Face Rising Attacks Over Ebola Reporting

Journalists in the Democratic Republic of Congo are facing increasing attacks and threats, particularly those reporting on the country's worsening Ebola outbreak. The Committee to Protect Journalists says reporters and media workers have been assaulted over Ebola awareness campaigns, with some accused of spreading misinformation about the disease. In one incident, at least six people attacked the editor of a community radio station in North Kivu. Another journalist was assaulted by youths armed with machetes. Other journalists have also faced threats, including an armed intrusion at a journalist's home and an attack on staff at Radio Terra FM. The attacks are causing concern regarding the safety of journalists who are attempting to combat misinformation during the health crisis and press freedom.

Cameroon Sets February 2027 Date for Parliamentary, Local Polls

The parliamentary and municipal elections will be held on 7 February 2027 in Cameroon. The elections will represent a serious political test for the ruling party of President Paul Biya. The elections will be the first nationwide vote since Biya controversially won his eighth presidential term in October 2025. The election was marred by deadly protests and fraud allegations. The ruling Cameroon People's Democratic Movement currently dominates parliament and local government but could face a stronger challenge from opposition parties. Political observers said that the opposition will seek to build on growing public dissatisfaction with the government and demands for political change. The vote is also expected to test whether the ruling party can maintain its grip on power after more than four decades under Biya's leadership.

Ghana Hires US Lawyer to Pursue Justice for Nationals Killed

Ghana has approved the appointment of prominent American civil rights lawyer Ben Crump to help secure justice for Ghanaians killed in the United States in recent months. The country's Permanent Mission in New York will engage Crump to assist with the cases at no cost to Ghanaian taxpayers. Ghana's Foreign Ministry said that the move reflects the government's commitment to protecting the rights and dignity of its citizens living abroad. The ministry also expressed appreciation for Crump's willingness to assist following a positive telephone discussion. Ghana has acknowledged the cooperation of US authorities as both countries pursue justice for the victims.

Close 

UN Chief Calls for End to Fossil Fuels at COP31

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has urged world leaders at COP31 in Turkey to end dependence on fossil fuels. He warned that the climate crisis is advancing faster than global efforts to address it. He called on governments to tax oil companies' windfall profits and accused the fossil fuel industry of using its influence to delay climate action. The summit comes amid growing climate disasters, including heatwaves, wildfires and deadly floods, but expectations for breakthroughs remain low. Several prominent world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, are also absent. Meanwhile, Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has called for renewed global commitment to climate action, while host Turkey is pushing for greater electrification across transport, buildings and industry by 2035.

World.title: South Africa: City Power Nears Completion of Joburg Repairs - South African News Briefs - November 12, 2026
World.content:
press review

Joburg Power Outage Delays Restoration to Key Facilities

Johannesburg City Power continues efforts to restore electricity after technical problems at the Mayfair substation, EWN reports . This has delayed the restoration of power to essential services, including Netcare Garden City Hospital. The outage has also affected residents and businesses around Auckland Park, who have been without electricity. City Power said that repairs at the Hursthill substation are about 95% complete. SABC broadcasting operations have returned to normal despite ongoing supply challenges.

24 Hospitalised After Ammonia Leak at Ekurhuleni Factory

Twenty-four employees have been hospitalised after an ammonia leak at the Festive Chicken facility in Olifantsfontein, Ekurhuleni, reports SABC News . The leak reportedly occurred when a pressure-release valve malfunctioned during routine maintenance, exposing workers to ammonia fumes and causing respiratory distress. Emergency services transported all 24 affected employees to nearby hospitals for treatment. Ekurhuleni Disaster and Emergency Services said that ammonia levels at the facility have since returned to zero.

Soweto Student Murder Accused to Return to Court

A 31-year-old man accused of murdering 22-year-old student Botshelo Mabua in Soweto is set to appear in the Protea Magistrates Court, reports EWN. Sizwe Yende was denied bail after being accused of strangling Mabua following an alleged argument in September. The State alleged that he pushed her, causing her to hit her head on a table, before strangling her. The case is expected to be transferred for trial proceedings. The National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) pledged to pursue justice in cases of gender-based violence and femicide.

More South African news

World.title: Malawi: Nationwide Protests Planned Over Malawi's Economic Challenges
World.content:
Frustrated Malawians are preparing to take to the streets in nationwide demonstrations on 17 November 2026, piling pressure on the government over worsening economic hardships and failing public services.

The protests, organised by a group calling itself Concerned Citizens, are set to take place in major cities and districts including Lilongwe, Blantyre, Mzuzu, Zomba, Kasungu, Mulanje, Balaka, Mchinji, Salima, Chikwawa and Phalombe.

According to a circular issued by the organisers, demonstrators will demand answers over persistent fuel shortages, foreign currency scarcity, electricity blackouts, shortages of essential medicines in public hospitals, water supply disruptions and alleged passport scandals.

The group says Malawians are no longer satisfied with assurances and want government to provide clear, time-bound solutions to the country's mounting challenges.



In a move likely to increase political pressure, the organisers are also calling for the resignation of three Cabinet ministers whom they blame for failures in key sectors.

The ministers named are Finance Minister Joseph Mwanamvekha, Health Minister Madalitso Baloyi and Energy Minister Jean Mathanga.

"The Concerned Citizens are demanding the resignation of the following Ministers," the circular states.

The planned demonstrations come as households and businesses continue to struggle with rising costs, shortages of essential commodities and unreliable public services.

Organisers say the protests are intended to force authorities to account for the country's challenges and outline when ordinary Malawians can expect improvements.

With anger growing over the state of the economy and public services, the demonstrations are expected to become a major test of public sentiment towards the government's handling of the crisis.

World.title: Kenya: Kenya's Last Ebola Patient Leaves Hospital
World.content:
A patient is carried to an Ebola treatment centre in the DR Congo.

Kenya had nine confirmed cases, while DR Congo continues to battle its deadliest outbreak of the disease.

Kenyan Health Minister Aden Duale said on Wednesday that the east African country had discharged its last remaining Ebola patient from a Nairobi hospital.

The final person to undergo treatment for the disease in Kenya had 11 contact cases, Duale said, who will also undergo 21 days of quarantine.

Kenya will be declared Ebola-free on December 23 if no one else exhibits symptoms until then.

"Through strengthened surveillance and contact tracing, all 135 contacts linked to the index case were successfully traced and monitored," the health ministry said.

"All nine confirmed cases remained within a single transmission cluster, with no community transmission recorded," it added.

The first of its nine cases, reported on October 6, came from a Kenyan man who had recently travelled back from the Demoratic Republic of Congo.

Seven patients recovered, and two passed away.

What is the state of the Ebola outbreak?

DR Congo on Wednesday reported 11,000 cases of the virulent, often fatal disease.

This current outbreak, which began in May, has become Congo's deadliest, claiming 5,387 lives so far.

There has also been one case reported in Nigeria, from a patient who had recently travelled from Uganda, which saw a small cluster of the disease.

World.title: Ghana: Ghana Engages U.S. Civil Rights Lawyer Ben Crump to Seek Justice for Ghanaians Killed in U.S.
World.content:
Approval has been granted to Ghana's Permanent Mission in New York to engage the services of celebrated US civil rights lawyer, Ben Crump, to assist Ghana in securing justice for all Ghanaians killed in the US in recent months.

The engagement will be at no cost to the Ghanaian taxpayer.

"Ghana will go every length to secure justice and safeguard the dignity of our dear nationals abroad," the statement said.

The Foreign Minister expressed gratitude to Ben Crump for the positive telephone discussion on the matter.

Related Articles

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Overhauls Key Government Positions
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia, November 11, 2026 - President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has announced a new wave of appointments and nominations across several government institutions, including the appointment of a new Mayor of Monrovia, two county superintendents, and ambassador-designates, as part of efforts to strengthen public administration and institutional leadership.

The appointments, announced Wednesday by the Executive Mansion, affect eight government institutions, including the Ministries of Foreign Affairs, Local Government, and Commerce and Industry, as well as the Monrovia City Corporation (MCC).

Other institutions affected include the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau, Agricultural and Industrial Training Bureau, National Insurance Corporation of Liberia (NICOL), and the Independent National Commission on Human Rights (INCHR).

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Among the major appointments is that of James Kpadeh Mulbah as Mayor of Monrovia, placing him at the helm of the capital city's administration.

In the Ministry of Local Government, President Boakai has appointed Wesley D. M. Nyenatoh, Sr. as Superintendent of River Gee County and Elijah G. Freeman as Superintendent of Grand Cape Mount County.

The appointments also affect the leadership of Grand Cape Mount County, with outgoing Superintendent Foley Kiatamba expected to be reassigned to another government position.

At the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the President has named Stephen J. H. Zargo and Jeremiah Solunteh as Ambassador-Designates. Their nominations are expected to proceed through the applicable confirmation process.

Meanwhile, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry will have a new Deputy Minister for Public Services, with Mr. Ceebee C. D. Barshell appointed to the position.

In other appointments, President Boakai named George Mulbah as Commissioner of the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau, while Mike T. Swengbe has been appointed Deputy Director General for Technical Services at the Agricultural and Industrial Training Bureau.

The President also appointed John-Charuk Siafa as Officer-in-Charge of the National Insurance Corporation of Liberia.

In a move to strengthen the leadership of the Independent National Commission on Human Rights, President Boakai has nominated four individuals to fill existing vacancies at the institution following the completion of the vetting process by the Chief Justice of Liberia.

The nominees are Cllr. Philomena T. Williams, Mr. Shiwoh Kamara, Mr. Domah Cooper, and Cllr. Mohammed E. Fahnbulleh, who has been re-nominated.

All four nominees are expected to serve as Commissioners of the human rights institution, subject to the applicable confirmation process.

Close 

The appointments come at a time when the Commission remains an important institution in promoting and protecting fundamental human rights, monitoring compliance with national and international human rights obligations, and holding public institutions accountable.

Meanwhile, President Boakai has expressed special appreciation to Abdullah S. Swaray for his service while holding over as Acting Managing Director of the National Insurance Corporation of Liberia.

The President emphasized that the new appointments and nominations are intended to strengthen government operations and improve leadership across the affected institutions.

He urged the newly appointed and nominated officials to discharge their responsibilities with integrity, professionalism, and dedication to public service, stressing that the interests of the Liberian people must remain central to their work.

The Executive Mansion noted that the nominations and appointments requiring legislative approval remain subject to confirmation by the Liberian Senate.

World.title: Nigeria: Nigerian Court Detains Journalist Daniel Ojukwu On Cybercrime Charges
World.content:
Abuja — The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on Nigerian authorities to immediately drop the criminal charges against journalist Daniel Ojukwu, release him unconditionally, and stop criminalizing the press for their work.

On November 10, a federal court in Nigeria's capital, Abuja, remanded Ojukwu, a correspondent with the privately owned Foundation for Investigative Journalism (FIJ), to the Kuje Custodial Centre until December 1 on cybercrime and criminal defamation charges, according to a copy of the charge sheet, which CPJ reviewed. Ojukwu, who traveled to the hearing from the southwestern Lagos state, pleaded not guilty to the 12 counts brought against him.

FIJ's founder and award-winning journalist, Fisayo Soyombo, who faces the same charges, was not in court but is expected at the next hearing, according to FIJ's lawyers, Oluseye Ayo Moore and Abimbola Ojenike, who spoke with CPJ.

"Nigerian authorities must swiftly drop the criminal charges against journalist Daniel Ojukwu and FIJ founder Fisayo Soyombo, and repeal laws that criminalize journalism," said CPJ Africa Director Angela Quintal. "Nigeria's cybercrime and criminal laws have too often been used to target journalists. With elections approaching, authorities must not ignore the damaging impact of these charges on press freedom and journalists' ability to report freely and without fear."

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The charges are linked to four related investigations FIJ published between late 2023 and early 2024, which uncovered a number of suspicious government contracts by the office of the special assistant to the Nigerian government on sustainable development goals, Princess Adejoke Orelope-Adefulire.

The investigations were also related to Ojukwu's secret arrest and 10-day detention in 2024, according to FIJ's lawyers.

Moore told CPJ that the case was adjourned until December 1 to give prosecutors time to respond to the bail application filed by the defense.

The journalists are charged with violating:

sections 27(b), 24(2)(a) of the Cybercrimes Act, which each carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in jail or a fine of 25 million naira (US$18,570)

sections 517 and 375 of the Criminal Code Act, which each carry a maximum sentence of two years

CPJ's calls and messages to Orelope-Adefulire for comments went unanswered. Her lawyer, Muiz Banire, defended the charges. He said that journalists should practice responsible journalism, but added, "Let them show you that what they published about my client is correct."

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Spike in Attacks On DR Congo Journalists Fueled in Part By Ebola Reporting
World.content:
The recent spike in physical assaults and threats directed at journalists in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has extended into November, as the worsening Ebola virus outbreak has triggered a backlash against reporters covering the spread of the disease in the eastern part of the country.

Fear surrounding the Ebola outbreak, which has exploded into the second-worst on record since it was detected in May, has led to attacks on medical workers and raised the risk for reporters trying to counter rampant misinformation, with CPJ documenting attacks on two radio stations in the past week.

On November 4, at least six unidentified individuals beat Jackson Mbusa Vagheni, editor-in-chief of Radio du Peuple Oïcha, a community radio station in the North Kivu province town of Oïcha, as he was leaving his office. He sustained injuries to his leg, arms, and back, and went to a local hospital for treatment.

Mbusa, who has since gone into hiding and continues to receive threats by phone, told CPJ that the attackers accused him of spreading false information about Ebola. "The local population in the town of Oïcha does not tolerate the awareness-raising work we are conducting in the media regarding the Ebola virus," he said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

On November 5, a group of unidentified youths armed with machetes entered Radiotélévision Bafwasende's (RTBD) offices, in the northeast Tshopo province town of Bafwasende, and punched journalist Finance Sianga Bilanga. The attack was believed to be connected to Sianga's involvement in Ebola awareness-raising activities, the radio station's director, Ibrahim Mulamba, told CPJ. The journalist was not injured thanks to the neighbors' intervention, he said.

Two weeks earlier, on October 24, Sianga had been attacked by unknown individuals following an RTBD report revealing that several local healthcare facilities had closed their doors and that medical staff had stopped coming to work, fearing threats from residents who view the Ebola epidemic as a fabrication, said Mulamba.

In an earlier incident involving Ebola-related reporting, Guillaume Munguakonkwa, a news presenter at community radio station Kamole FM, in the eastern South Kivu province locality of Nyangezi, was detained on July 27 and held for three days in a cell belonging to the intelligence service of the M23 and the Congo River Alliance (AFC), for producing a report on the Ebola virus. His voice recorder, mobile phone, and notebook were confiscated.

In two other recent incidents involving attacks on DRC journalists, CPJ was unable to determine whether they were targeted for their reporting.

On November 3, an armed man broke into the home of Zahabu Celemami, director of the YouTube-based news channel Clever Flash TV, in the South Kivu province town of Uvira, with the intent to kill him, Patient Debaba, the local president of the National Press Union of the Congo (UNPC), told CPJ.

When the intruder pointed his weapon at him, Zahabu lunged and seized the firearm. After a fierce struggle, the assailant fled. The next morning, Zahabu delivered the weapon to the local military intelligence office, which filed a report on the weapon seizure, reviewed by CPJ.

On November 7, an unidentified man burst into Radio Terra FM's offices, in the Ituri province village of Kolokoto, and ordered staffers to leave the premises while attempting to force his way into the studio, the station's director, Samuel Warom, told CPJ.

The man assaulted cameraman Mechak Piker and journalists Mungunuti Boaz, Innocent Jackson, and Dominique Ukochi, who sustained an injury to his right foot while attempting to come to his colleagues' aid. The assailant was taken into custody by the Congolese National Police (PNC) and was set to be transferred to the public prosecutor's office on November 10.

In February 2023, Radio Terra FM had been targeted with arson and death threats after the station raised awareness about corruption and environmental protection laws, Warom said.

Close 

Meanwhile, on November 6, individuals claiming to be close to the governor of Kasaï-Central province, Joseph-Moïse Kambulu Nkonko, sent a series of threats, reviewed by the CPJ, to members of the Collective of Investigative Journalists. The group, which includes journalists Jeff Mbuyi, Fabrice Mbumba, Jean-Pierre Kabue, Théodore Kadingu, and Vidram Mbuyi, had conducted an investigation into illegal gold mining in the Luiza territory, according to Jeff Mbuyi and Mbumba, who spoke with the CPJ. The report, which CPJ reviewed, was published by several local media outlets.

Following the investigation, the provincial assembly established a commission to review Kambulu's administration of the province, which the unidentified individuals blame on the journalist collective.

When CPJ attempted to seek comment via phone and messaging app the military governor of North Kivu, Maj. Gen. Somo Kakule Évariste, and the governor of Tshopo province, Paulin Lendongolia Lebabonga, they did not answer. Kambulu told CPJ he would instruct one of his associates to return our call, but they have not.

World.title: GOP senator says Republicans can 'forget 2028' as party looks to reclaim Upper Chamber

Sen. Jim Justice, R-W. Va., said the GOP can "forget" about taking back the Senate majority in 2028 after Democrats' blue wave secured the majority in both chambers of Congress following last week's midterm elections.

Eight Republican-held Senate seats were flipped, bringing the Democratic caucus to 55 seats after Democrat Scott Colom was projected on Wednesday to win Mississippi’s Senate race. The caucus could gain another seat if Democrat Mary Peltola holds onto her narrow lead in Alaska.

"You can forget 2028. Absolutely," Justice told the Washington Examiner of the next federal election.

"I hope and pray we don’t lose the presidency. But this is such a colossal blow that it is beyond belief how colossal this is to America," he continued.

GOP EYES SENATE COMEBACK AFTER DEMOCRATIC BLOODBATH, BUT ANOTHER POLITICAL NIGHTMARE COULD AWAIT

Justice joined President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other Republicans in partially attributing the party's midterm losses to the war in Iran, which led to surging fuel prices.

Gas prices are nearly 90 cents per gallon higher than a year ago, according to AAA, which listed the national average at about $3.94 per gallon on Wednesday, compared with $3.07 a year earlier.

"Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for," Thune told reporters earlier this week. "But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us."

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, who was chosen to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, Republicans' Senate campaign arm for the 2028 cycle, said the GOP must learn from their disastrous showing in the midterms.

"I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it," he said.

World.title: War of words between Michigan Wolverines-Oregon Ducks heats up as Dan Lanning responds to criticisms
World.content:
Well, the Big Ten Conference might not be having the best season on the field, but off the field? The drama just keeps brewing. And of all teams, this time it involves ... the Michigan Wolverines and Oregon Ducks?

The two teams, both having varying degrees of disappointing results thus far in 2026, face off on Saturday in Eugene, and despite the lack of history between the two programs, there's some bad blood rapidly brewing.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

It started thanks to already-embattled Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham. His first season in Ann Arbor has been, to put it mildly, well below expectations. While at Utah, the 66-year-old was known for being a calm, steady voice of leadership who seemed to always win the games he needed to win. The Utes punched well above their historical weight, and his penchant for stability. Whittingham was in Salt Lake City for 32 years, looked like a perfect fit for a Michigan program coming off years of turmoil.

MICHIGAN'S NEW HEAD COACH POURS COLD WATER ON OHIO STATE RIVALRY: 'HATE IS A STRONG WORD'

But the Wolverines' struggles started almost immediately. Whittingham dismissed the importance of the Michigan-Ohio State rivalry game, which put him on the wrong foot with most fans. Then the Wolverines required some questionable clock management from the replay review crew to pull out a miraculous 13-12 comeback win over Western Michigan. They rebounded to beat Oklahoma the following week, but lost to Iowa, Minnesota and Indiana from late September to late October.

Their offense has been dismal all season, culminating in an awful 15-6 loss to Michigan State last on November 7. Instead of progressing in his second year as a starter, Bryce Underwood has ranged from disappointing to unacceptably bad. To the point where Whittingham benched him for backup Tommy Carr. All this has led to speculation and outright discussion around Michigan that boosters are preparing to pull together enough to buy Whittingham out after just one season. It also might explain why the normally uncontroversial coach is making headlines.

MICHIGAN HIRED KYLE WHITTINGHAM TO FIX ITS MESS. INSTEAD, HE’S CREATED AN EVEN BIGGER ONE WITH WOLVERINES

At a news conference ahead of this weekend's game, Whittingham praised Oregon head coach Dan Lanning, then took a shot at the Ducks' immense financial resources.

"Outstanding football coach, defensive-minded coach. That’s his background. Tireless recruiter. He really does a great job recruiting, and it doesn’t hurt that you have $50+ million dollars at your disposal to, in essence outbid everybody," he said. "Not everybody, but a lot of people. But that’s not his fault. That’s a credit. I mean, that’s a credit to their program and their dedication and desire to win and the support they have. NIL is the name of the game in recruiting these days. It’s shifted so much.

"It used to be the facilities you had and the tradition and all these other things, and now it’s, ‘Oh, this is all great, but these guys have a hundred grand more for me. So that’s a little bit of a factor to say the least. But not to take anything away from Dan, because he is an outstanding recruiter."

Maybe there's some personal animus there, stemming from a fight between the two over a recruit or recruits? Regardless of the motivations though, Whittingham's right that the Ducks have significant advantages over other teams. Lanning though, unsurprisingly heard about it and, well, didn't love it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

On Wednesday, Lanning said he had "nothing to say," then said something back.

"I’ve got nothing to say to Coach Whit other than I think he’s an unbelievable coach, and I get it," he said. "They’re spending more of their money right now on their coaches that they’re letting go, so maybe it makes it hard to sign players.

"But I know they’ve signed a couple of guys that we weren’t able to compete with what they decided to do, and maybe a lot of that money is tied up for them in another player. I don’t know. But Coach Whittingham is an unbelievable coach. He’s a Hall of Fame coach. I’ve got nothing but respect for him."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

That is definitely more than "nothing" to say!

Both coaches are right about their fronthanded criticisms and backhanded compliments. Lanning deserves a ton of credit for helping keep Oregon's season (mostly) on the rails, recovering after losses to UCLA and Illinois to beat Northwestern and then Ohio State in Columbus. But the Ducks entered 2026 with championship aspirations in large part because of their very expensive roster.

Yes, Dante Moore got hurt against USC, but that came after Oregon was thoroughly dismantled by Oklahoma State. And the money they have allowed them to sign Dylan Raiola, who started at Nebraska in 2025, as a backup. A luxury few other teams enjoy. They can outbid almost anyone if they really want to, or if they value a player more than the other team.



So Whittingham is right that Lanning is a great recruiter, a very good head coach, and also has immense resources at his disposal.

Lanning is right to take a pot shot at Michigan's coaching staff problems, including the $10 million buyout owed to Jason Beck after just a few months of a three-year deal. And he's also right that Whittingham has been a great head coach his entire career. Just an incredible exchange of mutual praise, admiration, and sarcastic criticisms.

Before the season, Oregon-Michigan seemed like one of the big games on the calendar, must-see TV for college football fans. Most of the shine is off, now that the Wolverines are buried and Oregon is clinging to hopes of reaching the Big Ten Conference Championship, but the war of words off the field has made the on-field game must-see TV all over again.

World.title: Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski, Yankees' Cam Schlittler named unanimous Cy Young Award winners for 2026 MLB season
World.content:
Milwaukee Brewers’ Jacob Misiorowski and New York Yankees’ Cam Schlittler were named unanimous Cy Young Award winners on Wednesday, confirming what many believed would be the case as the two most dominant starters in baseball during the 2026 MLB season.

Misiorowski, who led a Brewers pitching staff to the franchise’s first-ever World Series title, received all 30 first-place votes by the Baseball Writers’ Association of America. Philadelphia Phillies’ left-hander Cristopher Sanchez came in second place, while Atlanta Braves veteran lefty Chris Sale finished third.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Schlittler, in his first full season with the Yankees, was a breakout star in a loaded rotation. He also received all 30 first-place votes, while Toronto Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease and Cleveland Guardians Parker Messick finished second and third, respectively.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

It was also announced on Wednesday that San Diego Padres closer Mason Miller and Blue Jays closer Louis Varland won the inaugural Reliever of the Year award for their respective leagues.

Misiorowski, the 24-year-old with a lightning rod for an arm that lives in the triple digits with his fastball, had the best ERA for a starter in baseball this season at 1.80, while collecting 252 strikeouts in 30 starts, which also led the league.

As the Brewers went on to win 103 regular-season games, "The Miz" pitched to a 0.80 WHIP, while owning a 6.6 fWAR which led all pitchers.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Misiorowski became the fourth Brewers pitcher to ever win the Cy Young Award, the latest being Corbin Burnes in 2021. Pete Vuckovich (1982) and Rollie Fingers (1981) collected the award as well.

Even sweeter, Misiorowski was the first pitcher since Hall of Famer Randy Johnson to win both the Cy Young and a World Series in the same season, which he did as a member of the Arizona Diamondbacks in 2001.

At 6-foot-7, Misiorowski’s fastball against Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Chicago Cubs during a June game became the fastest pitch ever thrown by a starter in the Statcast era after clocking at 105.5 mph. He averaged 100.6 mph on his fastballs, throwing more than 1,000 pitches at that speed or faster during the season.

In the American League, though, Schlittler, standing at 6-foot-6, also delivered a triple-digit four-seamer. Misiorowski certainly has him beat for the best fastball, but in his first full season with the Yankees, he was as dominant as they believed he could be following an impressive showing in 2025.

But nobody in the Bronx expected the 25-year-old to be the ace of a rotation that featured Gerrit Cole, the Yankees’ most-recent Cy Young winner in 2023, Carlos Rodon, and Max Fried.

Schlittler owned an AL-best 1.95 ERA with 239 strikeouts across 33 starts. The Yankees had the best ERA as a pitching staff in the regular season, and Schlitter was a key reason why, giving up one run or fewer in 21 of those 33 outings.

And it wasn’t a home crowd that got him going extra when it was his turn to take the mound. It seemed Schlitter relished moments on the road, owning a 1.16 ERA over 17 starts away from Yankee Stadium.

Schlittler, a Massachusetts native who grew up a Boston Red Sox fan and is now universally hated by the fan base he loves to troll on social media, is a product of the Yankees’ minor league system. As a seventh-round draft choice out of Northeastern, Schlittler wasn’t always throwing gas with a devastating curveball mixed in with a cutter and sinker.

After mechanical changes, adding muscle and more, the Yankees saw Schlitter’s velocity rising from the low 90s to the upper 90s, with times where he’d top out at triple digits. Like Misiorowski, Schlitter has the ability to not only blow it past you, but place his heaters wherever he wishes, making it that much harder to get on base.

Schlittler proved he wasn’t just a one-hit wonder after his tremendous Game 3 of the AL Wild Card Series in 2025, where he held his childhood team scoreless for eight innings with 12 strikeouts. He dominated his way through the Yankees’ schedule and ultimately picked up another win against the Red Sox in the AL Wild Card Series this past season, where he pitched Game 1 as the team’s ace.

Both pitchers have bright careers ahead of them, with one already notching a World Series ring under his belt.

World.title: Blue states elect Democrats who supported permanent cash handout policy as part of mayors coalition
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Proponents of guaranteed income programs are declaring victory following the midterm elections after several key allies won statewide and federal offices across the country.

Five former members of the Mayors for a Guaranteed Income (MGI) coalition — along with officials from partner organizations — won election to higher office, while voters approved multiple direct-cash ballot measures nationwide.

The most prominent victory came in Georgia, where MGI founding member and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected governor, becoming the first Black woman elected to lead the state.

GEORGIA GOVERNOR'S MANSION PROJECTED TO FLIP BLUE FOR FIRST TIME IN NEARLY 30 YEARS

"Support for guaranteed income has been steadily growing since we launched the first pilot in 2019," MGI President Michael D. Tubbs told Fox News Digital.

MGI noted that more than 60 bills involving cash-based policies similar to guaranteed income have been introduced across 15 states.

Tubbs, who served as mayor of Stockton, California, from 2017 to 2021, also founded Counties for a Guaranteed Income (CGI) and Legislators for a Guaranteed Income.

"Previous polling showed a majority of voters support direct, unconditional cash assistance, and now we've seen several champions who led guaranteed income programs at the local level ascend to higher office in the most recent elections," Tubbs said.

"I hope the newly elected Democratic House and Senate will continue to prioritize affordability and make guaranteed income a permanent policy for Americans."

MAYORS WANT TO KEEP HANDING OUT FREE CASH AFTER FEDERAL FUNDS DRIED UP

Mayors and commissioners move to Capitol Hill

Two current MGI members secured seats in the U.S. House of Representatives:

Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss was elected to represent Illinois’ 9th Congressional District.

Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti won Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District.

Neither Biss nor Cognetti responded to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

Meanwhile, Counties for a Guaranteed Income (CGI) — MGI's sister network — saw two of its prominent members elected to higher office:

Cook County Commissioner Donna Miller was elected to represent Illinois’ 2nd Congressional District.

Montgomery County Councilmember Will Jawando, a CGI founding member, was elected Montgomery County Executive in Maryland.

None of the other newly elected officials responded to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Local funding models take shape

Cook County, Illinois, previously made headlines for establishing what officials described as the nation's first permanent guaranteed income program at the county level. To sustain the program after federal funding from the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) expired, the Cook County Board of Commissioners approved $7.5 million for guaranteed income as part of its fiscal year 2026 budget.

Tubbs previously told Fox News Digital the federal government should follow Cook County's lead by establishing a federal direct-cash assistance program.

"We have wars in Iran, regime change in Venezuela. We get it, the healthcare system and the big, ugly bill," Tubbs said in March. "So, people are saying that social safety is being frayed.

"That wealth is further being taken from the many and given to the few, and there has to be a government solution because this is a government-caused problem. … Inflation, unaffordability, this is all a direct result of government policy," Tubbs added.

According to MGI, guaranteed basic income initiatives have expanded across the country, with more than 100 pilot programs launched since 2018. MGI has grown into a coalition of more than 150 mayors, promoting pilots that offer eligible participants payments of as much as $1,000 per month with no spending restrictions.

However, with federal pandemic relief dollars drying up, questions remain about whether local governments can afford to make these programs permanent through local taxes.

AS AMERICANS ARE CRUSHED BY AFFORDABILITY, GROWING TREND OF MAYORS PUSHING CASH HANDOUTS AS THE ANSWER

Advocates push federal action

Other progressive advocacy groups are pushing for permanent taxpayer-funded guaranteed income programs at both state and federal levels.

The Economic Security Project (ESP), founded in 2016 by a network of entrepreneurs, activists and philanthropists, has backed over 100 guaranteed income pilots nationwide.

ESP Director of Cash Initiatives Shafeka Hashash directed Fox News Digital to a post highlighting election results that favored guaranteed income advocates.

"Michigan. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed is a longtime cash champion. He spoke at the 2024 GI [Guaranteed Income] Now conference and contributed to our 2025 report ‘The Resilience Factor: Cash as a Tool Toward Better Health for Young Families.’ In one of the toughest Senate races in the country, his campaign centered on a single tagline: 'Money out of politics. Money in your pocket,'" Hashash wrote.

FORMER CALIFORNIA MAYOR PUSHES GUARANTEED INCOME AS FIX FOR AFFORDABILITY CRISIS

The Los Angeles Police Department identified the driver as Ihor Demianenko of Valley Village, who investigators determined was under the influence after Tuesday evening's deadly crash.

He was arrested on three counts of murder, and his bail was set at $6.03 million, police said.

The crash happened around 5:55 p.m. Tuesday when Demianenko was driving a white Toyota Sienna southbound on Lankershim Boulevard, just south of Chandler Boulevard, according to an LAPD news release.

MARIJUANA USERS MAY FACE HIDDEN DRIVING DANGER THAT STANDARD TESTS CAN MISS

Los Angeles Fire Department paramedics pronounced three women dead at the crash site. Police said the victims were Hispanic women between 40 and 60 years old whose identities have not been released pending notification of their families.

Two other women, both Hispanic and between 50 and 55 years old, were taken to a hospital in critical condition.

CALIFORNIA MOM HAS BOTH LEGS AMPUTATED AFTER SUSPECTED IMPAIRED DRIVER PLOWS INTO HER RESTAURANT LUNCH TABLE

World.title: White House warns congressional Democrats: Investigating us may be a crime
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Previewing the partisan battles to come, the White House fired a warning shot at House Democrats’ top investigator Wednesday.

The Trump administration is “monitoring” Democrats’ “abusive and capricious threats” to launch congressional probes, White House counsel Will Scharf said in a letter to Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to become chairman of the powerful Oversight Committee starting in January.

And, Scharf warned, those threats may be criminal and warrant their own executive branch investigations. His letter was shared with NBC News by a White House official.

While threats of political reprisal for partisan investigations are commonplace, the suggestion of a congressional probe constituting criminality is not.

When President Joe Biden occupied the White House, and Republicans took control of Congress, Democrats cried foul that Trump’s allies were only interested in launching partisan probes that damaged their political enemies.

But those high-profile investigations continued unimpeded. House Oversight Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., led probes into the international business dealings of Biden’s son Hunter Biden and brother James Biden.

In the letter dated Monday, Scharf rattled off numerous examples of Democratic lawmakers making cavalier threats of issuing subpoenas. For example, Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J., wrote on X, “We’re going to toss out subpoenas like Mardi Gras beads,” while Rep. Emily Randall, D-Wash., said they’ll be passed out “like candy.”

The White House pointed to Supreme Court rulings that have held that congressional investigations must be tied to a legitimate legislative purpose and must not be used to punish political opponents. But House and Senate committees under both parties have broad authority to investigate a range of matters, and they’ve rarely been stopped by the courts.

Likely House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., called the Scharf letter “outrageous,” telling reporters on Capitol Hill on Wednesday: “It’s factually inaccurate. It’s legally inaccurate, and it’s inaccurate in terms of the Constitution.”

“A Democratic Congress is going to be a check and balance on an out-of-control executive branch in the face of unprecedented corruption that they’ve unleashed on the American people. And if they don’t like it, consult the Constitution,” Jeffries said.

Scharf in his letter accused Democrats of seeking “to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” adding that “threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

Trump himself has used his office to target his political enemies. A year ago, the president accused Democrats of criminality, saying on social media that a video posted by Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., and other Democrats telling service members not to follow illegal orders amounted to “SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR, punishable by DEATH!”

The Trump administration failed to secure an indictment against those Democrats over the video, and a judge later found that their speech was protected by the First Amendment in blocking the Pentagon’s attempt to punish Kelly.

The president has also publicly called on his Justice Department to investigate Democrats who probed his family and business dealings, including Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James.

Responding to Scharf’s letter, Garcia invoked the separation of powers in a statement and said newly empowered congressional Democrats will stay the course in investigating the president and his administration.

“It appears Donald Trump has something to hide. Let’s be clear: Congress’ authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate,” Garcia said in a statement.

Garcia and other Democrats who will lead congressional committees beginning in January have made no secret of their interest in investigating Trump, as well as his family, businesses and administration.

As NBC News reported this month, the White House was gearing up for a defense even before Election Day, hiring staff in the counsel’s office, while individual current and former aides have hired lawyers.

“The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse,” Garcia said. “The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”

World.title: She’s delivered 2,000 babies. The measles outbreak changed her mind about vaccines.
World.content:
This is part of The Vaccine Divide, a data investigation into America’s potential loss of its measles-free status as the deadly virus roars back and childhood vaccine defenses continue to crack and crumble.

When Roberta Devers, a midwife in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, did a prenatal check on an expectant mom this week, the woman — a member of the Amish community in her third trimester — had been sick with measles.

Devers said she has cared for dozens of pregnant women infected with the virus since measles began spreading rapidly in the county in April. Lancaster County is largely rural, with sprawling family farms.

“Every single day,” she said, “someone’s calling to ask what they do. They’re pregnant and they’ve gotten it, or their babies have gotten it.”

Devers, 63, estimates she has delivered nearly 2,000 babies in her 38-year career. She has a degree in maternal and fetal health, but she is working as an unlicensed, traditional midwife in Pennsylvania, independent of the hospital systems and without physician oversight. State law bars traditional midwives from practicing medicine.

Devers said pregnant women with measles are having miscarriages. "While our Amish families believe God is always in control, they're emotional people, and like anyone else, they grieve the loss of a baby," Devers said. Hannah Beier for NBC News

Devers said she questioned immunizations as a young mother and never vaccinated her son.

“There was as much information against vaccines as there was about the efficacy of vaccines,” she said. “It was difficult to know who to trust and who to believe.”

Her experiences in Lancaster County’s outbreak have changed her mindset.

“Numbers and books became people,” she said. “It was humanized by watching what was happening to the mothers I was serving.”

World.title: What are childhood vaccination rates in your community and schools?
World.content:
This is part of The Vaccine Divide, an updated data investigation into America potentially losing its measles-free status as the deadly virus roars back and childhood vaccine defenses continue to crack and crumble.

As vaccination rates among children go down, the risk of getting sick from a vaccine-preventable illness such as measles goes up.

Use these maps to see the childhood vaccination rates for your community.

World.title: Behind the data: How NBC News tracked the decline in childhood vaccinations
World.content:
Editor’s note: This 2026 NBC News data investigation is an update of The Vaccine Divide, which was originally published in September 2025. The methodology for both projects is similar. The new data was collected from June to October 2026.

For “The Vaccine Divide,” NBC News gathered massive amounts of data from state governments and archives of public records. With the help of infectious disease researchers at Stanford University, NBC News filed scores of requests for documents, including materials obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, and wrestled different types of data into a standardized format to map and compare rates across thousands of counties.

Methodology

How NBC News collected the data

NBC News built a database of childhood vaccination and exemption information using data provided by state governments, primarily health agencies. The data combines public information available for some states and data provided directly to NBC News.

The data covers kindergartner vaccinations for each academic year.

After collection, the data was collated, and exemption rates were calculated in order to be analyzed. The analysis focuses on four facets of the data:

Medical exemptions: Exemptions granted when students have medical conditions that could make vaccination harmful. Nonmedical exemptions: Exemptions for students who opt out of required vaccinations because of personal beliefs or religious convictions. MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccinations: For states where data is subdivided by number of doses, MMR vaccination is counted by the second dose. Some states track measles, mumps and rubella immunization separately; in those states, measles was used to represent MMR rates. Up-to-date vaccinations: Students are considered “up to date” with their vaccinations if they have received the full vaccination series required for enrollment in their schools.

How the data was processed

With a hodgepodge of formats, jurisdictions and collection practices across states, the task required extensive work to ensure that possible inconsistencies in the data were managed.

Certain states, such as Ohio and New York, required further calculations to aggregate the state-supplied data.

Other states required hand input of hundreds of rows of tabular data.

All data was checked for accuracy.

Analyzing the data

This analysis of childhood MMR vaccination rates focused on states that provided MMR figures for the 2025-26 school year. Accompanying the analysis were several variant analyses, which confirmed that the results were robust. The variant analyses all yielded similar results, mostly within 1 percentage point. We also examined the scale of MMR vaccination rate decline across counties, with almost 4 in 10 counties declining by over 5 percentage points since 2019 and about 1 in 8 declining by that amount since 2024. Fewer than 2% of counties declined by 0.1 percentage points or less since 2019.

Variations in the data

Many states collect and report their data differently. Some use health districts instead of counties. Some states provided over a decade of data; others provided only two years’ worth. Some states redacted certain data because of privacy concerns.
