World.title: Nvidia's board preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang, sources say
World.content:
Nvidia's board of directors is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang soon, according to two sources familiar with the matter, following allegations that Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies believe was a Chinese asset.

The Trump administration is aware of the matter, the sources said.

The Wall Street Journal was first to report on the board's moves.

Nvidia's share price slid more than 8% in after-hours trading Wednesday after the Journal's report, extending a multi-day sell-off for one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies.

The company has faced days of turmoil following reports that American intelligence agencies believed Huang was the target of a Chinese spying plot.

Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993, and for years it was best known for designing graphics cards widely used for gaming. The company now designs the powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms, making its technology highly sensitive and subject to export controls limiting sales to China.

The New York Times reported last week on allegations that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who previously led a Singapore-based firm called Megaspeed International that bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips and hardware. U.S. intelligence agencies have believed for months that Alice Huang — who is not related to Jensen Huang — was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, the newspaper reported.

Bloomberg reported Wednesday night that Alice Huang has returned to China, her home country, citing people familiar with the matter. She is living in Beijing with the knowledge of Chinese security officials, one of the people told Bloomberg, which said it wasn't immediately clear when or why she went there.

In a message to Nvidia employees over the weekend, Jensen Huang wrote that he was "unfaithful to my wife" and apologized for hurting her and their children. He did not name the woman involved.

Nvidia's board said Sunday it had launched an independent investigation into allegations that the CEO "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." The board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."

Two law enforcement sources told CBS News the Justice Department is also investigating Megaspeed over potential violations of U.S. export restrictions on advanced AI chips. Some analysts have raised questions about whether the saga resulted in China — which is racing the U.S. for AI dominance — gaining access to Nvidia's technology through Megaspeed. The company has denied any involvement in illegal chip transfers.

China has denied all allegations, with Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun telling reporters on Monday that the "so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear."

Beyond the national security concerns, Nvidia is facing a securities lawsuit accusing the company of failing to disclose information to shareholders about Jensen Huang's relationship with the alleged spy.

Jensen Huang has a close relationship with the Trump administration. President Trump gave Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 computer chips to "approved customers" in China late last year, with the federal government taking a 25% cut of chip sales. The deal did not include Nvidia's more advanced Blackwell or Rubin systems.

The Nvidia CEO and other U.S. tech executives traveled to China with Mr. Trump earlier this year.

On Monday, Mr. Trump called Jensen Huang a "very high-quality person," saying during a White House briefing that "the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape." The president said he spoke to Jensen Huang to see how he was doing, and the executive "said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy."

World.title: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills 6, health authorities say
World.content:
An Israeli airstrike targeting the Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed six people and wounded at least a dozen more, Gaza's Health Ministry said.

The strike was carried out early Thursday, according to the Israeli military, which said it struck "a senior Hamas terrorist" and other militants "while they were operating within Nasser Hospital," without providing evidence.

Israel accuses Hamas and its allies of using hospitals as cover for military activity.

In the statement, the Israeli military said Hamas was using the hospital as "a command center for military and terrorist activities."

A Palestinian man inspects damage inside a building at Nasser Hospital following an Israeli airstrike in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, on Nov. 12, 2026. Ramadan Abed / REUTERS

The Hamas-controlled Gaza Health Ministry said the strike hit the hospital's surgery department and that a doctor was among the dead. An Associated Press journalist at the scene said parts of the building's second floor were destroyed.

Nasser Hospital in the city of Khan Younis is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in Gaza, whose healthcare infrastructure has been decimated by the yearslong war.

Israeli forces have previously attacked and raided Nasser Hospital. In 2025, the military killed five journalists — including AP contributor Mariam Dagga — when it struck a gathering point for local reporters at the complex.

The war started on Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 others hostage. Since then, Israel's retaliatory offensive has killed more than 74,600 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, which is part of the Hamas-run government but whose figures are generally considered reliable by the international community.

Israel has continued to strike Gaza despite a U.S.-backed ceasefire and controls at least 60% of the enclave. Since the truce went into effect in October 2025, Israeli strikes and gunfire have killed 1,622 people, health authorities say. Five Israeli soldiers have also been killed during that period.

World.title: 3 killed when SUV crashes into North Hollywood food stand
World.content:
Police say three people are dead after an SUV crashed into a food stand near a North Hollywood bus stop in Los Angeles on Tuesday night.

The collision occurred at around 5:55 p.m. local time near the Metro station at the corner of Lankershim and Chandler boulevards, according to the LA Police Department.

Firefighters said three people were pronounced dead at the scene, while three others were taken to a nearby hospital, two of whom were in critical condition at the time. As of 11 p.m., one of the victims remained in stable condition, while the other was still critical.

None of the victims have yet been identified by police, who said all three were between 40 and 70 years old. Witnesses told CBS LA the three women were street vendors in the area, and one had worked there for more than 15 years.

The critically injured individuals are also women between 50 and 55 years old.

Crews extricated one person, the driver, from the wreckage, according to LAFD.

"I'm heartbroken for the families of everyone impacted," Mayor Karen Bass wrote in a statement on X. "We will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available."

The scene of a crash in North Hollywood that left three people dead and several others hospitalized on Nov. 10, 2026. CBS LA

LAPD officers said the driver of the white SUV was in serious condition and was determined to be under the influence of drugs or alcohol at the time of the crash. Police identified him as Ihor Demianenko, a 61-year-old Valley Village resident. He was arrested on suspicion of three counts of murder.

Demianenko is currently being held on more than $6 million bail.

The circumstances surrounding the collision remain under investigation, but LAPD Major Collision Investigation Team and Valley Traffic Division detectives said that Demianenko was attempting to avoid another car that was driving "legally and safely" before the crash. Police said they would continue looking for security camera footage from the Metro bus station and businesses in the surrounding area as their probe continued.

"It'll be a prolonged but a very deliberate investigation to determine what happened here," LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell said. "Our hearts go out to the families of the victims that were struck here tonight."

Aerial footage showed the white SUV stopped on the sidewalk underneath a canopy, where the food stand was set up.

Friends and loved ones remember street vendors killed

Mourners identified two of the women as Teodora, a 57-year-old woman known fondly as Doris, and Maria, 73.

On Tuesday night, some of Doris' family members of one of the three women killed stopped by a growing memorial.

"There are no words to express the absence that she's gonna have over my life," Doris' daughter, Melissa Villalobos, said. "Every goal, everything that I do is gonna be for her. Everything that I achieve will be for her, because of every sacrifice that she has done for me."

She said she hopes that her mother is remembered as a selfless, independent and hardworking woman.

"She never neglected to give someone food, never neglected to give a bottle of water," Melissa Villalobos said. "I am grateful of that time that I had her for."

Los Angeles City Councilman Adrin Nazarian, who represents the area, has partnered with nonprofit organization ICON CDC to create a GoFundMe fundraiser to assist the families of the three victims. It can be found by searching for the keywords: "NoHo Metro Station Street Vendor Support Fund."

"We sat there and talked all day, two days ago," said Laduke Warwick. "Today, she's in heaven. I guarantee they're all in heaven."

He said their relationship began years ago when he was homeless. Though he's now housed, he'll never forget the day that Doris handed him a bacon-wrapped hot dog, a soda, and struck up a conversation with him.

"They're just such amazing people. I can't believe they left like that," Warwick said. "If I could say anything to them, I'd say thank you so much for all the amazing blessings that you have shared with me in a short moment of my life, that I can't even repay with words, money or kindness.

Local street photographer Jeff Wilson snapped some photos of Doris just four months ago, calling her an "anchor" of the community after more than a decade of serving food.

"Pre-COVID to COVID, past COVID to all the ICE crazy stuff, she was here," Wilson said. "She was always doing something, helping people."

The memorial continued to grow at the spot of the crash throughout the day Wednesday, with dozens of community members stopping by to pay their respects. Of the dozens who stopped, many remembered the trio of women who were always there to lend a helping hand to those who needed it the most.

"They're mothers, grandmothers. They're somebody's somebody," said Mike Sandoval, a regular customer. "They were out here every day. I had good days, I had bad days coming through this area, and every time I needed something they were always there."

World.title: At least 2 killed, 17 hurt in Brooklyn building collapse
World.content:
At least two people were killed and 17 others injured Wednesday in Brooklyn when one building collapsed and a second was significantly damaged, authorities said.

The collapse occurred just after 4 p.m. Eastern time Wednesday at a three-story building on Flatbush Avenue near Bedford Avenue in Flatbush.

The New York City Police Department said a building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. was completely collapsed, while the side of an adjacent building at 1323 Flatbush Ave. was torn off in the process.

According to police, the building that fully collapsed was occupied by residents at the time. Photos and video from the scene showed the exposed interiors of stairwells and apartments in the neighboring building. The cause of the collapse is under investigation.

Photos and video from the scene appear to show an entire side of one building collapsed. CBS News New York

The site next to those two buildings was vacant and under construction, and multiple people from both the collapsed building and the construction site were trapped, officials said.

More than 250 firefighters and EMS personnel responded to the site. New York City Fire Department Chief of Department John Esposito said a fire company that was in the neighborhood arrived on the scene less than one minute after the collapse.

"They encountered people trapped in the adjacent building that was part of the collapse. They immediately took action and removed those people from danger," Esposito said.

Two people were killed and at least 17 others were injured, including seven children, officials said. FDNY officials said that of the injured, four people were in critical condition and 13 were in stable condition, including one firefighter with minor injuries.

Officials have not yet released the ages of the victims who were killed.

FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said investigators do not know how many people may still be in the collapse zone or how many people are missing.

"We know that we're not finished here, and we will likely not be finished for quite some time," Bonsignore said.

"We will be here for several days until this entire site is searched for all potential victims," Esposito said.

Anyone who is unable to reach someone who many have been affected by the collapse is urged to call 311, or 212-639-9675 if you are outside New York City.

The FDNY says a major technical rescue operation got underway after a building collapse. Chopper 2

Firefighters could be seen sifting through the rubble by hand and breaking through a collapsed wall to search underneath it. K-9 units were also canvassing the debris.

"This has been an incredibly challenging and fast-moving situation, with precarious wreckage to navigate and dangerous voids beneath the surface. This type of rescue is exactly what the FDNY trains for," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a press conference Wednesday evening.

CBS News New York cameras captured crews pulling one survivor from the rubble at around 6:15 p.m. A man on the scene said that the survivor was his pregnant wife.

"The units are performing dangerous and heroic work," Bonsignore said.

Drivers were encouraged to avoid the area and should expect traffic delays and road closures, officials said. Flatbush Avenue was closed between Clarendon Road and Bedford Avenue.

The American Red Cross and New York City Emergency Management set up at reception center for displaced residents at the Flatbush YMCA. The Red Cross said they have registered eight adults and two children for assistance, so far.

The New York City Department of Buildings said its commissioner and investigators were sent to the site to assist with recovery operations and conduct structural stability inspections of nearby buildings.

The NYPD said the side of 1323 Flatbush Ave. was torn off in the collapse. Chopper 2

Meanwhile, city records show that a contractor was given a violation over activity at the vacant lot adjacent to the collapsed building, 2625 Bedford Ave. According to city records, the buildings department had issued a violation to a demolition contractor in April because inspectors said the building at that site had been demolished despite a city order to stop all demolition work. That violation is now listed as resolved, and the violation notice does not state why the city issued a stop work order in the first place.

DOB officials say plans had been approved for the construction of a three-story building at the site, and excavation work was happening prior to the collapse.

"When that happens at a construction site, when you're actually digging down very deep into the ground next to an existing building, that can often present a lot of precarious problems of destabilizing an existing building, and if proper precautions aren't taken, sometimes this is what happens," said Glenn Corbett, an associate professor of fire science at John Jay College of Criminal Justice.

It was unclear if that work had anything to do with Wednesday's collapse.

The Brooklyn District Attorney says his office is working with the DOB and law enforcement to determine if any criminal conduct contributed to the collapse.

World.title: Nvidia's stock dives as board weighs move to oust Jensen Huang
World.content:
Nvidia's stock price tumbled after the close of trading on Wednesday on news that the chipmaker's board of directors is preparing to oust longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

Nvidia this week launched an investigation into Huang, who admitted to having an extramarital affair. U.S. intelligence agencies have linked the CEO to a Chinese business executive, Alice Huang (no relation), who is suspected of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security.

The Trump administration is aware of the Nvidia board's plans, sources told CBS News. The Wall Street Journal was the first to report that board members were preparing to remove Jensen Huang.

Nvidia shares fell more than 8%, to $159.51, in after-hours trading. The drop continued a steep decline in the company's market value, which has sunk more than $450 billion since Nvidia announced the probe into Jensen Huang's conduct on Nov. 8.

Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, is seen in many circles as the face of the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector, with the company's advanced chips providing the critical computing resources that power frontier AI models.

His departure would be a major blow to Nvidia, which lacks any obvious successor to fill his shoes, according to Wall Street analysts.

"The news is obviously negative, as Jensen is (arguably) the most prominent executive at the most prominent company sitting at the center of the world's most important industry — someone who foresaw the rise of AI years before ChatGPT arrived and made sure the firm he founded would be prepared to capitalize on it," Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge said in a report.

Nvidia's code of conduct

Corporate governance experts said Jensen Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang appears to violate Nvidia's code of conduct. That policy highlights that personal relationships could create a conflict of interest for Nvidia, while Huang himself specifies in the code of conduct that the company's workers have a responsibility "to maintain high ethical standards."

Nvidia's code also instructs employees to ask themselves whether they could defend an action if it were made public on social media or known to colleagues. If not, the policy states, "do not proceed."

In a message to company employees on Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair, and he apologized to his wife and their two children, both of whom also work at Nvidia. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote.

Nvidia's 11-person board includes Jensen Huang, although the other board members are designated as independent, according to a regulatory filing.

President Trump said this week the FBI is also investigating romantic and business ties between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who was a senior executive at Megaspeed International. The Singapore-based company has been one of Nvidia's largest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and other advanced hardware.

The turmoil at Nvidia is also drawing scrutiny in Congress, with lawmakers expected to question company executives about whether its chips are being funneled to China through other countries.

Dan Ives, a tech analyst with investment adviser Yorkville Ives, said investors will now consider who might succeed Huang, what impact that could have on the company's short-term strategy and what any government investigations might reveal.

"Jensen is not replaceable by another CEO or group of interim executives, but Nvidia likely now has to move on without Jensen at the helm, which seemed like a Twilight Zone episode narrative before Sunday afternoon when the news broke," Ives said in a report.

World.title: SS United States sinks, will become world's largest artificial reef
World.content:
The SS United States, the fabled ocean liner, was scuttled toward the ocean floor on Wednesday in a controlled, explosive-free sinking that took place about 20 nautical miles off the Gulf Coast of Florida between the Destin-Fort Walton Beach region and Pensacola.

The 1,000-foot-long SS United States was sent to the bottom of the ocean in an hourslong sinking operation that began Wednesday afternoon and concluded later in the evening.

The ship will become the world's largest artificial reef, only adding to its long list of maritime achievements. The Destin-Fort Walton Beach metropolitan area says it already has about 580 artificial reefs off its coastline, the most for any region in the country.

Crews prepare to sink the former ocean liner SS United States to create an artificial reef off the coast of Destin, Florida, on Nov. 11, 2026. Tony Giberson/USA Today Network via REUTERS

The SS United States first set sail in 1952, at the time setting a transatlantic speed record for an ocean liner that still stands today.

It carried thousands of voyagers over its two decades of military service, including presidents, royalty, celebrities and even legendary CBS News broadcaster Walter Cronkite.

Its design was so revolutionary that even the Pentagon kept it a secret.

But by 1969, the SS United States was retired from service, and it wound up in Philadelphia in 1996. It remained docked there for decades, until Okaloosa County in Florida purchased the ship from the SS United States Conservancy for about $1 million in 2024 with the goal of deploying it as an artificial reef designed to provide a habitat for the Gulf's marine ecosystem.

Prior to sinking it, the county sent the ship to Mobile, Alabama, for a one-year preparation process that involved removing all environmentally unsafe materials, including non-metal items, wiring and fuel, the county said.

Holes were also strategically cut throughout the ship to ensure it remains upright when submerged.

The preparations were conducted in coordination with the Environmental Protection Agency and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection.

The approximately $13 million project to make the ship an artificial reef was funded by county tourist tax revenue. Okaloosa County hopes that the ship will serve as a jolt to the economy of the Florida Panhandle, providing a year-round destination for divers.

"I think it's going to be like Disney World," Jocelyn Collins, general manager for Emerald Coast Scuba, told CBS News. "You know, we're going to line people up and take pictures underwater."

World.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race in upset
World.content:
Washington — Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi Senate race, CBS News projects, delivering Democrats an eighth flipped Senate seat after the dramatic race had been up in the air for days.

Colom, 43, is a district attorney and seventh-generation Mississippian. He campaigned on cost-of-living and healthcare issues, while pledging to deliver for the Magnolia State where he argued Hyde-Smith hasn't. And he saw support from top surrogates like former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris, who joined Colom on the campaign trail in the weeks leading up to Election Day.

He will be the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction.

Colom thanked his supporters — and pointed to his campaign's long odds — during a victory speech late Wednesday at Tougaloo College in Jackson, Mississippi.

"Throughout this campaign, there were many times where I had to have faith. There were times that I couldn't get donors to answer the phone. They did not believe a moment like this was possible, but I kept the faith," he said. "I did my first town hall in Jackson, Mississippi. ... Less than 10 people showed up, but I kept the faith."

Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018, and was the first woman elected to represent Mississippi in Congress.

"While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," Hyde-Smith said in a video message Wednesday night. "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state."

The race became surprisingly competitive in deep-red Mississippi, heating up in the final weeks of the campaign. National Democrats announced last month that they were investing in ad spending in the race for the first time, and the Cook Political Report changed its rating from solidly Republican to leaning Republican, as the headwinds that faced Republicans across the map — an unpopular war in Iran and persistent affordability issues — even made their way to reliably red states.

The race appeared extremely close the day after the election, when at one point just a few dozen votes separated the candidates. But Colom's lead strengthened in the days that followed.

Heading into Election Day, the race appeared to be a steep uphill climb for Democrats. President Trump won the state by 20 points in 2024, and the state hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982. But the contest's competitiveness in the final stages of the campaign was illustrative of the broader political environment, which put seats on the map that Democrats wouldn't have dreamed of flipping at the beginning of the cycle.

"I want to make one thing clear: An election may come to an end, but our commitment to Mississippi never will," Hyde-Smith said added in her video. "I have always believed the public service is about something much bigger than any one person or any one election. It is about the people we serve, the values we hold dear and the future we leave for our children and grandchildren. And while my time in the United States Senate may be coming to an end, my love for Mississippi and determination to stand up for what is right never will. I will always be proud to call Mississippi home."

With the projected victory, Democrats add yet another seat to their majority, marking their eighth flip after the party won seats in North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas and Maine.

In January, Democrats will control at least 55 Senate seats to Republicans' 44, with Alaska's Senate race still a toss-up.

World.title: Pope declares Peru his "homeland" in final leg of South America trip
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV declared Peru his "homeland" on Wednesday as he arrived in Lima at the start of his historic visit, returning to the place that taught him how to be a pastor and where a nationwide party erupted to welcome the beloved "Padre Robert" home.

Leo seemed genuinely moved as he emerged from his charter plane, smiling broadly at nearly every turn of his first moments on Peruvian soil. The Vatican estimated that some 3 million people lined Leo's miles-long motorcade route into town, waving Peruvian and Holy See flags.

Some in the roaring crowds broke through the tight security to chase behind the car that transported him to the presidential palace, where Leo met privately with Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori. During the formal welcome ceremony in the palace courtyard, he sang the Peruvian national anthem alongside Fujimori and a children's choir.

Pope Leo waves to the faithful from the popemobile on his way to Peru's government palace in Lima on Nov. 11, 2026. Miguel Marruffo /AFP via Getty Images

In his first remarks to Fujimori and government officials, the Chicago-born Leo said the Peruvian citizenship he acquired in 2015 cemented a bond that began long before, crediting Peruvians with having formed him as a pastor by sharing their lives, joys and struggles with him.

"Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you," he said.

"That is why I can tell you, with deep gratitude, that I am also returning to my homeland," he said to applause.

Popemania descends on Peru, where Leo lived and served for decades

The visit to Peru marked the final leg of Leo's three-nation South America tour and its emotional highlight, given the more than two decades that Leo, formerly Cardinal Robert Prevost, spent in Peru as a missionary priest and later bishop. He has said it was here that he learned "what it means to be a shepherd." As a dual citizen of the U.S. and Peru, he's the first pope from each country.

"We love him so much because he's worked here, he knows our sufferings, he knows it all," said 85-year-old Evelina Cruz, who held a pope plush doll made by her niece as she waited for Leo to arrive.

Pope Leo XIV and Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori at a welcome ceremony as part of the pope's official visit to Peru at the Presidential Palace on Nov. 11, 2026, in Lima, Peru. Mariana Bazo / Getty Images

In preparation for the pope's visit, a huge 46-foot statue of the pontiff was unveiled in the port of El Callao. Baristas in Lima, the capital, were offering cappuccinos decorated with the image of the pope.

"My heart is so excited that it makes me want to cry with joy," said Zuly Castillo, who served as Leo's

secretary when he was bishop of the northern city of Chiclayo near the Pacific Coast.

Gustavo Morello, an associate professor of sociology at Boston College and the author of "Lived Religion in Latin America," said the trip was a "return to his origins, without any doubt."

"Peru is the crown of the trip, the homecoming of the first Peruvian pope, no matter where he was born," he said.

With hands raised and voices lifted in song, hundreds awaited the pope's arrival in Lima in front of the presidential palace. "Long live Christ!" the crowd sang, following a Catholic choir on the stage.

Popemania also hit Chiclayo, where Leo arrives on Friday. Leo is painted in colorful murals, emblazoned on T-shirts, baseball hats and even bobblehead dolls.

Over the coming days, Leo will celebrate Mass in all his old stomping grounds including at the nearby sanctuary of St. Turibius of Mogrovejo in Zaña, a city that is a hub of Afro-Peruvian culture, and where the pope often visited to pray to the saint of his devotion.

Since Leo knows his adopted country so well, his speeches will be closely watched, especially one he'll deliver from the square in front of Lima's cathedral Thursday "on the challenges and hopes for the future of the Peruvian people."

Pope to honor Peru's Indigenous peoples in the Amazon

The pope will honor Peru's Indigenous peoples by traveling to Pucallpa, in Peru's Amazon, to celebrate Mass. Illegal gold mining and the cultivation of coca leaves, the raw material used to produce cocaine, are affecting Peru's Indigenous peoples.

"The Amazon is a place where critical issues affecting development — such as the environmental crisis, the exclusion of Indigenous peoples, various forms of violence, and extreme poverty — all intersect," said Pérez.

Leo will also meet with popular groups of faithful and representatives of local traditions in Cusco — the capital of the Inca Empire, an important city of Spanish colonial rule and an important cultural

destination, including the nearby ruins at Machu Picchu.

The pope will celebrate Mass in Cusco's main square, where in 1781 the Indigenous hero Túpac Amaru II was killed following the most significant rebellion against the Spanish during the colonial era.

Pope arrives in Peru about one month after undergoing lung cancer surgery

The pope's arrival in Peru comes about one month after he underwent surgery in Italy to remove a nodular lesion from his right lung, during which surgeons confirmed he had lung cancer. The Vatican announced at the time that the 71-year-old had been diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, and that the surgery had been successful.

Just two weeks after he underwent the surgery, doctors cleared him to make the South American trip, which started in Uruguay and took him to Argentina.

During an address in Uruguay last weekend, the pope used his own experience with cancer to push for access to universal healthcare.

"Recently I experienced firsthand the limitations imposed by illness, and I received care for which I am grateful," the pope said. " … Ensuring that healthcare is accessible to everyone, regardless of their resources, is a duty that confronts every society."

At the start of his trip, the pope also confirmed that he voted by mail in the U.S. midterm elections in Chicago, the first sitting pontiff to vote in a U.S. election.

World.title: World's fastest ocean liner is sunk to break another record: largest artificial reef
World.content:
World's fastest ocean liner is sunk to break another record: largest artificial reef

toggle caption i Destin-Fort Walton Beach/Screenshot by NPR

The fastest passenger liner in the world crossed the Atlantic Ocean in less than four days. On Wednesday, it sank in five hours.

The SS United States, launched in 1951 and longer than the RMS Titanic, once transported four presidents, the Mona Lisa and a slate of 20th century movie stars. After decades spent rusting, and facing the scrap heap, its minders settled on a deal to turn the vessel into what's expected to be the world's largest artificial reef off the coast of Okaloosa County, Fla.

Crews removed plugs in the ship's hull, allowing it to fill with water without the use of explosives. After hours of delays, its final moments went quickly. The ship tilted onto its side and dipped below the waves.

Sponsor Message

The sinking marks a bittersweet coda to the era of gleaming behemoths that crossed the seas in elegant fashion. It is also the latest in an ongoing effort by coastal communities to lure thrill-seeking tourists away from international destinations, one that has so far generated surprising economic benefits.

"For those of us who love shipwrecks and love ships in general, it was way more tragic to see it sitting and rusting away at the dock," wreck diver and maritime enthusiast Karen Flynn told NPR.

toggle caption i Ingeborg Talliarek/Keystone/Hulton Archive/Getty Images

Her diving club, the Maryland-based Atlantic Wreck Divers, booked tickets and a charter boat just days after a date for the ship's "deployment," as the sinking is diplomatically described, was set.

"We've dove everything that you can around the world," Flynn said. "This will just be one more unique, new thing for us to dive."

A potential tourism boom

In many ways, Flynn and her club are the exact type of visitor that Okaloosa County is hoping to attract: divers planning to stay overnight who will spend a fair amount of money on equipment, food and lodging during their travels.

The Florida panhandle county has sunk hundreds of artificial reefs, many of which are ships or boats.

Sponsor Message

"Certainly this is the biggest that we've done," said Okaloosa County tourism director Jennifer Adams.

The United States, which is nearly 1,000 feet long, is now the centerpiece of that watery collection.

Reefs bring in roughly $10 million to $12 million in annual economic benefits for the county, Adams said. She expects that number to climb now, and for the county to recoup its $10 million investment in the United States in "a couple of years."

To fulfill that promise, the liner's transformation was designed to appeal to tourists, marine life and federal regulators, Adams said. Its hull was stripped of toxic materials and bulky components, and the ship itself was placed just over 20 nautical miles from the city of Destin's beaches.

"It should rest at a place where its upper decks … are not outside of the recreational diving limits," said Flynn, the diver.

toggle caption i SS United States Conservancy

Panhandle counties now have a claim to several big-ticket ships that could draw tourists. The SS United States joins the USS Oriskany — a 888-foot post-war aircraft carrier sunk by the U.S. Navy off Pensacola in 2006 — and is set to make the area home to the first and second largest artificial reefs globally.

Since 1940, Florida alone has created more than 4,000 artificial reefs, according to a state fish and wildlife commission tally. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration analyzed 2017 data on diving tourism around artificial and natural reefs. It calculated that visits to just a few of those reefs generated almost a billion dollars in annual economic benefits.

Economist Andrew Ropicki, at the University of Florida, says Okaloosa and its surrounding counties have something of a "critical mass" of these planned shipwrecks.

"You can capture more of those tourism dollars than [other areas]," he said.

But Ropicki also warned that an overinvestment in reefing might eventually lead to diminishing returns, as visitor interests shift or they become overwhelmed by choice.

Sponsor Message

Adams, the Okaloosa tourism director, told NPR plans are already in the works to sink "five or six" additional artificial reefs after the SS United States.

For now, however, she hopes the sight of such a unique ship below the surface of the Gulf of Mexico is enough to draw crowds.

Sovereign of the seas

Wednesday's sinking carries a far more complicated set of emotions for Susan Gibbs. She's head of the SS United States Conservancy — custodian through much of the ship's ill-fated stretch moored in Philadelphia.

"I'm full of a complex mix of sorrow but gratitude and pride and hope," she said prior to the sinking.

Gibbs is the granddaughter of William Francis Gibbs, who worked obsessively on the ocean liner almost a century ago. For a short period, after the end of World War II and before the age of the passenger jet, his creation was the pride of the American transportation industry.

"He would freely admit that he loved this ship a thousand times more than my grandmother," she said.

Now, seeing her grandfather's crowning achievement stripped and scuttled feels "complicated." Her organization sold the SS United States to Okaloosa County for $1 million in 2024, a fraction of its original cost.

But for Gibbs, it's a better fate for the vessel than a scrapyard.

"We felt that reefing was by far the more dignified solution," she said.

Karen Flynn, the wreck diver, agrees. She says even below the waves the ship will still have a sense of grandeur.

"There's something about looking out over that bridge … and seeing the nose of the bow and then seeing just the blue out in front of it," she said. "That is going to be a spectacular shot."

World.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins the closest Senate race in the country
World.content:
Democrat Scott Colom wins the closest Senate race in the country

Transcript

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

Mississippi's U.S. Senate race has finally been called. Democratic challenger Scott Colom will be the state's next senator. That is according to a race call by The Associated Press. Colom is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Mississippi since 1982 and the first African American to represent Mississippi since Reconstruction. Elise Catrion Gregg of the Gulf States Newsroom and Mississippi Public Broadcasting has been following this and joins us now. Hey, Elise.

ELISE CATRION GREGG, BYLINE: Hi there.

DETROW: I mean, a lot of historic markers there. Walk us through all of this.

GREGG: Yeah, absolutely. You know, Colom announced his run in late 2025, and it was seen as just kind of a long shot in a state that has been traditionally a Republican stronghold. And now he's won. When the votes first came in on election night, you know, Cindy Hyde-Smith seemed like she was ahead and, you know, for much of the campaign season, she was, you know, projected to be the winner. Although folks, you know, were aware of Colom's popularity. Here we are now. Latest results show he's roughly 5,000 votes ahead of her.

DETROW: Yeah. I mean, a Democratic victory in Mississippi is shocking, even in the context of the wave election that seemed to be building. Mississippi was not on the radar of that many people looking at states that could flip. It's a stunning loss for Republicans. What is the party saying?

GREGG: So we haven't gotten any official statements from Republicans in the state or from Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith just yet, although she has called to concede the race. But we do know that before this was all called, the state GOP said that they would be looking into legal options, possible litigation and just really closely monitoring the ballot count. And to be clear, both candidates have had volunteers and lawyers monitoring the count. But what I will say is that we're likely to see some legal action come out of this at some point or another. But, you know, it's very clear, as Scott Colom has said several times during his campaign, especially in recent days, the people of Mississippi have spoken.

DETROW: Mississippi doesn't have a recount law, right? It wouldn't be a set process that you know exactly what's going to happen?

GREGG: No, it's been interesting to see. There's no recount law, and we don't have runoffs for U.S. Senate race, so plurality wins, and the votes speak for themselves in this case.

DETROW: Elise last question - Scott Colom has this historic win, as we mentioned. What do we need to know about Colom?

GREGG: Yeah, so since 2016, Colom has been a local district attorney. His platform was on affordability, you know, healthcare accessibility, saving rural hospitals, which is a huge deal here in Mississippi. And he said that his work as a DA in an area that leans right has really informed just his push for bipartisanship and prioritizing issues that matter to Mississippians across the state. When he was a DA, a big priority of his was ensuring that innocent folks weren't being put in prison. In fact, that was part of his platform that helped him win against the previous DA.

And he has just had a really robust campaign over the last year or so. He's gone all the way to the coast to the very north part of Mississippi, through the Delta and central Mississippi. He's talked to folks from both parties. I think, notably, when President Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, for a rally for Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, Colom was in line with folks trying to get in, talking to them about what issues matter to them. He's run a really robust campaign, and I think that's resonated with the voters here in Mississippi.

DETROW: That's Elise Catrion Gregg with Mississippi Public Broadcasting and the Gulf States Newsroom. Thanks so much.

GREGG: Thank you.
