World.title: Following big Democratic wins, these swing voters are looking for results
World.content:
Following big Democratic wins, these swing voters are looking for results

toggle caption i Tara Anand for NPR

Republicans were dealt a stunning rebuke in last week's midterms. But swing voters, who could be decisive in the next election, are more interested in results than investigations or impeachment as Democrats prepare to take power in Congress.

"I am hoping that we don't experience a bunch of gridlock and a lot of whining and crying and just political infighting for the next two years," said Theresa, a voter from Pennsylvania who is participating in NPR's Swing Shift project. "I'm hoping we don't have that. I fear that we will have that."

NPR has agreed not to use the full names of the Swing Shift voters, so they can speak freely about politics without fear of personal or professional repercussions.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

Theresa voted for President Biden in 2020, President Trump in 2024 and split her ticket in this year's midterms. Like many voters, her top issue this year was affordability. In a voice memo sent to NPR days after the midterms, Theresa said she is eager for the cost of living to come down.

"I just don't remember it ever being as bad in our time," Theresa said. "And I'm just hoping we get some relief and we get some relief soon."

At 9:56 PM on election night, Wally in Georgia hit send on his voice memo. He had seen enough.

"Just checking in here with a quick note. I'm not surprised at all by the outcome tonight," Wally said. "I believe that this is a lot of Trump's doing and pushback on his style of politics and how he governs."

Wally voted for Trump in 2024 but swung back to Democrats in this year's midterms. He had initially supported Trump in hopes that a Trump presidency would shake up the political system, but that didn't happen and now he says the second Trump term has been exhausting. As he sees it, the decisive Democratic wins signal that the country is ready to move on.

Sponsor Message

"Trump has been shooting himself in the foot for many months now," Wally said. "But voting isn't the end of the game here. We have to hold Democrats to some sort of tangible change and not just promises about what they want to do."

For several of the Swing Shift voters, Tuesday's results came as a surprise.

Jason from North Carolina split his ticket, voting for Democrat Roy Cooper for Senate and the Republican incumbent for the House.

"My congressman was defeated this time by someone that no one's really ever heard of," said Jason, sounding almost puzzled by the blue wave that crashed on North Carolina.

That happened in a lot of places. Jason wants the incoming Democratic Congress to focus on the cost of living and steer clear of impeachment.

"My fear is that the Democrats now are going to spend the next 2 years not focusing on any of the things that they say Trump didn't do," said Jason.

Michelle in Michigan, voted for President Biden in 2020 but chose Republicans in 2024 and again in this year's midterms.

"This is the first time I think ever since I've been voting that not one of the people that I voted for won their election," Michelle said.

Michelle says she understands why so many people voted for Democrats, even if she didn't. Americans are tired, she said, of high gas prices, the cost of living and not being able to afford their groceries. They voted for change.

John from Pennsylvania said it felt like his state went from purple to blue overnight.

"I'm just very surprised," John said. "Not surprised that Democrats had a good night, but they had a very good night. Absolutely amazed that they won in Texas and places that just seemed like they were really red."

He voted for President Biden in 2020 and President Trump in 2024. In the most recent midterms, he stuck with Republicans despite concerns about the cost of living and the war with Iran.

Sponsor Message

Gerald in Georgia ran through the list of states where Democrats won senate races in disbelief.

"Come on man, Texas turned blue," Gerald said. "South Carolina turned blue, Ohio, Kansas. Like, this was a referendum of epic proportions."

Gerald is a Biden to Trump voter from Georgia, who has gone all in on MAGA. He's already looking ahead to a future without Trump leading Republicans.

"The Donald Trump era for all intents and purposes is coming to an end in 2028 for certain, if not before that," Gerald said.

Before that, though, Democrats will take power in Washington, at least in part.

Swing Shift voters said again and again when asked about their hopes and fears following these midterms that they hope that the incoming Democratic Congress will focus on the issues that impact their daily lives but fear more of the same broken politics.

"I will choose to hope because that's really all we can do is hope," said Michelle. "Hope that the politicians that were voted in will live up to the promises they made and that change will truly be made."

Even though John didn't vote for Democrats this year, he still wants them to tackle the cost of living.

"Over these next 2 years I hope they are concerned with and concentrate on the affordability issue," John said. "I hope they work with President Trump to try to lower prices. I just hope it's not two years of investigations and impeachment hearings."

Anything Democrats pass in a divided government would have to be signed by President Trump. The president has been inconsistent in recent days about whether he wants cooperation or combat with the new Congress.

World.title: How China gets around the U.S. ban on Nvidia chips
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The revelation that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a former executive of a Singapore-based company has raised concerns about China's ability to acquire advanced microchips restricted from the country.

Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who later became the controlling shareholder of Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed International.

The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing while developing a close ​relationship with the Nvidia CE O — accusations that China's Foreign ⁠Ministry has called "groundless."

Megaspeed has also drawn scrutiny from U.S. authorities over suspicions that it helped Chinese companies obtain advanced Nvidia chips, subject to Washington's export restrictions.

Meanwhile, the scandal has put the effectiveness of the U.S. restrictions on these advanced chips to China under a spotlight.

Here's a look at why China needs these top-tier chips, why the U.S. has banned them from export, and how China is still able to acquire them.

Why would China want Nvidia's chips?

Nvidia designs the world’s most powerful AI chips, which are considered the gold standard, analysts say.

"Their chips are at the forefront of the AI revolution," said Ryan Ellis, an associate professor at Northeastern University in Boston, whose research focuses on communication law and policy, infrastructure politics and cybersecurity.

Artificial intelligence takes a huge amount of graphics processing (GPU) capacity, added Dennis Wilder, a former senior U.S. intelligence officer and National Security Council director for China.

High-end chips, like those offered by Nvidia, provide a cheaper means of developing AI, without having to create more data centres to create more GPU capacity, Wilder said.

They also support the most advanced AI models, Ellis said, meaning a lack of access to those chips hampers development.

"Inside China, there is an incredible hunger and thirst for these chips," he said. "There's a thriving black market for the most advanced video chips in China."

Why did the U.S. block sales of these chips to China?

In October 2022, under the Biden administration, the U.S. Department of Commerce implemented export controls on advanced computing chips going to China. That means Nvidia's top-end chips, Blackwell Ultra and Vera Rubin — both GPUs used for AI models, are blocked from being sold to the country.

The U.S. government has two main reasons for blocking these sales: To maintain the country's global lead in AI development and to protect national security.

Whoever is winning the AI race — and able to train the best models — has the ability to be in the driver's seat for this next era of the AI revolution, said Chris Mattmann, who was the inaugural chief data and AI officer at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA).

WATCH | Nvidia shares slide following CEO affair with alleged Chinese spy: Nvidia shares slide as U.S. firm probes CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy | Duration closed caption 2:07 Nvidia shares dropped sharply after the U.S. tech giant launched an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a Chinese woman who U.S. intelligence agencies allege is a spy for Beijing.

While the U.S is still ahead of China, that gap is closing, Mattmann said. And anything that might "move the needle," like access to advanced chips, helps close that gap, he said.

The U.S. government is also trying to preserve national security, with concerns that allowing China access to such chips could help advance its military technology, potentially allowing the development of systems that might one day threaten U.S. interests.

"Export controls are always … trying to both allow a market to grow, but also to shape that market in such a way that it doesn't undermine national security," said Ellis.

U.S. President Donald Trump, however, has eased up on some restrictions, and now allows other Nvidia chips that were initially blocked — typically those used in consumer electronics — to be sold to China under certain conditions.

So how is China getting Nvidia chips?

Soon after advanced chip restrictions to China were implemented, an illegal smuggling and underground network was set up by many vendors to get the chips into China and sell them on to companies there, Germany's Deutsche Welle (DW) news agency reported.

The U.S. has cracked down on those vendors, where possible. In December 2025, the Department of Justice announced two Chinese men were in custody for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

A screengrab from CTI video footage shows a woman identified by Reuters as Alice Huang, after comparison with a photograph obtained separately, attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan, on May 22, 2025. (Reuters)

But there's also a legal loophole that can be exploited to send chips to China.

While Nvidia can't sell their most advanced chips directly to China or China-based companies, they can sell them to other countries, and third-party data centres can then rent out access to those data centres to companies affiliated with China.

WATCH | Nvidia investigates CEO's relationship with alleged Chinese spy: Nvidia opens investigation into CEO's relationship with alleged Chinese spy | Duration closed caption 6:50 Nvidia is opening an investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, after he admitted to having an affair. The woman in question is accused of being a Chinese spy, having allegedly passed information to Beijing, according to a media report. New York Times reporter Julian E. Barnes, who broke the news of Huang's relationship, says 'there is a long way to go on this story.'

For example, Nvidia could sell the chips to a Malaysian company that then turns around and rents that computing power to a Chinese company, Ellis said, and "that would be above board."

While some U.S. lawmakers believe this loophole should be closed, others believe it is a reasonable accommodation, Ellis said.

But, Ellis said, the current scandal suggests that what's often happening is that these chips are being sold to these other countries, where they are then moved straight into China.

Are the controls truly effective?

According to Ellis, U.S. export controls are "never going to be 100 per cent perfect."

But there could certainly be more spot checks and more aggressive oversight to make sure the purchasers of these chips remain the end users, he said. "The enforcement is missing."

The U.S. Commerce Department's enforcement arm, the Bureau of Industry and Security, is just not staffed well enough to enforce the restrictions, Wilder agreed.

For example, Reuters reported that China's Northwestern Polytechnical University purchased Nvidia H200 chips last month, according to records. The news agency also found that other Chinese universities have bought Nvidia chips barred from export, including several institutions that had close ‌links to China's ⁠defence industry or military research.

WATCH | Why D.C. has proposed an emergency hotline with Beijing: Can an AI 'red phone' stop a U.S.-China war? | About That | Duration 2:54 A spike in AI agents operating outside human instruction has prompted Washington to propose an emergency hotline with Beijing. Andrew Chang breaks down why the U.S. is opting to keep an open line on AI despite a longstanding rivalry and distrust. Images provided by The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty

The controls have also raised questions as to whether they are achieving the intended effect of slowing Chinese development.

Since the U.S. in 2019 excluded Huawei — and later China — from buying some of the world's most powerful computer chips and chipmaking machinery, Chinese semiconductor makers have rushed to become self-sufficient, developing their own chips and know-how.

Jensen Huang himself, who has advocated for looser export controls on China, has argued that continued U.S. sales to China would preserve American technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on U.S. technology.

"We have to, No. 1, make sure that we have national security and that we protect our nation, but we also simultaneously should go and compete, and grow our technology industry and maximize our exports," the Nvidia CEO told The Associated Press in June.

World.title: LinkedIn, Monster take down over 1,000 fake job postings after CBC investigation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

More than 1,500 misleading job postings — offering remote work, no experience needed — have been taken down from LinkedIn and Monster after a CBC visual investigation revealed the listings funnelled unsuspecting applicants to a multi-level marketing (MLM) company that asked for money.

CBC connected a network of travel-related pages posting suspicious jobs — positions like "Work From Home Travel Planner and Virtual Customer Support Representative" — to a U.S.-based MLM called Evolution Travel. Some of the roles promised to pay up to $75,000 US per year.

In reality, there was no job and no salary.

Applicants were quickly directed to join virtual information sessions, where they were asked to pay hundreds of dollars up front, followed by a monthly subscription fee. The program promised to teach members how to make money from booking travel as an independent agent and recruiting others into the program, taking a cut of their commissions.

WATCH | Investigating who's behind hundreds of fake job postings: Exposing who’s behind fake job ads online | Duration closed caption 10:19 Major job-seeking platforms host hundreds of listings for remote travel jobs that promise salaries up to $75,000 with no experience required. CBC Visual Investigations applied online and found that there is no job: The ads lead to a U.S.-based multi-level marketing scheme that asks unsuspecting applicants to pay up front. After flagging the listings to LinkedIn and Monster, nearly 1,500 were taken offline.

The companies went by names like Wanderwell Collective, Professional Travel Hub, Remote-Careers, Sky Land & Ocean Travel and Sunkissed Getaways.

The job postings made no mention of Evolution Travel or sign-up fees.

Many of the jobs did not require experience and promised to pay up to $75,000 US. (Illustration: Matthew Hoddy/CBC; LinkedIn)

"This is disgusting," said Jay Jones, a Chicago-based job listing investigator who CBC shared its findings with. "They catch you with the lure of the fake job. The money is great, [successful applicants] get to stay at home. You have to pay to get work — that's not how work works."

Misleading job postings — including ones that require payment or lead to MLMs — are strictly prohibited on platforms like LinkedIn and other job sites.

Jay Jones investigates misleading and fake jobs online. (CBC)

"It feels in so many ways that we're living in a funhouse mirror," said Vass Bednar, managing director of the Canadian Shield Institute, a public policy think-tank that focuses on economic resilience and digital sovereignty.

These postings risk "eroding confidence — confidence in the self and confidence that there is, frankly, meaningful work out there for people that is worth pursuing."

Jobs were 'misleading': LinkedIn

MLMs are not illegal in Canada or the U.S. However, in the U.S., companies and individuals could face fines if they are found to violate the U.S. Federal Trade Commission Act, which prohibits "unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce."

"I would consider [these job posts] misleading… and would invite enforcement by either the FTC, the state governments or other federal enforcement agencies," said William Kovacic, former FTC chairman and commissioner, with whom CBC also shared its findings.

One independent agent behind multiple travel businesses linked to misleading jobs ads CBC identified — Wanderwell Collective, Destination Knot, Aisle and Abroad, and Professional Travel Hub — was Diedre Norton. In one video posted to YouTube, Norton said she had a network of 300 recruits for Evolution Travel.

Even though Evolution Travel’s founder, David McCovy, praised her in online videos as being a top performer, Norton denied being affiliated with the program before hanging up on CBC News.

Screenshot of an online video showing Evolution founder David McCovy during a conference. (EvolutionTravelCafe/YouTube)

McCovy did not respond to CBC’s requests for comment.

A representative from Evolution Travel who only identified themselves by their title, chief operating officer, told CBC they have consistently told their independent agents not to post job ads on any platforms.

Late last month, LinkedIn took down close to 900 ads connected to Evolution Travel, saying it had removed them because they were "misleading and violated" company policy, adding "the companies behind them will no longer be able to post jobs" on the platform.

Monster took down 600 listings, saying it has "clear policies prohibiting misleading job postings and multi-level marketing opportunities, and we take action to remove listings that do not meet our standards."

Hundreds of job postings posted to LinkedIn and Monster actually brought applicants into the recruiting process for a multi-level marketing company, a CBC News visual investigation has found. (Illustration: Matthew Hoddy/CBC, LinkedIn, Monster)

Detecting fake jobs

Evolution Travel does not operate in Canada, but CBC journalists still came across the job posting in their feeds. They were also recommended in emails from LinkedIn.

The ads contained immediate red flags. The travel companies named in the ads had minimal to no presence online, and there were close to 1,500 postings, often with almost identical job descriptions.

Many of the jobs did not require experience and were remote. CBC found more than 1,500 misleading or fake jobs. (LinkedIn)

The jobs, in many cases, required no education, no prior experience and often did not require a resumé.

CBC applied for eight jobs on LinkedIn and Monster, attaching a blank document as a resumé in cases that required it. Upon applying, the team was sent automated emails to join a virtual information session by individuals connected to Evolution Travel.

CBC journalists were sent automated emails and asked to join a virtual information session by individuals connected to Evolution Travel upon applying for the jobs. (CBC)

Evolution Travel and its partner Archer Travel Services describe themselves as an international "home-based travel business" that trains its members to book travel and earn a commission.

But it's not just about booking travel. Archer Travel’s website describes Evolution Travel as its "recruiting partner" and describes it as a "network marketing" company — another term for multi-level marketing, according to the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

A compensation plan for members on Evolution Travel’s website shows a percentage of commissions and monthly bonuses are paid to the most effective recruiters, with membership tiers up to "8 Star Platinum" for recruiting 100,000 people.

Documents show compensation plans for Evolution Travel. (Evolution Travel)

None of this was mentioned in the information sessions CBC attended, which covered travel booking exclusively. When a CBC journalist posing as a job applicant asked about getting commissions from their own recruits, the session host said it was not covered in the information sessions and that the person who invited them into the program would address it.

Session hosts also didn’t disclose there is a hidden $50 annual fee in the independent contractor agreement, seen by CBC, when signing up.

A screenshot from an Evolution virtual session shows the packages attendees can pay to enrol in the program. (Evolution Travel)

Former FTC chairman and commissioner Kovacic said if he were still at the agency, he would be looking into the company.

"[Fees are] not presented in the initial interaction," he said. "It's shrouded in a way that's very important and would mislead users."

27,000 independent contractors

Job seekers have been complaining about Evolution Travel, its members and agents like Deidre Norton online and to the Better Business Bureau for years.

In 2021, Evolution Travel was among 1,000 companies put on notice by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission that they could face fines if they or their representatives made "misleading, or deceptive representations" about a "money-making opportunity."

Kovacic said a firm that "defied" FTC notices and continued to persist in these practices would be a "worthy target for an investigation."

CBC News found numerous complaints online about companies linked to the job postings. (Illustration: Matthew Hoddy/CBC, Reddit, Better Business Bureau)

Ron Archer, the CEO of Archer Travel Services, said that the company does "not condone illegal job postings and addresses them when we are made aware."

Yet in videos online, travel agents connected to Evolution Travel talked openly about using LinkedIn job postings to recruit people into the business.

Archer said they cannot "tell people how they train for their business" because they have "27,000 independent contractors around the world."

"LinkedIn is a big one," said one member in a June 2026 training video posted to YouTube. "We have quite a few different trainings on how to post on LinkedIn."

Jay Jones, who has gotten tens of thousands of jobs taken down from platforms himself, said companies like LinkedIn and Monster generate revenue through this traffic.

"There's no actual vetting of what companies get to be created, what jobs get to be listed," said Jones. "People coming [to LinkedIn] believing that there are real opportunities are greeted with this MLM nonsense."

For any tips related to this investigation, contact eric.szeto@cbc.ca or the visual investigation team’s inbox: vi@cbc.ca

World.title: American Airlines resumes flights to Haiti, providing a vital route into the country
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A major U.S. airline has begun flying into northern Haiti on a daily basis, providing a vital route into the country at a time when Americans have few options to get there amid U.S. government advice to avoid all travel to the Caribbean nation due to security concerns.

At the start of November, American Airlines relaunched daily non-stop service from Miami to the port city of Cap-Haïtien after a years-long absence that began during the pandemic and persisted through a prolonged period of instability that has followed in Haiti.

"We are ​excited ​to return ​to Haiti," the airline told CBC News via email, pointing to the important link the route provides between the two countries.

Yet the route is resuming at a time when the U.S. State Department is advising people not to travel to Haiti for any reason, as a result of the ongoing state of emergency in the country and general security risks — including crime, kidnapping and unrest. Canada's government is also currently warning people not to visit the country.

Haiti has endured a series of crises, including years of political chaos, widespread gang violence and a related wave of civilian displacement. The country also faces major challenges with hunger at the moment.

The State Department nonetheless sees value in Americans having another way to get to Haiti, telling CBC News that it "welcomes" the airline's new service to Cap-Haïtien — even though its travel advice is unchanged.

"The Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans," the State Department said.

A 'very complicated' journey lately

The return of the American Airlines service between South Florida and the western side of the island of Hispaniola, is likewise welcomed by members of the Haitian community in the U.S.

Wolf Pamphile, the founder and CEO of Haiti Policy House, a Washington, D.C.,-based think-tank, said travel to Haiti has been "very complicated" for those trying to get there from the U.S. — with Haitian carrier Sunrise Airways being one of the main options.

LISTEN | The Trump administration and Haiti: Front Burner 36:28 Why is Trump so focused on Haiti?

The United States has a large Haitian diaspora, particularly in Florida. But Pamphile said there are also many people with ties to Haiti living in parts of the northeastern U.S. — including in New York, New Jersey and Massachusetts.

He says the return of American Airlines to Cap-Haïtien gives Haiti-bound American air travellers more reliability and a level of customer service "that doesn't exist in the market right now."

For Florida resident Gilson Morusuma, American Airlines' re-entry into the Haitian market brings the prospect of better service and more competitive pricing for air travel to his home country.

But when speaking to The Haitian Times, he noted that while the return of the American Airlines route offers travellers like himself a new option, "it does not resolve the broader challenges facing the country's aviation sector or restore service to the capital."

Shift in air traffic

Pamphile says the security situation in Haiti's capital of Port-au-Prince has led to a shift in air traffic, to the point where Cap-Haïtien has become "the main hub" for many international flights to the island.

Pamphile noted that while Port-au-Prince faces gang-related security challenges, the situation is "drastically different" in Cap-Haïtien, which is about 200 kilometres north of the capital.

Pilots watch the runway from the cockpit of a plane landing in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti, in April 2026. (Clarens Siffroy/AFP/Getty Images)

Regarding security considerations surrounding its flights to Cap-Haïtien, American Airlines told CBC News it "conducts ​a comprehensive ​review ​of a variety ​of operational, safety and ​business ​considerations before ​starting service."

There were a spate of publicly reported incidents in November 2024 of gangs firing at aircraft in Port-au-Prince — including an American Airlines flight. As a result, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration banned U.S. flights from landing in the capital — a ban that's been extended into 2027.

The November 2024 incidents also led to a shutdown of the international airport in Port-au-Prince. Seven months after, Haiti's Sunrise airline operated the first commercial flight out of the capital, according to The Associated Press.

Fellow U.S. carrier JetBlue Airways used to fly to Haiti, but halted service in 2024 after one of its planes was shot at when departing Port-au-Prince.

In July, JetBlue president Marty St. George told the Miami Herald the airline had no plans to return.

JetBlue told CBC News it did not have "any updates or additional information to share regarding our service to Haiti."

Parallel advice from Ottawa

Like its U.S. counterpart, Global Affairs Canada is also telling travellers to avoid all travel to Haiti given the "extremely volatile" security situation in the country.

As such, two Canadian airlines that previously flew to Haiti have no immediate plans to restart flights to the country.

"We do not anticipate resuming our service to Port-au-Prince in the near future," Stéphanie Dussault, an Air Transat spokesperson, told CBC News via email. "We continue to assess the situation in Haiti, with the safety of our passengers and crew guiding any decision about future service."

That's also the case at Air Canada, which is not operating flights to Haiti at this time.

"We continue to closely monitor the situation and will assess opportunities to resume service when conditions allow," Yasmine Mehdi, an airline spokesperson, said in an emailed statement.

World.title: Anthropic IPO to test the first 'pure play' AI stock in a choppy market
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Anthropic's stock market debut is set to be big — a big valuation, big spending, big warnings, big uncertainty for investors and a big potential indicator of how the recently volatile artificial intelligence sector will fare in 2027.

In an amended U.S. regulatory filing Tuesday, San Francisco-based Anthropic set an expected initial public offering (IPO) price range of $70 US to $78 US per share. That implies a fully diluted market valuation of roughly $1.3 trillion US at the midpoint, climbing to $1.4 trillion US at the top end , marking the largest technology stock market debut on record.

"It's going to be one of the biggest IPOs in history," said Greg Taylor, portfolio manager at Vancouver-based PenderFund Capital Management.

The size of an IPO is typically measured by the amount of capital raised. Anthropic is aiming to raise up to $64.4 billion US directly through its public share offering. If that happens, it will rank behind only SpaceX's record-setting stock market launch in June .

Taylor expects Anthropic shares will start trading before America celebrates Thanksgiving, on Nov. 26. Wealthsimple, the popular Canadian financial trading app, lists an expected "IPO day" of Nov. 30.

Ernest Wong, head of research at Toronto-based Baskin Wealth Management, anticipates the stock will be a serious heavyweight when it starts trading on the Nasdaq exchange.

"There are only a handful of stocks in the world that are valued over $1 trillion US," he said. "It speaks to how big AI really is."

WATCH | What's next for Nvidia, after an alleged Chinese spy scandal: What the CEO cheating scandal could mean for Nvidia and AI | Duration closed caption 1:59 After Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, questions are being raised about the company's governance and deeper implications for the future of AI.

What is Anthropic?

Anthropic started as a niche AI research lab in 2021, when its founders left rival OpenAI because they felt it was too focused on profits, ignoring risks and giving too much control to investors.

The company gained momentum in 2024, when it released Claude 3.5 Sonnet. This version beat OpenAI's GPT-4o on major performance benchmarks at a fraction of the cost of previous frontier AI models.

Unlike Apple or Microsoft, Anthropic is not a traditional for-profit company. It's organized as a public benefit corporation, meaning its board has a legal mandate to balance public safety against maximizing shareholder returns.

Today, Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei is a leading advocate for AI safety , arguing the industry should slow development to let safety measures catch up.

In Anthropic's recent regulatory filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, 94 of more than 300 pages were dedicated to spelling out a long list of risk factors.

"Our AI models may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed," the company stated.

Anthropic says this may include, "behavior resembling blackmail or efforts to influence human decision-makers to preserve the model's continued operation," as well as actions that "pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

Big numbers

$1.4 trillion US is not the only eyebrow-raising figure associated with Anthropic's IPO.

The company's valuation has fluctuated wildly in recent months. $2 trillion US was recently on the table. In late May, private investors valued the company at $965 billion US, up from $380 billion US in February.

"There's a fairly big degree of optimism baked into these valuations as they're coming out," Taylor said.

"I don't think anyone can tell you what Anthropic is gonna look like five years out."

Dario Amodei, CEO and co-founder of Anthropic, attends the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January 2025. (Markus Schreiber/The Associated Press)

The company's sales have been brisk. According to regulatory filings, Anthropic earned more than three and a half times as much revenue in the first six months of 2026 as it did in the entire previous calendar year. Roughly 20 per cent of those sales came from two big unnamed customers.

At the same time, the AI giant has been spilling a lot of red ink. It booked a $80.7 billion US net loss this year through June, although this was mainly due to non-cash accounting charges. The company lost $42 billion US in 2025.

Anthropic also has big spending plans. The company does not build or own physical data centres. Instead, it rents high-performance computing power from cloud providers like Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud through massive multi-year service contracts.

According to regulatory filings, Anthropic has locked in nearly $900 billion US in cloud and computing deals that run through the 2030s and 2040s. Partners in these deals include Broadcom, SpaceX AI, Google Cloud, Amazon Web Services, and Microsoft Azure.

A blockbuster IPO

Anthropic's IPO isn't noteworthy for its massive size alone.

"Buying the Anthropic IPO is one of the first pure play AI investments out there," Taylor said.

Until now, investors looking to own a piece of the artificial intelligence boom have been mainly limited to far less AI-focused technology stocks such as Microsoft or Nvidia, which makes chips. Google, for example, is widely-considered part of the AI investment theme. But the company also has massive businesses unrelated to AI, like its Android smartphones, and YouTube.

"The only thing they do is create new AI models," Wong said of Anthropic. "It's certainly a missing piece of the puzzle, in the sense that you have the public company data from all of the various players that are involved in AI, except for the model companies, which are largely Anthropic and OpenAI."

If Anthropic's IPO is seen as a new benchmark for AI investment, its first trading sessions will come amid significant volatility for the technology sector.

Earlier this month, tech and AI stocks experienced sharp sell-offs and swift rebounds as markets entered correction territory. This was due in part to concerns about AI companies matching their big spending with sufficient profits. The situation was compounded by political concerns in the U.S. after the midterms about tighter regulation for AI and data centres.

At the same time, the recent scandal involving Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy adds a new dimension to AI investment concerns. The chipmaker's stock, seen as a bellwether for the AI trade, has erased billions in market capitalization in recent days on the Nasdaq, where Anthropic is set to debut.

Like the dot com bubble?

"The main risk for Anthropic is that essentially they have to compete with other model providers. It's a very competitive market," Wong said. "OpenAI makes their own models. SpaceX through Grok is a leading model lab. Certainly, Google and Meta are competing in this space."

He predicts the stock won't be for the faint of heart early on, as investors rank each new Anthropic product against peers and evaluate it's huge spending on data services.

"It'll be very volatile," Wong said.

Such has been the case with SpaceX since its Nasdaq debut in June. The stock surged about 19 per cent on day one. Since then, it's dipped as much as 22 per cent below its $135 US IPO price.

For Taylor, the AI sector's massive spending, blistering stock run-ups and tight business links between a handful of tech companies are all reminders of a previous investment frenzy that separated winners from losers in spectacular fashion.

"The dot-com bubble is certainly the one that's probably most real in a lot of people's minds," he said. "Everyone wanted a piece of the internet back in 2000."

While companies like Pets.com went bust, Google and Microsoft became household names.

"There's a lot of big parallels here with AI," Taylor said. "It's just figuring out who's going to win at the end of the day."

World.title: Shelter workers raise alarm as severe stomach bug hits Montreal's homeless population
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A severe stomach bug has spread through Montreal's homeless population, raising concern among shelter workers who say not enough is being done to contain it.

Shigella infection, also known as shigellosis, leads to diarrhea, stomach cramps and fever.

Its spread can be prevented by simple hygiene, such as handwashing, but the bacterial infection is affecting some of the city's homeless population, who don't often have access to clean water and washrooms.

One worker at the Old Brewery Mission, one of the city's largest shelters, said they don't believe the measures in place at the site are sufficient. They have reported the situation to the province's workplace safety board.

"Employees are not confident it's being taken seriously enough," said the person, whom CBC agreed not to identify out of concern for their job security.

"We don't feel supported."

Michelle Patenaude, executive director of CAP Saint-Barnabé, which operates three shelters in eastern Montreal, said her organization has been taking precautions to curb the spread of the bacteria. At one point, Patenaude said she was forced to restrict access to some services.

"We welcome particularly vulnerable people daily, in collective environments where infection prevention is a major challenge," she said in an email. "Nobody is taking this situation lightly."

Julien Montreuil, head of L'Anonyme, a group that works with people in encampments, said he believes the situation is under control for now. But he said that, for people who live in tents, even the basic hygiene advice from public health officials "can sometimes be complicated."

Advisory sent to medical staff

The problem was first flagged by health authorities in September, and then again in October.

Santé Québec, the Crown corporation responsible for the province's health network, circulated an advisory on Oct. 26 to front-line medical staff and specialists, obtained by CBC News, warning about a rise in multidrug-resistant infections of shigella among the city's homeless population that began in September in the east end.

The advisory said the "highly contagious nature of the infection," as well as "crowded conditions in shelters" and "limited access to sanitary facilities" could all contribute to transmission.

It also stressed the need to rapidly report cases in order to trace the spread.

In an email, Montreal Public Health said 45 shigellosis cases have been confirmed among the city's homeless population since late August. The city typically records about 150 cases annually across the entire population.

Spokesperson Geneviève Paradis said the agency has deployed staff to affected shelters to reinforce hygiene protocols. But Paradis said it is "crucial that none of these measures restrict access to the care, services and resources people need."

William Hodgson, a spokesperson for the Old Brewery Mission, said the shelter takes the situation "very seriously," and has been working with public health authorities.

"If communications weren't good enough, we want to be better at that," he said.

WATCH | Why this stomach bug is getting harder to treat: Stomach bug circulating among homeless population getting harder to treat | Duration closed caption 7:23 Toronto Public Health has reported at least 11 confirmed cases of Shigella infection, all among homeless people. The bacterial infection causes diarrhea, can be spread by as few as 10 bacteria and is becoming increasingly resistant to antibiotics.

Growing cases in Canadian cities

Shigellosis, one of the main causes of dysentery, spreads from person to person through an infected person's stool.

A microscopic amount of the bacteria on surfaces, in food or water can be enough to get someone sick. The bacteria also remains contagious for weeks after episodes of intense diarrhea.

The bacterial infection has become more common among homeless people in North American cities, including Vancouver, Edmonton and Toronto, and research indicates it is also increasingly resistant to antibiotics.

A recent study by researchers at the University of British Columbia found cases were on the rise among homeless people in Vancouver. The authors warned that greater outreach was necessary to crack down on the bacterial infection.

Dr. Carl Boodman, an expert in infectious diseases at the McGill University Health Centre, told CBC the bacterial infection is treatable and preventable.

He said outbreaks are linked, ultimately, to a lack of adequate housing and a lack of access to "public sanitation infrastructure for those who are experiencing homelessness."

World.title: Pilot killed in plane crash during Remembrance Day event in Quebec's Beauce region
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A pilot died in a plane crash during a Remembrance Day ceremony in Quebec's Beauce region Wednesday morning.

The Sûreté du Québec (SQ) says the pilot was a man in his 60s from the region.

He was alone in the plane at the time of the crash, according to SQ spokesperson Sgt. Audrey-Anne Bilodeau.

While police have not publicly identified the pilot, Radio-Canada is reporting his name was Daniel Parent. They say the 68-year-old was a member of a local flight club, the Club Aéronautique de Beauce.

The fatal crash took place in a wooded area close to the local airport in Saint-Georges, Que., about 100 kilometres south of Quebec City.

The city's mayor told CBC the crash occurred during a Remembrance Day ceremony.

"A formation of six aircraft was performing the Missing Man formation as part of the ceremony when one of the pilots crashed," Manon Bougie said via email.

Part of the aircraft wreckage in a wooded area, not far from the Saint-Georges, Que., airport. (Guillaume Croteau-Langevin/Radio-Canada)

It happened as the pilot was on approach for landing, according to the city's fire department.

Fire Chief Frédéric Morin said emergency crews arrived in less than six minutes, but were unfortunately unable to save the pilot, as the aircraft was already fully engulfed in flames.

"It was a deeply sad and tragic moment," said Bougie of the crash. "Our thoughts are with everyone affected by this terrible accident."

Sgt. Bilodeau said the aircraft being flown were all private planes with civilian pilots.

WATCH | Pilot killed during Remembrance Day event in Beauce region: Quebec pilot killed in crash linked to ceremony for Remembrance Day | Duration 1:17 A pilot has died in a plane crash linked to a Remembrance Day ceremony in Quebec's Beauce region Wednesday morning.

Resident heard crash, saw flames

Saint-Georges resident Michel Rodrigue, who lives about two kilometres from where the Remembrance Day ceremony was taking place, says he heard the crash.

The plane ended up landing in the woods across from his neighbour's property, which he estimates is about 100 feet from his house.

He described the sound of the crash as metallic, like the sound of sheet metal.

"My wife has flowers upstairs and I thought the cat had knocked over the flower cabinet," Rodrigue said.

"It turned out it was the plane crashing behind our house."

Rodrigue recalled looking outside and seeing flames. So he went to grab fire extinguishers.

"But two small fire extinguishers wouldn't have been enough for a fire that size," he said.

Condolences pour in

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon posted his condolences to the pilot's family and loved ones on X.

The premier has said he's closely monitoring the situation and is in touch with Domestic Security Minister Guy Lapointe Jr.

Several other provincial and federal politicians soon followed in sharing their sympathies.

Among them was federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon, who wrote on Facebook that he was saddened to learn of the pilot's passing.

The SQ initially said the pilot was seriously injured and then confirmed the death shortly before 1:30 p.m. The crash is still under investigation. (Edouard Dubois/Radio-Canada)

Provincial police are still on scene.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada is deploying a team of investigators to the site in order to gather information and assess what happened.

It's still not known what caused the plane to go down.

World.title: Ottawa had been aware of Stellantis-Roshel talks for months, source says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal government had been made aware for months about the possibility that Stellantis would sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to a light armoured vehicle manufacturer, a source has told CBC News.

The automaker announced on Monday that it plans to sell the plant to Roshel Inc., a move Prime Minister Mark Carney characterized as a "betrayal of the workers as it is a betrayal of the obligations to Canada."

A source with direct knowledge of the sale of the Stellantis Brampton plant said the federal government had been engaged regularly on the deal since August. The source said both the Prime Minister's Office and Industry Minister Mélanie Joly's office had been briefed on the details of what was going to be announced. CTV News first reported the government's involvement in the talks.

More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when Stellantis halted operations in 2023 to refit the facility to produce the Jeep Compass.

Both Carney and Joly have blasted the potential sale to Roshel. The minister is expected to hold a meeting of all stakeholders in Toronto on Thursday in an attempt to find a way forward for the laid-off Stellantis workers.

WATCH | Did Stellantis violate its deals with the federal government?: CBC speaks with Flavio Volpe about funding contract given to Stellantis by government | Duration closed caption 8:48 Get the latest on CBCNews.ca, the CBC News App, and CBC News Network for breaking news and analysis.

Ottawa didn't facilitate deal, minister's office says

A spokesperson for Joly said she "had no part in negotiating the deal with Stellantis or Roshel."

"The minister didn't meet with Roshel regarding this issue," Mathis Denis said.

"Reporting that the minister was involved in the Roshel deal is false."

"The minister, the department and the team would never have approved or agreed to a deal that lacked the union's approval. The minister would never have agreed to something the union doesn't accept," Denis said.

In a deal announced by the former Trudeau government in 2022, Ottawa said it would inject up to $529 million in Stellantis plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., to help them retool to increase production of electric and gas-powered vehicles.

Denis also said Joly or her team wouldn't approve a deal with Roshel if it broke Stellantis's commitments under that 2022 deal.

That same agreement also saw Ontario Premier Doug Ford's government pledge to support the plants with an investment of up to $513 million.

CBC News confirmed on Tuesday that Ontario has not provided the company with any funding for its Brampton retooling initiative because it didn't meet conditions related to job creation and project milestones.

Ford cautions against Chinese 'knock-down kits'

Ford wrote a letter to Carney on Tuesday, a copy of which has been obtained by CBC News, warning against the possibility that the plant would be used to assemble "Chinese-made knock-down kits" — where a Chinese auto manufacturer imports parts from overseas just to be assembled in Canada.

"We cannot undermine the future of Canada and Ontario’s automotive sector by allowing the introduction of Chinese-made knock-down kits at the Stellantis Brampton facility," Ford wrote in the letter, adding that he is pleased the federal government is aligned on that position.

"The economic impact of introducing kits to Ontario’s automotive sector would be devastating to Canadian automotive workers and to the thousands of businesses and workers across the Canadian automotive and auto parts supply chain."

WATCH | Poilievre calls on Joly to be fired over Stellantis plant closure: Poilievre calls on Joly to be fired over Stellantis Brampton plant closure | Duration closed caption 2:02 Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre blamed the Liberal government for failing to prevent the closure of the Stellantis auto plant in Brampton, Ont., and called on Prime Minister Carney to fire Industry Minister Mélanie Joly for her handling of the file.

Ford has come out aggressively against the idea of the Brampton plant being used as an assembly station for Chinese vehicles since the possibility was first suggested in a February report by Bloomberg News. The outlet suggested Stellantis was in talks with Zhejiang ‌Leapmotor Technology, a Chinese automobile manufacturer with headquarters in Hangzhou, China, at that time.

Asked about the Stellantis sale during an unrelated news conference on Monday, Ford again raised concerns about Chinese assembly kits.

"We can't bring in kits from China. Can't happen," the premier said. "That will bastardize the whole sector. Unacceptable. We need them to find a vehicle, a model that works."

World.title: Hegseth, wife and aides spark scolding from guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth following a Veterans Day ceremony.

Video shows Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.

As the group broke from taking photos, a loud laugh could be heard, and the soldier guarding the tomb shouted that "all visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's top spokesperson, said that "while commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoured — and will always honour — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe," he added.

WATCH | Hegseth and group appear to be rebuked: Hegseth delegation appears to be rebuked at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier | Duration closed caption 0:43 A U.S. army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier appeared to rebuke War Secretary Pete Hegseth, his wife and aides after loud laughter was heard from the group.

Incident follows near impeachment of Hegseth

The tomb is considered to be one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the U.S., being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from the First and Second World Wars and the Korean War. It has been guarded around the clock — rain or shine — by a soldier from the Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as "The Old Guard," since 1948.

Hegseth and his staff were at the tomb as part of a larger ceremony commemorating Veterans Day that was also attended by U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice-President JD Vance.

The incident comes a day after Hegseth narrowly survived an effort to impeach him by lawmakers in Congress.

The effort was led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats. However, while Hegseth's critics were not successful in Tuesday's vote, Republicans may have only delayed efforts to impeach him. With Democrats set to take control of the House of Representatives and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.

Hegseth slammed the effort on Tuesday at his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the U.S. Constitution for his removal.

WATCH | Hegseth survives impeachment vote: Republicans block impeachment push against Hegseth | Duration closed caption 2:43 The House of Representatives voted on Tuesday to shelve impeachment articles against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. Shortly after, U.S. President Donald Trump called outgoing Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie, who put forward the motion, a 'major loser.'

A core part of his argument included the assertion that criticisms of him and his handling of the U.S. military were tantamount to an indictment against the nation's service members and their successes.

"On the eve of Veterans Day, these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime," Hegseth said Tuesday.

"This is not patriotism," he said. "This is sabotage."

Following the reprimand at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, the reaction from Democrats was swift.

Rep. Gwen Moore said Hegseth demonstrated "his utter lack of fitness for his office."

"One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier," she wrote in a social media post.

Pete Hegseth continues to demonstrate his utter lack of fitness for his office. One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. —RepGwenMoore

It was not the first time members of Trump's team have caused controversy at Arlington National Cemetery.

During his campaign for a second term, Trump attended a ceremony in 2024 to honour U.S. forces killed in the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. A campaign staffer reportedly shoved a cemetery employee trying to prevent two people from filming and photographing the event.

WATCH | U.S. army confirms worker shoved by Trump staffer: U.S. army confirms Arlington cemetery worker 'pushed aside' by Trump staff | Duration 1:57 The U.S. army has confirmed claims that a member of Donald Trump's campaign 'pushed aside' a worker at Arlington National Cemetery who attempted to enforce rules against political activities there.

Trump, who had been invited by troops' families, later shared a video on TikTok showing him at the cemetery with a voiceover blaming the Biden administration for the "disaster" of the Afghanistan withdrawal.

U.S. law prohibits campaign or election-related activities within national military cemeteries.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Welcome to Barcelona, Venezuela – Photo of the Day
World.content:

World.title: Chile: Fatherhood Under Threat or Masculinity on the Defensive?
World.content:
A critique of Chile’s proposed False Accusations Law

By Andres Kogan Valderrama

HAVANA TIMES – Regarding a bill in the Chilean legislature which addresses false accusations and reports in family court proceedings, I would like to discuss how this initiative fits into antifeminist discourse and the activities of organizations seeking to perpetuate gender inequalities. I have worked on issues of masculinity for years, and as a father, I am particularly interested in discussing what we are defending when we talk about fatherhood.

First, I want to express my support for Colectiva Resistencia Materna Chile and Movimiento FemNNA, as well as the many other organizations and individuals who have warned about the risks this initiative poses to women who report violence and who have signed the letter opposing the proposed false accusations law (1).
