You couldn’t be too far right or too far left, but you could lean a little either way.

That broke down when Andrés Manuel López Obrador arrived on the scene. He hadn’t gone to a good private school, didn’t have a respected last name and wasn’t even from a major city. He was born in a small town in Tabasco, a place that looks more like Thailand and feels more like Costa Rica than the usual image of Mexico. He wasn’t exactly poor, but he was definitely not elite, and his political manners showed it. AMLO, as he is known, had not traveled the world, didn’t shop in Houston or spend summers in Spain. And whatever his politics (which are hard to pin down), moderation was not among them.

When he became mayor of Mexico City in 2000, the country’s main political goal was ending the PRI’s 71-year regime, and his freshness was welcome in a city that is huge, mostly progressive and the intellectual center of the country. He was audacious and, on balance, probably a good mayor: he changed the city’s political culture and paved the way for its later transformation. But when he ran for president, everything changed. The elites were alarmed to see an outsider so close to power. His razor-thin loss to Felipe Calderón in 2006, amid allegations of fraud, polarized the country, and his reaction, declaring himself the “legitimate president,” offended an elite that prized adherence to the unwritten rules of power.

By the time he won the presidency in 2018, López Obrador was more stubborn and polarizing than ever. But Mexico had also changed in the 18 years since he was elected mayor, and he understood that change better than almost anyone. Most Mexicans outside any elite were fed up. The “social mood” index of the Mexican polling firm Nodo showed alarming levels of anger. The Peña Nieto government had been so visibly corrupt and elitist that it finally woke up Mexico’s middle and lower classes.

AMLO used this to his advantage. He built a communication style based on constantly antagonizing the elite and its most visible figures, then waiting for them to lash back. What the elites didn’t understand was that every attack made him stronger. For his voters, AMLO was the legitimate voice of the people. The strategy also let him recreate the environment where he thrived most: the permanent campaign, fueled by friction.

AMLO was not a great president. To his credit, he reduced poverty as no one had before, and he took control of the public narrative so completely that he built a nearly unbeatable electoral machine. But he governed like an eternal candidate rather than a president. He decided with his gut more than with the vision of a statesman, polarized society, dismantled valuable institutions and infrastructure projects because he didn’t like them, and championed others that have yet to prove their worth. In many ways, his government was a huge missed opportunity. In that sense, though, it was no different from those of Peña Nieto, Calderón or Fox, which were also deeply flawed but never seemed to bother the elites.

A famous Mexican writer once told me that AMLO’s greatest contribution to Mexico City was paving the way for the mayors who came after him. So when he chose Claudia Sheinbaum, a successful former mayor of the capital with a PhD in engineering, as his party’s candidate, there was a lot of hope.

Sheinbaum is not AMLO. She comes from an elite I haven’t mentioned yet, the cultural elite, and above all, she was an effective mayor. She won the 2024 election by nearly 19 million votes over the runner-up, Xóchitl Gálvez, and her approval rating has stayed above 70%. Still, the elites don’t like her.

Her government looks nothing like AMLO’s. She has grown close to the business community and is promoting investment as few of her predecessors have. She has been pragmatic with the United States and has brought Mexico back onto the world stage. Her security policy is the opposite of AMLO’s: she has gone after the cartels and violence has dropped. And her infrastructure projects, including passenger rail lines connecting Mexico’s main industrial hubs, make sense for the country’s needs.

Part of the elite’s rejection has to do with style. Although her policies are very different from AMLO’s, her rhetoric is very similar, and that is deliberate: she knows how to speak to her large political base. But the elites wouldn’t like her even if she spoke differently. They dislike her emphasis on social programs and social justice, but above all they dislike what she represents. She represents otherness: a Mexico that doesn’t move in their circles, that doesn’t solve problems over coffee in Polanco or through class pacts. She isn’t interested in money or in pleasing Mexico’s powerful men. They don’t like that she wears Indigenous clothing, and they don’t like that she is the heir of López Obrador, whom they see as an uneducated, ill-mannered, far-left provincial.

Mexico has at least two elites: the cultural one, which more or less accepts Sheinbaum, and the economic one, which deeply dislikes her. And the economic elite’s rejection has less to do with her policies than with the otherness it cannot accept. That elite wants a sort of White Mexico, one that mirrors its Americanized or Europeanized values and aspirations, its social codes, the primacy of its class and even of its skin color. Sheinbaum reminds it that it is no longer in power, and that is unbearable. Mexico’s elites will keep disliking Sheinbaum no matter what she does. How much of that comes from an actual analysis of her government, and how much from a view shaped by class, is a question with a mixed answer, though one that leans heavily in one direction.

Emilio Lezama is a Mexican writer, political analyst and communications strategist based in Mexico City. As founder and director of Los Hijos de la Malinche, a strategic communications agency, he advises international companies and institutions on navigating Mexico’s political landscape, managing reputation and crises, and building public support for their projects. He is a columnist for El Universal, has written for The New York Times and El País and has published several books.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Mexico City man forced to buy event merchandise to obtain tortillas outside his own apartment
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Municipal authorities confirmed Monday that Mexico City is on track to welcome a record-breaking 65.9 million tourists in 2026 — a massive influx driven by a packed calendar of international concerts and sporting events that has effectively transformed central residential neighborhoods into perpetual venue concourses.

The capital’s tourism boom, which has generated over 120 billion pesos in hotel revenue and a 16% jump in lodging tax collections, was fully on display Tuesday morning when local resident Rodrigo Morales was forced to purchase a 1,200-peso commemorative stadium tour hoodie just to reach the tortilleria on his own block.

Morales, 34, reportedly found himself cut off from basic domestic staples after event organizers erected a temporary VIP concourse, three wristband authentication checkpoints, and a corporate sponsor village outside his apartment building to accommodate back-to-back stadium shows and motorsport crowds.

“I simply wanted half a kilo of warm corn tortillas,” said Morales, standing in a two-hour credentialing queue while wearing a neon-laminated media pass. “However, security staff informed me that the sidewalk leading to the corner shop had been designated an exclusive artist-merchandise corridor. My options were either to buy the limited-edition tour fleece or attempt to breach the soundboard barricade.”

City tourism officials praised the interaction as proof of the capital’s booming hospitality economy, noting that as visitor volume reaches double its level from 10 years ago, public infrastructure must seamlessly integrate with event monetization.

“With tens of millions of visitors flooding the capital, our goal is to ensure every square block offers the vibrant commercial flow of an arena,” explained a spokesperson for the local tourism ministry. “When a local resident buys official tour merchandise just to step over an idling broadcast truck and retrieve his groceries, that represents a direct victory for our economic projections.”

At press time, Morales reported that while his tortillas were completely cold by the time he cleared the final security metal detector, he remained optimistic about his evening plans, provided he could secure a general-admission wristband to access his own bathroom.

World.title: Sheinbaum calls NYT report on CIA’s alleged bargain with Chihuahua prosecutor ‘very interesting’: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📰 NYT report spotlights ex-prosecutor who allegedly partnered with CIA: Sheinbaum called the Times article on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, “very interesting.” The report says Zuany’s revoked U.S. visa was reinstated after he helped CIA officers train state forces and join missions. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said Tuesday that both the FGR and the Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office have outstanding arrest warrants for Zuany.

Sheinbaum called the Times article on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, “very interesting.” The report says Zuany’s revoked U.S. visa was reinstated after he helped CIA officers train state forces and join missions. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said Tuesday that both the FGR and the Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office have outstanding arrest warrants for Zuany. ⚖️ “ It’s illegal because it violates the National Security Law”: Sheinbaum said her government flagged the CIA’s participation in an April drug lab raid in Chihuahua as illegal as soon as it found out about it. Former Chihuahua attorney general César Jáuregui was detained last month on a treason charge. She said any collaboration with foreign agencies must respect the Constitution and the National Security Law, and that “in this case, [the law] wasn’t obeyed.”

Sheinbaum said her government flagged the CIA’s participation in an April drug lab raid in Chihuahua as illegal as soon as it found out about it. Former Chihuahua attorney general César Jáuregui was detained last month on a treason charge. She said any collaboration with foreign agencies must respect the Constitution and the National Security Law, and that “in this case, [the law] wasn’t obeyed.” 🏥 IMSS Bienestar doctor’s appointments up 55% since 2023: Director Alejandro Svarch said the public healthcare service for people without social security is on track to provide 58.3 million free consultations this year, up from 37.3 million in 2023. Specialist appointments are projected to rise 105%.

Director Alejandro Svarch said the public healthcare service for people without social security is on track to provide 58.3 million free consultations this year, up from 37.3 million in 2023. Specialist appointments are projected to rise 105%. 📈 Opposition-governed states lag: Svarch said “general consultations” rose just 4% between 2023 and 2026 in the eight states that haven’t joined IMSS Bienestar, which operates in 24 of 32 federal entities, while specialist appointments are forecast to rise 27%. “It’s the same country, the same period, but you can see the results are vastly different,” he said.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Wednesday morning press conference, President Sheinbaum responded to a New York Times report headlined “The Man Who Helped the C.I.A. Secretly Operate in Mexico.”

Published on Tuesday, the article focuses on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, the state where U.S. Central Intelligence Agency officers allegedly participated in a drug lab raid in April without the authorization or knowledge of the Mexican government. Two CIA agents and two Chihuahua police officials died in a car accident after the raid, a tragedy that helped bring the CIA’s presence in the state to light.

The New York Times report states that “[w]hen the Central Intelligence Agency was looking to quietly expand its operations in Mexico last year, it found an especially useful partner.”

“… To the C.I.A., Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a prosecutor and former police commander in the border state of Chihuahua, offered a different kind of partnership,” the report says.

“He could pair C.I.A. officers with Mexican police units on counter-cartel operations — and he was in a bind that made him uniquely cooperative, Mexican and U.S. officials said.”

That bind, according to the Times, was that Zuany’s U.S. visa had been revoked “because of his suspected ties to the very cartels the C.I.A. wanted to root out.”

The Times reported that Zuany’s visa was reinstated after he “shepherded C.I.A. officers as they trained Chihuahua State forces, joined those forces on certain missions and provided expertise during ground operations” during a period of more than six months.

Beyond Sheinbaum’s response to the New York Times report, another notable topic at today’s mañanera was the performance of IMSS Bienestar, Mexico’s public healthcare service for people without social security coverage through institutions such as the Mexican Social Security Institute, or IMSS, and the State Workers’ Social Security Institute, or ISSSTE.

The IMSS Bienestar scheme was established by the previous federal government and now operates in 24 of Mexico’s 32 federal entities. Eight states have opted against signing onto the scheme. Those states — Nuevo León, Coahuila, Durango, Jalisco, Querétaro, Aguascalientes, Chihuahua and Guanajuato — are all governed by opposition parties, rather than by Morena, Mexico’s ruling party.

NYT report ‘very interesting,’ says Sheinbaum

A reporter raised the New York Times report about Zuany, noting that it quotes the former prosecutor as saying that Chihuahua Governor Maru Campos was aware of the CIA’s presence in the northern border state, something that Campos denies.

Sheinbaum, who has previously been critical of the Times’ reporting on Mexico, said she read the report and described it as “very interesting.”

🇲🇽#México | Claudia Sheinbaum se refirió al reportaje de The New York Times sobre la presunta facilitación de operaciones de la CIA por parte de Guillermo Zuany, fiscal especializado de Chihuahua. La presidenta calificó la publicación como “muy interesante” y sostuvo que los agentes estadounidenses deben apegarse a la Ley de Seguridad Nacional. “En este caso no se respetó”, afirmó. #ClaudiaSheinbaum #Chihuahua #CIA #SeguridadNacional 🌐 Consulta #ElPortalDeÁngulo7

➡️ https://t.co/14SVC19UGG — Ángulo7 Noticias (@angulosiete) November 11, 2026

She subsequently noted that the former attorney general of Chihuahua, César Jáuregui, was arrested in connection with the CIA’s presence in the state. Jáuregui, who was detained by federal authorities on a treason charge last month, is accused of allowing CIA officers to participate in the drug lab raid in Chihuahua in April without authorization from the Mexican government.

Sheinbaum said that the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) has to continue its investigation of the case. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said on Tuesday that both the FGR and the Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office have outstanding warrants for the arrest of Zuany.

Sheinbaum said that Zuany’s alleged conduct is “very relevant” to investigations into the CIA’s presence in Chihuahua.

“It’s worth learning about who this person is and how he collaborated with one of the U.S. agencies,” she said.

Although the New York Times report states that CIA officers joined Chihuahua state forces “on certain missions” and that the CIA “began working” with Zuany “around 2025,” Sheinbaum asserted that “the article doesn’t say that there were operations [with the CIA] since 2025.”

“It says there was [CIA] presence,” she said.

Sheinbaum highlighted that her government pointed out that the CIA’s participation in the drug lab raid in Chihuahua was illegal as soon as it found out about it.

“It’s illegal because it violates the National Security Law,” she said.

“And the Federal Attorney General’s Office opened an investigation,” Sheinbaum added.

“Today, the [former] attorney general of Chihuahua is detained for this reason. The important thing is that … any collaboration [with foreign authorities] has to guarantee respect for the [Mexican] Constitution and the National Security Law,” she said.

“Any agent from a U.S. agency in Mexico has to comply with the National Security Law,” Sheinbaum said.

“In this case, [the law] wasn’t obeyed,” she said.

IMSS Bienestar chief reports sharp increase in doctor’s appointments

At the start of his presentation, IMSS Bienestar director Alejandro Svarch said that “for decades, where a person was born and the job they held determined the range of medical care they were able to receive.”

“Three years ago, IMSS Bienestar began transforming this reality,” he said.

“Today we are the largest network of public health services in our country and above all we’re an institute that is achieving results,” Svarch said.

He went on to report that the number of medical consultations provided by IMSS Bienestar is projected to increase 55% this year compared to 2023. IMSS Bienestar is on track to provide 58.3 million free doctor’s appointments this year, according to the data presented by Svarch, up from 37.3 million in 2023.

“That’s why we say the model works. The results are clear and compelling,” the IMSS Bienestar chief said.

Svarch noted that IMSS Bienestar operates in 24 of Mexico’s 32 federal entities, while eight states have their own public healthcare systems for people without social security coverage.

He reported that “general consultations” increased just 4% this year compared to 2023 in the eight states that haven’t signed on to IMSS Bienestar.

“It’s the same country, the same period, but you can see the results are vastly different,” Svarch said.

He also reported that the number of specialist doctor’s appointments provided by IMSS Bienestar is projected to rise 105% this year compared to 2023, while the increase over the same period in states where IMSS Bienestar doesn’t operate is forecast to be 27%.

“These results are not the product of chance,” Svarch said.

“They are the product of actions and a very specific implementation plan,” he said.

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Eat, dance, swim, run, repeat!
World.content:
One of the things I love most about living in Puerto Vallarta is the variety of entertainment and activities on offer. Case in point, this month you can 1) taste cuisine from some of Mexico’s top chefs at the 31st International Gourmet Festival; 2) listen to live jazz, rock and mariachi at one of Vallarta’s many great music venues; 3) compete in an open-water swimming race; or 4) run a half-marathon. OK, so the last two might not be for everyone, but you can cheer on the racers instead.

Read on to learn more about these exciting events.

31st International Gourmet Festival

Puerto Vallarta’s reputation as a culinary destination is on the rise. Earlier this year, two local restaurants, Icú and Pancho’s Takos, earned spots on the prestigious Michelin Guide’s recommended list, a first for the city. This month, Vallarta will host the 31st International Gourmet Festival from Nov. 12-22. The festival brings some of the most celebrated Mexican chefs together for 11 days of culinary events at more than 25 top-rated restaurants in Puerto Vallarta, Riviera Nayarit and Tepic.

Events include tasting experiences featuring food and wine from more than a dozen restaurants, dining “safaris” where you travel to a few selected restaurants in one night, multicourse fine dining at single restaurants featuring guest chefs and even a drag brunch.

On Nov. 17, the Technological University of Bahía de Banderas (UTBB) will host a panel of chefs who will discuss the latest trends shaping the culinary scene in Mexico. The panel discussion is free and open to the public. Tickets for the dining experiences are available for purchase on the festival website.

Live music up close and personal

I love listening to live music, especially in intimate settings where I can watch the performers up close. In my last events roundup, I promised to share some of my favorite venues. True to my word, here you go:

The Social Club: The Social Club is a modern-day speakeasy located at 447 Basilio Badillo in the Romantic Zone. Just a narrow black door marks its spot. If you’ve never been before, you could easily miss it. I feel transported to another era every time I visit. After entering the front door, you climb up a narrow staircase, pass through red velvet curtains and enter a small parlor-style room with tiny tables lit by tiny lamps. The “stage” is at the back of the room, just a few feet from the tables. Waiters clad in Prohibition-era outfits serve bespoke and classic cocktails. Doors open at 9 p.m., and music starts around 10 p.m., featuring many of the best local jazz musicians and many special events. This is one of our favorite date-night spots in all of Vallarta.

Aquí Nomás: In the mood for a Mexican folk music singalong? Then you want to go to Aquí Nomás in Versalles. On Friday and Saturday nights, the neighborhood cantina hosts a live mariachi band that plays all the classic songs that Mexicans seem to know by heart. On our first visit in early October, we had only planned on staying for dinner and venturing someplace for music. But, being early season, the other venues in Versalles were closed. Our waitress convinced us to stay, and we’re so glad we did. Around 10:30 in the evening, the band showed up — a full 10-person mariachi ensemble — and the tables filled up, too. Pretty soon, the band was passing the mic, and everyone was singing along. It was such a friendly, local vibe; we are looking forward to returning soon with the whole family.

Casita & Garden: Casita & Garden in the Romantic Zone offers a variety of live music from jazz to funk to rock and pop every night of the week except Sundays. Shows are held in its lovely outdoor courtyard during the winter season starting at 7 p.m. In addition to live music, you can sample wine and sake selected by their in-house sake sommelier, and fill up on sushi and wood-fired pizza. The venue also hosts private dinners and wine tastings, but they are popular, so it’s best to reserve well ahead of time.

For the sporting type

View this post on Instagram A post shared by CRUCE VALLARTA (@crucevallarta)

Coming from Boulder, Colorado — arguably the sporting capital of the United States — where every summer weekend is packed with running, biking and triathlon events, I was astounded to find a similar enthusiasm for sports in Puerto Vallarta. It seems there is a race of some sort every weekend. Yet I’ve found the events way more chill and the athletes much friendlier than in Colorado. (Even though they still crush the course.)

Since moving to Mexico, I’ve become an avid open-water swimmer, and recently joined a local swimming group. They convinced me to 

If running is more your speed, the next day, on Nov. 15, Puerto Vallarta is hosting its 22nd Annual Half Marathon. The 21-km run is a grand tour of the hotel zone and the Marina, starting at the Sheraton and heading north along Av. Francisco Medina Ascencio (aka the 200), winding through the Marina and returning to the Sheraton via Av. Francisco Medina Ascencio. There is also a 5 km distance. You can register for either distance online.

I hope to see you out there, enjoying great food, good music and fun sports.

Debbie Slobe is a writer and communications strategist based in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco. She blogs at Mexpatmama.com and is a senior program director at Resource Media. Find her on Instagram and Facebook.

World.title: Brazilian Homebuilder’s Profit Hits Record
World.content:
Photo: Wilfredor, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

BRAZIL · ECONOMY

Key Facts The company MRV&Co is a large Brazilian builder of homes, mainly for lower-income families.

The profit Its Brazilian arm earned a record R$315 million (about US$56 million) in adjusted profit.

The sales The Brazilian arm’s revenue rose 28.7% to R$3.4 billion (about US$609 million) in July to September 2026.

The turnaround Group cash generation reached R$427 million (about US$77 million), a year after a cash burn.

Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 74.2 points (November 2026 edition).

Prediction markets Polymarket gives a 90.5% chance that Brazil’s central bank leaves rates unchanged in December (12 November, 3:46 a.m. ET).

MRV&Co, a large Brazilian builder of affordable homes, said on Wednesday 11 November 2026 that its Brazilian homebuilding arm earned a record adjusted profit of R$315 million (about US$56 million) in the third quarter. Adjusted profit strips out derivatives and other non-cash items, and the group, listed on B3 (Brazil’s main stock exchange) as MRVE3, described the quarter as a record for sales, production, revenue and profit.

What Happened

MRV&Co released its third-quarter results on Wednesday 11 November 2026. The whole group, which also includes the rental arm Luggo, the land developer Urba and the US apartment builder Resia, reported adjusted net profit of R$201.6 million (about US$36 million).

Record Sales and Better Margins

MRV Incorporação, the Brazilian homebuilding arm that makes up most of the business, raised net revenue 28.7% from a year earlier to R$3.4 billion (about US$609 million). That is 24% more than in the second quarter, the company said.

Gross margin, the share of revenue left after building costs, reached 32.1%, the highest in seven years. It rose 1.4 percentage points from a year earlier and 0.9 points from the second quarter.

Net sales were R$3.0 billion (about US$538 million) in the quarter and R$11.0 billion (about US$1.97 billion) over the last 12 months. The company sold about 11,000 homes while launching about 9,300, which shrinks its stock of unsold units.

Cash Returns After a Strike Scare

The group generated adjusted cash of R$427 million (about US$77 million) in the quarter, against R$70 million (about US$12.5 million) in the second quarter. A year earlier it burned R$23.4 million (about US$4.2 million), and the nine-month total now stands at R$894.3 million (about US$160 million).

The main driver was asset sales by Resia and Luggo, which total R$2.2 billion (about US$394 million) this year. The company expects them to cut net debt by R$1.6 billion (about US$287 million).

In July, Resia sold two projects, Ten Oaks and Rayzor Ranch, for US$139 million, cutting net debt by US$87 million. Luggo sold three finished rental buildings with 437 units for R$166 million (about US$30 million), which brought in R$144 million (about US$26 million) in cash.

A strike by staff of Caixa Econômica Federal, the state-owned bank that lends under the housing programme, disrupted mortgage transfers in September. The company said sales were not hurt, although the delays held back cash.

A Bet on the State Housing Programme

Chief financial officer Ricardo Paixão said almost all of the company’s launches now come from Minha Casa Minha Vida, the federal programme that subsidises homes for lower-income families. Buyers pay 4.5% to 7% a year, a rate tied to the FGTS, the workers’ severance fund.

Paixão said that makes demand less sensitive to the central bank’s benchmark rate, called Selic. The rate committee, Copom, interrupted its cutting cycle at its 4 November 2026 meeting, which held Selic at 13.75%.

What It Means for You

If you hold Brazilian stocks through a US fund, the quarter shows that a large, recently troubled homebuilder can post higher profit and cash flow while rates stay high. Its American arm, Resia, which builds and rents apartments in the United States, is selling assets rather than starting new projects.

The business now leans on government-backed lending rather than on market mortgage rates, which narrows the risks from Selic moves. It also depends on the state bank Caixa working smoothly, as the September strike showed.

What Is Not Known

Published figures for consolidated net profit differ by definition, from R$152.7 million attributable to shareholders to about R$171 million for the whole group. We therefore lead with the adjusted figures that the company highlights.

It is not yet clear how fast Resia can sell its remaining US assets, or how much of the R$1.6 billion in debt savings will arrive in the next quarters. The company has not said when it expects Caixa’s delayed transfers to be fully released.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, gave a 90.5% chance on 12 November 2026 (3:46 a.m. ET) that Brazil’s central bank makes no change to its rate in December, with US$71,011 traded across the whole event. The same market priced a 25-basis-point cut (a quarter of a percentage point) at 6.2%.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

How Much Did MRV Earn in the Third Quarter of 2026?

The group reported adjusted net profit of R$201.6 million (about US$36 million), and its Brazilian arm earned a record R$315 million (about US$56 million). The company published the results on Wednesday 11 November 2026.

Why Did MRV’s Cash Flow Improve?

Asset sales by its US arm Resia and its rental arm Luggo drove adjusted cash generation of R$427 million (about US$77 million). A year earlier the group burned cash.

What Is Minha Casa Minha Vida?

It is Brazil’s federal housing programme, which subsidises homes for lower-income families. Buyers pay interest of 4.5% to 7% a year, tied to the FGTS severance fund.

What Is MRV’s Gross Margin Now?

The Brazilian homebuilding arm reached 32.1%, its highest level in seven years. That was 1.4 percentage points above the third quarter of 2025.

World.title: Uganda Opens Envoy Office for Buganda
World.content:
Photo: Todd Huffman / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

UGANDA · POLITICS

Uganda’s government on Wednesday 11 November 2026 opened an Office of the Senior Presidential Special Envoy in Charge of Buganda Affairs in Kampala. Buganda is a historic kingdom in central Uganda, and its ties with the central government have been strained at several points since the 1960s.

Minister for the Presidency Milly Babirye Babalanda, a cabinet minister attached to the president’s office, launched it at Mosa Courts, a venue in Nakasero, a district of Kampala, for the government. It is headed by Joseph Mukasa Sewava, whom local media first reported as the Special Envoy on Buganda Affairs to President Yoweri Museveni in December 2025.

Key Facts Who Minister Milly Babirye Babalanda launched the office for the government on Wednesday 11 November 2026.

What An envoy office for talks between the central government and the Buganda Kingdom, led by Joseph Mukasa Sewava.

Where Mosa Courts, Nakasero, Kampala.

Quote “Our common enemy is poverty, not one another,” Minister Babalanda said.

Not known Budget, staffing and legal basis were not given in the reports we found.

What the New Office Is For

The office is meant to provide a permanent channel for talks between the central government and the Buganda Kingdom, local media reported. Babalanda said it should be a bridge for dialogue, not merely a ceremonial office.

Babalanda also said, “When Buganda prospers, Uganda prospers,” and that no Ugandan should feel like a stranger in any part of the country. Sewava said, according to local media, that the office is not a political one and is meant to bring people together.

Why Buganda Needs a Channel

The kingdom’s ties with the state have been strained at several points since independence. In 1966 government troops attacked the Lubiri, the palace of the Kabaka, Buganda’s king, in Kampala, and in 1967 a new constitution abolished Uganda’s kingdoms.

The kingdoms were restored in 1993 as cultural institutions, and in September 2009 violent clashes followed restrictions on a planned visit to Kayunga by the Kabaka, Ronald Muwenda Mutebi II. Babalanda warned at the launch against a return to such confrontation, according to local media.

File photo, May 2015. The Independence Monument park in central Kampala. Photo: Ruslik0, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What Buganda Said

Katikkiro Charles Peter Mayiga, the kingdom’s prime minister, was represented by Patrick Luwagga Mugumbule, the Speaker of Buganda’s parliament, the Lukiiko. His message asked the office to strengthen communication between the kingdom and the government and to put Buganda’s concerns first, according to local media.

We found no separate statement from the Kabaka or from the administration at Mengo, the Kampala hill that is the kingdom’s historic seat. That leaves the kingdom’s full position on the new office open.

What Is Not Known

The office’s budget, staff and legal basis were not given in the reports we found, and they cite no statutory instrument. It is also not known what powers Sewava has beyond acting as a channel.

We found no figure that measures the office’s reach, so we do not put a number on its likely effect. The reports call the office a bridge, and the Katikkiro’s message asked it to put Buganda’s concerns first.

What It Means for Readers

In our assessment, a steadier relationship between the central government and Buganda could ease one source of political friction in central Uganda, where Kampala sits. No dated checkpoints have been announced, so the test will be whether the office produces public, dated outcomes.

Read more on Uganda’s army chief planning to step down, the court-martial of a former army deputy and the central bank’s decision to hold its key rate at 12%.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the new Buganda envoy office?

It is the Office of the Senior Presidential Special Envoy in Charge of Buganda Affairs, launched in Kampala on 11 November 2026. Local media describe it as a permanent channel between the government and the Buganda Kingdom.

Who runs the office?

Joseph Mukasa Sewava, also spelled Ssewava, heads it. Local media first reported him as the Special Envoy of President Yoweri Museveni on Buganda Affairs in December 2025.

What is Buganda?

Buganda is a historic kingdom in central Uganda, led by the Kabaka, Ronald Muwenda Mutebi II. Uganda abolished its kingdoms in 1967 and restored them in 1993 as cultural institutions.

Has the kingdom responded?

The Katikkiro, Charles Peter Mayiga, sent a message that was read at the launch, according to local media. We found no separate statement from the Kabaka.

Sources: Statements by Minister Milly Babirye Babalanda and Joseph Mukasa Sewava at the launch of the office on 11 November 2026, and the message of Katikkiro Charles Peter Mayiga read there, as reported by Ugandan media; no State House statement or gazette notice was cited in the reports we saw on 12 November 2026.

World.title: Sudan Leader Claims War Sides Hide Famine
World.content:
Herders move cattle in search of grazing and water in Sudan, March 2021. (Photo: Reem Ahmed Elomarabi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

SUDAN · HUNGER

Yasir Arman, a senior Sudanese political leader, said in a statement published on 12 November 2026 that both sides in Sudan’s war, the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, are covering up what he calls an imminent famine. He also accused international hunger monitors of holding back data that could push the world to act.

Arman is a leader of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement – Revolutionary Democratic Current, a political movement, and he is calling for a humanitarian truce. His claim is unproven: in May 2026 the UN-backed hunger monitor, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), did not classify any area as in Famine, but it listed 14 hotspots as at risk of famine.

Key Facts Who Yasir Arman, a leader of a Sudanese political movement, spoke on 12 November 2026.

Claim He claims both warring sides hide an imminent famine and that monitors withhold data.

Official picture The UN-backed hunger monitor, the IPC, counted nearly 19.5 million people in acute hunger in May 2026.

At risk The IPC listed 14 hotspots at risk of famine; no area was classified Famine.

Ask Arman wants an urgent humanitarian truce to open aid routes.

What Arman Said

Arman said millions of Sudanese face a real threat to their lives because of economic collapse, destroyed infrastructure, displaced farmers and herders, and a failed farming season in most key areas. He added that attacks on power and water stations and markets, sieges of cities and the lack of safe aid corridors raise the danger.

He said the organisations that give early warnings of famine are silent without justification and are holding back data held by UN agencies and aid groups. Publishing it, he argued, would push governments to press both sides to accept an official famine declaration.

He called for an urgent humanitarian truce, even a temporary one, so food and medicine can reach people. He said Sudan’s people alone are paying the price.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the Hunger Monitor Has Found

The IPC, short for Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, is the UN-backed system that rates hunger in five phases. Its May 2026 analysis counted nearly 19.5 million people in acute food insecurity, about 40% of the population, and listed 14 hotspots in Darfur, in western Sudan, and in South Kordofan as at risk of famine.

No area was classified Famine in that analysis, Famine being the top of the IPC’s five phases, although the IPC’s Famine Review Committee, its expert panel, confirmed Famine in El Fasher, in Darfur, and Kadugli, in South Kordofan, in November 2025. In February 2026 an IPC alert said child malnutrition had passed the famine threshold in Um Baru and Kernoi in North Darfur, though the IPC stressed that an alert is not a formal Famine classification.

File photo, 2010. A road bridge across the Nile at Khartoum. Photo: Petr Adam Dohnálek, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Why the Warning Is Hard to Test

Arman gave no figures of his own in the statement, and he did not say which data he means. An IPC alert of 12 October 2026 warned that conditions in Darfur and Kordofan were deteriorating, but we found no new formal Famine classification this year.

UNICEF, the UN children’s agency, said on 10 November 2026 that it expects 825,000 children under five to suffer severe acute malnutrition this year. It also said its own Sudan response is just one-third funded.

What Is Not Known

It is not known which data Arman means, or whether any famine finding is waiting to be published. We found no new formal Famine classification in 2026.

Arman’s account comes from a single published statement, and we could not confirm it with a second source. We treat it as his claim, not as established fact.

What It Means for Readers

For readers in the United States, a formal famine declaration could add pressure on donors, including Washington, to fund aid and on both armies to open routes. The funding gap is already visible in UNICEF’s one-third figure.

Read more on the Sudan famine risk warning, Sudan’s fuel shortage and hunger risk and UNICEF’s warning on drones and children.

More: Sudan news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Yasir Arman?

He is a leader of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement – Revolutionary Democratic Current, a Sudanese political movement. He spoke in a statement published on 12 November 2026.

What does Arman claim?

He claims both warring sides are covering up an imminent famine and that hunger monitors are holding back data. We could not confirm either claim.

Is there a famine in Sudan?

The IPC confirmed Famine in El Fasher and Kadugli in November 2025. Its May 2026 analysis classified no area as in Famine but listed 14 hotspots as at risk.

What is the IPC?

The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification is a UN-backed system that rates hunger in five phases. At area level the top phase, Phase 5, is Famine; for households it is Catastrophe.

Sources: IPC Sudan analysis of May 2026, as published in UNICEF’s release of 15 May 2026 (UNICEF); IPC alert of 5 February 2026, as reported by UN News, the UN’s own news service; UNICEF Geneva briefing of 10 November 2026 (UNICEF); Arman’s statement of 12 November 2026, published in Arabic by a Sudanese news site.

World.title: Somaliland Reportedly Executes Nine Convicts
World.content:
Hargeisa, the capital of Somaliland, seen from a hillside in 2024. (Photo: Mheidegger, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

SOMALIA · SOMALILAND · CRIME AND PUNISHMENT

Somaliland reportedly shot nine convicted murderers by firing squad on Wednesday 11 November 2026, according to Somali news reports that we could not confirm with an official source. The self-declared republic in the Horn of Africa, the region around Somalia and Ethiopia, broke away from Somalia in 1991 and had published no statement that we could find.

The reports place the executions in the Mandheera area of the Sahil region and say they were carried out under qisas, an Islamic law of retribution. Somaliland is campaigning for formal recognition, so how it applies the death penalty is likely to draw outside attention.

Key Facts Who Somaliland authorities reportedly executed nine men convicted of murder.

Basis Separate murder cases under qisas, Islamic retributive law, the reports say.

What We Know

Somali news reports say the nine were shot on Wednesday 11 November 2026 in the Mandheera area of the Sahil region. They say the men had been sentenced in separate murder cases.

The reports say the sentences were carried out under qisas, an Islamic legal principle that lets a victim’s family seek retribution. They give no names for the nine, no identities for the victims and no details of the cases.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Is Somaliland?

Somaliland declared independence from Somalia in 1991 and runs its own government and courts from its capital, Hargeisa. Few countries recognise it, and it is campaigning for formal recognition.

Our explainer sets out why Somaliland wants recognition. Another report covers China’s and Djibouti’s opposition to its statehood.

Money changers stack bundles of Somaliland shilling notes at a street market in Hargeisa, the Somaliland capital. Photo: Fiona Graham / WorldRemit, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Earlier Executions at the Same Site

Six men were executed at Mandheera prison in January 2020, local news reports said at the time, and six more in November 2020, according to a European Union statement. The firing squad is therefore a repeated practice in Somaliland, not a new one.

What Is Not Known

We found no statement from the Somaliland government or its justice authorities, and no reaction from human-rights groups or foreign governments. The identities of the nine, the dates of their convictions and any appeal steps are unknown.

The reports use near-identical wording, and we could not establish that they are independent of each other. We therefore treat the account as reported, not confirmed.

What It Means for Readers

For readers in the United States, the executions add a human-rights question to Somaliland’s bid for recognition. We will update this report if the government confirms the details.

Read more on Somaliland’s recognition drive and on the visa dispute between Somalia and Somaliland.

More: Somalia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Somaliland execute nine people?

Somali news reports say yes, on Wednesday 11 November 2026 in the Mandheera area of the Sahil region. We found no official statement confirming it.

Why were the nine executed?

The reports say they were convicted of murder in separate cases and sentenced under qisas, an Islamic law of retribution. Details of the cases have not been published.

Is Somaliland a country?

Somaliland declared independence from Somalia in 1991 and governs itself, but few countries recognise it. It is campaigning for that recognition.

Has Somaliland used the firing squad before?

Yes. Six men were executed at Mandheera prison in January 2020 and six more in November 2020, according to local reports and a European Union statement.

Sources: No statement from the Somaliland government or its justice authorities had been published when we checked on 12 November 2026. This report rests on Somali news reports of 11 and 12 November 2026 with near-identical wording, which we could not establish as independent; for 2020, a European Union statement of 28 November 2020 and local reports.

Key Facts The company Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled oil giant, earned US$7.7 billion in the third quarter of 2026.

Record output Production hit a record 3.51 million barrels of oil equivalent a day.

Cash and debt Operating cash flow rose 15% to US$12 billion, and net debt stood at US$57.8 billion.

Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled oil company, earned R$39.8 billion (US$7.7 billion) in the third quarter of 2026 while pumping more oil than ever before. Excluding one-off items, profit reached R$47.9 billion (US$9.3 billion), up 68% from a year earlier.

For US readers, Petrobras matters because its shares trade in New York as American depositary receipts (ADRs), certificates that let Americans own foreign shares in dollars. Its rising output also adds to the crude and diesel supply that world markets, including US refiners, rely on.

What Happened

Petrobras reported the results on Tuesday 10 November 2026. Net income of R$39.8 billion (US$7.7 billion) was about 24% below the R$52.4 billion (about US$9.4 billion) of the second quarter, but the company said oil production, refining and fuel marketing all set records.

Adjusted EBITDA, a measure of operating profit before interest, taxes and depreciation, reached R$85.8 billion (US$16.7 billion). Excluding one-off items it was R$94.5 billion (US$18.4 billion).

Record Oil and Diesel Output

Total operated production averaged 3.51 million barrels of oil equivalent a day, a unit that adds oil and gas together. About 2.96 million of that came from the pre-salt, deep offshore fields that lie beneath a thick layer of salt.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

Chief Executive Magda Chambriard said Petrobras had planned an average of 3.1 million barrels a day for 2026 and now expects 3.3 million to 3.4 million. It is the third consecutive quarterly production record in 2026.

Refineries ran at 99% of capacity, and diesel output hit a record 769,000 barrels a day. Chambriard called that run “essential to ensuring Brazil’s energy security during this geopolitical crisis”.

Live Company Intelligence Petroleo Brasileiro Petrobras SA ADR — the full investor dossier Company overview and the latest Rio Times coverage.

Cash, Spending and Debt

Operating cash flow, the cash the business generates before investment, rose 15% in a year to R$61.8 billion (US$12 billion). Petrobras invested R$33 billion (US$6.4 billion) in the quarter, including R$27.5 billion (US$5.3 billion) in exploration and production.

Gross debt was US$70 billion, down 1.2% from the previous quarter, and net debt was US$57.8 billion. The board approved R$15.3 billion (about US$2.7 billion) in dividends and interest on equity, a tax-friendly form of payout, as our report on the payout explains.

Taxes and government take paid through the first nine months of 2026 totalled R$251.3 billion (about US$45 billion at R$5.58 per US dollar). The company called it the highest cumulative amount on record for that period.

Where the Next Oil Comes From

Petrobras reported oil discoveries in the Equatorial Margin, a deep-water frontier off Brazil’s far north coast, at the Morpho well in block FZA-M-59. It also won 21 exploration blocks in Brazilian auctions and signed contracts for eight offshore blocks in Côte d’Ivoire, where it will operate with a 90% stake.

Two new floating production units, P-80 and P-82, have set sail for the Búzios offshore oil field. Each is designed to produce 225,000 barrels a day and both are due to start work in 2027.

What It Means for You

If you hold Petrobras ADRs through a US fund, the quarter shows a company with record output, lower gross debt and a continuing payout. Dividends are declared in reais, so their dollar value moves with the exchange rate, which stood near R$5.58 per US dollar this week.

Combined exports of crude oil and refined products averaged 1.251 million barrels a day in the quarter. That makes Brazil a meaningful supplier to world oil markets, which US drivers and refiners follow.

What Is Not Known

The company’s summary does not explain the roughly R$8.1 billion of one-off items that separate headline profit from the adjusted figure. It is also not yet clear how the board will split the payout between dividends and interest on equity.

Future profit will depend on oil prices, which Petrobras does not control, and on whether the new platforms start on schedule in 2027. Eleven platforms are now authorised to run above their original capacity without extra investment, the company said.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Profit Did Petrobras Report for the Third Quarter of 2026?

Net income was R$39.8 billion (US$7.7 billion), or R$47.9 billion (US$9.3 billion) excluding one-off items. The company reported it on Tuesday 10 November 2026.

How Much Oil Did Petrobras Produce?

Total operated production averaged a record 3.51 million barrels of oil equivalent a day, including 2.96 million from the pre-salt. The company now expects 3.3 million to 3.4 million for the full year.

Can Americans Own Petrobras Shares?

Yes, through American depositary receipts (ADRs) traded in New York, which let Americans hold foreign shares in dollars. The company pays dividends in reais, so the dollar amount depends on the exchange rate.

How Much Will Petrobras Pay Its Shareholders?

The board approved R$15.3 billion (about US$2.7 billion) in dividends and interest on equity for the third quarter. That is a form of shareholder payout, and its split is still to be settled.

What Happened

Net operating revenue rose 9.8% to R$3.67 billion (US$658 million), and adjusted EBITDA grew 4.1% to R$1.948 billion (US$349 million), the company said on Tuesday 10 November 2026. Reported net profit, which includes one-off items, fell 3.7% to R$711 million (US$127 million).

Engie Brasil blamed higher financial expenses tied to its investment cycle and greater depreciation as new renewable plants began commercial operation. It said the quarter was driven by its power generation and energy trading businesses.

Chief Executive Eduardo Sattamini said in a statement, translated from Portuguese, that the numbers show “the resilience of our business model and our ability to deliver sustainable value even in challenging scenarios”. He listed the completed transfer of shares in Jirau Energia, a settlement over a fee for using public assets, and progress on transmission projects as the quarter’s main advances.

Where the Money Went

Total investment reached R$662 million (US$119 million) in the quarter, and R$593 million (US$106 million) of it went into new projects. Most of that built power transmission lines, the high-voltage links that carry electricity between regions.

Three line projects led the spending: Asa Branca (R$244 million, about US$44 million), Graúna (R$155 million, about US$28 million) and Colibri (R$26 million, about US$5 million). Another R$170 million (about US$30 million) went into expanding and modernising the Jaguara hydroelectric plant.

Debt and the Jirau Deal

Net debt stood at R$25.28 billion (US$4.5 billion) at the end of September, up 3.1% from a year earlier. Leverage, which compares debt with annual operating profit, held at 3.1 times, and the investor-relations team said the company wants to keep it below three times.

Sattamini said the company completed the transfer of shares in Jirau Energia, owner of the Jirau hydroelectric plant on the Madeira River, and settled the renegotiation of the UBP. The UBP is the “Uso do Bem Público”, a payment that hydropower plants make for using public assets.

That renegotiation gave the second quarter a large accounting gain, which is why second-quarter net profit of R$1.96 billion (about US$352 million) was far above this quarter’s. Adjusted profit, which strips the gain out, was R$694 million (about US$124 million) in that quarter.

What Comes Next

The investor-relations team said the company has projects prepared for Brazil’s next battery storage auction, expected in December, where batteries store power for later use. A win would raise investment needs from 2027 and could change the path of its debt ratio.

The Asa Branca, Graúna and Colibri lines are transmission projects now moving through licensing and construction. The company said it is advancing licensing, engineering, supplier contracts and construction on all three.

What It Means for You

If you invest in Brazil through US funds, this result shows a power company growing sales while paying more to borrow. At about R$5.58 per US dollar, the quarter’s adjusted profit equals about US$128 million.

US firms that sell batteries or grid equipment should watch the December auction, a possible opening for energy storage in Brazil. Funds that own Brazilian utilities will watch whether leverage stays near 3.1 times.

What Is Not Known

The company’s announcement does not split the R$716 million between generation, transmission and trading. It has not said whether it will win the December battery auction or how much it would invest.

It is also unclear whether interest costs will keep rising, because that depends on Brazil’s central bank and on the company’s own borrowing plans. Investors will look for the answer in the next quarterly results.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Profit Did Engie Brasil Report for the Third Quarter of 2026?

Adjusted net profit was R$716 million (US$128 million), down 2.1% from a year earlier. Reported net profit was R$711 million (US$127 million), down 3.7%.

Why Did Engie Brasil’s Profit Fall?

The company blamed higher financial expenses tied to its investment cycle and greater depreciation as new renewable plants began operating. Revenue and EBITDA still grew.

What Is EBITDA?

Adjusted EBITDA is profit before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, a common gauge of operating performance. Engie Brasil’s reached R$1.948 billion (US$349 million), up 4.1%.

What Is Engie Brasil Planning Next?

It is preparing projects for Brazil’s next battery storage auction, expected in December, and pushing on three transmission lines. A win in the auction could raise its investment needs from 2027.

World.title: Peru Bank Giant Credicorp Earns US$566M
World.content:
Towers in the San Isidro district of Lima, Peru (Photo: Protontorniyo, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

PERU · BUSINESS

Key Facts Who Credicorp, a Lima-based financial group, trades on the New York Stock Exchange as BAP.

Profit Third-quarter profit was S/1.93 billion (about US$566 million), up 11.0% on a year earlier.

Why it matters The group set aside money for flood losses from El Niño, a climate pattern.

Outlook Management kept its 2026 return on equity target near 19.5%, and a longer-term goal near 22%.

Power Index Peru ranks 5th of 14 in Peru ranks 5th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 53.9 points (November 2026 edition).

Credicorp, a Peruvian bank group, had a strong quarter even as it braced for floods. Credicorp, the Lima-based owner of Banco de Crédito del Perú (BCP), reported on Monday 9 November 2026 that profit for July to September rose 11.0% to S/1,929.4 million (about US$566 million).

What Happened

Credicorp said net income attributable to its shareholders reached S/1,929.4 million (about US$566 million), which is 11.0% above the third quarter of 2025 and 2.6% below the second quarter of 2026. Its return on equity, a measure of profit against shareholder capital, was 19.9%.

Loans grew 14.8% from a year earlier and 4.2% from the previous quarter. Deposits rose 14.3% over the year, and cheap deposits such as current and savings accounts made up 73.2% of the total.

Net interest income, the gap between what the bank earns on loans and pays on deposits, grew 17.7% in a year. The net interest margin, or profit per sol of earning assets, widened by 36 basis points (0.36 percentage points) to 6.9%.

Bad Loans and the El Niño Cushion

The share of loans that are overdue and risky, called the NPL ratio, fell by 91 basis points in a year to 3.9%. Credicorp holds provisions worth 120.9% of those loans.

Provisions, money set aside for expected losses, rose 37.4% in a year. The company said it raised them because its quarter-end review moved its base case for El Niño, a warm-water climate pattern that can bring floods to Peru, to “Very Strong”.

The cost of risk, which is provisions as a share of loans, stood at 2.0%. Its CET1 ratio, a core measure of capital strength, was 11.9% at BCP and 15.1% at Mibanco, its small-business lender.

Yape and the Digital Push

Yape, Credicorp’s mobile wallet, had 17.0 million monthly active users, up 9.8% in a year. It made up 9.8% of Credicorp’s risk-adjusted revenue, against 6.4% a year earlier, as the wallet earns more from each user.

Yape’s loan book nearly quadrupled in a year to S/2.3 billion (about US$680 million). Credicorp’s “innovation portfolio”, its digital and new-business units, supplies 10.7% of risk-adjusted revenue, meaning revenue after loan-loss costs.

What It Means for You

If you own BAP shares or a Peru fund, the report shows earnings still growing while the bank pays for a possible flood. Provisions made now can cushion losses later, but they also reduce profit today.

The release estimates that Peru’s economy grew about 3.3% in the third quarter. It says inflation ended September at 4.5%, the highest since September 2023, while the central bank held its policy rate at 4.25% as of October.

Soles are converted here at 3.407 per US dollar (RT market data, 12 November 2026). For a closer look at Peru’s banking rules, see our report on Peru’s penalties for lending accounts used in extortion.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how severe El Niño will be or how much damage it will cause to borrowers. Credicorp’s extra provisions are an estimate, not a loss that has already happened.

The company did not say that profit will keep rising at this pace. The next quarterly report will show whether the 2026 return target of about 19.5% holds.

World.title: Somalia Seeks US$6.3 Billion for Climate
World.content:
Climate: Somalia

Key Facts —Who: President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, Somalia’s head of state, speaking at COP31, the 31st UN climate conference Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Africa story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time. —What: He says Somalia needs about US$6.3 billion through 2035 to adapt to climate change —Context: The same US$6.3 billion figure was presented at COP30, last year’s UN climate conference, in November 2025 —Open: The start year, donor pledges and the split between grants and loans are not known —As of: 12 November 2026

Somalia’s president told world leaders at COP31 that his country needs about US$6.3 billion through 2035 to adapt to a harsher climate.

A Plea at the COP31 Climate Talks

President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, Somalia’s head of state, addressed world leaders on Wednesday 11 November 2026 at the leaders’ session of COP31, the 31st UN climate conference, in Antalya, Türkiye. He said Somalia needs about US$6.3 billion through 2035 to finance climate adaptation.

No official transcript of the speech was available to us, so we report it as media accounts of his remarks. Our explainer on who wants what in Somalia gives the wider political background.

He asked for climate finance mainly as grants rather than loans.

Displaced people wait for a food handout at a camp near Jowhar, a town in Somalia’s Shabelle valley, in 2013. Photo: African Union Mission in Somalia Public Information (CC0) via Wikimedia Commons.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the President Asked of Lenders

He urged international financial institutions and climate funds to simplify their application procedures. He also asked for eligibility criteria that reflect how exposed a country is to climate hazards.

He said Somalia adds only a small share of global greenhouse gas emissions but is among the countries most vulnerable to climate change. The talks in Antalya, running from 9 to 20 November 2026, cover climate finance, adaptation, emissions cuts and the Paris Agreement, the global climate pact.

The Number Is Not New

The US$6.3 billion figure first appeared a year earlier. On Friday 7 November 2025 at COP30, last year’s UN climate conference in Belém, Brazil, Deputy Prime Minister Salah Ahmed Jama presented a US$6.3 billion national adaptation plan.

Jama asked for “more grants, fewer loans, faster access”. So the 2026 speech repeated the figure rather than raising it.

Jama also said Somalia had accessed only about US$300 million by 2020, under 1% of needs, and put direct climate-related losses at US$2.8 billion. Those two figures come from a single report of his speech.

The plan’s priorities were early warning systems, climate-smart agriculture, resilient health services, climate-proof infrastructure, and empowering women and youth.

What This Means for You

Somalia is a fragile state, and climate shocks can add to displacement and hunger. Our reports on river flooding in southern Somalia and on the US leaving an air base in Somalia cover the risks on the ground and the security side.

What Is Not Known

The exact cost table and the source document behind the figure in the president’s speech are not known, and the start year of the period is not stated in his reported words. Nor is it known which donors have pledged, or what part is already funded.

How much would come as grants and how much as loans is also unknown. The Green Climate Fund, a UN-backed climate fund, announced a US$100 million investment partnership with Somalia in March 2024, separate from the US$6.3 billion request.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does Somalia say it needs for climate adaptation?

President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud said on Wednesday 11 November 2026 that Somalia needs about US$6.3 billion through 2035 for climate adaptation.

Is the US$6.3 billion figure new?

No. Deputy Prime Minister Salah Ahmed Jama presented a US$6.3 billion national adaptation plan at COP30 on Friday 7 November 2025. The 2026 speech repeated it.

What does Somalia want from climate funders?

It wants climate finance mainly as grants rather than loans, and simpler application procedures with eligibility rules that reflect a country’s exposure to climate hazards.

What is still unknown about the funding request?

The start year, the source document for the figure, donor pledges, the grants-to-loans split and the share already funded are all not known.
