World.title: Poland turns to home-grown giant for its defense buildup
World.content:
"PGZ is different from other European companies,” Leszkiewicz said, adding that PGZ makes more than 700 products. "I could say we make almost everything. But what can be a strength can also be a weakness.”

Marek Świerczyński, a defense analyst with the Warsaw-based Polityka Insight Center for Policy Analysis, said: “He essentially has to use diplomacy to try to manage the other companies.”

Legacy defense industry

For decades after the end of communism, Poland spent little on defense and the military largely made do with antiquated Soviet-era equipment. Russia’s illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 and its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 changed that, and Polish defense spending surged.

“We have strong historical and current experience with armored vehicles and maintenance, repair and overhaul services,” said Leszkiewicz. “We also make wheeled vehicles such as the Jelcz, and our work on sensors and radar is developing well. We have long been strong in rifles and pistols.”

Aleksandra Kozioł, a defense analyst with the Warsaw-based Polish Institute of International Affairs, pointed out other notable Polish defense companies, such as the private WB Group, which specializes in communications networks, unmanned aerial vehicles, loitering munitions and fire control solutions.

“We want to improve in new technologies, especially unmanned vehicles as well as software and IT solutions,” Leszkiewicz said.

World.title: The Kremlin can hide the death toll. It can’t hide the graves.
World.content:
In recent months, Russian authorities have issued warnings that taking photographs of military graves could result in life imprisonment, while the Federal Security Service has patrolled the country’s cemeteries in search of offenders. Since the summer, several dozen people across Russia have been arrested. The official charge in these closed trials is treason — specifically, cooperation with Ukrainian intelligence services.

Russia’s losses since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine are staggering. Russia 200, a casualty-tracking database created by independent outlet Mediazona and the BBC’s Russian service, lists the names of nearly 283,000 dead soldiers, including details about the circumstances of their deaths. But Mediazona, which draws on open-source information like social media posts and reports in local media, does not have the resources and access to document every battlefield fatality.

Other organizations estimate the death toll to be significantly higher. The U.K. Foreign Office and Dutch intelligence services estimate Russia’s losses to stand at more than half a million, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced in July that 700,000 Russian soldiers had died fighting in Ukraine.

Even the most modest estimates of Russian losses in Ukraine far surpass Soviet casualties in Afghanistan, a conflict that lasted nearly a decade from its launch in 1979. Then, as now, the Kremlin strove to hide the true costs of war.

Relatives of those who died in Afghanistan were forbidden from engraving the place of their loved ones’ deaths on their gravestones. “You could not mark the grave in any way that indicated that the person had died in the war,” Jeff Jones, a professor of history at the University of North Carolina, said. “Some [relatives] were actually forced to hold funerals at night so that it wouldn’t draw attention,” he added.

Later, relatives were permitted to engrave the words, “died heroically while fulfilling an international duty,” but “died in Afghanistan” was never allowed.

World.title: Peru: Pope Leo XIV returns to his adopted homeland on historic visit
World.content:
The 71-year-old pontiff was greeted at the airport by President Keiko Fujimori before blessing children with disabilities and babies gathered on the tarmac. He later travelled through the capital in his popemobile, waving to crowds carrying Peruvian and Vatican flags.

 

According to Vatican estimates, around three million people lined his route into the city. At Lima's historic Plaza Mayor, Leo was welcomed at the Government Palace, where he paid tribute to the Peruvian flag and joined Fujimori and a children's choir in singing the national anthem. The pope later met the president privately before addressing officials and guests at the National Theatre.

The visit marks the final leg of Leo XIV's 12-day South American tour, following stops in Uruguay and Argentina, and carries particular personal significance for the Chicago-born pontiff. Formerly known as Robert Prevost, he spent more than two decades serving communities in Peru and became bishop of Chiclayo before his election as pope.

Having acquired Peruvian citizenship in 2015, he told officials that the country had shaped his understanding of pastoral service. "I am also returning to my homeland," he declared, recalling the families who had welcomed him into their homes and shared their lives with him. Affectionately known to many Peruvians as "Padre Roberto", Leo is also expected to visit the Amazon region, the Andean city of Cusco and Chiclayo during his stay.

World.title: Is Nvidia's Jensen Huang too big to fail? Why a replacement is difficult and the impact on AI
World.content:
Most affairs of the heart are kept private.

 

But for Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, his secret relationship has become public and that could have a global impact on artificial intelligence, as he is being investigated over his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and whether he disclosed confidential intellectual property.

Nvidia designs the world’s most powerful chips and has become an AI infrastructure company, reaching its arm into robotics as well as autonomous driving. Nvidia has also invested in many AI companies across the world, including in Europe.

The chips that it produces run AI systems and have become an important front for the United States’ rivalry with China to lead in technology, with Washington even restricting access to the chips for Beijing.

Huang had lobbied for the US to relax its chip export rules to China.

"Nvidia is kind of at the base of [the AI ecosystem]," said Carmem Domingues, a former White House Senior AI Advisor to the Biden administration.

"All the AI companies either owe money to NVIDIA and/or depend on them to actually run the models and continue developing and growing their businesses," she told Euronews Next.

A new leader?

As Nvidia’s board reportedly considers ousting him, there are questions over whether the saga could bring about another 2008-style financial crisis and who could replace him.

Huang is Nvidia, he created the company three decades ago, his keynotes are attended by packed audiences and he has a celebrity fanbase that follows him wherever he goes.

As to who could replace him, Domingues believes "there's not someone who is sort of prepped and ready to go next in line".

Despite his two children being part of the company, "it's unclear what exactly their roles are in or how ready they would be to take over", and anyone else in the company seems "unlikely", she said.

Even if Huang was removed, they would likely keep him in some kind of role and that would be "in a way quote-unquote enough of a punishment for any potential wrongdoing", she added.

If you pin the two countries as adversaries, the fact that they would be spying on each other is kind of expected. Carmem Domingues Former AI advisor to Biden administration

Shares in Nvidia fell about 8% in trading on the news that the company board was reportedly considering ousting him.

"All the AI companies… have this sort of roundabout funding of each other... So everything is very intertwined and disastrous in many ways. And one falling can bring down a lot," said Domingues.

In 2008, global financial services firm Lehman Brothers fell and took the hit, while many other companies were considered too big to fail.

"Would they [Nvidia] protect him [Huang] in the name of not letting the 'house of cards' fall down?... So is Jensen, in a way, too big to fail himself? In a way. Yes," said Domingues.

But the AI bubble was already showing signs of bursting long before the Huang news and the US midterm election results, which showed a backlash to data centres and AI.

"It's almost burst. We're looking at the past month and then the US election and looking at markets. And there are also other problems, other issues. For example, the data centres are struggling with infrastructure, with the power grids," said Sheikha Maytha Bint Maktoum, an investor and founder of mental health company MindFriend.

For her, many AI startup valuations are detached from business fundamentals.

"No book I have read could have prepared me to see a day where a company is completely built on something that could vanish tomorrow," she said.

"There’s a product, but you can copy that product, and that product has no revenue... it is at a loss and valued at $14 billion (€12.6 billion)."

But for Nvidia, she believes any financial disruptions to the company would be "temporary", as "Nvidia has for decades built such a strong infrastructure around this ecosystem, it’s very difficult for me to see that would have a long-term impact".

Impact on China?

The Huang story has mostly been framed in the West as a question of market stability: could trouble at Nvidia ripple through an AI economy built on circular funding?

But in China, the conversation tends to run in a different direction. Companies there have spent years trying to reduce reliance on American chips, and episodes like this reinforce the instinct.

For Chinese company Xynova, which makes robotic hands, the thinking is more around long-term independence.

"Usually Chinese companies want to be more independent, not rely on the supplies... if you have to rely on American companies for supply, then it’s a big bottleneck," Isabel Zhu of Xynova told Euronews Next at the Web Summit tech conference in Lisbon.

"Huawei... they are trying to develop the chips, they’re working so hard, and they advocate that they are the Nvidia in China."

In her personal opinion, the AI race only makes the country want to push harder.

"I have faith in Chinese companies. If you really want to do something, then that will happen," she said.

But for Domingues, the Huang investigation will not change anything in the so-called AI race.

Long before the Huang saga, she said it was already framed as an AI race, noting that the US AI Action Plan in 2025 is literally called "Winning the AI Race". So, the scandal will not change much.

"If you pin the two countries as adversaries, the fact that they would be spying on each other is kind of expected... Every movie about the Cold War is about a spy… I find it unlikely [that it would change the rhetoric]."

World.title: There's 'not much space for climate denial anymore', says climate expert
World.content:
University College Cork professor Dr. Louise Firth believes 2026 marks a "turning point" in global warming, as Europe experienced extreme weather events over the summer, in addition to a fuel crisis as stemming from the war in the Iran. She calls this "a case for action."

 

Dr. Firth calls on the international community to provide financial support to Pacific Island nations. Despite being neither the biggest polluters, nor the largest contributors to the climate crisis, they are "the ones that are going to experience it the most," she says.

Whilst the Trump administration officially skipped this summit, with the US not providing an official delegation, she believes that this year's summit still "shines a light" and can "provide impetus for more action," highlighting COP's usefulness, despite the missing delegation.

Dr. Firth is currently attending COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV welcomed by millions on return to his second home Peru
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has returned to Peru, the country he considers his second homeland, amid a massive popular celebration. Around three million people, according to Vatican estimates, gathered along the route of his motorcade through Lima to welcome the Pontiff, who, as part of his tour of Latin America, is beginning a six-day visit to the country where he spent more than two decades as a missionary and bishop.

 

"The Pope is Peruvian!" some of those present chanted, according to AP, as Leo XIV travelled through the streets of the capital, which were decked out with Peruvian and Vatican flags. The 71-year-old Pontiff, who was born in Chicago, looked visibly moved on his arrival and took part in the official welcome ceremony at the Presidential Palace, where he sang the national anthem together with the president, Keiko Fujimori, and a children's choir.

In his first speech to the authorities and the diplomatic corps, Leo XIV stressed the deep ties he maintains with the country, reinforced by the Peruvian nationality he acquired in 2015. "Today I understand how much of this land remains in me and how much of my own story also belongs to you," he said.

The Pontiff said that the years he spent in Peru, sharing the lives, joys and difficulties of its people, helped to shape him as a pastor. "That is why I can say to you, with deep gratitude, that I am also returning to my homeland," he added, to applause.

Leo XIV also used his first meeting with political representatives to call on Peru to confront the most painful chapters of its history with "justice and sensitivity", a reference to the deep divisions that still mark national politics.

Among those present was President Fujimori, daughter of former president Alberto Fujimori, who died in 2024 and whose rule during the 1990s was marked by violence, human rights abuses and the fight against the Shining Path guerrilla movement.

Pope Leo XIV and the president of Peru, Keiko Fujimori, wave after meeting at the presidential palace in Lima, Peru, on 11 November 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

A tour with a heavy emotional weight

The trip is the final leg of a Latin American tour that has taken the Pope to Uruguay and Argentina before arriving in Peru. He will stay in the Andean country for almost a week and is due to travel from the Amazon to the Andes, with a visit to Cuzco, at more than 3,400 metres above sea level, and an especially emotional return to Chiclayo, where he served as bishop for a decade.

The visit comes at a time of significant difficulties for Peru, marked by political instability, crime, rising living costs and recurrent natural disasters. In this context, the Pope called for citizens to be able to live and work "without fear" and urged the authorities to make greater efforts to prevent natural disasters and protect lives.

The Latin American tour has also been marked by his social appeals. During his stay in Argentina, Leo XIV argued for a more inclusive economy and greater protection for vulnerable groups, including the poor, migrants, the sick and prisoners, in remarks that were interpreted as a criticism of the spending cuts by Javier Milei's government.

World.title: Witkoff and Kushner arrive in Moscow seeking Putin's 'blessing' to bring Europe into Ukraine peace talks
World.content:
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on Thursday morning for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, seeking to build on two days of US-mediated negotiations between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi that ended without a breakthrough towards ending the war.

 

Putin's special representative Kirill Dmitriev welcomed the envoys in a post on X, sharing footage of their arrival at Moscow's Vnukovo Airport.

The talks on 10–11 November produced an agreement in principle on a major prisoner-of-war exchange, but left key differences unresolved over territory, post-war security guarantees and Europe's role in the negotiations.

Kushner said the meeting with Putin would focus on the outcome of the Abu Dhabi discussions and seek Moscow's "blessing" to bring European representatives into the negotiating process.

"We see some openings and some opportunities," Kushner told reporters, adding that the envoys would travel to Dublin afterwards to brief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

"We've relayed to President Putin directly several times and to his team, that the only way to get this done is to have them by our side. And I think that, they're receptive to it. And I believe that, hopefully tomorrow in Moscow, Steve and I will be successful, and President Putin will give the blessing for that to occur."

For Witkoff, who initially led the Trump administration's negotiations with Russia over Ukraine, this marks his tenth visit to Russia since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

Moscow insists on its terms

Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Putin would first receive a briefing from Moscow's delegation to the Abu Dhabi talks before hearing the US envoys' assessment.

The Russian president would then decide Moscow's next steps in the negotiations, Lavrov said, adding that Russia's position would remain focused on achieving the objectives of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, who led Russia's delegation in Abu Dhabi, was more explicit, saying Moscow would only be satisfied once it had secured victory and reached an agreement on its own terms, which would largely translate into Ukraine's capitulation.

Medinsky also dismissed the prospect of immediate European participation in the negotiations.

"Once they (the Europeans) develop a conscience, they will be able to participate in peace negotiations," he told reporters following the Abu Dhabi talks.

Until then, he claimed, European countries were complicit in "a collective deception of the Ukrainian people" and effectively shared responsibility for civilian deaths.

The statements suggest Moscow remains unwilling to compromise on its maximalist demands, despite renewed US efforts to negotiate an end to the war.

Abu Dhabi talks leave key issues unresolved

The negotiations in the UAE marked the first US-mediated trilateral talks between Ukraine and Russia in nine months.

Ukraine's chief negotiator Rustem Umerov said the discussions covered steps towards a broader peace agreement and the country's post-war reconstruction.

"The first step - to end the war and ensure security guarantees for Ukraine," Umerov wrote on X.

Kushner acknowledged that significant differences remained, but suggested that the discussions had identified possible areas of compromise.

"Some areas we see places where we can find compromises, others we need to have more discussions, but I think this was a good first step," he told reporters.

Zelenskyy, who is in Dublin for meetings with European leaders, said he hoped the US envoys would return from Moscow with concrete proposals.

"What's important is that the Americans flew to Putin with specifics. I would very much like them to return to Dublin with specifics," he said, adding that while he remained sceptical, "there is hope".

World.title: US: Survivor pulled alive from rubble after deadly Brooklyn collapse
World.content:
The mixed residential and commercial building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue gave way, collapsing into an excavation pit at 2625 Bedford Avenue. The structural failure also ripped open part of the neighbouring building at 1323 Flatbush Avenue, leaving its interior rooms and furnishings visible from the street.

 

Dozens of firefighters were seen combing through piles of rubble in aerial footage, working by hand and using power saws, drones, buckets and specialist vacuum trucks. At around 6.30 pm, rescue teams pulled a dust-covered woman, believed to be pregnant, alive from the debris and carried her away on a stretcher. Her identity and medical condition were not immediately known.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at least 10 people had been admitted to hospital, including four in a critical condition. According to the FDNY, 17 people were injured, seven of them children, while one firefighter suffered minor injuries. Some 250 firefighters and paramedics took part in the operation.

Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani confirmed that excavation work was taking place directly alongside the structure when it gave way. The cause of the collapse remains under investigation, while Fire Chief John Esposito said authorities could not yet determine how many people were missing. Search-and-rescue operations could last several days.

World.title: Gaza documentary ‘NAZA’ becomes one of the most watched docs of 2026
World.content:
Award-winning Gaza documentary NAZA by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor is on track to become one of the most-watched documentaries on theatrical release of 2026.

 

New figures, collated by producers The Guardian and JW Films, reveal that the film has been seen by a worldwide audience of 1,547,033 across 47 territories as of 6 November.

With $13.5 million in international gross, NAZA ranks among the best-performing documentaries internationally of 2026 to date.

Shot in secrecy at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv during the ongoing Gaza war, NAZA shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to its official synopsis.

The investigative doc features interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers, soldiers and whistleblowers. They describe how Palestinians are targeted and how strikes are carried out using AI and automated surveillance in military targeting systems - despite Israel being aware that civilians are present in targeted areas. The participants' faces and voices were digitally altered to protect their identities.

The 80-minute hot-button doc builds on reporting between 2023 and 2025 published by the Israeli-Palestinian +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call, and The Guardian. It left this year's Venice Film Festival with the Special Jury Prize and received a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation at the festival.

Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor at the Venice Film Festival - Saturday 12 September 2026 AP Photo

The documentary has performed best in Italy, where it was released by I Wonder on 29 September shortly after its world premiere in Venice. It made history as the third most-watched documentary of all time in Italian cinemas, behind only Fahrenheit 9/11 and The March of the Penguins.

In France, during a 48-hour event release, NAZA attracted an audience of over 82,000 admissions. The film screened in more than 260 theaters nationwide, with nearly 500 screenings over two days. It topped the box office on both days, making it one of the most-watched documentaries in French theaters in 2026.

The doc’s German distributor ImmerGuteFilme has reported 83.355 admissions in the territory to date, with its strongest day to date on Sunday 1 November. This is doubly impressive, as the war in Gaza and the German government’s support of Israel have divided the country and its cultural scene.

Graffiti showing directors Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham with the Hebrew writings "traitors" in Ashdod, Israel - 15 September 2026 AP Photo

Last month, we reported that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had attacked the makers of NAZA, accusing the film of contributing to “global antisemitic incitement”.

“It’s shocking. We are fighting global antisemitic incitement and when it comes from within us it is intolerable,” Netanyahu said in a video posted on Telegram. “And now two Israeli directors portraying the IDF (Israel Defense Forces) as war criminals receive applause at the Venice festival.”

Netanyahu's comments followed those of Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar, who directly equated criticism of Israel's actions to antisemitism and announced that he would “act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship” of the Israeli directing duo Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.

Netanyahu has called for a criminal investigation into soldiers and officers interviewed in NAZA. He has ordered for the filmmakers to be prosecuted for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests” and asked for attorney general Gali Baharav-Miara, IDF chief of staff Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, and Shin Bet head David Zini, to “act urgently to uncover the identity of all those who are involved or appear in the libel film”.

As reported by the Guardian, Ricardo Gutiérrez, the general secretary of the European Federation of Journalists, said: “These threats constitute a blatant act of intimidation against journalists who have simply been doing their job, in strict accordance with ethical standards and in the public interest.”

Regarding Netanyahu’s threats, he added: “I am not surprised by this outburst, which confirms that this regime is prepared to do anything to cover up its crimes against humanity and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.”

After NAZA 's cinematic run, the documentary’s free global streaming release on theguardian.com is planned for early December. The film is included in the shortlist for Best European Documentary at the upcoming European Film Awards.

World.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate seat in historic upset
World.content:
Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, becoming the first Black senator elected from the southern US state in more than 140 years, US networks projected on Wednesday.

 

Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. It was perhaps the most remarkable seat flip of a midterm election in which Democrats won back the majority in both the Senate and the House of Representatives.

CNN, NBC and CBS called the race on Wednesday, eight days after election night. With about 99 per cent of the vote counted, Colom led Hyde-Smith by 49.2 per cent to 48.7 per cent, a margin of 4,585 votes.

“Mississippi, our prayers have often changed the course of history,” Colom told a jubilant crowd of supporters in Jackson, the state capital, on Wednesday night. “God didn’t want us to get it the easy way. He wanted us to get it the Mississippi way.”

In a prayerful, solemn speech, he paid tribute to Mississippi’s long tradition of Black activism and faith in progress.

He will also be the first Democratic senator from Mississippi in nearly 40 years.

Hyde-Smith, 67, who has held the seat since 2018, conceded in a video posted on X.

“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

A blow for Trump

The result in one of the most solidly Republican states deepens the setback for US President Donald Trump. Voters across the country turned away from his Republican Party, even in states that had not sent a Democrat to Washington in decades.

Democrats will now hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate and Republicans 44. One race, in Alaska, has yet to be called.

Including Mississippi, Democrats flipped eight Republican-held Senate seats, with breakthroughs in South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Maine. Several of those seats had not changed hands for decades.

Control of both chambers of Congress gives Democrats the power to block legislation, investigate the administration and stop Trump’s appointments. The defeat also leaves the 80-year-old president as a lame duck for the final two years of his term.

The race went down to the wire, surprising many observers who had doubted how far the Democratic wave would reach. The wave was driven by mounting anger over Trump’s hardline immigration policy, the war in Iran and the rising cost of living.

“Blue Mississippi is here,” Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the Senate, wrote on X after the projections came in.

“Scott Colom is the only person who could’ve gotten this done. I knew it from the moment I met him.”

‘The power of prayer’

The first Black senator ever elected in the United States, Hiram Revels, was from Mississippi. He served during the Reconstruction era that followed the American Civil War.

In his speech, Colom described how Revels, a minister by training, used his powerful oratory to win the backing of other politicians for his run for the Senate.

“That’s an example of the power of prayer, and through our history, there are so many people that lifted this state up through the power of prayer in very dark times,” Colom said.

“It’s local people that have faith that Mississippi can make progress, and it’s local people like the people out here who had faith that we could win this election,” he added.

World.title: ‘Monstrous injustice’: King Charles condemns slavery as UK agrees to talks
World.content:
In this episode of Spotlight on Africa, we talked to scholars from the continent and the Caribbean about slavery reparations – a key topic discussed at this year’s Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.

Advertising

The Commonwealth is a 56-nation group of mostly former British colonies, 21 of them in Africa. King Charles III remains head of state in 15 of them, including the UK.

Its biennial Heads of Government Meeting took place from 1 to 4 November 2026 in Antigua and Barbuda.

In a final communiqué issued on Wednesday, the group said the time had come for “meaningful, truthful and respectful conversation towards forging a common future based on equity”.

Timetable of talks

While no timetable for talks was announced, the group welcomed the United Kingdom’s willingness to engage “in a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms”.

In his opening speech, King Charles III, who is politically neutral, called the slave trade “a monstrous injustice” that filled him with “profound personal sorrow”, but stopped short of a formal apology.

UN backs resolution calling slave trade ‘gravest crime against humanity’

For his part, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was open to saying sorry but ruled out paying the financial reparations demanded by some Caribbean countries.

Britain’s Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also said it was “not feasible” for the country to pay reparations for slavery, but that “there are things we can work on co-operatively”.

According to reports, Britain could issue a formal apology next year, during its G20 presidency.

Britain played a pivotal role in the slave trade, which saw between 10 and 15 million enslaved Africans taken to the Americas over four centuries.

The country abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery throughout the British Empire in 1833. It paid financial compensation, but to plantation owners rather than to the enslaved people themselves.

UN resolution

In March this year, the United Nations adopted a resolution recognising the transatlantic slave trade and the enslavement of Africans as the “gravest crime against humanity”, in a motion spearheaded by Ghana.

Ghana backs Jamaica’s petition to push UK for slavery reparations

For many countries, the time has come for formal apologies and concrete plans for slavery reparations.

To find out how these issues are being tackled on the African continent and in the Caribbean, RFI spoke to a panel of four guests:

Edem Adotey: professor at the Institute of African Studies in Accra, Ghana,

Joel Kibazo: Commonwealth spokesperson,

Matiangai Sirleaf: professor at the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law in the United States,

Verene A. Shepherd: Jamaican historian and one of three vice-chairs of the Caricom Reparations Commission.

This episode was mixed by Nicolas Doreau.

World.title: Bundeswehr study exposes widespread sexual harassment in German military
World.content:
Sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr is far more widespread than previously known, with younger women disproportionately affected. Defence Minister Boris Pistorius has called for a policy of "zero tolerance."

"It was clear to us from the outset that the analysis would uncover uncomfortable truths," Defence Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) told theBundestag on Wednesday. Earlier that day, he had presented the findings of the Bundeswehr's first study into unreported cases of sexual misconduct to the Defence Committee.

According to the findings, sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr is far more widespread than previously known. "The study has shown that only between one third and one sixth of cases are reported," Pistorius said, announcing an action plan to address the issue. "There is zero tolerance for sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr. This is nothing less than a matter of upholding the human dignity enshrined in our Basic Law. And that principle applies all the more within the Bundeswehr."

Women in Germany's military suffer widespread sexual abuse — study To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Many victims stay silent

The study examined incidents that had gone unreported, the so-called "dark figure" of cases that never reach official statistics. To this end, the Bundeswehr Centre of Military History and Social Sciences (ZMSBw) surveyed 45,000 service members, around 18% of whom responded. More than 8,100 questionnaires were evaluated and supplemented with individual and group interviews. According to the institute, the data are scientifically representative.

According to the study, younger women in the lower ranks are particularly affected by sexual misconduct. Among men, non-heterosexual soldiers are disproportionately affected. The perpetrators are predominantly male. Statistically, combat units do not differ from the rest of the armed forces.

Female service members in units with a higher proportion of women (more than 15%) are less likely to be affected.

Verbal harassment is by far the most common form of misconduct, according to the study. Some 72% of female soldiers and 31% of male soldiers said they had experienced verbal harassment at least once during their military service. In the 12 months preceding the survey, 38% of female soldiers and 16% of male soldiers reported experiencing verbal sexual harassment. 9% of female soldiers and 3% of male soldiers reported incidents of physical sexual misconduct. 2% of both women and men said they had experienced sexual violence.

The study also examined why service members chose not to report incidents. The most commonly cited reason was a desire not to draw attention to themselves. "There appears to be a lack of awareness of the reporting channels. And, for me, the decisive issue is trust in those channels," Pistorius concluded.

Why Germany struggles to recruit women soldiers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Greens call for independent reporting office for victims

In response, the Bundeswehr plans to improve awareness of how and where cases of sexual harassment can be reported. That is precisely where the environmentalist Greens, who are in opposition in the Bundestag, direct their criticism. Defence policy spokesperson Sara Nanni is calling for "an external reporting office, alongside the regular disciplinary process, with investigative powers and the authority to take disciplinary action where appropriate." Such an independent point of contact, she argues, is needed in cases where superiors within the Bundeswehr fail to fulfil their responsibilities.

Another consequence of the study is the expansion of support services for those affected. A counseling center established in early November will soon be available around the clock. Supervisors are also to receive enhanced awareness training and improved instruction. "Sexual misconduct will become part of training at every level, from the very beginning," said Bundeswehr Inspector General Carsten Breuer.

In addition, the way supervisors handle reported cases will become a standing criterion in their performance evaluations. "Anyone who fails to lead by example, tolerates misconduct, or does not address it consistently will no longer hold a leadership position," Defence Minister Pistorius stressed.

Germany rearms, but who will serve in the military? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Reported cases on the rise

The study was prompted by a growing number of reports of sexual misconduct received by former Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces Eva Högl. Most of those who approached her were female soldiers. Högl called for the study into unreported cases in 2024. The process gained further momentum following incidents at the Parachute Regiment in Zweibrücken that came to light at the beginning of this year and also involved allegations of sexual misconduct.

The current Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces, Henning Otte, described the figures revealed by the study as "dramatically high." The findings had also made it clear, he said, "that there is a lack of trust in the Bundeswehr's structures. The Ministry of Defence must now take this study seriously and translate its findings into a leadership culture that is truly lived in practice."

The Bundeswehr is in urgent need of additional personnel and has been actively recruiting women. However, the study's findings are unlikely to make attracting more female recruits any easier. Women remain significantly underrepresented across nearly all branches of the armed forces.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Intelligent women get less help at work, study finds
World.content:
Women who scored high on intelligence tests were seen as more hostile by their teammates and got less help, a new study finds. High-scoring men faced no such penalty. Research explains why.

High intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work. But a new study suggests that for women, it can also lead to worse treatment from colleagues.

Across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often. Men with high scores did not receive such treatment, and in one group, they were treated better.

The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them and whether that differs between women and men.

Since it was published this year, Nitya Chawla, an associate professor at UCL School of Management in London and the researcher behind the study, says women have written to her saying the findings matched their own experience at work. Some told her they had wondered whether they were to blame for hostility.

How was the study done, and what are its limits?

The researchers ran two studies. The first followed 432 business students at a US public university working in small teams on a consulting project for real organizations. The second surveyed 394 full-time employees working in teams at a financial company in China.

Intelligence here means cognitive ability measured with a standardized test of reasoning and problem-solving that employers use in hiring. Teammates were not told of anyone's scores. They rated one another, and a few weeks later each person reported how much help they had received and how often they had been undermined, for instance by having information withheld.

The effects were small, and the study shows a link, not proof that colleagues' perceptions caused the treatment. Participants reported help and mistreatment themselves, and the study did not look at race or ethnicity.

In the student group, the difference between women and men was no longer statistically significant when two participants with extremely low scores were included.

IQ 130 = Genius? The truth about IQ tests To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why are intelligent women seen as hostile at work?

The researchers point to social role theory, the idea that people expect men and women to fit traditional roles: men as capable and assertive, women as warm and supportive. A woman with high cognitive ability breaks that expectation, and colleagues may assume she lacks warmth.

"It's that automatic, implicit assumption that takes place alongside the presence of intelligence that then drives these more negative interpersonal behaviors," Chawla told DW.

In both groups, women with higher scores were rated as more hostile. Among the employees in China, they were also rated as less warm. Women seen as more hostile reported less help, both with their work and on a personal level, and more undermining.

The team also checked whether the women were simply behaving differently. Higher-scoring women were rated as somewhat more domineering, but that did not explain why they received less help or more mistreatment. The findings point to colleagues' assumptions, Chawla says, rather than to anything the women did.

Do men with high intelligence scores face the same treatment?

No, men with high intelligence scores do not face the same treatment. Among the students in the United States, a man's score made no difference to how his teammates rated or treated him.

Among the employees in China, men with higher scores were rated as less hostile, received more help and were mistreated less often. The authors suggest the difference between the two groups may reflect cultural differences in gender norms, but they did not test this.

Should women hide their intelligence at work?

No, Chawla says. "That would be really the wrong conclusion to draw."

Small effects still matter, she argues, because they are experienced day after day. Over time, this kind of treatment can lead to anxiety, self-doubt and a sense of not belonging. "These experiences and these feelings can become very, very burdensome over time," she said.

What can managers do about gender bias at work?

Chawla puts the responsibility on workplaces rather than on women. Managers, she says, should track how team members treat one another, and organizations should hold regular check-ins to see whether employees are getting equal support.

Individuals can ask themselves a simple question, she says: would they react the same way if that colleague were a man?

A tourist has reportedly died after falling from a paraglider in Bir Billing, known as India's paragliding capital, Indian media has reported.

The incident has raised concerns over the safety of commercial skydiving ventures in the popular adventure tourism spot located in the Kangra district of the Himalayan state of Himachal Pradesh.

Reports said the accident took place on Tuesday evening and identified the deceased tourist as a 26-year-old man from Uttar Pradesh's Noida.

News agency PTI cited police as saying the man had been on a tandem paragliding flight with a local pilot. He reportedly fell just six minutes after take-off.

The police have registered a case of death due to negligence against the pilot adding that a further probe into the incident was underway.

This is the second paragliding death to be reported in the densely forested and mountainous district in less than a month.

On October 25, a 47-year-old Bulgarian national was killed in a paraglider crash near Rising Star Peak in Kangra district's Dharamshala.

World.content:
Skip next section WATCH: Nearly 500,000 Russians dead: How long can Putin keep fighting?

11/12/2026 November 12, 2026 WATCH: Nearly 500,000 Russians dead: How long can Putin keep fighting?

Nearly half a million Russian soldiers may have been killed in Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine. Can Russia continue fighting at such an enormous human and economic cost?

Leaked records reportedly obtained from Russia's state statistics agency, Rosstat, identify more than 412,000 deaths linked to the war. British newspaper The Guardian reports that the true death toll could be closer to 500,000.

The full dataset has not been independently verified.

Some months saw more than 500 Russian soldiers killed every day. And the losses have fallen disproportionately on Russia's poorer and more remote regions.

In this DW News interview, Janis Kluge, head of the Eastern Europe and Eurasia research division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), examines what the leaked figures reveal about Russia's military losses, recruitment crisis and war economy.

The leaked data comes as US-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine conclude in Abu Dhabi without a breakthrough on ending the war.

The two sides have agreed to a prisoner exchange, but fundamental disagreements remain. Could mounting Russian losses eventually force Putin to compromise, or make him even more determined to continue the war?

World.title: Where the US's war with Iran stands after the midterms
World.content:
Almost nine months after it began, the war in Iran has calmed to the point where Donald Trump sees an end. But with the key issues of the conflict unresolved and political change in the US, what is the situation?

The US-Israel war with Iran, according to US President Donald Trump, "is effectively over" in a military sense. Trump's secretary of state, Marco Rubio, backed up the president, saying there is "no need for major combat operations" in Iran because economic pressure and negotiations between the warring parties are proving effective.

However, Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, has denied negotiations are even taking place. "All American claims about the continuation of negotiations with Iran are aimed at easing economic pressures and reducing oil prices," he told Lebanese channel Al Mayadeen.

Is the Iran war actually over?

While neither side has claimed the conflict is concluded in every sense, Ian Kelly , a former US ambassador who now works at Northwestern University in the US, considers the current situation is something like a "virtual ceasefire." He added that there is currently a significant deescalation but that the central issues are unresolved.

"I wouldn't say the war is over. I would say there's no shooting going on, nothing really significant," Kelly told DW. "But the real issue is opening up the Strait of Hormuz. What Iran wants, of course, is for the United States to withdraw its massive strike forces from the Gulf. But that won't happen until Iran agrees to open the Strait of Hormuz."

A critical shipping lane between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, the Strait of Hormuz has been a focal point in the US-Iran conflict. Iran's attacks on commercial ships in the strait have led to higher oil prices and have had other economic impacts that have affected living costs in the US and around the world.

Kelly, who also held several high-level roles at the US State Department, thinks the US midterm election results, which will see the Democrats take control of the House and Senate next year after catastrophic losses for Trump's Republicans, means Iran is sitting tight.

"I think that Iran is in a wait-and-see moment to see if the war will wind down because Congress acts to either cut off the funding or severely limit the funding," he said. But with Iran's resources also dwindling, it's a game of cat and mouse.

What has this conflict meant for Donald Trump and what's next for the US?

Trump and his party need the war to end, according to Kelly, for political reasons, as well as strategic.

"As long as the war is not resolved, it's going to be a real sticking point for the Republicans as they look at [the election in] 2028. They have to wrap it up before then," he said.

"A major contributing factor to the Republican defeat was how Trump has not followed through on some of his promises made in 2024. One of the big ones was no more forever wars, and he just went off and started another war that doesn't seem to have an exit strategy. It has weakened the Republican Party."

Trump weakened: Is Europe safer now? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The imminent change in US politics will naturally have military consequences long before the 2028 election.

”There is little likelihood that Congress will continue to fund this war at the kind of levels that they have been," said Kelly. "That's another reason that Iran is sitting back and just waiting to see where this all comes out."

What needs to happen for a compromise to be reached?

While the US administration claims it is happy with a status quo of containment through land and sea blockades, Kelly believes the authority of Trump and his party will be further diminished if the US can't achieve concrete progress on its stated main goals: gaining full control of the Strait of Hormuz and forcing Iran to give up its enriched uranium.

"Both of those are quite possible," Kelly said, adding that even attempting to achieve them threatens the current relative calm.

"The White House has really painted itself in a corner here by stressing that the main goal is to deny Iran a nuclear weapon. I don't see that as something that Iran is going to negotiate away, which means that they [the US] will probably have to use military force again. The White House is in a real pickle."

But there is also the question of how long Iran can bear the economic burden of the war without reaching a deal.

"Iran's limitation in the Strait of Hormuz is economic rather than military, because continuing the war has a significant impact on its economy," Ali Mohammadi, an expert in Iranian affairs based in France, told DW earlier this week.

Nevertheless, the strait remains a key source of leverage for Iran in any future negotiations.

What would the end of the Iran War mean for the world economy?

Kelly doesn't see the economic strain of the war subsiding anytime soon, especially in oil markets.



The Strait of Hormuz remains key to bothe Iran and the US Image: REUTERS

"The real issue for the markets is that as long as it remains a phony war, it's very difficult to see oil prices lowering. The prices that are being charged now factor in the possible return to instability, so it has to be some kind of agreement where all sides and the oil markets are confident that we see a return to status quo. It's going to be difficult to restore the markets' confidence that these tankers won't be shot at again," Kelly said.

Given the global consequences of the conflict, Kelly expects it to be a hot topic at this month's APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) summit in Shenzhen, where Trump and his counterparts in Russia and China, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, will reportedly meet.

"I think Russia is interested in keeping the United States tied down like this. China, though, is interested in resolving it because they are a big customer," he said. A G20 summit in Miami follows the APEC meeting in December.

While the impasse between Iran and the US shows little sign of being broken, the fighting has calmed, for now at least. What happens in the coming weeks in the meeting rooms of Shenzhen and Miami currently looks more critical to finding a solution than what happens on Iranian territory or waterways.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV returns to Peru to a big welcome, calls it his 'homeland'
World.content:
An estimated 3 million people greeted Pope Leo XIV in Lima as the Peruvian-citizen pontiff began a six-day homecoming visit to the country where he spent two decades as a missionary and bishop.

Pope Leo XIV opened the Peruvian leg of his South America tour on Wednesday, telling crowds in Lima that returning to the country where he served for two decades felt like coming home.

The Vatican estimated that about 3 million people lined his motorcade route, the Associated Press reported.

What did he say?

Leo holds Peruvian citizenship and spent more than two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and later as bishop of the northern city of Chiclayo before becoming pope.

Also a US citizen, he is the first pope from either the United States or Peru.

He sang Peru's national anthem with President Keiko Fujimori at the presidential palace.

"Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you," he said, adding that he was "also returning to my homeland."

Leo urged Peruvians to "cultivate honesty, integrity," and to accept that "no one has all the answers."

As bishop, Leo XIV, then Robert Prevost, had repeatedly criticized Fujimori’s late father, former President Alberto Fujimori Image: Luis Acosta/AFP

He also called for stronger disaster prevention in a country regularly hit by El Nino-linked floods and landslides.

Fujimori said Peru must face the “unfinished task” of reconciliation after decades of insurgent violence, state abuses and sharp political divisions.

What is happening in Peru?

The welcome comes as many Peruvians are weary of their leaders.

The country has had nine presidents since July 2016, and homicide rates have nearly doubled in five years.

Political science professor Alonso Cardenas told AP he sees "no sign of a reaction, no strategy" from Fujimori's government.

Peru remains a majority Catholic country, making up about 67% of the population Image: Anthony Nino De Guzman/AFP

Notably, the Catholic Church is more credible than any other Peruvian institution, theology professor Veronique Lecaros told AP, even as Pew data show Catholics falling from 76% of the population to about 67%.

Leo's six-day stay includes a trip to 3,700 meters (about 12,140 feet), considered risky after Leo had part of a lung removed in mid-October because of a malignant tumor. He is due back at the Vatican on November 17.

World.title: Nvidia board reportedly weighs ousting Huang amid alleged affairs with exec and suspected Chinese spy
World.content:
Nvidia's board is reportedly preparing to oust Jensen Huang amid reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The shake-up would leave the world's leading AI chip supplier without the co-founder who built it.

Nvidia's board was meeting Wednesday to decide whether to remove co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang, media outlets, led by The Wall Street Journal, reported.

Huang has led the company for more than three decades, turning it from a gaming chipmaker into the dominant supplier of chips for artificial intelligence.

Why is Nvidia's board considering replacing Huang?

The report comes as Nvidia investigates whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort after reports of an affair with a woman US intelligence reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him.

News that Nvidia might part ways with Huang sent the company's shares down about 8% in after-hours trading.

A reporter for the financial news outlet Bloomberg said on X that Nvidia's board was working with an outside firm to identify potential successors and considering an interim CEO while it searched for a permanent replacement.

US Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons asked President Donald Trump's administration to preserve records related to Nvidia's chip exports to China, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing a letter from the senators. The request also covers records related to Huang's alleged affair with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence.

What has Huang said?

Huang acknowledged in a note to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife. He did not publicly name the woman. The New York Times identified her as Alice H., a former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed who is not related to him. Beijing rejected the espionage allegation.

Shareholders sued Nvidia and Huang on Monday in a proposed class action suit accusing them of concealing the alleged relationship and the risks it posed to the company.

What do we know about the second alleged affair?

The New York Times identified the Nvidia executive as Kimberly Powell, the company's vice president of health care. Asked about the relationship, Huang told the newspaper, "I don't think you should be talking to me directly," before ending the call.

Nvidia and Powell did not immediately respond to requests for comment, Reuters reported.

World.title: Mississippi Senate race: Democrat Scott Colom defeats Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith
World.content:
The southern US state of Mississippi has elected its first Black senator in more than 140 years. Democrat Scott Colom has won the seat in a historic upset, according to projections.

Democratic candidate Scott Colom beat Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's US Senate race after a prolonged ballot-counting process, the Associated Press projected on Wednesday.

The narrow victory makes Colom, 43, the state's first Black US senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction and the first new Democratic senator chosen by Mississippi since 1947.

"All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this," Colom told a crowd of hundreds who gathered at Tougaloo College for his victory party. "I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters."

How Colom pulled ahead in Mississippi

During the campaign, Colom promised to represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society.

"It's got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better," he said.

The southern US state of Mississippi has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations.

Democrats extend their Senate majority

The Mississippi victory gives the Democrats a 55-44 advantage in the 100-member ​Senate. The winner of the Senate race in Alaska remains to be determined. The Democrats also won control of the House of Representatives, having gained 41 seats so far and holding a 254-to-168 advantage, with 13 races yet to be called.

What will Democrats do with their midterm mandate? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Mississippi election officials have been counting ballots for over a week in a race so close that Colom led by only a few dozen votes at some points. The latest media-tabulated results showed him ahead by more than 4,500 votes, or 0.5 ​percentage points.

The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose Republican Party suffered defeats in several states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the US South.

Republican rival concedes after close count

Hyde-Smith, 67, posted a concession video on social media, and a spokesperson confirmed she had called Colom to concede. Hyde-Smith was first elected in 2018 and consistently led in opinion polls in a state that ⁠Trump ​won by nearly 23 points in 2024.

Progress or not? Democrats, Republicans pick new leaders in Congress To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Democrats' Senate leader, Chuck Schumer, wrote on X, "Blue Mississippi is here."

Hyde-Smith had blocked Colom's nomination by former President Joe Biden to serve as a US District Court judge in northern Mississippi, citing his position on transgender issues. Mississippi's other US senator, Republican Roger Wicker, supported his nomination for the post.

Mississippi does not have a law mandating a recount for a close election.

World.title: El mapa electoral: ¿Qué dicen las encuestas en cada provincia?
World.content:
Simulamos las elecciones 20.000 veces con el clásico modelo de EL PAÍS: hay 150 escaños casi decididos y otros 150 probables, pero medio centenar sigue en el aire. Consúltalos uno a uno

Las encuestas tratan de predecir los votos del próximo 29-N, pero el modelo electoral que publicamos en EL PAÍS desde hace una década va más allá: estima el voto y los escaños en cada provincia, y les asigna probabilidades. A continuación mostramos sus pronósticos en cada territorio, con las encuestas publicadas hasta el 9 de noviembre.

En el interactivo puedes ver los escaños seguros (99% de opciones), probables (75%-99%) y en juego (25%-75%) de cada partido. En total hay 153 seguros, 150 probables y 97 en juego (suman más de 350 porque varios partidos se disputan los escaños). También puedes elegir una provincia y ver nuestra estimación allí.

Las provincias con más escaños en juego son las más grandes, Madrid (con 10) y Barcelona (con nueve). Pero hay pulsos muy reñidos en algunas provincias pequeñas. En Lleida, que reparte cuatro diputados, cinco partidos se disputan los dos últimos: Junts, PP, PSOE, ERC y Vox.

¿Cómo funciona el modelo?

El modelo parte de nuestro promedio de sondeos, lo proyecta a cada provincia con su historia y microdatos del CIS, y le añade la incertidumbre de las encuestas en el pasado. Después simulamos las elecciones 20.000 veces y contamos cuántas veces gana cada partido cada escaño. Así podemos clasificarlos en tres grupos: seguros, probables y en juego.

El siguiente gráfico muestra qué significan estas probabilidades. Puedes simular las elecciones una, dos, tres o cien veces para hacerte una idea intuitiva de cuántas veces se gana un escaño de cada tipo.

El modelo es sólido. Cada pieza la hemos puesto a prueba con otras elecciones generales. Por ejemplo, hemos probado varias formas de repartir el voto entre provincias, siguiendo técnicas habituales, y nos quedamos con la más precisa en votos y escaños.

El modelo es cauteloso. Y lo es por diseño: predecir cada provincia es difícil porque las encuestas pierden precisión a escala provincial. Un sondeo de 2.000 o 5.000 entrevistas no basta para estimar directamente el voto de Soria, Pontevedra o Castellón. Por eso no lo intentamos: lo que hacemos es usar el voto histórico de cada partido en cada provincia y lo que dicen en cada comunidad los microdatos del CIS, que acumulan decenas de miles de entrevistas. Además, las fuerzas locales no siempre salen en las encuestas y pueden sorprender al final: Teruel Existe gana escaño en una de cada cinco simulaciones. Y pasa algo similar con partidos pequeños en las provincias grandes: Podemos consigue un diputado por Madrid en el 60% de las simulaciones, y SALF, en el 24%. Si detectas cualquier omisión, escríbenos.

Y el modelo es confiable. Estas predicciones las hemos hecho muchas veces. Por eso sabemos que el modelo funciona y está bien calibrado. En 2023 dimos 189 escaños como seguros y se cumplieron todos, igual que en las dos elecciones de 2019 (156 y 153). Los que dimos como probables se cumplieron el 94% de las veces (365 de 388), en la parte alta del 75%-99% que prometíamos. Los errores de cada provincia se compensan en parte al sumarlos, así que el total es más fiable que cada provincia por separado. El modelo también acierta en el total nacional: en las generales de 2016 a 2023, los escaños de cada partido grande cayeron dentro de nuestra horquilla del 80% en 19 de 20 casos, más de lo prometido: es la cautela de la que hablábamos.

Si quieres seguir todas las encuestas del 29-N, apúntate el nuevo pódcast de Kiko Llaneras, en Spotify, YouTube, Apple Podcasts o iVoox.

Metodología

Las predicciones las produce un modelo estadístico basado en sondeos y en su precisión histórica. Es una versión renovada del que hemos usado en unas 40 elecciones desde 2016: en Andalucía, Castilla y León, Aragón, Extremadura, las europeas, las generales de abril y noviembre de 2019 y de 2023, y otras en México, Francia o el Reino Unido.

Funciona en cuatro pasos. 1) Un promedio de encuestas que pondera cada sondeo por su tamaño, su fecha y la precisión histórica de su encuestadora, según nuestro comparador. 2) Una proyección del voto a cada provincia con un modelo logístico, que parte de las generales de 2023 —y, para los partidos nuevos o que ahora concurren por separado, de las europeas de 2024 y las andaluzas de 2026— y se alimenta también con microdatos del CIS de cada comunidad. 3) La incertidumbre de las encuestas, calibrada con los errores de 44 elecciones en España desde 1986 y con una base internacional de miles de sondeos, según el tamaño de cada partido y los días que faltan para votar. Usamos distribuciones t de Student, con colas más anchas que una normal, y errores correlacionados entre partidos. Esos errores tienen una parte común a toda España, porque las encuestas suelen fallar en la misma dirección en todas partes, y otra propia de cada provincia. 4) 20.000 simulaciones de las elecciones, repartiendo los escaños según D’Hondt con barrera del 3% en cada circunscripción.

Un escaño es seguro si un partido lo gana en más del 99% de las simulaciones; probable, entre el 75% y el 99%, y en juego, entre el 25% y el 75%. En nuestras pruebas con las generales de 2016 a 2023, esas probabilidades están muy bien afinadas: los escaños en juego se cumplieron 202 veces, frente a las 195 que predecía el modelo.

En los gráficos nacionales agrupamos como Izquierdas a Frente Amplio, Podemos y las coaliciones Compromís-Front Valencià, Unidad del Pueblo Canario y Ara Més-Front Ampli; en cada provincia aparecen por separado.

Si quieres seguir todas las encuestas del 29-N, apúntate al nuevo pódcast de Kiko Llaneras, en Spotify, YouTube, Apple Podcasts o iVoox.
