World.title: Poland and US sign statement of intent on strengthening defence industry cooperation
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, have signed a statement of intent on strengthening cooperation between their defence industries. “Today, we are taking the next steps in our alliance,” declared Hegseth, while Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the move signalled that Poland is now “not only a model ally…but has become a strategic partner of the United States”. The Polish defence minister added that he would also push for equipment jointly manufactured by Poland and the US to be eligible for EU defence funding. “Poland is the US ambassador in the EU,” he declared. Wicepremier W. @KosiniakKamysz z #Waszyngton: to chyba moja najważniejsza i przełomowa wizyta w USA. To moment, w którym mogę powiedzieć, że Polska jest nie tylko modelowym sojusznikiem, ale stała się strategicznym partnerem USA. pic.twitter.com/75xdgzIaG0 — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) November 10, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz was welcomed by Hegseth in Washington to discuss a range of issues relating to security cooperation. A major item on the agenda was Poland’s desire for a new permanent US military base on its territory. After the meeting, Kosiniak-Kamysz told reporters that there was a “green light from the Pentagon” for the base, with the final decision now resting with the White House. He said that was expected to be made in early December. Hegseth, meanwhile, praised Poland for embracing the “NATO 3.0” concept, under which the US wants Europe to take on more responsibility for its own defence. “Poland is building one of the most formidable armies in Europe, ready to secure and defend its territory,” said the Secretary of War, who noted that Warsaw is “leading by example” with its high levels of defence spending. Hegseth also welcomed the fact that Poland is investing significantly in US equipment, including Abrams tanks, F-35 fighter jets, Apache helicopters and Patriot air-defence systems. “You are building a fully modernised, interoperable force, and our two nations are…giving military cooperation industrial depth as well,” said the secretary of war. Hegseth also reaffirmed Washington’s desire for a peace deal in Ukraine and “encouraged Kosiniak-Kamysz to continue Poland’s steadfast support of Ukraine”, said Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell. American defense technology is driving innovation and creating new opportunities for transatlantic industrial cooperation.@USAmbNATO Matthew Whitaker, Assistant Secretary of Commerce David Fogel @CommerceGov and @USAmbPoland Tom Rose met with Deputy Minister of Defence… pic.twitter.com/5etw1L3X5A — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) November 10, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the statement of intent he had signed with Hegseth was aimed at ensuring more US equipment was manufactured and maintained in Poland itself, including technology transfers. He also said that he wants to secure European funds for jointly produced US equipment. The EU’s SAFE programme of defence loans, for example, largely excludes US manufacturers. “We want American equipment manufactured by Polish-American companies to benefit from European funding. I will present such a position next Tuesday at the meeting of EU defence ministers,” said Kosiniak-Kamysz. “Poland is the US ambassador to the EU.” The meeting between the two defence secretaries also coincided with the Transatlantic Defence Industry Access Forum, which brought together 70 Polish and 80 American firms, with the aim of strengthening ties between the two countries’ defence industries. W ostatnich dniach dobra decyzja o utworzeniu w Polsce centrum serwisowego rakiet Patriot, a dziś podpisaliśmy kolejne porozumienie z USA, które przyspieszy współpracę naszych przemysłów zbrojeniowych. Chcemy, by więcej uzbrojenia powstawało i było naprawiane w Polsce. To nowe… pic.twitter.com/j24E2xON66 — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 10, 2026 Last month, the United States chose Poland as the location for a planned facility for servicing and maintaining Patriot missiles – the first to be located outside the US itself. In July, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles. In May, an agreement was signed to establish a centre in Poland for servicing the engines of Abrams tanks. That same month, President Donald Trump announced that his country would station an additional 5,000 troops in Poland, prompting Warsaw to formally request the establishment of a new US military base, which President Karol Nawrocki has suggested should be called “Fort Trump”. World.title: Two Ukrainians charged with spying and sabotage for Russia in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has detained and charged two Ukrainian citizens accused of carrying out espionage and acts of sabotage on behalf of Russia. The men, aged 24 and 25, were allegedly paid to conduct reconnaissance of critical infrastructure and military facilities across Poland. They are also accused of setting fire to several vehicles with the aim of stoking anti-Ukrainian sentiment. Funkcjonariusze Agencji Bezpieczeństwa Wewnętrznego zatrzymali w Mińsku Mazowieckim dwóch obywateli Ukrainy w wieku 24 i 25 lat podejrzanych o szpiegostwo i prowadzenie działań dywersyjnych na zlecenie rosyjskich służb specjalnych. ▶️ Mężczyźni rozpoznawali i robili zdjęcia… pic.twitter.com/G3i8hEsBHT — Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 10, 2026 The suspects were detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) on 3 November in Mińsk Mazowiecki, a town just outside Warsaw, the capital. ABW officers also searched their residences and other locations connected to the investigation, seizing data storage devices and narcotics. According to investigators, the suspects were tasked with setting vehicles on fire after changing their licence plates to ones used by Ukrainian military vehicles. This was “aimed at fueling anti-Ukrainian sentiment”, says the National Prosecutor’s Office. Prosecutors have charged the men under Poland’s espionage law with working against Poland on behalf of a foreign intelligence service – a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of five years – and sabotage on behalf of foreign intelligence, which is punishable by 10 years to life. At the prosecutor’s request, a court ordered both suspects to be placed in pretrial detention for three months. In recent years, Poland has seen a huge rise in cases of espionage and sabotage carried out on behalf of Russia. The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined. Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 Last month, a Polish man was jailed for five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of an airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. Shortly afterwards, the trial began of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage. World.title: “Strong traces of right-wing extremism” in activity of Kraków terrorist, says justice minister
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, says that investigators have so far found “very strong traces of right-wing extremism” in the activity of Michał Oksiński, the man who carried out Saturday’s mass terrorist shooting in Kraków that left six people dead. The perpetrator’s search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist who killed 77 people during two attacks in 2011. Żurek’s comments come amid intense debate and dispute in Poland over the beliefs and motives of Oksiński, who on Monday died from the injuries he sustained during a shootout with police that brought his rampage to an end. W. Żurek ujawnia nowe ustalenia po zamachu w Krakowie. Tłumik w samochodzie sprawcy i ślady zainteresowania Breivikiemhttps://t.co/nd1XPBlmrI — Radio Kraków (@RadioKrakow) November 10, 2026 On Tuesday, Żurek, who also serves as prosecutor general, spoke to local broadcaster Radio Kraków about the progress of the investigation into Oksiński. He confirmed that the perpetrator had not left behind any letter or other kind of message revealing his motives. “Those motives are being investigated,” said the minister. “There are very strong traces of right-wing extremism. I can already confirm some information because the services have access to the perpetrator’s computer. Indeed, visits to websites related to Anders Breivik are visible.” Żurek also pointed to the fact that, as prosecutors announced on Sunday, a so-called Gadsden flag (showing a snake above the words “Don’t tread on me”) had been found in Oksiński’s home. Prosecutors say a "Don't Tread on Me" flag was found hanging at the home of the perpetrator of the attack in Kraków They emphasise that the flag is not associated with any one ideology or organisation and that they are still trying to determine the shooter's motives and beliefs pic.twitter.com/yoNfh7cHwU — Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) November 9, 2026 Although the National Prosecutor’s Office emphasised that the flag is not associated with any one ideology or organisation, Żurek noted that it was displayed during the attack on the United States Capitol by supporters of Donald Trump in 2021. “We know well that during the attack on the Capitol, there were quite a few of these flags among far-right groups in the United States,” said the minister. “This flag [in Oksiński’s home] also sends a signal to the security services and the prosecutor’s office.” Żurek added that a search of the perpetrator’s workplace had also identified “symbolism there that could point to this thread [of right-wing extremism]”, but provided no further details. The minister noted, however, that investigators are also taking into account the potential for “mental disorders” playing a role in the actions of Oksiński, whose parents and sister were found shot dead in his home. Żurek’s remarks come following controversy in Poland over a statement by interior minister Marcin Kierwiński on Saturday, in the immediate aftermath of the attack, when he said that early indications suggest that Oksiński had held “very radical views”, including a “fascination with far-right ideologies”. Over the following two days, Kierwiński refused to provide evidence supporting those claims, and in a TV interview on Sunday evening said that he had simply been sharing “first hypotheses”. That led some right-wing opposition politicians and commentators to accuse Kierwiński of spreading false claims, either through incompetence or as a deliberate attempt to associate the attack with the right. However, speaking to Radio Kraków on Tuesday, Żurek said that “it seems that what Minister Kierwiński communicated in those first hours is confirmed by the evidence”. Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, is facing growing pressure to present evidence to back his claim that the Kraków shooter was driven by far-right ideologies, amid criticism from opposition parties that he is seeking to exploit the tragedy for political reasons. — Jakub Krupa (@JakubKrupa) November 9, 2026 On social media, many people have also been sharing alleged images of Oksiński’s past activities, both online and in real life, claiming that they show he held left-wing views. However, some of those images have proven to be false, such as one purporting to show him at a pro-refugee rally (the photograph is genuine, but the person in it was not Oksiński) and another purporting to show him shaking hands with Kierwiński (the image was AI-generated). Further alleged images from Oskiński’s social media accounts remain unverified and also depict posts that were made six or seven years ago. Another fake that is being widely shared. While the photo is genuine, the person highlighted is not the Kraków shooter. Other images from the event clearly show it isn't him, while fact-checkers @konkret24 actually tracked down the guy in the photo: https://t.co/4HeofUdOUm pic.twitter.com/pTfdkCZlAL — Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) November 9, 2026 On Monday, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski told Polsat News that there had been an “enormous wave of disinformation” in the wake of Saturday’s tragedy. He criticised “pseudo-journalists and politicians” who had shared such content. “Digital platforms acted very responsibly, removing this content quickly,” said Gawkowski. However, he added that X, the social media service owned by Elon Musk, had been an exception and was “where the most radicalisation occurred”. Meanwhile, the interior ministry’s spokeswoman, Karolina Gałecka, announced on Monday that they would notify prosecutors about the creation and dissemination of the AI-generated image of Kierwiński shaking hands with Oksiński. She said it had been spread by social media accounts associated with right-wing broadcaster Republika. World.title: What is at stake in Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal dispute?
World.content:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Poland’s escalating Constitutional Tribunal (TK) dispute is no longer simply a legal argument about contested appointments but a struggle over who defines constitutional legitimacy.

As the liberal-centrist government and right-wing opposition and president advance rival rule-of-law claims, the conflict risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent.

The roots of the crisis

Poland’s 15-member TK is a powerful body that rules on the constitutionality of the country’s laws. The roots of the current dispute trace back to late 2015 and began immediately prior to the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party taking office following its October parliamentary election victory.

In its final weeks in power, the outgoing government, led by the liberal-centrist Civic Platform (PO, now Civic Coalition: KO), fast-tracked the appointment of five tribunal members who were replacing those whose terms were set to expire in November and December.

Upon winning an outright parliamentary majority, the incoming PiS-led government refused to recognise these appointments, elected a slate of five new tribunal members, and party-backed President Andrzej Duda swore them in.

Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025

The tribunal (still largely composed of pre-2015 judges) ruled that three of the outgoing parliament’s appointments were lawful, so only two of the new ones could stand. PiS refused to accept this, creating the so-called “understudy” judges (dublerzy) controversy.

As further vacancies arose, the new parliament gradually installed its nominees, culminating in the appointment at the end of 2016 of one of them, Julia Przyłębska, as tribunal president. Przyłębska’s leadership was contested on procedural grounds, as was that of her 2024 successor Bogdan Święczkowski, a former senior prosecutor closely aligned with the 2015-23 PiS administration.

All of this led to the then-opposition parties and much of the Polish legal and the EU political establishments denouncing the tribunal as legally compromised and politically captured.

Total non-cooperation

Following the autumn 2023 parliamentary election, a new coalition government headed up by KO leader Donald Tusk embraced a policy of total non-cooperation with the tribunal, refusing to publish its rulings.

The battle for control took a new turn when, after initially not filling any tribunal vacancies, from March 2026 onwards the new parliament elected successive waves of new members, reaching eight by September.

However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki (who succeeded Duda in August 2025) refused to swear in five of these nominees, including former minister and close Tusk ally Maciej Berek. In response, the government took the unprecedented step of swearing in the contested nominees directly in parliament, a move that both Nawrocki and Święczkowski rejected as illegal.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

The conflict escalated sharply at the end of last month, when, backed by the government and tribunal members elected by the current parliamentary majority, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the five contested nominees but having the longest judicial tenure, asserted her seniority to order a one-month suspension of Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański in their official duties and assumed temporary control.

Justice minister Waldemar Żurek submitted requests to lift Święczkowski and Sochański’s immunity as the newly appointed members, and the new nominees entered the tribunal building under State Protection Service (UOP) escort.

This triggered protests by right-wing opposition supporters at the building’s gates, prompting a heavy police presence and tense stand-off. The severity of this was underscored when Nawrocki cut short an official visit to Senegal mid-flight, returned to Warsaw and entered the tribunal building in the early hours, condemning what he described as a violation of the constitutional order.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court. The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

Korwin-Piotrowska then convened a tribunal general assembly which critics argued lacked the legally required two-thirds quorum because only eight of its 15 nominal members (the newly elected ones, including the five who had not taken the presidential oath) attended.

Her supporters maintained that the quorum was met because the suspension of Święczkowski and Sochański, and exclusion of the last remaining “understudy” judge, reduced the pool of eligible members to 12.

The government’s “transitional justice” logic

For the Tusk government and its legal defenders, these exceptional executive and parliamentary countermeasures were framed through the logic of “transitional justice”: as painful and extraordinary but necessary to restore the rule of law after PiS had violated the constitution and European standards, systematically packing the tribunal with political loyalists.

Justifying its non-recognition of tribunal rulings, the government argued that the presence of three defectively elected “understudy” members and their successors, together with Przyłębska’s and Święczkowski’s procedurally flawed presidential appointments, fundamentally “contaminated” the entire body, thereby invalidating its rulings.

In its efforts to restore democracy, the government may sometimes take actions that are “not fully compliant with the law”, admits @donaldtusk. But he says this is because of the legal chaos deliberately created by the former PiS government https://t.co/AWlM6hRLie — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 11, 2024

To provide what it argued was authoritative external confirmation of this defect, the government relied heavily on landmark European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) and EU Court of Justice (CJEU) rulings which determined that, thus constituted, the tribunal could no longer be considered a legitimate body established by legal standards.

From this perspective, refusing to recognise the tribunal’s allegedly unlawful rulings was framed as the only available mechanism to neutralise a partisan weapon that PiS had left behind to block the government’s legislative agenda.

Alternative parliamentary swearing-in procedures were justified on the grounds that the president’s role in receiving oaths was purely ceremonial, not a constitutionally mandated requirement.

Despite his recent political role, Berek’s appointment was defended on the basis that he played more of a technocratic-expert role within the government, and was highly qualified to undertake the extraordinary transitional measures required to repair a damaged institution.

Defenders of the tribunal leadership’s suspension and occupation of its headquarters argued that by blocking the new nominees from taking up their roles, Święczkowski had paralysed the institution and decisive measures were necessary to restore its proper functioning.

A “coup d’état”?

PiS and Nawrocki, on the other hand, maintained that the Tusk government’s actions amounted to an authoritarian attempt to operate completely outside of constitutional powers, treating legality as an option when it conflicted with its political agenda.

They insisted that all of its 2015 appointments were in full accordance with the law, correcting an improper attempt by the outgoing PO-dominated parliament to entrench its influence after electoral defeat, and that the tribunal’s ruling on the legality of these three “understudy” judges went beyond its jurisdiction.

Successive tribunal general assemblies, they argued, validly and legally selected Przyłębska and then Święczkowski as presidents, and the Tusk government had no constitutional right to pick and choose which tribunal rulings it would recognise. They said that, by delaying the election of some new members when vacancies arose, the government violated existing procedures.

The constitution, they said, explicitly required these new nominees to take their oaths directly “before the president” and that by conducting improper parliamentary swearing-in ceremonies they had effectively renounced their offices.

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary” But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026

The candidacy of Berek, a recently active politician with doubtful professional qualifications, they said represented its own form of institutional capture and selective legality.

The suspension of the tribunal leadership and occupation of its headquarters amounted to an unlawful power grab or “coup d’état” that completely disregarded established constitutional procedures.

PiS rejected the “contamination” thesis and argued vigorously that Poland had never transferred jurisdiction over the organisation of the national judiciary to EU institutions and European courts, who had no authority to evaluate the legality of tribunal appointments.

They accused the EU political establishment of double standards, weaponising “rule-of-law” arguments to help a politically aligned government while ignoring the Tusk administration’s own executive overreach.

PiS also argued that by delegitimising a tribunal which had in the past ruled that the Polish Constitution superseded EU law, the Tusk government was paving the way for controversial social and economic policies to be pushed through without any domestic judicial oversight.

Tusk’s liberal critics

On the other hand, more ideologically supportive liberal critics of the Tusk government’s approach acknowledged the original 2015 irregularities but warned that selective non-recognition of an entire institution, combined with attempts to install a new tribunal without presidential participation, risked creating the same dual legitimacy problem that they accused PiS of having started.

They stressed that lasting repair required broad political consensus and careful adherence to formal procedures so that future majorities did not simply invert the non-recognition tactic. They noted the tension with earlier condemnations of PiS for elevating politically aligned figures or recently active politicians.

While sympathetic to the goal of reforming what they believed was a deeply compromised tribunal, these critics argued that, by employing legally questionable shortcuts and executive force, the Tusk government risked setting dangerous precedents and deepening the very disorder that it was claiming to correct.

Interestingly, the government’s broader “transitional justice” justificatory logic – that ordinary procedures would not adequately address a systemic capture and the priority had to be functional restoration rather than abstract purity – mirrored the arguments PiS itself advanced for its own judicial reforms after 2015.

The right-wing party argued that the post-1989 judiciary remained dominated by a post-communist elite that required deep structural overhaul rather than incremental change.

A high-risk escalation

The latest escalation is likely to entrench and intensify the profound systemic polarisation that characterises the Polish political scene, for a long-time embodied in the KO-PiS duopoly, with the conflict framed in existential terms of either “restoring the rule of law” or “defending the constitutional order”.

This fierce dispute lies at the heart of the Tusk government’s broader political “reckoning” (rozliczenie) agenda involving visibly removing PiS’s influence from key institutions.

For the ruling coalition, this was a central 2023 election campaign message, and being seen to deliver on it is an absolute political necessity to satisfy and mobilise its electoral base. A confrontational approach thus serves to consolidate the government’s support among these core voters, who have grown increasingly impatient and want to see decisive action.

However, the government’s strategy is fraught with political risk. High-stakes tactics risk uniting its right-wing opponents and alienating moderate voters increasingly exhausted by endless, hyper-partisan institutional confrontation, legal brinkmanship and the optics of police deployments around a key state body.

They provide the president and right-wing opposition with a powerful counternarrative of constitutional vandalism ahead of the next parliamentary election.

Escalation is also straining relations within the ruling coalition, especially among more conservative or legalistic coalition partners who believe that a more fundamental constitutional “reset” based on a cross-party settlement is required to break the impasse in the longer term.

The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has proposed a “constitutional reset” to resolve the crisis around the country’s top court. It would involve removing all current judges and choosing new ones in a more consensual process https://t.co/xDwpRUVHxG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 6, 2026

Internationally, although the EU political establishment remains supportive of the Tusk government’s actions, they invite uneasy scrutiny of the stability of Poland’s legal system and have drawn explicit criticism from the US embassy.

The reliance on a “transitional justice” framing that echoes PiS’s earlier justifications for systemic change, combined with the appointment to the tribunal of a recent minister despite prior criticisms of politicised nominations, also undercuts government claims of consistent principle and provides the right with a powerful narrative of hypocrisy.

Legal dualism

Ultimately, this bitter dispute has paved the way for a protracted and deeply destabilising “legal dualism” that could plague the Polish state for years to come, with a tribunal simultaneously legitimate and illegitimate depending on who holds power.

By treating the tribunal as an illegitimate entity when its nominees did not control it, the current government has established a precedent.

Even if it now appears to have secured a clear majority for its own nominees, a future right-wing government and sympathetic president will have every incentive to use the exact same playbook: treating the reconstituted tribunal as a captured instrument of the liberal establishment, and regarding it as no more legitimate than the Tusk government did the PiS-era one.

Consequently, the tribunal’s authority, and legal certainty in Poland more generally, have been further eroded, leaving the country without a widely accepted arbiter to resolve constitutional disputes. There are no immediate prospects for a durable resolution of this conflict.

World.title: Coalition of the Willing military exercises begin in Poland to prepare support for postwar Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Thousands of soldiers from 11 countries began military exercises in Poland today. They are the first organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing, with the aim of preparing for a role in supporting Ukraine following a potential future peace deal with Russia. The manoeuvres, which are being jointly led by France and the UK, are taking place in Nowa Dęba, around 100 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, and will last until 22 November. The development has been condemned by Russia, which says it shows that Western countries are ignoring Moscow’s “legitimate security concerns” and “fueling the spiral of escalation”.​ 🇫🇷🇬🇧 KOALICJA: The MNF-U is training to ensure a solid and lasting peace in Ukraine The Multinational Force-Ukraine (MNF-U), formed from the Coalition of the Willing and under 🇫🇷🇬🇧command, is launching its first major exercise: KOALICJA 📅 November 9–22, 2026 📍In Poland,… pic.twitter.com/Ikcl1uY8N2 — The 🇫🇷 Joint Staff – Military operations (@FrenchForces) November 7, 2026 The plans were first announced in July by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk following a summit of the Coalition of the Willing in Paris. The exercises, taking place on land, in the air, and at sea, are being conducted by the Multinational Force Ukraine (MNF-U), which serves as the military component of the coalition. “This exercise will show that the Multinational Force-Ukraine is a real, capable, readily deployable force that represents a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine’s long-term stability and security,” said Tom Bateman, the British lieutenant-general commanding MNF-U. The British Ministry of Defence says that the exercise, which has been named “Koalicja” (meaning “Coalition” in Polish), “will test Allies’ readiness to support Ukraine and rebuild their Armed Forces once the conflict ends”. France’s armed forces ministry, meanwhile, says that the aim is to ensure that MNF-U is “ready to deploy at the request of the Ukrainian government” in order to help “guarantee a robust and lasting peace in Ukraine”. Around 2,800 troops are being deployed for the manoeuvres, with AFP reporting that this includes 1,100 from France alone. The British defence ministry says it has sent 300 personnel, as well as Typhoon and Voyager aircraft. In addition, just under 2,000 Polish troops will take part, bringing the total to almost 5,000 personnel, reports Polska Zbrojna, a publication linked to the Polish defence ministry. Other countries taking part are Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Turkey. Poland’s defence ministry says the exercises will “demonstrate how quickly participating nations can mobilise and establish forces capable of supporting Ukraine after the end of the war”. However, although Poland is hosting the manoeuvres, the defence ministry reiterated the country’s position that “it would not send its own soldiers to Ukrainian territory” as part of any postwar settlement. Poland has made clear it intends instead to help provide logistical support. Nederland doet met enkele honderden militairen mee aan oefening Koalicja in Polen. De Coalition of the Willing traint er met 11 landen op snelle verplaatsing, commandovoering en bevoorrading ter voorbereiding op mogelijke steun aan Oekraïne na beëindiging van de oorlog. pic.twitter.com/JLE6W91HnZ — Ministerie van Defensie (@Defensie) November 9, 2026 France says that the deployment of forces to Ukraine would include sending instructors to help the country rebuild and strengthen its armed forces, while air missions would enable civlian aircraft to resume flying in Ukrainian airspace. At sea, MNF-U forces could help clear mines from shipping routes in the Black Sea. The maritime component of the current exercises is being led by Turkey through a simulated operational exercise, without deploying troops to Poland itself. France, the UK and Poland have emphasised, however, that the MNF-U forces would only be deployed once fighting in Ukraine has ceased and would not carry out peacekeeping or ceasefire-monitoring duties. Poland will host military exercises later this year with France and the UK to prepare for providing future security guarantees to Ukraine, says PM @donaldtusk. He also declared Poland's willingness to permanently host more troops from its European allies https://t.co/couian4FrP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 On Saturday, the spokeswoman for Russia’s foreign ministry, Maria Zakharova, condemned the exercises, saying that they make “absolutely clear that the West remains unwilling to take Russia’s legitimate security concerns into account and continues to fuel the spiral of escalation”. She described the deployment of any foreign armed forces to Ukraine as “absolutely unacceptable” and said they would “create additional threats to Russia’s security”. “Any military units in Ukraine will be regarded by the Russian armed forces as legitimate targets, with all the risks and consequences that entails,” warned Zakharova. Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova’s answer to a media question in connection with the first military exercises of the so-called Multinational Force – Ukraine under the Coalition of the Willinghttps://t.co/GiouEAmT6J — Jeff Franzius (@jk55044) November 9, 2026 The exercises come as Ukraine and Russia meet the United States and others for peace talks in Abu Dhabi this week. Ukraine has repeatedly insisted that European security guarantees would be necessary for any peace agreement. British defence secretary Wes Streeting suggested the exercises forecast precisely such a scenario: “This isn’t a hypothetical plan, it’s a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops.” Zakharova, however, says that the exercises are “yet another confirmation that the Europeans have no place at the negotiating table”. World.title: Polish government ministers suggest tighter gun controls after deadly terrorist shooting
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. In the wake of Saturday’s deadly terrorist shooting in Kraków, a deputy defence minister has called for debate on limiting the number and types of weapons people can own. Meanwhile, a deputy interior minister says the tragedy provides an “incentive” to revisit proposals to better register certain guns. Poland has among the lowest levels of gun ownership in Europe, though the number of firearms licences being issued has risen in recent years and some politicians have called for expanded access to guns. Saturday’s attack was carried out by a man who legally owned firearms. On Saturday, 24-year-old Michał Oksiński drove through the historic city centre of Kraków, which was packed with tourists and locals, firing at random from his car. He killed six people and injured over a dozen more. Later in the day, the bodies of the perpetrator’s parents and sister were found in his home, where they had been shot dead. Oksiński’s rampage was brought to an end in a shootout with two police officers, which left all three with serious injuries. On Monday morning, the police announced that Oksiński had died in hospital. One of the police officers remains in what is described as “serious but stable” condition. The man who carried out Saturday’s deadly terrorist attack in the Polish city of Kraków has died in hospital from the injuries he sustained during a shootout with police. One of the two officers who stopped him remains in serious but stable condition https://t.co/rT1YBXhkp7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 9, 2026 The incident has caused shock in Poland, a country that has never previously experienced this type of mass public shooting. Speaking to Polsat News on Sunday, deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said that the tragedy “is the best illustration that it makes no sense to talk about expanding access to firearms”. She added that “it’s already relatively easy” to obtain a gun licence, which can be granted to anyone aged 21 or over who has passed the relevant tests and declared that the firearm is for sporting purposes. Both Oksiński and his father had such licences and legally owned 11 firearms. “I would like to start a discussion about whether access to such a large number of weapons should actually be so easy,” said Sobkowiak-Czarnecka. “This is also a question of whether someone who uses weapons for sporting purposes should have so many different types of weapons stored at home.” Also speaking to Polsat on Sunday, Czesław Mroczek, a deputy interior minister, said that “weapons are certainly a challenge for us”. He noted that “in Poland we have had many cases of killings using black powder weapons, for which there is not even a register, let alone a permit procedure”. Such weapons use traditional black powder rather than modern smokeless powder and include firearms manufactured before 1885 and their modern replicas. According to a recent study by researchers from the Jagiellonian University in Kraków, they make up a considerable proportion of firearm-related fatalities in the country. While noting that the issue is not directly related to the Kraków attacks, Mroczek said that plans to include these weapons in a register had already been drawn up and “this event [in Kraków] is an incentive for us to reexamine the matter”. 🇵🇱 Poland's interior ministry says black-powder guns, currently exempt from registration, will be entered into the register. The Krakow attack is described as an impulse to review the whole permit system.https://t.co/Nh7dr46MJ7 — Олег Рощин (@oleg_roshchin) November 9, 2026 On Monday morning, the spokesman for the National Prosecutor’s Office, Przemysław Nowak, held a press conference at which he provided further details on their findings so far. He revealed that Oksiński had been found with two AR-15 rifles and two handguns on his person and in his car, as well as around 500 rounds of ammunition. He had earlier fired “several dozen, possibly several hundred, shots”. A further seven guns had been found at Oksiński’s home. The total of 11 firearms matched the number of weapons there were permits for, noted Nowak, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. “The entire matter related to the weapons and the firearms permits will be reviewed,” added the spokesman. “We know that, since March of this year, he [Oksiński] has held firearms permits for one rifle and one pistol.” Prosecutors have launched a terror investigation into Saturday’s shooting in Kraków, which left six dead. Three more bodies were later found in the suspect's home. Further details have also emerged about the heroic actions of police and medical personnel https://t.co/icBJWLRK7c — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 8, 2026 Although gun ownership in Poland is relatively low, it has been rising steadily in recent years, particularly since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with the total number of registered firearms owned by Poles surpassing 1 million, up from around 380,000 in 2014. Last year, a record 50,709 new gun licences were issued in the country in 2025, up 10.6% compared to a year earlier. Under Polish law, civilians can apply for licences for sporting, hunting, collecting and personal protection purposes. To obtain one, applicants must undergo medical examinations, pass a test, and join a relevant association, such as the Polish Sports Shooting Association, the Polish Hunting Association, or a collectors’ group. Licences for sports and collection purposes are the most popular types of permits, together making up 76% of last year’s permits. But the number of licences issued for “personal protection” has grown from just 81 in 2021 to 7,254 last year. A record 50,709 gun licences were issued in Poland last year and the total number of registered firearms has now surpassed 1 million. Gun ownership in Poland has risen particularly rapidly since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 https://t.co/axt2YS044Z — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 11, 2026 Access to firearms widened in 2023 under the former government, when parliament passed a law removing “unnecessary administrative and legal barriers.” That allowed members of uniformed services to apply for personal protection permits, a change lawmakers said was intended to “strengthen Poland’s defence potential”. However, some politicians, especially on the right, have pushed for ownership rules to be further loosened. In September, speaking at the opening of a shooting range, President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, called for “public discussion about responsible access to weapons”. “Even in the European Union, Poland remains at the bottom of the list in terms of access to firearms,” he said, quoted by Polsat. “Only about 1% of Polish citizens have access to weapons and are skilled at using them. Fortunately, I’m in that 1%.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Prague to Mark 37 Years Since Velvet Revolution With 160 Events
World.content:
Prague will mark the 37th anniversary of the Velvet Revolution on November 17 with more than 160 events taking place along Národní Street as part of this year’s Korzo Národní celebrations.

Organised by the association Díky, že můžem, the annual event will bring together concerts, theatre performances, public discussions, exhibitions and activities exploring democracy and freedom.



This year’s programme carries the motto “Let’s Not Stand on the Sidelines. Democracy Relies on Each of Us.” The organisers say the message reflects growing concerns about declining trust in society and the challenges facing democratic institutions.

One of the central moments of the celebrations will take place at 17:11, when the traditional song Modlitba pro Martu (A Prayer for Marta) will be performed from the balcony of the Metro Palace.

This year, the performance will form the finale of a theatrical production titled DŮM VŠECH (House for All), which begins at 17:00. Visitors unable to gather directly beneath the balcony will be able to watch the performance on large screens along Národní Street or through a live broadcast.

The day’s programme will begin earlier, with the popular Velvet Brunch, a charity event held directly on the street between 10:00 and 13:00. At 13:00, members of the Czech Radio Children’s Choir will perform the national anthem.

Other events include live podcasts, musical performances and discussions on social issues. Among the scheduled speakers and performers are Markéta Foukalová, Martin Brunner, Václav Kopta and Vietnamese community representative Quang Luong.

Havel, the Vietnamese community and Věra Čáslavská

Several parts of this year’s celebrations will focus on important anniversaries.

The programme will commemorate the 90th anniversary of the birth of Václav Havel, the playwright and former Czech president.

His legacy will be explored through the traditional Václav Havel’s Living Room, titled “For Vašek”, at Platýz Palace. Actors including Vojtěch Vondráček and Taťjana Medvecká will read texts dedicated to Havel.

Another anniversary concerns the Vietnamese community, which marks 70 years in the Czech Republic. The programme will include Lost in Translation, a discussion bringing together three generations of Vietnamese residents to examine questions of identity, belonging and life between cultures.

The celebrations will also remember gymnast Věra Čáslavská, ten years after her death. Her life and the relationship between sport and politics will be examined through a special lecture aboard the Educational Tram and a live recording of the Outsider podcast.

World.title: FlixBus Launches Direct Route Between Prague Florenc and Airport
World.content:
FlixBus will introduce a direct bus connection between Prague’s Florenc Central Bus Station and Václav Havel Airport on November 12.

The new service will operate 13 times a day in each direction, with the journey taking approximately 30 minutes.

The first bus will leave Florenc at 3:40 a.m., while the last departure is scheduled for 10:40 p.m. From the airport, services will run between 4:15 a.m. and 11:15 p.m.



Ticket prices will depend on demand and departure times. According to the FlixBus website, the usual fare is around CZK 79, including the booking fee. The cheapest tickets start at CZK 69, while some departures cost up to CZK 89.

The company expects the route to attract business travellers in particular. Passengers will have access to Wi-Fi and power outlets on board.

BusAir joins the competition

FlixBus is not the only company expanding its airport connections. A separate private service, operating under the name BusAir, began running between Prague’s city centre and the airport in late October.

Operated by UBUS, the service offers eight departures a day in each direction, with buses running every two hours. A ticket costs CZK 125 and remains valid for 24 hours.

Due to renovation work on the ceiling at Prague Main Railway Station and traffic restrictions on the city’s main arterial road, BusAir currently departs from Opletalova Street, close to the station. On the way to the airport, it also stops at Hradčanská metro station on Line A.

Both new services are entering a market where the main competitor is the Airport Express, operated by Prague Public Transit Company (DPP).

The Airport Express runs more frequently than the private alternatives, with departures every 20 to 30 minutes during the day and hourly services overnight. It is also currently the only direct bus connection between the city centre and airport operating throughout the night.

Standard Prague public transport tickets are not valid on the service. A single adult ticket costs CZK 200, although passengers can get a lower fare when purchasing it together with a train ticket.

World.title: Říčany Named Czech Republic’s Best Place to Live for Ninth Year
World.content:
Říčany has been named the best municipality in the Czech Republic for quality of life for the ninth consecutive year, retaining its position at the top of a nationwide ranking ahead of Prague.

The Central Bohemian town, located southeast of the capital, again led the Quality of Life Index compiled by the Obce v datech project. The ranking assesses 206 Czech municipalities with extended administrative powers.

At the other end of the table, Orlová in the Karviná District ranked last, while nearby Karviná finished second from bottom.



The geographical divide remains clear: the 14 highest-ranked municipalities are all located within 50 kilometres of Prague or Brno, while many of those at the bottom are found in former industrial and border regions, particularly in the Moravian-Silesian and Ústí nad Labem regions.

There have nevertheless been signs of improvement in parts of the Moravian-Silesian Region. Over the past eight years, Odry, Kopřivnice and Hlučín have each climbed by around 40 places in the ranking.

The picture is less positive in the Ústí nad Labem Region, where only six of the region’s 16 assessed municipalities have improved their position since 2018. Roudnice nad Labem was the only municipality in the region to record a substantial rise.

Pohořelice Makes the Biggest Leap

Pohořelice, in the Brno-Country District, has recorded one of the most striking improvements since the index was introduced in 2018. The town has climbed from 117th place to fifth this year.

Nepomuk, in the Plzeň Region, has made an equally large jump of 112 places and now ranks 24th. Kuřim has moved up 65 positions to 15th, while Mnichovo Hradiště has risen 46 places to 18th.

According to Jan Havránek of AQE Advisors, which developed the project, municipalities do not need to perform at the top in every category to improve their overall ranking.

For around half of the 30 municipalities that have improved the most, the stronger results were linked to a younger population, population growth and, in many cases, longer life expectancy.

The Quality of Life Index evaluates municipalities across several broad areas, including health and the environment, material security and education, and relationships and public services.

World.title: ROCK THE OPERA Returns to Prague for 25th Anniversary Concert
World.content:
Twenty-five years after conductor Friedemann Riehle helped pioneer the symphonic rock concert format in Prague, he is returning to the Czech capital for a special anniversary performance.

ROCK THE OPERA will take place on Sunday, 13 December 2026, at Smetana Hall in Prague’s Municipal House.

The concert will bring together the Prague Philharmonic Orchestra, rock musicians and vocalists for an evening dedicated to some of the biggest songs in rock history.



The anniversary also marks a full-circle moment for Riehle. On 29 October 2001, he promoted and conducted one of the first symphonic rock shows in Prague, combining a symphony orchestra with rock drummers and vocalists to give legendary songs a new sound.

What began as an experiment has developed into a long-running international project. Over the past 25 years, Riehle has conducted more than 100 symphonic rock concerts across Europe, performing everywhere from Iceland to Istanbul and appearing at venues including the Vienna State Opera, Berlin Philharmonie and Athens’ Odeon of Herodes Atticus.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by RONNIE GRACE | ROCK SINGER ⚡️ (@ronniegrace)

For the Prague anniversary concert, Riehle will be joined by Ronnie Romero, one of the best-known voices in contemporary rock. Romero has performed with several internationally recognised rock musicians and bands and will bring his distinctive vocals to the symphonic arrangements.

The programme will feature music associated with some of rock’s biggest names, including Pink Floyd, Queen, AC/DC, Led Zeppelin and U2.

Alongside Romero, the concert will feature vocalists Lucie Koutniková and Sabina Olijve, guitarist Jiří Rambousek and drummer František Hönig. The Prague Philharmonic Orchestra will perform under the direction of Friedemann Riehle.

Tickets are available via Ticketportal.

World.title: St. Martin’s Day 2026 in Prague: Where to Enjoy Traditional Goose
World.content:
St. Martin’s Day, which Czechs celebrate on November 11, is a holiday of good food and drink. Autumn slowly alternates with winter, and it begins to snow.

In the past, the economic year was ending at this time, and the landowners were preparing a feast for their people as a form of thanks, when they were also paid out their wages.

St. Martin’s Day in restaurants

You can be sure that almost every restaurant around mid-November will be offering its visitors a special St. Martin’s Day menu. What does it feature?

According to a tradition that has lasted for several centuries, geese were always roasted in the autumn, fresh cabbage was processed, and wine or beer was drunk. And today’s restaurants and pubs remain faithful to these basic ingredients.

Typically, you will be served liver pâté as an appetizer, followed by a strong broth with liver dumplings and noodles, which the chefs usually leave to simmer overnight, with the main course being roast goose with red or white cabbage and dumplings.

Where to taste St. Martin’s menu?

Restaurant Salabka (November 6 – 14): Choose from 3 to 5 courses featuring seasonal autumn ingredients and contemporary gastronomy. Available from November 6, alongside the regular autumn tasting menu.

More info here.

Pilsner Urquell Experience: until November 15, here you can find a St. Martin’s Menu for 1,095 Kč including goose liver pâté with cranberries, roast goose leg with red cabbage and Carlsbad dumplings, followed by traditional Czech potato cones with poppy seeds.

More info here.

GARE Restaurants: Celebrate St. Martin’s Day at three GARE Restaurants: La Gare, Les Moules and Pivovar U Supa, each offering its own take on the Czech goose-feast tradition. Highlights include goose pâté, traditional goose kaldoun and confit goose leg with poppy-seed potato dumplings, plums and fermented cabbage.

La Gare serves its festive menu during lunch from November 9–13. Les Moules offers its specialties from November 7 while stocks last, while Pivovar U Supa continues its goose feast until November 15.

La Gare | Les Moules | Pivovar U Supa

Restaurant Masaryčka: Here the highlight is a tender goose leg confit with caraway, served with braised red cabbage, plums and assorted dumplings (499 CZK). Alternatively, guests can enjoy homemade potato lokše filled with pulled goose meat, onion cabbage and apples (359 CZK). To finish on a sweet note, the menu offers apple strudel with vanilla sauce, walnuts, honey and cinnamon crumble (149 CZK).

World.title: All Aboard the Pajama Express: Prague Metro Supports Hospitalised Kids
World.content:
The Prague Metro will host a special pajama-themed journey on Friday, November 13, as part of the Czech Republic’s annual Pajama Day, an initiative supporting families of children undergoing long-term hospital treatment.

For the first time, a dedicated carriage will be reserved for passengers travelling in their pajamas. The special train, known as the Pajama Express, will operate on Metro Line A, with participants invited to board its first carriage at any station along the route.



The journey will begin at Depo Hostivař at 9:13 a.m. and end at Nemocnice Motol, the metro station serving Motol University Hospital. Hospital representatives will welcome participants upon arrival.

The initiative aims to highlight the difficulties faced by children who spend extended periods in hospital, often separated from their usual surroundings, and the importance of having family members close by during treatment.

Several public figures and bloggers are expected to join the journey. Among them will be actress Veronika Arichteva, patron of the project.

Now in its third year, Pajama Day has attracted around 400 registered participants. Schools, businesses, public institutions, theatres, hospitals and individuals across the country have signed up for this year’s edition.

The event is organised by the Ronald McDonald House in the Czech Republic (Dům Ronalda McDonalda Česko), which provides free accommodation for families of seriously ill children at Motol Hospital.

The facility allows parents to stay close to their children throughout lengthy hospital stays, reducing the burden of travelling between the hospital and home.

Passengers wishing to take part in the Prague event do not need to register separately. They simply need to wear their pajamas and board the first carriage of the special train at any station along Line A.

World.title: Three Days of Chocolate and Sweet Treats Await in Prague
World.content:
Chocolate lovers in Prague will have a sweet reason to head to Novo Plaza this weekend as ČokoFest arrives at the shopping centre for the first time.

The three-day chocolate festival will take place from Friday, November 13, to Sunday, November 15, offering visitors free entry and a programme filled with tastings, handmade sweets and activities for children.



Visitors can expect a selection of handmade chocolates, pralines, cakes and other sweet specialties, with plenty of opportunities to sample different products throughout the weekend.

Families with children will also find a range of activities, including chocolate workshops designed for young visitors. Meanwhile, Thermomix will host live demonstrations and chocolate tastings during the event.

ČokoFest will also offer the chance to win several prizes. One of the main giveaways is a weekend drive in a Chery Tiggo 7, provided by Mach Motors. Visitors can also enter to win a ČokoBox and other sweet prizes.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ČokoFest / Čokoládový Festival (@cokofestcz)

With Christmas just around the corner, the festival could also be a good place to find original gifts for chocolate lovers.

ČokoFest takes place at Novo Plaza Shopping Centre in Prague 4, and admission is free throughout all three days.

World.title: Micro Praha Festival Returns With 93 Watch Brands From 27 Countries
World.content:
The fourth edition of the international watch festival will take place at Fantova budova on November 28–29. Admission is free with online registration.

The Micro Praha Festival will return to Prague on November 28–29, bringing together 93 independent watch brands from 27 countries.



The fourth edition of the event will take place at Fantův sál inside the historic Fantova budova, near Prague’s Main Railway Station. Visitors will be able to discover new collections, try on watches and meet the people behind the brands.

Organisers say this year’s edition will be the largest so far, with microbrands and established independent watchmakers exhibiting alongside each other for the first time.

Brands from countries including Switzerland, Germany, the United States, Canada, France, the Netherlands, Japan, Taiwan and the Czech Republic will take part. Several exhibitors will be appearing in Prague and Central Europe for the first time.

Among the newcomers are New York-based Brew, known for watches inspired by coffee culture; MING, which focuses on experimental designs and engineering; Atelier Wen, specialising in watches with hand-crafted guilloché dials; and Lorier, a brand recognised for its vintage-inspired designs.

Chrono24 Joins as Main Festival Sponsor

The 2026 edition will also see Chrono24, the international online marketplace for luxury watches, join the festival as its primary sponsor and partner.

Representatives from the company will be present throughout the weekend to discuss the watch market, industry trends and the platform’s latest features. KB Bank is also listed among this year’s primary sponsors.

The festival was founded in 2023 by Bhanu Chopra and Ondrej Vislocký, two watch enthusiasts who wanted to create a platform for smaller independent brands in Central Europe.

Chopra is a watch journalist who previously served as editor-in-chief of Revolution USA, while Vislocký is a Prague-based photographer whose work has appeared in international watch publications and brand catalogues.

The two also co-own INFINTY Watches, a specialist retailer of microbrand and independent watches in central Prague.

World.title: Son of former Orbán-era state secretary accused of leading criminal organisation in tax fraud case
World.content:
Prosecutors have requested the pre-trial detention of a man suspected of leading a criminal organisation operating in the security and guarding sector, in a tax fraud investigation involving more than HUF 9 billion (approximately EUR 24.6 million) in alleged damage to Hungary’s central budget. The National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) confirmed that the suspect is the son of a former state secretary.

According to a statement from the Budapest Chief Prosecutor’s Office, the man ran a network of security companies and allegedly used the services of another criminal organisation operating a network of fictitious companies issuing fraudulent invoices. Together with his alleged accomplices, he is suspected of causing particularly significant financial damage to the state.

Investigators believe that between July 2019 and March 2023, the organisation registered employees who were actually working for the security companies as employees of fictitious companies belonging to the invoice-fraud network. The arrangement allegedly helped the businesses avoid paying taxes and other public charges.

NAV investigators questioned the man as a suspect on suspicion of budgetary fraud causing particularly significant financial damage, committed as part of a criminal organisation and as an instigator, as well as other offences.

Prosecutors seek pre-trial detention

The Budapest Chief Prosecutor’s Office requested the suspect’s pre-trial detention, arguing that his presence during the proceedings could only be guaranteed through the strictest coercive measure. Prosecutors also cited a realistic risk that he could obstruct the investigation or commit further offences.

A judge was expected to decide on the request on Thursday. The request itself does not mean that the suspect has been convicted or that pre-trial detention has already been ordered.

58 suspects in wider invoice-fraud investigation

The case forms part of a much larger investigation into the alleged invoice-fraud network. NAV carried out searches at nearly 40 locations on Tuesday, taking 23 people into custody and questioning them as suspects. This brought the total number of suspects in the investigation to 58.

According to the tax authority, the alleged perpetrators caused more than HUF 9 billion in damage to the central budget. Authorities had previously secured assets worth approximately HUF 4 billion, with a further HUF 1.2 billion secured during Tuesday’s operation.

NAV also confirmed that the head of the security-sector organisation is the son of a former state secretary.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar wrote on Facebook on Tuesday that NAV’s MERKUR tactical unit had detained the son of a former state secretary under former Interior Minister Sándor Pintér. Magyar also said that investigators had searched a former company belonging to Pintér.

World.title: PM Magyar vows to protect Hungary’s borders during speech in Germany on fall of Berlin wall
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has vowed to protect the country’s borders for as long as he leads the government, while outlining his position on migration during a speech in Berlin marking the 37th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall.

Speaking in the German capital, Magyar recalled the events of 1989 and quoted former German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who said that Hungarians had knocked out the first brick of the Berlin Wall. However, his address also focused on present-day European politics, with criticism of the continent’s political leadership and a call for a more responsive approach to citizens’ concerns.

Magyar criticises Europe’s political elite

Magyar argued that Europe’s political establishment had spent too long producing reports and dealing with bureaucracy instead of making necessary decisions, leaving ordinary people feeling abandoned.

He accused European politicians of speaking to citizens from an “ivory tower”, while warning that political extremes built on fear and hatred were gaining strength, partly with outside assistance. He said politicians should instead listen to people whose voices had previously gone unheard.

Photo: MTI

The Hungarian prime minister also stressed that migration could not be avoided in discussions about Europe. He argued that the debate over illegal migration had brought about a fundamental change in European thinking over the past decade, with positions Hungary had consistently represented now reflected in those of most EU member states.

“From the beginning, Hungary has maintained that member states have the right to determine their own migration policies. However, this must not mean that some countries pass the negative consequences of their decisions on to others,” he said.

“As long as I lead the Hungarian government, we will protect the external borders of my country and Europe,” Magyar added.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Focus on everyday issues and European sovereignty

Beyond migration, Magyar spoke about his experiences travelling around Hungary and meeting people in their everyday lives. He said politics should focus less on ideology and more on solving practical problems.

Transport, healthcare and education might not be the most exciting subjects, he acknowledged, but they are among the issues that matter most to citizens. He said he and his Tisza Party government were committed to addressing them.

Magyar also warned against the influence of lobbying interests and foreign states, arguing that Europe cannot be sovereign if it is unable to protect or provide for itself. He said European unity should be based on respect for national characteristics and listening to ordinary citizens.

Photo: MTI

Hungarian ministers accompany Magyar to Berlin

The prime minister travelled to Germany accompanied by Foreign Minister Anita Orbán, Economy and Energy Minister István Kapitány, Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi and Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai. Magyar also met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Tuesday.

The Hungarian prime minister last visited Berlin in June, when he and Merz discussed the war in Ukraine and European economic cooperation. The visit follows a joint government meeting in the Czech Republic last week with Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš. Austrian officials also held a joint meeting with the Hungarian government in May.

World.title: One of the most beautiful waterfalls in Hungary ranks among the world’s top 20 – photos
World.content:
One of Miskolc’s best-known attractions, the Szinva Waterfall in Lillafüred, has received further international recognition, featuring as the world’s 17th most beautiful waterfall in Worldworthy’s 2026 ranking. This recognition further strengthens the international reputation of Miskolc-Lillafüred as a tourist destination. Alongside the natural treasures of the Bükk Mountains, the city’s historic city centre, the spas of Miskolctapolca, the Avas Wine District and the ever-expanding range of culinary delights all contribute to making Miskolc a rewarding destination for a stay of several days.

The Szinva Waterfall in Lillafüred has been included in this year’s edition of The Worldworthy 100, which showcases the world’s best-rated waterfalls. According to the organisation, the ranking is compiled using independent criteria such as online reviews, press coverage and travelogues; it is not possible to apply for inclusion on the list or to pay to be included.

The Iguaçu Falls in Brazil topped Worldworthy’s 2026 ranking, with Mexico’s Cascada El Chiflón taking second place and the world-famous Victoria Falls in Zimbabwe coming third. The Szinva Falls in Lillafüred came 17th in this prestigious international ranking, representing Hungary as the only Hungarian site on the TOP 100 list, which features 42 countries.

The Miskolc attraction even outperformed such world-famous waterfalls as the Kuang Si Falls in Laos (18th place), the Rhine Falls in Switzerland (38th place), Yosemite Falls in the United States (40th place) and Seljalandsfoss in Iceland (50th place).

The unique spectacle of the Lillafüred waterfall is complemented by the forest setting of the Bükk Mountains. Hungary’s highest waterfall is situated next to the hanging gardens of the Palotaszálló, just a few steps from Lake Hámori. Thanks to the area’s romantic atmosphere, the historic hotel, the forest narrow-gauge railway and the walking trails, as well as the caves with their spectacular chambers, Lillafüred offers enough to keep visitors occupied for several days in its own right.

Visitors can also combine their nature walks with a visit to the thermal baths in Miskolctapolca, another popular holiday resort in the Miskolc area. The Cave Baths, built within natural cave passages, and the Ellipsum Adventure Baths offer a variety of bathing experiences all year round, making the town an attractive destination not only for excursions and active pursuits but also for those seeking relaxation; it can be an appealing destination for school holidays or even a week-long summer break.

If you missed it – Dining Guide Top100: Hungary’s best pizzeria has been named – and it’s not in Budapest

Miskolc took centre stage on the international stage in 2026

In 2026, Miskolc’s Edible Forest – Forest Gastro Express programme won the award for the world’s best sustainable tourism initiative at the Green Destinations international competition. This unique experience combines the natural treasures of the Bükk Mountains with local gastronomy. Under expert guidance, participants can learn about the forest’s edible plants and then sample dishes made from local ingredients. The programme was also included in the 2026 Green List, an international selection by the British travel magazine Wanderlust.

In Time Out magazine’s 2026 international selection, Lillafüred was ranked as the 19th most beautiful place in the world. The Palotaszálló, Lake Hámori, the waterfall and the Bükk forest complex form a natural and built environment that stands out even by international standards.

Similarly, according to Time Out’s 2026 guide, Miskolc is Europe’s 4th best value-for-money destination worth discovering. This ranking draws attention to the town’s affordable yet rich range of tourist attractions. Visitors can enjoy a wide variety of activities and experiences, whilst the city is becoming an attractive alternative for an increasing number of international travellers.

The success of the Miskolc Advent Tram has also extended far beyond the country’s borders. This special festive tram was voted Europe’s most beautiful Advent tram for the ninth time running in 2026 in an international public poll. The tram is one of Miskolc’s best-known attractions during the Advent season, drawing many visitors to the city every year.

Miskolc has become one of the key regional centres for gastronomic tourism in Hungary, and its range of restaurants has elevated it to the status of one of the country’s most significant gastronomic destinations. Many of the city’s restaurants feature in the recommendations of the international Michelin Guide and the Hungarian Street Kitchen guide, meaning that Miskolc now offers travellers a remarkable gastronomic experience on a par with the capital and Lake Balaton.

The character of the local dining scene is defined by creative chefs, seasonal and locally sourced ingredients, and dishes drawing on the flavours of the Bükk Mountains. The unique atmosphere of the Avasi Wine Quarter adds further experiences to the city’s gastronomic offering.

The Szinva Waterfall’s inclusion on the world list presents a further opportunity to further strengthen Miskolc’s position on the international tourism map. International recognition is showcasing Miskolc’s attractions to an ever-wider audience.

World.title: EU customs duty triggers shift in online orders from Asian webshops
World.content:
One-third of Hungarian consumers have scaled back the frequency of their purchases from Asian webshops since the introduction of a European Union customs duty on low-value parcels on July 1, a survey commissioned by delivery company DODO shows.

The representative survey, conducted by Ipsos, shows 29pc of Hungarian consumers have stopped using Asian webshops since the rollout of the EUR 3 customs duty levied on each product category for items valued up to EUR 150 from sources outside of the EU.

Around 5pc of survey respondents still buy as frequently from Asian webshops, but take care to limit their product categories per package.

About 29pc now buy products from Hungarian webshops that they earlier ordered from Asia, while a further 21pc now choose webshops based in other EU member states.

From November 1, the EU has slapped an additional EUR 2 handling fee per item on non-EU packages on top of the EUR 3 customs duty.

If you missed it: Shein and Temu shoppers hit by new EU fee as cheap orders now cost more

How do the new EU customs charges affect Asian webshops?

The new rules apply to low-value goods shipped directly to EU consumers from countries outside the bloc, including purchases from popular Asian online marketplaces such as Temu and Shein. Crucially, the EUR 3 customs duty is calculated according to product categories rather than the total number of products in a parcel.

For example, a package containing several identical T-shirts attracts a EUR 3 duty, while an order containing T-shirts, shoes and electronic accessories could incur EUR 9 in customs charges if the goods fall under three different tariff classifications. The additional EUR 2 handling fee, introduced on 1 November, further increases the costs associated with importing low-value goods.

Why is the EU tightening rules on low-cost imports?

The European Union introduced the measures to address the rapid growth of low-value e-commerce imports and create fairer competition between European retailers and sellers based outside the bloc.

According to the European Commission, the previous customs exemption gave non-EU businesses a competitive advantage and made it more difficult to tackle undervalued shipments and products that fail to meet EU safety standards.

The changes are part of a broader reform of the EU customs system, aimed at improving oversight of cross-border online shopping. For Hungarian consumers, the DODO survey suggests that the new charges are already influencing purchasing decisions, with domestic and EU-based webshops gaining attention as alternatives to Asian platforms.
