World.title: Rein Sikk: Culture is politics
World.content:
Cultural workers should not be afraid to show members of the Riigikogu some love — but they should also be ready to bite when necessary, Rein Sikk advises in his daily commentary on Vikerraadio.

I'm about to commit a crime against Estonia, but there's no other way. I'm about to criticize the salt of our earth, the pillars of our culture — the people who run our cultural and community centers. But there really is no other way.

My offense is intended to prevent a greater crime. Namely, the cultural catastrophe that the organizers of the cultural congress, scheduled for late November, have been warning about. They claim that over the past 28 years, the Ministry of Culture's share of the state budget has shrunk threefold.

And it continues to shrink... So what can be done to stop cultural funding from declining? To prevent us from having three times less culture? Presumably, we need to demand answers from those making the cuts — in other words, members of the Riigikogu.

The opportunity to ask questions is just around the corner. In a little over 100 days, on March 7, Estonia will hold its parliamentary elections. Broadly speaking, the country's fate for the next four years will be decided. That includes the fate of culture and cultural centers. The salaries of cultural workers. And whether theaters will receive funding to take their productions to rural areas.

I was naive, to put it mildly, and downright stupid, to put it bluntly, to think that with elections approaching, cultural centers would be packed with election debates. Not a chance! It turns out that cultural workers are afraid of politics.

With the help of the Estonian Association of Community Centers, I sent more than 70 letters to community centers across the country, asking whether they planned to organize election debates ahead of the vote. Only a tenth of the centers responded. Just two believed that hosting pre-election debates was part of a cultural center's duty and role.

One response read: "Here at our center in Pärnu-Jaagupi, we don't have to invite anyone ourselves. Before every election, political parties approach us about meeting with local residents. We host both debates and simple meet-and-greet events."

Another encouraging and commendable response came from Rapla County: "For years, I've organized events at my Varbola community center ahead of both parliamentary and local government elections. These include debates as well as separate meetings with individual political parties. Representatives of all parties have always been happy to attend ahead of parliamentary elections. The meetings are interesting."

Lüganuse in Ida-Viru County said it was not ruling out the possibility of a debate: "If there is interest and demand within the community, we are ready to help."

Most respondents said that if someone wanted to organize a debate, they were welcome to do so. But the centers themselves would not organize one. Cultural workers, they argued, should remain apolitical.

I have my doubts, and I disagree. In fact, culture is politics. Cultural policy is the most important kind of politics there is. Cultural policy is a matter of life and death for nations, including the Estonian nation. It is a question of language and identity. This applies to village cultural centers and village libraries alike.

Let me offer a few positive examples from my home area of Kadrina. For years, local high school students have organized debates between candidates ahead of both local and parliamentary elections. They have always been praised for the substance of these events. For 25 years, outspoken sauna-goers at the Kadrina sauna have been demanding answers from parliamentary hopefuls and government ministers alike. These meetings have become legendary and people speak so frankly that some politicians are downright afraid to attend.

I have moderated and organized debates on numerous occasions. Now I am urging every community center and public library in Estonia to organize debates of their own.

Debates aren't painful; they're wonderful. Debates aren't tedious; they're exciting. They are an opportunity and a duty for citizens to have their say in Estonia's affairs. To ask questions and make demands, to bargain for the best possible deal in exchange for their vote. To demand concrete answers to concrete promises. And to remember those answers. And when things go wrong, to demand that those elected explain themselves directly. It's as simple as that.

Besides, an election debate is a far more substantive event than having some political party pitch a tent outside your community center and lure people inside. After all, an individual voter entering a party's tent finds themselves surrounded by party members.

But in a community center or library, the people are in charge. That's precisely why these institutions were created in the first place. To bring people together to discuss matters that concern them. There will be plenty of time for song and dance afterward.

World.title: Shoppers in Estonia increasingly split purchases among multiple stores
World.content:
Grocery stores are built primarily in areas with sufficient population and purchasing power, which is why major retail chains are concentrated mainly in Tallinn, Tartu and Pärnu, Rimi Eesti CEO Kristel Mets says.

Unlike many Western European countries, Estonia's grocery retail sector is highly dominated by chain stores, while independent neighborhood shops and small corner stores are relatively rare, Mets noted in a Postimees interview.

Because competing grocery chains are often located close to one another, consumer brand loyalty is low and shoppers typically alternate among three to four different stores.

More than half of grocery store revenue now comes from products sold at promotional prices. Retail sales volumes are not growing this year, and any increase in turnover is driven solely by inflation and higher value-added tax.

Grossi and Meie chains are also expanding their presence in the grocery market by opening new and significantly larger stores in small towns and residential neighborhoods.

A Grossi grocery store in Lasnamäe. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

"Grossi has decided, essentially, that it will no longer build those smaller stores, but instead stores with 1,600 square meters of retail space. A 1,600-square-meter store is a very large supermarket, almost hypermarket-sized by Estonian standards," Mets said.

Online grocery shopping and home delivery volumes are growing rapidly, and the service is increasingly used to order groceries remotely for elderly parents or grandparents.

To combat theft, Rimi has launched a pilot project installing security gates at self-checkout exits that open only when customers scan their receipts.

Full story in Postimees.

World.title: Researcher: A third of Estonians have experienced things they cannot explain
World.content:
Although Estonia is considered one of the most secular countries in the world today, stories of ghosts, spirits and unexplained experiences have not disappeared.

How common are experiences considered supernatural among Estonians today?

This spring, a study commissioned by the Ministry of the Interior on Estonians' religious identity was completed. Among other things, respondents were asked whether they had ever had any supernatural or unexplained experiences. As a folklorist, I wasn't surprised that about a third of Estonians, or 34 percent, said they had. Of course, the report didn't go into much detail about what these experiences involved, such as prophetic dreams or unexpected coincidences surrounding the death of a loved one.

Death is an extraordinary event in itself and it gives rise to these kinds of stories and observations. But there are also quite a few cases in which a folklorist would recognize classic ghostly encounters: certain sounds, voices or footsteps.

It's not so much a question of belief as of experience — how people interpret these strange, striking experiences. How they give them meaning or, conversely, how they forget about them or set them aside so they won't be disturbed by them. The human mind is often surprising and these stories arise spontaneously. The question is whether a culture provides interpretive frameworks that can give them meaning.

I remember something you said in one of your lectures: that you personally know academics with materialist and rational worldviews who nevertheless talk about having had supernatural or unexplained experiences. What explains this contradiction, or is there even a contradiction at all?

Human beings are quite complex and strange creatures. We don't think in just one way, following a single, linear pattern. Instead, different ways of thinking come into play in different situations. The question is what circumstances lead us to talk about certain things in certain ways. We can be analytical, scientific and materialist, but there are social situations that call for a different interpretive framework. For example, when dealing with events that may be traumatic, unexpected or difficult to experience.

In Estonia, for example, many real estate agents know ghost stories. That's important information when deciding what to tell prospective buyers about a property. There are many old farmhouses where something has happened — deportations, violence or various accidents — and these events are often connected to ghost stories.

I remember a story told by a real estate agent who was showing prospective buyers a small, old house in Tartu that was in relatively poor condition. One beautiful sunny day, as they were viewing the property, a door slammed shut with an enormous bang. It was clear that something wasn't right in the house because there was no explanation for why the door had slammed like that.

A physics professor from the University of Tartu who lived nearby then told them the history of the house. An elderly woman had once lived there. One winter, she had slipped, fallen and injured herself so badly that she unfortunately died. In the storyteller's view, this explained why something was wrong with the house.

It's not surprising that this kind of interpretive framework works well in such a situation and that even a physics professor doesn't rule out that explanation. It would certainly be wrong to suggest that this somehow calls his expertise as a physicist into question. On the contrary, it demonstrates the vitality of culture and our ability to tell stories that fit particular situations remarkably well.

In Estonia, unexplained phenomena once again gained wider public attention after the restoration of independence, when there was a major wave of New Age spirituality. If you compare the material collected in Jakob Hurt's time with stories that have emerged in Estonia since the restoration of independence, what would you identify as the main differences?

Jakob Hurt was a clergyman and, interestingly, the word "devil," (kurat) referring to a figure who was still very important in Christianity, was virtually absent from his folklore collection questionnaire. Matthias Johann Eisen, who later became a folklorist, had already realized that the devil was becoming a figure of folklore and losing the position he had held in the Lutheran worldview. Sometimes it's surprising how quickly certain beliefs and storytelling traditions fade. Take the devil, for example. Just 150 years ago, he was a terrifying force, but that's no longer the case today.

When Estonia regained independence, themes related to technology and UFOs emerged very strongly, often in border regions. I remember how, on the remote island of Kassari, visitors from outer space began appearing alongside Finnish tourist buses. There is a connection between social developments and these kinds of supernatural experiences.

Now guardian angels, who were talked about less for a while, have reappeared in Estonian folk belief. And then there are entirely new figures originating in the digital world. Take Slender Man from youth folklore, for example. He's a terrifying humanoid created by an internet forum user in 2009. He's depicted in a manipulated photograph as a faceless man with long legs, dressed in black, who poses a threat to children. Initially, he was clearly fictional, but then people began telling stories about encounters with him. I've even heard firsthand accounts from people who say they've actually seen and encountered this figure. Folklore and the world of belief are changing.

So would it be fair to say that internet folklore brings us these global figures and that even the Estonian folklore entering our cultural memory today is, in a sense, part of this larger global village?

Absolutely, but in a way, that's always been the case. The world of belief is open to outside influences and many of those influences have been adapted and incorporated into local traditions. Today's world is particularly open.

For example, vampires were never traditionally part of Estonian folklore. They're more closely associated with Slavic folklore. But now you can ask any child and they'll be able to tell you what vampires are. The image of the romantic vampire, for example, has reached us through movies.

In one of your articles, you described a case in which a woman interpreted a frightening vision she had experienced as a child as a UFO encounter. Yet you also identified elements in her story that, in older folklore, might have been associated with the devil or a nightmare spirit. Does this mean that the experience itself can remain the same while people change the explanation they give it?

Yes, that can certainly happen, because the recurring motifs from which stories are constructed are the main means by which beliefs are passed down. A story presented as a true account also serves as supporting evidence that it all really happened.

That particular story was told shortly before Estonia regained independence. It was a time when Vahur Kersna's program "Monoloog tundmatuga" ("Monologue With the Unknown") was airing on ETV, bringing UFO-related topics very much into the spotlight. So it's hardly surprising that this interpretive framework immediately came into play and that the account of a strange being supposedly trying to abduct a child took on meaning in the context of alien encounter stories.

The idea of the devil stealing children and replacing them with his own offspring is itself part of Estonian folklore and broader international folklore. The fact that the figure is humanlike, or humanoid, is also characteristic. It points to the fact that human beings remain at the center of supernatural experiences and the stories surrounding them.

With internet folklore, it's understandable how stories spread around the world and bring us figures such as Slender Man, whom you mentioned earlier. But what's remarkable about unexplained phenomena is that descriptions of them show surprising similarities across the world, even historically. For example, there are similarities between the storytelling traditions of very distant cultures when it comes to sleep paralysis or near-death experiences. How might a folklorist explain these shared experiences?

David J. Hufford wrote a landmark book about people's nighttime terrors titled "The Terror That Comes in the Night." To my knowledge, Hufford is also the only person in the world to hold doctorates in both psychiatry and folklore studies. He studied the phenomenon of sleep paralysis and the storytelling tradition associated with it, known in Estonia as painaja or luupainaja, a nightmare spirit. His research focused on Newfoundland folklore, but he also compared it with folklore from Southeast Asia.

And indeed, similar images emerge: the perception of some being that is choking or tormenting you, the feeling of being unable to move and the awareness that you're actually awake but something is happening to you. There are also various recommendations for how to escape this state.

Medicine describes this condition as sleep paralysis, but folklore around the world offers different interpretations. It might be an evil person or there might be an erotic element involving affection or attraction. There are many stories in Estonia about someone becoming another person's nightmare spirit because of romantic feelings. These interpretations circulate and change.

The experience of dying is probably also similar around the world. There are states of consciousness that most likely don't depend on culture. Different cultures then add their own ideas, concepts and belief systems, which give meaning to the experience.

Another fascinating aspect of the spirit world is its linguistic dimension, because the Estonian language is full of different forms of the words for soul and spirit. We talk about hingevalu (heartache or pain of the soul), vaimujõud (strength of spirit), but also vaimuvaesus (poverty of spirit), hingetus (soullessness) and vaimustus (enthusiasm). What does the Estonian language tell us about how we perceive the world?

These are excellent examples of how language preserves certain beliefs and forms of knowledge that aren't supported by the modern worldview or scientific thinking. These concepts don't have a clearly defined place in scientific psychology. What is the soul? What is the spirit? Today, psychology operates with entirely different categories.

Charles Taylor once developed the idea that there are cultures in which people perceive themselves as physically open to the world and cultures in which people perceive themselves as enclosed within their bodies. In other words, there are cultures in which people perceive their own presence as extending far beyond the boundaries of the human body. It's precisely in these cultures that stories of supernatural experiences are especially common, along with strong beliefs in and fears of witchcraft and curses.

One might assume that Estonia is a culture in which people perceive themselves as enclosed within their bodies, but older folk beliefs and the Estonian language suggest otherwise. Even today, we talk about drafts passing through a person. People have spoken of illnesses contracted from the ground or of being able to pierce someone or something with their gaze. There are many such examples. Language is a resource for creativity, as well as for both artistic and scientific thinking.

You wrote in Müürileht that supernatural phenomena still involve a great deal of uncertainty and ambiguity, pointing to cracks in the materialist worldview. You also raised the question of whether science that doesn't dare question the validity of the prevailing worldview is still science or whether it has become a form of dogma. How should researchers approach the study of the supernatural scientifically?

I'm speaking here primarily as a scholar of culture. From a folklorist's perspective, we have no direct access to the experience itself. Instead, we study how people describe and interpret that experience. And that alone provides incredibly fascinating and diverse material.

A certain kind of uncertainty about how to understand things is characteristic of our time. When people perceive something that doesn't fit their usual understanding of reality and seems somehow supernatural or disturbing, they tend to look the other way rather than try to make sense of it.

This kind of ambiguity and uncertainty is very common, not only here in Estonia but elsewhere as well. For example, one of my colleagues in Copenhagen, Denmark, studies Danes' experiences with ghosts. For them, these are relatively unpleasant and surprising experiences because they lack the interpretive frameworks to make sense of hearing voices or seeing something in empty buildings.

Folklore studies certainly won't solve the mystery of the afterlife or the supernatural. But we can examine in considerable depth how people talk about their strange experiences and how those experiences shape their thinking and worldview.

It raises the question: Did it really happen this way or was it something else? All of this prompts us to reflect on human existence and the world. And that's precisely what science also strives for: to understand the world better and more deeply.

There isn't just one worldview at any given time, either. There are several. Still, I think we can be glad that a scientific, analytical and critical worldview predominates in Estonia.

World.title: Interior ministry to relax Estonia's surname change restrictions
World.content:
A draft amendment to the Names Act would remove restrictions on adopting surnames that are either too rare or too common. The Institute of the Estonian Language opposes lifting these restrictions.

Under the current system, people cannot adopt a surname that is too rare, meaning one held by fewer than 20 people. They also cannot adopt a surname that is too common, meaning one held by more than 500 people. The restrictions do not apply, however, when someone gets married or takes an ancestor's surname.

The new Names Act would eliminate restrictions on adopting surnames that are either too rare or too common.

"We have opted to ease the restrictions. People will be able to decide for themselves, when choosing a surname freely, whether they want one that is very, very common or one that is moderately common or rare in Estonia. This was purely a political choice," Interior Minister Igor Taro explained.

The Institute of the Estonian Language (EKI) opposes lifting the restrictions. Fred Puss, an onomastics expert at EKI, said people already have a fairly wide selection of ancestral surnames to choose from.

"That gives everyone a choice of around 100 names, provided they have Estonian ancestors, of course. That's quite a large selection of names that are not subject to any restrictions. People can also choose an entirely new name, which is not subject to any restrictions either," Puss said.

"Taking a very rare surname, for example, one held by just five people or even fewer, when the person wishing to adopt it has no connection to those people, seems somewhat unacceptable to the Institute of the Estonian Language or at least not a particularly good choice," Puss added.

Under the bill, there would also be no restrictions on adopting very common surnames.

"Allowing people to adopt very common surnames is a matter of political choice, concerning whether it should be easier to distinguish one person from another. Nowadays, however, personal identification codes serve that purpose in official procedures, so the prevalence of a surname should not be a factor," the researcher said.

Puss noted that different countries take different approaches. "In Sweden and Denmark, for example, it's actually the opposite: Of existing surnames, people can only adopt those held by at least 2,000 people. So only very common surnames can be adopted, not less common ones."

According to Puss, Estonia's pool of surnames has been enriched considerably over the course of history and the fact that many surnames have only a small number of bearers is a distinctive feature of Estonia that should be preserved. Taro, however, believes the change should not undermine the diversity of surnames.

"It's certainly a very good argument that we should preserve the diversity of surnames and that people should be identifiable by name to avoid confusion. At the same time, freedom of choice doesn't actually restrict that diversity. The Estonian language offers excellent opportunities to invent and create all kinds of surnames by combining words," Taro explained.

The most common surnames in Estonia are Tamm, Ivanov(a), Saar, Mägi and Sepp.

World.title: Riigikogu burns midnight oil to pass 2027 state budget bill's second reading
World.content:
The government's draft 2027 state budget passed its second reading at the Riigikogu early Thursday, after a session that began at 4 p.m. and ran past midnight.

All four opposition parties — the Center Party, the Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE), Isamaa and the Social Democrats (SDE) — each proposed suspending the second reading. That motion failed 47–50 in the 101-seat chamber.

The bill's passage followed warnings from SDE chair Lauri Läänemets that Estonia could end up without a state budget, after the opposition's amendments — including €20 million for special care services against the €7.47 million the Finance Committee added — went unheeded (link in Estonian).

Revenues are forecast at €19.4 billion, expenditures at nearly €20.2 billion and investments at nearly €1.2 billion, with 95 amendments submitted and three partially accepted.

Riigikogu Finance Committee in session. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Debate on the amendments ahead of the second vote began around 4 p.m. with a report from the Finance Committee and concluded shortly before 1 a.m. The committee itself proposed one multi-part amendment covering adjustments within and between ministries' areas of responsibility, and another allocating an additional €7.47 million from the government reserve to improve the availability and quality of special care services.

The bill passed its first reading in mid-October. Amendments are open until 5.15 p.m. on Wednesday, November 25, ahead of the third and final reading; only cosmetic changes such as fixing typos are permitted between second and third readings. The state budget act usually passes as one of the Riigikogu's final acts before it breaks for winter recess, which this year begins on Thursday, December 17.

Wednesday's sitting continued with the auditor general's annual review and further readings of draft legislation, and ran into Thursday morning.

The Reform-Eesti 200 administration is a minority government meaning if all opposition and independent MPs voted against the state budget's third reading, it would not pass.

World.title: Defense minister: Drones entered Estonian airspace from northeast and southeast
World.content:
Defense Minister Martin Herem said that NATO aircraft were monitoring the situation and Estonia had not authorized the use of its airspace during Ukraine's Wednesday attack on Ust-Luga in Russia.

Minister of Defense Martin Herem said Ukraine's attack on Ust-Luga began around midnight and continued until approximately 6 a.m. Wednesday. Most of the drones flew close to Estonia's border but remained in Russian airspace.

At around 3:30 a.m., one drone briefly entered Estonian airspace from the direction of Latvia before continuing toward Russia. Several drones that reached Ust-Luga subsequently turned west and circled over the Gulf of Finland in Russian airspace. Some briefly crossed into Estonian airspace over the gulf.

At approximately 5:30 a.m., an explosion occurred aboard a Russian Baltic Fleet vessel in the Gulf of Finland. Smoke was subsequently observed rising from the ship, which then headed back toward St. Petersburg.

"All we know beyond that is that the Ukrainians have said they attacked the ship," the minister said.

Herem said Russian air defenses had been heavily engaged during the attack. Publicly available information indicated that Russia had suffered losses, although he noted that such losses were not unusual during major air defense operations.

"I wouldn't characterize Russia's losses as a failure. Rather, this was a very large-scale and well-organized Ukrainian attack in this war," he said.

Herem reiterated that Estonia had not authorized Ukraine or any other country to use its airspace for military operations. Ukraine had never requested such permission.

Estonia has contacted Ukraine for an explanation of the airspace violations and Herem said the two countries would coordinate their response. To his knowledge, Russia had not approached Estonia about the incident.

NATO air policing aircraft operating from Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia were already airborne before drones entered the Baltic states' airspace. Turkish fighter jets stationed in Estonia were among the aircraft involved.

However, Herem stressed that detecting a drone does not necessarily mean it can be safely intercepted.

"If a drone is flying very low, the aircraft is higher up and there are civilians or other objects in the background, you simply don't shoot it down," he explained.

"If it's very close to the border and Russia is on the other side, shooting it down isn't sensible either. Incidentally, Russia does exactly the same thing: Near its own border, it only engages drones when it can fire toward its own territory."

He added that sleet and drones' small heat signatures could further complicate interception.

Herem said the Estonian Defense Forces has maintained heightened readiness against drones since the spring, with sensors and, where necessary, weapons deployed on the ground. Information sharing with Finland, Latvia and Lithuania was also working well.

He saw no immediate need to change Estonia's air defense procedures.

"We have to assess whether destroying a drone poses a greater danger than allowing it to continue and intercepting it somewhere safer. But we certainly won't enter Russian airspace to shoot down these drones," Herem said.

More detailed air threat warnings needed

On civil protection, Herem acknowledged that relatively little could be done to protect the public from isolated stray drones. However, several Estonian ministries are working on a more detailed air threat warning system that would allow residents to track potential threats visually.

"It shouldn't just be a siren and some message. People should be able to see whether something is heading toward Krabi, Võru, Kohila or Rapla and make their own decisions based on that information," he said.

Early-morning EE-ALARM SMS threat alerts for Southeastern Estonia. September 1, 2026. Autor/allikas: Aili Vahtla/ERR

Such a system would also help reduce public anxiety, Herem added, expressing hope that progress could be made within the next six months.

He cited Ukraine as an example, where mobile applications allow residents to monitor drones in the air, identify their types, see their direction of travel and, in some cases, view predicted flight paths and estimated arrival times.

"That's the direction we're aiming for," Herem said.

World.title: Rally experts on Ott Tänak's WRC return: he has a hunger his rivals lack
World.content:
Ott Tänak is returning to the World Rally Championship stage after a year's absence, to the delight of Estonian rally fans.

Tänak made his public announcement last week and he will be joined by his compatriot and co-driver Martin Järveoja at the team with which the pair won the 2019 title – Toyota.

This followed a year's hiatus this year, after the Estonians finished the 2025 season for Hyundai, with Tänak fourth in the drivers' table.

More critical rally fans, however, are asking whether Tänak at 39 can still have the sharpness needed to compete for a further World Championship title or titles. Veteran and nine-time WRC title winner Sébastien Ogier was 41 when he won his most recent world title last year, they note; fellow Frenchman Sébastien Loeb was 38 when he won his ninth title, in 2012. Others say that experience matters. So what can be made of Tänak's chances this time around?

"Thirty-nine is no age at all in motorsport," rally expert Margus Murakas told "Spordipühapäev."

"If we are talking specifically about rallying, it is certainly a discipline where experience is required. Experienced drivers can objectively assess the situation and what is going to happen. Take the multiple French world champions, for instance, who have always had a clear plan. Ott and Martin also always have a clear plan on how to approach a race from the very first yard, be it tire choices or deciding where to attack, they stick to that plan and get to the finish line," Murakas said.

"Experienced drivers pick out those special stages where they feel comfortable and can see an opportunity to beat their rivals. They achieve a certain result or build up a lead, and then start defending it. I think it is impossible to drive the 300 competitive kilometers, which is currently the minimum for a WRC rally, flat out from the first meter to the finish," he added.

In Murakas' assessment, Tänak is even the leading favorite for this year's WRC title.

"Absolutely. I don't think he and Martin would have made this decision if they hadn't convinced themselves that they could compete for the very top spot," the expert noted.

Also appearing on "Spordipühapäev" was Margus Kiiver, who has followed rallying for years, worked at the EAL, the national autosport union, and the Estonian Olympic Committee, (EOK), and been involved in organizing Rally Estonia. He, too, believes Tänak and Järveoja have the potential to launch a serious title challenge.

"I don't believe the decision to return was made on the basis of 'let's go and see what happens.' Ott Tänak is known as an athlete who is very clearly goal-oriented. He has set himself a clear objective. Since 2019, when he won his first world title, the goal has naturally remained the same. Things simply haven't gone the way they should have," Kiiver said, adding Tänak may have taken a step back from top-level WRC racing, but has been behind the wheel a lot in other categories and in testing.

"I'm inclined to think that, compared with the drivers who have competed in the World Championship this year, Ott has covered more kilometers this year. All the testing he has done while getting to know the car. At the same time, he has maintained a good physical shape," he noted.

Tänak and Järveoja after clinching the WRC world champion title in Catalunya, back in 2019. Source: Toyota Gazoo Racing Team

Kiiver also believes Tänak has one major advantage over his rivals.

"He has something that many other drivers don't have – a hunger. He hasn't competed for a year, apart from that one rally in the U.S. (in September — ed.). He is hungry to compete, and I think that is one of his plus points."

"Perhaps there is also some indication in the fact that he is not the only one who has tested these new Toyota models. Testing has different objectives, so you cannot make direct comparisons, but you can get some sense of where you stand compared with [reigning champion] Elfyn Evans, Oliver Solberg or Kalle Rovanperä."

"We don't know how much information circulates within the Toyota team, but there is some data on which to base such a decision. Maybe I'm talking complete nonsense here, but I think that is the only way you can get some sense of where you stand compared with the other drivers," Kiiver said.

Given Tänak's influence on Estonian sport, the show's participants found it worthwhile discussing how motorsport has managed during the year now drawing to a close without a man competing at the highest level of the WRC and what should now be done to make the most of the renewed interest for the benefit of the sport. The same questions are relevant to Estonia's premier domestic event, Rally Estonia.

Some relatively new names did emerge this year, Kiiver noted.

"Estonian motorsport did quite well. We added more world titles, with Robert Virves and Jakko Viilo in the WRC2 class. On the other hand, we had Paul Aron, who was very much in the picture in Formula 1, taking part in free practice sessions. Admittedly, he did not get to race," he said.

"Looking at it in that light, it wasn't a bad year overall. Rally Estonia also managed without Ott, although it took a lot of work to get people out to the stages. Quite a lot of spectators actually came to watch the young Estonians compete. Both the media and fans focused a little more this year on our young drivers, who had inevitably been in the shadow of Ott Tänak and Martin Järveoja before," Kiiver added.

Outside of their home country, how eagerly was Tänak and Järveoja's return anticipated in the wider rally world?

Kiiver said very much, adding: "I believe it was very eagerly anticipated. The WRC is going through a period of transition. It has a new promoter, whose biggest efforts will start to bear fruit next season, and a colorful character like Tänak certainly adds a lot to the championship."

"I would venture to state that Ott Tänak is an even bigger name around the world than we can conceive of. He is highly respected among rally fans worldwide," the expert went on, noting that while Tänak may be a man of few words, those comments he does make are always on point.

"The WRC is getting back a very serious and highly goal-oriented professional," Kiiver concluded.

Background:

Tänak is joining a veritable stable of drivers at Toyota – not only will new world champion Elfyn Evans (Wales) be his teammate, but so too will be Takamoto Katsuta, from Japan, Toyota's home country, Norwegian-Swedish driver Oliver Solberg and Finn Sami Pajari. The team will continue to run the Yaris, but will also be entering the all-new GR Celica Rally1 next season.

The first race as per tradition is the Monte Carlo rally in January 2027.

World.title: Crude oil from northern Iraq smuggled to Iran, Afghanistan
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Crude oil and major petroleum products are being smuggled from the Kirkuk and Sulaymaniyah fields into Iran via the Bashmaq and Parviz Khan border crossings, according to an Iraqi intelligence investigation.

After being mixed and repackaged to avoid international sanctions, the illicit oil eventually finds its way to markets in Afghanistan and Iran.

According to intelligence findings reported by Al Arabiya News, the network uses what investigators call the “eastern route.”

Operators use official papers to secure oil quotas assigned to areas in Sulaymaniyah before diverting some of the supply to smuggling networks.

Crude oil and main derivatives are transported to the Iranian border by small and medium-sized tanker trucks. The supplies enter Iran through Iraqi Kurdistan’s Bashmaq and Parviz Khan border crossings.

The smuggled Iraqi oil is processed and combined with Iranian petroleum products at small refineries once it enters Iran.

The mixed gasoline is sold under false origin certificates to get over international restrictions, with Afghanistan being the main destination for the re-exported products.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi established a multi-agency investigating group to confront larger oil smuggling networks.

Iraq’s Federal Commission of Integrity opened an investigation targeting the oil smuggling network.

World.title: Iraq Museum in Baghdad to reopen on December 1 following two-year closure
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announced the official reopening of the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, scheduled for December 1 (1-12-2026), following an extensive closure that lasted for more than two years.

According to an official document published by the Ministry’s General Directorate of Public Relations and Media, Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Dr. Ali Al-Dakhili confirmed the decision to reopen the landmark cultural institution to domestic visitors, international tourists, and researchers from around the world.

The reopening follows extensive renovation and curatorial preparations across the museum’s historic exhibition halls, which house tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian, and Assyrian antiquities.

The document highlighted several key artifacts and curated wings prepared for public display:

Assyrian Statues and Reliefs: Featuring monumental winged bulls (lamassu) and stone carvings depicting legendary Assyrian monarchs.

Cuneiform Collections: Ancient clay tablets and historical prisms recording legal codes, administrative decrees, and foundational texts of ancient Mesopotamia.

Abbasid and Islamic Galleries: Intricately carved wooden mihrabs, monumental calligraphic friezes, and fine decorative architectural panels.

Mosaics and Stone Relics: Classical stone carvings, glasswork, and multi-era mosaics recovered and restored across diverse historical periods.

The ministry characterized the December 1 reopening as a pivotal milestone for Iraq’s cultural recovery and heritage tourism, framing the reactivation of the country’s flagship museum as a national celebration and an enduring bridge linking modern Iraqis and the global community to the roots of world civilization.

World.title: Spain’s De la Fuente hopeful teen star Yamal can face England
World.content:
Prague – Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said Wednesday he is optimistic Barcelona winger Lamine Yamal will be fit to face England in the Nations League at the weekend.

The 19-year-old winger will miss the world champions’ visit to face the Czech Republic in Prague on Thursday with a knee problem and is set to join up with Spain after that game.

Yamal played for Barcelona in the 2-1 La Liga win over Atletico Madrid on Sunday and on Monday Spain said he would not travel to face the Czechs.

“He got hurt in the last match, he had some discomfort in one knee, he went for the usual treatment, a scan in Barcelona, and they saw he had inflammation and fluid in the knee — that meant he needed rest,” De la Fuente told reporters.

“Our medical staff and his medical staff have a fantastic relationship, and I decided that his trip here should be avoided without knowing whether he’d be in any condition to play.”

The coach said he had spoken to the winger and his recovery was looking positive ahead of England’s visit to Madrid on Sunday.

“He’s doing a series of exercises with his physio and with the club that indicate the recovery is going well,” continued De la Fuente.

“We believe, I’m optimistic, that on Friday he’ll be with us.”

De la Fuente dismissed the idea that Yamal, who came third in the Ballon d’Or voting in October, has any special privileges compared to his La Roja team-mates.

“He has no privileges, and his team-mates are relaxed about it, because we treat everyone the same,” added the coach.

“In similar situations we would have done exactly the same for any other player, and the players know that.”

– Unstoppable run –

Spain have won all four games so far in Group A3 and sealed qualification to the quarter-finals.

De la Fuente’s side are unbeaten in their last 43 competitive outings, and the coach said it provided his team with extra motivation.

“We want to keep setting new milestones, and this is another one,” explained De la Fuente.

“None of us would probably ever have thought we’d even reach 35, because we already felt those were astronomical numbers, but having reached 43, you think, my goodness, we want to get to 44, of course we do.”

Spain won their previous outing away in Croatia with a brace from Arsenal’s Mikel Merino.

The midfielder is frequently used as a substitute by De la Fuente to great effect, with Merino netting vital goals against Portugal and Belgium in the World Cup off the bench this summer.

Merino said he would like to be a starter for Spain but he would not kick up a fuss.

“Of course, what player wouldn’t like to get (more) minutes?” Merino told reporters.

“You’ll never hear me complain about the coach’s decision, I will respect it… but all players want to be important, have minutes and enjoy themselves on the pitch.”

World.title: Iraq can serve as diplomatic bridge between US and Iran: US envoy
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – US Special Envoy for Iraq and Syria Tom Barrack stated that Iraq can serve as a diplomatic bridge between the United States and Iran.

Speaking at the Chatham House Iraq Initiative event in London, Barrack pointed out that Iraq may serve as a “magic key that unlocks the door” for a new sort of dialogue that Washington is unable to conduct directly.

Barrack emphasized that Iraq and Iran have “hand and glove” policies due to their shared 1,500-kilometer border, close religious connections, and extensive historical engagement.

Barrack also called for foreign investments, especially from American, French, Italian, and Middle Eastern corporations, to construct new pipeline infrastructure alongside current lines to help Iraq reach its goal of producing 10 million barrels of oil per day.

The US official underlined that Iraq’s largest obstacle to drawing in the international investment necessary for long-term prosperity and stability is still establishing the rule of law and clear regulations.

World.title: Al-Zaidi orders foundation stones laid for 1M land plots by 2027
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi directed local and federal authorities on Wednesday to lay the foundation stones for the ambitious “One Million Residential Plots” initiative (the Watan Initiative) across all governorates before the close of 2026.

Chaired by Al-Zaidi, the Seventh Regular Session of the High Commission for Coordination Between Governorates focused on reviewing intergovernmental mechanisms to accelerate infrastructure delivery and streamline stalled development portfolios.

According to a press statement released by the Prime Minister’s Media Office and carried by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), the General Coordinator for Provincial Affairs presented a comprehensive operational report confirming that groundbreaking has already taken place across four governorates: Karbala, Najaf, Nineveh, and Anbar.

Preparations are finalized for immediate foundation laying in Basra and Maysan, while Saladin, Diyala, and Dhi Qar have completed all statutory and administrative clearances. To expedite delivery, provincial investment commissions were formally empowered to handle technical contracting workflows for the housing rollout. Al-Zaidi also issued directives to accelerate the counterpart initiative allocating one million agricultural plots nationwide.

Addressing inter-provincial connectivity and road safety, the Prime Minister ordered the formation of a ministerial steering committee led by the Deputy Prime Minister for Service Affairs, with the Minister of Construction, Housing, Municipalities, and Public Works and the General Coordinator for Provincial Affairs serving as members.

The committee is tasked with conducting an immediate operational audit of arterial highways connecting Iraqi governorates to prioritize widening, resurfacing, congestion relief, and commercial freight optimization.

The High Commission adopted a comprehensive package of executive decisions to regulate urban expansion, municipal revenues, and public services:

World.title: ‘Dictator’ Infantino needs psychiatric help, says former FIFA chief Blatter
World.content:
Berlin – Former FIFA boss Sepp Blatter has slammed current chief Gianni Infantino, calling his successor a “dictator” and suggesting he needs psychiatric help, in an interview with Der Spiegel published Wednesday.

Blatter, 90, criticised Infantino’s decision to create the FIFA Peace Prize award for US President Donald Trump in the lead-up to this year’s World Cup, hosted in the US, Canada and Mexico.

He was also critical of Infantino’s post-World Cup plans to sell off part of the commercial rights of the competition in the future, which was scrapped after a fierce backlash.

“FIFA is suffering. It is currently led by a person who has allowed himself to be blinded,” Blatter told the German magazine.

The Peace Prize, he said, was “embarrassing”.

“Why would he do something like that?,” Blatter asked. “Infantino awards a peace prize to someone who wages war against Iran shortly afterwards? That’s madness.”

Blatter said it was easy for Infantino to secure support for his own re-election from national football bodies.

“‘If you vote for me,’ he tells the national associations, ‘you will get much more money than before.’

“He is a dictator. People in FIFA tell me that no one is allowed to ride in the elevator with him. He is ‘untouchable’.”

Speaking of Infantino’s World Cup sale plans, Blatter said: “Infantino no longer knows any borders. He doesn’t understand any of this.

“I mean, maybe Infantino should be sent to a psychiatric ward one day.”

President of FIFA from 1998, Blatter resigned in disgrace in 2015 amid corruption allegations, including accusations he had sought to buy votes for his presidency.

Charges were brought against him but Blatter was eventually cleared in two trials but was banned from football by FIFA’s ethics committee.

Blatter told the magazine he had “no regrets” from his time in charge of the organisation.

The Swiss was also critical of FIFA’s decision to suspend a red card awarded to USA striker Folarin Balogun after Trump intervened ahead of a crucial match at this summer’s World Cup.

“The red card. That’s the worst. Statutes can be interpreted. But rules of the game must apply to everyone, you can’t interpret them.”

Japanese official Kozo Tashima has announced plans to run against Infantino in his re-election bid, but Blatter named World Athletics president Sebastian Coe as his pick to take over FIFA.

“It is not important who is running. What is important is that the incumbent president is no longer elected.

“Coe was also chairman of the FIFA Ethics Committee. He is a strong personality. A president from the motherland of football, England, would be good.”

Blatter said he had not spoken with Infantino since early 2016.

AFP has contacted FIFA for a response.

World.title: Iraq, Bahrain review regional developments
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and the King of Bahrain, Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, discussed on Wednesday bilateral relations between the two countries and approaches to enhance joint cooperation in different sectors.

During their phone conversation, the two leaders addressed regional developments, ongoing efforts to de-escalate tensions and promote stability, and the importance of coordination on issues of mutual interest, according to a statement released by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

Al-Zaidi renewed his invitation to the King of Bahrain to visit Iraq. He also commended Bahrain’s stance and its positive role in the region, emphasizing the importance of promoting relations between the two countries and expanding the horizons of cooperation.

The king of Bahrain praised Iraq’s contribution to regional peace and stability, expressed his great admiration for the Iraqi people, and reaffirmed his country’s support for the Iraqi government’s initiatives.

The two leaders’ discussion comes a few days after Bahrain formally decided to send its ambassador back to Iraq, signaling a major diplomatic step forward.

Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein and Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani made the announcement on Saturday following a phone conversation.

The major development took place after Iraqi al-Zaidi made a formal visit to Manama.

Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa, the crown prince of Bahrain, described al-Zaidi’s trip as historic, pointing out that it was the first time an Iraqi prime minister has visited Bahrain since 2003.

Zayani emphasized that reinstating the ambassador demonstrates Bahrain’s commitment to enhancing joint cooperation and reinforcing communication channels to support regional stability, according to the Iraqi Foreign Ministry.

In the past few years, relations between Iraq and Bahrain have occasionally been strained. In June 2019, Bahrain recalled its ambassador after demonstrators broke into the embassy’s headquarters in Baghdad.

In April 2026, Manama summoned Iraq’s chargé d’affaires due to regional security concerns, despite the appointment of Khalid al-Mansour as a new ambassador in 2024 to improve relations.

World.title: Iraq plans to build gas pipeline linking south to north
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Oil Ministry has ordered a feasibility study to build a national liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) pipeline running from the southern part of the country to the northern provinces of Nineveh and Kirkuk.

The project aims to resolve domestic distribution bottlenecks, bridge a growing supply deficit, and create export capacity for surplus fuel.

Deputy Oil Minister for Gas Affairs Ezzat Saber announced the plan on Tuesday following meetings with ministry officials and oil company representatives.

The pipeline would deliver LPG straight to northern distribution networks in Kirkuk and Nineveh from southern production hubs.

In addition to stabilizing domestic supplies, the project is intended to allow Iraq to export surplus LPG to foreign markets.

The Iraqi government has not yet disclosed the precise route, estimated cost, pipeline capacity, construction schedule, or collaborating companies.

Iraq produces around 4,500 tons of LPG per day compared to a domestic demand of 4,700 tons, resulting in a daily shortage of roughly 200 tons.

With more motorists switching from gasoline to gas, domestic consumption has significantly increased. The number of vehicles using gas rose to 95,000 in July 2026, up from just 70,000 in March.

To replace slow tanker-truck transport with direct pipeline delivery, the new line complements larger network upgrades, such as a 3,000-cubic-meter LPG depot in Najaf that started trial operations in August 2026.

World.title: India must create, not just adopt inventions: Narayana Murthy calls for respect, better pay for teachers & researchers
World.content:
BENGALURU: India must move beyond adopting inventions developed elsewhere and become a nation that creates them,

founder NR

said Thursday, stressing that this transition would require greater respect for teachers and researchers, better pay and sustained investment in education and research.

In a recorded address at the Infosys Prize announcement in Bengaluru, Murthy argued that while India had made progress in areas such as space, atomic energy, vaccines and generic medicines, it continued to lag in several areas that directly affect citizensâ lives.

The country needs to build a culture of innovation, backed by strong schools, better-trained teachers and researchers who are equipped and recognised for their work, he said.



âA nation becomes economically powerful when it uses invention and continuous innovation to raise its per-capita income and improve the lives of its citizens. Invention and innovation are the two children of an inquiring mind, fortified by higher education and research,â he said.

Murthy outlined four stages of economic development through invention and innovation. In the first, a nation neither invents nor innovates, and does not even use othersâ ideas to improve its peopleâs lives.





In the second, it adopts inventions and innovations made elsewhere without improving them. In the third, it uses higher education and research to improve existing ideas. The fourth is when a nation develops its own inventions.

Assessing Indiaâs position, he said its achievements in atomic energy, space, vaccines, the Green Revolution and generic medicines placed it in the second stage in most areas, while its Global Delivery Model represented the third.

However, in making cities liveable, pollution-free and free of traffic congestion, and in providing clean, safe water, India remained at the first stage.

He cited the US, western Europe, China and Japan as countries that had reached the fourth stage, and said India must aspire to do the same in every area affecting the lives of its poorest citizens, including those in remote villages.

The transformation, he said, must begin in classrooms. Schools need to encourage independent, critical and analytical thinking, Socratic questioning and the ability to relate theory to the real world.

While the National Education Policy (NEP) had started this journey, Murthy proposed a way to accelerate it by bringing in 10,000 accomplished retired science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) teachers from India and developed countries.

They could run 2,500 'Train the Teacher' colleges across states and Union territories. Each team of four could train 100 primary and 100 secondary schoolteachers annually, taking the total to 5 lakh teachers a year.

Within five years, those trained would themselves become trainers.

Estimating the cost at about $100,000 per trainer a year, or $1 billion annually and $20 billion over 20 years, he said the investment was affordable for a country aspiring to become a $5-trillion economy. Invoking a line attributed to former Harvard president Derek Bok, he said: âIf you think education is expensive, try ignorance.â

But training alone would not suffice. âWe must respect our teachers and researchers, pay them better, equip them well, and honour them.

They are the role models for our young people,â he said.

Murthy also recalled that Infosys instituted the Infosys Prize in 2009 to support research in India. Congratulating this year's laureates, he said the award was not a lifetime achievement recognition but was intended to spur them towards bigger work and greater honours.

He urged India to cultivate global standards of productivity, discipline and hard work, while retaining the humility to learn from cultures that perform better.

World.title: The Australian in Indira's Tihar compound: When Sonia Gandhi carried lunch for Charles Sobhraj's accomplice
World.content:
NEW DELHI: On Christmas Day 1978,

carried a home-cooked lunch into Tihar Jail for her imprisoned mother-in-law,

, and, at the former Prime Minister's request, enough extra for a young Australian woman she describes as the accomplice of serial killer Charles Sobhraj.

The episode appears in Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia Gandhi's memoir, released on November 10. It is set in the week Indira Gandhi spent in Tihar after the

, the combined opposition formation, came to power in the elections that followed the Emergency. Sonia writes that she visited the jail daily during that period.

Christmas, she recalls, had always been a special day in the household, especially for the children, even when Sanjay and Rajiv were little boys.



"The celebration had no religious meaning for us, but it was a festive day when we exchanged gifts and decorated the house with colourful baubles and red poinsettias," she writes.

"But on this Christmas my mother-in-law was in jail. I felt that I had to do something special to keep our spirits up."

A friend offered to send sliced ham with roast potatoes and a small Christmas pudding, while Sonia would prepare "a good soup and some vegetables".





The plan soon had to expand.

"At my mother-in-law's request, the food had to be enough also for the three women who took turns guarding her and a young woman prisoner in her compound," Sonia writes. She identifies the prisoner as "an Australian girl, the accomplice of the dreaded Charles Sobraj, convicted for multiple murders of young tourists in Thailand, Nepal, and India".

"My mother-in-law felt sorry for her," Sonia writes.

Then came a hitch. "When it turned out that she didn't eat ham, we quickly had to change the menu and prepare a roast chicken instead."

There was resistance from within the jail as well. The day before, Indira Gandhi had sent a note saying that "under no circumstances" should her daughter-in-law deliver lunch. Sonia was to have her Christmas meal with Rajiv and the children.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

"I couldn't do it," she writes.

She went to Tihar with the food, a book as a small gift, and cards from the children.

"I rushed back rather late, but satisfied that I could celebrate with her briefly and also have lunch with Rajiv and the children," she recalls.

"As it happened, she was released the next day and came home."

The passage offers a rare domestic glimpse into one of the most dramatic periods of modern Indian politics: a former prime minister in jail, her daughter-in-law shuttling between kitchen and cell, and a Christmas lunch stretched to include guards and a fellow prisoner linked to a notorious killer.

World.title: Owaisi, Aazad announce alliance for UP polls; send message to Akhilesh
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

chief

and Nagina MP Chandra Shekhar Aazad on Thursday announced their alliance, Samajik Parivartan Morcha, for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections, with Aazad being the candidate for chief minister.

The two leaders made the announcement at a joint press conference in Lucknow, bringing together their parties ahead of the state polls.

Azad said the coalition was open to other parties, including the

and Congress, if they wanted to contest the elections in support of the alliance to prevent the

BJP

from returning to power in Uttar Pradesh, PTI reported.

Rejecting the description of the grouping as a "third front", Azad said it could become a political platform for deprived, oppressed and marginalised sections of society.



"People have been calling it a third front, but it is not a third front. It is the Samajik Parivartan Morcha. If you understand its depth, you will realise that it is the first front," he said.

He said the alliance aimed to bring together weaker and deprived communities and help them use their electoral strength to gain political power and address their concerns.

Invoking B R Ambedkar, Azad described political power as the "master key" to resolving people's problems.





He argued that communities without their own political organisations could not effectively safeguard their interests, regardless of their population.

Azad also cited Ambedkar's formation of political organisations, including the Scheduled Castes Federation, the Indian Labour Party and the Republican Party of India, saying he had recognised that existing political parties would not adequately represent marginalised communities.

He further alleged that successive governments had failed to fulfil promises to bring deprived communities into the mainstream, tackle poverty and prevent atrocities against them.

While AIMIM has a limited electoral presence in Uttar Pradesh, Owaisi has influence among sections of the minority community. Azad has been seeking to expand his support base among young Dalit voters.

World.title: Suspected Pakistani drone recovered near International Border in J&K's Samba
World.content:
NEW DELHI: A suspected Pakistani drone was recovered from an agricultural field near the International Border in

's Samba district on Thursday, officials told news agency PTI.

The drone, identified as a DJI Matrice 300 RTK, was found near Border Outpost Lalfamkima, around 800 metres from the International Border, during a search operation launched by the

(BSF).

No payload was found attached to the drone at the time of its recovery, officials told PTI.

The drone has been sent to the Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) for a detailed examination.

Investigators are expected to analyse the device to establish its technical details and gather information about its origin, ownership and possible flight history.

According to officials, the BSF launched the search operation after troops spotted suspected drone movement from across the border in the early hours of Thursday.

The personnel subsequently activated the anti-drone mechanism before carrying out the search.

World.title: India simplifies visa rules: Categories cut to 9 from 13, application fields reduced by up to 70%
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Having simplified its visa regime by cutting the total visa categories to 9 from 13 and sub-categories to 23 from 49 and also reducing the information sought from foreign applicants across all 23 sub-categories, the ministry of home affairs (MHA) will be MHA updating its IT systems by year-end, to grant visas per new rationalisation.

"The step aims at making it (visa regime) more compact, coherent and responsive to the requirements of foreign nationals visiting India," the home ministry said in a statement on Wednesday. As part of the revamp, the main visa categories were first cut on 22 to 13 and sub-categories to 49 from 63 in October last year, and further to 9 and 23 respectively on August 27 this year. This simplification was done after studying the visa system followed by the developed countries as well as the global standards.



"The consolidation of similar purposes of travel is aimed at providing greater clarity and ease in identifying the appropriate visa category while facilitating legitimate foreign arrivals," said a ministry spokesperson.

Currently electronic visa or e visa is processed by electronic travel authorization under 13 sub categories. The e-visa facility is available to nationals of 172 countries.

The MHA has also made visa application simpler, cutting the fields/columns by upto 70% across all 23 sub-categories of visas.





"The initiative aims to significantly reduce the information required from foreign nationals, while retaining essential details necessary for visa processing. This will reduce time and effort required to complete the application and also enhance administrative efficiency by facilitating more focused scrutiny and processing of visa application," said MHA.

The rationalisation of visitor visa, earlier called tourist visa, allows flexibility for short and long stays.

The name visitor visa reflects a broader range of permitted purposes beyond conventional tourism. The category has been organised into two sub-categories, V-1 and V-2. V-1 covers short-term activities such as business meetings, medical consultations, wellness retreats, and short term courses. It is granted for 30 days with multiple entries.

V2 is for longer-duration visits, with validity of 1, 5 or 10 years, as specified.

The medical visa framework retains separate provisions for treatment under conventional and AYUSH systems. M-1 Visa covers medical treatment other than treatment under AYUSH systems, while M-3 Visa covers treatment under AYUSH systems. M-1 and M-3 Visas, including their e-Visa variants, will be granted for one year as a default option with multiple entries.This arrangement gives patients greater predictability when treatment involves multiple consultations, follow-up appointments or staged procedures.

In the student visa category, S-1 covers school and college education while the S-2 is meant for PhD and research scholars in Indian universities.

Business visas shall now also divided into B-1 and B-2. B-1 Visa covers long-term, licence-based business activities, including foreign nationals seeking to establish industrial or business ventures in India. B-2 Visa covers short-term, contract-based business activities, including Production Investment Business, conferences, sports, performative arts and films.

A specific provision has also been made for foreign subject-matter specialists, engineers and technical personnel engaged by Indian companies. Such personnel may be granted a production investment business visa under the B-2 category through the e-Visa platform. This was earlier granted under e-B4 visa nomenclature.

"This differentiation gives businesses greater clarity when planning long-term investments as against short-term contractual assignments.

The dedicated provision for technical specialists can facilitate timely deployment of expertise for setting up and operationalising industrial facilities, transferring technology, etc," as per MHA.

The ministry said the changes in visa regime reduce overlap between visa categories and make the framework easier to navigate for visitors, patients, students, researchers, investors and business professionals. The rationalisation is intended to support legitimate travel, education, healthcare and economic engagement with India through clearer, purpose-based visa options, subject to applicable eligibility criteria and conditions.

World.title: Kulgam CRPF attack: Manhunt intensifies for LeT affiliated terrorist Md Lateef Bhat
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Security agencies have intensified their manhunt for Mohammad Lateef Bhat, one of four active terrorists featured on a recently released wanted poster by Jammu and Kashmir Police, following his identification as a suspect in Wednesdayâs attack on CRPF personnel in Kulgam.

Bhat, a resident of Khrewan Chadder in Kulgam, is considered one of the few remaining local terrorists active in the valley. He is affiliated with the Kashmir Revolutionary Army (KRA), a proxy group floated by Pak-based

(LeT) to conceal its direct involvement.

Operating across South Kashmir, particularly in the Kulgam, Shopian, and Anantnag districts, Bhat is known to exercise influence over local over ground worker (OGW) networks.



Investigating agencies suspect Bhatâs involvement in several recent terror strikes in the region. These include the July 22 fatal shooting of J&K Police Head Constable Aashiq Hussain in Anantnag and the July 31 targeted killing of two migrant workers from Chhattisgarh, Deepak and Bhupendra, in Kulgam.

Security forces noted that Bhat operates differently from standard modules. âKnown to be possessing an AK-47, he executes swift strikes either alone or in small groups before immediately blending into the local population,â said a source.





In July 2026, Bhat was trapped alongside top LeT commander Zakir Ganie during a security force siege on a house in Shopian. While Ganie was neutralised in the encounter, Bhat is learnt to have managed to break through the cordon and escape, evading a massive follow-up search operation.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

While law enforcement agencies state that the other three individuals listed on the wanted posterâ Bilal Ahmad Mir, Abid Qayoom Lone, and Mohammad Umar Mir â are currently operating from across the border in Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir (PoJK), Bhat remains the sole local operative actively grounded in South Kashmir.

Authorities had last week issued a public appeal for information on the whereabouts of the four suspects, promising strict confidentiality and a cash reward. Inputs can be shared directly with security agencies through designated helplines, they had said.

World.content:
The amendment follows a draft proposal issued in February 2025, when FSSAI invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders. The authority said it considered the feedback received before finalising the regulations.

NEW DELHI: The next time you pick up a milk packet, a curd carton or a paneer pack, you may notice a new symbol on the label. From July 1, 2028, all milk and milk products, including composite milk products, will have to carry a distinctive, standardised blue-and-white droplet logo, providing a uniform identification mark for the category.The logo features a white droplet against a blue square background. FSSAI officials told TOI that the mark is intended to help consumers readily identify products in this category at the point of purchase, strengthen their awareness and understanding of the regulatory identity of milk and milk products, and facilitate quicker recognition of relevant information on product labels. It is also aimed at bringing greater consistency to labelling practices.The requirement has been notified through the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Second Amendment Regulations, 2026, published in the Gazette on November 9. The amendment to the 2020 labelling regulations will come into force on July 1, 2028.The authority has prescribed minimum dimensions for the logo according to the area of the package's principal display panel. The blue square must measure at least 6 mm on each side for panels up to 100 sq cm, 8 mm for panels measuring 100 to 500 sq cm, 12 mm for panels measuring 500 to 2,500 sq cm, and 16 mm for panels larger than 2,500 sq cm.The Gazette also specifies the minimum dimensions of the white droplet inside the square. For the smallest, 6 mm logo, the droplet must be at least 4.56 mm high and 3 mm wide. For the larger logo sizes, these dimensions increase to 6.08 mm by 4 mm, 9.12 mm by 6 mm and 12.16 mm by 8 mm, respectively.The amendment follows a draft proposal issued in February 2025, when FSSAI invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders. The authority said it considered the feedback received before finalising the regulations.

World.title: India slips 5 spots on climate change performance index
World.content:
India has slipped five ranks down to 28th position on the Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI) 2027, released on Wednesday by prominent Germany-based environmental think tanks on the sidelines of the ongoing UN climate conference (COP31) and its leadersâ summit in Antalya, Turkiye.

This is the third consecutive fall for India in the annual CCPI ranking. Significantly, the country was among the top 10 performers for six years in a row till 2024. India, which ranked 31st in 2014, entered the top 10 for the first time in 2019 and climbed as high as seventh rank, based on its high performance on the renewable energy front.

Energy use , GHG emissions led to India rank dip: Study authors

CCPI, compiled by Germanwatch and NewClimate Institute, uses a standardised framework to compare the climate performance of 64 countries and EU as a whole, which, put together, account for over 90% of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.



The performance of countries is assessed in four categories: GHG emissions (40%), renewable energy (20%), energy use (20%) and climate policy (20%).

Changing trends

Responding to TOIâs question on the reason behind Indiaâs fall in the rankings, the lead author of CCPI, Jan Burck, and co-author Madlen Peter said the country lost most ground in the energy use and GHG emissions categories. âIndiaâs emissions and energy use per capita remain comparatively low, but both have risen in recent years.





The CCPI rates both trends very low,â they said.

The authors, however, appreciated Indiaâs progress in expanding clean energy and recognised the challenge of meeting growing energy neÂ­eds across the country. âThe rapid expansion of solar and wind power is a positive development. Indiaâs renewable energy trend is rated high, although renewables still accoÂ­unt for a relatively small shÂ­are of its overall energy suÂ­pÂ­pÂ­ly.â

The authors said India could use energy more efficiÂ­eÂ­nÂ­tly, invest in grids and storage to make better use of renÂ­eÂ­wÂ­able power and set a clÂ­eÂ­ar tiÂ­metable for reducing coal use to improve its performance.

Denmark (ranked 4th) again topped CCPI, followed by Lithuania and Luxembourg (at 5th and 6th, respectively), with the top three ranks remaining vacant, as in previous years, in the absence of a perfect score for any country.
