On the other hand, the worldâs largest emitter, China, is ranked 56th, whereas others in the league, Russia (66th), the US (67th) and Iran (68th), are the three worst performers in the overall rankings, with the report noting that none of the 65 largest emitters are on a Paris Agreement-compatible pathway.

Pakistan, at 26th position, is ranked above India. Itâs primarily due to comparatively lower GHG emissions in a relatively much smaller economy. The report also said the UK continues to be the only G20 country among the high perÂ­formers. It said 10 G20 countries received an overall âvery lowâ rating, including twin COP presidencies Turkiye (53rd) and Australia (54th), even though G20 bears special responsibility for climate mitigation, as its members account for over 75% of global GHG emissions.

World.title: Owaisi names Chandrashekhar Azad as Uttar Pradesh CM face of Samajik Parivartan Morcha
World.content:
Asaduddin Owaisi’s All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (AIMIM) and Chandrashekhar Azad’s Azad Samaj Party (Kanshiram) announced the formation of a new alliance, the ‘Samajik Parivartan Morcha’, ahead of the Uttar Pradesh Assembly polls, at a joint press conference in Lucknow on Thursday (November 12, 2026).

“We have decided to form Samajik Parivartan Morcha. I can say with confidence that this will be a strong Morcha to stop the BJP from coming to power in UP for the third time,” Mr. Owaisi said.

“If SP, Congress or any other party wants to join us to stop BJP from coming to power, we are open to it,” said the Nagina MP Mr. Azad.

Mr. Owaisi announced that Mr. Azad will be SPM coalition’s Chief Ministerial face for the 2027 State election.

“I am happy to announce that our brother Chandrashekhar Azad will be the chief president of the SPM and its chief ministerial candidate in Uttar Pradesh,” Mr. Owaisi said.

The AIMIM chief said the alliance would focus on issues concerning backward and Dalit communities, the oppressed and marginalised sections, irrespective of their caste, alleging that these communities had so far been used merely as vote banks by political parties.

He said the morcha would raise issues such as the deteriorating condition of education, unemployment among the State’s youth and problems faced by farmers.

‘A front for social change’

“This is not a third front, but a front for social change. Our alliance is strong on the ground, and it will grow even stronger. It is the alliance of deprived, downtrodden, marginalised, oppressed and exploited people and groups, our promised is to eradicate poverty and helplessness, to put an end to the caste-based violence and oppression inflicted upon us, in Uttar Pradesh,” said Mr. Azad, Lok Sabha MP from Nagina.

He said, those who spoke of uplifting the poor, marginalised social groups, of bringing them into the mainstream, went on to become MLAs, MPs, Chief Ministers, and even Prime Ministers. “Yet, these marginalised community remains exactly where it has always been. The truth is that governments kept changing, announcements kept being made, and even today, the Bahujan community remains deprived of basic amenities, in Uttar Pradesh these communities face injustice through bulldozer raj.”

The alliance between the two parties could pave the way for the first declared non-Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), non-Congress political front in Uttar Pradesh, with both parties considered marginal players eyeing to consolidate Scheduled Caste (SC) and minority voters in the politically crucial state.

“The alliance will be aiming to focus on Dalit and minority voters, as both leaders have long been associated with these vote blocks, but getting votes or winning your own seat and making your candidates victorious is a different issue,” said Asad Rizvi, a political analyst based in Lucknow, adding that the State is increasingly transforming into bipolar politics, between NDA and INDIA bloc, and it would be a huge challenge for the new alliance to make an impact.

(With inputs from PTI)

World.title: Villagers panic as leopard kills cow near Hasanur
World.content:
A cow was reportedly killed in a leopard attack near Hasanur in Thalavadi taluk on Wednesday (November 11, 2026), raising fresh concerns over attacks on livestock in villages bordering the Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve.

The cow, which had been left to graze near the reserve forest, was found dead on the roadside along National Highway 948 (Dindigul-Mysuru), which passes through the reserve. Villagers suspected that a leopard had attacked and killed the animal.

Earlier, V. Periyasamy of Bungalow Thotti was found dead along a stream near the forest fringes on October 4. The Forest Department confirmed that he had been killed in a leopard attack and subsequently intensified surveillance in the area.

The department said in a press release that cages had been installed at two locations to capture the leopard posing a threat to the public. Two leopard cubs, aged about a year, were trapped near Bunk Thottam at around 5 a.m. on October 22. A male leopard, aged five to six years, was captured at P.K.P.N. Thottam at around 6.45 a.m. on October 23.

A forest veterinarian examined all three animals and found them healthy. They were subsequently released into the dense forest, the release said.

The latest incident has renewed fears among villagers that leopards continue to venture out of the reserve forest in search of prey, despite the capture and release of three animals last month. The fact that the cow was reportedly attacked during the daytime has added to their concerns. Residents have urged the Forest Department to intensify surveillance and take measures to protect livestock grazing near the forest fringes.

World.title: Dubai-based Keralite loses ₹2.11 crore in alleged forex trading scam run through Telegram
World.content:
An expatriate from Kochi in Keralam has been allegedly cheated of more than ₹2.11 crore in an online forex and stock market trading scam after falling prey to a fraudulent investment platform operated through Telegram groups and a fake trading website.

The 41-year-old from Rayamangalam in Kunnathunadu, currently working in Dubai, allegedly lost the money after an unidentified gang fleeced him after impersonating as associates of a stock market intermediary. The Ernakulam Rural Cyber Crime Police have registered a case based on a petition filed by the victim’s friend.

The First Information Report was registered on November 11 under Section 318(4) (cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Section 66(D) (cheating by personation using computer resources) of the Information Technology Act.

The victim was allegedly lured by an online  for a company named ‘Handtec Markets’ in October. The company claimed to be a stock market intermediary and promised substantial returns through a special trading strategy, with little to no losses. He was then added to a Telegram group and the fraudsters convinced him to invest by claiming that they dealt only in high-return stocks and boasted a track record of delivering substantial profits to investors. He was then given a link that took him to an allegedly fake forex trading platform and was provided with a user ID and password to access his account.

The website displayed a trading dashboard resembling a genuine stock market platform. He claimed to have transferred money in multiple instalments to several bank accounts shared by the operators through a Telegram channel linked to an Indian mobile number, says the FIR.

However, he was unable to withdraw his ‘accumulated profits’ and the operators turned incommunicado leaving him with neither the promised returns nor his original investment. Police have issued notices to banks concerned to collect details of at least four bank accounts involved in the alleged scam. They are suspected to be mule accounts used for organised cybercrime network. The police suspect the involvement of a north Indian cybercrime syndicate, though the identities of the accused are yet to be established. The Telegram channel, the web links and the fake trading portal are also being examined to track down the accused.

World.title: Wife allegedly stabs husband to death with kitchen knife in Bengaluru
World.content:
A 35-year-old woman allegedly stabbed her husband to death with a kitchen knife following a domestic dispute over their inability to have children at Lakshmipura in Kempegowda Nagar police station limits in Bengaluru.

The deceased has been identified as Rajasekhar (44), who worked in a private bank. His wife, Malashree (35), has been accused of committing the murder.

According to preliminary information, Rajasekhar allegedly used to drink and subject his wife to physical and mental harassment. The couple, who had no children, frequently quarrelled over the issue, with Rajasekhar allegedly blaming and assaulting his wife.

On November 11 night, Rajasekhar reportedly returned home drunk and got into an argument with his wife. As the quarrel escalated, Malashree allegedly lost her temper, picked up a kitchen knife and stabbed him in the chest.

Rajasekhar suffered serious injuries and collapsed in a pool of blood. He was subsequently shifted to Victoria hospital, where he was declared dead.

World.title: NIA to probe online radicalisation of Indian youths by Pakistan-based gangster Shahzad Bhatti
World.content:
The National Investigation Agency has registered a case to probe the online radicalisation of Indian youths by Pakistan-based gangster Shahzad Bhatti and other ISI agents with the intention to carry out terror attacks in the country, officials said on Thursday (November 12, 2026).

The probe stems from a case registered by the Uttar Pradesh Anti-Terrorist Squad (ATS) in April this year.

The FIR named eight accused in the case, including Bhatti, an Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) agent based in Pakistan. ISI is Pakistan's spy agency.

The Central Government had in September declared the Pakistan-based Shahzad Bhatti Network (SBN) a terrorist organisation under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.

The action was taken as the Centre believed that the SBN was involved in "terrorism and has participated in various acts of terrorism in India."

Others named as accused in the NIA's First Information Report (FIR) included Md Hamad Barkati, Abid Jatt, Major Hamid, Major Iqbal — all of whom are ISI agents — and one Major Anwar based in Pakistan.

The NIA also named Tushar Chauhan alias Hijbullah Ali Khan, a resident of Uttar Pradesh, and Sameer, a resident of Delhi, as accused in the case. The two were arrested by the UP ATS in April this year.

The Uttar Pradesh ATS, investigating the presence of Pakistani sleeper cells created through social media, had found that these two men were allegedly in direct contact with Pakistani operatives and "planning a major disruptive act".

During the investigation, it emerged that Pakistani gangster Bhatti, Jatt and radical Pakistani YouTubers, allegedly acting on instructions from the ISI, were attempting to radicalise Indian youths and entice them with financial incentives to disturb internal peace and communal harmony, Uttar Pradesh's Additional Director General of Police (Law and Order) Amitabh Yash had said.

World.title: Inside Secunderabad’s new community hub for art and theatre
World.content:
Secunderabad’s old-world charm gets a cultural boost with Platform 51, a new arts destination in Vikrampuri Colony, Karkhana, bringing music, theatre and art closer to home.

Community-driven space

Set in a four-decade-old house in a quiet residential neighbourhood, the space is surrounded by trees and retains its architectural character. It is being reimagined as a multicultural hub with a café, amphitheatre and banquet hall. “Platform 51 will be a community-driven space focused on healing through art forms such as music, pottery and painting,” says co-founder Prerna Kirthi.

For Kriti, Secunderabad is more than a location. At a time when West Hyderabad, with its IT offices and rapid development, is seen as the city’s growth centre, she has consciously chosen to return to her roots. “My biggest inspiration has been my principal, Yogendra Guruwara of Sherwood Public School, who gave me the roots to stay grounded and the wings to fly. I dream of travelling across the world, but want to return to my roots in Secunderabad.”

Challenging journey

Platform 51 has been a challenging journey for Prerna, who works at a design college in the city. The idea emerged during a theatre workshop, when she envisioned a café and a space for activities promoting mental and physical well-being.

She leased the property in February 2025, but was left with the financial and operational burden when investors pulled out. Architect and theatre director RK Shenoy eventually stepped in as investor and co-founder. “I wanted to give up, but RK instilled hope,” recalls Prerna.

“Once you're invested in a project, you believe in it and work hard to make it happen. Neither of us knows how to swim, but we took the plunge because I believed in her resolve,” says Shenoy, founder of ARKA Design Studio and Dramanon theatre group.

Textured effect

Renovation began in February this year, with demolition taking three months. Built on rock, the house’s natural elevation lends itself to dramatic, multi-level spaces. Shenoy reused broken tiles, reopened sealed walls and exposed brick to retain the building’s raw texture and architectural character.

The 700-square-feet performance space, with a stage and green room, accommodates 51 people, giving the venue its name. Its 50-cm-thick walls, with exposed brick and textured patterns, act as natural sound diffusers, eliminating the need for microphones. “Plastic chairs reflect sound, which is why venues use absorbing materials. Here, the walls diffuse sound naturally, making it a space where performers don’t need mics,” says Shenoy.

Though not officially open yet, Platform 51 has hosted events, while trial runs help iron out operational issues. Plays and a Sufi night are also planned. “The objective is to create a space to explore and experiment with art forms and discover meaning in creative ways. The idea is to get people off their phones and into the space,” says Shenoy.

World.title: The digital recruiter | Shahzad Bhatti
World.content:
Over the past two years, the name of a social-media influencer from Pakistan has been surfacing in several terror-related investigations in India.

What started as a bid by the individual identified as Shahzad Bhatti to establish fear and clout in the border State of Punjab soon spread to 14 States, with several young men finding themselves behind bars under the stringent anti-terror law, the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA), for acting on his directions. Their assigned tasks included pasting posters glorifying Bhatti and his associates, installing CCTVs near critical installations, which were being live-streamed into Pakistan, or making extortion calls.

World.title: Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw to flag off Goa-Mangaluru-Bengaluru Vande Bharat Express, tour Dakshina Kannada and Udupi districts on November 13
World.content:
Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw will visit Dakshina Kannada and Udupi districts on November 13 to launch the Goa-Mangaluru-Bengaluru (Madgaon-Yesvantpur) Vande Bharat Express at Mangaluru Junction, and to dedicate a few development projects to the nation.

According to Dakshina Kannada Member of Parliament Captain Brijesh Chowta, Mr. Vaishnaw will arrive in Mangaluru on his first-ever visit to the region on November 12 night. He will flag off the VB Express at noon and travel by the same train till Subrahmanya Road station. En route, he would interact with passengers at Kabaka Puttur. His visit to the region is expected to usher in a new era of railway infrastructure development, the MP said.

Capt. Chowta said the new Vande Bharat Express is expected to considerably reduce the travel time between Bengaluru and Mangaluru thereby promoting business, tourism, and other commercial activities.

Udupi visit

According to Udupi-Chikkamagaluru MP Kota Srinivas Poojary, the Railway Minister will inspect Udupi Railway Station at 8.45 a.m. on November 13, followed by a visit to Sri Krishna Mutt at 9 a.m. As the Union Minister for Information and Broadcasting, he would inaugurate a new FM Station near Ajjarkad in Udupi city at 10 a.m. before proceeding to Mangaluru.

Schedule in Mangaluru

In Mangaluru, Mr. Vaishnaw is expected to hold a review meeting at the Deputy Commissioner’s office at 10.30 a.m., inspect Mangaluru Central Railway Station, flag off the VB Express along with Prime Minister Narendra Modi (through video conferencing) at noon, and travel to Subrahmanya Road by the inaugural special VB Express.

During his visit to Subrahmanya, Mr. Vaishnaw would dedicate the newly-electrified 55-km Subrahmanya Road-Sakleshpur ghat section and the Subrahmanya Road Railway Station building, redeveloped under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme, to the nation.

World.title: At COP31, PM Shehbaz calls for grant-based finance, resilience funding for climate-vulnerable countries
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday called for grant-based finance and improved resilience and adaptation funds for climate-vulnerable countries at COP31, being held in Turkiye’s Antalya.

This year’s summit focuses on transitioning toward a low-carbon future.

Delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya as global greenhouse gas emissions show little sign of falling and wars, inflation and other crises compete for political attention.

Addressing the summit, PM Shehbaz highlighted Pakistan’s efforts at promoting clean energy, but warned that “national effort cannot replace a fair and just global response.”

“When climate disasters strike, vulnerable countries need timely help and finance that does not deepen their debt”, PM Shehbaz noted, adding that Pakistan called for “grant-based finance, including public-private partnership, alongside significant enhancement of resilience and adaptation funds, which amount to survival funds, especially for struggling economies.”

He said clean energy sources provided nearly 55pc of Pakistan’s energy needs, adding that the country was advancing electric mobility and had set a target to cut projected emissions by about 50pc by 2035.

Recalling the 2025 floods in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Buner, the prime minister said, “In August 2025, a young man in Buner was just two days away from his wedding when flash floods swept through his village. A home preparing for celebrations became a house of mourning.”

“Their grief was personal, yet the warning signs continued to be global,” the prime minister cautioned, noting that this was the story of “millions of people in Pakistan and across the developing world”.

“People who have contributed the least to climate change bear its heaviest consequences,” he remarked.

Addressing the summit, PM Shehbaz also recalled the 2022 floods in Pakistan, noting the economic damage and mass displacement the catastrophe caused.

More than 1,700 people lost their lives, and economic losses exceeded $30bn,” the prime minister said.

PM Shehbaz recalled his speech at the UN General Assembly in 2022. “I had warned that what is happening in Pakistan will not stay in Pakistan, and unfortunately, that warning has become a stark reality.

“The future we feared has become the present we are living,” he said.

Underscoring the need for global solidarity, the premier remarked, “Climate change knows no borders and no nation can face it alone. Solidarity must mean real action.”

At this, he expressed gratitude to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan for his country’s support for Pakistan during the 2010 and 2022 floods.

Addressing the summit, PM Shehbaz also warned against the weaponisation of water.

“No nation should be allowed to put the lives and livelihoods of people downstream at risk. Water-sharing agreements must be honoured in letter and spirit,” the premier said.

Concluding his address, PM Shehbaz said world leaders had gathered at the summit to “shoulder a shared responsibility to protect life on this earth.”

“Let our success be measured not by promises we make here but by the families we protect, the resources we deliver, and the meaningful action we sustain,” he hoped.

On Tuesday, PM Shehbaz addressed a high-level dialogue on clean energy transition, titled ‘ 35 by 35: Powering the Future ’, where he highlighted Pakistan’s solar power boom.

“In just two years, Pakistan has added nearly 22 gigawatts of rooftop solar capacity — a quiet revolution by ordinary citizens seeking affordable power and a cleaner, more predictable future.”

World.title: 'Significant evidence' of placer gold in Punjab rivers, says CM Maryam at minerals investment forum
World.content:
Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz said on Thursday that there was “significant evidence” of “sufficient quantities” of placer gold flowing in the province’s five rivers.

She was speaking at the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum in Islamabad, an initiative aimed at harnessing the country’s mineral resources and attracting domestic and foreign investment in the mining sector.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar also addressed the event, which was attended by the chief ministers of Balochistan and Sindh, as well as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi.

Maryam said Punjab was the land of five rivers and that gold was “literally flowing” in all five, particularly in the areas of Mianwali and Attock.

Describing Pakistan as a “pot of gold”, she said its wealth lay both above and beneath the ground and needed to be explored and converted into tangible wealth.

“The wealth beneath Punjab was never a problem, never a problem, just like the whole of Pakistan, just like all four provinces and the federating units. The chaos above ground was the actual problem,” she said.

Maryam said the provincial mines and minerals department’s revenue stood at around Rs10 billion two and a half years ago but had since increased to Rs40bn.

“And it is just the beginning,” she added.

She also highlighted the province’s iron ore reserves, saying Chiniot had 261.5 million tonnes of iron ore.

She said the provincial government was taking steps to facilitate investment in the mining sector and create an enabling environment for investors.

The Punjab chief minister said her role as chief executive of the country’s most populous province was to facilitate investors and create an enabling environment by eliminating red tape, bureaucratic delays and unnecessary hurdles.

The provincial government was offering one-window facilitation to ensure investors did not have to run from pillar to post to complete the necessary procedures, she added.

Maryam said the government was also making substantial capital investments to reduce investors’ capital expenditure and prevent them from having to tie up funds in purchasing expensive land.

Additionally, the government was offering concessional financing of up to Rs5 billion and would provide solar-powered energy solutions to investors to help offset high energy and fuel costs.

Dar says provincial partnership vital for mineral development

Dar said Pakistan’s constitutional framework made provincial partnership indispensable, adding that the provinces were essential partners in the national undertaking and that their constitutional authority and ownership of mineral resources must be respected.

Addressing the event, he said the federal government was working alongside provincial governments and their leadership through national coordination, investment facilitation, policy alignment and international engagement.

Dar said Pakistan’s mineral resources were central to the next phase of the country’s economic transformation, stressing the need to diversify exports, strengthen the industrial base and attract long-term investment.

He said Pakistan possessed substantial and diverse mineral resources, including significant copper and gold potential along the Tethyan metallogenic belt in the west of the country. The country also had deposits of iron ore, chromite, lead, zinc, coal, rock salt, marble, gypsum, gemstones and other industrial minerals.

The deputy PM said the Reko Diq copper-gold project in Balochistan demonstrated the potential of international expertise, national participation and provincial ownership in attracting major long-term investment.

He stressed that Pakistan’s ambition should extend beyond extracting minerals and exporting them in raw form, saying the country needed to develop the capacity to process and refine them, as well as manufacture mineral-based products domestically.

Dar said Balochistan was central to Pakistan’s mineral future, adding that the development of its resources should contribute meaningfully to the provincial economy and the well-being of its people.

He also emphasised the importance of local employment, skills development and the participation of Pakistani companies, saying local communities must be active participants in and beneficiaries of mineral development.

The deputy prime minister further stated that environmental protection, workers’ safety and the rehabilitation of mining sites were essential to a successful minerals industry.

The Reko Diq copper-gold project in Balochistan is one of Pakistan’s most ambitious mining ventures, with significant potential to boost the country’s mineral wealth through the extraction of gold and copper.

Designed as an open-pit mining and processing operation, the project will initially process 45 million tonnes of ore annually, with capacity expected to double to 90m tonnes after the completion of Phase 2.

The mine has an estimated operational life of 37 years, which could potentially extend to 80 years through further exploration and resource development.

World.title: President, PM condole martyrdom of 10 policemen in Kohat, vow to continue fight against terrorism
World.content:
President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday expressed grief over the martyrdom of 10 police personnel in a terrorist attack on a police team in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Kohat district.

Eighteen terrorists were killed and 10 police personnel were martyred on Wednesday when a police team came under attack while returning from an operation against elements involved in illegal gold mining.

In his message, the president said the sacrifices of the KP police in the fight against terrorism were a source of pride for the entire nation.

The president extended his heartfelt condolences to the families of the martyred personnel and expressed solidarity with them.

He said cowardly terrorist attacks could not weaken the nation’s resolve, which remained unwavering in its commitment to eliminating terrorism from the country.

President Zardari said police personnel and other law enforcement agencies were making sacrifices to protect the lives and property of the people.

He also prayed for the speedy recovery of those injured in the attack, saying the sacrifices of those who laid down their lives for the peace, stability and security of the country would always be remembered.

Prime Minister Shehbaz reiterated the government’s resolve to eradicate terrorism from the country.

The prime minister, who is currently in Turkiye on a three-day official visit to attend the COP31 summit, strongly condemned the attack and paid tribute to the martyred KP police personnel.

Calling them national heroes, he said the brave officers and personnel of the provincial police force had set an example of devotion to duty and courage by laying down their lives for the peace and security of the country.

The premier also extended his heartfelt condolences to the families of the martyrs and prayed for the elevation of the ranks of the departed souls and strength for the bereaved families.

He said the killing of 18 terrorists during the operation demonstrated the professional capabilities, courage and unwavering resolve of the KP Police in the fight against terrorism.

He also described the “nexus between criminal elements and Fitna al-Khawarij” as a nefarious attempt to spread unrest in the country, vowing that such elements would not be allowed to succeed in their designs under any circumstances.

Fitna-al-Khawarij is a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan.

PM Shehbaz also reiterated that no compromise would be made on Pakistan’s peace and stability.

The prime minister further said the courage and steadfastness shown by police personnel and other law enforcement agencies in the fight against terrorism were commendable, adding that the entire nation stood shoulder to shoulder with the country’s security forces.

In a statement released yesterday, the KP Police said police personnel were conducting a joint operation with the local civil administration in the Darabukach locality near Kohat city.

“When the police party was returning after completing the operation, Fitna-al-Khawarij attacked the police party at the behest of criminal elements,” the statement read.

“Police personnel fought the attackers with great bravery and courage, as a result of which 18 khawarij were sent to hell,” it noted, adding that 10 personnel of KP Police “embraced martyrdom while fighting bravely”.

KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi has sought a detailed report on the incident.

According to images shared by KP Police on their X account, the martyred cops included Deputy Superintendent of Police Haidar Zaman.

KP has been facing security challenges for long.

According to Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies , the country’s security environment continued to show considerable volatility from Oct 30 to Nov 5, with renewed terrorist activity in parts of KP and the former tribal districts, alongside intensified counterterrorism operations and changing patterns of militant violence.

World.title: Debutant Saqib Khan takes seven as Pakistan restrict Sri Lanka to slender lead
World.content:
Debutant fast bowler Saqib Khan produced a remarkable seven-wicket haul as Pakistan restricted Sri Lanka to a slender 12-run first-innings lead on the fourth day of the opening Test at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Thursday.

Sri Lanka, who resumed their innings at 404 for four, were bowled out for 446 in 117.2 overs after losing their last six wickets for just 42 runs.

Pakistan had declared their first innings at 434 for nine, leaving the visitors with only a narrow advantage despite having appeared firmly in control after the third day.

Saqib finished with outstanding figures of seven for 130 in 34 overs, equalling the record for the most wickets by a Pakistani bowler on Test debut and becoming only the fourth player from the country to claim a seven-wicket haul in his first Test innings.

His performance turned the tide after Sri Lanka had dominated much of the contest through their experienced middle order.

The visitors had taken charge on the third day through a massive partnership between Dhananjaya de Silva and captain Kusal Mendis.

De Silva top-scored with a commanding 167 off 246 deliveries, including 20 boundaries, while Mendis contributed a fluent 119 from 202 balls, hitting 10 fours and four sixes.

Their unbroken fifth-wicket partnership had frustrated Pakistan’s bowlers for much of the previous day and set a new record for Sri Lanka against Pakistan, surpassing the previous best of 207. Mendis also became the first Sri Lankan to score a century in his maiden Test as captain.

However, Pakistan returned with renewed purpose on Thursday, with Saqib leading the charge.

He provided the decisive breakthrough by dismissing Mendis for 119, ending the crucial association and giving the hosts an opportunity to run through the remaining batting order.

Saqib continued to trouble the lower order, claiming the wickets of Sonal Dinusha, who made 20, Milan Rathnayake (12), Lahiru Kumara (0) and Asitha Fernando (4), among others.

His sustained accuracy and ability to extract assistance from the surface ensured Sri Lanka could not turn their strong position into a commanding first-innings lead.

Mohammad Abbas supported the debutant with two wickets, while Razaullah took one as Pakistan wrapped up the innings.

The late collapse prevented Sri Lanka from building a substantial advantage on a surface that had earlier offered some assistance to the seamers but had also allowed well-set batters to score freely.

Pakistan’s first-innings total had been built around valuable middle-order contributions, with Saud Shakeel narrowly missing a century after scoring 93.

Debutants Tayyab Arif and Mohammad Taha had also struck half-centuries, while Arafat Minhas added a brisk 52.

World.title: Israeli strike kills 6 at southern Gaza hospital: civil defence
World.content:
An Israeli strike killed six people and wounded around 20 at Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza, a civil defence official told AFP on Thursday.

The Israeli military confirmed the strike. Gaza’s civil defence agency said the bodies of those killed and more than 20 people wounded in the strike had been recovered from a building at the medical complex.

“The death toll from the Israeli strike inside Nasser Medical Complex, west of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, has risen to six,” civil defence spokesperson Mahmoud Bassal told AFP.

Nasser Hospital confirmed the six deaths in a statement.

The Israeli military claimed it carried out an “aerial strike to eliminate the threat they posed, after the Hamas had established a presence within the hospital complex and used it as a command centre”.

Hazem Qassem, spokesman for Hamas, called the strike on Nasser a war crime, adding that he held the US-backed Board of Peace in charge of overseeing Gaza’s ceasefire plan responsible for failing to prevent the strike.

A seventh person was killed by Israeli fire in central Gaza’s Al-Bureij camp Thursday, Bassal said.

Nearby Al-Aqsa hospital confirmed receiving the body and said the man was shot dead by Israeli forces. Israel’s military said it was looking into the death.

Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire that came into effect in October 2025, after two years of an Israeli offensive in Gaza triggered by an attack of unprecedented scale carried out by the Palestinian group against Israel on October 7, 2023.

On Tuesday, Israeli forces killed seven people, including a 13-year-old boy, in the Gaza Strip, according to local emergency services, while the Israeli military claimed it had targeted “military operatives”.

More than 1,590 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to the Gaza Ministry of Health. During the same period, the Israeli military has reported the loss of seven soldiers, as well as one civilian contractor.

World.title: US marine guard appears to rebuke Hegseth's delegation at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
World.content:
A US Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier appeared to rebuke Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s delegation on Wednesday after laughter could be heard as they climbed the steps of the solemn site, according to a video of the incident.

Hegseth, his wife and senior aides could be seen taking pictures and speaking to each other on the steps of the memorial at Arlington National Cemetery following a Veterans Day event.

Immediately after the laughter, the sentinel moved toward the group and, from a distance, shouted toward them: “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.”

Sitting at the heart of Arlington National Cemetery, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is a sacred site and the grave of three unknown American service members, including one from World War One. It is widely known as a place for mourning and for reflection on military service, and sentinels guard the site 24 hours a day.

Asked about the incident, which was first reported by CNN, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement: “The secretary and the entire department have always honoured and will always honour the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe.

“While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.”

Hegseth, a former Army National Guard soldier who served in Iraq, prevailed this week after the House of Representatives rejected a Republican lawmaker’s effort to impeach him.

At a rare Pentagon press conference on Tuesday hours before the vote, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a farce and defended his record, which includes championing the unpopular war on Iran, launching strikes on suspected drug vessels in Latin American waters and firing senior military officers.

Democrats who won control of both chambers of Congress last week have promised to investigate Hegseth for his stewardship of the US military and have not ruled out another impeachment effort.

World.title: Democrats seek bipartisan action to curb Trump’s immigration drive
World.content:
WASHINGTON: Democratic lawmakers have called for a bipartisan immigration deal, seeking changes to President Donald Trump’s enforcement policies and legal status for long-settled immigrants.

The appeal came as Democratic officials in several states and cities moved to limit their agencies’ role in federal immigration operations.

Members of the House and Senate, including lawmakers elected last week, held a news conference outside the US Capitol.

The group included progressive and centrist Democrats who said the election results offered an opportunity to revisit an approach that had become politically costly for Republicans.

Representative Veronica Escobar, whose Texas district includes the border city of El Paso, said she wanted far-reaching reform but recognised that legislation could not pass without Republican support.

“As we continue to have Donald Trump in the White House, and without a supermajority in the Senate, we need Republican support,” she said, adding that comprehensive reform would therefore have to be bipartisan.

Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona urged both parties to pursue an agreement before the current congressional session ends, or continue negotiations in the next one.

Republicans had long made immigration reform conditional on securing the border, he said.

“We have that right now. We did the job. Now let’s figure out how to right-size our immigration issue. Let’s figure out how to keep families together.”

Representative Sylvia Garcia of Texas proposed starting with the Dream and Promise Act, saying it could provide a basis for broader changes after Democrats assume control of Congress in January.

The lawmakers’ appeal for federal legislation coincided with efforts by Democratic state and local administrations to narrow the role of their police and detention agencies in enforcing federal civil immigration rules.

In Houston, Mayor John Whitmire has also issued an order barring city police from contacting Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) about administrative immigration warrants during routine traffic stops and minor, nonviolent violations.

Police may still contact ICE when a person is being booked into jail for a new offence carrying possible jail time and also has an administrative immigration warrant.

The order also removes earlier provisions requiring officers to wait for extended periods for ICE agents to attend traffic stops or detention scenes.

Whitmire said he had consulted Texas’s newly elected governor, lieutenant governor and comptroller before acting. He described the move as an attempt to ease anxiety in immigrant communities and said he hoped other cities in the state would follow.

“This is the right thing to do at the right time,” he said. “I do this to begin a healing process.”

Whitmire opposed a 2017 Texas law prohibiting sanctuary-city policies when he was a state senator. Houston’s move follows major Democratic gains in the state: Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, while James Talarico won a Senate seat.

Abbott had earlier threatened to hold back more than $110 million in public safety grants from Houston over its limits on cooperation with ICE. Austin and San Antonio are also reviewing their arrangements with federal immigration authorities.

Similar changes are underway elsewhere. Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger has ordered state law-enforcement agencies to end their agreements with ICE under the 287(g) programme, which authorises participating local and state officers to carry out specified immigration enforcement duties.

Maryland Governor Wes Moore has signed legislation ending formal 287(g) partnerships between ICE and state or local law-enforcement agencies.

The change requires nine sheriffs’ offices to withdraw from their agreements.

In New York, legislation signed by Governor Kathy Hochul requires existing arrangements involving local detention facilities and federal civil immigration detention to end by November 25.

California, meanwhile, continues to apply its California Values Act, which restricts the use of local police resources for federal civil immigration enforcement.

In January, Democrats are expected to use their new congressional committee leadership to scrutinise the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, investigate enforcement practices and detention conditions, and seek testimony and records.

But a Democratic majority will not by itself enable lawmakers to undo the president’s central immigration policies. Trump can veto legislation, while Senate rules will make it difficult to pass major measures without broader support.

Trump conceded after the Republican losses that his administration had been “too tough” on immigration in some respects. Yet his appointment of Stephen Miller, a leading architect of the crackdown, to a senior White House post points to continued resistance to a substantial change in direction.

Vice President JD Vance, seen as a possible Republican presidential candidate in 2028, has suggested that enforcement tactics could be adjusted, including through a greater focus on businesses that hire undocumented workers.

His comments indicate that debate over how the administration applies its immigration policy may continue, even as Trump retains its central objectives.

World.title: Mississippi Democrat flips US Senate seat in stunning upset after 140 years
World.content:
In a historic upset, Democrat Scott Colom has won his US Senate race in traditionally conservative Mississippi, networks projected Wednesday, making him the first African American elected to the chamber from the southern state in more than 140 years.

Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, prevailed over Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in perhaps the most extraordinary seat flip of an already extraordinary US midterm election, in which Democrats crushed the Republicans to reclaim the majority in both chambers of Congress.

In a prayerful and solemn speech, Colom praised Mississippi’s long tradition of Black activism and faith in progress.

“Mississippi, our prayers have often changed the course of history,” Colom told the jubilant crowd of his supporters in Jackson on Wednesday night. “God didn’t want us to get it the easy way. He wanted us to get it the Mississippi way.”

Colom’s win in the deep South adds sting to the stunning rebuke of President Donald Trump as voters around the country shunned his Republican Party, even in states that had not sent a Democrat to Washington in decades.

The latest win, called Wednesday by US news outlets that included CNN, NBC and CBS, will give Democrats 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with 44 for Republicans and one race — in the state of Alaska — still outstanding.

The midterms result was a personal humiliation for 80-year-old Trump as a Democratic wave swept through the Republican heartland, leaving him as a lame duck president for the remaining two years of his term.

The Democratic flipping of Congress signals an end to Trump’s stranglehold on US politics and gives Democrats the power to block legislation, probe his administration and thwart his appointments.

Including Mississippi now, Democrats flipped eight Senate seats that had been held by Republicans, scoring historic breakthroughs in South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Maine —several of which had not changed hands for decades.

Hyde-Smith, in office since 2018, conceded the race in a video posted to X.

“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” the 67-year-old senator said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

The race in ruby red Mississippi went down to the wire — a surprise for many observers who doubted the scale of the Democratic blue wave riding on mounting anger over Trump’s harsh immigration policy, the war in Iran and rising cost of living.

CNN called it for Colom on Wednesday, eight days after election night, with some 99 per cent of the vote in and the Democrat ahead of Hyde-Smith by 49pc to 48.7pc, a difference of 4,585 votes.

“Blue Mississippi is here,” the US Senate’s top Democrat Chuck Schumer proclaimed on X after the projections came in.

“Scott Colom is the only person who could’ve gotten this done. I knew it from the moment I met him.” Colom is set to become the first Democratic senator from Mississippi in nearly 40 years.

The first Black senator the United States ever elected, Hiram Revels, was from Mississippi and served during the Reconstruction era after the Civil War.

In his speech Colom referenced how Revels, a minister by training, inspired other politicians to support Colom’s Senate run through his powerful oratory.

“That’s an example of the power of prayer, and through our history, there are so many people that lifted this state up through the power of prayer in very dark times,” Colom said.

“It’s local people that have faith that Mississippi can make progress, and it’s local people like the people out here who had faith that we could win this election,” he added.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
