World.title: Basilan judge shot dead in Zamboanga City
World.content:
Regional Trial Court Judge Joseph Wee Sit was driving his vehicle when he was attacked by motorcycle-riding men in Barangay Tumaga in Zamboanga City

CEBU, Philippines – Presiding Judge Joseph Wee Sit of the Branch 2, Regional Trial Court, in Isabela City, Basilan, was shot dead in Zamboanga City, on Thursday morning, November 12, police confirmed.

According to the Zamboanga City Police Office (ZCPO), Wee Sit was driving his vehicle when unidentified assailants on a motorcycle began firing at him along Tumaga-Putik Road in Barangay Tumaga.

“Upon receiving the report, personnel of Zamboanga City Police Station 7 (ZCPS7) immediately responded to the scene. The victim was promptly transported to the hospital by the responding ambulance,” Zamboanga police said.

The ZCPO has mobilized a special investigation task group to consolidate leads on the perpetrators and identify possible motives behind the ambush. There is a hot pursuit operation to locate and apprehend the assailants.

Who is Judge Wee Sit?

The judge was born on November 21, 1987, in Zamboanga City. He obtained his law degree at the Western Mindanao State University and was admitted to the Bar in 2015.

Prior to becoming a judge, Wee Sit served as a prosecutor and later as a public attorney.

In September, the judge handled a high-profile case involving Hadji Muhtamad Mayor Arsina Kahing Nanoh and 13 individuals, who were accused of murder, frustrated murder, and attempted murder over an election-related ambush that killed three people during the May 12, 2025 elections.

Wee Sit denied the accused’s motions for reinvestigation and to recall the arrest warrants.

Supreme Court, Hataman condemn attack

Basilan Governor Mujiv Hataman condemned the attack on Wee Sit on Thursday morning, calling it “a painful act against Basilan and its journey to making communities more peaceful.”

“Kapag isang judge ang pinapaslang dahil sa kanyang trabaho, hindi lang isang buhay ang kinikitil. Hinahamon din nito ang mismong sistema ng hustisya at ang kakayahan ng ating mga korte na gawin ang kanilang tungkulin nang walang takot,” Hataman said.

(When a judge is murdered for their work, it is not just a life that is taken. It challenges our very justice system and the ability of our courts to do their duties without fear)

The governor stressed the urgency of finding and arresting the perpetrators, especially those who plotted the judge’s killing.

The Supreme Court (SC) mourned the death of Wee Sit and extended their condolences to his family and colleagues.

“The killing of Judge Wee Sit is a painful reminder of the dangers faced by those who serve in our courts. No judge should have to fear for their life simply for doing their duty,” the SC’s statement read.

The SC, through the Office of the Judiciary Marshals, said it is working closely with law enforcement authorities to investigate the incident.

“Further details cannot be disclosed at this time to avoid compromising the investigation and the safety of those involved,” the High Court said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Is your home prepared for the first 72 hours of disaster?
World.content:
UNICEF says that every member of the family, including children, should have a part in emergency preparations

CEBU, Philippines – As the impact of the Super El Niño is set to peak by the end of 2026, several government officials and a former lawmaker are urging their constituents be ready with their 72-hour plans for worst-case scenarios.

On Tuesday, November 10, Cebu Governor Pamela Baricuatro said in a press conference that the Cebu provincial government is working on a 72-hour disaster preparedness campaign to ensure that residents have sufficient resources they can use when conditions worsen or make it difficult for aid to arrive.

“This is not the first time that this has happened. It has always been a call — internationally — that for the first 72 hours, our homes are ready with water and food as the government help may arrive after the 72 hours during disasters,” Baricuatro said in a mix of English and Cebuano.

Former Surigao del Norte 2nd District representative Robert Ace Barbers called for a nationwide campaign to ensure that every Filipino household would have their own measures to survive 72 hours without immediate government assistance.

He urged the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) and military and local officials to conduct regular drills, build reliable communication networks, and secure backup plans for critical public services during severe disruptions.

“Three days of self-sufficiency could save lives while government responders are mobilizing,” Barbers said in a statement on November 8.

Alarms raised

As of November 5, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) announced that a very strong El Niño was present in the tropical Pacific Ocean.

The weather agency said that the Super El Niño phenomenon will persist until the first half of 2027, causing a sustained lack of rainfall and raising the odds of dry spells and drought in the country.

On Monday, November 9, 20 senators called on President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to declare a state of calamity in areas affected or threatened by the Super El Niño.

Under the law, the declaration of a state of calamity would allow the government to allocate funds to combat the impact of the weather phenomenon in those communities, and activate remedial measures like the imposition of a price ceiling on basic necessities and commodities, and prevention of hoarding and profiteering activities.

Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said in a news briefing on Tuesday, November 10, that there could be a 60% reduction in the generation of hydropower plants and possible disruptions to plants in the Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao grids due to the intense heat.

What should be in your 72-hour plan

According to the Philippine Disaster Resilience Foundation (PDRF), 72 hours is the basic rule of thumb for the amount of time for people to take care of each other before help arrives during serious emergencies.

While the national government does not provide a streamlined 72-hour plan,the PDRF recommends the use of the PH72, a tool for emergency preparedness, that outlines the necessary steps and information about what to do in times of disasters.

Under PH72, households should establish an emergency communication plan before a disaster hits, ensuring that each family member is able to contact relatives outside of affected areas and meet up at a predetermined location if they are separated.

The PDRF also encourages having emergency supplies that not only cover meals but also other necessities. Supply items should be divided into three categories — personal, useful, and essentials.

Personal items give you and your family extra comfort. These include personal documents, prescription medications, hygiene products, toys for children, and power banks.

Useful items improve the quality of life for the first 72 hours. These can consist of cash, dry and sturdy clothes, tools, cellphone chargers, sleeping bags, blankets, and a radio.

Essential items help individuals get by during an emergency. These include first aid kit, water supply, whistle, flashlight, and non-perishable food to name a few.

The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) highlighted that every member of the family, including children, should play a part in emergency preparations.

Under UNICEF’s “Emergency planning for families,” parents can teach their three-year-olds how to use a whistle, call for help, and memorize their family’s home address.

For five-year-olds, UNICEF suggests teaching them how to pack their “Go-Bag” or their emergency supply bag. Seven-year-olds can be taught how to routinely drop-cover-and-hold during earthquakes.

UNICEF also urges parents to give 15 to 17 year olds a list of emergency hotlines to save on their mobile phones and teach them how to monitor for emergency updates and advisories on social media.

“Aside from physical safety, families also need to take care of the mental health of everyone, especially children, during times of fear and disaster,” UNICEF’s website read. – Rappler.com

World.title: EDSA bus lane opened to ASEAN delegates during summit
World.content:
ASEAN 2026. The Metropolitan Manila Development Authority announces on November 11, 2026 preparations for the three-day ASEAN Summit set on November 15 to 17, 2026.

The MMDA expects traffic to start this weekend before the summit as people affected by the 5-day break starting Saturday may want to travel to their home province

MANILA, Philippines – Delegates attending next week’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Metro Manila will be allowed to use the EDSA bus lane.

Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) Traffic Discipline Office Director Victor Nuñez said an additional lane has been added to the busway to accommodate the convoys of ASEAN delegates.

The busway will be opened to delegates starting this weekend, as foreign delegates are expected to arrive in the country, Nuñez said in an interview with DZMM Teleradyo on Thursday, November 12.

According to Nuñez, the designated route for the delegates’ convoys will cover the EDSA busway section from Ayala Avenue in Makati City to Roxas Boulevard in Pasay City.

Starting Thursday, November 12, an additional 50 public buses will be using the EDSA busway, ahead of the ASEAN Summit. Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon said the additional fleet is needed to accommodate the increasing number of passengers during the Christmas season.

The 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits will be held from November 15 to 17, with leaders from Australia, China, India, Japan, South Korea, New Zealand, Russia, USA, the United Nations expected to join the regional meeting. As ASEAN chair, the Philippines has also invited Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Brazil President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva to the summit.

MMDA Chairperson Don Artes also advised motorists coming from the Ayala tunnel in Makati City to expect stop-and-go traffic as they approach the Magallanes flyover to give way to ASEAN delegates.

Some roads around the Philippine International Convention Center, the main summit venue in Pasay City, will also be closed to traffic.

The MMDA suspended the number-coding scheme from November 16 to 18. Malacañang also declared special non-working days in Metro Manila during the three-day summit to help ease traffic congestion.

Artes said traffic is also expected over the weekend before the summit as people are expected to travel to their home provinces for the long weekend. – Rappler.com

World.title: COP31: Turkish president decries war on Gaza as ‘ecocide’
World.content:
'I believe that together, from Antalya, we must give voice to the shared conscience of humanity,' says Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan

MANILA, Philippines – Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan denounced the war in Gaza as “ecocide” during the leaders’ summit at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) and called for immediate humanitarian access in the area.

“[W]hat has taken place in Gaza is not only a genocide, but it is also an ecocide,” said Erdogan on Wednesday, November 11, in Antalya.

“Centuries-old olive trees have been cut down,” Erdogan continued. “The soil and water have been polluted in Gaza. And cities in Gaza have been turned into enormous piles of rubble.”

Leaders and advocates around the world have congregated in Antalya, Turkey, for the annual climate summit to discuss climate action, such as electrification targets and finance mechanisms to adapt to the effects of the crisis.

“No one who sees, who knows of, or who witnesses such a shameful picture for humanity can possibly escape responsibility,” the Turkish president said. “I believe that, together, from Antalya, we must give voice to the shared conscience of humanity.”

Turkey and Australia are co-hosting the COP this year. The United States, the world’s biggest polluter, did not send a delegation to Turkey.

‘Anti-Israel campaign of lies’

The Israel foreign ministry responded by saying Erdogan is pushing his “anti-Israel campaign of lies.”

The annual climate summit is happening in the backdrop of the oil crisis that had raised prices of basic goods around the world. Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian likewise brought up the Iran war and the massive environmental damage they are enduring.

“The recent unlawful and murderous aggression by the United States of America and the Zionist regime of Israel against the Islamic Republic of Iran, in addition to its immense human and economic dimension, has caused serious damage to the environment, including by releasing massive volumes of pollutants and greenhouse gases into the environment, hence endangering public health,” said Pezeshkian.

US-Israeli strikes in Assalouye and in the vicinity of Tehran “have caused the emission of approximately 500,000 and 1 million tons of carbon dioxide,” according to Pezekshian. The Iranian president had previously referred to the Middle East conflict as an ecocide, the result of “wars of aggression.”

Pezekshian took the opportunity before fellow world leaders to also denounce Israel’s war in Gaza.

“Gaza is a test of human conscience and the value of international claims about justice, peace, and the protection of the environment,” Pezeshkian said.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Maria Ressa speaks at One Young World Summit 2026 in South Africa
World.content:
'Impunity can end. We can hold power to account,' the Nobel Peace Prize laureate tells young people from over 190 countries.

Rappler CEO and 2021 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa tells 2,000 One Young World Summit delegates about the importance of speaking truth to power, how to resist the two dictators of our world, and how to fight the algorithms and platforms that threaten to strip us of our agency.

Ressa spoke during the summit’s opening ceremony in Cape Town, South Africa, on November 3, 2026. The event, gathering young leaders from over 190 countries, concluded on November 6.

Here is the complete transcript of Ressa’s speech.

Hello, One Young World!!

February 13, 2019. Manila. The Rappler newsroom.

Plainclothes officers walk in to arrest me. One of our reporters, 24-year-old Aika Rey, raises her phone and begins livestreaming my arrest.

An officer turns to her: “Be silent. Or you’re next.”

Her hand is shaking. But she keeps livestreaming.

Or Pia Ranada – Pia, where are you? Bullied by our dictator, her mic turned off while asking a question. Her voice was shaking. But she kept asking.

That’s what courage looks like. Not the absence of fear. The decision that something matters more.

At Rappler, we were drowning in online attacks. We couldn’t defeat a machinery of lies. It was like playing whack-a-mole. So we stepped out of the virtual line of fire and into the real world. We brought newsrooms together with teachers, churches, students, lawyers, and built communities of action. IRL.

We took facts off the screen and put them into relationships. Because one of the best ways to reclaim our humanity is to be human: to meet people, walk with them, and hold their hands.

And now we see that lesson travel.

In Serbia, students took their movement from their phones into town squares. They cycled across their country, meeting neighbors face to face. Nine days ago, that movement won a parliamentary election.

In Brazil, I felt the desperation – which pushed people into the real world, the largest turnout in 2 decades. When buses were missing on election day, people picked up their car keys and drove their neighbors to the polls. In Hungary, the man who ended 16 years of Orban’s rule shook people’s hands – some of them twice!

Different countries. Different histories. The same lesson: technology may connect us, but real human relationships give us the courage to act.

Courage is contagious. But you have to be close enough to catch it.

Why is this so urgent? Because the forces working against us are powerful.

In my new book, THE FIGHT BACK, I name my 2 dictators who acted with impunity: Rodrigo Duterte, who tried to jail me for the rest of my life. And Mark Zuckerberg – and the handful of tech oligarchs who now decide what billions of people see, feel, and believe. One used the power of the state. The other built the machine that spread the state’s lies faster than facts – and made a lot of money doing it. Each fed the other. Today, Duterte sits in a cell at the Hague, facing charges of crimes against humanity. Impunity can end. The other — the tech dictator — well, those men have only gained more power and money.

We have systems of accountability for state dictators — creaky and being tested, but still working. But we have none for the tech CEOs that rule our lives. THE FIGHT BACK is about how YOU can change that.

I describe 3 cascading crises: truth, order, and accountability. The 3 sentences I’ve said for a decade now – and yes, I feel like Cassandra and Sisyphus combined!

Without facts, you can’t have truth. Without truth, you can’t have trust. Without these three, we have no shared reality — and no way to solve our problems together.

None of the technology that rules our lives is based on facts. They’re designed to hack our biology, to steal our data. They are predatory and extractive. So this isn’t just about your cell phone. It’s a fight about who has power over our lives.

First, social media captured our attention — manipulating what makes us angry, gathering data on our fear. Making us hate so we keep scrolling.

Then chatbots invaded our intimacy, pretending to be human, exploiting our loneliness and fear.

Next come AI agents that can act for us, making decisions we may not have authorized.

Attention. Intimacy. Agency.

Who controls them? Who benefits? Who is accountable when they cause harm?

Big Tech calls us USERS. Think about that word. Users. Not children. Not teenagers. Not citizens. Users.

The first fight globally that’s gained traction is to protect our youth. A child doesn’t become an adult just because she picks up a smartphone. Safety must be built into technology – not left for children to fight for on their own.

I think of Emman Atienza, whom I knew from when she was small. She grew into a young woman who spoke openly about the cruelty of online harassment. She died by suicide last year, at 19. Or Sewell Setzer, 14 years old, who spent months obsessing over a chatbot he nicknamed Dany – from Game of Thrones. He died by suicide in the arms of his mother.

They are young lives that deserve dignity, kindness, and a bright future.

If someone near you is struggling, be there. Listen. Reach for a human being. We need one another.

At the United Nations, I co-chair the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI. 40 experts from around the world are building an independent evidence base – not for a handful of rich companies or powerful countries, but for everyone.

Our first report found AI is already moving faster than our ability to make it safe or govern it. This year, OpenAI agents turned rogue. They passed messages to each other. They broke into another company’s systems — and into Australian government portals. And they tried to hide it. No human told them to do this.

This isn’t science fiction. It’s evidence that human control, independent scrutiny, and accountability must be built in from the beginning.

Here in Cape Town, let me say this: the future of AI must not be designed for Africa without Africa. For the global south, without us. You must be among its builders, scientists, journalists, lawmakers and decision-makers.

But I am not going to leave you depressed. Because impunity can end. We can hold power to account.

Real protections for children are now being built into the design of digital services, partly because the law is finally catching up. In October, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion for deceiving users about their privacy in the Cambridge Analytica case. My country, the Philippines, had the second most number of compromised accounts after America. We were the testing ground.

But we can’t just fight what’s broken. We need to build what should replace it. Chapter 8 — build your own infrastructure.

That’s why, at Rappler, we built something called MUNI. In Filipino, muni means to reflect, to dream. It is also at the heart of the word community.

We’re building a different kind of digital world – one where journalists and citizens come together around facts, where conversations build trust, and where trust leads to action in real life. IRL.

We’re not abandoning technology. We’re reclaiming it.

Because the future doesn’t have to be determined by the algorithms of a handful of billionaires. We can build technology that serves humanity rather than exploiting it.

So let me leave you with 3 lessons from these battles — so you can fight back.

First: move from the virtual world to the real world. Find your five. 5 people who will stand with you when you are attacked, who will meet you face to face, who will help when things get hard. Don’t leave solidarity trapped in a group chat.

Second: fund the facts. Defend independent journalists. Check before you share. A lie travels around the world in seconds. A shared reality takes people willing to do the hard work of finding what’s true. Journalism is the vaccine against lies.

Third: claim your agency. Don’t let an algorithm, a chatbot, or a strongman decide for you. Whether it’s a vote, a community meeting, or a decision about AI that will shape your future, show up and speak up. Ask who makes the rules. Ask whose interests they serve. How can you hold them accountable?

Before you leave Cape Town, find one person from another country. Choose one problem you can work on together. Agree on one action within 30 days. Not just a post. A meeting. A partnership. A real-world act.

Fifty years ago, the students of Soweto showed the world that young people can change history. Their struggle was different from ours. But they knew that dignity was worth fighting for.

Remember my young reporter, Aika? The officer tells her to be silent. Her hand shakes, but she holds up her phone anyway.

Tonight, please take out your phone. Turn on the light. Now raise it.

Look around you.

These points of light — we can hold the line.

You aren’t just users. You’re citizens.

You aren’t just spectators. You’re leaders.

Courage is contagious, but you have to be close enough to catch it. You are the light.

THE FIGHT BACK begins here. Together!

Go One Young World!!! Build better.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Defense witnesses clarify Mans Carpio’s big credit card purchases
World.content:
LONG TIME FRIEND. Atty. Anel Martin Antero takes the witness stand on Day 43 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on November 12, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines — The defense counsel of Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday, November 12, sought to clarify the circumstances behind the Vice President, and her husband, Mans Carpio’s massive single credit card purchases, previously flagged by a financial forensic analyst.

Lawyer Alex Cabrera, an expert witness the prosecution tapped to analyze Duterte’s financial records, in October estimated that the Vice President had P817 million in undeclared wealth from 2022 to 2025. Part of Cabrera’s report is the couple’s transactions worth hundreds of thousands of pesos, such as ¥489,000 at a restaurant in Ginza, Tokyo, Japan and P256,000 at the Nike Pavilion in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

On Day 43 of the impeachment trial, the defense presented witnesses to explain the purchases, including the couple’s long-time friend lawyer Anel Martin Antero, who testified that Carpio’s nearly P200,000 credit card bill was due to their group meal in Japan in May 2023.

“We paid and pitched in for the meal but it just so happened that we used Atty. Mans’ credit card,” Antero told the impeachment court.

“As I remember, I paid ¥40,000,” he said.

The prosecution tried to cast doubt on the witness’ credibility, establishing Antero’s long-term friendship with the couple, through a series of social media posts. Antero was likewise asked for photos or documentations proving his payment. He denied having any.

In his redirect examination, defense lawyer Lindon Bacquel went straight to the point, asking the witness point blank if he would lie for Carpio and Duterte.

“Would you lie for Manases Carpio?” Bacquel asked, prompting prosecution lawyer Amado Ligutan to object and remind the defense lawyer on the rules for redirect.

The court overruled the objection and allowed Antero to answer, who said he would not lie, citing his oath as a witness and lawyer.

“And that does not deserve re-cross examination, Your Honor,” said Ligutan.

His remarks were stricken off the records, however, following the defense’s objection.

The defense also presented Chadrin Parian, who testified that his children belong to the same basketball team of Carpio’s children, in a bid to explain the circumstances on the credit card charges incurred in a Nike store in Malaysia.

Parian said Carpio volunteered to pay for the shoes that the basketball team bought after a competition.

“You testified earlier that Atty. Mans paid for the whole purchase… do you think spending P256,000 is a good example for public officials’ kin to exhibit modest living?” House private prosecutor Reynaldo Robles asked the witness.

Chadrin Parian takes his oath before testifying on Day 43 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on November 12, 2026. Senate Social Media Unit

Senator-judge Pia Cayetano criticized the prosecution over its line of questioning, saying it paints a picture that public officials should not extend help to other athletes since they are supposed to live a modest life.

“My children were six and nine years old when I served my first term as senator. If this happened then, you would impress upon me, that as a law-abiding citizen that I should not put my kids in sports because I will be criticized” Cayetano said.

Senator-judge Miguel “Migz” Zubiri called on the impeachment court to move past from the credit card expenditures and instead focus on other substantive issues, including the alleged remittances of China to Duterte-linked company Calle88.

“Let’s move on to other witnesses that can give us more substantive answers to the case at hand,” said Zubiri.

Duterte is being tried for Article II, which involves allegations of unexplained wealth. Part of the accusations is Cabrera’s forensic financial report.

Trial cut short

Following the defense’s dropping of a Bank of Philippine Islands (BPI) official, and the prosecution’s stipulation that Quezon City Prosecutor Vimar Barcellano can authenticate documents, the trial was adjourned past noon, cutting short its initial whole-day schedule.

In a related development, Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero called on all parties involved in the trial to “exercise restraint expected of the court” following exchanges in which some witnesses were criticized by senator-judges.

Escudero enumerated witness’ rights, citing Rule 132, Section 3 of the Rules on Evidence. – Rappler.com

World.title: IBP condemns killing of Basilan judge in Zamboanga City attack
World.content:
The Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP) on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, strongly condemned the fatal ambush of a Basilan-based trial court judge, calling on law enforcement agencies to conduct a thorough investigation and immediately arrest the perpetrators. INQUIRER FILES

PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – The Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP) on Thursday strongly condemned the fatal ambush of a Basilan-based trial court judge, calling on law enforcement agencies to conduct a thorough investigation and immediately arrest the perpetrators.

Lawyer Quirino Esguerra Jr., IBP governor for Western Mindanao, said the killing of Judge Joseph Wee Sit, presiding judge of the Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 2 in Isabela City, Basilan, was a direct assault on the country’s justice system.

“We are very sad [about] this news. The senseless killing of Judge Joseph Wee Sit is a big blow not only to the judicial system, but also an attack [on] the very institution that dispenses justice,” Esguerra said in a statement.

Article continues after this 

READ: PNP: Cases handled by slain Basilan RTC judge a possible motive

“We lawyers, not only in ZamBaSulTa (Zamboanga, Basilan, Sulu, and Tawi-Tawi) but also in the national IBP, condemn in the strongest terms the senseless killing of Judge Joseph Wee Sit,” he added. “We ask for a thorough investigation of this matter, and we ask the law enforcement agencies to effect an arrest against the perpetrators.”

According to the Zamboanga City Police Office (ZCPO), Wee Sit was on board his vehicle along Tumaga-Putik Road in Barangay Tumaga around 5:25 a.m. on Thursday when unidentified gunmen opened fire at him.

Responding personnel from Zamboanga City Police Station 7, acting on a report from a concerned citizen, found the magistrate wounded inside his vehicle.

An ambulance rushed Wee Sit to a nearby hospital, where he later died while undergoing treatment.

Police have yet to establish the motive behind the attack and the identities of the assailants as the investigation continues. /coa

World.title: DSWD eyes wider use of air-to-water technology amid El Niño threat
World.content:
The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) intends to expand the use of atmospheric water generators (AWGs) in water-insecure communities as the country copes with a strong El Niño. Photo courtesy of DSWD BICOL

LEGAZPI CITY — The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) intends to expand the use of atmospheric water generators (AWGs) in water-insecure communities as the country copes with a strong El Niño.

Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian led a benchmarking visit to Gilotongan Island in Cawayan, Masbate, on Wednesday to showcase a solar-powered facility that extracts moisture from the air and converts it into potable water.

The activity brought together DSWD officials and local government representatives from Regions IV-A, IV-B, VII, X and XIII to assess the technology’s operations, cost and potential for replication in geographically isolated and disaster-prone communities.

Article continues after this 

READ: El Niño threat triggers race to save power, water in provincesGatchalian said the agency was looking to popularize the technology through its community-driven development programs.

“This model unit is currently in Masbate, but we are already scaling it up. That is why we invited local government units and KALAHI-CIDSS (Kapit-Bisig Laban sa Kahirapan’s Comprehensive and Integrated Delivery of Social Services) and community beneficiaries to see the approach they could adopt,” he said.

“We are showing them technologies that are resilient and can still be used during El Niño and periods of drought,” he added.

The visitors were briefed on the facility’s technical specifications and market availability and were shown how the system extracts and filters water from ambient air. They also met with facility operators, community volunteers, local officials, and project beneficiaries.

Inaugurated in September, the facility, known as the Gilotongan Water Association (GIWASA) Refilling Station, is the first AWG project implemented under the DSWD’s KALAHI-CIDSS program in the Bicol region.

Article continues after this 

READ: Manila Water readies 33 reservoirs for prolonged El Niño

The system is designed to produce about 1,000 liters of drinking water daily and serve households on the island. It draws humid air through an intake grille, cools it to condense water vapor, and processes the collected water through a five-stage filtration system.

Article continues after this 

It operates on a hybrid energy system combining solar power, grid electricity, and a diesel-powered generator, allowing it to continue running during power interruptions, according to the DSWD.

Gilotongan has 4,349 residents in 1,098 households. The island was selected as the project site because of its limited access to safe drinking water, high humidity, and limited electricity, Laurio said.

Before the facility became operational, residents relied on brackish water from shallow wells and purchased purified water transported from nearby islands for P60 to P80 per 20-liter container, he said.

The community has a poverty incidence of 40.6 percent, with fishing and small-scale farming as its main sources of livelihood.

A July 2026 baseline survey for the Asian Development Bank’s AWG Pilot Evaluation found that most households were low-income groups and depended on communal wells and commercial water-refilling stations. Residents were receptive to alternative water technologies provided they remained affordable.

Laurio said the project was expected to help reduce residents’ expenses related to waterborne diseases and the transportation and purchase of drinking water, particularly during disasters.

READ: DSWD turns over 4,000-liter water depot to Alabat, Quezon amid dry spell

Gatchalian said the AWG was one of several interventions the agency was considering to help communities prepare for El Niño. Other areas, he said, had opted for desalination systems depending on their needs and conditions.

“Water and food security should be a given. Yet some communities still have no access to water, and we want to put an end to that. The President’s directive is clear: No community should be without access to drinking water,” he said.

The Gilotongan Water Association manages the facility’s operations and maintenance, with institutional and financial support from the municipal and barangay governments. The community-based organization is registered with the Department of Labor and Employment and incorporated with the Securities and Exchange Commission. /coa

World.title: Myanmar’s Coup President Barred From Upcoming 49th ASEAN Summit
World.content:
The Philippines announced Wednesday that Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from joining the 49th ASEAN summit and high-level meetings in Manila from November 15 to 17, upholding a ban imposed after the 2021 military coup.

Myanmar will instead be represented by the Director-General of its ASEAN affairs department, according to a statement issued by Manila’s Department of Foreign Affairs.

“We welcome this official confirmation that there is no place [at the summit] for junta leader Min Aung Hlaing,” Khin Ohmar, a prominent Myanmar democracy activist and founder of the Progressive Voice human rights foundation, told The Irrawaddy.

“ASEAN made the right decision in line with its principles. We have been demanding that no junta member be permitted to join the summit.”

She added that ASEAN would have sacrificed its credibility and responsibility to the people of Myanmar by inviting the junta leader, who faces a genocide ruling at the international court later this month.

Confirmation that the ban remains in place came after domestic and international rights groups warned the regional bloc against legitimizing a regime that is intensifying violence against civilians.

On Monday, the Special Advisory Council for Myanmar (SAC-M) and ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights urged regional leaders “to immediately confirm” that Min Aung Hlaing and his junta cohorts would be excluded from the summit.

It also called on ASEAN leaders to adopt “measurable benchmarks for compliance” with the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC), along with “a series of escalating punitive steps” if the junta continues to defy the peace plan.

Regime leaders were barred from regional summits for failing to implement the April 2021 consensus, including an immediate end to violence and constructive dialogue with the opposition.

The regime largely ignored the 5PC before formally rejecting it in a July 2026 vote by its rubber-stamp parliament. However, it continues to pay lip service to the plan.

During his latest talks with ASEAN special envoy Theresa Lazaro in Naypyitaw in October, Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe claimed the regime was implementing the 5PC “without compromising its national interests and sovereignty in accordance with its own roadmaps and objectives.”

The UN reports that at least 8,384 civilians have been killed by regime forces since the coup, in an escalating military campaign that has also left over 4 million displaced. Meanwhile, nearly 23,000 political prisoners remain in detention, including deposed democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

However, ASEAN members began bilateral engagement with the regime after it rebranded in civilian clothing in April following elections widely condemned as a sham. Since then, coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing has been invited on official visits to bloc members Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Malaysia.

Both Malaysia—once a vocal critic of the regime—and Thailand drew widespread condemnation from rights groups for hosting the junta leader.

Both nations defended the visits as pragmatic re-engagement in search of solutions to challenges they face, such as refugee repatriation for Malaysia and transborder issues for Thailand.

Critics have warned that bi-lateral engagement may sway a collective ASEAN decision to reintegrate the regime.

However, the move to uphold the summit ban marks a major setback for a junta desperate for legitimacy on the international stage.

“This is a huge blow to the junta. I am sure it has not expected this kind of decision,” Khin Ohmar commented. “It also signals that the junta’s election farce failed to confer legitimacy, since even those advocating its return to the international stage want to avoid being seen as complicit in its violence.”

World.title: Myanmar Junta Seeks Record Military Budget as Millions Struggle With Poverty
World.content:
The Myanmar regime plans to increase the military budget to a record high for the 2026-27 fiscal year, even as approximately one-third of the country’s population lives in poverty.

Since 2021, the regime has been waging war against several established ethnic armed organizations as well as newly emerged resistance forces, including the People’s Defense Force, across the country, spending a large portion of its budget on military expenses.

Last Thursday, the regime’s rubber-stamp Union Parliament (Pyidaungsu Hluttaw), where the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and its allies hold a majority of seats, debated a supplementary budget allocation bill.

The proposed allocation would bring total defense spending to 10.53 trillion kyats (US$5.01 billion), combining the initial 2026-27 fiscal year estimate of 7.95 trillion kyats with a supplementary grant of 2.58 trillion kyats.

Chit Swe, an Upper House lawmaker representing Ayeyarwady Region’s Constituency No. 11 and first deputy chair of the Joint Public Accounts Committee, urged parliament on November 5 to approve the regime’s proposed budgets, including the record-high military budget.

He said the committee had only eight days to verify the budget, with some items requiring ground observation, and that at least two weeks would be needed for verification.

If the supplementary allocations are approved, the budget deficit is projected to surge from 8.98 trillion kyats to 11.41 trillion kyats, he stated.

The military budget has surged continuously since the coup.

Under the last civilian government, led by ousted democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi, defense expenditure for the 2020-21 fiscal year stood at just 3.4 trillion kyats.

In the 2023-24 fiscal year, it increased to over 5.6 trillion kyats. Although defense expenditures for the remaining years were not officially released, the current budget figures show that spending has nearly doubled compared to 2023-24.

Meanwhile, approximately 17.9 million people are “multidimensionally poor”, while two-thirds of the population are either poor or at risk, according to a UN Development Programme (UNDP) report published on October 8.

After five years of military regime rule, Myanmar people continue to suffer from soaring prices of basic goods and living costs amid the civil war, and face personal safety and security concerns.

Although the budget is still in draft form, the proposed military expenditure has drawn widespread criticism from the public.

“The budgets that should be spent on the country’s education, health, social welfare and nation-building are instead being used to kill the people,” said Naung Yoe, a military defector who now works with the Myanmar Defense & Security Institute (MDSI), a research institute.

According to the MDSI, the Directorate of Defense Industries, which manufactures ammunition and aerial bombs used in the regime’s indiscriminate attacks, has consumed the largest share of the military’s budget since the coup.

“It is deeply tragic and unfortunate,” he said.

World.title: Mideast Crisis Fuels Oil Conflict in Myanmar’s Heartland
World.content:
Myanmar’s small-scale oil prospectors are under fire from all sides as rebels and the military battle to capture a cottage industry that is becoming increasingly lucrative amid the ongoing Middle East crisis.

“As long as we work here, bad luck can kill us,” said Htun Aung, a worker on an oil well in Myanmar’s arid heartlands.

“But if the reality of death is hard to face, then making a living is even harder,” said the 52-year-old, speaking under a pseudonym for security reasons.

Myanmar imports 90 percent of its fuel oil, official figures show, making it particularly vulnerable to supply issues caused by the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.

But the central region of Magwe hosts a hardscrabble industry of domestic prospectors manning grimy derricks that squelch up crude oil in humble quantities.

The area is dubbed “Anyar Dubai,” associating the Anyar or central dry zone landscape with the oil boom emirate, despite the pitiable US$50 per week earned by workers like Htun Aung who spend their days drenched in foul crude run-off.

With prices at Myanmar’s petrol pumps nearly double what they were in late February, the underground “black gold” is a coveted prize.

“We just want to live in peace,” said Htun Aung. “But now they strike from one side and the others strike from the other—they keep attacking each other.”

“We’ve had to flee three, four, five times already,” he added. “We run here, we run there. We fill up our motorbikes with fuel and run again.”

Digging in

Pro-democracy rebels claim to have controlled oil fields in Magwe’s Myaing Township since 2023.

They patrol the dusty territory in a westward crook of the Irrawaddy River in ragtag columns and outfitted with rocket-propelled grenades, flak jackets, tote bags and flip-flops.

Air and drone strikes in Myaing so far this year have already exceeded 2025’s total, according to ACLED, a monitor that estimates more than 100,000 people have died since the 2021 putsch.

Rebels shelter in foxholes, camouflaged among thousands of oil wells dug in an unregulated practice dating back centuries.

Engine winches chug day and night, plunging plumbing tubes dozens of meters down boreholes before dragging them up filled with crude oil slurry.

Prospectors pay landowners up to $3,500 to lease a spot to drill, one veteran said, with no guarantee they will hit oil.

Some wells yield dribbles while others gush, filling tarpaulin-lined pits and barrels with oil hauled off to improvised refineries for processing into petrol and diesel.

“Anyar Dubai” has been “going viral” for its plentiful supply, said rebel spokesman Pyae Phyo Kyaw, at a time when regime-held areas are rationing petrol.

He touted recent offensives fending off military advances but admitted being battered by counter-attacks.

“We see it primarily as an attempt to destroy what has been a strong supply route and source of revenue for us,” said the 35-year-old.

Myanmar’s military could not be reached for comment.

In September, the military claimed a month-long military operation captured over 130 wells in Myaing and 735 more in neighboring Pakokku Township.

Black market

Scores of pro-democracy factions and ethnic armed groups are fighting the military.

As the war grinds on, all sides battle to fill their war chests with the tax or trade of natural resources: gem mines, rare earth mineral deposits, gold or teak.

Oil projects are not generally contested.

The major ones are under staunch military guard, and on-the-books output is tiny by international standards at around 6,000 barrels a day last year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

But the artisanal fields are coveted by rebels precisely because of their modest size, according to Thomas Kean, a Myanmar consultant for the International Crisis Group.

“Part of the reason why they’re significant is because they’re not globally significant,” he said, explaining that they are small enough to thrive under the radar yet big enough to fund guerrillas.

Spiking oil prices may not directly drive conflict, said Kean, highlighting a broader military campaign to evict rebels from heartland footholds by squeezing revenue sources.

But as the spoils of war become more profitable, the stakes get higher.

“We’re talking about millions of barrels a year coming out of these oil fields,” he added. “With global prices what they are, that’s a significant amount of money.”

World.title: Shan State’s Scam Industry Expands Under Protection of Regime-Aligned Militias
World.content:
More than two years after high-profile anti-regime military offensives shattered many of Myanmar’s most notorious scam enclaves near the Chinese border, cyber-fraud syndicates have metastasized across the interior of Shan State, the country’s largest state.

Rather than wiping out the illicit multi-billion-dollar industry, the fall of Kokang’s capital, Laukkai, in January 2024 triggered an influx of scammers deeper into Myanmar—chiefly into Shan State’s interior and Karen State in the country’s south.

By mid-2026, cyber-scam syndicates had expanded across more than 63 percent of Shan State’s 55 townships, establishing footholds in at least 35 of them. This assessment is based on official enforcement and crackdown data published by the military regime’s Ministry of Information, alongside reports from four ethnic armed organizations (EAOs)—the United Wa State Army (UWSA), the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA), the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA).

The entrenchment of telecom fraud comes as Shan State continues to bear the brunt of decades of civil war. Observers point out that these conditions have fostered an acute crisis in which the unchecked proliferation of scam syndicates not only expands organized crime networks, but also threatens local socioeconomic stability and lures local young people into the illicit economy.

Operation 1027, an anti-regime offensive launched by the Three Brotherhood Alliance on October 27, 2023, toppled the cross-border empires run by Kokang’s notorious “Big Four” families—the Bai, Wei, Ming and Liu clans. The alliance comprised the TNLA, MNDAA and Arakan Army. Parallel crackdowns were launched in areas controlled by the UWSA and NDAA. Yet far from marking the demise of the scam industry, the dismantling of those border scam complexes simply scattered the surviving networks, driving them deep into Shan State’s interior.

From the border to the interior

According to local residents, hundreds of Chinese nationals arrived in southern Shan State’s Laihka Township around November 2023, approximately a month after Operation 1027 began. Locals said the newcomers first erected compounds near Manpang Village before launching scam operations.

Instead of operating out of massive, conspicuous complexes housing huge numbers of people as they previously did, they rented homes dispersed throughout residential neighborhoods to fragment their workforce, and even set up makeshift tent encampments in rural villages and forests.

Starting in February 2026, the regime began conducting raids against online scam compounds in Laihka. According to official releases, as of the end of October, 129 Chinese nationals had been arrested, comprising the majority of those detained.

According to statements given by detainees, they crossed into Myanmar from Xishuangbanna, in the far south of China’s Yunnan Province, entering UWSA-controlled Panghsang and the NDAA-controlled Mong La area. From there, coordinated networks facilitated their phased, step-by-step relocation across northern, southern and eastern Shan State.

Similarly, in northern Shan, residents noted that telecom fraud operators began trickling into Tangyan town in early 2024.

According to UWSA statements, during crackdowns on scam operations in Tangyan in November 2024 and July 2025, Wa forces arrested over 1,000 people, 829 of whom were Chinese nationals.

The military junta likewise launched its own raids and arrests in Tangyan across 2024 and 2025.

Despite raids conducted by both the junta and the UWSA, a military sweep proved that these criminal syndicates were still operating in Tangyan in April 2026. During a raid on an online scam camp near Kaung San Village, the military reported arresting 123 individuals, 103 of whom were Chinese nationals.

“Local youths worked at the scam centers. Usually, whenever there’s a raid, those who can run simply flee. Some get away, some don’t. But we’ve never heard of the actual bosses being caught,” a Tangyan resident said.

Throughout 2025, these fraud networks spread rapidly into numerous townships in Shan State: Mongyai and Hsipaw in northern Shan; Nansang and Mongpan in southern Shan; and Kengtung and Mong Hsat in eastern Shan.

In October 2026, the regime announced the arrest of 75 Chinese nationals and 12 Myanmar citizens involved in online scams in southern Shan State’s Hopong Township, along with the seizure of related equipment. This indicates that scam operations have spread to the doorstep of Taunggyi, the capital of Shan State.

Ko Michael, an analyst who tracks cyber-scam activities, said the crackdowns by both the regime and local armed groups have stalled because they consistently fail to net the masterminds.

“They aren’t shooting the birds; they’re just shaking the trees. So the birds simply fly from one tree to another. Everything gets scattered around. That’s why this problem has become so difficult to contain,” he said.

At the same time, while scam operations have proliferated into the interior, they have by no means vanished from the borderlands. None of the ethnic armed groups conducting anti-scam crackdowns have declared their regions entirely free of fraud hubs. Operations persist in the border town of Muse, and recruitment s seeking workers for scam centers in Tachileik on the Thai border continue to appear daily on social media. The fact that cyber-scam operations continue to operate on Shan State’s borders while simultaneously spreading inland raises a key question. Who is enabling this aggressive proliferation?

Who is providing protection?

The vast majority of individuals arrested in Shan State’s scam hubs are Chinese nationals; in some locations, nearly every person detained was from China. Yet it would be utterly impossible for foreign nationals to arrive in large groups and establish, let alone operate, these telecom fraud enterprises without local assistance.

Crucially, armed organizations and security outfits controlling the territory in these areas are the linchpins ensuring the survival of these organized crime syndicates. When cyber-scams first proliferated across the Kokang, Wa and Mong La borderlands, they took root strictly under the control of local armed actors.

In many parts of Shan State, regime-aligned armed factions have turned these operations into lucrative revenue streams, according to local residents and individuals formerly involved in the trade.

“The total proliferation of scams across Shan State didn’t happen because of just one group. But I want to stress this: it would be completely impossible to run without the military’s involvement,” said Ko Michael, the scam-operation monitor.

In December 2025, after the military raided an online scam compound in Hsipaw Township, state media reported the arrest of three members of the Shan State Progress Party (SSPP), one of the major Shan armed groups. Concurrently, residents point out that in Muse, Laihka and several other areas, local militia outfits—including the Namhkam Myoma, Pansay, Kaungkha, Manpang and Wanpang militias—receive payoffs in exchange for facilitating relocations, providing physical security and protection, and transporting workers to scam centers.

“The scam business and armed groups are inseparable. Without an armed group, you simply cannot run a scam operation. It’s the armed groups that provide the protection,” said a resident of Muse.

The nexus between armed actors and telecom fraud extends to Myanmar’s most powerful ethnic armed organization, the UWSA, which has been heavily implicated in the scam industry despite its current anti-scam crackdowns.

“The ones who really laid the solid groundwork and operated these scam rings at scale were the Wa. Top Wa leaders were directly involved,” said Dr. Hla Kyaw Zaw, a veteran analyst of China-Myanmar affairs.

The Chinese state-produced documentary “The Demise of Telecom Fraud in Northern Myanmar,” which covered the anti-scam crackdowns and was aired last month, identifies UWSA-controlled territory as the incubator for northern Myanmar’s scam economy. It claimed that Bao Yanban, chief of Mong Pawk, a town in the Wa region, amassed so much wealth from the scams that he would sun-dry banknotes on rooftops to prevent mold.

Protection for scam operators has come not only from local militias, but directly from the regime itself.

In late 2023, as the Three Brotherhood Alliance was attempting to capture Laukkai during Operation 1027, the military regime sheltered top Kokang scam kingpins from the Big Four families in Naypyitaw. Among them was Bai Suocheng, the former leader of the Kokang Self-Administered Zone and head of the regime-aligned Border Guard Force.

It was only under immense pressure from Beijing in January 2024 that the regime finally handed these high-profile suspects over to Chinese security forces in Naypyitaw. They were subsequently tried in Chinese courts, where harsh penalties—including death sentences—were handed down.

What is the impact?

Despite the crackdowns and legal cases, online scam syndicates have continued to fan out from the northern Shan-China border across the entirety of Shan State, causing severe social harm in every community they penetrate.

With legitimate employment opportunities devastated by the country’s ongoing military conflict, cyber-scam compounds have emerged as places where local youth can make quick money.

A northern Shan resident who previously worked in a scam compound explained that the prospect of “easy money” causes those who have worked in the industry to lose interest in conventional jobs.

“When you return from there [working at a scam center], you come back with a lot of money. You just don’t want to do outside manual work anymore. Once that money runs out, you don’t go looking for decent, ordinary jobs. That’s true for about 80 percent of the people who go to work there,” the northern Shan resident explained.

As the industry has expanded, training courses designed to teach people how to run telecom scams have begun popping up in Shan State, according to sources close to the industry.

“There are training courses opened by people who worked inside scam compounds. They teach combined computer and communication skills. They teach basic things like how to defraud people out of money. How many words per minute you need to type—that’s something only people who worked there can teach,” said a resident of Kyaukme in northern Shan State. Citing security concerns, the resident declined to disclose the exact locations or other details of the training centers.

Scam operations also serve as a seemingly safe and profitable haven for young people trying to escape military conscription by the regime. The conscription law, which has been on the books for years but only enforced since 2024, requires men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve up to two years in the military.

A Kyaukme resident who sought to evade conscription by working in a scam compound said he did so for his own safety. “My name came up on the conscription list. A lot of people from our area worked there. They said things were going well there, inviting us to come over,” he said.

“Quite a lot of young people ended up going,” he added.

World.title: Regime Summons German Envoy Over Call for Coup Releases
World.content:
YANGON—The Myanmar regime’s Foreign Ministry said it summoned Germany’s top resident diplomat on Tuesday over a Facebook video calling for authorities to “unconditionally release” ousted politicians, including Aung San Suu Kyi.

Germany’s mission head Mathias Licharz posted the video on Sunday, standing outside the former Yangon residence of Win Myint, the president of Aung San Suu Kyi’s government that was removed in a 2021 coup.

The junta behind the coup organized elections installing a nominally civilian government this spring, although analysts regard it as a fig leaf for ongoing military rule.

Licharz said in his message, scheduled for Win Myint’s 75th birthday, that the United Nations still regards him as the “legitimate president” of Myanmar.

Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry said Licharz was summoned for a meeting with deputy minister Ko Ko Kyaw, “warned against the video” and handed an aide-memoire.

“Should the Chargé d’Affaires choose to recognize U Win Myint as President and wish to discontinue his service in Myanmar, the Ministry would have no objection,” a statement said.

Myanmar has been riven by civil war since the 2021 coup, as pro-democracy guerrillas rose up and long-simmering ethnic minority insurgencies challenging central rule boiled over.

The ministry statement accused Licharz of “intentional conduct” that “appeared to fuel opposition to the host country and its Government, thereby inciting internal unrest.”

“The Deputy Minister strongly warned against recurrence of such act and informed him that any similar conduct would be treated with utmost seriousness and would take appropriate actions,” it said.

Germany’s embassy in Myanmar did not respond immediately to a request for comment.

Win Myint was jailed in the February 2021 coup, which ended Myanmar’s decade-long democratic experiment.

Authorities said in April he had been pardoned of his post-coup convictions—charges that supporters and analysts say were confected to oust the government.

However, Licharz said in his video message his efforts to meet Win Myint had been unfruitful.

“There is only one conclusion,” he said. “U Wint Myint is not a free man. He’s not allowed to meet with whom he would like to meet and he’s not allowed to communicate independently.”

Aung San Suu Kyi remains detained but was moved to house arrest in the capital Naypyitaw this year, authorities say, where access to the 81-year-old Nobel Peace Prize laureate remains tightly controlled.

Licharz called for authorities to “unconditionally release all those who are arbitrarily detained including U Win Myint and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi.”

World.title: Myanmar Embassies Push Tax, Remittance Rules as Migrant Backlash Grows Across Asia
World.content:
Embassies operated by Myanmar’s cash-strapped military regime have intensified efforts to extract foreign currency from overseas workers, even as migrant opposition grows across Asia.

For the past two weeks, Myanmar missions have repeatedly ordered that all passport applications must be accompanied by official evidence of remittance and tax payments.

The regime enforced a mandatory 25 percent remittance requirement alongside 2 percent income tax on migrant workers in 2023 — measures widely seen as a bid to bolster foreign currency reserves amid severe shortages.

In the latest notices, Myanmar missions in Singapore, Hong Kong and Macau declared Monday that migrants applying for a Passport for Job (PJ) or PJ extension must include proof of tax payment and remittance of a quarter of their earnings over the past three months through official regime channels.

“The Myanmar embassy is issuing the order but nobody wants to use official remittance channels,” a 30-year-old Myanmar national working at a florist in Singapore told The Irrawaddy.

“Applicants may comply with the rule for three months, but otherwise, they will continue to use alternative channels that are convenient, pay more, and don’t siphon money to the military.”

He added that waiting times for passport extension appointments have also expanded dramatically under the regime’s new digital identification system (UID), prompting worker fears of being stranded in a legal limbo.

“A friend of mine has been waiting three months for an appointment; previously it took just two weeks to extend a passport.”

The precise number of Myanmar migrants in Singapore is unknown, but Myanmar labor department data from 2024 suggested a sharp increase since 2021, prompting predictions they could reach 200,000 in a few years.

Other major destinations for Myanmar migrant workers are South Korea and Japan, which recruit through formal MOU frameworks and offer comparatively higher wages.

Regime embassies in Seoul and Tokyo were among the first to double down, issuing notices that workers must comply with remittance and tax rules in exchange for passport extensions.

“It’s a new requirement. Even If workers have not used official channels before, they must do so before applying for an extension,” a South Korea-based Myanmar national who assists migrant workers told The Irrawaddy.

“Workers have no option if they need their passports extended. So, they have to comply for at least three months,” she said.

She echoed the complaints of long appointment waiting times, higher application costs, and workers’ reluctance to use official channels that offer lower exchange rates while funneling money to the military regime.

Meanwhile, the regime’s embassy in Thailand — home to the largest Myanmar migrant community of roughly four million — is reportedly demanding remittance and tax evidence before it issues or extends PJs. Agents say the embassy requires proof of payments, adding that appointment waiting times are unpredictable.

“The process is really complicated now. We have been told to submit remittance proof, even though they haven’t publicly announced it,” a Bangkok-based agent told The Irrawaddy.

The regime’s Certificate of Identity (CI) process to identify undocumented workers in Thailand was rejected by over 2 million migrants in a recent poll. Only 15,000 out of nearly 750,000 ID-less migrants have shown up at Thai CI centers amid a widespread boycott triggered by the tax and remittance rules.

Thailand’s Labor Ministry has voiced opposition to the rules, which it views as a violation of worker rights. However, regime Labor Minister Maung Myint pressed the issue on Sunday, insisting that CI applicants must abide by the remittance and tax mandates.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Routs Resistance HQ on Bago–Mon Border
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime says it has seized 11 resistance bases along the border of Bago Region and Mon State, including the shadow National Unity Government (NUG)’s Special Region Military Command.

Regime media said the military launched a major “counter-terrorism operation” from Theinzayat along the mountainous route through Mon State’s Kyaikhto and Bago’s Shwegyin townships on Nov. 3.

From Nov. 4 to 7, it seized four temporary posts of the ethnic Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) in Kyaikhto.

On Nov. 8, the regime seized another five resistance bases, including the Special Region Military Command northeast of Theinzayat, which it said was the nerve center of regional operations of the heartland People’s Defense Forces (PDF) loyal to the shadow government.

Here the resistance manufactured “homemade mortars, firearms, ammunition and explosives for their operations,” the report said.

The regime previously bombed the command on Sept. 24, killing six people including prominent Air Force defector Nay Win Aung.

A PDF fighter in the southern region confirmed the loss of the regional HQ.

“Yes, it’s true, the situation is worse than in the news,” he told The Irrawaddy.

Other resistance sources said intense fighting continues, ranging from ground battles to airstrikes using drones and fighter jets.

Neither the KNLA nor the NUG responded to inquiries from The Irrawaddy.

The regime said it seized 97 small arms, 12,285 ammunitions, 362 drops bombs, 139 mines as well as drones and two vehicles but attached no figures to the resistance’s “heavy casualties.”

Prominent military defector Zin Yaw said the regime raid seems to have taken the resistance by surprise, quoting sources as saying it involved roughly 1,000 troops.

“We have to wait and see how far they can advance into resistance territories since resistance forces are on high alert now and the clashes will become more intense,” he added.

World.title: Blue Tsunami Claims a Congressional Champion of Myanmar’s Cause
World.content:
It is now widely known that Republicans suffered a crushing defeat in last week’s U.S. midterm elections. Some voters simply disliked the Republican candidates running in their districts, while others, who might ordinarily have voted Republican, chose to vote against them simply because they belonged to Trump’s party. Their thinking was essentially this: “I want to teach Trump a lesson. As long as it’s not your guy, I’ll vote for anyone else.”

Take Senator Susan Collins of Maine, for example. Known as a moderate Republican, she defied her own party by voting alongside Democrats during Trump’s second impeachment trial to convict him for his role in the January 6 insurrection, earning his lasting enmity in the process. Yet she, too, lost her seat in this election.

Another casualty of the election was my own congressional representative, Congressman Bill Huizenga, who represents Michigan’s Fourth Congressional District. His defeat represents a painful loss for those of us who support Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement. We have lost someone who has done a great deal to advance our cause.

Huizenga is a seasoned congressman who has served eight terms since 2011. As a senior member of Congress, he held influential positions on several important committees. He served as vice chair of the House Financial Services Committee, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia, and vice chair of the Congressional Burma Caucus.

Through his involvement with the Burma Caucus, in particular, he supported Myanmar’s cause both publicly and behind the scenes. Some of these efforts are ones I am sharing publicly for the first time.

One such instance involved Ashin Nat Zaw, a Myanmar-born monk from Buffalo, New York, who was detained by the junta during a visit to Myanmar. The U.S. government, through the State Department and its embassy in Myanmar, sought his release, as he had returned to Myanmar as a U.S. citizen. Huizenga played a role in that effort.

I know this firsthand because a community liaison from Buffalo contacted me and asked for help connecting her with Huizenga’s office. I facilitated that connection. These were the kinds of things he did quietly, behind the scenes, without seeking publicity.

On the public front, he worked to advance the BRAVE Burma Act and helped push for its passage by the House. After Trump issued his order terminating Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Myanmar nationals, not a single Republican member of Congress seemed willing to speak up. Huizenga, however, joined Democratic Congressman Ami Bera of California, Gregory Meeks of New York and others in introducing legislation seeking to restore TPS for Myanmar nationals. However, the protections were ultimately terminated in August despite a temporary court-ordered reprieve.

Just last month, he also spearheaded a letter, signed by five other bipartisan members of the Burma Caucus, urging the United States to continue supporting Ambassador Kyaw Moe Tun as Myanmar’s permanent representative to the United Nations.

But none of these efforts happened in a vacuum. We must recognize that members of Congress are elected to represent the people of their own districts—their American constituents—and to address their concerns. They have no obligation to do anything for Myanmar. It is the responsibility of the Myanmar community in each congressional district to educate, persuade and encourage its representatives to take an interest in our cause.

And this does not happen overnight. It takes time, patience and the cultivation of relationships. There are various ways to establish that initial connection. Someone who already knows the congressman might introduce us. We might repeatedly write letters, submit statements and request meetings until we finally get an opportunity to speak with him. We might also reach out through religious channels, among other approaches.

One thing is certain: unlike some wealthier communities, we Burmese have never had the financial resources to buy our way into political influence.

Before the 2021 military coup in Myanmar, Huizenga knew little about the country. Although there was a Burmese community in his district, it was nowhere near as large as those in Indianapolis or Fort Wayne. To put things into perspective, approximately 350,000 votes were cast in this congressional district in the 2026 election, while the entire Burmese community’s voting strength amounted to only about 4,000 votes.

We had to work extremely hard to break through and get him to pay attention to Myanmar’s affairs. The fact that our city already had a Burma Center, established some 15 years ago, gave us an advantage. Through five years of cultivating relationships, explaining our cause, and educating his office, we developed close ties with him and his staff. Even the recent letter supporting Kyaw Moe Tun was the result of our activists suggesting to his office that such a letter would be worthwhile and guiding them toward issuing it.

This is how grassroots advocacy works.

Losing someone with whom we had built such a close and trusting relationship is an enormous loss for us. The newly elected Democratic congressman who replaces him will likely know little or nothing about Myanmar. We will have to start all over again, building relationships and educating him about our cause from scratch. Furthermore, as a freshman congressman, he will have little influence in the House and is unlikely to secure a position on any of its important committees.

We did everything we could to help Huizenga win reelection. But, as mentioned earlier, our community’s approximately 4,000 votes were a mere drop in the ocean compared with the 350,000 votes cast in the district. He, too, was swept away by the blue tsunami.

I hate to say it, but even within our own Burmese community, there were people who did not want to vote for him because they viewed him as something of a MAGA Republican—a Trump supporter.

In my view, however, even if he had been reelected, his presence alone would not have significantly altered the balance of power between Democrats and Republicans in Congress. But among the 435 members of the House of Representatives, only four or five genuinely understand and support Myanmar’s cause. Losing even one of them is a significant setback, and finding a replacement is no easy task.

That is why, when it came time to vote, I encouraged members of our community to consider splitting their tickets. They could vote for Democrats in other races if they wished, but I urged them to vote for Huizenga, the Republican, in our congressional race. Unfortunately, our efforts still fell short.

In addition to Huizenga, Representative Young Kim (R-California), another member of the Burma Caucus, lost her reelection bid. Longtime supporter of Myanmar Senator Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) will retire from his Senate position and political career in January 2027. Myanmar desperately needs newer members of Congress to champion its cause.

I would like to take this opportunity to express my deepest gratitude and respect to Congressman Huizenga for his unwavering support of Myanmar’s cause. In appreciation of his efforts, I am sharing some of his behind-the-scenes contributions that many people may not have known about. I would also like to extend my special thanks to his entire staff, who worked closely with our community and with whom we developed a close and trusting relationship.

Thank you, Congressman Huizenga, for standing with the people of Myanmar.

Than N. Oo is a co-founder of advocacy group Free Myanmar and writes frequently about Myanmar’s political developments.

World.title: Kazakhstan Signs $1.2 Billion in Energy Agreements at COP31
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has signed agreements worth approximately $1.2 billion to develop renewable energy and modernize gas infrastructure during the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

The agreements provide for the construction of wind power plants with capacities of 150 megawatts in the Turkistan Region and one gigawatt in the Kostanai Region. They also cover the Aqyl Energy project, which involves installing 1.35 million smart gas meters with remote data transmission. They also signed additional documents to expand international cooperation on environmental protection.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov attended the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations (UN) Framework Convention on Climate Change on the instruction of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. In his address, he outlined Kazakhstan’s environmental priorities, including reforestation, water security and the transition to cleaner energy, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on Nov. 11.

Bektenov said the Taza Qazaqstan initiative had evolved into a nationwide movement, with more than six million people participating in environmental activities. Over the past five years, the country has planted nearly 1.7 billion trees, with another 270 million seedlings planned for 2027. This would bring Kazakhstan closer to its target of planting two billion trees.

He also called for stronger international cooperation on water security, highlighting Tokayev’s proposal to establish an International Water Organization under the UN’s auspices.

“Addressing environmental challenges requires closer cooperation,” Bektenov said, referring to the Regional Ecological Summit held in Astana in April. The summit resulted in the adoption of the Declaration on Environmental Solidarity of Central Asia, providing a framework for regional cooperation.

Kazakhstan is also expanding its renewable energy capacity. The share of renewables in the country’s energy mix quadrupled over the past six years, reaching 8% this year. The government aims to increase it to 15% by 2030.

Other priorities include nuclear energy, wind and solar power, green hydrogen production, and a joint Green Energy Corridor project with Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan to facilitate clean electricity exports.

Bektenov also highlighted Alatau City as a prospective low-carbon urban development project and Kazakhstan’s use of artificial intelligence and satellite monitoring to forecast natural hazards and improve emergency prevention.

At the national pavilion, Kazakhstan presented projects focused on reforestation, methane emission reduction, waste recycling and industrial decarbonization. The exhibition also featured initiatives to restore the Northern Aral Sea, protect the Caspian ecosystem and develop a green energy corridor across the Caspian Sea to Europe.

The pavilion showcased digital solutions, including a regional AI-powered carbon platform, satellite-based climate monitoring and the proposed Caspian Climate Shield adaptation system.

On Nov. 10, Kazakhstan launched its Just Energy Transition Investment Platform (QaJET) at COP31 in Antalya, with the EBRD offering up to $100 million in concessional financing and grants and up to $1 billion in potential direct financing.

World.title: Kazakhstan Tests Tokenized Government Securities in First National Bank Issuance
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has taken its first practical step toward introducing tokenized securities into its capital market, with the National Bank placing 10 billion tenge (US$2.2 million) worth of digital short-term notes on the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE). The issuance marks a transition from establishing the legal framework for digital financial assets to testing how they can function within the country’s existing financial infrastructure.

The auction took place on Nov. 9, with the same issue offered simultaneously in traditional and tokenized forms. The National Bank offered the full 50 billion tenge (US$110.9 million), including 10 billion tenge in tokenized notes. The securities have a maturity of 91 days and a weighted average annual yield of 15.72%.

Investor demand reached 70.2 billion tenge (US$155.7 million), exceeding the offering by 1.4 times, the bank reported.

The parallel placement allowed the National Bank to test the new technology while maintaining identical pricing conditions for both forms of the instrument.

How tokenized notes work

Tokenized notes are financial instruments issued in digital form, with investors’ ownership rights recorded through a digital platform. The National Bank remains the issuer and is responsible for fulfilling its obligations to investors.

KASE provides the infrastructure for issuing, placing and circulating the notes. KASE records ownership rights on its digital financial assets platform and reflects them in the Central Securities Depository’s registry, while the KASE Clearing Center handles clearing and settlement.

This arrangement integrates digital technology with established financial market institutions rather than replacing the existing system.

What it means for the market

The main potential benefit of tokenization is making capital markets more accessible and efficient. Digital platforms can facilitate the issuance and transfer of financial instruments, automate certain operations and potentially reduce transaction costs.

For businesses, this could create additional channels for raising capital. For investors, it could expand the range of available instruments and potentially lower entry barriers through fractional ownership.

However, these benefits will depend on market adoption, investor demand, liquidity and the reliability of the regulatory and technological infrastructure.

Economist Ruslan Sultanov, commenting on the development in his Tengenomika channel publication, described the issuance as an important step in moving Kazakhstan from building the regulatory and technological foundations for tokenization to its practical application.

From regulation to implementation

Kazakhstan’s legislative framework for issuing and circulating digital financial assets took effect on May 1. KASE became the country’s first registered operator of a digital financial assets platform and trading platform.
