National Bank Chairman Timur Suleimenov said the next priority was to expand the infrastructure’s practical use, attract new issuers and broaden the range of digital financial instruments.

KASE is also prepared to assist potential issuers with structuring transactions, onboarding and preparing securities for placement.

The first issuance demonstrates that tokenized instruments can operate within Kazakhstan’s existing financial market infrastructure. The next test will be whether businesses and other market participants adopt the technology more broadly, turning an initial transaction into a functioning segment of the domestic capital market.

World.title: Astana to Host World Taekwondo Grand Prix Final for First Time in 2026
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan will host the World Taekwondo Grand Prix Final for the first time on Nov. 28-29, bringing together some of the world’s leading athletes in Olympic weight categories, the Kazakhstan Taekwondo Federation reported.

The tournament will be held in Astana and will serve as the final event of the prestigious international competition series, which awards ranking points and helps determine the world’s top taekwondo athletes.

Only athletes who qualify through the world rankings will compete in the final, making it one of the key events on the international taekwondo calendar. The Grand Prix series plays an important role in the sport’s Olympic qualification system, with ranking points contributing to the selection process for the Olympic Games.

Hosting the 2026 final reflects the development of taekwondo in Kazakhstan and the confidence of the international federation in the country’s ability to stage major sporting events.

The tournament is also expected to provide an important competitive opportunity for athletes preparing for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.

Earlier, Kazakhstan has officially been selected as the host country of the 2027 World Taekwondo Championships (WT), marking the first time the global competition will take place in Central Asia.

World.title: Kazakhstan Launches Locally Produced Stadler Coaches on Astana-Almaty Route
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has launched its first passenger train equipped with locally manufactured Stadler coaches on the Astana-Almaty route, marking a new stage in the country’s railway fleet renewal and its cooperation with Swiss rail manufacturer Stadler.

Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), the national railway operator, has already received more than 100 coaches, with a contract providing for the phased delivery of 557 coaches by 2030.

The first train departed from Astana’s Nurly Zhol railway station on Nov. 11 and will run daily as passenger train No. 3/4 on the Nurly Zhol-Almaty-2 route. It leaves Astana at 1:10 p.m. and arrives in Almaty at 8:30 a.m. the following day.

The coaches are manufactured in Kazakhstan using Stadler’s Swiss technology and adapted to the country’s climatic conditions. They are designed to operate in temperatures ranging from minus 50 to plus 45 degrees Celsius and have an expected service life of 40 years.

“The coaches from Stadler from Switzerland are based on Swiss technology. They have individual temperature control in each compartment, allowing passengers to adjust the temperature by two degrees up or down. This makes the journey really comfortable,” said Stefan Giese, chief director for maintenance and repair, in a comment to the Astana Times.

He added that the coaches follow European design standards adapted to Kazakhstan’s operating environment and will gradually be deployed on major railway routes across the country.

Compartment coaches accommodate 40 passengers, while open-plan sleeping coaches seat 58. The facilities include climate control, individual lighting, 220-volt power outlets, USB and USB-C ports, Wi-Fi, video surveillance and dedicated luggage areas. Special arrangements have also been made for passengers with reduced mobility. Each train includes a buffet coach.

Speaking at the launch ceremony, Deputy Minister of Transport Zhanibek Taizhanov said the project represents not only an upgrade of passenger rail transport but also an investment in domestic industrial development.

“The project is being implemented directly in our country. It is not only about renewing railway transport but also about developing domestic industry, creating jobs, introducing modern technologies and improving the qualifications of Kazakh specialists,” he said.

Taizhanov described cooperation with Stadler as a joint investment and industrial project aimed at the country’s long-term development. He added that the launch was only the beginning of a broader effort to make modern, safe and comfortable coaches a standard across Kazakhstan’s railway network.

According to KTZ, its passenger transportation subsidiary has accepted more than 100 Stadler coaches. The contract предусматривает the delivery of 557 passenger coaches in stages through 2030, followed by servicing and maintenance.

The next Stadler-equipped train is scheduled to enter service on the Nurly Zhol-Semei route on Nov. 13.

Tickets are available through the national railway ticketing website, bilet.railways.kz, and at railway ticket offices.

World.title: Tokayev Highlights AI-Driven Security Risks at CSTO Summit in Moscow
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for stronger cooperation among member states of the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) to combat international terrorism, counter illicit drug trafficking and strengthen information security amid the growing influence of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies on Nov. 11, Akorda reported.

Tokayev thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for hosting the meeting and praised Russia’s chairmanship of the CSTO this year, describing it as productive.

The meeting was attended by Belarus’ President Alexander Lukashenko, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon and CSTO Secretary General Taalatbek Masadykov. The leaders reviewed key aspects of cooperation within the organization, assessed its activities in 2026 and outlined priorities for the coming period. They also exchanged views on pressing international and regional security issues.

The meeting concluded with the adoption of a Joint Statement by the CSTO Collective Security Council. The leaders also signed a series of documents aimed at further strengthening the organization’s collective security framework based on the shared interests of its member states.

Kazakhstan also called for stronger international dialogue and mutual trust at the International Forum on Collective Security in Moscow, held on Nov. 10. Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi emphasized that a stable international order should be grounded in international law and the willingness of countries to maintain dialogue despite serious disagreements, stressing that Eurasia’s future should not be shaped by confrontation or dividing lines.

World.title: Kazakhstan Invites US Businesses to Partner in Critical Minerals Sector at B20 Summit
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has invited U.S. businesses to develop long-term industrial and technology partnerships in critical minerals, highlighting its resource base, infrastructure, regulatory framework and skilled workforce.

Kanat Sharlapayev, chairman of the Presidium of the Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs, outlined these advantages at a B20 Summit panel on Central Asia-U.S. public-private partnerships in Washington on Nov. 9-11.

Sharlapayev described Kazakhstan’s competitive advantages as Superfecta, combining four factors: diverse mineral resources, developed infrastructure, predictable regulation and qualified personnel, the chamber’s press service reported on Nov. 11.

“From 2022 to 2025, capital investment in metal ore mining in Kazakhstan increased by approximately 62%, while total investment in geological exploration grew 2.5 times to reach $1 billion,” he said.

He highlighted opportunities in deeper mineral processing, technology transfer and industrial development, citing the Sarytogan graphite project, with resources exceeding 65 million tons, Taza Metal Technologies’ high-purity manganese sulfate production and the Akbulak joint exploration project between Kazgeology and Cove Kaz Capital Group, where rare earth elements, including neodymium and praseodymium, have been identified.

International companies operating in Kazakhstan include Rio Tinto, Fortescue, Ivanhoe Mines, Arras Minerals, B2Gold and East Star Resources.

On the sidelines of the summit, Sharlapayev met with Dan Levine, founder and managing partner of Tenfore Holdings, to discuss cooperation in advanced manufacturing, robotics, smart logistics and artificial intelligence.

He also met Heidi Crebo-Rediker, senior fellow in the Center for Geoeconomic Studies at the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), to discuss private investment in infrastructure and critical minerals, public-private partnerships and long-term financing for small and medium-sized businesses.

The B20 Summit is taking place in Washington on Nov. 9-11 as part of the U.S. presidency of the G20. Kazakhstan’s business delegation includes representatives from industry, energy, agribusiness and transport and logistics.

World.title: Kazakhstan Wins Coursera Award for Digital Transformation of Higher Education
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Science and Higher Education has received the Coursera Learning Excellence Award 2026 for integrating international online education into the national higher education system and expanding digital and artificial intelligence (AI) skills development.

The award was presented at the London FWD event, which brought together education technology platforms Coursera and Udemy and key partners from Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA). Other organizations recognized included consulting firm EY, British bank Nationwide and Italian technology company bIP. The event was led by Coursera Chief Executive Officer Greg Hart, the ministry reported on Nov. 6.

The award recognizes Kazakhstan’s progress in integrating international online courses into university curricula and developing digital competencies relevant to the modern economy.

More than 292,000 students earn Coursera certificates

Kazakhstan began its partnership with Coursera in 2022, making the initiative an important part of its higher education transformation.

Through the program, students have gained access to thousands of international online courses and professional certification programs offered by leading universities and industry partners.

More than 292,000 students have earned certificates, bringing the total to more than 682,000. Cumulative learning time has surpassed 5.35 million hours, and Kazakh universities have recognized 163,098 academic credits.

This year, the ministry allocated 38,184 Coursera licenses across 100 higher education institutions. More than 100 universities are integrating platform courses into their academic programs and recognizing online learning outcomes as part of formal education.

The latest award follows the 2025 recognition of Minister of Science and Higher Education Sayasat Nurbek, who received the Coursera Learning Hero Award.

The ministry continues to prioritize digital education, international partnerships and the development of skills needed in the modern labor market, including AI competencies and entrepreneurship.

World.title: Foreigners to Obtain IIN in Kazakhstan Within One Working Day Under New Online Pilot
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs is launching a pilot project allowing foreign citizens to apply for individual identification numbers (IINs) online through the QazETA mobile application. The service will be available via the MAQ digital migration services platform, with applications processed within one working day, according to a ministry order.

The pilot project was introduced under Order No. 825 of Nov. 2, which entered into force on Nov. 9.

Under the new procedure, foreign applicants must register or log in to the QazETA application and consent to the processing of their personal data. They must then photograph their identity document, complete biometric authentication and a liveness check, and confirm their geolocation, reported inbusiness.kz on Nov. 10.

The system will automatically generate an application, allowing users to review the information and provide any additional details if necessary.

Authorities will then verify the applicant’s entry into Kazakhstan through the Berkut Unified Centralized System. If the verification is successful, the application will be forwarded to the Ministry of Internal Affairs for review.

The ministry will check the application’s completeness and accuracy, verify that the submitted information matches the attached identity documents, and ensure that no duplicate IIN has been issued.

Once all requirements are met, the ministry will generate an IIN and forward it to the relevant information system. Applicants will be able to check the result through the MAQ platform in the QazETA application, using the sections titled “View IIN Application List” or “View IIN.”

Users will also be able to view and download their IIN registration certificate.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s proposed hourly wage system: Who stands to benefit – workers, employers or state?
World.content:
Introduction of hourly wages in Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan plans to introduce a minimum hourly wage from 2027. The announcement was made on 11 November by Deputy Minister of Labour and Social Protection Zaur Aliyev during a meeting of the Milli Majlis Committee on Labour and Social Policy. According to Aliyev, the new system will initially apply to agricultural production and the catering sector.

Back in 2024, we reported that the introduction of hourly wages was under discussion in Azerbaijan. The main provisions of the proposed amendments to the Labour Code have now emerged.

The government and MPs have presented the initiative as a way to make employment more flexible and bring informal employment into the formal economy. However, critics have raised a different question:

Who will benefit from hourly wages, and could the system be used to split full-time positions into part-time roles in the public sector?

What does the draft law propose?

According to media reports, the draft law provides for hourly wages in two cases: when an employment contract is concluded for less than one month or when the working week does not exceed 20 hours. The Cabinet of Ministers will determine which sectors the new system will apply to.

The draft law also includes several safeguards for employees:

If an employee works less than one hour in a day, they must be paid at least the minimum hourly rate. Any part of an hour must be paid as a full hour.

For part-time employees paid a monthly salary, wages cannot fall below the minimum wage calculated in proportion to their working hours.

In organisations funded by the state budget, hourly wages can only be introduced if the organisation’s existing pay system allows for them, according to APA.

The minimum hourly rate has not yet been announced. According to Musa Guliyev, chairman of the Milli Majlis Committee on Labour and Social Policy, the draft law stipulates that:

The minimum hourly rate cannot be lower than the hourly equivalent of the minimum monthly wage.

However, the deputy minister of labour and social protection said that the proposed minimum hourly rate would be set above this level.

Since January 2025, Azerbaijan’s minimum monthly wage has stood at 400 manats (approximately $235). According to calculations by economist Natig Jafarli, this translates into around 2 manats and 50 gapiks per hour (approximately $1.47) for a five-day working week, or around 2 manats (approximately $1.18) for a six-day working week.

What do authorities say?

Musa Guliyev believes that hourly wages could make it easier for women with young children, students and pensioners to enter the labour market. According to him, the current minimum monthly wage system creates “inequality and social injustice” for part-time, seasonal and short-term workers.

However, the minimum wage cannot serve as a universal benchmark for all working arrangements.

Guliyev described hourly wages as a “social instrument that helps formalise informal employment”. Deputy Minister Zaur Aliyev, meanwhile, said the changes would allow for greater flexibility in applying the minimum wage system and make wage calculations more transparent.

The introduction of hourly wages has not come as a surprise. In May 2026, the government, the Confederation of Trade Unions and the Confederation of Entrepreneurs of Azerbaijan signed a General Collective Agreement for 2026–2028, committing to securing legislative amendments introducing a minimum hourly wage.

What concerns have critics raised?

Natig Jafarli, an economist and chairman of the Republican Alternative Party, raised three questions in a social media post.

The first concerns the benefits for workers. What would they gain from the introduction of a minimum hourly wage? Jafarli gave an example: if someone were hired for two hours a day and paid 5 manats (approximately $3), “who would benefit from this?”

The second question concerns the public sector. According to Jafarli, nearly half of all salaried employees work in the public sector, and it would be difficult to introduce hourly working arrangements for teachers, doctors, police officers and judicial employees. According to figures from the State Statistical Committee, as of 1 September, 834,200 of Azerbaijan’s 1,776,800 salaried employees, or around 47%, worked in the public sector.

The third question concerns the private sector. Jafarli argues that hourly wages should not be “imposed on the private sector, but rather encouraged through incentives”. In his view, employers spend time and money recruiting and training staff and may therefore have little incentive to hire two or three hourly paid employees instead of one full-time worker.

Economist Akif Nasirli argued last year that Azerbaijan was not ready to introduce such a system. He identified the lack of effective mechanisms to monitor compliance with labour legislation as the main obstacle.

Human resources manager Royal Ahmadov told Bakupost on 6 November that introducing hourly wages would not automatically lead to higher salaries. According to him, much would depend on the minimum hourly rate and how working hours are recorded.

“The main goal is not to provide employers with cheaper labour,” he stressed.

Could full-time positions be split into part-time roles?

Jafarli’s most serious concerns relate to the public sector. He believes the new system will primarily be used in state-funded organisations.

The economist gives the following example: a ministry employing 100 people on an average salary of 1,500 manats (approximately $882) could hire another 100 employees without dismissing anyone. If each of the two employees sharing a position worked four hours a day and earned 600 manats (approximately $353), the cost of one full-time equivalent position would fall from 1,500 to 1,200 manats (approximately $706).

According to Jafarli, this would allow the authorities to report the creation of “new jobs”, while saving the state budget 300 manats (approximately $176) per full-time equivalent position.

The economist describes this as “an attempt to create the appearance of sweeping changes without changing anything in substance”.

Government representatives have not yet responded to the criticism. However, the draft law does not exclude state-funded organisations from the new system: hourly wages would be permitted where the organisation’s existing pay structure allows for them.

Jafarli’s example of a four-hour working day also falls within the conditions set out in the draft law, as it would amount to a 20-hour working week over five days.

These concerns come against a backdrop of declining public-sector employment. In 2025, the number of public-sector employees fell by 2%, equivalent to around 17,000 jobs. Employment also declined in education and public administration, while private-sector employment grew by 5.2%.

Who could benefit?

Supporters of the new system argue that workers currently employed without formal contracts stand to benefit the most. MP Razi Nurullayev explained the reasoning last year:

“Workers will be paid for the hours they actually work.”

Economist Khalid Kerimli said in May that the current monthly wage system is primarily designed for full-time employees. In his view, introducing a minimum hourly rate would help protect the rights of part-time workers and give the Labour Inspectorate greater scope to monitor compliance with labour legislation.

However, Kerimli stressed that “introducing a minimum hourly wage does not mean an increase in the minimum wage”.

The impact of the reform will therefore depend on two decisions that have yet to be made: setting the minimum hourly rate and approving the list of sectors in which it will apply.

The new system will first be introduced in agricultural production and the catering sector. If hourly wages help bring informal employment in these industries into the formal economy, supporters’ expectations will be met. However, if the system leads to full-time positions being split into part-time roles and lower labour costs, critics’ concerns may prove justified.

World.title: Court removes leaders of Coalition for Change from hearing on banning political parties in Georgia – day 10 recap
World.content:
Georgia opposition ban trial

On 11 November, Georgia’s Constitutional Court held the tenth day of hearings on a lawsuit brought by ruling party Georgian Dream seeking to ban five opposition parties.

The hearing was at the question-and-answer stage, with judges questioning representatives of Georgian Dream, which brought the case.

Context. The case sets a precedent. The lawsuit was signed by 88 MPs from the ruling party. It seeks to ban five opposition groups: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. Georgian Dream argues that these parties have violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits political parties that seek to overthrow or forcibly change the country’s constitutional order. The ruling party cites their refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the current government as one of its arguments. The application also accuses them of attempting to overthrow the government. The application also accuses Unity – National Movement of undermining the country’s independence and territorial integrity. The stated reason is the party’s alleged responsibility for the August 2008 war with Russia over South Ossetia, when the United National Movement was in power. All five parties deny the allegations. The court must deliver its final ruling by 24 June 2027. A simple majority is required to uphold the lawsuit, meaning at least four of the seven judges must vote in favour.

The main development on 11 November was the removal of Coalition for Change leaders Nika Gvaramia and Maia Kopaleishvili from the courtroom by Constitutional Court Chairman Revaz Nadaraia for arguing with the court and the plaintiffs.

Unless their request to be allowed back into the proceedings is granted, Gvaramia and Kopaleishvili will be barred from attending further hearings until the case is concluded.

Both have been among the most active representatives of the defendants. Kopaleishvili is a former Constitutional Court judge.

What led to Gvaramia and Kopaleishvili being removed

Judge Eva Gotsiridze asked the plaintiffs whether they had evidence that the opposition parties had taken part in or incited violence. In response, Georgian Dream MP Archil Gorduladze named Murtaz Zodelava and Paata Burchuladze. Both have been charged in connection with the events of 4 October 2025, when a group of activists attempted to storm the presidential palace.

Gorduladze said both men were linked to the United National Movement.

Nika Gvaramia objected: “Neither of them was a member of that party. If people were prosecuted simply because someone happened to be their former classmate, half of Georgia would be in prison – because all of you who have ruined this country were classmates!”

“As for those who have ruined it – well, here you all are!” Gorduladze retorted.

Gvaramia then asked whether being friends with someone meant belonging to the same political party: “If I acknowledge that someone is my friend, does that mean we are all conspirators plotting a coup?”

Constitutional Court Chairman Revaz Nadaraia deemed the exchange disruptive and ordered Gvaramia, followed by Kopaleishvili, to leave the courtroom.

Maia Kopaleishvili: “This is a show of force”

Kopaleishvili described her removal from the courtroom as a restriction on access to justice. “This was a deliberate act. It was an instruction from Georgian Dream,” she said. She then asked Nadaraia: “Why are you laughing? Have you already made your decision?”

Nadaraia replied that a formal request could be filed, adding that it was regrettable that Kopaleishvili did not know the law despite having worked at the Constitutional Court for 10 years.

“This is an insult,” Tengiz Tevzadze, another representative of Coalition for Change, told the presiding judge.

“Keep your colleague in check,” Nadaraia retorted.

Before those ordered to leave the courtroom departed, Nadaraia asked them: “For the past two days, have you deliberately been trying to get yourselves removed? Are you perhaps just trying to avoid answering questions?”

As she left, Kopaleishvili told the judges that they should be guardians of the Constitution, not people who restrict the rights of participants in legal proceedings. “This is a show of force,” she said.

She added that Georgian Dream would probably be pleased that the defendants would no longer be able to ask questions.

A day earlier, on 10 November, Nadaraia had repeatedly threatened to remove Kopaleishvili from the courtroom and accused her of trying to discredit the court.

Gvaramia, meanwhile, threatened to file a motion to have the presiding judge recused.

170 injured police officers and photographs on a laptop

The first point of contention during the day’s hearing concerned the evidence.

Judge Vasil Roinishvili asked the plaintiffs whether they had calculated the material damage caused to the state by the defendants, both domestically and internationally.

He cited problems related to visa regimes, critical international resolutions and cases of law enforcement officers being injured during mass unrest.

Gorduladze replied that around 170 law enforcement officers had been injured in November and December 2024 alone.

Opposition representatives demanded to know where this figure appeared as evidence in the lawsuit.

“Did we not agree to skip the examination of evidence, Mr Chairman?” Gvaramia asked sarcastically, referring to a decision taken the previous day.

“The court did not skip anything. Please do not exaggerate,” Nadaraia retorted.

Gorduladze then opened photographs of injured police officers on his work laptop and showed them to the court.

This triggered another verbal clash with Gvaramia. The presiding judge issued him a warning and threatened to remove him from the courtroom.

Giga Lemondzhava, another representative of Coalition for Change, also tried to speak. Nadaraia refused to give him the floor, saying: “Take your seat, or I will order you to be removed. I am not giving you the floor.”

The presiding judge explained that at the questioning stage, the parties were required to accept their opponents’ answers, even if they found them unsatisfactory.

Ana Buchukuri, a representative of the Gakharia for Georgia party, demanded that the court reprimand Gorduladze for making “offensive remarks” about the defendants.

Judge Gotsiridze: “Seeking to ban five parties at once is unprecedented”

Judge Eva Gotsiridze questioned the plaintiffs about the criteria for banning political parties.

She noted that seeking to ban five parties at once was truly unprecedented.

Gotsiridze also pointed out that the lawsuit describes several other parties as “anti-constitutional”, yet the plaintiffs are not seeking to ban them.

In her view, the term “anti-constitutional” was being applied to political parties too loosely. Following this logic, she said, more than 10 parties in Georgia – effectively a majority – could be classified as anti-constitutional.

The judge questioned whether the criteria proposed by the plaintiffs were sufficiently clear, suggesting they might be too vague, and asked how such an approach could be reconciled with democratic principles.

What happens next

The hearing will resume on 12 November at 12:00, with the question-and-answer stage continuing. This time, judges will question representatives of the opposition parties.

The presiding judge said the questioning is expected to continue until next Tuesday.

Hearings in the case have been held at the Constitutional Court in Batumi since 21 October. Since then, the defendants have filed around 14 motions, of which only one has been granted, and that only in part.

News in Georgia

World.title: ‘Who could be closer friend to us than Armenia?’ – Key takeaways from Iran’s vice-president’s visit to Yerevan
World.content:
Вице-президент Ирана – об объемах поставок газа в Армению

Iranian Vice-President Seyed Hamid Pourmohammadi arrived in Yerevan to attend the 19th session of the Armenian-Iranian Intergovernmental Commission. Armenian journalists asked him about economic ties and Iran’s position on the Armenian-American TRIPP project project, known as the “Trump Route”, which would run through Armenian territory. Armenian media also wanted to understand why Iran’s religious and secular authorities hold different positions on the issue.

Seyed Hamid Pourmohammadi stressed that Tehran’s official position was reflected in statements by Iran’s Foreign Ministry.

“Armenia and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan are our reliable partners, and we remain in constant contact. Tehran considers it important that the countries of the region themselves ensure and maintain security and peace. Iran welcomes any steps aimed at preserving and strengthening peace and security among the countries of the region,” the Iranian vice-president said.

Just days earlier, Ali Akbar Velayati, a senior adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, had sharply criticised Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan over the TRIPP project. Velayati accused Pashinyan of making Armenia increasingly dependent on the West, saying this “opens a new chapter of hostility and tension in the South Caucasus”. Velayati’s remarks prompted a response from Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei. He stressed that the Armenian authorities had assured Tehran that the implementation of the TRIPP project, near Iran’s borders, would involve neither the deployment of US military forces in the region nor any changes to existing borders. Baghaei added that, although Iran enjoys excellent relations with Armenia, it would continue to monitor developments and make its position public if necessary.

On increasing Iranian gas supplies to Armenia

Against the backdrop of discussions about a possible increase in the price of Russian gas supplied to Armenia, journalists asked whether Iran could increase its gas exports to the country.

“Iran is one of the countries with the largest gas reserves in the world. And if we have the capacity to export gas, who could be a closer friend to us than Armenia, to whom we would export it?” the Iranian vice-president replied.

Pourmohammadi said that one of the commissions established under Armenian-Iranian cooperation deals specifically with energy issues. According to him, the two sides discussed all possible areas of cooperation in this sector, including supplies of gas and diesel fuel, as well as issues related to Armenia’s long-term energy security.

However, the specific details of the agreements reached with Iran have not been disclosed.

Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan, who co-chairs the intergovernmental commission on the Armenian side, offered only the following details:

“There is not a single area in which we have not reached agreements. These include trade, energy (particularly gas and electricity), opportunities to expand existing project agreements, as well as infrastructure development and its mutual integration.”

The Iran–Armenia gas pipeline has a designed capacity of more than 2 billion cubic metres of gas a year. However, only a small fraction of this capacity is currently being used. Since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline has been under the control of Russian company Gazprom. Some experts believe that Iran cannot increase its gas exports without Russia’s consent. However, in July this year, Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan said there were no restrictions on receiving gas under the Armenian-Iranian “gas-for-electricity” programme. The programme began in 2009 and has already been extended until 2030. The minister assured that Armenia could at least double its gas imports from Iran.

Outcomes of the intergovernmental meeting

The Armenian government said that the intergovernmental meeting covered the implementation of joint projects in the following areas:

energy;

transport;

trade;

infrastructure;

business ties.

Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan particularly emphasised Armenia’s readiness to develop regional connectivity. He expressed confidence that unblocking regional transport links “would create new opportunities for the countries of the region”. In this context, he stressed the importance of Iran’s support for the Crossroads of Peace initiative. The Armenian government’s project aims to fully unblock transport links to and from Armenia in all directions.

The two sides also signed a memorandum of understanding following the intergovernmental commission meeting.

Connectivity also on the agenda of bilateral meetings

According to the Armenian prime minister’s office, Nikol Pashinyan discussed joint Armenian-Iranian programmes during his meeting with the Iranian vice-president. He said their successful implementation would “help develop and expand bilateral relations”.

“The interlocutors discussed issues related to the development of Armenia-Iran border infrastructure, joint road construction projects, as well as cooperation in energy, agriculture and other sectors,” the statement said.

Pashinyan and Pourmohammadi also discussed the unblocking of regional transport links and the opportunities this process could create for both countries.

Armenian Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan also discussed regional connectivity and the unblocking of transport links with the Iranian vice-president. Following their meeting, officials said that both countries saw “great potential” for further developing trade and economic ties and elevating bilateral relations to a strategic level.

World.title: Georgian authorities respond to Metropolitan Iov’s scathing sermon
World.content:
Georgian metropolitan criticises government



Metropolitan Iov (Akiashvili) of Ruisi and Urbnisi has sharply criticised the Georgian government, saying the ruling team has run out of steam and that the country needs better governance. In his sermon, the clergyman also addressed relations between the Church and the state, accusing the authorities of seeking to bring the Church under their control, turning a blind eye to corruption and neglecting national interests.

A sermon delivered on 10 November at Urbnisi Cathedral was published on the diocese’s social media page. Particular attention was drawn to Metropolitan Iov’s remarks, in which he criticised not only the government but also the Church’s senior leadership.

The metropolitan said the Georgian authorities lacked faith and were distant from the Church, warning that growing ties between the Church and the state threatened the independence of the clergy. He noted that, as the state provides funding to the Church, it is becoming increasingly difficult for clergy to speak openly about the government’s failings.

He also addressed the situation within the Church, saying that a significant proportion of the clergy had come to resemble government officials. He pointed out that while priests urge their congregations to endure poverty, help those in need and practise humility, their own behaviour is quite different.

The metropolitan also raised the issue of transparency in state funding for the Church. In his view, parishioners should know how every tetri (the smallest unit of Georgian currency) allocated to the Church is spent.

“Each of you, as parishioners, should know what the money is spent on and where every tetri goes,” he said.

Metropolitan Iov also recalled the reigns of David the Builder and Queen Tamar, noting that during periods of Georgia’s historical greatness, secular rulers worked in harmony with the Church. In his assessment, however, the current government has departed from this historical example.

A significant part of the sermon was also devoted to the so-called State Security Service “dossiers”. According to the metropolitan, the circulation of materials documenting private conversations and the personal lives of members of the clergy was intended to discredit the Church. He also recalled a statement by Bidzina Ivanishvili, in which he suggested that it was legitimate to criticise the Patriarch because he, too, was human and could make mistakes.

The so-called “dossier scandal”, involving the State Security Service (SSS), concerns alleged secret recordings and documents that emerged in the media in September 2021. The materials reportedly contained recordings of private conversations and phone calls, as well as information about the personal lives of senior representatives of the Georgian Orthodox Church, including metropolitans, bishops, priests and monks.

The documents pointed to widespread surveillance and wiretapping of the clergy. They covered internal Church disputes, relationships between members of the clergy, their private lives and political views. The authenticity of the recordings and the precise circumstances in which they were obtained have never been fully established.

The scandal became particularly serious because the State Security Service was named as the alleged source of the leak. The authorities were forced to respond to the allegations and seek to identify those who had made the documents public. However, it remains unclear to much of the public who was behind the collection and dissemination of the material.

Iov questioned why the identities of those who circulated the recordings had still not been established, despite promises from the authorities.

The metropolitan criticised the government over the spread of drug addiction and gambling addiction, the promotion of casinos, corruption and demographic problems. He noted that young people were leaving the country and villages were becoming deserted, while the scale of new construction, against the backdrop of a declining population, raised questions.

Iov also addressed the issue of David Gareji (the subject of a long-standing territorial dispute between Georgia and Azerbaijan over an undemarcated section of their border running through the sixth-century monastery complex – JAMnews), saying that the authorities’ response to the territorial challenges facing Georgia was inadequate.

“We must sound the alarm, because things cannot continue like this. It has become clear that the current government has completely exhausted its potential. Just as changes of government are commonplace around the world, we too should choose a better government in the future,” the metropolitan said.

He added that discussing the need for a change of government did not mean being hostile towards it, and that pointing out the government’s mistakes was a duty of the clergy.

Government and opposition reactions

The metropolitan’s sermon prompted mixed reactions from representatives of the government and the opposition.

Levan Machavariani, a Georgian Dream MP, said Metropolitan Iov’s political assessments were detached from reality and incorrect. He said he regretted that a senior clergyman was using the Church and the pulpit to make political statements.

Machavariani said the authorities were ready to provide comprehensive answers to any questions raised by the clergy. However, he stressed that such issues should be discussed through consultations before being made public.

“The people of Georgia know perfectly well how our government treats the Mother Church. If any problems or questions arise, we are accustomed to discussing them in a constructive manner,” the MP said.

Metropolitan Iov’s remarks were also criticised by Giorgi Gabunia, chairman of the parliamentary Committee on Culture. He described the metropolitan’s accusations as unfounded and said any confrontation between the Church and the state ran counter to the country’s interests. According to Gabunia, attempts are being made both inside and outside the country to provoke a conflict between the Church and the state.

The opposition took a different position from the ruling party. Pikria Chikhradze, a member of the Lelo – Strong Georgia party, described Metropolitan Iov’s sermon as significant and forceful. In her view, the Church’s criticism of the authorities may even have come too late.

Chikhradze drew attention to the so-called State Security Service “dossiers”, noting that the materials contained information about the private lives and correspondence of members of the clergy. In her view, it was virtually impossible to imagine that information on such a scale could have been collected without state involvement.

She also recalled the so-called “cyanide case” (a high-profile criminal scandal in 2017 involving allegations of a plot to murder a senior figure within the Georgian Orthodox Church – JAMnews), which, she said, still left many questions unanswered. Chikhradze argued that both cases were linked to attempts to undermine the Church’s authority.

The opposition politician said that Bidzina Ivanishvili could not tolerate the existence of independent institutions or influential figures capable of shaping public opinion. As an example, Chikhradze cited a plan to establish cannabis plantations, noting that the Church’s firm opposition had played an important role in halting the project. She also pointed out that, despite the Church’s objections to tax breaks for casinos, the authorities had gone ahead and adopted the relevant legislative amendments.

Pikria Chikhradze

Levan Bezhashvili, one of the leaders of the Unity – National Movement party, welcomed the metropolitan’s remarks. He said that Iov himself often criticises the party and is not a supporter of the National Movement, but that this did not diminish the significance of his latest statement.

“He made a very good statement – well done,” Bezhashvili said.

He added that Metropolitan Iov’s assessment reflected a reality recognised by both society and the Church.

Representatives of People’s Power, a pro-Russian movement that supports the ruling party, also responded to Metropolitan Iov’s criticism.

Tamta Megrelishvili said the metropolitan had used the church pulpit to deliver a political appeal, presenting his partisan position as a religious duty. She argued that accusing the authorities of “lacking faith” and calling for a change of government undermined the Church’s authority.

“In essence, this is an open political call from the church pulpit for a change of government,” Megrelishvili wrote.

Another People’s Power representative, Davit Kartvelishvili, took a much harsher view of Metropolitan Iov’s remarks. He accused the cleric of aligning himself with Saakashvili’s political camp and suggested that his calls for a change of government were driven by personal interests. Kartvelishvili also recalled previous allegations against Iov concerning the situation within his own diocese.

Pro-government commentator Davit Chikhelidze said Metropolitan Iov was accusing the authorities of “turning away from faith”, even though, in Chikhelidze’s view, the metropolitan’s own actions did not reflect the values he claimed to defend. He argued that the sermon harmed the country’s interests and was “playing into the enemy’s hands”.

The Church and Georgian Dream: Why Metropolitan Iov’s Statement Matters

The Georgian Orthodox Church occupies a unique position in the country’s political life. Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has established itself not merely as a religious organisation but as one of the most influential institutions in Georgian society. For decades, its authority has far outweighed that of individual political parties or government officials. As a result, maintaining good relations with the Church has been a major source of political legitimacy for virtually every Georgian government.

Georgian Dream, which came to power in 2012, forged particularly close ties with the Church. Bidzina Ivanishvili and members of the ruling team publicly emphasised the unique role of the Orthodox Church, while some influential members of the clergy openly expressed support for the new government. Over time, these ties became a key element of the ruling party’s political and ideological identity.

However, relations between the Church and the authorities have not always been smooth. Clergy members have previously criticised decisions made by the ruling team on a number of issues, including an initiative to legalise cannabis cultivation, as well as gambling and other matters of public concern. Nevertheless, such direct criticism of the government’s overall political course by senior Church figures remains rare.

What makes Metropolitan Iov’s statement particularly noteworthy is that he goes beyond criticising individual government decisions. He questions the established relationship between the state and the Church, raises concerns about the clergy’s financial dependence on the government and internal problems within the Church, and directly tells the authorities that they have exhausted their capacity to govern the country.

The statement carries additional weight given that, following the political changes of 2012, a significant part of the Church was favourably disposed towards Georgian Dream. Metropolitan Iov himself acknowledges that Church representatives supported the government, although he no longer regards that support as unconditional loyalty.

Trust between the Church and the government became a particularly contentious issue in 2021, when media outlets published materials suggesting possible covert surveillance by the State Security Service (SSS). Thousands of documents pointed to possible surveillance of clergy members, politicians, journalists and diplomats. The scandal raised serious questions both within the Church and in Georgian society more broadly, but those responsible have yet to be identified.

It is also worth noting that, according to the Centre for Social Justice, the Orthodox Church received more than 283 million lari (approximately $109,158,525) from central and municipal budgets between 2020 and 2024.

Georgian metropolitan criticises government

World.title: Georgia’s population grows but ages: What has changed over past decade?
World.content:
Georgia’s demographics in 2015–2025

Georgia‘s population has grown over the past decade, but this increase masks significant demographic changes. Growth has been driven primarily by migration, while an increasing proportion of the population lives in urban areas and the share of elderly people continues to rise.

According to updated data from Georgia’s National Statistics Office (Geostat), the country’s population increased by approximately 209,000 between 2015 and 2025, reaching 3.93 million.

However, this growth does not mean that the population is increasing through natural change — that is, births exceeding deaths.

On the contrary, Georgia has recorded negative natural population growth in recent years, with deaths outnumbering births. This means that migration into the country has been the main driver of overall population growth.

According to Geostat, particularly sharp demographic changes began in 2022. Over the following three years, Georgia’s population increased by nearly 170,000. During this period, net migration was exceptionally high, with the number of people entering the country significantly exceeding the number leaving.

The most notable shift in migration patterns occurred in 2022, when Georgia recorded more than 200,000 immigrants. High positive net migration continued over the following two years. Together, the years 2022–2024 accounted for the overwhelming majority of the positive net migration recorded over the past decade.

However, population growth was not observed across all regions of Georgia. The increase was concentrated mainly in Tbilisi, Adjara and Kvemo Kartli. Population numbers declined in most other regions, while remaining virtually unchanged in Mtskheta-Mtianeti.

These figures suggest that population growth has been unevenly distributed across the country, with residents becoming increasingly concentrated in a few urban centres.

Georgia’s urban population continues to grow

Over the past decade, Georgia’s urban population has increased, while its rural population has declined. In 2015, around 57% of the country’s population lived in urban areas, compared with 62% in 2025. This means that the country’s overall population growth has been driven entirely by an increase in urban residents, while the rural population has shrunk.

Georgia’s age structure is also changing. The population is gradually ageing, with the number of people aged 65 and over increasing by nearly 30% over the past decade. This age group now accounts for around 18% of the total population.

At the same time, the number of children has increased, while the working-age population (those aged 15–64) has declined. This means that, despite overall population growth, the proportion of people of working age is decreasing, while the share of elderly residents continues to rise.

There have been no significant changes in the population’s gender composition. Women continue to outnumber men, although the gap has narrowed slightly.

According to Geostat, the figures have been recalculated to take into account the results of the 2024 national population census. The adjustments aim to bring demographic data for the past decade into line with the latest census results, providing a more accurate picture of population trends over time.

The updated data highlight several key demographic trends in Georgia: the population is growing, primarily due to migration; people are becoming increasingly concentrated in urban areas; and the age structure is changing, with a growing proportion of elderly residents.

According to the latest Geostat figures, the 2024 census showed that Georgia’s population stood at 3.93 million, an increase of 5.8%, or 216,000 people, compared with 2014. Women account for 52% of the population, while men make up 48%.

World.title: No examination of evidence: day nine of hearings in Georgia’s case to ban opposition parties
World.content:
Georgia party ban trial: Day 9

On 10 November, Georgia’s Constitutional Court continued hearings in the case concerning a possible ban on opposition parties. The court had scheduled a question-and-answer session. However, before questioning began, opposition representatives submitted two motions, one of which concerned the examination of evidence.

The motion triggered serious disagreements. Heated arguments repeatedly broke out during the discussion, and Constitutional Court Chairman Judge Revaz Nadaraya lost his composure several times.

Ultimately, the court rejected one of the two motions submitted by the opposition and granted the other only in part. The opposition considered the way the court handled the second motion tantamount to rejecting it.

Once the court had dealt with the motions, the question-and-answer session began. The first questions went to the claimant, the ruling Georgian Dream party.

As at previous hearings, Judge Nadaraya again threatened to have representatives of the respondents removed from the courtroom. He also continued to deny some opposition representatives the opportunity to speak.

Georgia’s Constitutional Court is hearing a case that could lead to a ban on opposition parties. The case sets a precedent. Eighty-eight MPs from the ruling Georgian Dream party filed the application. They are seeking to have five opposition groups declared unconstitutional: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. Georgian Dream argues that these parties have violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits political parties that seek to overthrow or forcibly change the country’s constitutional order. The ruling party cites their refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the current government as one of its arguments. The application also accuses them of attempting to overthrow the government. The application also accuses Unity – National Movement of undermining the country’s independence and territorial integrity. It argues that the party bears responsibility for the war with Russia in August 2008. The case relies mainly on the findings of a temporary parliamentary investigative commission. The respondents reject the allegations.

What happened during the unusually heated court hearing on 10 November? Our report from the courtroom.

“Give us a chance to defend ourselves”: Lelo files motion on the examination of evidence

At the start of the hearing, Levan Samushia, one of the leaders of the opposition Lelo party, asked the judges to examine the evidence before moving on to the questioning stage.

The evidence includes written documents, video recordings and other material in the case file that the court may rely on when reaching its decision.

Samushia supported his motion by citing the Organic Law on the Constitutional Court and the court’s rules of procedure. He sought to convince the judges that the law provides for a separate stage of examining evidence, which must take place before the question-and-answer session.

Under Article 20, paragraph 6 of the Constitutional Court’s rules of procedure, “after examining the evidence, the presiding judge gives the parties the right to question each other”.

“Put simply, they are trying to suppress political parties. That is exactly what is happening here from a legal point of view,” Samushia told the full bench of judges.

He urged the court not to skip this crucial stage, invoking the principles of a fair trial and the binding requirements of the law.

Other opposition parties backed Samushia’s motion, saying they had also planned to make a similar request.

From the outset, Constitutional Court Judge Revaz Nadaraya did his utmost to portray the motion as unfounded.

“So you want to start by examining the documents attached to the case file? Open all of them?” the judge asked.

“Yes,” Samushia replied.

“Criminal procedure law works differently here,” Judge Nadaraya insisted, showing no intention of backing down.

He was referring to the inquisitorial principle, arguing that, unlike in ordinary courts, the parties in the Constitutional Court do not have the exclusive right or responsibility to obtain or request evidence. The court itself plays the leading role in this process.

“The adversarial principle has not been abolished along with the inquisitorial principle,” Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, interjected from his seat. “We must not skip this stage.”

“Are you suggesting that we open and watch every link? View programmes lasting half an hour or more?” Judge Nadaraya asked again. [*Georgian Dream’s application relies primarily on the findings of the parliamentary investigative commission, but it also includes numerous links. You can see how many by following this link – JAMnews.]

“The claimant should specify the exact minute and second in each programme. That way, we can save the court’s time,” Samushia insisted, sticking firmly to his position.

“What do I have to do with the events of 7 November? I was a first-year student” – Berdia Sichinava

Berdia Sichinava, a representative of the party founded by former prime minister Giorgi Gakharia, who previously served in Georgian Dream, also joined the discussion.

He pointed to what he described as the absurdity of holding him accountable and scrutinising him over cases in which he himself, as a prosecutor, had brought charges against the previous government.

“Take the case of Nora Kvitsiani, for example, which the investigative commission’s report mentions. Are the accusations directed at me, Berdia Sichinava? I was the prosecutor who issued a ruling in 2016 recognising that Nora Kvitsiani’s rights had been violated. I took part in the proceedings that ultimately led to her acquittal.”

He also referred to the case of Sulkhan Molashvili:

“I would like to know whether the case of Sulkhan Molashvili concerns me too. I was the prosecutor who recognised his family as victims and returned their country house to them.”

One of the main arguments in Georgian Dream’s application is that the United National Movement introduced systematic torture and inhuman treatment in penitentiary institutions while in power, and that the party should therefore face a ban. The application cites several high-profile cases from the previous administration, including those of Nora Kvitsiani and Sulkhan Molashvili. However, Georgian Dream does not specify which evidence relates to each individual. Instead, it claims that all the evidence applies equally to everyone named in the case. Sulkhan Molashvili was the former head of the Chamber of Control. Authorities arrested him in 2004, and he later said that he had suffered torture and inhuman treatment. Nora Kvitsiani was arrested after a special operation in the Kodori Gorge in 2006. Her arrest and prosecution formed part of wider concerns about repressive measures against opponents of the government then in power.

“What do I have to do with the events of 7 November? I was a first-year student,” Berdia Sichinava asked. [The application accuses the United National Movement of violently dispersing a protest on 7 November – JAMnews.]

“So what are we supposed to do now – read out the court rulings as well?” Revaz Nadaraya asked, seizing on a new argument and pointing out that the parliamentary commission’s report referred to specific court decisions.

“The court cannot base its decision on this report [by the parliamentary commission]. It could, however, rely on the facts presented in it – although those facts would still require further examination,” Gvaramia said. He reminded the judges that the report came from a temporary parliamentary investigative commission and represented a document containing political assessments.

“How dare you speak to me like that? I will file a motion to recuse you” – Gvaramia confronts judge

The discussion dragged on and repeatedly descended into heated arguments.

“Suppose I want to examine the records of my own questioning. How am I supposed to know whether you will rely on that testimony when reaching your final decision? How can I find that out without examining it together with you?” Gvaramia asked.

He also reminded the judge of previous motions that the court had rejected, pointing out that they concerned legal issues. [Since the start of the proceedings, the defence has submitted around 14 motions. The court has granted only one, and even then only in part – JAMnews.]

Judge Nadaraya grew angry and repeatedly interrupted Gvaramia.

“If we are going to argue, we will get nowhere. You have your procedural rights, and I have mine. I know them perfectly well. Please let me finish,” Gvaramia said.

“You seem to think you have the right to do whatever you please. That is simply not the case,” the judge replied.

“What tone are you using with me?! What makes you think you have the right to speak to me like that?! I will file a motion to recuse you. Please do not interrupt me!” Gvaramia exclaimed, no longer concealing his anger.

“Stick to the substance of the motion. There is no need to bring up what we have or have not granted in the past,” Nadaraya said sharply.

“It is not for you to decide what I can talk about!” Gvaramia retorted.

“It is precisely my job to decide that. Either you comply with the court’s instructions or…” The presiding judge left the sentence unfinished.

“I am explaining the grounds for my motion. Let me speak! You cannot conduct the proceedings in such a one-sided manner!” Nika Gvaramia insisted.

“Maya, would you like my seat?” Judge Nadaraya asks Maya Kopaleishvili

Constitutional Court Judge Revaz Nadaraya lost his temper again when Maya Kopaleishvili, an ally of Nika Gvaramia, tried to join the discussion. Kopaleishvili is a former Constitutional Court judge who frequently highlights cases in which judges have breached procedural rules.

Speaking from her seat, Kopaleishvili tried to explain why examining the evidence was important.

“Ms Kopaleishvili, perhaps I should give you my seat? Why are you speaking? Did you ask for permission to speak? Do you have some special privileges?” Judge Nadaraya asked sternly.

“I don’t have any, but apparently you do,” Kopaleishvili replied.

The judge did not allow Maya Kopaleishvili to put forward her arguments. Throughout the hearing, the presiding judge was particularly harsh towards her and repeatedly threatened to have her removed from the courtroom. He accused her of trying to discredit the court.

“There seems to have been a misunderstanding” – Eva Gotsiridze

“It seems there has been a misunderstanding,” Judge Eva Gotsiridze said, trying to make herself heard above the noise and defuse the tension. She explained that the examination of evidence actually formed part of the question-and-answer stage.

“For example, during cross-examination, you can ask: ‘What evidence supports the allegation that you are guilty?’” she suggested to the opposing side.

Gotsiridze repeated the argument that the Constitutional Court chairman had made several times. She noted that the court could not, for instance, check each of the 1,005 links listed in the footnotes to the application. She cited this figure as an example, although the actual number of links in the footnotes is indeed very large.

She also recalled another argument raised by a fellow judge: some of the evidence consisted of court rulings, and “you are hardly going to ask us to review those as well”.

“Then why does the examination of evidence stage exist at all? Why do other cases include it?” Nika Gvaramia asked Gotsiridze.

In response, Eva Gotsiridze said that lawmakers could not have anticipated exactly how proceedings before the Constitutional Court would unfold in practice when they drafted the legislation. She again stressed that the examination of evidence was “woven into the question-and-answer stage, particularly when the parties question each other”.

Maya Kopaleishvili also wanted to respond to this clarification. However, the presiding judge once again refused to let her speak.

“You are not allowing me to comment on this motion. That is wrong,” Kopaleishvili told Judge Nadaraya.

“Yes, yes, that’s right! Absolutely right! Enough has been said already,” the judge replied.

“Do you know what this tells us? It tells us that the court… is afraid,” Kopaleishvili retorted.

“Ms Kopaleishvili, this is the second time you have said that someone is afraid. I will have you removed from the courtroom! Out!” the judge snapped.

“Mr Chairman, are you trying to intimidate me now? Do I look like someone who can be intimidated?” Kopaleishvili replied, refusing to back down.

“No, no – I have absolutely no such intention,” the judge replied. But he still did not give her the floor.

No separate stage for examining evidence: the court’s ruling on the motion

After the heated exchanges, the panel of judges withdrew to deliberate. The half-hour they had requested stretched into an hour.

“Granted in part,” the judges announced when they returned to the courtroom. They explained that they would consider any evidence whose relevance to the case became disputed. However, they would not hold a separate stage devoted exclusively to examining evidence.

“The panel reached a unanimous decision,” Judge Nadaraya stressed.

“A legal absurdity”: the court rejects the opposition’s second motion

Before Nadaraya, who appeared pleased with the decision, could resume the hearing, Nika Gvaramia asked to speak and submit a second motion.

He proposed that, if the court upheld the application, it should delay enforcement of its ruling by at least one month. All the opposition parties joined the motion.

Gvaramia explained that this period would allow the parties to apply to the European Court of Human Rights for interim measures.

“Mr Gvaramia, you spoke for so long and presented so many arguments that you could write a separate article about them. These issues require examination and analysis. In my view, we cannot decide this today. It would be irresponsible. Let us leave these motions without consideration: rejecting them or granting them would be equally irresponsible,” Constitutional Court Judge Eva Gotsiridze replied.

“What kind of research would that require? If I had proposed something that called for setting up an entire scientific institute to resolve a single question, then, well, I am not quite that ambitious,” Gvaramia retorted.

Representatives of the ruling party opposed the motion. Archil Gorduladze argued that granting it would amount to prejudging the court’s final verdict.

“If the court grants this motion, it will effectively announce in advance that it intends to set a specific deadline – ‘X’ or ‘Y’ – for enforcing its decision. Nothing like this exists in legal practice,” Gorduladze said.

“If anything truly has no precedent in legal practice, it is banning five different political parties in a single court case,” Gvaramia replied.

The court rejected this motion too. Despite Eva Gotsiridze’s comment, the full bench reached its decision immediately, without even withdrawing to deliberate.

“Granting this motion has no constitutional or legal basis. It would be a legal absurdity,” Revaz Nadaraya said, stressing that “the full bench is unanimous in its position”.

He explained that the court could decide whether to delay enforcement in its final ruling, so there was no need for a preliminary decision.

Where does the state end and the ruling party begin? The question-and-answer session

After the court had dealt with the motions, the question-and-answer session began. Judge Vasil Roinishvili asked the first questions.

He asked Archil Gorduladze to clarify where the boundary between the state and the ruling party lay, and to explain how far a political party should be held responsible for government decisions and actions.

Gorduladze said that the state and the party were not the same thing. However, he argued that a party bears responsibility for the laws and political course that its representatives help shape. He cited the foreign agents law as an example, noting that Georgian Dream had still secured a mandate from voters in the election despite passing it.

Roinishvili raised an argument put forward by the opposition: responsibility for criminal acts should rest with the individual officials involved, not with the political party itself. Gorduladze replied that human rights violations under the United National Movement government had not been isolated incidents. He said an entire system had encouraged criminal behaviour and protected those responsible.

Judge Eva Gotsiridze then took over the questioning. She asked Gorduladze to clarify whether a party should be held responsible for failing to distance itself from its leaders’ actions or for failing to respond appropriately to their behaviour.

She also noted that most of the people mentioned in the case had faced criminal charges only after the change of government. The opposition regarded this as a leading question.

Gotsiridze also asked about the meaning of the term “constitutional order”. She wanted to know whether Euro-Atlantic integration, enshrined in Article 78 of the Constitution, could be considered an integral part of the constitutional order, and whether violating this provision could provide grounds for banning a political party.

Giorgi Kakhiani, another representative of Georgian Dream, replied that the court should interpret Article 78 alongside other constitutional provisions. Tornike Cheishvili, meanwhile, described it as a transitional provision designed to achieve a temporary goal.

The judge then asked: if the government violates Article 78, does that amount to a breach of the constitutional order? And could it justify banning a political party? The question prompted laughter in the courtroom.

Gotsiridze raised several more issues, including the circumstances in which a party could be required to distance itself from the actions of its own leaders. She postponed hearing the answers until the following day.

“The decision has already been made – they are just trying to dress it up nicely”: reactions after the hearing

After the hearing, Georgian Dream accused the opposition of turning the proceedings into a performance.

“They are trying to turn a legal process into something resembling a televised debate or show. They know perfectly well that their unconstitutional actions have absolutely no legal basis. They are trying to achieve their goals through demagoguery alone,” Archil Gorduladze said.

The opposition, meanwhile, focused on the question of examining evidence.

“The way the court is handling the evidence raises serious questions. I do not know how it intends to resolve this situation. Essentially, it has simply skipped an entire stage of the proceedings. This is completely unacceptable and does not comply with the law,” Nika Gvaramia said after the hearing.

He added that the decision to ban the parties had effectively already been made: “Now they are just trying to make the whole thing look respectable – rather like trying to make a corpse look presentable.”

“The Constitutional Court operates under the inquisitorial principle: it must examine all the evidence, including material that the parties themselves have not submitted but which is necessary for a well-founded decision. However, the court must examine this evidence during the proceedings, with the parties present, rather than behind closed doors in the judges’ deliberation room,” former judge Maya Kopaleishvili wrote on social media after the court refused to let her speak during the hearing.

During the hearing itself, she had warned the judge that if he refused to let her speak in court, she would present her arguments publicly on Facebook.

In her view, the court should have prepared better for a case involving a ban on political parties. “The court could have included a special section in its rules of procedure, for example, setting out how it should examine evidence.”

Berdia Sichinava said the proceedings had only made the court’s alleged bias more apparent. He added that the judges’ haste to reach a decision had also become unmistakable.

“Of course, there can be no other conclusion. This is a fundamental issue. A case of such importance to the country cannot proceed without examining the evidence. I am certain that the question-and-answer session will make it even clearer that this is all nothing but a bluff.”

The court will resume hearings on the application on 11 November. Further sessions are also scheduled for 12 and 13 November.

The Constitutional Court in Batumi began hearing the case to ban political parties on 21 October. The stage at which the parties presented their explanations and arguments has already concluded.

Last week, the court took a 10-day break to mark its 30th anniversary. The judges celebrated the occasion alongside senior representatives of the Georgian Dream party.

Georgia party ban trial: Day 9

World.title: ‘This restraining measure cost man his life’: Armenia debates opposition figure’s death in prison
World.content:
Death of opposition politician in Armenian prison

Arsen Gevorgyan, an opposition politician, died this morning at a prison in Armenia. Gevorgyan had stood as a candidate for head of the Stepanavan community in local elections, representing the opposition Strong Armenia party. However, authorities arrested him on suspicion of vote-buying just days before the election.

The prison authorities have not disclosed the cause of his death. Media outlets reported that Gevorgyan had apparently suffered a heart attack. His relatives said he had never “complained of any health problems”.

The opposition Strong Armenia party blamed the authorities for Arsen Gevorgyan’s death. It said his arrest on “groundless charges” formed part of a “smear campaign”.

“Those who ordered the unjustified discrediting and arrests of hundreds of people bear responsibility for the death of yet another opposition figure in prison,” representatives of Strong Armenia said.

Human rights defenders are calling for a thorough investigation into the circumstances of Arsen Gevorgyan’s death.

The issue has also sparked widespread discussion on social media. Some users argue that the authorities imposed an excessively harsh pre-trial measure on the opposition politician, which may have contributed to his death. They therefore hold the Armenian authorities responsible.

Stepanavan was the only community where Strong Armenia, led by pro-Russian businessman Samvel Karapetyan, fielded a candidate in the local elections. Authorities detained Arsen Gevorgyan, who was running for head of the community, on 21 October – four days before the election. A court ordered his pre-trial detention for two months that same day. According to the Anti-Corruption Committee, Gevorgyan had bribed several dozen voters, urging them to vote for Strong Armenia. He denied the charges. His party colleagues, meanwhile, described the case as political persecution.

What the authorities have said

The Penitentiary Service said that Arsen Gevorgyan, born in 1980, who was being held at the Nubarashen penitentiary, suffered a sudden deterioration in his health early in the morning. The medical officer on duty administered first aid.

“An ambulance was called at around 07:55. At approximately 08:30, medical staff pronounced Arsen Gevorgyan dead,” the statement said.

The authorities also said that Gevorgyan had not complained about his health during his time in the facility.

Journalists asked Justice Minister Srbui Galyan today who would be held accountable if an investigation found that Gevorgyan had not received adequate medical care. Galyan did not answer the question. However, she confirmed that Gevorgyan had not complained about his health while in the penitentiary.

“Unfortunately, incidents like this happen both around the world and in penitentiary institutions,” the minister said, offering her condolences to Gevorgyan’s family.

According to Galyan, 20 inmates died in penitentiary institutions in 2025 and four in 2026.

The Investigative Committee has opened a criminal investigation into Arsen Gevorgyan’s death. A forensic medical examination will follow.

Human rights defender’s view

Daniel Ioannisyan, a human rights defender and coordinator of the NGO Union of Informed Citizens, says the authorities must conduct a “thorough and transparent investigation” into the circumstances of Arsen Gevorgyan’s death.

In particular, he wants answers to the following questions:

“Did Gevorgyan have any chronic illnesses that he had reported to the prison administration?

When did Gevorgyan’s health begin to deteriorate? When did he (or his cellmates) alert prison staff? How did the staff respond, and exactly what steps did they take, minute by minute?

When did medical personnel learn about the problem, and what measures did they take, minute by minute?”

“The public should receive answers to these questions as soon as possible,” Ioannisyan wrote on his Facebook page.

Reactions on social media

Most comments on social media express outrage over the opposition politician’s death and the court’s decision to remand him in custody.

Here are some examples:

“Another political murder.”

“Look, the leader of Strong Armenia is to blame. He provided the money for distributing bribes during the election campaign. What does Nikol [Pashinyan] have to do with it?”

“Far more dangerous criminals are walking free, while they jailed a man for offering a bribe. They could have simply placed him under house arrest.”

“Pre-trial detention was clearly a disproportionate measure. And this measure cost a man his life. Where could he have fled from your so-called justice? And who can actually escape your justice – assuming it even exists?”

“The state is responsible for the life of anyone in its custody. And the head of state is Nikol Pashinyan. Nikol, this happened under your system. You must answer for it: what condition was the man in, did he receive medical care, and why did a man whose guilt a court had not established die in prison?”

“This is another stark reminder of the tragic consequences that political persecution can bring. We demand a full, independent and impartial investigation into all the circumstances surrounding his death.”

Death of opposition politician in Armenian prison

World.title: Which sectors of Georgia’s economy are most dependent on Russia?
World.content:
What does Georgia depend on Russia for?

Since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, remittances and other financial inflows from Russia to Georgia have risen sharply. Although these flows have declined somewhat in subsequent years, Georgia remains heavily dependent on Russia in several sectors.

The Russian market remains particularly important for Georgian wine and other traditional export goods. Russia has also increased its share of Georgia’s natural gas supplies.

A study by BM.ge examines Russia’s influence on Georgia’s economy over the past five years. It covers data on foreign trade, foreign direct investment, remittances, tourism and the energy sector from 2021 to 2026.

This article provides a brief overview of the study’s main findings.

Revenue from Russia has fallen, but dependence remains

One of the key indicators in the study is the ratio of revenue from exports to Russia, tourism from Russia and remittances from Russia to Georgia’s nominal gross domestic product (GDP).

According to BM.ge’s calculations, in 2022 these three sources accounted for 14.4% of Georgia’s GDP. By 2025, the figure had fallen to 5% – below the 6.2% recorded in 2021.

The main reason for the decline was a sharp drop in remittances from Russia. In 2022, people and businesses transferred $2.07bn from Russia to Georgia. By 2025, the figure had fallen to $468m.

Moreover, between January and September 2026, remittances from Russia fell by a further 11.5% compared with the same period a year earlier, reaching $304.8m.
