However, these figures do not necessarily mean that Georgia’s overall economic dependence on Russia has declined by the same margin. The indicator does not account for imports from Russia, dependence on energy supplies or other economic ties.

Trade: imports are rising, while traditional exports remain concentrated in the Russian market

Between 2021 and 2025, trade between Georgia and Russia increased.

In 2025, Georgia’s exports to Russia totalled $749.3m, while imports from Russia reached $1.94bn. Total trade turnover stood at $2.69bn. Imports were approximately 2.6 times higher than exports.

Over the same period, Russia’s share of Georgia’s total exports fell from 14.4% to 10.3%. However, the picture looks different when it comes to exports of locally produced goods: Russia’s share of these exports rose from 17.7% in 2021 to 20.8% in 2025.

This means Russia remains an important market for goods produced in Georgia. Dependence is particularly high for traditional export products.

In 2025, Russia accounted for around 64% of Georgia’s wine exports and 56% of its exports of spirits. In the first nine months of 2026, Georgia exported $119.8m worth of wine and $92.9m worth of spirits to Russia.

According to the study, such a high concentration in the Russian market leaves Georgian producers vulnerable to changes in demand and potential trade restrictions.

Energy: Russia’s share of gas supplies has increased

One of the sectors most visibly dependent on Russia is energy, particularly natural gas supplies.

Citing data from GNERC (the Georgian National Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission), BM.ge reports that Georgia imported 397 million cubic metres of natural gas from Russia in 2021. By 2025, the figure had risen to 886 million cubic metres. Over five years, gas imports from Russia increased 2.2-fold.

As a result, Russia’s share of Georgia’s gas supplies rose from 15.3% to 27.9%. Nevertheless, Azerbaijan remained by far the largest supplier in 2025, accounting for 71.7% of Georgia’s natural gas imports.

Russia is also an important supplier of oil and petroleum products to Georgia. A key factor in this area is the oil refinery in Kulevi, which began operations in October 2025. Initially, the facility processed Russian crude oil.

The European Union added the refinery to its sanctions list in July 2026, but postponed the restrictions until 25 January 2027. According to the company that owns the facility, the refinery stopped processing Russian oil on 23 August 2026 and switched to non-Russian crude.

As for electricity, Russia supplied 62.4% of Georgia’s electricity imports in 2025.

However, these figures need to be considered in context: a significant share of the electricity imported from Russia goes towards supplying occupied Abkhazia.

According to BM.ge, around 74.5% of the electricity Georgia imported from Russia in 2025 went to Abkhazia.

Tourism: visitor numbers and revenue tell different stories

Russia remains one of the main sources of tourists for Georgia.

In 2025, Russian citizens made 1.58 million visits to Georgia, an 11.1% increase on the previous year. Between January and September 2026, they made 1.31 million visits, 4.9% more than in the same period a year earlier.

However, Russia’s share of Georgia’s tourism revenue has declined.

In 2022, Russia accounted for 25.3% of revenue from international travel. By 2025, this figure had fallen to 14.8%.

Georgia earned a total of $4.69bn from international tourism in 2025, with Russian visitors contributing $694m.

The study also notes that trends in arrivals from other countries affect the overall number of tourist visits.

Therefore, an increase in visits by Russian citizens does not necessarily mean that Russia’s share of Georgia’s tourism revenue is also growing.

Investment: Russia’s share of foreign capital remains relatively small

Russia accounts for a relatively small share of Georgia’s total foreign direct investment (FDI), compared with other economic indicators.

In 2021, Russian FDI in Georgia totalled $87.7m. By 2023, it had risen to $131.2m, before reaching $109.5m in 2025.

At the same time, Russia’s share of Georgia’s total FDI fell from 6.8% in 2021 to 5.8% in 2025.

In the first half of 2026, most Russian investment went into the property and construction sectors.

According to data that BM.ge obtained from Georgia’s National Statistics Office, 71.8% of Russian investment – amounting to $26.7m – went into real estate.

What does the study show? The key findings

The analysis concludes that falling revenue from Russia does not provide a complete picture of Georgia’s economic dependence on its northern neighbour.

On the one hand, Russia’s share of remittances and tourism revenue has declined, as has its share of Georgia’s total exports.

On the other hand, Russia’s share of Georgia’s natural gas supplies has increased, while it remains the main export market for Georgian wine and other traditional products.

The study’s author also stresses the importance of reducing economic vulnerability.

According to BM.ge’s analysis, this requires diversifying export markets, finding alternative energy suppliers and steadily reducing Georgia’s economic dependence on Russia.

The study also serves as a reminder that economic relations with Russia are not merely a commercial matter. Previous embargoes on Georgian goods have shown that Moscow can restrict access to its market for political reasons.

What does Georgia depend on Russia for? The Georgian-Russian border and the road towards Lars. Photo: Davit Pipia / JAMnews, 2022.

World.title: Caspian Geo launches 3D seismic survey at Azerbaijan's Goshadash structure
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 12. Caspian Geo has begun 3D seismic surveys on the Goshadash structure in the Azerbaijani sector of the Caspian Sea, commissioned by SOCAR Exploration.

According to a statement from SOCAR Exploration, the surveys are being conducted using on-bottom (OBN) seismic receivers.

In addition, it is noted that this is the third seismic survey project carried out under the leadership of SOCAR Exploration over the past 12 months. Previously, the company conducted two similar campaigns abroad.

The data obtained will enable a comprehensive assessment of prospective targets and will serve as the basis for planning further exploratory drilling.

Will be updated

World.title: European Political Community summit gets underway in Dublin
World.content:
DUBLIN, Ireland, November 12. The European Political Community (EPC) summit is getting underway in Dublin, bringing together leaders from up to 50 European countries and partner states, Trend's special correspondent reports.

The meeting is being held at the Dublin Convention Centre and co-chaired by European Council President António Costa and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin. Canada has also been invited to attend as a guest.

The summit is being held under the motto "Europe – strong, secure and connected". Discussions are focused on European security, Russia's war against Ukraine, economic competitiveness, energy security, transport infrastructure development and stronger regional connectivity.

Particular attention will be given to Europe's defense capabilities, countering cyberattacks, disinformation and other hybrid threats, as well as sharing responsibility for European security between European countries and the United States.

The economic agenda covers innovation and digital infrastructure development, stronger transport links, reliable and affordable energy supplies, and improving the resilience of the European economy to external shocks.

The EPC brings together EU member states and countries outside the bloc. Established in 2022 following the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine, the European Political Community serves as a platform for political dialogue and coordination among European countries. The format does not involve creating new EU institutions or adopting legally binding decisions.

For Azerbaijan, participation in the summit is particularly significant in terms of energy cooperation, the peace process in the South Caucasus and transport connectivity. Azerbaijan continues to play an important role in diversifying natural gas supplies to Europe, particularly through the Southern Gas Corridor.

Meanwhile, amid progress on the peace agenda between Azerbaijan and Armenia, prospects for ensuring long-term stability in the South Caucasus remain an important aspect of European policy in the region.

The development of the Middle Corridor, which connects Asia and Europe via the South Caucasus and offers additional opportunities to expand trade and transport links, is another key area of focus.

The next EPC summit is scheduled to take place in Azerbaijan in May 2028. This will give Baku an opportunity to host European leaders and continue dialogue on regional and broader European issues.

Following the conclusion of the EPC summit in Dublin, a separate informal meeting of the leaders of the 27 EU member states will take place on November 13.

World.title: Turkmenistan, UNFPA discuss demographic and youth development priorities
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 12. Turkmenistan and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) have discussed cooperation on demographic resilience, youth development and gender equality within the framework of their 2026-2030 Country Programme, according to a press release from the Turkmen government.

The discussions took place during a meeting between UNFPA Executive Director Diene Keita and Turkmenistan's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Vepa Hajiyev.

The two sides reviewed the main areas of their long-standing partnership and discussed ways to advance cooperation under the current Country Programme.

Particular attention was given to joint efforts within multilateral platforms, including the UN Commission on Population and Development and the UN Commission on the Status of Women.

The meeting also addressed youth development and Turkmenistan's preparations for presenting its Voluntary National Review in 2027. The review forms part of the country's reporting on progress toward the UN Sustainable Development Goals.

The sides also discussed opportunities for cooperation during Turkmenistan's upcoming chairmanship of the Group of Landlocked Developing Countries in 2027.

The discussions focused on aligning bilateral cooperation with Turkmenistan's priorities in population policy and social development, as well as its participation in international initiatives.

Turkmenistan's domestic youth policy was also outlined in several state documents. Under the Law on State Youth Policy, adopted in a revised edition in September 2022, young people are defined as citizens aged 14 to 35.

The law establishes the state's approach to youth participation in the country's social, economic, political and cultural life. It covers education, employment, entrepreneurship, healthcare, sports and cultural activities, and provides for support for young families, talented young people and youth associations.

In September 2026, Turkmenistan approved a new State Programme on Youth Policy through 2031, along with an action plan for its implementation. According to the government, the programme aims to identify and support young people interested in science, education and advanced technologies, while creating conditions for their participation in the country's socio-economic, political and cultural development.

Responsibility for implementing the programme was assigned to relevant ministries, government agencies and the administrations of the country's regions, Ashgabat and Arkadag. The new programme follows the previous State Programme for 2021-2025.

Turkmenistan's Strategy for International Cooperation of Youth for 2023-2030 was approved by a presidential resolution in June 2023. According to the official announcement, the strategy aims to develop international youth partnerships in line with Turkmenistan's legislation and international agreements.

Its implementation was assigned to relevant ministries, government departments and the administrations of the country's regions, Ashgabat and Arkadag.

World.title: Irish PM highlights Azerbaijan’s role in strengthening Europe’s energy security
World.content:
DUBLIN, Ireland, November 12. Azerbaijan’s participation in the European Political Community (EPC) provides opportunities to strengthen Europe’s energy security and address broader economic and security challenges facing the continent, Irish Prime Minister (Taoiseach) Micheál Martin said, Trend's special correspondent reports.

Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the EPC summit in Dublin, Martin noted that the forum brings together European countries and partners beyond the European Union, enabling them to develop common approaches to major regional and international challenges.

He highlighted Azerbaijan’s participation in the EPC framework as an example of how cooperation can produce tangible results, particularly in energy supplies and the broader security of the European continent.

"If you look at Azerbaijan coming within the EPC fold, there were significant developments from that in terms of supplies and so on, in terms of both the economic security of the continent and also security in respect of hybrid attacks," he said.

Martin stressed that energy connectivity, technological cooperation and people-to-people ties are among the key issues requiring closer coordination between European countries and their partners.

He also pointed to the importance of cooperation in ensuring affordable energy supplies, protecting critical infrastructure and securing access to critical raw materials and rare earth minerals.

According to the Irish prime minister, informal discussions within the EPC framework can also facilitate progress on major political and security issues.

Martin said the forum's broader format allows participating countries to discuss shared challenges and develop common solutions beyond the scope of traditional EU-level meetings.

World.title: Uzbekistan joins $720M climate investment initiative
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 12. Uzbekistan will participate in a $720 million international climate investment program aimed at accelerating industrial decarbonization, promoting green technologies and strengthening climate resilience in developing economies.

According to Uzbekistan's National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change, the Transformation Pathways Initiative (TPI) was approved by the Board of the Green Climate Fund (GCF) in October 2026 and presented at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, on November 11.

The total financing package amounts to $720 million, of which $187 million will be provided by the GCF. The remaining $533 million is expected to come from co-financing.

Uzbekistan is one of 10 countries selected to participate in the initiative, which is being implemented with the involvement of the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) and international investment firm Finance in Motion.

The program is designed to provide businesses with greater access to long-term climate financing for energy-efficient technologies, renewable energy projects, greenhouse gas emission reductions, and the modernization of industrial production processes.

Priority areas include industrial enterprises, small and medium-sized businesses, and the development of climate-resilient agri-food systems.

Funding will be provided through direct investments and loans to businesses, including through local financial institutions. The initiative also provides technical assistance in preparing investment projects, assessing climate impacts and improving companies' investment attractiveness.

At the global level, the program is expected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by more than 31 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent and strengthen climate resilience for over 1.4 million people.

For Uzbekistan, participation in the initiative is expected to open up additional opportunities to attract international capital for industrial modernization, resource-efficient technologies and green economy development.

Potential areas of cooperation include improving energy efficiency in the textile, chemical and construction industries, expanding distributed renewable energy generation, introducing circular economy technologies and modernizing the agro-industrial sector.

Uzbekistan's National Committee for Ecology and Climate Change is working with international partners to explore opportunities for developing a pipeline of investment projects under the program. The process will involve relevant ministries, commercial banks and industrial enterprises.

The initiative is aligned with Uzbekistan's national priorities of reducing greenhouse gas emissions, improving energy efficiency, and transitioning to a low-carbon economic model. Specific financing allocations for participating countries will be determined as investment projects are developed and selected.

World.title: Kazakhstan's Air Astana Group Q3 revenue rises 20.6% to $529.1M
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 12. Kazakhstan Air Astana Group's revenue and other income increased by 20.6% to $529.1 million in the third quarter of 2026, compared with $438.6 million in the same period of 2025, according to the company.

The company said this represented an improvement in revenue growth compared with the first half of the year, supported by continued pricing strength and Air Astana's planned reallocation of capacity towards higher-margin international routes.

Despite continued cost pressures, quarterly earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization and rent (EBITDAR) remained broadly in line with the previous year, increasing by 0.4% to $105.6 million, compared with $105.2 million in the third quarter of 2025.

However, the EBITDAR margin decreased by 4 percentage points to 20%, compared with 24% a year earlier, as higher revenue was largely absorbed by increased costs. FlyArystan posted a particularly strong performance, with EBITDAR increasing by 33.9% and its margin improving by 3.1 percentage points in the third quarter.

For the first nine months of 2026, revenue and other income increased by 17.9% to $1.293 billion, compared with $1.0968 billion in the same period of 2025.

EBITDAR decreased by 5.7% to $247.3 million, compared with $262.2 million a year earlier, while the EBITDAR margin declined by 4.8 percentage points to 19.1%, compared with 23.9%.

The company noted that the stabilization of EBITDAR in the third quarter represented an improvement in the year-on-year earnings trend, although the nine-month performance continued to reflect pressure on the Group's cost base.

Air Astana Group operates Air Astana, a full-service airline that launched its first flight in 2002, and FlyArystan, a low-cost carrier established in 2019. The Group is listed on the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange, the Astana International Exchange, and the London Stock Exchange.

World.title: Türkiye's Pegasus Airlines to launch flights to three Uzbek cities
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 12. Pegasus Airlines will launch direct flights from Istanbul to Bukhara and Andijan in December 2026, with flights to Termez scheduled to begin in March 2027.

According to Uzbekistan's Tourism Committee, the airline announced the new routes on November 11 during a presentation in Tashkent.

Flights between Istanbul and Bukhara will begin on December 14, while services to Andijan are scheduled to start on December 18. Flights to Termez are expected to launch on March 1, 2027.

Initially, the Bukhara and Termez routes will operate three times a week, while flights to Andijan will run twice a week.

The new routes will connect Uzbekistan's regional tourism destinations with visitors from Türkiye, Europe, the Middle East and other markets through Pegasus Airlines' network, which covers more than 160 destinations in 58 countries.

The route expansion follows agreements reached during talks between Chairman of Uzbekistan's Tourism Committee Abdulaziz Akkulov and Pegasus Airlines management during his working visit to Türkiye. The discussions focused on expanding affordable air travel, attracting transit passengers through Istanbul and promoting Uzbekistan's tourism potential internationally.

The new connections will improve access to several regional destinations. Bukhara is known for its historical and cultural heritage, while Andijan provides access to the Fergana Valley. The Termez route will connect travelers with the archaeological and historical attractions of the Surkhandarya region.

The cooperation framework also includes joint marketing campaigns, familiarization trips and business-to-business meetings with tour operators. The parties will also consider launching flights to Karshi and Nukus in the longer term.

The expansion of air connections is part of Uzbekistan's broader efforts to increase international tourist arrivals and strengthen its position in the global tourism market.

World.title: Turkmenistan signs five new agreements with international organizations in Antalya
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 12. Turkmenistan has signed five cooperation documents with UN agencies and the International Water Management Institute in Antalya, covering climate action, energy transition, industrial development and water management, the Turkmen Foreign Ministry reported.

The documents were signed yesterday during the working visit of Chairman of the Halk Maslahaty of Turkmenistan Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov to Türkiye.

The package includes the Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate Action, signed by the Minister of Education of Turkmenistan in cooperation with the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF).

The signing ceremony was attended by Gernot Laganda, Director of UNICEF's Climate and Environment Programme and head of the organization's delegation to COP31, as well as Jalpa Ratna, UNICEF Representative in Turkmenistan.

Another document is an agreement with the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) on implementing the third phase of the work plan for the management of the phasedown of hydrochlorofluorocarbons in Turkmenistan for 2026-2030.

The package also includes a project document titled "Supporting the Energy Transition in Remote Settlements of Turkmenistan." It was prepared by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) office in Turkmenistan jointly with the country's Ministries of Environmental Protection and Energy.

In addition, Turkmenistan signed the Country Programming Framework for 2026-2030 with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).

The fifth document is a memorandum of understanding between the State Committee for Water Management of Turkmenistan and the International Water Management Institute. It provides for cooperation in the field of water resources management.

World.title: When Evan Gershkovich was arrested by the FSB he feared the worst
World.content:
Yekaterinburg, Russia, 2023. American journalist Evan Gershkovich is sitting in a restaurant talking to a source.

A number of masked men enter.

They inform the American that he is being arrested by Russia's main intelligence agency, the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation.

Known as the FSB, it's the successor to the Soviet-era KGB, where Russian President Vladimir Putin previously worked.

Gershkovich is now the first US journalist to be arrested in Russia since the Cold War. He is hooded and thrown in a van before the agents get to work.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, who as a Russian secret service KGB served in the German Democratic Republic, was equipped with a house card of the responsible Ministry of State Security service. (Supplied: BSTU)

Vladimir Putin's details are seen on the Stasi identification card found in Germany.

"The hood gets ripped off at one point," Gershkovich told 7.30.

"There's operatives sitting next to me and a man across from me in a suit. He asks, 'Who do you work for?' I say the Wall Street Journal.

" The hood goes back on [and] fists pummel my midsection and the hood comes back off again. "

The question is repeated before Gershkovich arrives at a station and is charged with espionage.

Lefortovo pre-trial detention centre in Moscow, Russia. (Reuters: Shamil Zhumatov)

The charge strikes fear into the foreign correspondent. He knows Russia under Putin has a reputation for doing whatever it takes to silence enemies of the state.

In 2018, former Russian spy Sergei Skripal and his daughter, Yulia, were targeted in an assassination attempt with deadly nerve agent Novichok. They would ultimately survive the poisoning.

Former Putin opponent Alexei Navalny survived an attempt on his life undertaken with Novichok before his eventual death in February 2024, in one of Russia's harshest prisons.

And in August 2023 former Putin ally Yevgeny Prigozhin perished in a plane crash, while a number of other former allies have disappeared.

Gershkovich told 7.30 that his main fear was torture.

City view of Yekaterinburg in Russia where Evan Gershkovich was initially detained. (Reuters: Evgenia Novozhenina)

"I've reported on cases where somebody's brought to a station, strapped to a chair, electrodes are attached to various parts of their body, and they're electrocuted, simply for the fact of trying to get them to sign papers that attest to the fact that they're guilty in a fabricated case," he said.

Life in the 'exchange bank'

The fear was real but for Gershkovich, the torture would not come. The FSB and Russian authorities had something else in mind.

Gershkovich realised he had been set up as Russia looked to replenish its "exchange bank".

That "bank", Gershkovich says, is all about Russia having a number of foreigners it can use in exchange to get some of its own incarcerated back.

In his case, the main target was Russian hitman Vadim Krasikov, who was serving jail time in Germany, having been convicted in 2019 over the brazen daylight murder of a former Chechen militant in a Berlin park in 2018.

The judge called the killing of Georgian citizen Zelimkhan Khangoshvili "state terrorism", adding that the order had almost certainly come from Putin himself.

Among the evidence he cited for Russian state involvement were Krasikov's official Russian papers containing a false identity, and the fact that Russian law empowered Putin to order the murder of state enemies abroad.

The IK-3 penal colony, where Russian opposition politician Alexei Navalny served his jail term. (Reuters)

Gershkovich said he knew almost immediately prisoner exchange would be the case once he had arrived in his "really tiny" prison cell that measured 2.4 metres by 3 metres by 3.7 metres.

"It has a bed running on one wall, a bed at the end perpendicular at the window, a desk running down the other, and it's so thin that only one person can fit walking up and down that space, and you eventually have a cellmate," he told 7.30.

"So there are two of you living in the cell, and you can only walk up and down six or seven steps.

"On my second night in prison on TV, I'm watching the main evening news show and one of the hosts says to the other host 'we've replenished our exchange fund'.

"The Russians use that as a catch-all for the foreigners that they hold to be swapped."

Gershkovich says he was treated relatively well compared to other prisoners he knew about.

"I've been reporting obviously on stories of Ukrainian civilians, Ukrainian POWs, Russian political prisoners," he said.

"[They] were tortured, deprived of hot food, hot showers, told they're never gonna see their families again, that's not happening to me.

"Really early on, my mattress is thicker than my cellmate's. Before the US ambassador comes to visit, the prison warden comes and checks in on me, asks how I'm doing.

"Eventually, there's even a moment where I say 'I'm surprised how much you're checking in on me'. He says, 'Of course, we care about your health.'

" I joke, 'Well, the package has to be whole and undamaged or its value will go down,'" and he checks [over] his shoulder, gets all serious and says, 'I didn't tell you this, but yes.' "

While it had become clear to Gershkovich that he was waiting for a swap, the death of Navalny was a blow and he remembers it as a moment that was likely intended to strike fear.

Russian opposition politician Alexei Navalny was a major opponent of Putin. (Reuters: Shamil Zhumatov)

He heard the news while he was on his one hour a day on the jail's roof, his only time outside the tiny cell.

"We're on this walk and suddenly the radio, which never happens, switches to the news and we hear that Alexei Navalny has died, and then it switches back," he said.

"I think they did that for the Ukrainians who were being held in the prison, the Russian political prisoners, perhaps myself too, very deliberately to send a message to us."

Before his death, there had been reports Navalny could form part of a prisoner swap deal in exchange for Russian assassin Krasikov.

But six months later, the swap happened in Türkiye, and the journalist was released alongside fellow Americans Paul Whelan and Alsu Kurmasheva.

What Russians think of Putin

Gershkovich used his 16 months in prison to learn more about Putin's Russia and what people really thought of a leader he said was growing more authoritarian while the war in Ukraine rolled on.

Vladimir Putin in Red Square in Moscow. (Sputnik: Yuri Kochetkov/Pool via Reuters)

"When Putin came to power it coincided with this big oil and gas boom," Gershkovich said of his May 2000 inauguration as president for the first time.

"At the same time, he made really clear what would happen politically if you tried to challenge him.

"The social contract that was essentially developed was your life will get better, money is pouring in as long as you stay out of politics.

"That is essentially the logic of the regime over the next 20, 25 years, except that it gets more and more repressive.

"By the time I go to prison, what I, and I think the best sociologists and researchers working on Russia will tell you, is that 15 per cent of people really support Putin in the war, 15 per cent really are anti-Putin and anti-war."

He said the rest would abstain from making any comment on the war, such was the fear Putin wielded on either side of the prison walls.

Evan Gershkovich reunites with his mother while US President Joe Biden looks on after a successful prisoner swap between the US and Russia. (Reuters: Kevin Mohatt)

Gershkovich said one prison guard perfectly encapsulated the example, telling him: "The news is so bad, I try not to follow it. I go to my dacha, my country house, I fish."

"So I asked him what he thought about the war," Gershkovich said.

"He smiled and zippered his mouth shut, put a finger to his mouth and kind of shrugged his shoulders. And what he was telling me is, I think, 'I don't support the war, but I can't talk about it.'

" I think the vast majority of Russians are somewhere in that camp. "

World.title: Marsh dodges Sandpapergate questions in testy press conference exchange
World.content:
Australia's one-day captain, Mitch Marsh, has refused to address key aspects of the Sandpapergate ball-tampering scandal as journalists peppered him with questions at a press conference.

Marsh, who was bowling when Cameron Bancroft was spotted hiding a piece of sandpaper in his pants during the 2018 series, spent most of the 12-minute press conference straight-batting questions about the infamous South Africa tour and Usman Khawaja's explosive allegations.

The very first question put to Marsh was: "Did you know that sandpaper was being used to tamper with cricket balls in South Africa?"

"Jeez, you hit a six off the first ball there, mate. Well done," Marsh replied.

Loading Instagram content

"I respect that certain people have told their stories, but I'm not here to share mine.

"I know that might sound weird, but it's a big week for us, and it's an important time for this one-day group.

"I really respect that Uzzy has told his story. He's written his book, and my focus is really on tomorrow."

Marsh was continually peppered with questions about why he was not willing to speak on the topic.

"I've personally moved on," he said.

Mitch Marsh says he has no ill feelings towards Usman Khawaja for the allegations made in his book. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

"I respect that others probably haven't, but I have, and I hope that's respected.

"This is my choice to not go back there. Who knows? Maybe I'll write a book one day."

Marsh insisted he held no grudges against Khawaja.

"I respect Uzzy for telling his story and for writing his book, and I don't sit here coming from a place of judgement," Marsh said.

"Everyone's got their story. Some will be willing to share it, and others might not, purely on the basis of the fact that they've moved on.

"It's really important that at some stage we do."

Australia's Test captain, Pat Cummins, is set to front a press conference in Sydney tomorrow morning and has promised to answer "any and all media".

AAP

World.title: Surgeon among six killed in Israeli air strike on Gaza hospital
World.content:
Palestinian health authorities say a surgeon is one of at least six people who have been killed in an Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza.

The attack happened in the early hours of Thursday morning, local time. Video from the scene shows extensive damage to one of the compound's buildings.

Gaza's Civil Defense agency said the surgery department was hit and that at least 20 people were injured in the blast.

Israeli strikes kill eight people in Gaza, medics say Israeli strikes killed at least eight Palestinians, including five police officers, in the Gaza Strip in two separate attacks, according to medics and the Hamas-run interior ministry.

Hours after the strike, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said a "senior Hamas terrorist and additional terrorists" had been using the hospital as a command centre.

"Targeting a medical facility that includes patients receiving treatment and teams performing their humanitarian and professional duty represents a serious attack on the health system and a flagrant violation of international laws and conventions that ensure the protection of medical facilities, employees and patients," Gaza's health ministry said in a statement.

"The ministry confirms that the continued targeting of hospitals and their medical facilities exacerbates the suffering of the sick and wounded, and threatens what remains of the ability of the health sector to provide its services, in light of the catastrophic conditions in the Gaza Strip."

Rizk Abu Shaira was the surgeon who was killed, the ministry said.

Hamas labelled the strike a "fully fledged war crime".

At least six people have been killed in an Israeli air strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, in southern Gaza. (Reuters: Ramadan Abed)

Israeli group condemns attacks on health system

Israel regularly justifies attacks on medical and humanitarian facilities by insisting they lose their protections under international law if they are used by Hamas for terrorist activities.

In this instance, the IDF said Hamas had been using Nasser Hospital as a command centre and claimed the buildings were being used to store weapons and conduct interrogations.

The IDF released graphics showing the building it hit, but did not provide any further evidence to back up its claims about its use by Hamas.

Measuring Israel's expansion across the Middle East ABC analysis reveals the extent of Israel's expansion on four fronts: Lebanon, the West Bank, Gaza and Syria.

"The IDF and the [Israel Security Agency] strongly condemn the Hamas terrorist organisation's cynical exploitation of civilian and medical infrastructure for military purposes, while endangering the lives of patients, medical personnel, and civilians," it said in a statement.

"Prior to and during the strike, steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians, including the use of precision munitions and aerial surveillance."

The IDF also released audio of what it said was a warning issued to the health ministry for Hamas to cease using hospitals across the strip, or risk further action by the military.

"Israel's genocide in Gaza continues under the guise of a ceasefire," Israeli advocacy group Physicians for Human Rights Israel said.

"Repeated attacks on hospitals and healthcare workers are further devastating an already shattered healthcare system, denying Palestinians in Gaza access to essential medical care and the ability to recover and live in dignity.

"The international community's inaction and continued impunity enable these attacks on Gaza's healthcare system. As long as those responsible are not held accountable, the attacks will continue."

Nasser Hospital targeted multiple times

Palestinian health authorities say more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the October 2025 ceasefire, many of them civilians, including women and children.

The death toll in Gaza now stands at more than 74,600 people.

Nasser Hospital has been targeted a number of times during the three-year long war in Gaza, triggered by Hamas' deadly attacks on Israel in October 2023.

UN inquiry on Gaza and the West Bank Israel has continued to commit genocide in Gaza since last October's ceasefire, according to a report from UN-commissioned experts. Israel has rejected the findings as "misinformation".

On August 25 last year, the hospital was the scene of a "double-tap" strike by Israeli forces.

The IDF claimed it was targeting a Hamas terrorist when it opened fire on a camera operator who had placed his camera on the outside of the hospital to film the Khan Younis skyline.

Minutes later, as emergency workers and fellow journalists were crawling over the site of the attack, another strike hit the building.

Twenty-two Palestinians were killed that day, including five journalists.

Among them were journalists working for the Associated Press and Reuters. The agencies and other media outlets condemned the strikes.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu labelled that incident a "tragic mishap" and the IDF said it had launched an investigation into the matter.

Its findings are yet to be released.

Gaza's health ministry says the strike on Nasser Hospital was a "flagrant violation of international laws". (Reuters)

Israeli attacks across Gaza have reportedly increased in recent days, despite the ceasefire being in place.

Progress towards the next stage of the ceasefire remains stalled, with Hamas saying it will lay down its weapons only if Israel stops launching strikes and withdraws from territory.

Israel says it will only stop once Hamas demilitarises and no longer poses a threat to the country.

Both sides have been criticised for the delays, although the Trump administration-backed Board of Peace has ratcheted up its rhetoric against the Israeli government in recent months, accusing it of avoiding holding up its side of the bargain.

World.title: FA scrambles for Jordan alternative with Socceroos reluctant to travel
World.content:
Socceroos players remain unwilling to travel to Jordan as Football Australia (FA) scrambles for alternatives to playing an upcoming friendly in Amman.

But US Soccer's decision to withdraw its team from the under-17 World Cup in ‌Qatar over safety concerns is not expected to affect either the Socceroos or their Joeys counterparts.

The Socceroos and Joeys are both in camp in Doha ahead of their respective friendlies and World Cup campaigns.

Popovic refuses to blacklist Socceroos who pull out of Jordan friendly Australia coach Tony Popovic insists Socceroos players who are reluctant to play Jordan due to security concerns will not be blacklisted from the national team set-up if they elect to withdraw from his squad.

The senior team is due to face Qatar on Saturday (AEDT) before travelling to Amman to face Jordan on November 18.

The latter is the issue, with PFA boss Beau Busch saying last week that Socceroos players had "overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated".

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) advises Australians to reconsider their need to travel to Jordan "due to the unpredictable security situation" and the "threat of terrorism".

FA had been keen for the game in Jordan to proceed, but has said it was monitoring the security situation in the area.

The friendlies against Qatar and Jordan were arranged as preparations for January's Asian Cup, but the postponement of the tournament to December 2027 due to conflict in Saudi Arabia has decreased their significance.

Martin Kugeler has flown to Doha to find a solution. (Getty Images: Ayush Kumar)

FA heavy hitters including chief executive Martin Kugeler and football director Heather Garriock flew to Doha this week, as did Busch and men's head of player relations Jon McKain.

Players are not expected to back down and agree to play in Jordan, likely leaving cancellation or relocation as the options.

One option is Australia remaining in Qatar and playing Jordan in Doha.

But that proposal is understood to have been met with some reluctance from both the Qatari and Jordanian football associations.

Jordan has already had to deal with Indonesia pulling out of a friendly this window.

Playing the Jordan game somewhere in southern Europe is another option, along with cancelling or postponing the game altogether.

Coach Tony Popovic, due to speak to media in his pre-match press conference on Thursday night, has indicated no players would be blacklisted from future selection if they withdrew from his squad for security reasons.

Elsewhere, in ‌a letter sent to players, US Soccer said it was cancelling its team's pre-tournament camp and its participation in the under-17 World Cup "in light of current circumstances".

US Soccer cited US State Department's Level 3 travel advisory for Qatar and related ‌directives for ‌embassy ⁠staff and families.

But the Joeys are not expected to follow the US in withdrawing from the under-17 tournament in Qatar, while the Socceroos are understood not to have issues with being in Qatar.

World.title: Kiwi duo Ponga and Waaka claim Golden Boot awards after stunning seasons
World.content:
New Zealand duo Kalyn Ponga and Stacey Waaka have been named the men's and women's Golden Boot winners after outstanding individual seasons at their respective clubs.

Ponga scored six tries as he led Newcastle to the NRL grand final before scoring two further tries for the Kiwis at the Rugby League World Cup despite suffering a broken arm.

Waaka, a cross-code star, scored nine tries for the Warriors in just 10 NRLW appearances and added nine tries in four World Cup appearances.

Both players will be in action for New Zealand's men's and women's sides in their respective World Cup finals this weekend as they take on Australia.

Ponga is New Zealand's eighth men's Golden Boot winner, joining Hugh McGahan, Stacey Jones, Benji Marshall, Shaun Johnson, Roger Tuivasa-Sheck, Joseph Manu and James Fisher-Harris.

Waaka is the third New Zealand player to win the women's award, joining Raecene McGregor and Georgia Hale.

Ponga edged out his Cup final counterpart Reece Walsh, Samoa powerhouse Francis Manulelua, Tonga centre Robert Toia and Kiwi centre Casey McLean who were all shortlisted for the men's award.

The Wheelchair golden boot was taken out by England's Rob Hawkins ahead of Friday night's final in Wollongong between England and France.

World.title: Data centre industry butts up against community challenges
World.content:
The peak body representing data centres in Australia say its members are still grappling with "getting community consultation right" after several AI companies have either dumped or paused their plans for building centres across the country.

South Australia has today seen the first sign of data centre development in retreat, with Quantum DC announcing it will pause plans to build a 1200-megawatt AI data centre in Tungkillo, in the Adelaide Hills, following deep frustration, anger and protests from the surrounding community.

In New South Wales, another AI data centre proposed for Sydney's south, on the Cooks River, was scrapped over the weekend, the latest in a series of proposed NSW data centres to be dumped following community opposition.

Peak body Data Centres Australia does not represent Quantum DC.

Speaking broadly, its CEO Belinda Dennett said the challenge with community engagement was choosing the right time.

"Communities want early engagement, but they also want detailed answers, so there is a bit of a trade-off.

"Often, early engagement means you don't have all those answers around design plans, around energy source, around how much water that may use."

She said there was great potential and interest to build data centres in South Australia, but operators and investors wanted policy certainty.

"That's the challenge for all the states at the moment, the challenge of not having federal rules in place … we don't have that policy certainty," she said.

"The quicker we have certainty, the more viable I think Australia's going to be."

Tungkillo's rolling hills won't have a data centre, for now. (Supplied: Magdalene Lippett)

All sides of politics welcome pause

On Thursday, political parties including the Liberals, One Nation and the Greens welcomed the pause on the Tungkillo development, while the SA government criticised the developer for its consultation process.

The Greens went a step further, calling for a data centre moratorium.

SA's minister for artificial intelligence (AI), Chris Picton, said the Tungkillo announcement highlighted why the state government was keen to get legislation through the parliament to enable proper regulatory control.

"[It's] going to be critical to making sure that we can think through all these issues with data centres to make sure that can be managed in an appropriate way, whether that be issues about energy, or water, or land use," Mr Picton said.

Opposition leader Ashton Hurn said it didn't make sense for a data centre at Tungkillo to be built on "prime agricultural land", but there was also a need to make sure the community understood why data centres are needed.

"No-one really wants them in the backyard because no-one really understands what they're needed for in the first place," Ms Hurn said.

"We believe that a vehicle to do that is including them in the royal commission," Ms Hurn said.

When details of the state's Royal Commission into Artificial Intelligence were released in early October, its terms of reference did not include data centres.

Mr Picton said it wasn't remiss of the government not to include them: "They are completely separate things.

"Data centres have issues, but they're infrastructure issues … They're issues about energy use, water use and where the land is."

Community protests against the Tungkillo data centre seem to have had an effect. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

The Greens, One Nation and the Liberal Party united in the upper house on Wednesday to establish a parliamentary inquiry into data centres, which was not supported by Labor.

One Nation SA leader Cory Bernardi said the party would like to see a pause on data centres until the inquiry is finished.

"But we're also recognising that data centres per se are not bad," he said.

"We have a data centre here in the metropolitan area of Adelaide that hasn't caused any fuss at all.

"But what we want is a community licence for it."

World.title: Ex-wife of police prosecutor tells court of assault just after C-section
World.content:
A NSW police prosecutor assaulted his then wife as she held their newborn baby while recovering from birth complications, a court has heard.

Family and domestic violence support services: NSW Domestic Violence Line on 1800 656 463

Lifeline on 131 114

Men's Referral Service on 1300 766 491

Mensline on 1300 789 978

Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578

Emergency services on Triple Zero (000) if you need immediate care

MZ, whose identity the court suppressed to protect the victim, was taken into custody in July, after a jury convicted him of 11 offences related to domestic violence.

These include two counts of sexual intercourse without consent, two counts of common assault, five counts of assault occasioning bodily harm, intentionally choke a person without consent, and sexually touch another person without consent.

The 50-year-old man, a police prosecutor whose career with the force spanned more than two decades, appeared via audio-visual link in the NSW District Court.

He sat idle and expressionless as his ex-wife and her two children read victim impact statements.

"You did not simply hurt me, you changed the course of my life and the life of my children," his ex-wife read from the courtroom.

She read through pages of testimony maintaining composure, but her voice began to waver when she detailed the abuse her children had to witness.

"After the C-section of our second child, you assaulted me when I was recovering from complications," she said.

" I was physically weak and recovering…My eldest daughter had to intervene to protect me from you. "

One incident, she said, caused her to realise he would not change.

"The time when you assaulted me when I held our child was one of the most frightening moments.

"Even holding our baby was not enough to stop you. That's when I began to understand that nothing would make you stop."

The court heard that she faced a power imbalance when accusing a police prosecutor of domestic violence offences.

"The blue shirt you hid behind was meant to represent safety…instead it became the same blue shirt I learnt to fear," she said.

She also said the years spent pursuing the matter through the courts forced her to relive trauma.

"You do not get to write the end of my story," she said. "I survived everything you did. I survived you."

The court heard the abuse left her two children suffering from post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and living with a distrust of law enforcement.

Court heard MZ was sexually abused as a child

Judge Philip Hogan heard closing arguments as members of MZ's family watched from the gallery, among them his father, brothers and sister.

The defence, represented by barrister Arjun Chhabra, said the serious offences warranted a jail sentence of just under 10 years after mitigating factors were considered.

"MZ described an incident of sexual abuse when he was a child by a trusted figure," the court heard.

Mr Chhabra said his client had been diagnosed with PTSD, and that his work as a police prosecutor exposed him to criminal matters that left him triggered — particularly around an incident of domestic violence in 2020.

"It is likely that his symptoms reduced his capacity to manage stress during periods of heightened conflict," Mr Chhabra said.

He said MZ's career in the NSW Police Force would make him a target in jail, and that the time he would serve in protective custody would be more onerous.

"That he may come face to face with people he arrested or prosecuted…that is a real punishment… and that ought to be reflected in the sentencing exercise," Mr Chhabra said.

'No expression of remorse'

The Crown, represented by barrister Rohan Cooley, said a serving police officer should have known better.

"The offender must have known because he was a police officer that this would be a consequence," he said.

He acknowledged the report of sexual abuse and PTSD, but did not believe it "impaired his ability to appreciate the seriousness or potential consequences of his actions".

Mr Cooley told the court MZ had shown no sense of wrongdoing over his actions.

"There's clearly no expression of remorse," he said.

The defence had previously acknowledged the absence of an expression of remorse.

Judge Hogan adjourned the matter for sentencing at Gosford District Court on December 11.

He has been suspended from the NSW Police Force without pay while his employment is under review.

World.title: With Jensen Huang under pressure, Nvidia finds itself with no succession plan
World.content:
When reports of an espionage plot against Nvidia's Jensen Huang first emerged, the company stood by their chief executive.

Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo released a statement saying Mr Huang was committed to keep leading the firm "without interruption".

Before its probe into Mr Huang's romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy was even underway, Nvidia said it had "no reason to believe" either US national security or company secrets had been compromised.

Two days later, Nvidia's board is reportedly meeting to decide whether to oust Mr Huang.

How Nvidia came to investigate Jensen Huang's affair The chief executive of the world's most valuable company and a close ally of Donald Trump admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Here's what we know.

Overnight, the New York Times reported he had a second extra-marital affair with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, the company's vice-president of health care, who also reported to him.

This week, shares in the multi-trillion-dollar tech giant tumbled, while Nvidia and Mr Huang have faced a ‌proposed class action accusing them ‌of ⁠defrauding ‌shareholders.

But what is perhaps most extraordinary is that Nvidia has no obvious successor to Mr Huang, who has run the company since it was created 33 years ago.

Holding the position of co-founder, president and chief executive, Mr Huang has created an unusually flat corporate structure with about 60 executives reporting directly to him.

He once said he did not believe in succession planning, according to the Wall Street Journal, despite his family being woven into the company's fabric.

Jensen Huang's daughter, Madison (left), is a senior marketing director at Nvidia and Spencer (right), his son, is a product line manager in robotics. (Thu Hoang Ly/The Mercury News/Getty Images)

Mr Huang is the only Nvidia insider on the company's board, which operates without a permanent chair. Instead, a lead director is chosen annually by a majority of board members.

"Jensen is not replaceable … there is no other person on the management team bench that can step in seamlessly as CEO," tech analyst Dan Ives told Reuters.

Following the first reports this morning the board was preparing to oust him, Nvidia's share price dropped about 8 per cent in after-hours trade.

That brought it 33 per cent lower than its peak in early October.

Jensen Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife after reports emerged he had developed a relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), a data centre executive at the centre of the alleged spy plot. (Reuters: CTI)

Mr Huang's departure could leave the world-leading chip maker and global AI trade in an even more precarious position, according to investment analyst Jun Bei Liu.

"He's the face of Nvidia and Nvidia has been front and centre of the AI build-out," she said.

"If we look at how many new cloud data centre businesses have been sponsored in this circular financing world, it's pretty much all by Nvidia.

"There's just a lot of uncertainty to come … not just for Nvidia, it's for the whole AI, the circular financing, the AI build-out, all the ⁠businesses that they co-invest and sponsor."

Huang's star power

Mr Huang has spent decades building Nvidia into a leading developer of graphics processing units, the hardware that AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic rely on to operate.

One of the world's most valuable companies, Nvidia hit a market capitalisation of $US5.7 trillion ($8.3 trillion) at its peak in early October.

Jensen Huang is one of the world's most influential figures in the tech and AI industry. (Reuters: Kim Soo-hyeon)

In America's pursuit to win the AI race against China, Mr Huang has emerged as a close ally of Donald Trump and one of the few people known to have a direct line to him.

He has been to the White House at least five times since Mr Trump returned to office and just months ago accompanied him on a trip to Beijing.

Mr Huang's star power also extends to other tech billionaires such as Larry Ellison and Elon Musk, who famously begged him for more Nvidia chips. (Already, the SpaceX founder has suggested he would hire him).

NYT tech reporter Ryan Mac told the ABC's Afternoon Briefing that Mr Huang was a person "that sets the tone when it comes to AI regulation or lack thereof".

"He is an agenda-setter, someone that has a close relationship with Donald Trump and influences policy not just in the US but globally.

"This is arguably the most important person in the tech industry, certainly in AI," he said.

Mac, one of the reporters who broke the story of Mr Huang's second alleged affair, said it was "incredibly unclear" who would be tapped to succeed the Nvidia boss should he depart the company.

"He has this kind of gravitas, this 'key man' placement in the company that would be very hard to replace," he said.

World.title: The pushback on data centres is democracy at work
World.content:
NationalNSWData centres Editorial The pushback on data centres is democracy at work The Herald's View Editorial November 12, 2026 — 8:00pm

November 12, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The AI and data centre boom is not turning out to be the godsend some claim. Environmental problems and the future of work are among the big questions our society is facing, but community groups worried about data centres in their backyard are not waiting for the answer. In September, the industrial property giant Goodman Group backed away from building an $800 million, 24/7 data centre at Lane Cove amid resident protests and concerns by utility providers Sydney Water and Ausgrid that it would strain existing infrastructure and increase electrocution and fire risks. A proposal to build a data centre in North Katoomba was knocked back last June after local opposition, and last week a new data centre beside the Cooks River was scrapped following Kogarah residents’ protests. A NEXTDC Data centre in Artarmon in Sydney. Dominic Lorrimer In western Sydney, the Herald’s Ellie Busby reports a group of mostly young 20-somethings is rallying the community to protest against technology company AirTrunk’s plan for a $9 billion facility, the nation’s largest data centre development, which would be built in Kemps Creek and near three schools. There have been similar outcomes in Victoria. The pushback against artificial intelligence infrastructure construction emerged as hot button issue that contributed to the Democrat landslide in this month’s US midterm elections.



Australia is a significant data centre market in the Asia-Pacific region. Earlier this year, Westpac Economics said the boom had helped make Australia the second-largest investment destination for data centres, after the US. Investment is estimated to top $155 billion in the coming decade, most slated for Sydney and Melbourne. Currently, about 165 data centres operate around Australia and 225 are planned. Related Article Data centres ‘Stop the slop’: Meet the young people fighting western Sydney’s data centre rush There are arguments in their favour. The NSW government credits data centres and renewable energy for boosting business investment and helping to prevent the state economy from falling into recession. By embracing AI infrastructure, Australia has a better chance of reaping the economic, security and workforce benefits of the technology of the future. However, both governments and AI companies have failed to effectively explain these benefits to voters, so anger over data centres in the suburbs is mounting.



The NSW government talks about balance. Its guidelines now require the needs of communities, households and businesses to be protected, and for centres to pay for the energy and water and to manage the environmental impacts of operations. A parliamentary inquiry this week suggested smarter planning controls were needed to encourage companies to build in special precincts and avoid unwanted US-style data centre clusters in densely populated suburbs. The Albanese government has introduced new rules to force data centres to source round-the-clock power from entirely new renewable sources located in the same state to limit their impact on the grid and avoid price spikes. Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles this week even went so far as to say suburbs were the wrong place to build data centres, and they should be constructed a long way from where people live. In some circles, the term NIMBY is an insult. Yet, given the well-documented problems associated with data centres, it is difficult to be negative about residents motivated by concerns about proliferation in their neighbourhoods. There might be reasons why centres need to be built in suburban areas (transmission speeds, proximity to power), but AI companies have failed to make their case to the affected communities. Regardless of the benefits or costs of data centres, these campaigns are evidence of people power and democracy at work. They’re pleasing proof that, should there be enough of a groundswell, the AI companies and governments will heed local sentiments. World.title: Victorian election hot seats: The social media app that could hold major voter sway in Ringwood
World.content:
Despite running for the seat of Sydenham, in Melbourne’s western suburbs, Liberal candidate Nathalie Moussi can’t call herself a local.

In fact, she owns a house in Torquay just minutes from the beach and says she splits her time between that property and another in Melbourne that’s outside the Sydenham boundary.

If she wins on election night, then she’ll move, she says.

Nathalie Moussi is running as the Liberal candidate in the seat of Sydenham. Facebook

The revelation is a blow to the Liberals’ campaign to unseat Labor from its once-safe seat.

As former NSW premier and federal senator Kristina Keneally discovered in her disastrous 2022 campaign, voters care deeply about where candidates live.

After being parachuted into a long-time Labor seat far from where she lived, Keneally and the party were stunned by a huge swing against them and saw the electorate opt for independent candidate Dai Le instead.

Moussi now confronts a similar risk.

One Nation candidate Joh Bauch also owns property in Truganina, south of the electorate.

The Star Weekly reported in 2024 he lived in Deer Park, which is located outside the seat’s boundary. Bauch did not return multiple requests for comment or confirm if he lives in the seat of Sydenham.

Local councillor and One Nation candidate for Sydenham, Joh Bauch. Joe Armao

While there are no formal rules around whether a candidate must live within the electorate when they run for office, it’s the kind of detail that matters to a lot of voters when choosing their representative.

“People in the western suburbs are very patriotic about living in the west,” said Maria Kerr, who is running as an independent in Sydenham and lives in Delahey. “I think it’s vitally important the candidate lives in the seat. They need to understand what the issues are on the ground.”

Moussi defended herself by pointing to her ownership of the popular Luxor Function Centre in Taylors Lakes.

“For the past 15 years, I’ve invested in Sydenham, built my business, employed local people and supported the community,” she told The Age.

“I believe representing a community is about more than where you sleep at night. It’s about the contribution you’ve made, the jobs you’ve created and how hard you’re prepared to fight for local people.”

One Nation did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaCrime Woman injured in mistaken identity firebombing linked to campaign against developer Cameron Houston and Chris Vedelago November 12, 2026 — 7:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. An innocent couple asleep in their Cheltenham townhouse were the unintended victims of a targeted campaign of violence by the Finks outlaw motorcycle gang against besieged property developer Simon Pitard. A 52-year-old woman sustained serious burns after the Bay Road property was firebombed in a pre-dawn attack on October 28. The damaged Bay Street property. Cameron Houston The woman’s 57-year-old partner was not injured by the arson attack, which police believe was a case of mistaken identity with the wrong property being torched. A police spokeswoman confirmed the anti-bikie Echo Taskforce was investigating the Cheltenham attack, along with the firebombing of Pitard’s home in Brighton and a drive-by shooting at an Arcare aged care centre in Maidstone.



The police spokesman also confirmed the victims of the Cheltenham attack had no links to Pitard. This masthead can also reveal the campaign of threats and violence against Pitard began more than two years ago, when he was viciously bashed in April 2024. Embattled property tycoon Simon Pitard. Arsineh Houspian Three underworld and property industry sources, who asked not to be identified because of safety concerns, said Pitard required reconstructive surgery to his face following the assault. In 2022, Pitard was banned from managing any corporation for 3½ years, following the collapse of Steller Property Group in 2019 with debts of $617 million. The 44-year-old was director of more than 40 companies that were placed into liquidation.



Pitard co-founded Steller Group with Melbourne businessman Nicholas Smedley who were involved in the redevelopment of the Continental Hotel in Sorrento when the company spectacularly collapsed in 2019. Police outside an Arcare facility in Malvern on Wednesday. Despite being pursued by a conga-line of creditors, Pitard maintained his lavish lifestyle and continued to reside in a Brighton mansion registered under the name of his wife, Skye Pitard. Property records reveal her father, Russell Knowles, co-founder of Arcare Aged Care, holds a caveat registered against the property on Manor Road, suggesting he has a financial stake in the property. On October 27, several masked men rammed the front gates of Pitard’s residence on Manor Street and doused accelerant over two luxury cars, which were both destroyed in the blaze.



Related Article Exclusive

Organised crime Melbourne nursing homes under police guard as bikies target prominent aged care chain The campaign of intimidation targeted at Pitard took an unexpected turn last week, when his father-in-law’s aged-care empire came under attack. On October 6, elderly residents at the Arcare facility in Maidstone awoke to the sound of gunfire as two masked men in a white SUV fired ten shots at the home. This masthead revealed earlier this week that Victoria Police immediately deployed officers to protect other aged-care centres operated by Arcare, with police cars stationed outside homes across Melbourne. Police cars were parked outside two homes, while private guards patrolled two other centres earlier this week.



On Wednesday night, a police van was spotted outside an Arcare address in the inner east. Less than a day after the Maidstone shooting, the Finks were identified as an “organised crime priority” by Victoria Police, which formed a specialist taskforce to target the gang. Detective Superintendent Wayne Cheesman put the gang on notice, but made no reference to the attack on the Arcare facility, or Pitard’s home. “My message to the Finks … and to any outlaw motorcycle gang that chooses to cause harm in our community is very clear: if you choose to continue your involvement in serious and organised crime, Victoria Police is coming for you.” But no arrests have been made almost a week after the drive-by shooting in Maidstone, while the deployment of marked police cars, vans and cameras outside several aged-care centres places further strain on the force’s resources.



A source, with knowledge of the threats, said Knowles had recently engaged several former members of the Australian Defence Force to provide “close personal protection services” for his daughter and extended family. A letter to residents’ families from Arcare state operations manager Prab Kaur, sent on Monday, said the organisation had increased wellbeing support for residents, visitors and staff after the Maidstone incident, adding that it was also working closely with police and regulators. Simon and Skye Pitard have been approached for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: More wet weather on the way after storms lash Brisbane
World.content:
NationalQueenslandExtreme weather More wet weather on the way after storms lash Brisbane Dominique Tassell and William Davis Updated November 12, 2026 — 7:50pm ,first published November 12, 2026 — 8:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Brisbane may not be out of the woods just yet, with more wet weather possible a day after destructive storms swept the city. Warnings were issued for south-east Queensland by the Bureau of Meteorology before 6pm on Thursday, with the River City on the fringe of one alert area. It said severe thunderstorms likely to produce damaging winds, large hailstones and heavy rainfall that could lead to flash flooding would primarily affect towns to the north-west of Brisbane. Trees fell in Regents Park, Logan, on Wednesday afternoon. Kingaroy, Cherbourg, Taroom, Monto, Yarraman and Gayndah were listed as among the areas that could be hit hardest.



Hail measuring about six centimetres was recorded at Churchable before 5pm, and 75 millimetres of rail was recorded within an hour at Mount Moffatt. The bureau forecasted rain or more thunderstorms in parts of Brisbane until next Tuesday. Loading “It’s a bit of a stormy next few days,” senior meteorologist Robert Lawry said. “There is a chance in Brisbane that we could see some thunderstorms overnight into the early hours.



“We’ll probably get thunderstorms again tomorrow afternoon and early evening, but it’s not super likely to get them into the city … it’ll be more out towards the west. Related Article Queensland Rail Brisbane passengers trapped in train for six hours “Then as we go into Saturday, there’s definitely storms expected again for Brisbane … there’s storms again forecast for Sunday, and there is a chance of those being severe.” As of 6pm on Thursday, about 25,000 properties in south-east Queensland remained without power following a lashing that damaged homes and brought trees down onto traffic. Parts of the region recorded between 50 and 80 millimetres in just half-an-hour, leading to flash flooding.



Wind gusts of up to 96km/h were recorded at Brisbane Airport, leading to delays and diversions. Intense gusts tore down trees and lifted a trampoline out of a backyard in Regents Park, Logan, while large hailstones were recorded west of the Gold Coast. A falling tree knocked out traffic lights before crashing into cars on Aspen Circuit in Logan Reserve about 4pm. Another tree came down on Logan Road in Eight Mile Plains, striking two vehicles just before 5pm. A trampoline was lifted onto a road in Regents Park amid the heavy storms. Sophie Stewart SES crews responded to more than 320 requests for help across the state’s south-east.



Most requests for assistance were related to fallen trees affecting structures or blocking the entry or exit to properties, and many needed tarpaulins for leaking roofs. Among the hundreds of requests, 243 callouts were from Logan City. On Thursday morning, 11 schools in the area were closed. Burrowes State School, Corymbia State School, Crestmead State School, Jimboomba State School, Logan Village State School, Marsden State High School, Marsden State School, South Rock State School, Yarrabilba State School, Yarrabilba State Secondary College and Yugumbir State School were closed. The weather is expected to ease on Friday before a resurgence in storm activity at the weekend. “Into the weekend, we do see those thunderstorms reinvigorate as another surface trough develops across inland parts of Queensland,” meteorologist Jonathan How said. World.title: Has the Christmas beetle really returned to Brisbane?
World.content:
NationalQueenslandWildlife Has the Christmas beetle really returned to Brisbane? Marissa Calligeros November 12, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For many who grew up in Brisbane, Christmas beetles are synonymous with the start of the festive season. Locals remember the shiny, iridescent insects emerging en masse each year to crawl across lawns, congregate around lights and smash into glass doors. This spring, large beetles spotted across Brisbane’s suburbs have attracted attention and raised hopes the Christmas beetle has returned in greater numbers after decades of apparent decline. Loading Some, however, are likely imposters.



Early November rains this year brought forth large numbers of the native brown cockchafer beetle in south-east Queensland. Queensland Museum entomologist Dr Nicole Gunter said this was a species easily mistaken for the Christmas beetle. A brown cockchafer beetle on Brisbane’s southside this month. Marissa Calligeros “They are in the same family of beetles, but different subfamilies,” she said. Christmas beetles were also frequently mistaken for the Argentine lawn beetle.



The imposters are dull brown. In contrast, the real thing is shiny, often an iridescent green or metallic brown in keeping with the season, and twice as large. In welcome news, however, Gunter said south-east Queensland’s wet start to November also made conditions ripe for legitimate varieties of Christmas beetles to emerge. Christmas beetles have notably thicker legs than other beetle species. From left: an Argentinian scarab beetle, a cane beetle species, and a Christmas beetle. Catherine Strohfeldt There are more than 35 species of mainland Christmas beetles, with about 10 of those found in and around Brisbane. “We’re definitely seeing them at the moment,” Gunter said.



“It is the perfect time of the year to be seeing them. We have had good rain last year, and we’ve also had a reasonably wet spring so far.” One of the easiest ways to distinguish a real Christmas beetle from the fake kind is to look at the insect’s legs. Summer hummers: The genuine Christmas beetle (centre), with the Argentine lawn beetle (right) and native chafer (left). Nick Moir “A Christmas beetle’s legs are really robust and strong, and they’ve got these really big claws that are used for gripping,” Gunter says. “Often the main part of their legs will be either a sort of yellowish brown, or a reddish brown.



“Generally, the last sections of their legs are a darker colour – they’re either a really darkish red, or black. Those legs are quite characteristic.” Their heads are also highly distinctive. They have a shovel-like extension called a clypeus, which gives them a duck-bill appearance . A Christmas beetle spotted on North Stradbroke Island in late September 2026. The Christmas beetle is identifiable by its thick, reddish-coloured legs with dark parts at the end, and its duck-bill like head, as well as its iridescent green colour. Adult Christmas beetles live in dry bushland and rainforest, emerging from pupation in the wet summer months, around Christmas. For the rest of the year, the beetles live underground as grubs, feeding on decaying plant matter and nibbling roots.



“The good news is, these are seasonal insects,” Gunter said. “So if we have a few good years of rain, and there are areas of habitat that are still suitable for them, it does mean that these populations have the opportunity to bounce back.” Christmas beetles common in the south-east, from left: Anoplognathus porosus, Anoplognathus boisduvalii, Anoplognathus pallidicollis, Anoplognathus concolor. Catherine Strohfeldt Backyard enthusiasts without a science degree can use the Australian Museum’s Christmas beetle ID app – and contribute to a citizen science project that tracks Christmas beetle populations as they fluctuate from year to year.
