World.title: ‘Stop the slop’: Meet the young people fighting western Sydney’s data centre rush
World.content:
NationalNSWData centres ‘Stop the slop’: Meet the young people fighting western Sydney’s data centre rush Ellie Busby November 12, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As the battle against data centres in NSW rages on, a new contender has emerged to take on the major industrial developers: an emerging group mostly of twenty-somethings from western Sydney. Stop the Slop, made up of a core group of eight people, has been rallying residents to oppose the developments planned for Sydney’s west, which is fast becoming a data centre hub. Christie Duong and Nirvana Prasad from Stop the Slop stand near where a data centre is proposed in Kemps Creek. Sitthixay Ditthavong Dozens of data centres are operating in or proposed for suburbs stretching from Marsden Park to Kemps Creek. Christie Duong, who started the group, said the data centre resistance in the US inspired her to learn more about the developments proposed in her own community. After that, Duong said, the floodgates opened.



She discovered the scale of the data centres planned for western Sydney, connected with other young people from across the region, and they began campaigning against these projects on social media. The response was positive: their posts gained the attention of a younger audience, and many were excited there was finally movement in Sydney’s west against the projects. “The reason why we’re focusing on western Sydney in particular is the fact that it’s perceived to be a data centre hub with a few data centres already existing there, and how they will continue to pop up,” she said. “We want to knock out all of [the data centres] because they’re just shady in general.”



The group has been advocating against the $7 billion plan for a data centre development in Kemps Creek, located near three schools. If approved, it would see US technology company AirTrunk develop data hall buildings across 52 hectares of vacant land. Related Article Data centres These Sydney schools teach 1500 students. A $9b data centre is moving next door The facility would have a power capacity of 1.2 gigawatts, which is roughly equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of about one million Australian homes. In a video posted on Instagram, Duong explains the scale of the project would be the equivalent of 52 football fields. One comment asks: “wtf why have we got this epidemic of data centres?” Duong said: “I feel like if this gets approved, then what does it mean for the others? Like, how far can [data centres] push this?” Project manager Plan PM said in a statement they had undertaken extensive stakeholder engagement, received feedback and were actively working with the relevant bodies to find solutions to the matters raised. Amendments to the project were submitted in July, and included reducing it from six buildings to three.



There has been recent success in communities taking on industrial property giants and winning. Goodman Group abandoned plans for a hyperscale data centre on Sydney’s north shore in September following outrage among residents. An application for a data centre in the Blue Mountains was withdrawn in June after significant community backlash. This month, a proposal for an AI data centre on the banks of the Cooks River was scrapped. The Kemps Creek data centre is planned to be built on 52 hectares of vacant land. Sitthixay Ditthavong Duong had been inspired as residents across NSW banded together to stop these developments, but she believed the “organising landscape” in western Sydney required a different approach. “I think, as it’s been shown, visibility is important, but I think there are other things in the background that make things fall through, and we really want to be strategic about how we target [data centres] as well, and what it means for western Sydney as a data centre hub,” she said.



She says Stop the Slop members, who range in age between 21 and 32, are hopeful they can have similar success by hosting education sessions and continuing to reach people through social media. Campaigns against data centres in western Sydney have ramped up recently, with the $1.1 billion Project Pluto data centre in Guildford West the latest to receive significant pushback from residents. Data centre projects in Sydney. The development, which would be built next door to a sports ground and operate 24 hours a day, didn’t receive any submissions from the public, with many in the community saying they weren’t notified of the plans. A petition to stop the project, which was approved in July, has been signed by more than 5000 people. Goodman Group was contacted for comment.



Data centres have become a major political flashpoint. A NSW parliamentary inquiry last week said the government should plan for large-scale data centre development in precincts, supported by shared energy and water infrastructure, rather than as isolated developments. Related Article AI Cooks River AI data centre scrapped after local outcry Among the 23 recommendations was requiring AI companies to properly listen and respond to community concerns. Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles this week said the suburbs were “not a place where you would have data centres”. As Stop the Slop grows in supporters, Duong wants governments to pay attention.



“I think it is the time, it is important that they listen,” she said. “Things are at stake for them.”

World.title: Pat Cummins’ captaincy is about to face its biggest moment of truth
World.content:
SportCricketBall tampering Opinion Pat Cummins’ captaincy is about to face its biggest moment of truth Andrew Wu Sports Writer November 12, 2026 — 7:43pm

November 12, 2026 — 7:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Pat Cummins has won big matches for Australia with both bat and ball. He has advocated on climate change, and stuck up for his teammates in the aftermath of Justin Langer’s axing as coach. Friday is as big a test of his leadership as those moments. Cummins has nearly always met the moment in the 15 years since he was presented with his baggy green in Johannesburg. His task now as Test captain is to unite a dressing room and re-unify Australian cricket after a bruising week for the game. Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins is going to face the media on Friday morning. Getty Images For all the work Cummins and his teammates have done in rebuilding the reputation of the national men’s team, the prevailing view of the side, according to the Australian public this week, is they are cheats. Lying cheats as well. Cricket Australia’s hasty investigation in 2018 left many gaps, which Usman Khawaja’s warts-and-all memoir and David Warner’s social media posts have filled. Warner is likely to say more on Friday when he suits up in the Kayo Sports commentary box in Perth for the opening one-day international against England.



While there has been much angst in and outside the dressing room at the candid nature of Khawaja’s book Sabr, much of the criticism of the chapter dedicated to one of Australian sport’s biggest scandals has played the man rather than the ball. Usman Khawaja with Cummins back in 2018 - the year of sandpapergate. Getty Images Whether friendships forged under the baggy green are lost forever is a matter for Khawaja and his former teammates to discuss. Of more significance is how Cummins addresses the central premise of Khawaja’s claims: that the whole team knew sandpaper was being used. Perhaps Cummins can give ground on Khawaja’s argument that the entire team was complicit as they all stood to gain from an illegally altered ball that hooped around corners. The fining of every player in an XI for a slow over rate is an example of cricket’s one-in, all-in approach to certain indiscretions.



What would be more surprising is a confession to knowledge of the sandpaper plot when Cummins has been adamant from the start he did not know. Related Article Ball tampering ‘Not here to share mine’: Marsh deflects Khawaja’s sandpaper allegations He made this point publicly in 2021 when he was a signatory to the statement made by the rest of the Cape Town attack – which also included Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon – after Cameron Bancroft’s interview with journalist Donald Macrae in The Guardian. Australian cricket missed that opportunity to take the skeletons out of the closet. They have the chance again. One of Cummins’ problems is many in the public do not believe him or the fast bowlers. There is enough scepticism that a body language expert gave his analysis on Starc’s and Khawaja’s media appearances this week to assess the veracity of their comments.



Some will never give Cummins the chance, based on their disagreement with his progressive politics, but even more fair-minded cricket followers are sceptical of the idea a bowler would not know if the condition of their only tool of the trade was altered. Editor's pick Exclusive

Ball tampering ‘You can’t say sandpaper’: Coach allegedly told Smith, Bancroft to lie Cummins, though, is wedged. The more emphatic he is to convince the doubters, and support his fellow bowlers, the more he runs the risk of disenfranchising Steve Smith, one of the three players who copped lengthy bans over the scandal. Smith is central to Cummins’ ambitions for the team in the next eight months in their goal of conquering India in India and ending what will be a 26-year drought in England. He remains the team’s best batter in a troublesome top six, an excellent slipper and his onfield tactical acumen alleviates much of the pressure on Cummins as a bowling captain.



Smith, the former captain, has been silent on the matter as he recuperates from a neck injury in his adopted home of New York. Loading Any schadenfreude he felt when Khawaja’s claims were first aired must surely have faded the longer the issue has dragged on, and the closer it gets to his arrival back home, likely to be early next week when he joins NSW teammates as he prepares for the upcoming Test series against New Zealand. Not everyone around the team is convinced Smith’s neck injury was the sole reason he withdrew from the recent decider in Cape Town, Australia’s first Test at the venue since the tumult of 2018, and there are concerns how the dredging of the past is affecting him. Smith can shed more light on these matters if the plans for him to speak publicly next week in Sydney go ahead.

World.title: They used to battle in a Melbourne backyard. Now they’re facing off in a Test at Murrayfield
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby They used to battle in a Melbourne backyard. Now they’re facing off in a Test at Murrayfield Iain Payten November 12, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Edinburgh: When Isaac Kailea was growing up in suburban Melbourne, playing bruising games of backyard footy with his brothers and “cousins”, the common goal was to grow up and play for the Wallabies. Remarkably, at least two of the backyard crew did go on to play Test rugby – and another two are on track to make it, as well. Isaac Kailea getting ready for action at Wallabies training. Getty Images But Kailea was the only one to fulfil the original dream of doing it for the Wallabies. His backyard rival turned rugby role model, Sione Tuipulotu, did it for Scotland, and the pair will face off for a second time at Murrayfield on Monday morning (AEDT). Tuipulotu’s younger brothers Mosese and Ottavio – who both played for the Waratahs – are now also playing professionally in Scotland, and both are tipped as good chances to follow in Sione’s footsteps one day.



“I grew up with him and his younger brothers as well. We pretty much just call each other cousins, I call his dad my uncle,” Kailea said. “Our dads met in Melbourne, they’re both of Tongan heritage, and there’s a couple other families there, all Tongan as well, that we all grew up with. Wallabies prop Isaac Kailea (aqua shirt, back row) and Sione Tuipulotu (white t-shirt, front row) posing with their brothers and cousins in Melbourne. “So a lot of boys and a lot of a lot of pretty rough games in the backyard. But he [Sione] was always sort of the leader amongst the kids. He was the oldest. “We never played a proper organised match together, but we played a couple of times in the backyard, and he used to run amok. He’d smash us.” Tuipulotu progressed up the ranks in Victorian junior rugby, played a record three years for the Junior Wallabies and eventually became the first homegrown player to debut for the Melbourne Rebels in 2016.



But after struggling to get game time at the Rebels, Tuipulotu moved to Japan, and then with Scottish heritage through his grandmother, the fiery centre moved to Glasgow in Scotland. He debuted for the Scots in 2021 and was made captain in 2024. “It started at the Rebels, and all my younger cousins and myself as well, we really wanted to follow in his footsteps, Kailea said. Sione Tuipulotu playing against Australia in November, 2024. AP “He was a really good role model for all of us. Obviously, it was a bit tough for him in Australia, and he went on his own little journey, through Japan, and now he’s ended up in Scotland. And now his brothers are over here as well, chasing the dream. So it’s pretty crazy, to be honest. “I’ve met his nan before. She’s still got a pretty thick Scottish accent, so yeah, I wasn’t I wasn’t too surprised when I found out that he was going to Scotland. I knew he always had that connection.



“In Melbourne … there’s some unreal players that I don’t think ever really get recognized, and for him to sort of move out of Australia and get recognized is really good.” Kailea debuted for the Rebels in 2021, and moved to NSW after the Melbourne club was shut down in 2024. The 125kg prop made his debut for the Wallabies in 2024, and even played against Sione on the spring tour later that year. Isaac Kailea in action for the Wallabies in July 2024. Getty Images “I sort of had that one circled. I said, ‘I’d really love to play in that game’,” Kailea said. “He can be pretty lippy on the field, just as he is off it. So, yeah, he was throwing a bit of chat, but nothing too crazy. I don’t think he’d get too disrespectful.



Related Article Australian rugby Wallabies wary of Scotland’s Finn-and-Sione show “He’s probably one of the most competitive people I know, so when he puts on that Scottish jersey, no matter who he’s playing, he’s going to give it 100 per cent. Whether he goes extra hard because we’re Australia, I couldn’t say. I just know he’s always putting in that effort.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: People, you can go your own way in voting
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters People, you can go your own way in voting November 12, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Photo: Matt Davidson To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Just because the Coalition is suggesting an order of preferences doesn’t mean a voter has to follow that suggestion. A voter can allocate the required numbers on the ballot sheet in any way they choose. We are not all just sheep who have to follow what others want us to do, following any party’s or any candidate’s leaflet handed out at a polling booth. We are individuals with individual choices, values and opinions. Please put a lot of thought into how you will vote and allocate your preferences according to your principles, not that of a party machine. Many independent candidates’ leaflets only ask voters to allocate the No.1 to them recognising voters’ ability and intelligence to think for themselves in regard to preferences.

Jenny Callaghan, Hawthorn Labor, time to go into the wilderness

Unlike your correspondents (Letters, 12/11), I am not overly concerned by Jess Wilson’s decision to preference One Nation ahead of the Greens and Labor. Opinion polls indicate that the Coalition will almost certainly be in a position to form government with a comfortable majority in the Legislative Assembly. In this circumstance, One Nation will only have a potentially significant role to play in the Legislative Council. However, even in that house the new government will be able to negotiate with other parties as well as One Nation in order to pass its legislation. As for me, I won’t be deliberately preferencing One Nation ahead of Labor when I follow the Liberals’ how-to-vote card. Rather I will be sending a message to the Labor Party that it needs to spend some time in the political wilderness in order to examine why it lost its way so badly.

Ivan Glynn, Vermont The choice is all ours, and enjoy the sausage

The Liberal Party in Victoria making the decision to preference One Nation has drawn many responses to The Age letters pages. How many voters take and follow party how-to-vote cards? Here’s a thought: if you want to vote for the Liberal Party first, you can still place One Nation last on your ballot paper. You are allowed to think for yourself. Even better, last Saturday in New Zealand’s election, that nation voted free of campaigners, how-to-vote cards and roadside signage at polling places. It’s the law. New Zealanders can vote without interference or annoyance. It seems that they have to do their homework before arriving to vote. Wouldn’t it be wonderful if we could say the same in Australia? Not only do we have the right to vote, we more importantly have the right to think for ourselves. Don’t let a party, any party, determine how you place your preferences. Do your homework. Say politely, ″⁣no thank you″⁣, when offered a how-to-vote pamphlet at a polling booth. Just enjoy your democracy sausage.

Gryff Jamieson-Ballard, Castlemaine



System imperfect, but it’s preferable

First-past-the-post elections are hardly the panacea your correspondent (Letters, 12/11) wishes for. Take the seat of Hawthorn with seven candidates standing. In today’s crowded contests, the most popular candidate might earn 30 per cent of the vote with the other 70 per cent going to the other six candidates. A first-past-the-post system would elect an MP that 70 per cent did not prefer. Our preference system considers the wishes of the majority, however imperfectly, in a way that first past the post cannot do.

John Gwyther, Coongulla It comes down to competency and policy

The Victorian government does not deserve another term. Both the Coalition and One Nation have shown themselves incompetent at the simplest task of picking candidates. So independents or greens at least stand for something – the environment and the planet or a more civilised and thoughtful political discourse. Take your pick, but don’t vote for anyone who does not deserve it through competence and policy.

Greg Cooper, Mount Martha THE FORUM Tax gas dodgers

Every electric vehicle on the road reduces our reliance on imported fuel, and every home battery helps shave the evening peaks that drive up wholesale power prices. Both help ease the cost of living. So why is the Albanese government considering cutting support for these clean, efficient technologies (“Green energy perks face budget axe in bid to curb inflation”, 12/11)? A better option sits in plain sight: a levy on gas exports. The Australia Institute estimates a 25 per cent levy would raise about $17 billion a year, and argues it would steer more gas into the local market, easing gas and electricity prices. Don’t tax the households doing the right thing; tax the gas giants who are dodging their share.

Isabelle Henry, Ascot Vale



Hung parliament wish

My wish for the Victorian election is a hung parliament with independents holding the balance of power in the Legislative Council (Letters 12/11).

That would help rein in Labor’s profligate spending and the Liberal/One Nation propensity to slash funding to health, education, climate change mitigation and community services, plus keep a lid on the culture wars.

Jane Ross, San Remo Labor’s fallen standards

An often quoted cliche is: the standard you walk past is the standard you accept.

When applied to politics, the standards the Labor Party has at best, accepted, and at worst facilitated, are not able to be ignored. Regardless of all other voting permutations, the Labor Party needs to be placed last in the coming state election.

Mike Pantzopoulos, Ashburton Wilson’s conundrum

Jess Wilson has decided to preference One Nation ahead of Labor and the Greens unless in specific electorates a One Nation candidate holds or expresses extreme views. What a dilemma for her if a One Nation candidate, although highly unlikely, was in favour of keeping the Treaty in place.

Mark Hulls, Sandringham Doomed outcome

The only things that preference deals produce are uncomfortable bedfellows and unworkable governments (“Liberals to put Labor, Greens last”, 11/11). There’s no point in doing deals to facilitate electoral success if you then cannot enact and deliver policies as promised. Any government dependent on short-term preference deals is doomed to long-term frustration and failure.

Jenifer Nicholls, Windsor What follows protest?

Well said to your correspondent (Letters, 12/11). Lodging a ″⁣protest vote″⁣ just for the sake of protesting, without any consideration for the long-term implications, would be a bit like shooting yourself in the foot by way of protest. You are probably going to be worse off either way. There are no magic bullets in either context.

Helen Moss, Croydon



Qantas, it’s over

Dee Madigan (Comment, 12/11) hit the nail well and truly on the head.

I have always tried to fly with Qantas as I believed it to be the best airline. I, too, was excited when Alan Joyce left the company and Qantas appointed Vanessa Hudson to lead it.

Now, after having continued to support them, those days are coming to an end. I am currently going through a small and, some would say, petty dispute with Qantas over quite a lot of frequent flyer points following an international flight. So much for loyalty after choosing them for 50years. Maybe it’s time to walk away from this relationship.

Wendy Daniels, Hawthorn Mental health failings

I commend Dr Mark Langley (Letters, 11/11) on reminding us of the government’s failure to look after the mental health of our community following the closure of the state mental and psychiatric hospitals and their associated outpatient facilities.

I had an extensive career in our mental hospitals including a brief position as acting Psychiatric Superintendent at Ararat Mental Hospital including J Ward, which was termed Victoria’s Ward for the Criminal Insane. I also helped run the outpatient psychiatric services at Prince Henry’s Hospital which preceded the Monash Medical Centre. In all of these, the public had free and immediate access to public psychiatric services. We turned nobody away. As I commented in my submission to the Royal Commission into Mental Health although there were evils in the mental hospitals including institutionalisation and a lack of agency among inmates, when we closed the system we abandoned the mentally ill. As I put it, we threw out the baby with the bath water.

Successive governments never implemented alternatives for public psychiatric care. Also, in the modern world the balance between individual and community rights has become distorted so that it is so difficult to compel those with a lack of insight to have effective treatment and rehabilitation.

The consequence of this has been a contribution to violence and lawlessness. The shortage of public psychiatric beds including beds in forensic psychiatry and the unwillingness to lock up violent offenders during the long wait before trial is endangering our community.

Dr Norman Rose, Kilmore Failure of funding

Your correspondent (Letters, 11/11) is wrong in suggesting ″⁣deinstitutionalisation has failed”. Research in the 1970s clearly demonstrated improved therapeutic outcomes for long-term psychiatric patients could be achieved in the community. However, the success of deinstitutionalisation was also shown to be dependent on the establishment of high-quality community mental health services that provided assertive and ongoing social interventions and support, and targeted therapeutic interventions.

Those of us who were proponents of deinstitutionalisation in the 1980s stressed to government that a failure to adequately fund community-based treatment would result in a failing system and poor care for those with chronic illness. Unfortunately, we then had the Kennett era.

Effectively, government took the money from the sale of psychiatric hospitals and put it into general revenue, while establishing a threadbare system of community treatment. It’s not deinstitutionalisation that has failed, rather for decades governments have failed to adequately fund appropriate treatment and supports. The irony is that the same 1970s research also showed that community-based treatment was cost effective, so long as it was adequately funded and maintained.

Dr Peter Cook, Essendon Numbers with Wilson

While it is true that 40 per cent of Australians voted Yes in the Voice referendum, as your correspondent correctly says (Letters, 11/11), it is equally true that 60 per cent voted No. In Victoria, the No vote was slightly lower but still a significant 54 per cent against. From the day she was appointed Liberal leader Jess Wilson has made it clear she would “tear up” the Treaty. If she does win government, as seems likely, a majority of Victorians will have given her an undeniable mandate to repeal legislation that, thanks to the overwhelming No vote in 2023, should never have been brought before parliament in the first place.

Greg Hardy, Upper Ferntree Gully Policies at odds

Definition of hypocrisy: The Liberals expel a candidate for making disparaging remarks about Indigenous people, yet they want to disparage First Nations people by expelling the Treaty.

Linda Lewis, Watsonia



How to reshape Labor

As Shaun Carney argues (Comment, 12/11) the shine has left the PM. But what to do? Anthony Albanese has been at the game of politics for most of his life. Is he going to change his political character now? Is he even capable of doing so?

In the UK, a sinking Labor government has had its fortunes reversed by the installation of Andy Burnham as PM. Not much essentially has changed in terms of policy, but there’s now a sense of a government with strong leadership, a clear direction, and a great communicator in the top job. Australia’s fundamentals are so much better than the UK’s, and yet we have a government that is floundering, led by someone who seems embarrassed to talk up his own government’s achievements – notably, making housing affordable for the first time in decades. There’s plenty more to do to fix 20 years of policy neglect and widening inequality, but there’s the basis of a good story to tell here. Labor is terrified of leadership change, for good reason. While polling shows a significant drop in support for Labor, more alarming is the tangible slide in the government’s credibility, which, once lost, is virtually impossible to recapture. Time for a switch à la Burnham?

Greg Gardiner, Brunswick Wrong priorities

Illustrator Megan Herbert nailed it with her cartoon (12/11). However, it could have had the word “perchance” before “ready by late 2030s”. Wouldn’t it be good, if instead of giving $368 billion to the US on a vague promise of useless hardware, we invested the money in education, health and sustainability?

John Laurie, Riddells Creek Myer was the apex

Your correspondent is correct (Letters, 11/11). Invoking the glorious past of David Jones is false nostalgia in Melbourne. When I was first in Melbourne in 1979 there was no DJs and Myer represented the pinnacle of retail experience. The food hall was dazzling.

Helmut Simon, Thomson The halcyon days

David Jones is an interloper. In colourful mosaic and tiled signage, the name Buckley and Nunn Limited remains on the DJs’ Bourke Street building, a reminder of the halcyon days when about a dozen department stores operated in the CBD.

Jim McLeod, Sale



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Politics

Anthony Albanese says, ″⁣Australia is a proud leader on climate change.″⁣ What utter hypocrisy.

Reg Murray, Glen Iris An exciting new cartoon coming soon ″⁣Donald The Lame Duck and his Daffy mates″⁣. Stay tuned.

Ian Holton, Yarraville If ″⁣first past the post″⁣ is not an option, then voters have to do our own research, and vote for the candidates we prefer.

Wendy Brennan, Bendigo



I’ll see your pothole promise and raise it one million. How childish. We need politicians with vision to improve society and the environment.

Ralph Frank, Malvern East “You shall be judged by the company you keep.” So the Liberals have put One Nation ahead of Labor.

Rod Cripps, Parkdale Frightening to realise people will vote for this combination. Time to stop. Reflect. And why scrap Victoria’s Treaty with First Nations people?

Virginia Krumins, Albert Park Furthermore

Re: “Aged care homes guarded”, (11/11). Old age is inconvenient enough, without driveby shootings.

Lawrie Bradly, Surrey Hills A rising number of Qantas workers definitely don’t call Australia home.

Luigi Soccio, Daylesford



Qantas the flying kangaroo that escaped overseas.

Doug Springall, Yarragon Megan Herbert (11/11) reveals a huge absurdity – believing that outmoded technologies can overcome a cyberattack on our defences.

Kay Moulton, Surrey Hills It’s wrong that small voting centres are being closed. At least offer free transport to another centre.

John Walsh, Watsonia Finally

Usman Khawaja should have named his book True Grit.

Paul Custance, Highett

World.title: Victorian election hot seats: The social media app that could hold major voter sway in Ringwood
World.content:
Despite running for the seat of Sydenham, in Melbourne’s western suburbs, Liberal candidate Nathalie Moussi can’t call herself a local.

In fact, she owns a house in Torquay just minutes from the beach and says she splits her time between that property and another in Melbourne that’s outside the Sydenham boundary.

If she wins on election night, then she’ll move, she says.

Nathalie Moussi is running as the Liberal candidate in the seat of Sydenham. Facebook

The revelation is a blow to the Liberals’ campaign to unseat Labor from its once-safe seat.

As former NSW premier and federal senator Kristina Keneally discovered in her disastrous 2022 campaign, voters care deeply about where candidates live.

After being parachuted into a long-time Labor seat far from where she lived, Keneally and the party were stunned by a huge swing against them and saw the electorate opt for independent candidate Dai Le instead.

Moussi now confronts a similar risk.

One Nation candidate Joh Bauch also owns property in Truganina, south of the electorate.

The Star Weekly reported in 2024 he lived in Deer Park, which is located outside the seat’s boundary. Bauch did not return multiple requests for comment or confirm if he lives in the seat of Sydenham.

Local councillor and One Nation candidate for Sydenham, Joh Bauch. Joe Armao

While there are no formal rules around whether a candidate must live within the electorate when they run for office, it’s the kind of detail that matters to a lot of voters when choosing their representative.

“People in the western suburbs are very patriotic about living in the west,” said Maria Kerr, who is running as an independent in Sydenham and lives in Delahey. “I think it’s vitally important the candidate lives in the seat. They need to understand what the issues are on the ground.”

Moussi defended herself by pointing to her ownership of the popular Luxor Function Centre in Taylors Lakes.

“For the past 15 years, I’ve invested in Sydenham, built my business, employed local people and supported the community,” she told The Age.

“I believe representing a community is about more than where you sleep at night. It’s about the contribution you’ve made, the jobs you’ve created and how hard you’re prepared to fight for local people.”

One Nation did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

World.title: Woman injured in mistaken identity firebombing linked to campaign against developer

Exclusive NationalVictoriaCrime Woman injured in mistaken identity firebombing linked to campaign against developer Cameron Houston and Chris Vedelago November 12, 2026 — 7:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. An innocent couple asleep in their Cheltenham townhouse were the unintended victims of a targeted campaign of violence by the Finks outlaw motorcycle gang against besieged property developer Simon Pitard. A 52-year-old woman sustained serious burns after the Bay Road property was firebombed in a pre-dawn attack on October 28. The damaged Bay Street property. Cameron Houston The woman’s 57-year-old partner was not injured by the arson attack, which police believe was a case of mistaken identity with the wrong property being torched. A police spokeswoman confirmed the anti-bikie Echo Taskforce was investigating the Cheltenham attack, along with the firebombing of Pitard’s home in Brighton and a drive-by shooting at an Arcare aged care centre in Maidstone.



The police spokesman also confirmed the victims of the Cheltenham attack had no links to Pitard. This masthead can also reveal the campaign of threats and violence against Pitard began more than two years ago, when he was viciously bashed in April 2024. Embattled property tycoon Simon Pitard. Arsineh Houspian Three underworld and property industry sources, who asked not to be identified because of safety concerns, said Pitard required reconstructive surgery to his face following the assault. In 2022, Pitard was banned from managing any corporation for 3½ years, following the collapse of Steller Property Group in 2019 with debts of $617 million. The 44-year-old was director of more than 40 companies that were placed into liquidation.



Pitard co-founded Steller Group with Melbourne businessman Nicholas Smedley who were involved in the redevelopment of the Continental Hotel in Sorrento when the company spectacularly collapsed in 2019. Police outside an Arcare facility in Malvern on Wednesday. Despite being pursued by a conga-line of creditors, Pitard maintained his lavish lifestyle and continued to reside in a Brighton mansion registered under the name of his wife, Skye Pitard. Property records reveal her father, Russell Knowles, co-founder of Arcare Aged Care, holds a caveat registered against the property on Manor Road, suggesting he has a financial stake in the property. On October 27, several masked men rammed the front gates of Pitard’s residence on Manor Street and doused accelerant over two luxury cars, which were both destroyed in the blaze.



Related Article Exclusive

Organised crime Melbourne nursing homes under police guard as bikies target prominent aged care chain The campaign of intimidation targeted at Pitard took an unexpected turn last week, when his father-in-law’s aged-care empire came under attack. On October 6, elderly residents at the Arcare facility in Maidstone awoke to the sound of gunfire as two masked men in a white SUV fired ten shots at the home. This masthead revealed earlier this week that Victoria Police immediately deployed officers to protect other aged-care centres operated by Arcare, with police cars stationed outside homes across Melbourne. Police cars were parked outside two homes, while private guards patrolled two other centres earlier this week.



On Wednesday night, a police van was spotted outside an Arcare address in the inner east. Less than a day after the Maidstone shooting, the Finks were identified as an “organised crime priority” by Victoria Police, which formed a specialist taskforce to target the gang. Detective Superintendent Wayne Cheesman put the gang on notice, but made no reference to the attack on the Arcare facility, or Pitard’s home. “My message to the Finks … and to any outlaw motorcycle gang that chooses to cause harm in our community is very clear: if you choose to continue your involvement in serious and organised crime, Victoria Police is coming for you.” But no arrests have been made almost a week after the drive-by shooting in Maidstone, while the deployment of marked police cars, vans and cameras outside several aged-care centres places further strain on the force’s resources.



A source, with knowledge of the threats, said Knowles had recently engaged several former members of the Australian Defence Force to provide “close personal protection services” for his daughter and extended family. A letter to residents’ families from Arcare state operations manager Prab Kaur, sent on Monday, said the organisation had increased wellbeing support for residents, visitors and staff after the Maidstone incident, adding that it was also working closely with police and regulators. Simon and Skye Pitard have been approached for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: More wet weather on the way after storms lash Brisbane
World.content:
NationalQueenslandExtreme weather More wet weather on the way after storms lash Brisbane Dominique Tassell and William Davis Updated November 12, 2026 — 7:50pm ,first published November 12, 2026 — 8:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Brisbane may not be out of the woods just yet, with more wet weather possible a day after destructive storms swept the city. Warnings were issued for south-east Queensland by the Bureau of Meteorology before 6pm on Thursday, with the River City on the fringe of one alert area. It said severe thunderstorms likely to produce damaging winds, large hailstones and heavy rainfall that could lead to flash flooding would primarily affect towns to the north-west of Brisbane. Trees fell in Regents Park, Logan, on Wednesday afternoon. Kingaroy, Cherbourg, Taroom, Monto, Yarraman and Gayndah were listed as among the areas that could be hit hardest.



Hail measuring about six centimetres was recorded at Churchable before 5pm, and 75 millimetres of rail was recorded within an hour at Mount Moffatt. The bureau forecasted rain or more thunderstorms in parts of Brisbane until next Tuesday. Loading “It’s a bit of a stormy next few days,” senior meteorologist Robert Lawry said. “There is a chance in Brisbane that we could see some thunderstorms overnight into the early hours.



“We’ll probably get thunderstorms again tomorrow afternoon and early evening, but it’s not super likely to get them into the city … it’ll be more out towards the west. Related Article Queensland Rail Brisbane passengers trapped in train for six hours “Then as we go into Saturday, there’s definitely storms expected again for Brisbane … there’s storms again forecast for Sunday, and there is a chance of those being severe.” As of 6pm on Thursday, about 25,000 properties in south-east Queensland remained without power following a lashing that damaged homes and brought trees down onto traffic. Parts of the region recorded between 50 and 80 millimetres in just half-an-hour, leading to flash flooding.



Wind gusts of up to 96km/h were recorded at Brisbane Airport, leading to delays and diversions. Intense gusts tore down trees and lifted a trampoline out of a backyard in Regents Park, Logan, while large hailstones were recorded west of the Gold Coast. A falling tree knocked out traffic lights before crashing into cars on Aspen Circuit in Logan Reserve about 4pm. Another tree came down on Logan Road in Eight Mile Plains, striking two vehicles just before 5pm. A trampoline was lifted onto a road in Regents Park amid the heavy storms. Sophie Stewart SES crews responded to more than 320 requests for help across the state’s south-east.



Most requests for assistance were related to fallen trees affecting structures or blocking the entry or exit to properties, and many needed tarpaulins for leaking roofs. Among the hundreds of requests, 243 callouts were from Logan City. On Thursday morning, 11 schools in the area were closed. Burrowes State School, Corymbia State School, Crestmead State School, Jimboomba State School, Logan Village State School, Marsden State High School, Marsden State School, South Rock State School, Yarrabilba State School, Yarrabilba State Secondary College and Yugumbir State School were closed. The weather is expected to ease on Friday before a resurgence in storm activity at the weekend. “Into the weekend, we do see those thunderstorms reinvigorate as another surface trough develops across inland parts of Queensland,” meteorologist Jonathan How said. World.title: Has the Christmas beetle really returned to Brisbane?
World.content:
NationalQueenslandWildlife Has the Christmas beetle really returned to Brisbane? Marissa Calligeros November 12, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For many who grew up in Brisbane, Christmas beetles are synonymous with the start of the festive season. Locals remember the shiny, iridescent insects emerging en masse each year to crawl across lawns, congregate around lights and smash into glass doors. This spring, large beetles spotted across Brisbane’s suburbs have attracted attention and raised hopes the Christmas beetle has returned in greater numbers after decades of apparent decline. Loading Some, however, are likely imposters.



Early November rains this year brought forth large numbers of the native brown cockchafer beetle in south-east Queensland. Queensland Museum entomologist Dr Nicole Gunter said this was a species easily mistaken for the Christmas beetle. A brown cockchafer beetle on Brisbane’s southside this month. Marissa Calligeros “They are in the same family of beetles, but different subfamilies,” she said. Christmas beetles were also frequently mistaken for the Argentine lawn beetle.



The imposters are dull brown. In contrast, the real thing is shiny, often an iridescent green or metallic brown in keeping with the season, and twice as large. In welcome news, however, Gunter said south-east Queensland’s wet start to November also made conditions ripe for legitimate varieties of Christmas beetles to emerge. Christmas beetles have notably thicker legs than other beetle species. From left: an Argentinian scarab beetle, a cane beetle species, and a Christmas beetle. Catherine Strohfeldt There are more than 35 species of mainland Christmas beetles, with about 10 of those found in and around Brisbane. “We’re definitely seeing them at the moment,” Gunter said.



“It is the perfect time of the year to be seeing them. We have had good rain last year, and we’ve also had a reasonably wet spring so far.” One of the easiest ways to distinguish a real Christmas beetle from the fake kind is to look at the insect’s legs. Summer hummers: The genuine Christmas beetle (centre), with the Argentine lawn beetle (right) and native chafer (left). Nick Moir “A Christmas beetle’s legs are really robust and strong, and they’ve got these really big claws that are used for gripping,” Gunter says. “Often the main part of their legs will be either a sort of yellowish brown, or a reddish brown.



“Generally, the last sections of their legs are a darker colour – they’re either a really darkish red, or black. Those legs are quite characteristic.” Their heads are also highly distinctive. They have a shovel-like extension called a clypeus, which gives them a duck-bill appearance . A Christmas beetle spotted on North Stradbroke Island in late September 2026. The Christmas beetle is identifiable by its thick, reddish-coloured legs with dark parts at the end, and its duck-bill like head, as well as its iridescent green colour. Adult Christmas beetles live in dry bushland and rainforest, emerging from pupation in the wet summer months, around Christmas. For the rest of the year, the beetles live underground as grubs, feeding on decaying plant matter and nibbling roots.



“The good news is, these are seasonal insects,” Gunter said. “So if we have a few good years of rain, and there are areas of habitat that are still suitable for them, it does mean that these populations have the opportunity to bounce back.” Christmas beetles common in the south-east, from left: Anoplognathus porosus, Anoplognathus boisduvalii, Anoplognathus pallidicollis, Anoplognathus concolor. Catherine Strohfeldt Backyard enthusiasts without a science degree can use the Australian Museum’s Christmas beetle ID app – and contribute to a citizen science project that tracks Christmas beetle populations as they fluctuate from year to year. World.title: ‘Stop the slop’: Meet the young people fighting western Sydney’s data centre rush
World.content:
NationalNSWData centres ‘Stop the slop’: Meet the young people fighting western Sydney’s data centre rush Ellie Busby November 12, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As the battle against data centres in NSW rages on, a new contender has emerged to take on the major industrial developers: an emerging group mostly of twenty-somethings from western Sydney. Stop the Slop, made up of a core group of eight people, has been rallying residents to oppose the developments planned for Sydney’s west, which is fast becoming a data centre hub. Christie Duong and Nirvana Prasad from Stop the Slop stand near where a data centre is proposed in Kemps Creek. Sitthixay Ditthavong Dozens of data centres are operating in or proposed for suburbs stretching from Marsden Park to Kemps Creek. Christie Duong, who started the group, said the data centre resistance in the US inspired her to learn more about the developments proposed in her own community. After that, Duong said, the floodgates opened.



She discovered the scale of the data centres planned for western Sydney, connected with other young people from across the region, and they began campaigning against these projects on social media. The response was positive: their posts gained the attention of a younger audience, and many were excited there was finally movement in Sydney’s west against the projects. “The reason why we’re focusing on western Sydney in particular is the fact that it’s perceived to be a data centre hub with a few data centres already existing there, and how they will continue to pop up,” she said. “We want to knock out all of [the data centres] because they’re just shady in general.”



The group has been advocating against the $7 billion plan for a data centre development in Kemps Creek, located near three schools. If approved, it would see US technology company AirTrunk develop data hall buildings across 52 hectares of vacant land. Related Article Data centres These Sydney schools teach 1500 students. A $9b data centre is moving next door The facility would have a power capacity of 1.2 gigawatts, which is roughly equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of about one million Australian homes. In a video posted on Instagram, Duong explains the scale of the project would be the equivalent of 52 football fields. One comment asks: “wtf why have we got this epidemic of data centres?” Duong said: “I feel like if this gets approved, then what does it mean for the others? Like, how far can [data centres] push this?” Project manager Plan PM said in a statement they had undertaken extensive stakeholder engagement, received feedback and were actively working with the relevant bodies to find solutions to the matters raised. Amendments to the project were submitted in July, and included reducing it from six buildings to three.



There has been recent success in communities taking on industrial property giants and winning. Goodman Group abandoned plans for a hyperscale data centre on Sydney’s north shore in September following outrage among residents. An application for a data centre in the Blue Mountains was withdrawn in June after significant community backlash. This month, a proposal for an AI data centre on the banks of the Cooks River was scrapped. The Kemps Creek data centre is planned to be built on 52 hectares of vacant land. Sitthixay Ditthavong Duong had been inspired as residents across NSW banded together to stop these developments, but she believed the “organising landscape” in western Sydney required a different approach. “I think, as it’s been shown, visibility is important, but I think there are other things in the background that make things fall through, and we really want to be strategic about how we target [data centres] as well, and what it means for western Sydney as a data centre hub,” she said.



She says Stop the Slop members, who range in age between 21 and 32, are hopeful they can have similar success by hosting education sessions and continuing to reach people through social media. Campaigns against data centres in western Sydney have ramped up recently, with the $1.1 billion Project Pluto data centre in Guildford West the latest to receive significant pushback from residents. Data centre projects in Sydney. The development, which would be built next door to a sports ground and operate 24 hours a day, didn’t receive any submissions from the public, with many in the community saying they weren’t notified of the plans. A petition to stop the project, which was approved in July, has been signed by more than 5000 people. Goodman Group was contacted for comment.



Data centres have become a major political flashpoint. A NSW parliamentary inquiry last week said the government should plan for large-scale data centre development in precincts, supported by shared energy and water infrastructure, rather than as isolated developments. Related Article AI Cooks River AI data centre scrapped after local outcry Among the 23 recommendations was requiring AI companies to properly listen and respond to community concerns. Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles this week said the suburbs were “not a place where you would have data centres”. As Stop the Slop grows in supporters, Duong wants governments to pay attention.



“I think it is the time, it is important that they listen,” she said. “Things are at stake for them.”

World.title: Pat Cummins’ captaincy is about to face its biggest moment of truth
World.content:
SportCricketBall tampering Opinion Pat Cummins’ captaincy is about to face its biggest moment of truth Andrew Wu Sports Writer November 12, 2026 — 7:43pm

November 12, 2026 — 7:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Pat Cummins has won big matches for Australia with both bat and ball. He has advocated on climate change, and stuck up for his teammates in the aftermath of Justin Langer’s axing as coach. Friday is as big a test of his leadership as those moments. Cummins has nearly always met the moment in the 15 years since he was presented with his baggy green in Johannesburg. His task now as Test captain is to unite a dressing room and re-unify Australian cricket after a bruising week for the game. Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins is going to face the media on Friday morning. Getty Images For all the work Cummins and his teammates have done in rebuilding the reputation of the national men’s team, the prevailing view of the side, according to the Australian public this week, is they are cheats. Lying cheats as well. Cricket Australia’s hasty investigation in 2018 left many gaps, which Usman Khawaja’s warts-and-all memoir and David Warner’s social media posts have filled. Warner is likely to say more on Friday when he suits up in the Kayo Sports commentary box in Perth for the opening one-day international against England.



While there has been much angst in and outside the dressing room at the candid nature of Khawaja’s book Sabr, much of the criticism of the chapter dedicated to one of Australian sport’s biggest scandals has played the man rather than the ball. Usman Khawaja with Cummins back in 2018 - the year of sandpapergate. Getty Images Whether friendships forged under the baggy green are lost forever is a matter for Khawaja and his former teammates to discuss. Of more significance is how Cummins addresses the central premise of Khawaja’s claims: that the whole team knew sandpaper was being used. Perhaps Cummins can give ground on Khawaja’s argument that the entire team was complicit as they all stood to gain from an illegally altered ball that hooped around corners. The fining of every player in an XI for a slow over rate is an example of cricket’s one-in, all-in approach to certain indiscretions.



What would be more surprising is a confession to knowledge of the sandpaper plot when Cummins has been adamant from the start he did not know. Related Article Ball tampering ‘Not here to share mine’: Marsh deflects Khawaja’s sandpaper allegations He made this point publicly in 2021 when he was a signatory to the statement made by the rest of the Cape Town attack – which also included Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon – after Cameron Bancroft’s interview with journalist Donald Macrae in The Guardian. Australian cricket missed that opportunity to take the skeletons out of the closet. They have the chance again. One of Cummins’ problems is many in the public do not believe him or the fast bowlers. There is enough scepticism that a body language expert gave his analysis on Starc’s and Khawaja’s media appearances this week to assess the veracity of their comments.



Some will never give Cummins the chance, based on their disagreement with his progressive politics, but even more fair-minded cricket followers are sceptical of the idea a bowler would not know if the condition of their only tool of the trade was altered. Editor's pick Exclusive

Ball tampering ‘You can’t say sandpaper’: Coach allegedly told Smith, Bancroft to lie Cummins, though, is wedged. The more emphatic he is to convince the doubters, and support his fellow bowlers, the more he runs the risk of disenfranchising Steve Smith, one of the three players who copped lengthy bans over the scandal. Smith is central to Cummins’ ambitions for the team in the next eight months in their goal of conquering India in India and ending what will be a 26-year drought in England. He remains the team’s best batter in a troublesome top six, an excellent slipper and his onfield tactical acumen alleviates much of the pressure on Cummins as a bowling captain.



Smith, the former captain, has been silent on the matter as he recuperates from a neck injury in his adopted home of New York. Loading Any schadenfreude he felt when Khawaja’s claims were first aired must surely have faded the longer the issue has dragged on, and the closer it gets to his arrival back home, likely to be early next week when he joins NSW teammates as he prepares for the upcoming Test series against New Zealand. Not everyone around the team is convinced Smith’s neck injury was the sole reason he withdrew from the recent decider in Cape Town, Australia’s first Test at the venue since the tumult of 2018, and there are concerns how the dredging of the past is affecting him. Smith can shed more light on these matters if the plans for him to speak publicly next week in Sydney go ahead.

World.title: They used to battle in a Melbourne backyard. Now they’re facing off in a Test at Murrayfield
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby They used to battle in a Melbourne backyard. Now they’re facing off in a Test at Murrayfield Iain Payten November 12, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Edinburgh: When Isaac Kailea was growing up in suburban Melbourne, playing bruising games of backyard footy with his brothers and “cousins”, the common goal was to grow up and play for the Wallabies. Remarkably, at least two of the backyard crew did go on to play Test rugby – and another two are on track to make it, as well. Isaac Kailea getting ready for action at Wallabies training. Getty Images But Kailea was the only one to fulfil the original dream of doing it for the Wallabies. His backyard rival turned rugby role model, Sione Tuipulotu, did it for Scotland, and the pair will face off for a second time at Murrayfield on Monday morning (AEDT). Tuipulotu’s younger brothers Mosese and Ottavio – who both played for the Waratahs – are now also playing professionally in Scotland, and both are tipped as good chances to follow in Sione’s footsteps one day.



“I grew up with him and his younger brothers as well. We pretty much just call each other cousins, I call his dad my uncle,” Kailea said. “Our dads met in Melbourne, they’re both of Tongan heritage, and there’s a couple other families there, all Tongan as well, that we all grew up with. Wallabies prop Isaac Kailea (aqua shirt, back row) and Sione Tuipulotu (white t-shirt, front row) posing with their brothers and cousins in Melbourne. “So a lot of boys and a lot of a lot of pretty rough games in the backyard. But he [Sione] was always sort of the leader amongst the kids. He was the oldest. “We never played a proper organised match together, but we played a couple of times in the backyard, and he used to run amok. He’d smash us.” Tuipulotu progressed up the ranks in Victorian junior rugby, played a record three years for the Junior Wallabies and eventually became the first homegrown player to debut for the Melbourne Rebels in 2016.



But after struggling to get game time at the Rebels, Tuipulotu moved to Japan, and then with Scottish heritage through his grandmother, the fiery centre moved to Glasgow in Scotland. He debuted for the Scots in 2021 and was made captain in 2024. “It started at the Rebels, and all my younger cousins and myself as well, we really wanted to follow in his footsteps, Kailea said. Sione Tuipulotu playing against Australia in November, 2024. AP “He was a really good role model for all of us. Obviously, it was a bit tough for him in Australia, and he went on his own little journey, through Japan, and now he’s ended up in Scotland. And now his brothers are over here as well, chasing the dream. So it’s pretty crazy, to be honest. “I’ve met his nan before. She’s still got a pretty thick Scottish accent, so yeah, I wasn’t I wasn’t too surprised when I found out that he was going to Scotland. I knew he always had that connection.



“In Melbourne … there’s some unreal players that I don’t think ever really get recognized, and for him to sort of move out of Australia and get recognized is really good.” Kailea debuted for the Rebels in 2021, and moved to NSW after the Melbourne club was shut down in 2024. The 125kg prop made his debut for the Wallabies in 2024, and even played against Sione on the spring tour later that year. Isaac Kailea in action for the Wallabies in July 2024. Getty Images “I sort of had that one circled. I said, ‘I’d really love to play in that game’,” Kailea said. “He can be pretty lippy on the field, just as he is off it. So, yeah, he was throwing a bit of chat, but nothing too crazy. I don’t think he’d get too disrespectful.



Related Article Australian rugby Wallabies wary of Scotland’s Finn-and-Sione show “He’s probably one of the most competitive people I know, so when he puts on that Scottish jersey, no matter who he’s playing, he’s going to give it 100 per cent. Whether he goes extra hard because we’re Australia, I couldn’t say. I just know he’s always putting in that effort.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Gang controversy fails to dent support for Te Pāti Māori's top performers
World.content:
Two Te Pāti Māori candidates caught up in the controversial gang meeting have emerged as the party's strongest performers this election, raising questions about how Māori voters view political engagement with gangs.

Mata producer Annabelle Lee-Mather said Oriini Kaipara had worked incredibly hard in her electorate, meeting with the Sikh community, visiting every kura kaupapa and dramatically increasing her winning margin.

Lee-Mather said it's significant that Kaipara and Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke, the party's two strongest performers, were both at the centre of the gang meeting controversy.

She said their results suggested Māori voters had a different set of values when it came to who their MPs engaged with and how they approached issues involving gangs. Rather than being punished at the ballot box, both candidates appeared to have been rewarded for their mahi.

Former senior parliamentary staffer Jason Ake agreed that too much energy had been wasted fighting over deck chairs on the same side of politics, pointing to the gang controversy as an example of unnecessary division.

Meanwhile, Te Tai Tokerau remains on a knife-edge, with Te Pāti Māori's Aperahama Edwards holding a narrow 436-vote lead over Green MP Hūhana Lyndon five days after election night.

Ake said the result was critical for the balance of power in Parliament. If the seat flipped to the Greens, the left could lose a seat from its overall parliamentary bloc.

He described Te Tai Tokerau as a bellwether for Māori politics. When Te Tai Tokerau moved he said, Māori across the country often moved with it.

Five days after a marathon election night, Mata host Mihingarangi Forbes is joined by veteran political journalist Tina Wickliffe, Ake and Lee-Mather to unpack the overhangs, hangovers and political headaches.

Who's left standing, who's nursing a sore head, and what does it all mean for Māori?

Mata host Mihingarangi Forbes (C) with producer Annabelle Lee-Mather (L) and political journalist Tina Wickliffe. Mata

Te Pāti Māori's comeback saw the party win five of the seven Māori electorates. Wickliffe said the result demonstrated the party still had significant support in its electorates, but now was the time for a reset. She believed Te Pāti Māori should consider repositioning itself on Parliament's crossbenches.

The election also saw former Te Pāti Māori MPs Tākuta Ferris and Mariameno Kapa-Kingi fail to return to Parliament after being pushed out of the party and attempting political comebacks under new banners.

Ake wasn't surprised Ferris lost Te Tai Tonga, pointing to the electorate's strong Labour history.

Kapa-Kingi's newly established Te Tai Tokerau Party also failed to gain traction. Wickliffe said West Auckland voters, who made up the southern end of the electorate, were unlikely to back a Northland-branded party.

Lee-Mather said the sheer size of the Māori electorates made party infrastructure critical. Candidates needed established networks to carry their message into every nook and cranny. When Te Pāti Māori imploded, Ferris and Kapa-Kingi lost much of the machinery and support they needed to compete.

World.title: All Whites outclass India in series opener
World.content:
New Zealand's football series against India is part of the celebration of a century of sporting contests between the two nations, but the home side showed little mercy in a 5-0 victory on Thursday night in Auckland.

Returning home for the first time since the World Cup, the All Whites starting side was primarily A-League players, alongside captain and English Premier League player Chris Wood.

Wood played a part in confusing India's defence in the fifth minute, which lead to the opening goal of the game to New Zealand off an Indian defender.

The All Whites had several more opportunities in the first half an hour that they failed to capitalise on, including a sitter for Logan Rogerson.

Indian goalkeeper Vishal Kaith pulled off several top saves to keep his side in the contest and make the All Whites find different ways to get past him in the first half.

Jesse Randall, who scored for Scottish club side Dundee United at the weekend, continued that form for his country, when he added New Zealand's second and his fourth in an All Whites shirt in the 34th minute.

Randall scored his second less than 10 minutes later, after some good hustle in the box by former Auckland clubmate Francis de Vries, who had initially crossed the ball to set up Wood.

By halftime, the All Whites had their highest score against India, after beating them 2-1 in 2018 and drawing 0-0 in 1981.

India made five changes to start the second half, whereas the home side went unchanged.

Wood finally scored his first goal of the game just before the hour mark, with a header, after a spell of struggling to score for club or country.

Just after the captain's goal took the score to 4-0, the All Whites made five changes, with Wellington Phoenix defender Matt Sheridan coming on to make his debut.

Corban Piper and Nathan Walker also made their debuts, when they were subbed on in the 73rd minute.

The All Whites' fifth goal came for Lachie Bayliss, after he had been threatening to score all night.

New Zealand had a chance to extend the lead from the penalty spot, but in his 50th match, Bill Tuiloma's shot was saved.

The second game of the series is in Christchurch on Sunday and will end All Whites coach Darren Bazeley's tenure.

World.title: Coroner orders NZ Rugby to turn over concussion docs
World.content:
Warning: This story discusses suicide.

NZ Rugby has been ordered to release more than 1000 documents to the coronial inquiry into the deaths of professional rugby players Shane Christie and Billy Guyton.

Christie - a former Māori All Blacks, Highlanders and Tasman player - died by suspected suicide, aged 40, in August last year.

Guyton - a former Māori All Blacks, Blues and Tasman player - died by suspected suicide, aged 33, in May 2023.

The pair were good friends and both were diagnosed after their deaths with chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease linked to repeated head trauma.

Coroner Ian Telford joined the inquiries into the two deaths at a case management conference on Thursday.

He also signalled an inquest would be held, but it was too early in the inquiry to set a date or venue.

Much of the hearing was concerned with NZ Rugby's disclosure of material.

The organisation's lawyer, Tanzam Hossain, said it had provided more than 6000 documents to the inquiry so far.

However, more than 1000 documents uncovered by its searches of policies and procedures relating to its handling of concussion had not been turned over to the lawyers of Christie or Guyton's families, or the coroner.

Daniel Kalderimis KC, one of the lawyer's representing Guyton's whānau, told the court the sport's body had taken an "impermissibly passive approach" to disclosure, "bordering on leisurely".

"Our biggest concern with how New Zealand Rugby has responded to date by trying to limit what it wants to provide by way of those policies is that it knows also that its knowledge of the risk and what sort of precautionary approach might need to be taken is what this is all going to be about," he said.

"We don't have any confidence that we have that."

NZ Rugby had searched for documents using terms such as 'Billy' or 'Billy* Guyton', but not for 'Guyton', Kalderimis said.

"That's an obvious miss," he said.

"Secondly, it has not searched generally for documents that postdate Mr Guyton's death, which was in May 2023, even though it has offered up as relevant its own concussion policies after that date. You can't only provide the good stuff after that date."

Other nations had grappled with the effect of concussion injuries in sport and the issue of CTE, and the world would be watching the inquiry into Guyton and Christie's deaths, Kalderimis said.

"What we need to know is not what they're offering, which is current concussion policies in place in 2026," he said.

"We need to know what was [NZ Rugby's] position at the time and was there a precautionary approach? If so, what did it look like?

"How was it manifested? Who did it?

"We say that New Zealand Rugby cannot say to this inquiry that they don't have people who know about this. There will be people who have thought about this."

Shane Christie was farewelled with a haka at his funeral in September 2025. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Then there were disclosure requests that had not been undertaken.

"We mentioned specifically, when we were here last time, text messages needed to be searched," Kalderimis said. "They simply have not been searched.

"The time for doing this disclosure in a collaborative way - with NZ Rugby providing us with statements first and then some documents later, and then telling us all the difficulties they're experiencing - is over. This inquiry is going to be one that the world looks at."

NZ Rugby's handling of the inquiry to date led coroner Ian Telford to express his frustration.

"It'll come as no surprise to you that I'm starting to lose patience with this exercise and I want to bring it to its conclusion," Telford told Hossain.

Hossain said NZ Rugby could produce the uncovered documents quickly and was happy to do so.

Many of the documents could be of no help to the inquiry, she said.

In terms of further documents to be produced, she asked for further direction from the court.

"Ms Hossain, how on earth can I do that? I'm just a coroner," Telford responded.

"How can I possibly know what you've got on your computers in New Zealand Rugby? Categories of documents about matters I don't understand.

"If you were to ask me to direct now those categories or those specific search terms, I have to be blunt and frank, I wouldn't know where to start."

Hossain said NZ Rugby faced the same difficulty in "attempting to search for this information".

"I think New Zealand Rugby know that we're talking about two individuals and they know what the matters are that are touching this inquiry," Telford responded.

"If not, we can try and enunciate that even clearer, but I think it's really obvious what the global issues are that are before this inquiry."

The court heard there had also been an attempt to extract data from Christie's phone and more than 52,000 passwords were attempted.

That effort would continue, but police advised 94,000 attempts remained and it was unclear if it would ultimately be successful.

Telford ordered NZ Rugby to turn over the 1091 outstanding documents to the inquiry and to undertake further searches for information of relevance.

The matter will next be called again in court early next year.

World.title: Kāpiti Coast Airport confirms it will close at end of November
World.content:
Kāpiti Coast Airport has confirmed it will close on 30 November, a decision which the local MP has slammed as "cruel, unfair and unnecessary".

A spokesperson for owners NZ PropCo said the airport will close at 7pm on 30 November, and until then would "continue to operate under its existing certificate and safety requirements".

Kāpiti Aero Club said earlier today that Kāpiti Coast Airport Holdings had asked it to surrender its lease - which is in place until 2033 - on 30 November, and to vacate the land by 28 February 2027.

Sounds Air chief executive Andrew Crawford told RNZ he's also been informed by the airport's chief executive it will close on 30 November.

The airport, owned by NZ PropCo, had entered a conditional sale and purchase agreement that required the airport to close.

Key people in aviation in the region have been talking about the potential closure for days.

Ōtaki MP Tim Costley said he was really concerned about the closure date.

"It's really soon, particularly if they're [the aero club's] lease went well into the 20-30s from what I've heard, to suddenly being told you have now three weeks.

"This just seems cruel, unfair and unnecessary."

Costley said there were pragmatic ways the airport could keep operating now, while the owners go through a process to sell it. He said the land was being sold for housing development, but this required a council zoning change through a public process, which was far from guaranteed.

"We don't need it [as housing]. We have more than 5000 houses going in across Kāpiti."

The airport was needed as a critical piece of infrastructure for medical and civil emergencies, Costley said, as well as regional connectivity.

In the last year, about 15 Life Flight aircraft landed at Kāpiti Coast Airport when they couldn't land in Wellington, he said.

Costley said he had heard from two people who credited the airport with saving their life or partner's life in a medical emergency.

Audio player for " Pending closure of Kapiti Airport could land in legal territory " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2552965%2Fkapiti-coast-airport-confirms-it-will-close-at-end-of-november

Pending closure of Kapiti Airport could land in legal territory Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Closure would be a 'terrible loss' for community

Kāpiti Aero Club executive member Peter Merwood said the club was taking legal advice about the request to surrender its lease.

"We have a lease which gives us rights over the airport until 2033, so the question is why would we give that up, we have a legal entitlement to the land."

Merwood said the closure would be a "terrible loss" for the community.

The club, open since 1983, currently had 13 staff, operates a fleet of more than 10 aircraft, had 250 members and had trained hundreds of pilots who now worked in the aviation sector, he said.

"Today we've got on the books 50 people that are actively being trained and they might being going for a private pilot's license, a commercial pilot's license."

The next nearest training areas were Feilding or Wellington, though Costley said Wellington was not suitable for all types of training due to the numbers of commercial flights flying in and out of the airport.

"Once an airport like Kāpiti is lost, it's gone, it'll never come back," Merwood said.

Mayor says council inundated with emails

Kāpiti Coast mayor Janet Holborow said the council had been inundated with emails asking them to stop the re-zoning of the airport - but it's not that simple.

"It's important to understand that council can't just vote to stop a change of designation."

She said the council had tried to negotiate with the airport owners.

"It's a frustrating situation due to the fact that the asset is in private ownership. Council is not in a position to buy the land or fund the infrastructure needed to keep it operating."

Holborow said councillors must remain impartial throughout the zoning change process, following the Resource Management Act 1991.

She said the council made a mistake selling the airport off in 1995, and were asking the government to step in now.

"What is clear is that we need to work together and put pressure on our local MP and the government to save our airport."

She said the council had provided funding and loans in recent years to ensure the air services continued to operate between Kāpiti and Auckland.

However, challenging economic conditions had seen both Air New Zealand and Air Chathams pull out of providing services from Kāpiti Airport.

World.title: RNZ board assured unlawful overdraft did not need approval
World.content:
RNZ's board says it was assured by its then-chief financial officer that it didn't need approval for a $5 million overdraft.

On Monday, the public broadcaster revealed a shock $12m budget blowout, after a litany of financial blunders that included the overdraft that breached the Crown Entities Act.

By law, RNZ required ministerial sign-off to set up the overdraft.

RNZ chief financial officer Hilary Parker resigned unexpectedly in early October.

Board chair Brent Impey said a director did ask Parker in writing whether ministerial approval was required.

The query came after the board signed off on the overdraft, but before it was formally entered into.

"The assurance given at that time was that RNZ did not require approval from either the minister of finance or the shareholding ministers to establish the facility," Impey said.

"This matter will form part of what the independent review needs to consider and it is important that this process is undertaken with consideration of all relevant information in due course.

"As a result, I will not be commenting further on this matter," he said.

Chief executive Paul Thompson took responsibility for the blowout and said internal reports gave an inaccurate picture of the finances, meaning the scale of the loss only became clear in October.

RNZ CEO Paul Thompson VNP / Phil Smith

While carrying out the broadcaster's annual audit, EY identified a breach of the Crown Entities Act - emphasising it in RNZ's annual report.

"We draw your attention to Note 12 on page 32 about the Group not complying with sections 160 and 162 of the Crown Entities Act 2004, in that the Group entered into a financing arrangement without the authority of the Minister for Media and Communications and the Minister of Finance."

The breach concerned a $5m overdraft that was set up without ministerial approval.

RNZ said the $5m overdraft was initiated to provide RNZ with a safety net in the event one of its land sales was delayed, so the company could manage significant one-off costs, but was never used.

By law, RNZ needs sign-off from two ministers to borrow money, which it last received in 2006 for up to $3.5m.

On Checkpoint, Impey accepted the organisation had broken the law.

"Now, how did that happen? That's very difficult to explain.

"That there was a loan with Westpac and again, the Crown Entities Act was breached."
