An RNZ spokesperson said the board approved a temporary $5m overdraft facility on 9 June, 2026.

Former RNZ chief financial office Hilary Parker LinkedIn

Public law expert and barrister Mai Chen said the fact that ministerial approval wasn't obtained raises questions.

"You've got people in highly paid positions who don't seem to understand that they're a Crown entity, they're subject to the Crown Entities Act," she said. "Why did they do it without going through the right process?"

Chen said it was concerning that the board appeared to be unaware of the breach and more broadly in the dark about RNZ's financial position.

Asked if RNZ management was aware of its obligations under the Crown Entities Act, RNZ pointed to section 160 of the Act - that outlines the need for ministerial sign-off - in its borrowing policy.

It said no internal or external legal advice was sought before entering into the overdraft.

"The independent review will establish what happened and why," the spokesperson said.

A Westpac spokesperson said the bank didn't comment on specific customers' banking details.

World.title: 'A sad state of affairs': The scale of sexist and racist abuse in politics
World.content:
About one in three comments made to candidates on social media in the lead up to and during the 2026 election campaign was abusive - with women receiving "the sharper end", according to new data.

An analysis of almost 150,000 comments on 34 candidate and campaign accounts between 1 August and 6 November showed that, overall, negative comments outnumbered positive ones by more than two to one.

It comes after RNZ reported threats against MPs had risen astronomically in recent years, and revealed a specialist parliamentary security team handled more than 200 requests for help in just three weeks.

The analysis covered 24 accounts owned by women and nine by men, examining more than 110,000 comments on women's accounts and more than 30,000 on men's.

Of the comments women candidates received, about half were negative while only 18 percent were positive. That compared with 38 percent negative comments and 27 percent positive for men.

Jacqueline Comer, chief product officer and co-founder of Areto Labs, who is based in Aotearoa New Zealand, told RNZ it reflected global trends.

Comer said every candidate in the campaign had to scroll past some of this, whatever their party, but she noted women got the "sharper end of it".

"More viciousness, more slurs, more attacks on their identity, more of the worst," she said.

"We tend to file that under the rough and tumble of politics. It isn't. It's a cost we've quietly attached to standing for office, and women are paying more of it."

Of the comments women candidates received, about half were negative while only 18 percent were positive. 123RF / Rawpixel Ltd

The Canadian tech company which conducted the analysis, Areto Labs, found the abuse women received was more severe, with 5.1 percent of comments labelled as extreme - twice the rate for men at 2.4 percent.

Comer described "extreme" as anything that no one would disagree was "extremely toxic or abusive".

"Things like rape threats or just vicious, really pointy racist abuse, where there's certain phrases that we've all agreed as society that are unacceptable.

"Things like that are just a lot more aggressive."

Personal attacks were the most common abuse for every candidate, and racism was the most common form of identity-based abuse - detected more than twice as often as sexism.

Comer described the focus on race as "a bit unique".

"Usually, if there's more women than men in the data, you tend to see sexism as the higher one. But here, it's racism, which is quite a sad state of affairs, really."

Identity-based abuse made up a fifth of the abuse women received (20 percent), against an eighth for men (12.5 percent).

Women also received far more gender-related abuse than men, at nearly four times the rate. That included sexist, transphobic and homophobic comments, gender microaggressions and body shaming.

Comer said it was hugely concerning, and asked who was attracted to a combative environment.

"We'll start to see a shift in the types of people who are running for office as well, where you potentially they get that sort of dopamine hit and rush from combat rather than from collaboration."

Sir Peter Gluckman Supplied / University of Auckland

Prior to the election, RNZ spoke with former chief science advisor Sir Peter Gluckman about the political landscape. One issue he raised was the way social media drove "short-termism".

He also noted the way in which political discourse had become more abusive, reflecting the way anonymous and ad hominem attacks had become easier to make online.

"That's the sad reality of what social media has done. It's changed the way we have discourse. 50 years ago, this would not have been acceptable forms of conversation."

Politicians unsurprised

RNZ approached all political parties in Parliament for their response to the analysis, and received replies from Labour and the Greens.

The Greens' Tamatha Paul told RNZ it wasn't surprising. She described having to pay someone to moderate her social media because of the issue. She was also part of a Parliament trial to use an AI tool to moderate her social media platforms to detect negative sentiment, abuse or death threats.

She described it as "going to pretty great lengths" to "protect my own peace" as well as uphold a safe online forum for her followers.

Green MP Tamatha Paul. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Paul described having to have "Parliament security guards and four uniformed police officers" at every electorate debate during the campaign.

"We had to have a layer of physical protection, so it's not even just in the online space.

"I almost envy people who only get online abuse because it always inevitably turns into physical, real threats."

Paul then told RNZ she'd dealt with a death threat on Wednesday where somebody had told her they planned to "murder" her.

The past political term had made her want to work across the aisle on social media regulation, "because these platforms are not being accountable for the harm that they're allowing to happen".

"They're not being accountable for the democratic chilling effect that it's having, and that women don't want to participate in politics anymore because we have to pay for it physically with our safety, which is an expectation that isn't required of men."

Labour's Carmel Sepuloni. RNZ / Angus Dreaver

Labour's Carmel Sepuloni said she frequently received comments which were racist and misogynistic, many of which targeted her physical appearance.

"Like many women in politics, I make a conscious effort to shut it out, to the point where I'm concerned I've become desensitised to it. But I don't think anyone can be exposed to that kind of vitriol day after day without it taking a toll."

She said politicians should be challanged and held to account: "That's how democracy works.

"But criticism and abuse are two very different things, and no one should face threats, personal attacks or hate just for doing their job."

Sepuloni was worried most about the "long-term cost".

"I'm concerned for women's mental health given what we now endure online, and that it will drive good people out of politics or put them off standing in the first place.

World.title: Election aftermath: Each party's wins & regrets - and that phone call
World.content:
Audio player for " The Aftermath 2026: How each party is feeling post-election... and that phone call " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2558513%2Felection-aftermath-each-party-s-wins-and-regrets-and-that-phone-call

The Aftermath 2026: How each party is feeling post-election... and that phone call Caucus Download MP3 59m

Analysis: Regrets, Frank Sinatra had a few. But too few to mention. The party leaders and strategists competing in the general election campaign, however, will have plenty of them to ponder while they wait for the 400,000 special votes to be counted.

Who has the most regrets is yet to be determined. While the centre-right bloc of National, ACT, and New Zealand First are in the box seat, a hung Parliament or even centre-left win are well within the realms of possibility. If the specials deliver the same percentage changes as they did in 2023, the Greens will gain a seat and New Zealand First will lose one. With Opportunity just 0.26 percent away from an extra seat and Wairarapa in the balance, there are no guarantees.

But there are - or should be - regrets, and in this week's episode of Caucus, reviewing the preliminary election results, highlighted where the parties must be kicking themselves.

History will most harshly judge the two major parties, as they fell to their lowest combined vote in the MMP era. You might call it the Purple Plummet; 3.5 percent below the previous lowest combined vote in 1996.

Then, Jim Bolger's National Party barely clung to power with 33.9 percent of the vote after forming a coalition with New Zealand First. It's notable that coalition didn't survive the term and Christopher Luxon's 29 percent National Party would be even weaker.

Labour should be shaking its head at its performance in Auckland. Counting the city's 22 electorates, Labour won only eight. While it added two to the six it won in 2023 and can see some green shoots in the west, it was still well below the 12 it won during the red wave election in 2020. In short, it wasn't enough. National still owns every Auckland electorate north of the harbour bridge and much of the east. Crucially, it held Maungakiekie and Takanini. Until Labour can at least match National in our biggest city, it will struggle. And the results suggest that until Aucklanders' bitter memories of the second Covid lockdown fade or Chris Hipkins goes as leader, that won't change.

The Greens are rightly delighted to have delivered their second record vote in a row. Chloe Swarbrick came of age this election, looking like the grown-up in most of the rooms she entered. But its oft-stated goal was to "change the government", so on that front the Greens failed. And they only have to look at Nelson and Wairarapa to see a missed opportunity. While the coalition partners largely offered themselves as repeat-government, with Winston Peters even telling Hutt South voters to give their electorate vote to Chris Bishop, the left lacked joined-up thinking. In Nelson and Wairarapa, two seats everyone knew would be close, the Greens candidate vote was bigger than the gap between National in first and Labour in second. If the Greens had recognised the overhang threat and explicitly told its supporters in those two seats to vote for the Labour candidate, they could be the ones in the box seat now.

Te Pati Māori, while it says otherwise, must question its choice to engage (and be so explicit about) a cynical overhang strategy that encouraged the (for now) election-winning overhang on the right. New Zealand First was just a year ago promising new levels of success and a transformative 2026 election.

While it achieved its best result since 2002, it remains behind ACT, could still lose a seat, and has yet to resolve what to do about Michael Laws. ACT and Opportunity, at this stage, have the fewest campaign regrets. ACT's David Seymour looked the most serious candidate in most debates and led his party to its third record result in a row. As Jo Moir says in the podcast, he appeared constrained by the deputy prime ministership. But in truth that encouraged a self-discipline that did him credit. Opportunity, of course, became the first party under MMP to enter parliament without an incumbent MP. It may yet hold the balance of power.

Those two parties' biggest regrets may be to come. ACT could yet find itself in Opposition. Seymour since the election has already said the result "anchors" future governments to the right and has declared National's supermarket policy "dead on arrival". Such bold statements come with a whiff of hubris and he will want to take care not to overplay his 11 percent hand. Opportunity may yet rue having to choose between two unpopular leaders and potentially unstable governments.

And what of National? Voters have sent the message they prefer its people to its brand. That has implications for the party it will need to act on. But, while he won't see it this way, the biggest regret of the campaign must be Luxon's decision to promise New Zealanders he would not, no-way, no-how pick up the phone to Opportunity's Qiulae Wong after the election, before immediately doing that exact thing.

Politics requires the craft of compromise, so politicians often feel compelled to be economical with the truth. But seldom has a New Zealand politician so brazenly and repeatedly made a promise he clearly intended to break. Trust is built through a combination of competence and intent. Yet clearly Luxon never intended to keep his word. So the breach of trust is historic. Disastrously, it comes at a time when people's trust in core social institutions is already dangerously low. If Luxon remains prime minister, he will enter the role with his credibility in tatters, having damaged New Zealanders' trust in our political system. That is a heavy legacy to carry. But the regret, sadly, is something all of us will have to live with.

World.title: Justice boss won't step down after review reveals culture marred by leadership issues
World.content:
Audio player for " Review over former Lotto presenter finds numerous issues in Justice Ministry " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/crime-and-justice/2558048%2Fjustice-boss-won-t-step-down-after-review-reveals-culture-marred-by-leadership-issues

Review over former Lotto presenter finds numerous issues in Justice Ministry Checkpoint Download MP3 9m

Ministry of Justice secretary and chief executive Andrew Kibblewhite says he won't step down after a review into the Justice Ministry revealed a culture marred by leadership, decision-making and accountability issues.

The review was ordered in August following its handling of a former employee, with outgoing Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith saying his confidence in the agency was "seriously shaken".

Former Lotto presenter Russell Harrison was suspended for five years on full pay - more than $500,000 - as he faced charges relating to organised crime following a global FBI sting.

The Public Service Commission carried out the review and described the Harrison case as "a microcosm for our broader findings".

It found leaders were not sufficiently focused on public trust and confidence, too accepting of flawed internal advice and overly concerned about legal action. Staff who tried to speak up were not listened to.

'I'm grabbing that with both hands'

Kibblewhite told Checkpoint he was accountable and had to "own" the report, but believed he was the one to lead the ministry through its changes.

"We've got a culture that has some work ons and I 100 percent agree to that. We've also got a culture that's got a whole lot of strength and the report calls that out. It talks about the staff and how committed they are and how engaged they are.

"Our most recent court participation, court participant satisfaction survey, we had the highest ever satisfaction results that we've had in the courts.

"There's a lot going on that's indicative of culture. This report says we've got more work to do and I absolutely buy that, but that doesn't mean that I'm going to resile away from taking the leadership that's needed to move it forward.

"I'm grabbing that with both hands."

Kibblewhite said the Harrison case was problematic, and decisions were made at the beginning, and were not tested sufficiently afterwards.

He said the ministry wasn't keeping its eye on the ball.

"We've owned that and we've recognised that we need much stronger reporting up to the senior leadership team and making sure that the decisions are really challenged when they need to be, and I think we've fixed that," he said.

Kibblewhite said the report showed work was needed, and steps were being taken to ensure people felt like they could speak up.

A new policy to boost that was launched six weeks ago, he said.

"This is an active area of work for us. It's an active area where we are making progress, but look, I absolutely acknowledge the voices that come through in the report.

"We've got more to do. I'm just really confident that the things we have in train are moving us in the right direction. And I've got some really good solid evidence that for lots of people, that's the case."

Justice system under 'intense pressure'

The report also highlighted a justice system under "intense pressure", with challenges that are persistent, complex and difficult to resolve. That included more people going through the court system, more complex cases, cost pressures and workforce and infrastructure constraints.

"At the same time, expectations of service quality, accessibility and timeliness continue to rise while the ministry leads major change through Te Au Reka, one of the most significant court administration reforms ever undertaken in New Zealand and a programme representing a significant investment."

Te Au Reka is a new digital case management system.

Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche suggested tweaks around the edges of the ministry would not cut it.

"The pressures facing the justice system have been building for many years and will not be resolved through harder work, additional process, or further organisational complexity.

"The ministry has an opportunity to move beyond managing today's pressures and towards helping shape a justice system that is more effective, accessible, trusted and sustainable."

No clear direction, staff exhausted

Staff told the review it was not clear what they were working towards. They said there was no shortage of planning and strategy documents, but they were "overly bland at best and at worst confusing".

One manager said the strategy was "an aspirational document with some fluffy words" and questioned what it meant in practice.

Staff were stuck dealing with whatever immediate priorities were placed in front of them by the government of the day, and wondering whether they are focusing on the right things.

The review said clarifying the ministry's vision as strategy must be its single most urgent priority, and leadership, culture and performance would flow from that.

Frontline staff reported no clear plan for addressing demand and backlogs, instead resorting to temporary measures like overtime. Such patch-up solutions resulted in overworked and exhausted staff, the report said.

The suspended staff member was a former Lotto presenter. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Focus weighted towards policy, not the courts

The review found the ministry produced high quality policy work, but that received more attention and resource than operations.

"For example, we were surprised that there is no room in the ministry's executive team for a manager dedicated to the District Court (the busiest court in Australasia)," it said.

They were equally surprised about thin resourcing allocated to support judges with judicial policy and the future development of the courts.

"We strongly suggest this be re-examined."

One interviewee commented: "...they sometimes seem like people running a hospital who've never been on a ward. Everyone in that place must understand, live and breathe the work of the courts, not just the frontline."

World.title: Addo-Carr free to leave Eels as club rejects extension opportunity
World.content:
Josh Addo-Carr is free to leave Parramatta immediately after the Eels advised the former Test winger the club would not offer him a contract extension beyond 2027.

After a series of bizarre twists and turns, the Eels have decided Addo-Carr is not wanted after next season and he can start hunting for a new NRL club.

The development comes despite the NRL integrity unit clearing the 31-year-old to return to Parramatta after failing a roadside random drugs test in October.

The ex-NSW State of Origin and Kangaroos star received an unexpected lifeline when his B sample came back negative earlier this month.

"The Parramatta Eels would like to provide an update regarding Josh Addo-Carr following a driving incident in September," an Eels statement read on Thursday.

"After reviewing all relevant information, including the negative result of the B sample, the club has cleared Josh in relation to the issues raised following the incident.

"The NRL has also confirmed it will not be taking any further action, and the club now considers the matter closed.

"Separately, the club has informed Josh and his management that it will not be seeking to extend his current contract beyond the end of the 2027 season."

The Eels will keep the door ajar for Addo-Carr to see out his 2027 contract, but will not stand in his way if he secures a new contract with a rival club.

The 31-year-old is due back at pre-season training with the Eels next week, as his management looks to secure the flyer a future elsewhere.

AAP

World.title: Cummins to 'respond properly' to Khawaja claims tomorrow
World.content:
Australia Test captain Pat Cummins is set to break his public silence on the sandpaper scandal after taking time to "better understand" the allegations of ex-teammate Usman Khawaja.

Test captain Cummins announced on social media that he would speak to reporters tomorrow morning at Cricket NSW's headquarters in Sydney.

"Happy to speak with any and all media about the events of this week," Cummins posted today.

"I've taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy's allegations so I can respond properly."

Cricket Australia is yet to confirm an official time but Cummins said he would speak at 9:30am AEDT between a training session and the start of day three of NSW's Sheffield Shield clash with South Australia.

Many in Australian cricket circles have been demanding Cummins publicly respond to Khawaja's explosive claims in his book about ball tampering in Australia's Test team.

Khawaja told Nine Newspapers of the plot to use sandpaper on the ball in the infamous 2018 Test against South Africa in Cape Town: "It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us."

The retired batter also wrote of Australia's ball tampering in the preceding Ashes Test series against England.

Cummins and fellow fast bowlers Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood, and spinner Nathan Lyon, have previously denied knowledge of Australia taking sandpaper onto the Cape Town ground. Starc reiterated that stance on Tuesday.

AAP

World.title: Vescio won't quit this habit even if 'it's uncomfortable to watch'
World.content:
There was a moment in Darcy Vescio's press conference for their 100th game where they hesitated on a word.

The inaugural Carlton player has long been a voice and face for the competition, including for the LGBTQ+ community, and particularly so after coming out as non-binary in 2021.

They have always championed that AFLW is for everyone — and everyone is welcome.

Want to win an AFLW flag? Club culture matters, data shows AFL Players Association CEO James Gallagher says the gap between AFLW clubs getting workplace culture right is widening and the results can be seen on the field.

But while that is true, they do not exactly want everyone to feel comfortable at their home semifinal on Saturday.

As Princes Park, Carlton's HQ, is used as a home venue for many teams, a lot of the Blues' opposition have become very familiar with the ground.

North Melbourne star Ash Riddell spoke very publicly about loving the ground ahead of the Kangaroos' qualifying final with Carlton last week.

"You want [opposition] people to not feel… welcome," Vescio said, to laughter.

"When they come here. Even heading into last week's game … Riddell was very public in saying she loves playing at Ikon Park because they've built great memories here and they're really home here.

"So that's something we do want to wrestle back."

Darcy Vescio is the first Carlton player to reach 100 AFLW games. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

Vescio has said it has been tough to watch other teams play at their home during finals series. Carlton did not make the final eight from 2022 to 2024.

The Blues will have that opportunity when they come up against Hawthorn this weekend in a semifinal.

When Vescio runs out for that game, they will become the first Carlton player to reach 100 games in the AFLW.

Over the course of their career, Vescio has also played a pivotal role in the AFLW collective bargaining agreement negotiations over the years, helping drive the league's pay, conditions and professionalism forward.

"That adds, not weight, but it makes the footy experience a lot more rich," Vescio said.

"I love the game and every challenge that that brings, physically and mentally."

Darcy Vescio sees their role as more than just a football player despite 100 AFLW games. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

"But when you can extrapolate further and see the way you can shape things and push the game into a better space and I guess impact different communities who might not have always seen themselves in footy, for me, that adds to my experience of being a human playing footy.

"From the outside, it can be tempting to just want footy players to just focus on footy. But the reality is when you step out onto the field, you're a fully formed human with a brain and with things going on in your life.

"So if you're able to, I guess, service all areas of yourself whilst playing footy, it just makes it feel like a lot more worthwhile experience."

A lot has changed over the 11 seasons Vescio has played, including the number of teams in the competition (from eight to 18), season length and start date, and the skills and evolution of the game on-field.

Darcy Vesio has been a stalwart of the competition since its conception. (Getty: Morgan Hancock)

One thing for Vescio themself, is the length of their socks.

"They're a bit of a fidget toy for me at this point. They kind of come up, they come down. But I am enjoying the long socks," they said.

"I feel like for a long time the socks we were given were very small, like I've got size 11 feet, so they were really squeezing in and some games they would be around my heel.

"So I feel like after 10 seasons of that, I'm trying to just hit back with maximum length. But yeah, I know it is uncomfortable for some people to look at."

World.title: What is in Usman Khawaja's book Sabr and what did he actually say about Sandpapergate?
World.content:
Usman Khawaja's revelations about the sandpaper scandal have reopened a massive rift in Australian cricket: who knew what? Who's lying? Who's telling the truth.

Much of the problem lies in the ambiguity of language that Khawaja has used in his interviews and moreover in his newly release autobiography, Sabr, which he is now publicising.

When Khawaja told the Nine newspapers that "It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," what exactly did he mean?

Was he inferring that the entire team knew about the plot to sandpaper a cricket ball during the third Test in Cape Town in 2018?

Cameron Bancroft was banned for nine months and Steve Smith for a year for their roles in the sandpaper scandal. (Photo by Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images/Getty Images) (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman)

That clearly is how most of Australia understood that statement.

Or was he saying that everyone in the Australian set-up needed to take responsibility?

We don't know and that is because of Khawaja's deliberate attempts to not name names as he told Sarah Ferguson on 730 this week, "it's never been for me about pointing fingers."

"This is my story," he wrote in his book.

Loading...

But what is clearly inferred from the book is that even if he wasn't pointing fingers at individuals, the knowledge of the ball tampering was widespread and discussed within the team and on the field.

So, what exactly is in Khawaja's book?

The sandpaper chapter is dedicated to three players who were banned for their involvement in the incident, then captain, Steve Smith, Cameron Bancroft and "my childhood friend David Warner".

"The truth will set you free," he wrote.

The set-up happened before the first test in Durban when he alleges a member of the coaching staff told the team: "I don't care what you have to do, or how, but we need to get it moving in the air."

The Australians celebrate the final wicket of the first Test in Durban in 2018. (Getty Images: Lee Warren/Gallo Images)

"It was so much harder to bat when the ball was moving in the air, particularly when it was reverse swinging. "We had to keep doing what all of us had been doing for years in domestic and international cricket: finding a way to make it go reverse. "We were all complicit. "Reverse swing on those older, flatter Test wickets was how you won matches, come day four and five."

The first reference to sandpaper in the chapter comes in reference to the size of the change rooms during the South Africa series.

"Of course I bloody knew what was happening with the sandpaper. "There wasn't much in those small change-rooms that got past me. It was a room full of banter and it was very hard to hide anything. Let alone when you used sandpaper on the ball and it would leave these huge swirl marks on it."

Sandpaper, he explains, is readily available in cricket change rooms, because batters use it to clean up their bats.

On day two of the second test at Port Elizabeth (now Gqeberha), he described an experiment to use sandpaper on a cricket ball.

Steve Smith and David Warner appeal for a wicket during the second Test of the series. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

"What we saw was unbelievable. The ball was completely dry and extremely scuffed on the side we'd sandpapered. There was no way it wouldn't reverse if we bowled with it. Everyone had a look at the ball and was laughing their heads off."

He wrote that a plan was hatched to sandpaper the ball in the Test immediately after breaks in play when the umpire would drop the ball on the boundary before the players went onto the field.

Cameron Bancroft offered to do the deed, because David Warner was conscious that the TV cameras were focused on him.

Khawaja recounted Bancroft saying: "No worries — it'll be easy."

"At this stage, Steve Smith put his hands up and said, 'I don't want to know about anything about this,' and walked out of the room."

Smith used almost the exact same words to describe his actions in a press conference during his subsequent one-year ban.

Nevertheless, the plan went ahead as Khawaja described in his book.

Australia cut through the South African batters after Cameron Bancroft had taken to the ball with sandpaper. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

"The next session, we absolutely went through the South Africans. Bangers (Bancroft) had walked on the field after the break, picked up the ball that the umpires had left on the field, and given it a few twists and turns. The ball came up a treat. The shiny side was shiny and the buffed and, thanks to the sandpaper, the reverse side was really rough and dry. "Every time during that session the ball was passed to me at gully, I'd take a look and think, wow, even I could reverse swing this ball. It was ridiculous. The bowlers went to work and bowled beautifully. Reversing it around corners. We got four wickets for 28 runs. "It was moving so much that, at one point, one of the bowlers said in the huddle after a wicket, 'Guys, it's going heaps now. Just don't do anything else to it, because it's silly how much it's going'.

Khawaja doesn't name the bowlers who took the four wicket in the book, but the scoreboard shows Mitchell Marsh took two, while Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc took one each.

Even so, Australia lost the test. Khawaja claimed that the South African bowlers were reverse swinging the ball "everywhere", starting after about 21 overs.

"We didn't know what they were doing with the ball — all we knew was that they were better than us at getting it go reverse. And we were using sandpaper!"

Come the third test at Cape Town, drizzle was making the ball wet and hard to swing.

Khawaja described a member of the coaching staff approaching Bancroft who he was sitting next to.

"Bangers, whatever you're doing, we need more of it. It's wet out there — we just need more of it," Khawaja says the coach said.

Khawaja wrote the sandpaper helped take the wet surface layer off the ball, making it dry and more conducive to reverse swing.

It was the next session when the infamous shots of Bancroft trousering a small yellow sliver of sandpaper were broadcast on the big screen at Newlands.

Bancroft, he wrote, was "catatonic".

Cameron Bancroft was called over by the umpires after being caught with the sandpaper. (Gallo Images via Getty: Ashley Vlotman)

"Every one of the boys on the field was shitting themselves."

Khawaja wrote it was after the game he had a conversation with the team manager, Gavin Dovey.

"We need to cop this as a team. We did it as a team, so we cop it as a team. "[Dovey] said I was right but that two guys in the team disagreed."

During a subsequent team meeting, Khawaja wrote he expressed the same view that the entire team should accept responsibility.

"There was silence when I said that. Most of the guys agreed, but Painey (Steve Smith's replacement as captain, Tim Paine) knew not everyone felt that way. And so, my idea fell flat."

Khawaja concludes the chapter saying: "I can only speak for myself, and it's very clear I knew what was going on."

Khawaja wants the rest of us to draw our own conclusions.

World.title: Warner hits out as batting coach calls Khawaja claims 'absolutely false'
World.content:
The fallout from Usman Khawaja's 2018 South African tour ball-tampering allegations shows no sign of abating after Australia's former batting coach Graeme Hick weighed in to insist they were "absolutely false".

Hick's strong denial of Khawaja's assertion that the whole team knew of the plan to use sandpaper to alter the state of the ball in the series eight years ago also dragged David Warner back to social media as he launched further barbs at Cricket Australia.

In his new book, former Test batting luminary Khawaja's revelations about the infamous "sandpapergate" tour have received both strong support and vehement denials.

The latest rebuttal of his claims has come from former Zimbabwe-born England batting star Graeme Hick, who joined paceman Mitchell Starc and former head coach Darren Lehmann.

Sandpapergate continues to wound Australia Usman Khawaja and David Warner's Sandpapergate revelations may have set the scene for civil war in Australian cricket as the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continues to captivate and damage.

Hick, who worked with the Australian team from 2016 to 2020, told the Sydney Morning Herald: "I have seen the various statements around the coaches and I'm very disappointed with the broad nature of them.

"Khawaja puts it simply: 'It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.' To me, what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false.

"In regard to any discussions around the ball-tampering in Port Elizabeth or Cape Town, I will say in true honesty that I did not hear or know anything.

"My first knowledge of all this was, like many, when it appeared on the big screen in Cape Town as I was sat on the outside balcony at the time."

Khawaja's fellow opener Warner, who was one of three players who took the blame for the 2018 sandpaper scandal at Cape Town along with captain Steve Smith and batter Cameron Bancroft, has backed Khawaja's stance and thanked him, saying: "It's 100 per cent accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."

After reading Hick's comments, Warner returned to social media with another post that seemed to imply the English Test player was hardly at the heart of the team as Cricket Australia's appointment after the popular Michael Di Venuto resigned.

"Let's get the facts straight," Warner wrote. "Graeme Hick was only appointed because Cricket Australia was unwilling to pay Michael Di Venuto what he deserved.

"As players, we valued Michael so highly that we even offered to contribute from our own salaries to retain him.

"These discussions were taking place during the New Zealand tour. That alone speaks volumes about how highly we regarded him and how determined we were to keep him involved. Adds to why Graeme has spoken!!"

AAP

World.title: The Wallabies-Scotland rivalry born in a Melbourne backyard
World.content:
Sione Tuipulotu used to smash Isaac Kailea in their Melbourne backyard battles, but Wallabies prop Kailea hopes to get revenge when his "lippy" cousin leads out Scotland at Murrayfield.

Tuipulotu is another who got away from Australian rugby, a centre who forged his own path before using his ancestry to become Scotland's Aussie braveheart, an inspirational captain who led them to victory over the Wallabies two years ago.

None of which surprises his old mate Kailea, who as a kid always looked up to the guy he saw as a role model in their close-knit Tongan community in Melbourne.

It is also why Sunday's (Monday AEDT) international also means so much to 26-year-old Kailea, who came off the bench in that 2024 clash when Tuipulotu scored a try in the Scots' 27-13 victory.

"If I get the chance again, I'd love to get a win over him," Waratahs loosehead Kailea said, reflecting on the close bond between his family and the Tuipulotu brothers, Sione and younger rugby-playing siblings Sese and Tavi.

Tuipulotu toured Australia with the British and Irish Lions last year. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

"Sione's probably one of the most competitive people I know, so when he puts on that Scottish jersey, he's going to give it 100 per cent.

"Whether he goes extra hard because we're Australia, I couldn't say. I just know he's always putting in that effort, especially now he's their captain.

"I know him quite well. I grew up with him and his younger brothers, we pretty much just call each other cousins. Our dads, both of Tongan heritage, met in Melbourne, and there's a couple of other Tongan families there we all grew up with.

"So a lot of boys, a lot of pretty rough games in the backyard, but Sione was always the leader among the kids, as the oldest. We played a couple of times in the backyard. He used to run amok — he'd smash us to bits.

"The younger kids just followed his lead, and the leadership he showed there is something I can see him doing now with Scotland. Even the way he talks, it's still the same. It's pretty cool to see."

Kailea said the rest of the younger boys saw saw Tuipulotu as a role model, especially once he played for the Melbourne Rebels.

Kailea has joined his "cousin" on the international stage. (AAP Image: Joel Carrett)

"It was a bit tough for him in Australia, he went on his own little journey, through Japan, and now he's ended up in Scotland, and his brothers are over here as well, chasing the dream," Kailea said.

Hooker Tavi plays alongside Tuipulotu at Glasgow Warriors and centre Sese is at Edinburgh Rugby.

"It's pretty crazy to be honest," Kailea said.

In that 2024 clash, Tuipulotu played like a man with something to prove.

"He can be pretty lippy on the field, just like he is off it, so he was throwing a bit of chat, but nothing too crazy. I don't think he'd get too disrespectful," smiled Kailea, recalling how Tuipulotu collected the match trophy off his Scottish gran, Jaqueline Thomson.

He also got flattened by a thunderous tackle from Joseph Aukuso-Suaalii in that match which actually caused an arm injury to the Australian and left Tuipulotu reflecting: "I've never been hit like that in my career."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: The women's RLWC final is a fight against fate
World.content:
The women's Rugby League World Cup has ended up exactly where it was fated to be, with Australia to face New Zealand in the final for the third tournament in a row.

Barring the kind of upset that sends bookies broke, this was the only way it could be given the Jillaroos and Kiwi Ferns have romped their way through with a near contemptuous ease.

Only Fiji, a delightful surprise packet in their maiden tournament who lost to New Zealand by six in the group stage and Australia by 16 in the semi-final, managed to run either of them close. The former is the only game of the World Cup to be decided by one score or fewer.

Australia names teams for World Cup finals Australia has named its men's and women's sides for this Sunday's Rugby League World Cup finals against New Zealand.

Even counting the valiant efforts of the Bulikula, Australia and New Zealand have outscored their opponents by a combined 272-20 and 182-24 respectively.

Fiji's emergence and Papua New Guinea and Samoa's continued development are positives but if the journey truly matters more than the destination this one has been a trudge.

It has felt inevitable from the start and perhaps it was. There could have been improvements to the draw — Australia had no business playing a team like Wales — but none that would have changed this outcome.

A tournament like this and a final like this, where Australia are deserved 20-point favourites given they've only lost to New Zealand once in the past ten years, is the wrong end of the double-edged sword women's rugby league is trying to wield.

The Jillaroos are the game's lone superpower, without peer or rival, because they are the end-product of almost a decade of transformation via the NRLW.

Australia have done it easy through much of this World Cup. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

They play the same sport as developing nations, but they're in a different game to nations like Wales, France and Papua New Guinea.

There's a value in having a team that stands so tall because they're a gold standard to aspire to for some and a target to aim at for others.

They are proof of what is possible for women's rugby league with investment from the bottom up and the top down, as well as giving it the patience for that investment to rise to the top.

It makes the Jillaroos an incredible creation and victory on Sunday would confirm what most already know — that this is the greatest collection of talent in the history of women's rugby league.

Lopsided women's rugby league The rise of Pasifika rugby league teams in the international men's game contrasts with a widening gulf in the women's game.

Just as the 2017 final, the last before the start of the NRLW, signalled the beginning of a new kind of history so would a Jillaroos win here be the capstone on Australia remaking the game in their own image.

It would mark their fourth World Cup final win in a row, pulling them past New Zealand who currently have three with the last coming back in 2008.

Their dominance is a by-product of the game's progress but it's also so complete and smothering it's become a problem. The things that have made them great have worked too well.

Australia have moved so far and so fast not only is there nothing left for them to overtake, they can barely see New Zealand over their shoulders. They must keep looking though, because there is nobody else to see.

New Zealand are the only team to come close to Australia in recent years. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

They are Everest and New Zealand are the only other team who have even been able to try to climb a mountain before. Everybody else is stuck at base camp.

As talented as their opponents are — and with Raecene McGregor at halfback, Mele Hufanga and Stacey Waaka in the centres and inspirational captain Georgia Hale leading a forward pack who could skin a crocodile their talent is considerable — just playing well is not enough for New Zealand to win.

They'll need an off night by the Australians, a few bounces of the ball, perhaps a referee call or two falling their way, just to bring them into the contest.

A win is possible, but it would be the greatest upset of this era and when the second-best team in the world needs a fair bit of luck to take it to the best, things have gotten way too top heavy.

Australia's World Cup record breaker helps nobody Australia ran up the biggest win in women's international rugby league history with its World Cup victory over Wales but it was the kind of result that served little purpose other than stuffing the stats sheet.

Australia have taken giant strides while everyone else is trying to catch up with smaller steps.

The great-grandparent rule might help in the short-term if it allows more elite talent to filter through to other nations.

Any potential NRL investment in Super League would surely include a women's component and that would give the game in the northern hemisphere a boost it sorely needs.

Both moves would build on the progress of this World Cup, which has mainly come through in excellent television ratings even if the contests haven't been close.

But further development is required before there's any thought of a standalone World Cup, which will likely be tabled until 2034 at the earliest because it cannot happen until this game is for more than one player.

There are glories that lie outside ultimate victory and those can be easier to find once teams like Fiji, Samoa and Papua New Guinea have more time to develop but when it comes to Australia that's a hard thing to remember.

They are the best by such a margin the rest are barely in sight, a grim fate they can confirm with glory on Sunday.

World.title: Swimming embraces short and sharp with new Swim GP competition
World.content:
No sport is immune from a fight for relevance in a jam-packed sporting marketplace.

And Swim GP is Swimming Australia's latest attempt to blend sporting entertainment, just 12 months on from its last foray into the genre, Australia vs The World in Brisbane.

This year, the nation is keeping things in-house with a slightly tweaked format involving teams of domestic swimmers.

"I think it's a really exciting opportunity," three-time Commonwealth Games champion Jenna Forrester told ABC Sport.

"I wasn't actually at Aus vs The World last year, so this is going to be my first time doing an event like this.

"But I got to watch some of it on TV and I thought that it was a really cool concept."

Swimming's revolution begins with pumping night at The Valley Swimming stepped out of its tried and trusted format in a novelty, multi-event competition in Brisbane on Friday night.

A cool concept but not an unfamiliar one.

Swimming has toyed with events like this for more than 30 years, since the Qantas Skins events in the mid-1990s.

Before COVID, the International Swimming League (ISL) came in to shake up the perceived monotony of conventional competition and act as a vehicle to keep interest in the sport high between Olympics.

The league has not been seen since 2021, partially as a result of COVID, partially due to the Russia-Ukraine war. The ISL's principal backer is Ukrainian businessman Konstantin Grigorishin.

However, later this year, the ISL will return with a one-off All-Star Match at the London Aquatics Centre on December 19.

The International Swimming League (ISL) took place before COVID. (Getty Images: Catherine Ivill)

That is despite there being legal issues between World Aquatics and the ISL: World Aquatics settled with a group of 263 swimmers in September 2025, who said they were denied a chance to compete, and therefore earn money, in ISL competitions.

World Aquatics paid those swimmers a combined $US4.6 million, and allowed them to participate in independent competitions such as the ISL without losing their ability to compete in the Olympics.

There is also a separate, ongoing lawsuit between the ISL and World Aquatics.

The ISL also played a role in forming the College Swimming League (CSL) in the USA, which had its first competitions in September.

The league brings together 12 programs from three of the biggest NCAA conferences: the SEC, ACC and Big Ten.

The ISL aimed to give international swimmers more visibility, and hopes to do the same for college swimmers with the CSL. (Getty Images: Catherine Ivill)

The league featured multiples, four-team competitions, with 30 events at each competition. That includes Skins events and a "jackpot" scoring rule.

Chief executive Rob Kent told Reuters the league was designed for a TV audience and for each meet to last a TV-friendly two and a half hours.

TV-friendly is exactly what Swim GP is going for too.

"I think it's just going to be a year-by-year thing that will just keep getting better and better as the event progresses," Forrester said.

"It is really exciting and it definitely is a bit different to what we're used to."

Skins matches, multi-round elimination races, play a big role in Swim GP, as do mystery relays and power plays, much in the same way they did in Brisbane last year.

It will also provide high-intensity race prep for swimmers outside of the major championships.

"It's a really exciting opportunity, and short course as well, so it'll be short and fast," Forrester said.

Jenna Forrester's versatility was instrumental in her early selection. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"It'll be good race practice and good race practice in coming together as a team, because that's something that's really important in swimming.

"It is an individual sport, but when we go away on the Australian team we really focus on the culture and bringing that Australian spirit.

"I think this will be kind of a good practice into turning swimming into more of a team sport."

At Swim GP, Australia's best and brightest able-bodied and para swimmers have been split into four teams: Team Kraken, Wahoo, KingTide and Tsunami.

Each team has platinum athletes as their headliners: KingTide has Flynn Southam and Lani Pallister; Kraken selected Kyle Chalmers and Mollie O’Callaghan; Wahoo had Meg Harris and Sam Short; Tsunami went with Kaylee McKeown and William Petric.

The first overall pick went to Wahoo, who selected sprint specialist Ben Armbruster.

Ben Armbruster is a versatile sprinter. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Armbruster is as versatile a sprinter as they come.

The 24-year-old won Commonwealth and Pan Pac gold in the 50-metres butterfly, having reached the semifinals of the 50m freestyle at the Paris Olympics and the final of the 50m backstroke at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham.

Mel Marshall used her first pick, second overall, to select Forrester for KingTide.

"To be second pick, that was kind of crazy to be honest," Forrester said.

"I'm curious to see what events they have because I feel like a lot of it will be kind of sprint events. I'm interested to see how I go trying to do some of those.

"It really just shows that I've had a pretty good year, I guess.

"Maybe that hasn't really settled in for me yet, maybe some other people are seeing it before I am."

Tech.title: Nvidia is reportedly preparing to fire Jensen Huang
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang

Nvidia’s board is preparing to dismiss CEO Jensen Huang following a report from the New York Times about a second alleged extramarital affair, just days after he admitted to a separate affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, The Wall Street Journal reports. The second alleged affair was with an executive who reports to him, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell, according to the Times.

The Nvidia board will meet as soon as today to decide on Huang’s future at the company, according to the Journal. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Verge.

Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were allegedly captured together at a hotel in San Jose during Nvidia’s GTC developer conference in March, two unnamed sources told the Times. The Times has not seen the video. Rumors about a potential affair between the two had long circulated at Nvidia, an unnamed source told CNBC, partially because Powell does not have a health or science background.

Nvidia’s stock fell more than 7 percent in after-hours trading Wednesday.

Since Nvidia and Huang confirmed an extramarital relationship with Megaspeed executive and alleged spy Alice Huang and a subsequent investigation over the weekend, the company has said it retained former US attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to handle it, but today’s rumor suggests it won’t wait for those results to act. Last year, Huang hired crisis communications firm Heller known for handling public sex scandals, according to Wired. Its founder has advised several powerful men who faced public scrutiny, Wired reported, like former congressman Anthony Weiner and writer Jeffrey Toobin. Heller did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Verge.

Tech.title: Hands on with Home Assistant’s new ‘smart home multi-tool’
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

All the smart home news, reviews, and gadgets you need to know about

Nabu Casa — the commercial side of the Open Home Foundation, which runs Home Assistant — just launched the Home Assistant Connect Aux-2, a multi-function box designed to help you bring more non-smart devices into your smart home. It’s part of Home Assistant’s ongoing efforts to become more user-friendly. And it’s working.

I’ve been testing the Aux-2 for a couple days and I’ve found it unsurprisingly useful and surprisingly easy to set up. The Aux-2 is a $69 box about the size of a deck of cards. It has 2.4GHz Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Ethernet, USB-A, USB-C, a digital/analog audio jack, a Grove port for interfacing with peripherals like sensors, buttons, and LEDs, and a pair of RS-232 serial ports.

The sticker is nature’s way of saying “don’t use these ports unless you know what you’re doing.” The rear of the device is simpler, with just a reset switch, USB-C, and Ethernet (which supports PoE).

It can bridge Bluetooth devices into your Home Assistant setup. Its USB port lets you plug in a Nabu Casa Z-Wave or Zigbee antenna in case your Home Assistant hub isn’t in a good spot. You can control devices like TVs, AV receivers, solar inverters, and more via serial connector. And you can connect an amplifier or powered speakers to its audio jack to stream music to older audio equipment.

All of these things leverage Home Assistant’s capabilities as an open-source platform. The Aux-2 is based on ESPHome, an open platform for making DIY smart home devices from cheap, flexible ESP boards, and it uses existing Home Assistant/ESPHome integrations for all its features. The serial integration was developed earlier this year; Music Assistant and SendSpin, which power the audio-out feature, are in active development.

I have a Home Assistant install, but even after several years it is not my primary smart home platform simply because of friction and time constraints. Instead, I have a hodgepodge of Google Home, Apple Home, and a few devices that are only in Home Assistant. The situation is not ideal.

But the Aux-2’s capabilities perfectly intersect with two things I’d been meaning to do anyway, one of which I’m already using Home Assistant for. First, I have a garage fridge, because I live in Texas. I also have children, which means sometimes the fridge or freezer door gets left open. I want to know when that happens before all my food goes bad.

A couple years ago, I set up a few Aqara temperature sensors, connected to Home Assistant via a now-discontinued Zigbee dongle, and set up an automation to alert me if the fridge or freezer get too warm. But they frequently drop connection (probably because they’re inside a fridge in the garage), they chew through coin cell batteries, and they have no displays, which means I also have a cheap Acu-rite hygrometer in the fridge so I can see the temperature without pulling out my phone. Someone tipped me off to Govee’s Bluetooth hygrometers, but I’d need a Bluetooth proxy to get them into Home Assistant. That happens to be a feature of the Aux-2.

I also have a set of in-wall speakers in my living room that I’ve never used. I’d been meaning to get an amp, but analysis paralysis set in. Do I get a Wiim Amp? A stereo receiver? A cheap Bluetooth amp? Do I try to get them to work with my four Sonos speakers? Maybe my ancient Google Home speaker? Turns out I do nothing for five years. Maybe the Aux-2 could help.

Setting up the Aux-2 was much easier than I expected. I plugged it into my computer via USB-C and was able to download and install the latest firmware right from a browser. I could also add my Wi-Fi credentials. Then I unplugged it, moved it over to my media console and connected it to power (it takes USB-C or power over Ethernet), and did the rest of the setup in the Home Assistant interface.

We love a setup wizard. Screenshot: Nathan Edwards / The Verge

In HA, I was prompted to install ESPHome, which discovered the Aux-2 and sent me to a “set up your ESPHome device page” that walked me through the capabilities. Enabling Bluetooth proxying took a couple of clicks; I added the Govee Bluetooth integration and put batteries into the sensors and they showed up automatically. Mercifully, they maintained their Bluetooth connection through three walls and a fridge, and now my fridge monitoring setup works again.

The audio capability took a little longer, but most of that was spent hooking the speakers up to the amp I ended up buying and setting up Music Assistant, which I didn’t have installed. Music Assistant lives on your Home Assistant hardware and can play from many different services — from Spotify to YouTube Music to local files and more — and to many different outputs, like Sonos, Wiim, AirPlay, Google Cast, and others, but they all need to be configured, and that took a beat. Not a long beat: less than half an hour total.

I can now play music to the in-wall speakers using Music Assistant. Sendspin, the whole-home audio standard (also developed by the Open Home Foundation) is supposed to be able to let you group speakers from different protocols under certain conditions, but I haven’t gotten that working yet. The standard is still in development, and I’ve also been busy, so I’m not sure if that’s a me problem or a them problem.

I would also like to see the Aux-2 show up as an AirPlay or Spotify Connect target, which (again) is probably just a thing I need to set up.

You can’t go wrong. Screenshot: Nathan Edwards / The Verge

Serial control is the most intriguing feature of the Aux-2, and it’s unfortunately the thing I haven’t yet had time to test. But the ability to hook in things like solar inverters, TVs, and receivers is fascinating and one I want to look into further when I get the chance. Maybe I’ll hook it up to my LG TV.

The Aux-2 doesn’t do anything you couldn’t do already with an ESP32 board and various accessories, or even other ESP-based devices. The Apollo Automations Cast-1, for example, costs $35 and supports the same music-casting and Bluetooth proxy features I’m actually using from the Aux-2 at the moment. You could bodge together something even cheaper with DIY parts.

That’s not a knock against the Aux-2. That’s the whole point. The ecosystem is open by design, which I find endlessly refreshing. Both Nabu Casa and Apollo fund the Open Home Foundation, which develops Home Assistant and ESPHome (and Sendspin and Music Assistant), and both provide hardware that’s a little easier to use than DIY options. But there’s nothing stopping you from making your own devices. It’s actively encouraged.

I bought a three-pack of ESP32 boards for $16 three years ago. I could have built a Bluetooth proxy from one of those. I could have built an LED controller. I could have built a soil sensor, or a media player, or any of a dozen other things. I didn’t do anything at all.

But now that I’ve used the Aux-2 and dipped my toe into the ESPHome waters, maybe I will.

Tech.title: United won’t let your AI agent book your flight
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

United says it won’t let personal AI assistants book tickets on the airline, citing both privacy and regulatory concerns.

The company says it hasn’t yet seen many people try to use AI agents to book their flights, The Wall Street Journal reports, in line with observations from other businesses like Doordash. But United is concerned that agents could expose customers’ information or make purchases they didn’t intend, and potentially skirt federal rules about the kind of information airlines need to share with customers — like having them attest that their bags don’t have explosives.

While agents can still show users United flights, they won’t be able to actually complete the transaction on their behalf. The decision, and others like it, could limit the potential usefulness of newer personal AI assistants like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots. “To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman,” United CEO Scott Kirby said at an event on Tuesday, according to the Journal.

Across sectors, businesses are grappling with whether to let AI agents transact on their sites, and United is not alone in blocking access for unauthorized agents. eBay appeared to block agents from browsing the site, and several major banks have also placed restrictions on them. United suggests it could reconsider its decision based on future advancements. “As third-party AI agents advance, we see the opportunities they present. However, at the same time, allowing them to interact directly with a United account or booking could involve sensitive actions, and we want to make sure we have established protections for travelers first.”

Tech.title: Loot boxes, influencers, and addictive features face an EU crackdown
Tech.content:
is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Gaming, social media, and e-commerce platforms are facing a fresh wave of sweeping European Union rules that aim to make “your online experience fairer.” The newly proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA) published by the EU Commission on Wednesday is designed to tackle practices that exploit consumers into spending more of their time and money online, including misleading prices or availability, addictive design features like gaming loot boxes, undisclosed influencer marketing, and more.

“The Act will protect consumers of all ages shopping and browsing for goods or services online,” the EU Commission said in a news bulletin. “It will also mean fairer competition for businesses, which are expecting to save EU consumers up to €13.7 billion ($15.1 billion) a year.”

Here’s an overview of what the DFA proposal includes:

A ban on manipulative marketing practices and so-called “dark patterns” that push consumers into making decisions they might not otherwise make, such as fake claims about a product almost being sold out.

A requirement to give consumers the choice to turn off addictive features, such as persistent prompts, endless scrolling, and autoplay of videos. Restrictions around addictive design also apply to “AI companions and general conversational chatbots.”

Restrictions on unfair practices that encourage overspending, such as banning gambling-like features (pay-to-win and pay-to-progress, for example) for minors.

Requiring influencers to clearly disclose advertising content, and restrictions to prevent them from exploiting the trust of children.

Restrictions on unfair personalised ads and prices that target minors or take advantage of sensitive data.

Making subscriptions and digital contracts easier to cancel, with prompts to remind customers about upcoming automatic renewals and free trial periods coming to an end.

Requiring clear and transparent pricing, especially around dynamic pricing and purchases using virtual in-app currency. When consumers wait in virtual queues for cultural and sports event tickets, companies will have to show the current price in real time and at the highest possible price.

Giving consumers the right to communicate with a human customer service representative, and clear rights using an AI agent to make purchases.

The scope of the restrictions being proposed is broad, and could have a significant impact on major parts of the online digital landscape, from the “rabbit hole” algorithms across YouTube, TikTok, and Meta platforms, to AI chatbots and apps like DuoLingo that relentlessly nudge users to keep interacting with them. Some gaming organizations have already slammed the DFA proposal, describing its restrictions around virtual currencies, loot boxes, and offering micro-transactions to minors as being “unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate.”

Given this is a draft proposal, the DFA will undergo various approvals through the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union before being passed into law, and its current measures could be changed or removed entirely as part of that process. When (or if) it does come into force, the EU Commission says companies who violate the regulations could see fines of up to six percent of their worldwide annual turnover.

“Our consumer protection rules will help ensure that businesses compete on the merits of their products and services - not on their ability to exploit consumers or evade the rules. We are not making it harder to do business. We are making it harder to do business unfairly,” EU Commissioner Michael McGrath said in remarks following the DFA draft publication. “We cannot have 21st-century consumers protected by rules that have not kept pace with the 21st-century economy.”

Tech.title: Toyota’s Scion is back, starting with an American-made, 25-mph kei truck
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Toyota is dusting off the Scion badge for a radically different mission. Rather than targeting youth-market hatchbacks, “Scion by Toyota” is being positioned as an experimental mobility incubator — and its first vehicle is an authentic Japanese-style kei truck built in Indiana.

Kei vehicles, which are built to satisfy Japan’s light vehicle regulations, are enjoying surging popularity around the world, including here in the US. More than 30,000 used kei trucks have been imported into the US since 2020, with roughly 7,500 units entering the country each year. Even President Trump is a fan, telling reporters last year that he authorized the Department of Transportation to approve their production.

Toyota looks to be the first to test the American market’s appetite for the tiny trucks. The choice to use the Scion brand, which was discontinued in 2016, would seem to indicate that the automaker is hoping to appeal to younger car buyers. But more than that, Toyota says it sees Scion as a testing ground for utility, outdoor adventure, and customization that wouldn’t typically fit in any of its other models.

When it lands in the second half of 2027, Scion’s KEI-01 sports a 660cc three-cylinder gas engine paired with a continuously variable transmission. It won’t win any drag races, but it should delivery enough power for stop-and-go driving while using a minimum amount of fuel.

Previous Next

















1 / 10

It’s true super power comes from its diminutive dimensions. At roughly 11 feet long and under 5 feet wide, the KEI-01 is about half the footprint of a full-size pickup. It can easily thread through cramped alleys, narrow barn aisles, garden gates, or busy campus pathways where standard trucks can’t fit.

The truck features an on-demand 4WD system with a push-button locking mode. If you’re cutting across muddy farm turf, gravel work paths, or wet slush, power splits to all four wheels to keep the truck from spinning out or getting stuck.

Inside, the vehicle looks pretty cheap, with lots of black plastic and a noticeable absence of any premium materials. That will hopefully help keep the price nice and low — though Toyota hasn’t disclosed any trim options yet. Japanese imports typically range from $6,000 to $12,000.

Because it is certified under federal Low-Speed Vehicle (LSV) rules — also used for golf carts and golf cart-adjacent vehicles — its top speed is strictly capped at 25 mph. The truck bed features three sides that fold completely flat, removing the need to lean over high-metal sides to drop in cargo. The KEI-01 can hold up to 600 pounds of soil, tools, or gear, and can easily tow small utility trailers or mowers.

Unlike an open utility cart or ATV, this tiny truck has a fully sealed cabin equipped with both heating and air conditioning. The extended roofline gives drivers extra headroom, reclining seats, and interior storage behind the seats to keep tools dry and secure. True to classic Japanese utility imports, the steering wheel is on the right side of the cab. Beyond the cool factor, curbside delivery and stepping directly onto sidewalks or worksite shoulders is quicker and safer.

To make the KEI-01 to conform to the rules and regs of auto manufacturing in the US, Toyota is investing $34 million into its Princeton, Indiana manufacturing plant to stand up local assembly and add roughly 50 jobs. Production kicks off in the second half of 2027, but everyday drivers won’t be able to buy one off the lot immediately.

Scion by Toyota is launching the mini-truck strictly as a fleet-focused pilot program targeting corporate campuses, farms, municipalities, and local delivery operators, distributed through a specialized group of existing Toyota dealerships. While Toyota notes it may consider opening up sales to consumer retail down the road if demand justifies it, the initial rollout is very much treated as an experiment to evaluate real-world US utility.

The KEI-01 was joined by two adventure-themed concepts that show Scion’s new focus extends far beyond budget hatchbacks. The SxS Concept packs a 300-plus-horsepower hybrid turbo setup for high-speed off-roading, while the modular BKE Concept explores compact personal mobility. Together, they signal that Scion’s second act is aimed squarely at niche utility and experimental recreation.

Images by Toyota

Tech.title: Google’s Tabletop AI experiment lets you build custom collaboration apps
Tech.content:
Google has cooked up a new experimental AI tool called Tabletop that generates customized collaborative hubs to help you coordinate with family, and friends. The Tabletop platform shares some visual similarities with workplace management apps like Asana and Monday, but with a built-in AI feature that allows you to vibecode personalized interactive tools by describing them, such as savings trackers, chore charts, event plans, and more.

“Just add in your links, files and ideas, then prompt @tabletop — or pick a starter template — to generate custom interactive trip itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters and tournament brackets,” Google Labs design and engineering lead Roman Nurik said in the blog post. “Once your space is ready, drop the invite link in your group chat to let everyone jump in and use it at the same time like a Google Doc.”

Access to the Tabletop beta is rolling out via a waitlist, and currently limited to people over the age of 18 in the US. Some of the example use cases that Nurik provides in his video above would clearly require giving kids or teens access to Tabletop, however, and using this for personal family planning looks like a compelling alternative to stuffy workplace software, so that age requirement might only be in place while Tabletop is in public testing.
